column121: The previous week of flying was the most demanding experienced in over XX years of flying. In hindsight; these challenging events diminished and taxed my mental and physical abilities on subsequent flights leading to inadvertent decisions possibly contributing to my rejected takeoff.  On 3 out of last 4 flights encountered nearly identical events with the Environmental System Controller (ESC) Level 1 Alerts of Pack Flo/ Pack Disagree/ Bleed Off anomalies on two different aircraft during Max Thrust Takeoff with Anti-ice On flights. In the first flight event the anomalies presented on upwind; climb-out were corrected automatically by the ESC and Auto Anti Ice mode. Bleed Air Off; Pack Disagree; Pack Off; Level alerts all extinguished automatically. There was no input from the crew and the Level 1+2 checklists were reviewed for reference by crew. In the second flight event; relying on system knowledge; the previous flight; and anticipating the ESC would respond accordingly in same fashion it was discussed with crew that the ESC in Auto Mode would automatically resolve a pack flow disagree issue level 1 alert noticed late in taxi with a higher demand airflow presented in the system; when we were to run-up the engines for deice concerns for :30 seconds; in position prior to takeoff. Numerous distractions such as short taxi; checklist completion; deice fluid on windscreens making taxi turns difficult due to limited visibility on side windows; and significant deice delays made our departure later than normal allowing more body and mental fatigue to set in. The air synoptic was illuminated due to manual selection of Anti Ice because this air frame did not have an auto anti feature on it. This is important to note because it was normal looking to see AIR for our takeoff setup conditions. After engine run-up and brake release received a level 2 alert Pack not off alert; Pack Flow Disagree resulting in a decision to abort takeoff with a low speed <50 knots reject. Contacted MX resulted in a Block turn back and MX deferral for a malfunctioning Pack.Third flight event; subsequently occurred two days later with Bleed Air off/ Pack Disagree/ Pack Off level 1 alerts occurring on climb out on same aircraft first instance happened on. Close observation revealed in fact the ESC in combo with the Auto Anti Ice again fully resolved any anomalies without any input from the crew. It became more obvious to me the Auto Anti Ice feature once detecting no need for Anti Ice usage is securing Anti Ice allowing the ESC to revert to normal ops eliminating any level 1 or 2 alerts. Thus the ESC must be prioritizing the airflow; protecting the system if a potential leak is detected; turning off packs and bleeds in its process when Anti Ice was ON. On the rejected Takeoff the Anti-Ice was Manually turned ON; the ESC attempted to secure the Pack Flow /Disagree but was unsuccessful in doing so. The decision to conduct a low speed reject was correct but may have possibly been avoided by first contacting MX before takeoff. Checklist were reviewed by the crew but it was fully anticipated the ESC to resolve the Pack issue on run-up before brake release. In the future; it will be my priority with any confusing level alerts to involve MX early to form the best team based consensus and strengthen decision making.
column123: After deicing and during taxi out we received a level 1 alert for 'Pack 3 FLOW DISAG'. Level 1 checklist references: 'Consequences NONE'. It was our understanding that this was a cycling pack flow issue that the system controller would resolve with higher demand flow on run up once takeoff power was applied. This was our second leg for the night and we were already dealing with a lengthy delay; de-icing; icing conditions; snow; wake turbulence avoidance of a departing heavy jet and having to do an engine run up while holding in position in order to clear the engines of icing before releasing the brakes for take off. At the point of brake release to initiate the takeoff roll; neither of us noticed if the level 1 alert was still displayed. Once takeoff power was applied and we reached approximately 40kts ground speed we received a level 2 PACK 3 NOT CLOSED alert. The captain elected to reject the takeoff as is in accordance with company SOP. We cleared the runway with no further indecent and returned to the blocks where maintenance deferred pack 3. We ultimately departed without further incident and completed the flight as originally planned.  In hind sight we should have delayed the take off and mitigated the level 1 PACK FLOW DISAG alert before taking the runway.

When we said we hadn't; he said if we'd had the vaccine; he would let us in; but of course we hadn't had that either.  Manager X pulled us aside and said that this official was simply trying to make a name for himself; and she again apologized; even though it was clearly not her fault.  It occurred to us later that perhaps he was fishing for a bribe; but while that's very common in small GA airplanes; I've never had that happen as part of an airline crew. Unfortunately; I was not able to get the name of the health official.By this point; we had the Flight Operations Manager involved; and he was working on getting us seats on the plane back to ZZZ as it was clear we weren't going to be allowed into ZZZZ. column121: Descent and approach were briefed with expectation of [Runway] XXL at ZZZ. ATC advised during descent to expect Runway XYR. ATC was advised that we were a 747-8 and a request for [Runway] XXL was made. ATC advised that Runway XXL was not available unless operationally required. Runway change checklist was performed and performance obtained for [Runway] XYR. Captain briefed that a right turn [off] [Runway] XYR was not allowed except for Taxiway E. However we did not expect to make this exit so he briefed a left turn at [Taxiway] K or roll to the end. Arrival and landing were normal; after slowing through 60 kts. we were past [Taxiway] E and the Captain stated that he would be exiting left on [Taxiway] K. As we began our left turn toward the high speed taxiway I noticed a line of lights on the ground marking the taxiway closed. These were very dim and low to the ground. Very hard to see. I said very affirmatively; STOP; STOP Barrier. The Captain [stopped] the aircraft and then corrected taxi course. The aircraft did encroach on the first few feet of Taxiway K but not far enough that he couldn't correct back onto the runway. On our rollout ATC did issue an invalid taxi clearance that was a distraction. The taxi clearance was corrected after our [query] and the remainder of the taxi was uneventful. Post flight review of NOTAMS (Notice to Airman) and ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service) revealed that the taxiway was NOTAM closed and was missed on our part. The poor lighting of the taxiway closure barrier was a large factor in us not seeing it sooner.
column123: Prior to top of descent we briefed and prepared to fly the ILS (Instrument Landing System) approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ. Our airport briefing page does say that arrivals between XA:00 and XB:00 should expect Runway XYR for landing; but goes on to state that 747-8 aircraft should expect XXL. Upon check in with ZZZ Approach; we were told to expect [Runway] XYR. I reminded the controller of our aircraft type and queried whether [Runway] XXL was available. We were told that due to noise abatement procedures at that time of day that we could only use [Runway] XXL if it was due to operational necessity. After a quick discussion with the Captain; we decided that due to our light gross weight; we could accept [Runway] XYR. We quickly reprogrammed the FMS (Flight Management System) and briefed the new approach; to include the many 747-8 taxi restrictions and the fact that taxi to parking was likely to be somewhat complex. We decided that a left turn off the runway on Taxiway Kilo was the most likely scenario. While we did these things quickly; I felt that we had covered all of our bases and did not feel rushed or that the workload was too high. What both the Captain and I missed however; was the fact that [Taxiway] Kilo was closed. We had both reviewed the NOTAMs (Notice To Airmen) and ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service); but since we were planning on landing on [Runway] 8L; I believe we both simply failed to register the Taxiway Kilo closure; as it did not apply to our original taxi plan. The approach and landing were uneventful and both the Captain and I were focused on identifying Taxiway Kilo in order to vacate the runway. At no point during our approach or rollout did Tower relay any instructions on how we could expect to vacate the runway. As we began to make the turn for [Runway] Kilo; the IRO (International Relief Officer) forcefully stated 'Stop! Stop'. He had managed to pick up the extremely dimly lit barricades that marked the closure. The Captain managed to get the airplane stopped before we were committed to Taxiway Kilo. Around the time we stopped; Tower transmitted that [Taxiway] Kilo was; in fact closed; and that we could expect to make a right turn off the runway at Taxiway Charlie. This was an invalid clearance; as the -8 is restricted from using that portion of [Taxiway] Charlie. As we were about to query Tower; I believe he realized our aircraft type and issued a clearance to taxi clear of the runway at the end. The rest of the taxi was uneventful. I think there are several take-aways from this incident. First; the IRO was worth his weight in gold this morning. Had he not spoken out in a timely and forceful manner; I think there was a very good chance we would have impacted the barriers or at the very least been unable to continue our taxi. The IRO was the last link in the error chain and that link held strong. Second; I think both ZZZ Approach and the Tower Controller were both unaccustomed to a 747-8 arriving at that time of morning. Landing on [Runway] 4R presents a number of taxi challenges to a -8; and perhaps the best practice may be for -8 crews to declare 'operational necessity' and request [Runways] 8L or 8R unless there are other extenuating circumstances. In the event we must land on [Runway] 4R; a simple 'plan to vacate the runway at X' from Tower would be extremely helpful. Finally; while I do believe the way our situation evolved created somewhat of a setup regarding the closure of Taxiway Kilo; the information was in fact available in the NOTAMs and via ATIS. I overlooked that information largely due to an incorrect expectation bias. I am aware of my ultimate responsibility to digest that information and will make an effort in the future to pay more attention to the 'Plan B' options in addition to the expected one.

Also; I added that if we did have to take any delays we would be declaring emergency fuel. ATC set us up immediately for a close pattern for [Runway] XXL. It was evident due to lack of recency the FO was struggling with the conditions that day.  Also; be vigilant on [Runway] XXL as I have had issues on windy days before where the tree line ends and the field begins. With the second attempt we had a 15 knot increase with the wind shear caution message.
column123: I was the Pilot Flying. The Wind shear changes in combination with the amount of time since I've been flying in the airplane were contributing factors. column121: Please reference ZZZ [airport]; ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID.  We were assigned the ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID and departed Runway XXR at ZZZ. It was a busy phase of flight and we were task saturated at the time. Getting an ECAM message for a pressurization fault was an added distraction. I was a little slow to respond but I've been off work almost X weeks and I'm still shaking off the cobwebs.Not pointing fingers; but a change to our SID would have been nice to know BEFORE we took off so we could expect; brief; and build the change into the FMS. column121: Coming to ZZZ on the ILS [Runway] XXR; we were continually slowed by ATC for spacing of traffic ahead and behind.  At about 1;200 MSL on glide path still IMC Tower told us to go-around.  I was PF and hit GA button and advanced power levers.  We went through missed approach procedure; but as flight guidance was attempting to be set the aircraft was also capturing the level off of 2;000 MSL so took a little longer to complete.  Meanwhile we were a little late on turning to 195 heading.  ATC queried us as we were in the turn.  We had also climbed to 2;180 feet before stopping and returning back to 2;000 immediately.  After we got settled ATC vectored us back to ILS with no further issues.  ATC told us they had to send us around because aircraft on final for parallel Runway XXL behind us had gotten .99 miles from us.  Spacing needed to stay a min of 1 mile.I should have paid more attention to altitude and started turn to 195 even if flight guidance wasn't quite set yet.  Also pulled back power sooner or not add as much to avoid going through altitude.
column123: During our arrival into ZZZ; when told to run base (heading approximately toward ZZZZZ [Intersection]); we were slowed to 170 KIAS.  We were maintaining 4;000 feet throughout base turn and intercept turn onto final.  Once established on final (approximately 20 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection]) we were slowed further to 160 KIAS; with traffic approximately 4 NM in front of us.  Once we intercepted the glideslope; we maintained approximately 1;000 feet above the preceding traffic; but gained to within 3 NM distance.  Meanwhile; ATC vectored a airline flight onto final for [Runway] XXL close behind us.I told the First Officer (PF) to potentially fly a half-dot high on the glide slope to avoid any potential wake from the preceding aircraft.  Once we reached approximately 10 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] we were slowed further to 150 KIAS.As we continued down the approach; the TCAS showed us to be approximately 2.5 NM from the preceding traffic; with the traffic behind us close in trail (unable to tell the specific distance).  At approximately 600 AGL; ZZZ Tower issued a Go-Around; with nonstandard missed approach instructions (Right turn heading 195; climb and maintain 2;000).  The First Officer initiated the Go-Around and the Captain (PM) proceeded to re-program the Flight Guidance.Due to the light passenger load; the subsequent climb rate caused the Flight Guidance to immediately switch from a Climb indication to an Altitude Capturing indication; which caught the Captain off-guard; and he tried to re-configure the Flight Guidance back to a Climb indication.  The Flight Guidance again sequenced to an Altitude Capture indication.  At this point; the Captain (PM) noticed the aircraft was off course to the left approximately 35 degrees and was rapidly approaching 2;000 feet.  The Captain brought this to the attention of the First Officer while also simultaneously acknowledging ATC stating 'Turn right heading 195.'  The Captain also prompted the First Officer to reduce the power setting; as the airspeed was approaching maximum flap speeds.  The missed approach up to leveling off at 2;000 feet was all hand-flown (i.e. not with the autopilot).Once the aircraft was established on the appropriate heading; altitude; and configuration; ZZZ Approach vectored the flight around for a second attempt at the ILS 16R; which occurred without further incident.  In researching the First Officer's seniority; he has been here less than X years (Date).  After debriefing the flight; he stated that that was his first Missed Approach / Go-Around in the actual aircraft EVER.Since we had been slowed down significantly early during the approach; we knew we could expect to be sandwiched in between other aircraft.  However; we did not know that ATC needed only 1 mile separation between aircraft on parallel ILS approaches (told to us by ATC during our second attempt).  There was no mention of spacing requirements on our first approach.Due to 'COVID loads;' the aircraft type climb rates are very good; requiring steeper than normal attitudes so as to not exceed flap speeds.  This factor; combined with the First Officer's relative inexperience with missed approaches; caused a momentary loss of situational awareness by the First Officer.This required the CA to not only re-configure the flight guidance for a missed approach; but also ensure the First Officer did not over speed the flaps; communicate with ATC; and ensure the aircraft was following appropriate flight guidance (which was a non-standard missed approach).Also contributing to the loss in situational awareness was the altitude at which ATC issued the Go-Around:  600 AGL.  This caused a significant startle factor in both the Captain and First Officer.  Had ATC mentioned anything about a potential missed approach; we would have been much more prepared.Last-minute ATC-issued Go Around instructions (below 1;000 AFE); caused by inadequate spacing with simultaneous parallel approach aircraft.RECOMMENDATIONS:1.  ATC NEEDS to let crews know 'be ready for a missed approach' if there is potential for a spacing issue.  We were given our Go-Around instructions at 600 AGL.  This is a very high-risk area to issue a Go-Around; when spacing throughout the entire approach was tight.  Some sort of notification to us would have primed for a potential Missed Approach and therefore could have avoided any loss of situational awareness and subsequent heading / altitude deviation.2.  STOP ISSUING NON-STANDARD MISSED APPROACH INSTRUCTIONS.  The ILS [Runway] XXR's Standard Missed Approach instructions are to fly runway heading to 900 feet; then climb on heading 195 to intercept the ZZZ 210 degree radial; maintain 2;000 feet.  This is VERY similar to what we were assigned (heading 195; climb to 2;000 feet).  However; when we're given nonstandard missed approach instructions; not only do we have to interpret what it is ATC actually told us; but also program that into the Flight Guidance.  This programming is CONTRADICTORY to what our normal Flight Guidance programming procedures are.  Had ATC simply said 'fly the published missed approach;' that could've aided in our appropriate handling of the aircraft.LESSONS LEARNED:Don't trust ZZZ ATC to not screw up.  If spacing looks tight; brief a missed approach; even if it's done on the Final Approach Course.  Also; do not trust your fellow crew member to fly a perfect Missed Approach.  Watch them like a hawk for course; airspeed; and altitude management; and IMMEDIATELY speak up if there is even a minor deviation.

column121: After making the turn at ZZZZZ intersection at FL300; we had a bleed 1 leak caution message. We ran the QRH and isolated system 1 and after a few minutes the message returned forcing us to continue the checklist through the descent portion. As we were waiting the three minutes before the descent; I initiated contact with AIRINC to reach dispatch as our ACARS had just lost coms most likely to it transitioning from one frequency to another. However with the need for a descent arising we lost communication with AIRINC before establishing any plan with dispatch. We requested priority handling with ZZZ Center and initiated a turn towards ZZZ as the thought of continuing towards ZZZZ or ZZZZ1 was the longest stretch of open water on the route and worst case scenario we were 60-80 miles north of the coast and ZZZZ2 was the closest [authorized] airport around if we had to continue the checklist and shut down the engine. As we got closer to ZZZZ2 while still 130 miles from ZZZ we were able to get an ACARS connection and get dispatch caught up on the situation. They did not realize how bad the situation was and thought we were closer to ZZZZ and ZZZZ1 than we actually were. As the aircraft was stable and the bleed temp of system 1 was around 50C; the system still held almost 70psi throughout the flight indicating one of the valves was still open and not properly closed; we confirmed with dispatch that it was safe to continue beyond ZZZ to ZZZ1 for an uneventful landing. Throughout the communication black out center was very professional and extremely helpful. I hope our thanks and appreciation for their work can be passed on to the controllers working with us.
column123: Prior to ZZZZZ1 [fix]; flight sent an ACARS message stating a Bleed Leak. Flight followed the QRH and three minutes later the message returned requiring a diversion to nearest suitable. There was quite a bit confusion going on because the flight also attempted to contact us via ARINC. The ARINC call failed; and the flight seemed to be in an ACARS dead spot as well. A few minutes later; I received multiple ACARS messages stating the flight was diverting to ZZZ. Per the flight's location; ZZZZ1 seemed like the closer; more suitable option and would've had the flight avoid going EOW (Extended Over Water) at 10;000 [with priority handling]. After running numbers for ZZZZ1; flight informed me over ACARS that ZZZ or ZZZ1 was closer. Although [our equipment] showed the flight over ZZZZ1; in reality the flight was 250 nm to the east; indeed much closer to ZZZ or ZZZ1. With that information; we decided ZZZ1 was a more suitable airport. In addition to runway length; ZZZ ops informed us that pax would not be allowed off the aircraft due to customs issues. Flight landed and blocked in.While I was certainly caught off guard and should've opened the QRH a few minutes faster; I was seriously hampered by our lack of equipment accuracy; ACARS dead spots; and ARINC being unable to raise the flight. It's hard to have an accurate; timely discussion over ACARS when both sides of the situation are working quickly on fixing the problems. If this were being done via remote dispatching; I do not wish to imagine the consequences. In the future; I will remind myself to remain calm and follow step-by-step actions to reach a quicker; less confusing end.

column123: Upon arrival a ZZZ; we received a new cabin crew for the flight to ZZZ1. ZZZ to ZZZ1 was to be the flight deck crew's second flight using the same aircraft.   During the pre-flight; the aft cabin crew called the flight deck and advised us that the emergency equipment that is stowed in the two most aft overhead compartments were not located in their proper location.  TO fully understand; I also went aft to see for myself.  The FA showed me in her manual; the proper location and orientation of the equipment.  I went back to the flight deck; verified the same information in the aircraft operating handbook.  I advised the Captain of the discrepancy.  Maintenance was called.   This discrepancy was found on the second leg of the day; while utilizing the same aircraft.  The location of the equipment was inverted in its actual location vs. the location as stated in the manuals.Cabin crew may have not been facing forward in the cabin when pre-flighting the emergency equipment.  While the equipment was stowed in an overhead bin correctly; with the proper associated placards; the actual location of the equipment did not match the location stated in the manual.  As an example Oxygen is to be in the port side overhead.  Its actual location was starboard.  It is possible that during a pre-flight that a crew member facing aft will simply associate that the oxygen is 'on my left side'   This aircraft also had new overheads and added capacity within the last year. During that change; the equipment may have been installed incorrectly. Cabin crew may need to have greater situational awareness as to the actual right and left side of the aircraft; regardless of their orientation within the cabin.

column121: Prior to initiating descent to ZZZZ1; the flight crew contacted ZZZZ Center and advised that we were unable to accept RNP-1 (Required Navigation Performance) arrival procedures. At this point; Center instructed the flight crew to fly an RNP-1 arrival despite having been informed of the incapability and the flight crew reiterated the fact they were unable to accept the arrival. Instead; the flight crew requested to fly direct to ZZZZZ waypoint for the start of the RNP RWY (Runway) XX approach. However; Center ignored this request and instructed the flight crew to fly direct to ZZZZ1 VOR and expect the VOR-A approach (Jeppesen Plate [Page]). When the crew once again requested to fly direct to ZZZZZ for the RNP RWY XX; Center repeated the instruction to fly direct to ZZZZ1 and expect the VOR-A approach without further acknowledgement or explanation of denial. The flight crew speculated that Center's refusal to assign the RNP approach was due to misinterpretation of the flight crew's inability to accept the RNP arrival; and efforts to clarify this case were also ignored by Center. The Captain (Pilot Monitoring) selected the VOR-A approach in the MCDU (Multi-Purpose Control Display Unit) and verified the route information while the First Officer (Pilot Flying) briefed the approach plate. At this time; both crew members observed what appeared to be inconsistencies between the MCDU approach database and the Jeppesen approach chart; specifically that the waypoint on Chart X did not match the waypoint shown in the MCDU routing; nor did the MCDU approach procedure indicate the required procedure turn under routing [FLP page] or Procedure Turn Info page [NAV - Page 2 - Patterns - Procedure Turn]. As the workload for the flight crew increased due to the inconsistency between chart and MCDU database; Center's refusal to assign a more effective approach; continuing descent towards mountainous terrain; and multiple segmented and non-standard clearances from Center that threatened to interrupt critical flight deck operations (notably the approach briefing); the flight crew elected to fly the VOR-A approach under raw data (green needles). All elements of the planned approach thus far mentioned became void after the flight crew received the hand-off to Approach Control who instructed them to fly direct to the airfield and complete a visual left-hand traffic pattern from overhead the runway.This flight crew highly recommends that an investigation be conducted into inconsistencies observed between the Jeppesen approach plate for the ZZZZ1 VOR-A Approach [Chart] and the MCDU database for the EJET fleet; namely the incorrectly labeled waypoint identified as ZZZZZ1 on the chart. This flight crew also highly recommends that effective communications be made between [Company] Flight Operations and the [Country] Air Traffic Control agency to ensure better understanding of which procedures [Company] flights are able to conduct and which procedures they are not; specifically the differences between RNP-1 'Arrivals' and RNP Approaches.

column121: After I briefed the A Flight Attendant; she asked if I would be wearing a mask whenever they came in the cockpit for a lavatory break.  I informed her as per our protocol I am not required and for operational safety reasons I do not wear my mask in the cockpit. She then informed me that they would not enter to give us a break unless I wore a mask.  I then initiated calls to Dispatch and Operations to inform them of this problem.  I understand their concerns and respect their decision.   Yet; I do not understand why they would take issue with cockpit members facing forward and unmasked when they are continuously exposed to passengers in the cabin who have their mask off while eating or drinking as well as children who are not required to have a mask.On a recent flight my First Officer and I had a hard time understanding the ATC Controller due to the muffled sound because they were wearing a mask.  It is also difficult understanding a First Officer who is wearing a mask in the loud cockpit environment.  Safety of flight is my priority followed by mission and passengers.  I regret the inconvenience this brought to passengers and company alike but this difference in protocol needs to be resolved without imposing non safety operational constraints on the cockpit.   I realize this is a novel disease and the information from the CDC and NIH [National Institutes of Health] is at times confusing and conflicting but believe that we should not take information to extremes and compromise operational safety.Lack of cohesive policy between Cockpit and Flight Attendant protocols that plays between personal concerns over operational safety.  I also feel misinformation or agenda also play a role on differences regarding relative issues.Keep the current Pilot protocol which works well and imposes minimal restrictions regarding operational safety.  Clarify Flight Attendant protocols so they do not conflict with the cockpit.   To each individual this pandemic is relative and emotional.  Any preconceived or personal perception cannot be satisfied by one fits all protocols; so I believe individuals overly concerned should be required to get the vaccine.  I will at the earliest opportunity get vaccinated for myself; family and coworkers.

column121: We were entering the terminal area with given heading descending from 11;000 feet down to 4;000 feet from the South west of the airport for RNAV 28. Passing through 5;000 feet we called the 'airport insight' and received the clearance for the visual approach for Runway 28. By the time we were abeam the airport flap 1 was down and altitude was 2;400 feet descending to 2;200 feet which was final approach segment altitude. Even though I was fully aware of the presence of obstacle (1;687 feet) on the path of our downwind I was confident that 500 feet margin and few thousand feet right of the course would give us good margin for safety. As we were getting close to the tower crane 'terrain' aural message came and after 2-3 second later 'terrain! pull up!' message came. I applied immediate max power and established pitch between 15-20. The message lasted few seconds and we climbed about 2;700 feet. After the conflict was resolved I intercepted the final course and follow the PAPI to the runway as normal operation.When we have received the visual clearance about 20 miles away I bugged the altitude down to 2;200 feet assuming within the 10 mile radius to the airport there cannot be anything that can pose threat to our path. Even though I was aware of the Tower; I didn't mention it during my briefing and considered it a big threat. When the Captain brought me an attention about the Tower once we were getting closer to it and asking me to turn inside the final approach point I delayed his suggestion wanting to intercept the final course outside the FAP. I could have been clear to ask him his intention or worries as we are nearing the obstacle and get the concurrence from both of us that 500 feet is enough or not.1. Better understanding of EGPWS logic could have given me the conservative altitude margins. 2. Detailed briefing; I could have planned better plan by flying higher or going around the tower instead of over flying it. 3. Rushing; I could have gone further out and fly higher to intercept instead of tightening my base turn to join right at the FAP.

column121: In ZZZ we attempted to start number two engine using APU air and it spooled up abnormally slowly; and I noticed that the EGT seemed to lag. At 45% N2 the start stagnated and decayed until a 2.5% N2 decrease and Engine Fail indication on the ECAM. We stopped the start; then following guidance in our paperwork; we started number one (which also stagnated a little bit but then started normally) and then attempted a second start on number two using cross-bleed from the number one engine. We allowed the engine to spool up to 25.7% N2; then added fuel. At starter cutout; the engine hung again; dropping to about 43.2% N2 and hanging there before slowly spooling up to about 43.8% N2 when it timed out for the start and Engine Fail was indicated on ECAM again. Our Quick Reference Handbook said we could attempt a second start after the first hung start; but that maintenance action was required if the second start failed. At that point we requested a tug and BTB to our parking space. This is where Maintenance Control got involved. At first they suggested that we defer the APU bleed; however it was obvious to me that the air was not the problem (we used a separate source for each start); so I told him the APU bleed deferral was not sufficient. Then he suggested that a problem with the Integrated Drive Generator might be causing the hung start and suggested we defer that; and I agreed it could be tried. As part of the maintenance action during start the Inetgrated Drive Generator was disconnected and deferred; and the Airworthiness Release in the log book was signed off; then we continued getting the jet started and were on our way. During the flight the APU was running as required by the deferral; and at 36;000 ft. it automatically shut down. I attempted to start the APU; and on the second try; it started. I requested and descended to a lower altitude of 30;000 ft. and the APU operated normally for the rest of the flight. If I had not been able to start it; I would have had to advise ATC and divert. I wrote up the APU under a P code for momentary or transitory malfunction. In ZZZ1; maintenance checked the APU for any failure codes; did the repetitive inspection for oil quantity for the Integrated Drive Generator deferral; and signed off the APU. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed the situation and agreed that the APU was not malfunctioning and may have had a momentary problem with operating at high altitude. We accepted the jet for the leg to ZZZ2. With a fresh Airworthiness Release in the log book; we started the number one engine first; then started number two using cross-bleed at the request of maintenance. The number two engine came close to exceeding time limits; but did eventually spool up. We were filed for 33;000 ft.; and at that altitude the APU did the same thing--it shut down--and we were able to get it started again on the second try. We requested and descended to 29;000 ft. for the remainder of the flight. Again; the APU operated normally from there on; and again; I wrote it up with a P code for the shut down. I also made a comment in the logbook about the number two engine start; even though our flight paperwork said that comments for a successful start were not needed. There I made a note that the EGT from fuel introduction to the point where the start stagnated; then started to spool up; seemed abnormally low and was at least 50 degrees cooler at 45% N2 than the other engine. The stagnated start was evident from fuel introduction until after started cutout when it became apparent that the engine was not ready to continue the start on its own. The Integrated Drive Generator has nothing to do with the EGT during start. I suspect something else is going on here; perhaps a Electronic Engine Control problem with the fuel mixture at high altitude; or a sensor malfunction. On further reflection; I feel that the deferral of the Integrated Drive Generator was inappropriate for the problem we had; and I should not have accepted it. It created a problem where we could have been forced to request priority handling and divert. It is likely that whatever is wrong with our engine starts does not pose a safety of flight risk once we get the engine going; so it makes no sense to do a deferral that could compromise safety. Until this is figured out; the guidance needs to be specific and it needs to go out to everyone in the maintenance and crew pipelines and it should be operations friendly. My recommendation is that everything in the fuel system be checked in case it is causing the starting problem for cold engines at high altitude. I think that the bleed system is less likely to be the issue because of the low EGT I saw during all four start attempts on that engine. I also recommend that maintenance be able to attempt at least one more start before the aircraft is taken out of service; and that crew get more guidance concerning the problem. 'Maintenance action' is not enough to let a Captain know what to expect or what to accept. I also have felt for a long time that our systems manual has been scrubbed of a lot of detail about systems with which we do not directly interact; so we are less able to make informed decisions and instead have to rely on experience. That will not always save us from making the wrong call. Everyone in this situation acted in good faith; and I am not writing this report to cast any doubt on anyone. I only want to point out a safety issue that we can avoid in the future.

column121: I believe complacency played a role in this error. I am always checking and double checking my work but unfortunately I missed an important piece of information on the Center of Gravity (CG) and Passenger Count (PC) data. Next time I will slow down and thoroughly check my work without rushing and recognize my complacency.We arrived to our aircraft in the morning to perform our duties for the first leg out of two for the day. Boarding was complete and I received the cargo sheet and CG/PC Data from the gate agent. As I plugged the numbers in for departure I noticed the passenger count seemed low.  Thinking that it was due to the slow season and COVID I continued to run the numbers for our takeoff data. With the low passenger count I figured we were going to also need a ZFW reset from the dispatcher. I confirmed with the Captain and went ahead and contacted Dispatch with our new ZFW and confirmation of our CG. New numbers were sent back and we took off uneventfully.While in cruise the Captain requested a lavatory break. Upon his returned; he voiced his concern with the passenger count from what he saw in the cabin while checking our CG/PC. That is when we realized that the incorrect CG/PC was given to us. As we were starting our decent; the Captain transferred the controls to me while he referenced the COM and tables to calculate our correct weight along with the landing data and Vapp. As a precaution we also added few knots to the Vapp. The Captain completed the tasks and I confirmed that all the information was correct and within safe parameters for a safe landing.  We had sufficient runway and the field was VMC at the time of landing. The landing was uneventfully and we continued to the gate.

The PF executed the RA escape maneuver to comply with the RA. I then told ZZZ Departure that I had the GA aircraft in sight; as we still hadn't been given any traffic alerts. column121: For the ILS Runway 04R at ZZZ; performance numbers were run for a Flaps 30 landing with a good stopping margin at Autobrakes 3. ATIS winds were calling approximately 070/13 - no gusts. Upon switching to Tower at ZZZZZ on the localizer course and tracking the glideslope; Tower cleared us to land with winds now gusting to 20. As PF (Pilot Flying); I elected to add 4 knots to the Vtarget and as an added Safety measure at ZZZ; I selected Autobrakes MAX to compensate for a slightly increased approach speed. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) attempted to quickly re-run the performance data; but the gusts were not yet accounted for in the METAR. Rather than going heads down any longer inside 1;000 feet AGL; we agreed a 4-5 knot addition to VTarget and using Autobrakes MAX would be more than sufficient to account for the gust factor.At approximately 500 feet AGL; we received a GPWS Too Low Flaps Alert. The PM immediately called for the go-around and it was initiated. A quick scan of the flap handle and I realized that I had neglected to call for Flaps 30 from a Flaps 15 setting; and the Before Landing Checklist was not run. We were quickly vectored around for another uneventful ILS. The minor distraction of adding a gust factor and changing the Autobrakes setting sent me out of a normal approach configuration sequence and we ended up both missing the final flap setting and subsequent checklist.With the normal ZZZ procedure of not contacting (and often not switching to) Tower until reaching the fix at about a 5-mile final; it's possible for us to miss out on cues to changing weather on the ground. We were number 3 or 4 in a sequence of landings on 04R. Had we switched to Tower five or more miles sooner; we may have caught the gusting winds earlier and had more time to type in the adjusted winds and send away for the performance numbers prior to 1;000 feet AGL. This was another series of events combined with mild fatigue that led to poor task prioritization on our parts.
column123: The short version is that we got 'Too Low; Flaps' at 500 feet because we were at Flaps 15. We went around. Planned winds were 070/7. Tower winds were 070/12G20. I re-ran the performance landing numbers at 1;500 feet; but did not override the METAR and got back the numbers for 070/7. The PF (Pilot Flying) chose to add 5 knots to VTarget and we agreed to go from Medium to Max braking and continue.There is no guidance I am aware of as to when we would be required to re-run our landing numbers. I should not have tried to re-run the landing numbers at that point. That would have eliminated the distraction that led to not selecting our planned final flaps or running the Before Landing Checklist.

column121: While in line for takeoff on Taxiway for XXR; we received a notification from the flight attendants that the cabin was filling up with smoke which was coupled with a foul odor akin to burning rubber. We smelled the odor at the same time the flight attendants notified us of the smoke. I asked them if it was thick enough to block view of the back of the aircraft and if they thought we needed to evacuate right away. They answered no to both questions. I then told them that we would be moving to a cargo ramp to run a QRH and if they thought at any point we would need to evacuate while moving to call me back and we would stop immediately. I also informed them that the next time we stopped would be the last time we would move without calling them and that once stopped; if they felt the need to evacuate; they were to do it. We taxied to the cargo ramp just south of taxiway after alerting ATC that we were [requesting priority handling] and would be pulling off to the side to run a QRH and to have the fire trucks standby. We ran the entirety of the smoke fire fumes QRH; which had us deactivate the PACs (Air Conditioning Packs) and close the bleed valves. We elected to not drop pass O2 or go on O2 ourselves as we were not having any adverse reactions; but just dealing with an unpleasant smell in the flight deck. We called the flight attendants at this time and asked about the passengers' condition and they stated that everyone was fine. The smoke slowly dissipated throughout the rest of the event. At this point; we decided to go back to the gate as the smoke was no longer producing from the vents and the passengers were not complaining about any issues when asked. We cancelled [priority handling] but requested that crash rescue follow us to the gate. Once arriving at the gate with the aircraft shut down and the flight deck door open and main cabin door; we had one woman reportedly having bronchitis coughing to a large extent. She was the first off. I was not aware she had an adverse reaction until pulling into the gate. We deplaned everyone as quickly as possible and had Maintenance confirm that PAC 2 was the culprit. To my knowledge; all passengers refused medical attention. We later got another aircraft and had all passengers board.The probable cause was something happened with the Right PAC as we were single engine no APU taxiing to XXR with Engine 2 running.

column121: TCAS RA on arrival into ZZZ [airport]. Assigned descent to 7;000 feet and vectors to final by ZZZ Approach. We reached 7;000 feet and noted approach was extremely busy where the Controller was being stepped on seemingly more than half of her transmissions. While level at 7;000 feet the TCAS noted a proximate target converging from 1 o'clock; 400 feet below. We attempted to contact Approach but there was zero opportunity to get a word in due to the sheer amount of communication on frequency. I advised the Captain PF to 'get ready' while we attempted to locate the aircraft visually. A few seconds later the TCAS noted traffic and ordered a very shallow climb. I announced to ZZZ Approach that we were responding to an RA; but I believe I was blocked; the frequency still jammed with constant communication. A very short time later the controller issued traffic to us and I again advised 'Climbing on RA.' Controller replied 'Roger' I believe and the event was over shortly after. We returned to 7;000 feet and were vectored for the visual; but the controller still had to vector us around multiple VFR targets on our way to the runway. Most significantly we were cleared for the visual approach; but were restricted to flying and intercepting between 5 and 7 NM from the airport due to area traffic. This caused a perceived limitation that pilots are not used to. The CA/PF then overflew the Localizer slightly attempting to maintain these limitations. The aircraft was clearly stable by 1000 feet and we continued in to land; but this was following an incident due to the same cause.Cause was due to the intense level of traffic in ZZZ Approach's airspace. I spoke with a contact at ZZZ [Approach] later who noted the Controller had 15 active aircraft not including the VFR targets attempting to get clearance from the closed airspace; Practice IFR traffic; and VFR flight following requests. The Controller was doing an excellent job and maintained a very professional demeanor throughout. There was just no reasonable way for Controller to maintain communications with the volume of aircraft. I am not sure; but this could have been a result of reduced staffing due to COVID. Maybe there was an East and West ZZZ [Approach] sector available; but no staffing to accommodate. My suggestions would be to either split ZZZ Approach or to draw a new arrival for ZZZ airport to reduce the amount of communications and possible routes needed for the controllers.

column121: Flew ZONNA1 arrival to TUS. I was PF (Pilot Flying) and did the arrival briefing prior to descent which included terrain hazards and the MSA. Both pilots had terrain selected. Approach control gave us a clearance to turn right to 270 and descend to 10;000' for sequencing. Soon after this clearance we entered IMC. Passing north and abeam Mt Lemmon at about 10;300'; we got an EGPWS TERRAIN PULL UP warning. I executed the EGPWS Recovery Action. Almost immediately we went VMC. After passing the MSA of 10;700 and visually verifying terrain clearance; I resumed normal flight; leveled at 11;000' and informed ATC that we had responded to a GPWS terrain warning. They acknowledged and gave us a descent to 9000'. Remainder of flight was uneventful.Either the Terrain system gave us a false alert or we were given a clearance to descend below the radar minimum altitude. We never got any indication on the Terrain display. STAR page showed us north of Mt Lemmon and the terrain depicted around it. While we had good terrain awareness; I should have queried Approach about an IMC descent below the Sector MSA.I recommend a Radar Minimum Altitudes chart be included in the Jeppesen pages for TUS.

column121: ATC turned us onto the approach while still at 4;000. Told us to 'maintain 3;000 till established cleared ILS [Runway] XXL. FO (First Officer) put in 3;000 in the altitude selector and I acknowledged it. Once established; instead of selecting 2;700 feet for the FAF altitude he rolled the altitude selector to 3;300 and started a slow descent. Stated he was going to just control the altitude himself. I thought that was strange; but let him do it figuring it was just a technique he liked to do.As we approached 2;700 feet; he was still descending at ~700 FPM; so I realized he was going to blow through the altitude. I told him he needed to stop descending and return to the FAF altitude until we intercepted the GS. The first time I said this he seemed confused and didn't really do much. I said more sternly that we needed to climb back to the proper altitude. This time he initiated a climb back to the proper altitude and we were still stabilized and fully configured by 1;000 feet AGL. ATC did issue us a low altitude alert as we were climbing back to the proper altitude and we got a single 'Glideslope' callout from the aircraft.The cause was the FO's improper use of the altitude selector and VS (Vertical Speed) mode. Contributing was me allowing him to do the method he did instead of asking him to just put the FAF altitude in the altitude selector till GS intercept.I should have insisted that the FO put the FAF altitude in the altitude selector; especially in IMC. I also told him afterword's that he could have just stayed at 3;000 once established and intercepted the GS from there since at that point we were already close to GS intercept.
column123: Cleared ILS [Runway] XXL; we were given an intercept heading and told to maintain 3;000 feet. The Controller kept us close and fairly high before clearing us for the approach. We were at 4;000 feet when cleared. Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring); First Officer was PF (Pilot Flying). Once established; PF started down with vertical speed to capture glide slope by 2;700 feet at ZZZZZ. PF moved altitude knob up to 3;300 feet from 3;000 feet instead of to 2;700 feet causing us to go below published altitude by almost 500 feet. Was immediately corrected and aircraft was stabilized. Given a close proximity intercept; task saturation was high with intercepting; radio communications; and configuring aircraft. Should have cross checked better and stated intentions more clearly (PF to PM).If crew starts to feel rushed or task saturation is high; ask for longer final or a more stable intercept from ATC. Never let cross checking suffer due to task saturation; should always come first. PM should state approach intention more clearly while getting established. Don't have tunnel vision (Example Focusing on getting configured and not having correct altitude set).

column121: Operating flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After landing on Runway XX; exited on Taxiway A and turned left on Taxiway C; and believing that Tower had actually cleared us to taxi to the gate; we started to slowly taxi; when Tower called us and asked that we call Ground. We called Ground and he stated 'You started to taxi without calling us; and crossed Runway XX; which is an active runway'. We had barely started to taxi on C. We had read the NOTAMs; and in fact; Runway XX was 'NOTAMed CLOSED'; so it could not be an 'Active' at all. Regardless; we asked Ground for taxi clearance to the gate; and received clearance to the gate via 'C.' We did not want to argue with the Ground Controller; but we do know that Runway XX is Closed at ZZZ1; so it's not Active in any way. We asked the Ground Controller if we should 'expect any paperwork'; and he said 'no'. I do not believe we did anything wrong; but it's better to be safe and proactive; and learn from our possible mistakes.We had flown into ZZZ1 previously (a few days before) and due to controller shortages or consolidation of ATC positions (During COVID-19 times); the Tower normally gives us the taxi instruction after we cleared the landing runway. This time; we cleared the runway and thought we had heard the Tower tell us to 'taxi to the gate' (as they have been doing recently). We started to slowly taxi on Taxiway C and that's when Tower asked us to 'call ground for taxi;' something they had not done in the past 3-6 times we had landed there recently. So; probably I was expecting the same ATC procedures to happen; but regardless; in the future; will come to a stop on the taxiway and not move until further taxi clearance is received.I would suggest to avoid being complacent; and instead of expecting the same type of ATC handling from small airports as we may be getting every day during COVID-19 (combined controller positions; where there is perhaps combined Tower and Ground; or even Approach/Tower/Ground Controller); and instead treat it just like a busy airport.

column121: I returned to work after a 3 month absence. I am still qualified on the module. I was assigned as the trainer to Mechanic Y. I was training him on the stator case assembly. The procedure that I was taught; and which had been in use as long as I can remember; was to slide the case and vane assembly; so that approximately one third of it overhung the table surface. Then the bolts were tightened from below with a ratchet with a socket and long extension; repositioning the case and vane assembly as necessary until all bolts were tightened. At the time of the incident; I was not in the work area; having gone to the restroom.Support the case with a hoist and sling before tightening the bolts. This should be added to the job card.
column123: One week after return from 3 months off and being the first time working on this unit as a trainee.On Graveyard shift I was working on the module and order # XXXX. I was tightening the bolts of the vanes. The bolts are tighten from the bottom while the case sits on the table. To access the bolts part of the case is moved slightly beyond the edge of the table. The chair moved; the wrench and its extension did come off the bolt head causing the case to slide off the table and fall to the floor approximately 30 inches.There was no visible damage to the case because it fell directly on my arm and that cushioned the fall. Inspection will be called to inspect the unit.I would add to the job card to support the case with a hoist before tightening the bolts. Or developing a fixture that would allow to reach the bolts from the bottom without having to move part of the case off the edge of the table.

column121: I was performing a functional test of the stall protection computer. On step XX; the task tells you to put the aircraft in the weight off wheels configuration. On the first page of the task for putting the aircraft in the weight off wheel configuration you are told to pull and tag Circuit Breakers (CB): CB P-1; A12; A13; A14; G14; & CB P-1 lower U7. On the second page to pull and tag CB P-1 lower T7; T8; T9; CB P2; N6; H8; CB P2 lower S1; V5 and CB P-5; B10.I pulled the circuit breaker on the first page but failed to pull the circuit breakers on the second page of the task. On the next step on the functional test of the stall protection computer you are told to set the air data test set to 90 kts and the altitude to 18;000 feet. During this step is when we noticed smoke coming from the left pitot probe. I ran out to check the pitot probe and saw that I melted the pitot probe test head to the pitot probe. I quickly removed heat from the pitot probe.To pay more attention to the Aircraft Maintenance Manual and to double check all the correct circuit breakers are pulled.
column123: While performing a functional check of stall protection system we were required to put aircraft in weight off wheels and put aircraft at 18;000 feet and 90 kts using pitot static test set. Causing the heat to still be on to the LH probe.We quickly removed heat from probe.Pay more attention to AMM task and I should have double checked the CBs my partner pulled.

column121: I was deadheading on Aircraft X. I identified myself to the A Flight Attendant (FA) (as I always do) as a safety and security asset.The flight was nearly full.  During boarding a man who I later learned was Mr. X approached my seat.  He was wearing a camo gaiter around his neck which was partially covering his mouth but was not covering his nose. As he approached; I identified myself as a crew member and politely asked him to pull his mask up over his nose.  He complied but said that I should pinch my mask tight over my nose.  I didn't quite hear what he said so I queried him.  He said; 'You should pinch down on your nose to close the gap at the top of your mask.'   My mask was an NP95 which had no gaps anywhere around my face.  It was my sense that the man was being sarcastic and antagonistic.  I said nothing further to him.I advised the FA A what happened before we pushed back.  She told me that the man had boarded without his face covered and was told to cover his face.  Thus he had pulled his face covering off his face between the time he boarded (when he was told to put it on) and the time he approached me; which was no more than thirty seconds. He clearly had no intention of complying with the mask policy.  FA A asked me to brief the Captain about the incident and asked if I would talk to the CSR agent whom she wanted to speak with Mr. X. I agreed.  Before departure I walked into the jet bridge and spoke with FA A and the CSR.  I briefly explained what I observed and what he said to me then I went back onto the airplane and took my seat.  A short time later I observed Mr. X walk back down the aisle past me.Sometime during the flight FA A advised me that Mr. X had been [violating other regulations].  She advised me that Mr. X demanded to know the crews names (including mine) but that she did not give him any names. She was clearly concerned about this and I could see how his actions were distracting to the flight crew and were thus interfering with their duties.  She told me that she was going to have CS meet the aircraft and asked me to stay as a witness.  FA A as well as the rest of the inflight crew were nothing but polite and professional the entire flight; when I observed her dealing with Mr. X or otherwise.After leaving the aircraft I was standing in the jet bridge and spoke with a CS Supervisor.  Mr. X walked by me and said in an aggressive and hostile tone; 'I want your name.'  I told him that I could not give it to him and that I could not speak with him about this matter.  He again demanded my name and moved closer to me.  I backed up.  He then raised his camera and said; 'I'm taking your picture.'  I stated; 'Do not take my picture.'  He said; I'm taking your picture.'  I quickly turned around and walked around the jet bridge corner toward the aircraft door.   I do not know if he took my photograph or not but felt that his forcing his camera in my face was one of belligerence; hostility; and aggression.  I felt threatened.  All of this simply because he was asked to properly wear his mask.  After the CSR Supervisor and Mr. X walked into the terminal; I remained in the jet bridge as I did not want to encounter Mr. X again.When the CSR Supervisor walked back onto the jet bridge; I explained to her that I could not have my photograph taken and suggested that if he loitered around the terminal waiting for me that she please call law enforcement.  I asked her if she felt he was being hostile and or belligerent.  She agreed that he was.  After some time; Mr. X left the area; and I departed the terminal.Based on his behavior and actions I would strongly urge that Mr. X is not allowed to fly on our airline in the future.

column121: It wasn't supposed to be a very long leg or a long day. The plan was to fly from ZZZ to ZZZ1; grab a quick snack and go to ZZZ2 for the overnight and good food. But; that wasn't what happened.  Snow flurries forced us into unplanned deicing. Bad alternates required reworking and refueling. In the middle of deicing; a sudden snow squall sent visibility plummeting and negating any holdover times. New takeoff alternates then had to be amended onto the paperwork; and re-validating required new paperwork. To describe our departure out of ZZZ as a struggle would be an understatement. But; ever so slowly and methodically; we did eventually depart to ZZZ1. It was on arrival that we were notified that our overnight had changed and to contact scheduling on the ground. So; you can imagine that when we landed in ZZZ1; we were mentally bruised; hungry; tired; and on edge. The landing was normal; as was the taxi to our planned gate. What confused us is what we saw upon turning to face south; looking at [Gate X]. There was nothing. No rampers; or wands or even lights. It was a completely empty and dark. I set the parking brake and asked my FO (First Officer) to send another in range report and commented that we should probably call ZZZ1 OPS and see if they had changed our gate. FO dutifully called OPS on the number two radio so I dialed the north ramp frequency into radio one to monitor. At that exact moment the ACARS message returned as my FO was repeating what OPS had just said; gate change to [Gate Y]! I released the parking brake and began a slow turn to the right when I realized I wasn't at an outstation in the middle of nowhere or on an uncontrolled ramp. I had lost all situational awareness and was in the middle of ZZZ1 moving without permission! I immediately stopped the aircraft and called North Ramp with the gate change. column121: We departed on time for a XX minute flight. Climbing through 10;000 feet I chimed the flight attendants and we continued our climb to 21;000 feet. Center was telling me to expect bad rides all the way to our destination. So when we leveled off at 21;000 feet. I made an announcement stating that the ride was going to be rough and that I would keep the seat belt sign of the entire flight. I also asked the flight attendants to remain seated for the duration of the flight as well or so I thought. The ride was not good. Continuous light occasionally moderate turbulence. The arrival is challenging on a good day and today was no exception. We were dealing with a complex arrival; turbulence; icing and multiple changes to speed and altitude. We were cleared to descend via the arrival with no speed restrictions with about a 90 knot tailwind.We would be early. Around the time that we started our descent I noticed that someone was trying to use the door code to gain access to the cockpit. I immediately declined it and made sure door was locked. The Pilot Flying and I both thought that was strange so I tried calling back to a Flight Attendant to see what was going on. That was the first indication something was wrong. When I turned on the speaker for the cabin I could hear an audible cycling noise. When I tried to chime the flight attendants I couldn't hear the chime and I could not hear any voices on the interphone. I tried to make a quick announcement but nothing was coming out back in the cabin. As the Pilot Flying and I were extremely busy managing the descent and approach we heard a knock at the door and could faintly hear a voice. Pilot Flying turned around and saw a note on the ground that said INTERPHONE INOP.I wanted to get up and grab the note to try and write something back but we were too busy. A few minutes passed. The cockpit door lock code was entered again and I denied it a second time. I tried to yell as loud as I could that we got the message. I think they must have heard that time because they stopped knocking on the door. We landed and began our taxi to the gate. After clearing the active runways I had Pilot Flying call maintenance and inform them that our Cabin Interphone and Public Address system was inoperative. We taxied to the gate and shutdown. After the shutdown checklist was complete and before the forward door was opened I got up to check on the A Flight Attendant and see if everything was OK. He was visibly upset. After the passengers got off the other two Flight Attendant's joined us up in first class to discuss what had happened. A Flight Attendant said that it was the scariest flight of his life. He said that after we had hit a rough patch of turbulence the cabin lights in the plane started to cycle on and off. They were still doing it after I went back to talk to them. He then had tried to call me to see if everything was OK but couldn't reach me. He thought that maybe we had lost pressurization and that we might have been incapacitated. He tried the door code to maybe get a peek inside to see if we were OK. He left a note under the door in hopes that we would grab it and write back. Only after the last time that he tried the door lock and I denied it did he hear me yell through the door. The other two flight attendants were also upset that they couldn't communicate with me. I spent at least 15 minutes with them trying to explain why I couldn't respond to them even though I wanted to.Trying to unlock the cockpit door without my authorization put me on high alert. This is not something I expected. If this had been a different flight with more time I would have taken their note and responded to it and sent it back. That would have been the best way. I tried yelling through the door; but it is loud in the cockpit and only on the second time did they hear me. If we had lost pressurization the masks in the back would have dropped and they would have felt it in their ears. The first time I denied his access to the cockpit door he should have known we were OK. I cannot just open the cockpit door without knowing who is behind it. My first priority is to fly the aircraft. I just didn't have enough time to respond to them the way they wanted me to.I tried to address all of their concerns and I did understand that they were upset. I wrote up the Public Address system as well as the Interphone system with their input to give the mechanics all they needed to fix the system. Maintenance came on board and reset the system. I tested the PA and both forward and aft intercoms with the Flight Attendants and in front of maintenance to make sure everything worked. Maintenance signed off the system and we than headed back. After our initial conversation about what had transpired I thought all Flight Attendants were OK just a little rattled but good enough to continue. If I had known they still had reservations about what had happened I would have immediately responded to them. My crew always comes first.

column121: My first attempt at writing this portion did not save so I will attempt it again. We had an A321 sharklet. Every portion of the beginning of the flight leg from gate departure; takeoff and climb up to the fume event was normal and routine. At sometime above 10;000 ft. we got a call from our #1 FA (Flight Attendant) telling us that the FAs in Economy Class more towards the rear of the aircraft were smelling a sweat odor and a more robust glue type odor. I believe from my prospective that the odor came from the back from the wings black wards because we did not smell anything in the flight deck and no one smelled anything in first class; #1 FA or forward section of the cabin behind 1st class section. Captain began trouble shooting the problem with the QRH guidelines and the FAs that was smelling the odors. One of the FAs was feeling ill from the fume which was strong in the area they were working. Passenger in that area smelled the odors as well. Captain asked if she can continue or do we need to get back to the gate in ZZZ so she can seek medical attention. She was not sure if she wanted to continue on toward ZZZZ1 or return. Captain asked the #1 FA to monitor the FA's condition and if she worsened we will return to ZZZ. While we were discussing the QRH fume trouble shooting pages and making plans to return to ZZZ or another airport that may be closer to our position if we continued to fly farther away from ZZZ; the #1 FA called and told us the FA that was feeling ill was on O2 and was not getting better. So we notified ATC that we will be returning to ZZZ which was the best option to land. We [were given priority handling] to expedite our return to ZZZ and so the FA can get the medical attention she needed. As we began to descend into ZZZ I remember it was below FL180 and through landing that the odors began to infiltrate the flight deck and the #1 FA and passengers began smelling it too. We donned our O2 masks. It was a sweaty smell and it also had an Elmer's glue order to us. The odors continued until we arrived to the gate. The FA that was really ill went to the hospital and the remaining flight crew continued with us to ZZZZ1 with a replacement FA.I don't know of any causal factors that would cause a fume event other than fixing the problem of the source that caused the fumes from escaping and preventing and future leaks from going into the cabin.The only thing that would prevent this from happening would be a complete redesign of the airplane systems that keeps the cabin ventilation isolated from any possible fume leaking into the cabin.

column121: Taxing from the device pad for departure we came very close to coming in contact with Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y had been given clearance to taxi to the runway while we were still finishing up de-ice and neither the Captain or myself as First Officer gave it much thought. When we finished the de-ice process I called for taxi and we were given clearance to taxi. The Runway Visual Range was being reported at the time of 1;000 ft. so the visibility was obviously a contributing factor in the described events. As we were on Taxiway A approaching an intersection; I began to notice some lights on the right hand side of the airplane. I assumed that I was seeing hangar lights as they did not appear to be moving. Looking back this was due to the fact that ourselves and Aircraft Y had roughly the same ground speed and therefore the lights were staying in the same position on my window.As we got closer the Captain and I both realized at about the same time that what we were seeing was Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y must have seen us about the same time because we both came to a stop. When we stopped on the slick taxiway we were probably no more then 20 or 30 ft. away from Aircraft Y. We began to taxi away and as we did I asked ground to verify that we were in fact cleared to taxi to the runway. They stated that we were. Aircraft Y then asked the same thing and ground replied that they as well were cleared to taxi to the same runway. Due to the 1;000 ft. Runway Visual Range I know that Tower could not see where either of us were. I think that the normal low visual procedures of reporting when passing certain points would have saved this from happening. I think that Ground thought that Aircraft Y was already at the end of the runway when we were cleared for taxi and for some reason Aircraft Y was delayed.
column123: We were departing. ATIS prevailing visibility was 1/4 mile in freezing fog. After start we went to device pad 1 and completed Type I and Type IV deicing. Ground gave us taxi instructions and to hold short the ILS critical area. Taxi was uneventful until reaching an intersection. Aircraft Y had been cleared to taxi to the same runway and we nearly met at the intersection. We both applied brakes. Aircraft Y told Ground they would 'give way to...' us. After starting to taxi we called Ground to confirm our taxi instructions. Aircraft Y did the same. We were both cleared all the way to Runway 12. Aircraft Y was cleared to taxi before us and either taxied slow or delayed their start. Ground could have confirmed their position before clearing us to taxi.

column121: After takeoff at acceleration altitude I called for 'flaps 0; climb checks; pitch mode.' Once we were clear of the traffic we were handed off to another frequency on which we were told to look for yet another aircraft in close proximity. By the time we were clear we were through 10;000 feet and due to the distractions we forgot to complete the climb check. I initially began accelerating and reached about 265 knots before I decided to slow to complete the second part of the ice test. Once the test was complete (at around 18;000 feet) I began accelerating and again reached about 265 knots before we realized the flaps were still set to 9. We slowed; retracted the flaps; contacted Maintenance and continued the flight without further incident.No real suggestions. It was human error on my part. I should have been more vigilant and will be in the future.

column121: In our initial climb to 6;000 feet we were instructed by Departure to turn off course and given a fix to fly to. I confirmed the fix with the CA (Captain) and pressed Nav Mode on the FMS. I looked over to my PFD to set the new altitude assigned by Departure and the CA looked away at the same time. Shortly thereafter; Departure called and asked us if we were turning on course. We both looked up and realized that the Nav mode had not captured the course. I immediately turned the heading bug towards the course line on the display; while the CA notified the Controller that we were correcting and turning on course.While compensating for winds and flying via the heading bug; we started to analyze the problem. Shortly after changing the AP to the CA's side; we were able to correct the Nav issue; as the AP was functioning properly on the CA's side; I continued as the pilot flying. About 45 minutes out; the CA left the flight deck to use the LAV. As he returned; he noticed that we had about 8 status messages that popped up sometime after he had left the flight deck. I was engaged with a short conversation with the FA (Flight Attendant) and did not notice the display of messages until he returned. The status messages were flight control related; noting flight spoilers; rudder; etc. The CA referred to the QRH for landing data as a precautionary measure; in the event of a total system failure to those systems. The CA Then notified ATC of our potential systems status and requested deleting the LAHSO restrictions. ATC was unable to comply.Later; as we were given an intercept angle to intercept the final approach course; I selected the NAV button and was waiting for the intercept. We had a [heavy aircraft] on our left and we were paying close attention to that traffic; when we noticed that the aircraft had blown through the center line and was deviating right. The CA then asked me what was going on and while trying to process the information; I replied; 'I have no idea.' At that time Tower called to query our actions; It was as if the aircraft had a mind of its own and before I was able to kick off the autopilot; the CA then asked for the flight controls. We landed without incident and all flight control systems were operational throughout the landing phase; as all the spoilers had deployed. The AP had remained on the CA's side throughout the entire approach.Hindsight; I told the CA; that the one course of action we could have taken at the onset of discovering that the AP/Nav was not recognizing my side; we should have changed roles and allowed him to be the Pilot Flying. With the unexpected behavior of the FMS during the critical phase of flight; I was in total agreement with the CA's actions and decisions; I believe his actions were appropriate and timely while operating in the essence of safety for the passengers and crew.

column121: I checked in with the gate agent prior to my flight to ZZZZ. Approximately 10-15 minutes prior to departure; the A1 FA informed me that she was informed that we had boarded without minimum crew. I fly this trip nearly every week and it's generally always a bit of a scramble at the last minute to get the form completed by all crew members prior to departure.  In addition it is a very difficult form to electronically fill out for the first time.  I believe the FA was only trying her best to complete the form prior to boarding. Perhaps a reminder to both cockpit and cabin crew that a COVID-19 declaration form is required for entry into ZZZZ.  And that the form takes a while to complete as it NOT intuitive and can take a few attempts to complete it and requires sufficient WiFi or cellular signal.

column121: During the DINGO 5 arrival into TUS; after waypoint MAVVA; I continued on the charted 075 degree heading passing through the Runway 11L localizer course; not complying with the textual instruction to intercept the I-TUS localizer course. ATC gave me vectors back around to re-intercept the localizer course; and a normal landing was made.The cause of the event was a failure to cross-check the textual instructions with what is displayed on the chart. Contributing factors were as follows: 1) A 'Descend Via' clearance was not issued. ATC instructed to 'Descend and maintain 8;000 feet; and EXPECT a visual approach.' I misinterpreted that to mean he would provide vectors to the final approach course; or clear me for a visual approach passing MAVVA.  2) I found the verbiage on the chart confusing where it states 'Runway 11L EXPECT approach clearance'. I interpreted that to mean once established on the 075 heading from MAVVA; not upon intercepting the localizer; as normally you would not intercept a localizer without ATC clearance or prior to accepting a visual approach.To avoid a recurrence of this event; a thorough briefing covering all noted and textual information should be conducted and cross checked prior to every landing. While my briefing did cover all of the information on the plan-view of the arrival; I missed a crucial piece of information solely located in the textual description that was not well depicted nor defined on the plan-view. It would have been helpful if ATC had offered us a visual approach earlier; directed us to intercept the localized after MAVVA and THEN expect approach clearance; or have the instruction to Intercept I-TUS localizer clearly printed on the plan view. It is worthy to note; the ATC controller stated 'Yeah; you're not the first airliner to do this' both over the frequency and on the telephone while speaking with him after landing. This leads me to believe that this could be a common mistake that could be corrected easily with a revised; emphasized; note on the arrival chart.
