column121: I was First Officer and pilot monitoring for a reposition flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. When I arrived to the airplane; the Captain was already there with multiple maintenance technicians working through a dual inoperative GPS situation. The consensus was to defer both GPS units; along with the associated MEL items. After processing our 9 MELs during our pre-flight discussion we waited approximately two hours for a flight plan to be filed due to the issue with ADS-B being inoperative.During the after-start checklist; the CONT CAB ZONE TEMP fault appeared on Master Caution recall. We complied with the QRH and MEL and contacted Maintenance Control for deferral under the 'flight crew placard' option. The Captain and I discussed the phrase in the QRH; 'if the light extinguishes when Master Caution System is reset; no further action is required' - and he noted that this does not alleviate us from the need to defer the item per the MEL XX-XXY. Along the same time; the Captain noted that the 'dispatch alert' box was unchecked; so after the deferral was complete we resumed normal operations.After takeoff we experienced two additional master recall lights - 'Anti-Skid Inop' and the 'Reverser' on the overhead panel.Shortly after we leveled off at cruise altitude the dispatcher asked if we had added a new deferred item after pushback. We responded that we had; that it was XX-XXY. He advised us to fill out a report; despite the 'dispatch alert' box not being checked.The reposition flights after long-term storage lend themselves to multiple maintenance related issues and could be planned ahead to be operated by Functional Check Flight pilots.The filing of our flight plan took nearly two hours. Not knowing the exact cause of the issue; it would be helpful for future flights to review the process for filing flights with inoperative GPS and ADS-B to minimize future delays.
column123: Aircraft X was a reposition flight for aircraft (tail) in storage several months.  The aircraft was dispatched with multiple MELs.  We waited over two hours for Dispatch to be able to get ATC to accept a flight plan into the system for a clearance.A Control Cab 'Zone Temp' light illuminated during Master Cation recall during the after-start checklist.  QRH procedures were followed and Maintenance control was contacted for a crew MEL (XX-XXY) before departure despite the misleading 'No further action required' guidance in the QRH.Two more master caution lights were encountered after takeoff (Master caution 'anti-skid and reverser.')Dispatch sent an ACARs message after level off advising us to submit a report for not getting an amended release for XX-XXY before departure.  We responded that a Dispatch alert is not required for XX-XXY.  Dispatch responded 'They give us a heads up anyway.'  We did not believe we violated any maintenance/dispatch procedures but were led to believe we had.Reposition flights from long term storage are a severely irregular operation and should be conducted by the Functional Check Flight department.

column121: Landed on a runway with snow removal equipment on it. While on rollout; the low visibility obscured runway activity until no other choice was available.Onboard equipment failed; distracting crew from making radio positions reporting to ZZZ traffic. Event occurred after Tower had closed for the night.Good accident prevention was conducted by all vehicles and aircraft involved; and no other problems occurred.This could have been a classic example of 'Chain of events causing a accident.'  A late departure because of icing conditions at origin. Weather at arrival airport causing snow removal equipment to be on runway for extended periods of time. A minor problem during the approach to landing phase distracted the crew; and company procedures required crew to be playing the role of both flying and non-flying pilot at the same time.      In this case; I believe; safety would have been better served if once the decision to hand off control was made; we didn't change back 600-400 feet above the ground. Once the decision was made our roles would have been clearer; and airplane radio communication would have been made at the critical trigger points.
column123: On approach to ZZZ Approach vectored my flight to join the ILS [Runway] XX. They cleared us for the approach and told us to contact ZZZ on the CTAF frequency. The vector brought us in at 2;000 feet MSL and outside of ZZZZZ final fix. We had tuned and identified the ILS frequency. I was flying the aircraft and had intercepted the localizer. The glide slope needle on the Captain's ADI flagged. The FO's instruments were still working so control of the aircraft was transferred just outside of the final approach fix.  As we descended on the approach; I was monitoring the FO's progress. I had forgotten to make the needed radio call outs; (in the blind) on the CTAF frequency; to announce our presence on the approach and our intentions to land. On the landing roll; we saw the snow removal equipment clearing the runway at the far end.We were alerted to the presence of the snow removal operation upon our roll out on the runway. We also realized that the radio; although properly tuned into the stand-by position on the #1 radio; had not been switched over.The weather at ZZZ was a ceiling of 1;200 feet and visibility of 1 3/4 miles with blowing snow according to the ASOS. (There was nothing to advise us of snow removal activities in progress.) The instrumentation problem caused an unexpected transfer of control of the aircraft to a student pilot who was on his OE training. The transfer was completed successfully; but I was concerned about monitoring the progress of the student on the ILS approach. My attention was on the approach and I failed to make the needed callouts on the CTAF frequency to announce our arrival at ZZZ. The visibility prevented us from seeing the snow removal in progress as we approached the runway.We switched over to the proper frequency and proceeded to taxi in to the FBO.We could have used an alert from Approach control as to the presence of the snow removal equipment working on the surface at ZZZ or have that information broadcast on the ASOS.

column121: While on visual approach to COS [Runway] 35L; crew both identified a very large building under construction with crane offset between 1.7 to 2 miles from the runway threshold. At approximately 1.5 miles from threshold; received EGPWS (Electronic Ground Proximity Warning) 'Obstacle; Pull Up!' warning. Aircraft was stable and on visual glide path as verified by FMS 3 degree visual glide path indicator and also visually with Runway 35L PAPI. Sink rate at time of incident was 500 ft. per minute. As the building was either directly underneath or just behind aircraft; no other obstacles were noted and aircraft was stable and on glide path; PIC (Pilot-in-Command) decided this was an erroneous warning and elected to continue flight. Landing was uneventful. During debrief; both crew members agreed that the message was erroneous and must be an anomaly caused by the new construction and a go-around at that time would be futile. If the weather was not CAVU (Ceiling and Visibility Unlimited) an immediate go-around would have been performed. There is a current NOTAM (01/037) regarding a crane at this location but the crane was offset from the flight path and at 300 ft. AGL. An issue exists with the EGPWS system and this new building construction that will trigger false warnings and may cause aircraft to go-around unnecessarily.

column121: While turning into Spot XXX on the cargo apron in ZZZZ; the plane was unable to stop in a timely manner due to what I believe was contamination on the apron. Due to the lack of braking ability the CA (Captain) briefly deployed the thrust reversers and the plane was then able to slow and we regained braking ability. I was not aware that there was difficulty braking until the CA deployed the reversers. We then proceeded to finish the turn into [spot] without issue. The entrance to the ramp was well cleaned and mostly free of contaminants; and according to the Captain; the braking condition was very good. However; further into the ramp; the contamination became present; although it was not very visible; almost like it was black ice on top of the pavement. When we exited the plane after shutting down and securing; the ramp and parking area was covered in a transparent; very slippery layer of ice with slush scattered sporadically throughout. I believe that this ice existed on the apron just outside of the parking spot as well. There was no active precipitation and all of the airport surfaces we had been on up until that point had had good breaking conditions. Thankfully the CA was able to control the aircraft without causing damage to the plane or surroundings. I do not have an exact recollection of the ground speed when we had the difficulty breaking; but I would estimate it to be in the range of roughly 5-7 knots. We notified the ground crew of the difficulty braking and hopefully they took actions to decontaminate that area of the ramp for the next aircraft.I believe the transition from well-cleared; contaminant free areas; to the contaminated area caused the braking issue. It was also night and the light did not reflect off of the ice on the contaminated areas of the ramp; making it difficult to see the contamination. I thought the Captain was maintaining a safe speed for the conditions and was surprised when the reversers were deployed.I would suggest that the entirety of the ramp is cleared to the same standard in the future if able. Crews should also be extra vigilant of contamination that is not easily visible in low light; or poorly lit conditions.
column123: Normal arrival. While taxiing to Stand XXX we were following a company aircraft. Due to the light weight of our aircraft it kept accelerating while at idle thrust. When entering the cargo ramp; the pavement was bare and wet. The last 500 feet of taxi had thin frozen slush. The aircraft ahead slowed; and we were slowing to turn into our stand; when the Captain noted the aircraft was sliding. He applied full brakes to no effect; then deployed reverse thrust on both engines; slightly above idle. The aircraft slowed and stopped after sliding about 50 feet. The reversers were stowed and the aircraft turned into the stand and parked. As it approached the stop point it again slid about 5 feet in the attempt to stop. Reverse thrust was not used a second time. Less than 30% n1 in reverse.[The cause was] thin ice on the ramp. Taxi speed about 8-10 knots. Unnoticed change in braking effectiveness. Fatigue from a 15+ hour day.Reverse thrust was a last ditch effort to not scrape paint. Parking brake might have worked also. Even creeping to the stop point; the aircraft still slid about 2 feet past the stop point.

Once I realized this; I immediately called my coordinator; who verified that the NOTAM for the airspace closure did not allow us to even drop down once entering the airspace; and was only published for overflights; and at XC:00Z I ACARSed to return to gate; since even if they departed immediately; which they had just started the deice process; they would be pushing it to make it into the airspace in time (they were already filed fast). The flight returned to gate and was delayed several hours in order to allow for arrival to ZZZ [Center] after it opened at XF:30Z.I missed the original emails stating the closure which would have given myself; the crew; and the coordinator a heads up to be careful of our times deicing. It is hard to check every email. For ATC-0 events; I believe there should be other forms of notification to dispatchers to prevent this from happening. I do not believe ATC-0 NOTAMs attached for pilot paperwork; as the Captain said he did not see it; and reviewing the paperwork; I did not either.

column121: In preparing for the flight; I could not determine the engine-out minimum cleanup altitude departing Runway 16R for an engine failure that occurs after D3.0 IRNO. The complex special EFP reads 'EO - Established on H325 and above 5;500 feet MSL' - a condition that will not be reached if climbing via IRNO LOC SOUTH COURSE per the EFP. After talking to the Chief Pilot on Call; who then made inquiries to other internal resources; it was determined that 5;500 feet MSL is the minimum cleanup altitude. In fact; at the minimum all-engine climb gradient of 440 ft./NM any departing aircraft will be above 5;500 feet MSL (1;085 ft. AAE) before D3.0 IRNO. However; with an all-engine minimum cleanup altitude of 7;400 feet MSL an engine failure can occur with the flaps extended. The EFP does not provide a minimum cleanup altitude for that case.Our departure was uneventful; and our light-weight [aircraft] reached 7;400 ft. MSL as we crossed D3.0 IRNO. Winds were out of the south at 45 kts. On a side note; the [Runway] 16L/R EFP for IRNO OTS (Out of Service) appears flawed. If IRNO and IAGY are both OTS the procedure specifies runway heading to 8;500 feet MSL. At max crosswind for a V2 of 131 KIAS of 70 kts.; drift angle will be 32 degrees. With a ground track of 196 (degrees); the terrain at 7;862 feet is almost precisely on course from the FMG R-205 decision point. The crosswind limits appear to be for the early turn to H325; but may need to be more restrictive for a 164 heading climb to 8;500 feet MSL.

column121: Departing RJAA. I was PF (Pilot Flying). Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring). Relief FO (First Officer) was sitting in observer seat. We were within a close margin of max structural weight but within all limits. It was briefed that the best angle speed (258 kts.) and flaps up maneuver speed (254 kts.) would exceed the 250 [kts.] below 10;000 ft. restriction so we opted to keep Flaps 1 until passing 10;000 [ft.] so that we could maintain maneuverability. Once we cleaned up to Flaps 1; I opened the speed window and manually set speed to 240 kts. The overspeed margin was currently 250 kts. The underspeed margin was around 225 kts. Flaps 1 maneuver speed was about 235 kts. Upon reaching 10;000 ft.; I put 245 kts. in the speed window to initiate an acceleration that would then continue past 254 kts. for the Flaps Up speed as the flaps transitioned. The transition was going as planned until we hit some moderate wake turbulence from crossing traffic. The speed started to shoot up dramatically towards the upper limit. I applied some back pressure while keeping the AP engaged to get the nose up and arrest the speed increase. I was able to arrest most of the speed increase but it still resulted in a 1 or 2 kt. overspeed. At this time; the turbulence became more intense and both the low and high speed regimes converged. I disengaged the AP/AT (Autopilot/Autothrottle) and hand flew to best maintain airspeed as I anticipated a drop in airspeed on the other side of the wake turbulence. The airspeed started to drop but was arrested with manual input. Once the high and low speed margins stabilized and the turbulence subsided; we re-automated the aircraft and continued our departure without incident.I did not anticipate the wake of crossing traffic to be such a factor in our tight tolerances. When so close to max structural weight on TO (takeoff); the transition from Flaps 1 to Flaps Up is always on a razor thin margin. Any significant wake; turbulence or even wind shift will put you into and undesired airspeed regime. I would suggest not loading the aircraft right up to max weights and this has always been an issue for flap transition on the 767.

column121: During Climb we Leveled at 17;000 departure switched us to ZZZ Center on XYZ.AA. Upon check in with ZZZ Center we were given the clearance to climb and maintain flight level 290 and 270 knots.  The Captain who was the pilot Monitor at the time read back those instructions and I set the altitude preset to FL290.  During the climb coming through approximately 220/230 we were given traffic at our 2 to 3 o'clock which wasn't a factor. Then while climbing through FL250 ATC called us asking what our altitude was; he then told us that we were assigned FL190.  He then cleared us to FL300. Flight continued without further issue.As pilots we take responsibility for any deviation of this nature and if there's questions it is our duty to ask and ask again to repeat if needed. I have however; noticed that since we've started flying more frequently since COVID that there are many more miscommunications on the radio than normal.I think we need to recognize that with what's been happening with COVID over the last year we as a group have lost a little proficiency especially with regards to radio calls and procedures. A lot of us have been out on the leaves that includes both pilots and controllers. What I didn't realize was I had left them extended below 1;000 feet. column121: We operated Aircraft X from ZZZ to MDW; and the majority of the flight was uneventful. Mr. Y was my Captain and PF; and we had setup well in advance for the RNAV RNP Y approach for Runway 22L at MDW according to their latest ATIS. Later we received an ATIS update showing that the ILS for Runway 31C was active; so we re-configured and briefed that; still with plenty of time. We had discussed the possible need of diverting to ZZZ1 rather than our filed ALT1 of ZZZ2 and ALT2 of ZZZ3; but the visibility at MDW stayed above the minimums we needed for either the RNAV or ILS approaches to 22L/31C respectively.Fast forward to our first approach attempt: we're established on the ILS to 31C; fully configured well before the FAF and I was thinking we've got it made. We broke out at around 1;700 MSL and inflight visibility was not an issue and better than reported. From around 2;000 feet and down we experienced constant light and moderate turbulence; but no icing or precipitation. Captain had turned the autopilot and autothrottles off to help deal with the winds that were gusting from 260 degrees at 21 to 39 knots. We were also landing with stall protection ice speeds; adding 10 knots to our Vref and Vapp speeds.Everything was going great until somewhere between 1/2 to 1 mile from the approach end of 31C we got multiple 'WINDSHEAR' automated call outs from the airplane. Captain elected to go-around which we did; re-configuring as needed and I let MDW Tower know at around 400 feet AGL per the SOP. They gave us a heading and altitude to fly; asked us the reason for the go-around and handed us back off to Chicago Approach. We cleaned up the airplane and got vectored in for another ILS approach to 31C behind an Air Carrier Y.The second ILS approach was almost identical to the first; albeit with slightly less wind and turbulence. This time; even though we were ready for the conditions and knew more of what to expect; we managed to catch a gust of wind right in the flare and didn't touch down on Runway 31C until between the first third and the midpoint of the runway. Captain did a great job of thinking quick and performed a rejected landing; setting and calling 'TOGA' almost immediately after touchdown and off we went. We reconfigured again; got vectored around and handed off to Chicago Approach again and came around for a third attempt at Runway 31C.The third time Captain was able to land normally and well within the touchdown zone; but when he applied the brakes we found out that the '5/5/5' runway condition codes advertised for 31C were optimistic at best with the airplane noticeably sliding and skidding as we rolled out. We also noticed that there was blowing snow obscuring at least 50 percent of the runway surface. Captain advised MDW Tower of the braking action we experienced; calling it 'poor' and; to their credit; they immediately directed the broom and plow teams out to clear Runway 31C again. The rest of the flight was normal as we taxied into our gate.If there's anything I learned tonight; it's that just because you're on short final that doesn't mean you're going to land. Also: just because the Air Carrier Y flight that landed ahead of you reported 'braking action good' doesn't mean you will. I remember being on short final during our first ILS approach to 31C feeling complacent that we 'had it made' being on the ILS rather than RNAV RNP approach with its higher minimums and having broken out early at 1;700 feet. My go-around call outs also could have been crisper and more prompt; but that was mostly due to the 'startle' factor which was my own fault.My one suggestion would be for the airport operations crews at MDW to conduct their own braking action tests more often and with a more pessimistic eye. When the ATIS states RCCs are '5/5/5' the Air Carrier Y flight that landed ahead of you reports 'braking action good' and yet you experience significant wheel slip/skid due to icy runway surface conditions upon landing; thatindicates someone is being either dishonest or overly optimistic on their own braking action reports. If we or our Dispatch had known that the 'real' RCCs for 31C at MDW were actually 3/3/3 or even 2/2/2; we most likely would not have had the required landing performance numbers that we needed to land at MDW's shorter runways and would've gone to ZZZ1.

column121: Descending via the NIIXX 2 arrival for the ILS Runway 35R in CAVOK conditions. Around the BSTON Intersection we were given a westerly to northwesterly radar vector and cleared to descend and maintain 10;000. As we got closer to the final approach course (somewhere between DEANE and DRUMM) we were cleared to descend and maintain 8;000 and cleared direct to the FRONZ Intersection (FAF for the ILS). The Controller asked if we had 35R in sight; after a pause; we had the runway in sight and advised ATC. We were then cleared for the visual approach to 35R. The FAF altitude at FRONZ is 7;000 so that is what we set in the MCP while descending through approximately 8;800 in FLCH. We had just gotten the '2;500' call from the Radio Altimeter and made our call outs. As we descended through 8;000 I noticed the Radio Altitude around 1;800 and descending. A quick look at JeppFD PRO showed our aircraft position just south and east of the DRUMM Intersection. I called out the altitude and the fact that we need to go back up to 8;000 (our last cleared altitude prior to the approach clearance) until we are north of DRUMM. I reset the MCP to 8;000 and verbalized that we need to climb back up. The Captain selected a V/S climb back to 8;000. We joined the approach course and followed the G/S and landed without incident.ATC never mentioned anything to us about violating airspace or going below the DEN Class B. Though it is nice to get directs; etc. However; I believe the direct to FRONZ clearance; if not really familiar with the DEN Class B; can set crews up to possibly violate airspace and even lead to an unstable approach.Once parked at the gate with all checklists complete; we debriefed and there certainly was some confusion as to exactly where we were when we descended below 8;000. We had a jump seat observer who thought we might have been a little low as he has a lot of General Aviation experience in the DEN area.

column121: The FO was on the very first leg of OE. The flight proceeded perfectly until arriving in the ZZZ1 [airport] terminal area. ZZZ Center descended us and never handed us over to the local [ZZZ] TRACON. Instead; we were told to expect holding instructions. It was clear the Center Controller was very busy (he was doing an exceptionally good job). Instead of issuing holding instructions we were asked where we wanted to hold. We told him we wanted to hold at ZZZZZ [Intersection]; the initial approach fix for the ILS Runway XX to ZZZ [airport]. He issued instructions to hold south. We asked if we could hold north inbound; right hand turns. He issued instructions 'cleared as requested' with no EFC. He asked how much fuel we had onboard and we replied 2 hours. I didn't push the EFC because it was clear he was saturated and we were holding at 11;000 feet above a lower layer in VFR conditions. ATC explained to other aircraft that ZZZ [TRACON] was ATC Zero and he was the only Controller handling all aircraft going into and out of 4 controlled fields. It was difficult to simply get a break on the frequency so I decided to just be patient.We had been sending ACARS messages to the company enroute and didn't get any responses; this is not that unusual; usually Dispatch will reply with 'OK' but not always. When we were issued holding instructions we sent Dispatch an ACARS message 'Holding at OM for Runway YY ZZZ; no reason given' and once again; we did not receive a reply. Incidentally; I instruct all my OE pilots; as I did in this instance; to look for the 'VHF IN PROGRESS' display after selecting SEND on an ACARS message to be certain the unit actually sent the message. In all cases it did.The airport pages indicated that ZZZ2 [airport] was just XX miles away and we knew they were not affected by this situation. The weather at ZZZ2 was also good. Our FMC fuel reserve was 4.0 since we had no alternate. At first I wanted to use 7.0 as a decision point on fuel. My thought it would probably take 20 minutes to get to ZZZ2 if needed and I wanted a cushion so I added 3.0 to the FMC fuel reserve to make my decision. If we hit 7.0 on the fuel it would be time to contact Dispatch and go to ZZZ2. While we were doing all this ATC was relying on us to contact aircraft going into and out of the airports below to issue instructions. Needless to say we were a bit busy. We were told to descend first to 8;000 feet in the hold; then to 6;000 feet. On several occasions VFR aircraft popped up on our TCAS (no alerts were issued) as we were holding in Class E airspace above the ZZZ Class D and the ZZZ1 Class C. We were keeping a keen eye outside. At one point ATC issued instructions to climb to 8;000 feet in the hold for traffic. Again; the Center Controller was doing an exceptionally good job. We were told on several occasions what our sequence was going into ZZZ; third; then second; then next.  Our intent; of course; was to get into ZZZ safely.ATC was issuing phone numbers for aircraft to call when on the ground. I was a bit confused as to why; I thought the towers were open; but paid it no mind. We heard the Controller mention COVID as the reason to another aircraft. Unfortunately; the aircraft landing ZZZ in front of us; Aircraft Y failed to call the phone number. This haunted ALL landings into all 4 airports. The Controller explained to another aircraft that his procedures precluded him from clearing any other aircraft for approaches into any of the four fields until had had a cancellation from the Aircraft Y. In fact; ATC had us attempt to call him on the frequency.I considered whether we could get in VFR but we could not get down into the class D with ZZZ Center and there was a layer between us and the field (I've forgotten where it was but probably about 3;000 feet). I then considered our fuel considerations; rather than using the 4.0 FMC fuel reserve I decided to use the actual FAR fuel reserve of roughly 3.6. The FO stayed on top of duties not only contacting other aircraft but complying with my requests as the flying pilot very well. Finally; when we reached 6;600 pounds of fuel remaining I asked the FO to contact Dispatch via ARINC phone patch. We had already looked at the ARINC Services page in the Jepps early on and determined that ARINC had a surface on ground frequency of XYX.XZ at ZZZ1; and we would be able to get a hold of them down low. I asked FO to come up with a diversion plan. FO worked with Dispatch who recommended ZZZ2 (of course) and said the fuel required would be 1;100 pounds at 10;000 feet. This seemed too low; I didn't see how we could climb to 10;000 feet; fly XY miles; and shoot an approach and landing on 1;100 pounds (and change) of fuel; so we declared minimum fuel and requested an immediate direct vector to ZZZ2. At no point did we use the words 'Mayday' or 'Emergency'. We were instructed to fly a heading (I believe it was 045 degrees) and issued climb instructions to 10;000 feet. We immediately complied and began to set up for an approach into ZZZ2.The FO did a great job juggling responsibilities; getting ATIS and setting up for the approach; contacting ZZZ1 local; etc. At one point ATC queried our fuel status and the FO initially used the word Emergency but then quickly corrected and said we had declared Minimum Fuel. We landed on ZZZ2 Runway XXL with 3.7 on the fuel. We pulled off the runway and asked ATC for a position where we could sit and call the company.We called Dispatch on the cell phone and were instructed to go to the 'Maintenance Ramp.' We complied and were met with a follow me car where we parked; right next to an aircraft with a full load of passengers (obviously there for the same reason; we were later joined by another aircraft). We were immediately met with a set of stairs and a representative who asked what we needed. Dispatch immediately gave us a field load and we ordered thirteen thousand pounds of fuel. We arranged for the proper fuel load. It took some time for the fuel truck to arrive.We then had to coordinate getting paperwork to the aircraft. While Dispatch and the team did a great job of getting that all set up; the young lady driving back and forth had to go quite a ways to get our paperwork which took a great deal of time.Once we had our paperwork we were able to depart for the short flight to ZZZ. We completed the legs without further incident.I am uncertain what drove ZZZ TRACON to close; whether it was a scheduled cleaning due to COVID or some type of emergency. We reviewed the ATC and FIR NOTAMs and did not have anything mentioning the closure. Clearly this was the beginning of the delay. Then; it was further exacerbated by the crew of Aircraft Y jet failing to call the phone number after landing. Had they called we were next to be cleared to land and we would not have diverted.Several suggestions: We need clear and concise ACARs policies in the FOM. Each and every time Dispatch receives a message from a crew inflight they should ALWAYS reply. Perhaps this is a policy with Dispatch; but since it is not in the FOM and once in a while we do not hear from them we have no idea and I was not concerned about not getting replies; until we mentioned holding to them and I got no reply. That's when we hopped on the ACARS Services chart and noted that ZZZ1 had a ground based frequency and we could reach them from our holding position (incidentally; many of our pilots don't even know that table exists). Second; It is not unusual for ACARs not to work. This needs to be cleaned up. We are constantly writing up aircraft for 'NO COMM' and ACARs failures and they don't work. Honestly; I'd say ACARS works correctly about 2/3 of the time; certainly not the spirit of FAR 121.99. Granted we have ARINC; but crews will rely on ACARS just to find out after the fact that dispatch never got anything from us. Next; if this was a scheduled COVID cleaning we should have known they were going ATC Zero before we arrived in the terminal area. Dispatch was even caught off guard about it. ATC must develop a means of communicating this so we don't find out so late in the game. They should also consider issuing a TFR. Perhaps the FAA should consider a new type of TFR for COVID. Frankly; I am a small aircraft owner and use it frequently. I don't want to be told I can't fly over class D airspace while in Class E airspace simply because they are cleaning TRACON. On a beautiful sunny day there are going to be aircraft all over. If I were flying GA in the area and knew the TRACON was down I'd probably stay away just because I don't want to get run over by a transport. Finally; the company should consider what paperwork we REALLY need at the aircraft. For instance; we can already get performance via ACARS. We can pull up our NOTAMS on our tablet. That would leave signing fit for duty and the release. Perhaps we could give Dispatch all the pertinent info (they already had the ZFW weight and balance) so all they needed was fuel onboard and they could simply give us the necessary numbers for departure. Next; send us an ACARS message for signatures - we could print 2 of them and leave one with the rep on the ramp. Had we been able to do that we would have been out about an hour earlier and would NOT have taken another delay. Incidentally; we obtained our PDC via ACARS in ZZZ2 correctly and it worked properly all the way back; including the summary page.

column121: Captain was pilot monitoring. FO (First Officer) was pilot flying. Passing through 4;000 feet MSL on climbout from ZZZ we noticed a fuel imbalance developing - right wing main tank fuel indication already 400 pounds lower than left wing. Right wing main tank fuel appeared to be feeding at approximately twice the rate of the left and it appeared that the center tank fuel was not feeding at all. Engine fuel flow readings appeared normal and equal. By 10;000 feet MSL the imbalance had increased to the point that the IMBAL alert was activated. We coordinated with ATC to level off at 12;000 feet MSL in order to reduce fuel flow and begin taking appropriate action. Upon leveling at 12;000 feet MSL we observed the right fuel tank quantity feed rate appear to normalize and then observed a 50 pound increase in right main tank fuel quantity. Fuel imbalance at that point was 1;100 pounds. We initiated the IMBAL checklist in the QRH. Observing what then appeared to be normal tank quantity indications for a crossfeed operation; we coordinated with ATC to continue our climb and proceed on course to the destination knowing we would also coordinate with Dispatch and maintenance promptly to determine if proceeding to ZZZ1 was advisable. As soon as we established climb fuel flow settings and pitch attitude; the right main tank quantity began to decrease again at what appeared to be the same abnormal rate observed during the initial climb. We then requested priority handling initiated the return to ZZZ (nearest airport) and started the APU as a precaution. I advised Dispatch; the cabin crew; and the passengers of the situation using SOP. As soon as we stopped the climb to initiate the return to ZZZ the right main fuel tank indication again stopped decreasing at an abnormal rate. We concluded the IMBAL checklist and for the remainder of the flight we observed no further indications of abnormal rate of decrease in right main wing tank fuel. During the descent; I spoke with the flight attendants and they confirmed that there were no visible indications of fuel leaks on either wing or engine. column121: After pushing off gate and starting 1 engine; we received an Elevator Servo Fault ECAM message. We went through all QRH procedures to resolve the problem to no avail. After calling ZZZ Operations to coordinate a return to the gate; we were informed that we were not allowed to return to the gate for a maintenance problem without Maintenance Control authorization. This seems to be in conflict with 14 CFR 121.533; 14 CFR 121.535 regarding Captain's Pilot in Command authority; as well as the MEL preamble which states that Maintenance Control's role is that of technical consultation (Not Command and Control). In any event; we eventually reached Maintenance Control via personal cellphone; and; eventually; Maintenance Control concurred that we should return to the gate. We returned to the gate; maintenance personnel troubleshot the problem to no avail; and the aircraft was taken out of service. My concern is that; in this scenario; the flight crew was forced to go through a Maintenance Control process that has 3 possible outcomes. First; Maintenance Control directs some off book procedure over the phone that 'fixes' the problem. Second; Maintenance Control directs us to flight crew placard the malfunction (which is not allowed by the MEL in any event). Neither one of those outcomes are acceptable with a primary flight control malfunction. The last possible outcome; and the only realistic outcome; is to return the aircraft to the gate; which we were frustrated from doing by this Maintenance Control permission regimen. I am concerned we are being pushed into possibly unsafe operation as our judgment is automatically questioned by a corporate policy that directly conflicts with Federal law.[Reporter stated the need for a revision of] company policy regarding maintenance troubleshooting.We [flight crews] need clearer understanding of the roles and responsibilities of Maintenance Control versus the PIC.

column121: This narrative highlights two incorrect published crossing altitudes on two different arrivals that can lead to altitude deviations and aircraft overspeeds. The first is the PASLY 4 (10-2C) arrival to BNA at GROAT intersection. The crossing is depicted to cross GROAT at or below FL 230. It is always 1000 out of 1000 times given to cross GROAT at FL 220 usually by Memphis Center and has been for at least five years. Sometimes this occurs very late. This can lead to a situation where the aircraft was on the path; is now high; and the aircraft then pitches down at the last minute to meet the unpublished altitude of 22;000 ft. This pitchdown can lead to an overspeed and a situation that still does not meet the crossing. The second instance is on the ENDEE 6 Arrival into MDW (10-2). The fix in particular is KAMBL and the published crossing is between FL 270-FL 240. The unpublished crossing that is given; very late; is to cross KAMBL at 24;000 ft. Now the aircraft is in the same situation as the PASLY 4 Arrival; only you may have a 100 plus kt. tailwind to deal with as well. Both these situations persist but are preventable by simply changing the published altitude. Finally; there are several Pilots who are rusty from not flying; due to low utilization; whose situational awareness and lack of currency make this situation even more grave. Please fix these easy to remedy issues and trap the known errors. Thank you. We did not have a deviation. I am only reporting to highlight these issues.

column123: With the A.P. and A.T. off; I was P.F. on the visual approach to Runway XX.  ATC calls out traffic at our 2 o'clock that will be close to us for another runway. The Captain later said he thought I said 'We're set to TA only.'  The approach continued normally with us going to managed speed; gear down; as we started down the glide slope inside the FAF.  Just after I called for flaps 3 around 1;400 feet AGL; I noted the Aircraft Y a little above us and the appropriate distance to the right joining up with us.  I was still slowing the aircraft at that moment; and the RA went off 'Climb; Climb.'  I asked the Captain 'We are not in TA only?'  He responded 'Well we are going to have to go.'  I momentarily considered going around; but thought continuing the approach was actually the safest course of action when the RA immediately stopped.  We continued the approach and landed uneventfully.  The RA happened the moment the Aircraft Y was joining the other localizer course.  What I should have done is gone around.  Following the RA is the right thing to do unless it is unsafe to do so.

column121: While on approach to ZZZ in day VMC conditions; crew was instructed to fly direct 'ZZZZZ' - the FAF for ILS XX - for a visual approach to [Runway] XX. The crew had been left high by both Center and Approach; but was able to reach the 5;000 ft. and slow prior to intercept. The PIC/PF (Pilot Flying) briefed the SIC/PM (Pilot Monitoring) on speed/energy management and airspeed 'windows' prior to the approach. After reporting runway in sight and receiving the approach clearance; the PF initiated descent to 4;500 ft. (the FAF altitude) and began to lessen the intercept angle; and PM prompted gear down and flaps 22. Aircraft still slightly overshot the localizer but was able to capture both LOC and GS which happened simultaneously. 4;500 ft. is within 1;300 ft. AGL of field elevation; and due to the short distance both vertically to the runway and laterally (just outside 4 miles); the PM/PIC anticipated an unstable approach and called a go around. The PF pressed the TOGA (Takeoff Go-Around); disconnected the autopilot; and called 'check thrust flaps nine' and the PM set flaps 9 and checked the thrust to discover the PF had not yet increased thrust to detents. Concurrently with the 'check thrust flaps 9 actions'; and 'Sink Rate' EGPWS warning occurred; and momentary hesitation by PF prompted PM/PIC to take control and initiate the immediate action in response to the 'sink rate' AURAL as required for the EGPWS escape; with a 'Pull Up' Aural warning occurring concurrently with the initiation of the EGPWS escape procedure. (At the time of initiation the EGPWS escape; PIC noted an 1;800 fpm descent rate). Upon reaching a safe altitude; the aircraft configuration was cleaned up in line as normal; and flight continued back for ILS without further incident. One error was made during EGPWS escape; which was PIC only increasing thrust to detents and not to max. Upon completion of the flight; crew debriefed on a number of key items. These included energy management and the approach profile in the AOM; go around procedure and ensuring power is set concurrently with pitch and callout when conducting a missed; and the EGPWS escape maneuver.Crews should act very early to mitigate unstable approach situations; including in a situation like this requesting a lower altitude earlier and a vector out to the IAF in lieu of the FAF; this can alleviate the chances of an unstable approach long before the issue manifests. Missed approaches should be initiated immediately upon identification of an unstable approach. In the event of a missed approach; crews should ensure the action is taken decisively including the increase of power; and both pilots should remain involved in the process. Should a GPWS warning be received; decisive; immediate action should be taken - as per the AOM - superseding normal missed approach actions due to the time critical nature of high vertical speed close to the ground. Captains especially should keep a close eye on FOs conducting operations at outstations - in this situation; having approach offer a better vector to join or taking an actual ILS clearance may have prevented the situation from manifesting at all.

column121: Arriving into ZZZ the altimeter setting was showing 0996 mb; so during our arrival brief we covered the VNAV limitation for altimeters lower than 29.70/1006 and put special emphasis on using FLCH (Flight Level Change) when transitioning. Transition level was FL070. ATC began descending us in small steps; they gave us a descend to FL070 but when we were passing FL080 they gave us a descend to 6;000 ft. then further lower to 5;000 ft.; during those step downs I missed switching the altimeter setting to the local 0996mb. Then when we leveled at 5;000 ft. ATC verified the altimeter setting stating that we were 400 ft. lower than we should have. I immediately realized my mistake; set the correct altimeter setting; took corrective action and called for the approach checklist. Since the airplane wasn't reacting as fast as I wanted; I disconnected the auto pilot; corrected the altitude and continued manual flying all the way until we landed. There is no excuse for missing an altimeter setting during transition. There were many factors/distractions that took place for this to happen and they all came pretty close together: long duty day; our bells to the flight attendants; re-route to a point not in our route; use of wing and Engine anti-ice; heavy rain during descent so continuous ignition was set; multiple small step downs from ATC; VNAV limitation; all of them occurring often simultaneously. We; as crew; came together and managed all threats that were thrown at us as best we could to bring the airplane safely to the ground.I will; from now on; better prioritize on the stuff that I delegate and ask my crew to keep an eye on me and remind me of things that could make us incur a deviation like this one. Even though we all had our hands full; I should have asked someone for some sort of reminder about the transition level.
column123: At the conclusion of a long duty day and the second flight leg of the day; I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) en-route. This was my second leg as PM (6th leg as flight crew) in an international theater in nearly 3 years. Prior to descent and during the approach briefing as well as once the relief pilots entered the cockpit; we discussed the lower altimeter setting of 0996mb and the associated procedure per Company limitations from not using VNAV when transitioning from QNH (Height Above Sea Level) to QNE or QNE to QNH when below 1006mb. We felt very prepared for the arrival and descent into ZZZ. The transition altitude of 7;000 ft. was also briefed however as we proceeded; we encountered winter weather requiring extra vigilance (icing conditions and heavy precipitation). ATC descended us in multiple small increments below 10;000 ft. but the last prior to this event was a descent to 5;000 ft. With the added attention to the weather and ensuring proper use of FLCH instead of VNAV during what should have been the transition; both the pilot flying; and the pilot monitoring did not switch the altimeters at the proper time to the local setting of 0996mb. Upon level-off at 5;000 ft.; ATC came over the radio to verify local altimeter of 996mb and stating the observation of being 400 ft. low. I quickly realized my altimeter was incorrect and took corrective action and confirmed the pilot flying did so as well both with the altimeter and the flight path. One of the observer pilots also confirmed and stated the MSA for situational awareness. The pilot flying disconnected the auto pilot and continued to intercept the localizer path while returning to the cleared altitude. The aircraft was hand flown to landing with no further incident.Multiple links in the chain led up to this event and while we thought we had sufficiently briefed the several unique environments (low altimeter/Company limitation; winter weather) we also were distracted by being vectored to a point not on an arrival or the approach expected. It only goes to show that even with the best preparation and briefing that events can change and compound quickly and while attention to detail is most crucial during all phases of flight; extra vigilance is needed for approach and arrival; especially in areas that have not been flown to in recent months or years. Ultimately; the crew worked together to safely return the aircraft to the desired state and ensured a lesson learned for the future when operating in areas with differing transition altitudes.

Soon mechanics were seen on both sides of the aircraft frantically giving the set parking brake signal. Both Captain and First Officer immediately and simultaneously pushed down brake pedals. Captain then set parking brake. Move team plugged in headset. Captain asked the question what happened? column121: Enroute ZZZ-San Salvador at FL390 we were able to ascertain through ATC Control that Runway 25 was in use and that we could expect to proceed via CAT VOR and execute the ILS Y 25. The FO (First Officer) was the Pilot Flying and thoroughly briefed the approach and his expectations for altitudes; automation modes and aircraft configuration throughout the approach. We were turned over to San Salvador Approach approximately 70 miles from the airport descending to FL200. San Salvador Approach cleared us direct CAT VOR; cross VOR above 5;000 [ft.] cleared ILS Y Runway 25. Both pilots confirmed clearance; altitudes and automation as we proceeded. As we neared CAT we were around 8;000 [ft.] at 240 kts.; still on the VNAV path. Although the FMC appeared to like the profile we both agreed it was time to slow down to meet the briefed approach profile. The FO selected vertical speed and dialed the speed back in the MCP window. With the selected vertical speed we weren't slowing down so I recommended Level Change. We slowed; configured and continued the approach passing CAT VOR. I set 2;500 [ft.] in the altitude window to fly outbound from the VOR as we completed the landing checklist. Once crossing the fix at [8.0 nm] we turned inbound via LNAV and set the FAF crossing altitude of 1;600 [ft.]; approach mode selected. We were in VFR conditions with the airport in sight on my side of the aircraft. As we turned towards the airport and descended I noticed we seemed low since we were more than 8 miles away and below the glide path. I looked back at the FMC and noticed fix [7.8 nm] with a crossing altitude of 2;500 [ft]. Shortly afterwards ATC asked what our altitude was and I replied 1;600 [ft.]. At that point both the FO and I realized we had missed [7.8 nm] on the procedure and should have crossed it at 2;500 [ft.]. [7.8 nm] is not clearly depicted on the approach plate with a crossing altitude nor is there an altitude depicted for the turn inbound. Also; we flew the procedure properly if the automation was in VNAV; but it wasn't. Although it was nighttime we were in VFR conditions with the airport in sight throughout the procedure. No GPWS cautions. At no time did I feel the procedure unsafe.
column123: I was the PF.  CENAMER approach cleared us to descend out of FL390 to FL 200.  We were expecting the ILSY Rwy 25.  We briefed the approach thoroughly and I explained I would stay in VNAV until lined up on final approach where I would select APP for the ILS.   Well above FL200; we were handed off to ElSal approach.  They told us to proceed to CAT VOR and cleared us for a full approach ILS Y Rwy 25 approach with procedure turn.  HOWEVER; we were high before arriving at CAT so I selected to use vertical speed and open the speed window to control speed.  The CAPT suggested I use LVL CHG instead since it would do a better job getting down and controlling speed.  I did so; while  flaps and gear helped slow us.  I was still well above 3500'; over the VOR beginning the procedure turn outbound to D8.0.  Still in LVL CHG; We were able to fully configure and be on the VNAV PATH at 2500' at D8.0.  We completed the LANDING CHECKLIST.  At this point we had the airport in sight and never lost contact the whole time.  We were both using TERR MODE for obstacle clearance.  After passing D8.0 I asked the CAPT to select the next lower altitude of 1600' as depicted on the approach chart; and he did so.  In my haste to get at the correct altitude; slow down and  configure for landing; I did not  realize I had not reselected VNAV.  The autopilot descended us to 1600' as we turned toward final.  We crossed D7.8 at 1600' vice 2500'..  There was no GPWS warning and we had the airport in sight the whole time.  On final approach I selected APP and we noticed we looked low and at the same time; the control tower queried us about our altitude.  That was when we noticed our error but were already capturing the glideslope at that time.  We continued the approach; landed safely and taxied to our gate without further incident.

column121: During the boarding of [Aircraft X] ZZZ - ZZZ1; I noticed a message on [Software] from the gate agent to station operations to inform the ramp personnel that there was a 'motorized wheelchair' on the jet bridge to be loaded onto the aircraft. I made a note to make sure we were provided notification of the wheel chair and when it did not come through the automated weight and balance data I asked the ramp lead. He just told me that it was 'very light' so he scanned it as a normal bag. I asked him if it was electric and if it had a battery and he said he did not know. He did not understand why I needed to know so after explaining that it was Dangerous Goods and required notification; he went to check it. I decided to go down with him to the cargo bin to make sure he knew what we needed. When he went in the cargo bin there was not a belt loader available so I was not able to also get in; and it was surrounded by bags so I was not able to see the base of it myself. He looked for several minutes; then informed me that it was 'not electric' and had 'no battery or electric parts' at all. I clarified this with him multiple times; both while standing at the cargo bin and also over the headset in the cockpit. After the flight was complete; we saw the agents in ZZZ1 unload it and the passenger get on it. I asked her if it was motorized and she said that it was. I asked her what type of battery it had and she said it was lithium ion and it was removable. She also showed me exactly where the battery was and how it could be removed. She also said that someone; it was unclear who and whether or not it was a [Company] employee; told her not to 'give too much information' during her check in process or she might have trouble flying with it. She couldn't remember if she had told the agent if it was a lithium ion battery. Regardless; multiple employees should have been able to figure out along the chain that it was motorized somehow; which meant it had to be electric.The cause was the ramp's misunderstanding of our DG (Dangerous Goods) policies and not being able to identify DG loaded on the aircraft; as well as possibly the passenger not reporting it as DG during check in.This is now the second time I have had an undeclared lithium ion wheelchair carried in the cargo bin in the past year and a half; which is indicative that this may be a larger issue than just one single missed item. Also; given that the ramp lead had no idea that electric wheelchair batteries had to be declared; it is impossible to know how many other events have happened where we simply didn't see the passenger after the flight.

column121: While approaching MCO Gate XXX to park the aircraft; we noticed that the Marshaller had two wands that were flickering on/off. Neither the left and right Wing Walker's had lighted wands.  I stopped the aircraft; set the parking brake; made a radio call to MCO Operations asking for six lighted wands (two for the Marshaller; two for the left Wing Walker; and two for the right Wing Walker). One of the supervisors saw that the wands being used by the Marshaller were flickering on/off.  One of the Ramp Supervisors took one of the inoperative wands from the Marshaller and discarded it by throwing it across the ramp I spoke to the two Ramp Supervisors; and they explained the following:1. This situation happens all the time in MCO where the safety equipment (lighted wands) do not work properly at night.2. If we go to an adjacent gate to obtain wands; there is a 50/50 chance that we will find lighted wands that work (all the time; not just tonight).3. There is no manager on duty tonight.  All managers left for home earlier in the evening.  The managers do not preflight the equipment to ensure it is working properly and ensure that we have adequate numbers of lighted wands before the managers go home for the night (ongoing issue).  4. We have communicated the problems about the safety equipment not operating properly many times to our managers; and nothing ever happens to fix the problem.5. Other pilots have mentioned the same concern about lack of operating safety equipment to MCO Leadership and still nothing improves.6. One Ramp Supervisor explained that he has worked at four different (Company) Stations.  He said that MCO is by far the least prepared with ramp equipment; safety equipment; etc.  The (Company) VP of Ground Operations needs to ensure that all stations have adequate safety equipment and that it is used consistently when required.  The MCO Station Manager needs to get involved and ensure his/her (Company) Ground Operations Team has an adequate amount of properly working lighted wands every evening before the Ramp and Operations Managers retire for the evening.  The ramp agents need to be trained that the use of the lighted wands is mandatory to ensure the aircraft arriving at night can be safely parked in the safety zone.  No exceptions!

column121: While on approach into CHO we were being vectored by Potomac Approach on frequency 126.4. We were on a right downwind being vectored for the ILS Runway 03. It was IMC conditions with light to moderate rime ice accumulating on the aircraft. At 3;000 ft. MSL we were given a right turn; a base turn; toward the final for Runway 03. We were just outside; south of the fix WULDU. I noticed were getting close to the localizer course for the final approach; and Potomac had not issued a turn for us to intercept the approach. I prompted Potomac approach and tried to establish communication. There was no answer on 126.4. I prompted again; and still there was no answer from Potomac. At this time we crossed over the localizer course without a turn to intercept given from Potomac. I had guard (121.5) already tuned in on comm 2. I heard Potomac approach trying to hail us on 121.5 on guard and advised us to switch to frequency 132.85. I switched to 132.85 and they gave us an immediate turn to the right to reestablish us on the localizer course. The coverage on 126.4 for the area was lost and I confirmed that with Potomac that we were trying to contact them. Apparently a Learjet overheard us trying to transmit on 126.4 and relayed it to Potomac. Once we re-established communication; Potomac gave us that right turn to intercept but it was 'too late'; The aircraft GPWS detected terrain and gave us a 'Terrain; Terrain' 'PULL UP' audio warning. I directed the First Officer to Climb the aircraft and disregard the instruction from Potomac Approach. We climbed up to 3;500 ft. MSL and got the aircraft clear of the terrain. I advise Potomac what had happened and that we were unable to intercept the approach from the vector that they gave us. Potomac than gave us more vectors to get re-established on the approach. From there we landed with no further issues. I conversed with Potomac about the drop in radio coverage on frequency 126.4. They agreed and confirmed that they could not hear us and we could not hear them on 126.4.[Problem was identified by] flight crew scan. No communication from ATC have prompting them several times. Having Guard (121.5) on comm 2 and have our audio on to re-establish communication. Being aware of the terrain in the area and seeing the aircraft GPS position on The Jepp charts. [Cause was] loss of two-way communication on 126.4 between our aircraft and Potomac approach lead us to not receiving an instruction to intercept the localizer course. Without that instruction we continued on our heading and had to re-establish communication via guard and switch to a different frequency that has radio coverage in the area. All of this lead to vectors in an area with terrain and caused us to be in a position where the aircraft GPWS was activated. [We] contacted ATC. Followed the aircraft GWPS system and climbed to avoid terrain. Advised ATC that we were responding to a GWPS annunciation. [Suggest] better radio coverage equipment is needed for the area around CHO. Suggest the importance of ALWAYS monitoring 121.5 on Comm 2 for flight crews.

column121: On the ZZZZZ6 we were told to level at 7;000 feet for traffic. This was my 3rd trip on IOE and was practicing hand flying the departure. It was turbulent and we were in and out of IMC. Since we were extremely light due to light loads we were climbing at an extremely fast vertical speed. Passing through 6;000 I announced that I was going to use TCS to reduce the rate of climb to about 1;000 since there was traffic above and I wanted to avoid a RA. I corrected the VS to about 1;000 ft/min. I was not quick enough to override and reduce the autothrottles to avoid increasing airspeed. The airspeed quickly and momentarily increased to 270 knots as we were leveling at 7;000 feet. I reduced the autothrottles too late and while reducing them altitude deviated by 140 feet high. Both deviations were short and immediately corrected. Nothing was mentioned by ATC. We were later given higher once the traffic passed. The combination of hand flying in turbulent conditions in IMC and leveling at a low altitude with light loads was a recipe for distraction and error to occur. I could have eliminated some of these variables by engaging autopilot earlier or reducing autothrottles quicker. The CA and I debriefed and talked through what led to the event and how to prevent it in the future.I learned that when possible reduce extra variables that could lead to an error. I am new to flying with the company and new procedures; was hand flying in turbulent conditions and IMC; light loads with good performance; and was given a low level off. That is a lot of variables at once and the ones that I could control are the earlier use of automation to help alleviation some of the task saturation. Hand flying in turbulent conditions and maintaining altitude can be difficult and the autopilot can alleviate and sometimes do a better job to avoid deviations. Additionally I learned not to lag on overriding the autothrottles when using in FLCH mode. From this experience I feel that I can better identify and evaluate a handful of risks in a certain situation and will take prompt action to reduce these risks in a timely manner. The CA and I had a productive debrief and agreed on what variables led to the deviation and how to prevent in the future.

column121: On a descent into DEN; we were cleared to descend via the CLASH 3 Arrival. I confirmed that the final altitude was 9;000 ft. and selected it in the altitude window. About 10 miles from EVRLY; we experienced wake turbulence for about five seconds; and then experienced it again. I selected Vertical Speed and leveled off the descent to get above the wake turbulence. After we were clear of the wake turbulence; I selected a 2;000 FPM descent to get back on my vertical path. At that time; we were told to switch to Denver Approach. Upon checking in with Denver Approach they changed our runway to 35L. At this point I was concerned about changing the approach in the FMC. I forgot to re-engage the VNAV. Because I forgot to re-engage the VNAV; the aircraft did not slow down to 250 kts for EVRLY. The aircraft also continued a descent below 12;000 feet.; which was the lowest altitude at TWNSN. The aircraft continue to descend until I notice the deviation. By this time I was leveling at 10;000 feet. and was below the 11;000 feet. altitude required for PNBAL. ATC advised me to slow the 210 knots; and gave me a vector for the final approach to Runway 35L. They also gave me a descent to 9;000 feet. The rest of the arrival went as planned.
column125: B737 Captain reported distractions from a wake turbulence encounter on arrival into DEN contributed to altitude and speed deviations.

column121: The deicing crew at ZZZ briefed myself and the First Officer (F/O) where the deicing was going to take place and we requested FULL AIRCRAFT DEICE with Type 1 and WINGS AND TAIL ANTI ICE with Type 4. After we pushed back and parking brake was set; the QRH was complied with for configuring the airplane for deicing as instructed by the deicing crew. The ice-truck drove past the nose to the left side and disappeared. Approximately; 15 minutes later; the truck rolled up from the right side and told us over the radio that the deicing was completed without giving us the pertinent data that we need like the type of fluid used for the deice and anti-ice. Moreover; we were not given the start time for the anti-icing. The first officer had to ask them for the information even to the point of getting clarification for the type 4 used in the anti-icing. This baffled us! As we tried to figure out what was going on; I asked my F/O if he had heard the sound of the spraying on the fuselage. He said no he really didn't hear it and I didn't hear it. So just to make sure; I asked the F/O to verbally ask if Type 1 was WHOLE FUSELAGE and TYPE 4 FOR WINGS AND TAIL; iceman said YES!  So we got the holdover time; and stated to taxi out but I had my doubt on what was done. As I was telling the F/O that we will need to pullover and do a pre-takeoff check by going in to the cabin to inspect at least the wings; we got a call from the flight attendants telling us that the windows were still glazed over with ice.I decided to return to the gate to do another walk around inspection. When we arrived at the gate at my F/O did the second walk around inspection; he came back angry and furious; and rightly so because the airplane was still ENCASED IN ICE! I too was very angry with the UNSAFE Job the iceman did for us and LIED about it. And please note that there was NO precipitation since we arrived at the airport.
column123: During the night in ZZZ they had gotten freezing rain; so when we got to the airplane (10 minutes before departure due to the road conditions) we already knew that we had to deice; which my walk around affirmed that. At this point everything was pretty normal except for the fact we were late; (we did not rush nor did I feel rushed) and we had to deice. We ran all checklists and pushed back; we ran the QRH for de-icing and called OPS for deicing/ anti icing; and my exact verbiage was 'parking brake set aircraft configured for de-icing full body wings and tail Type I and wings and tail Type IV' when they were done which looking back; it didn't seem to have taken the usual amount of time; it was way shorter! We finished up with the QRH; started the engines; ran the checklists and started to taxi; to which we may have taxied 100 yards when the FAs (Flight Attendants) called and said that the windows in the back were covered in ice; the CA (Captain) was also listening to this; I than told ground that we needed to stop and work a problem; he stopped the airplane and we discussed the issue and both determined we CANNOT takeoff with ice on the airplane; we both made the decision to gate return and inspect the airplane; we got to the gate ran the parking checklist and they brought up the Jetway; I exited the airplane to do another walk around and discovered the airplane still covered in ice! When I returned to the Jetway the CA was talking to the station manager; I shared what I had seen on the walk around and returned to the flight deck and re-repaired the aircraft for departure; I was not part of the discussion with the station manager or the Chief Pilot; I was briefed by the CA as to what each had said; and the thing that gets me the most is that the Chief Pilot was making excuses for ZZZ Operations; as they 'don't do it very often'! Come to find out the person spraying our aircraft was the stations de-icing trainer!! After all the decisions and a call to dispatch for a new flight plan we pushed back again ran checklists; got property de-iced ( we think and hope) and departed about two and a half hours late for a uneventful rest of the flight.

column121: We were being vectored from the northwest to the ILS approach and descending to 2;000 ft. when Tower asked if we had the airport in sight. This was my first time in ZZZ and although I thought I saw the airport I was not in a hurry to call it in sight; just to be sure. I verbalized that with the First Officer but he had been there before and was comfortable calling the airport in sight; so I did. Our initial vector would have taken us just outside the Final Approach Fix. However; when Tower issued clearance for the Visual Approach; the First Officer turned to a heading that would take us inside the Final Approach Fix. At the same time; he continued to descend while configuring with flaps (I think at either 10 or 15) and landing gear; and the speed brake extended. As the descent continued; Tower issued an 'Altitude Alert' and instructed us to adjust immediately. I cannot remember the exact verbiage; but there was a mention of our altitude being 1;200 ft. and perhaps something about 'minimum vectoring altitude.' The First Officer immediately adjusted his attitude to level off at around 1;200 ft. and continued to fly towards the runway center line. We were approximately abeam the Final Approach Fix at this point. He then asked for more flaps; ultimately Flaps 30; for the landing. I realized at about that point that he still had the speed brake extended and told him. He immediately stowed the speed brake and intercepted the visual glide path to the runway. I think he asked me at about that point if I was okay to continue. He was on the glide path and stabilized; so I said 'yes.'On landing rollout I noticed what sounded like an open microphone on the Tower frequency. Since there didn't seem to be any other aircraft on the frequency; I suspected it was coming from our aircraft. The Tower made a broadcast to all stations on the frequency that they were broadcasting on an active ATC radio frequency; and that they should cease immediately. When I made the '80 kts.' call out on landing roll; I heard myself over the radio. That confirmed that the First Officer was holding down the microphone button in his grip on the yoke. As soon as he loosened his grip; the transmission stopped.
column123: I was the pilot flying. Based on the weather reported we briefed the RNAV Arrival to be followed by the ILS Approach. We made special note that we were not to utilize the Autothrottle for the approach due to MEL(Minimum Equipment List) restriction. The arrival went as planned until we were given a vector off the arrival and then direct to the Final Approach Fix and a descent to 2;000 ft. As we were a bit high and fast; the speed brake was being utilized to expedite descent. While proceeding to the Final Approach Fix; the weather was acceptable to proceed visually so we reported field in sight and were cleared for the Visual Approach. Due to the high intercept angle to the Final Approach Fix I turned to establish a more acceptable intercept angle to capture the localizer. My perception looking outside was that we were quite high so asked the Pilot Monitoring to set Touchdown Zone Elevation. I failed to engage Vertical Nav for better situational awareness in relation to my vertical path and relied solely on the visual sight picture until on final. While on a dogleg to final we received an ATC Altitude warning alert telling us that we were below the sector altitude. We were approximately 1;100 ft. just abeam of the Final Approach Fix on a dogleg to final. I then stopped the descent until approaching final approach course and engaging Approach mode for glideslope capture. Continued the Visual Approach to a landing.

column121: We had been vectored off of the WAZKO1 RNAV Arrival toward the final approach course for the RNAV Runway 4 at ELP. We broke out of the overcast around 9;000 ft. and were approaching KANTR at 7;500 feet. There was a lot of ambient light from the city below and the reflection of that light from the overcast above as well as the fresh layer of snow on the surface. Approach cleared us for the approach and gave us 'Direct KANTR; Maintain 7;200 ft. until KANTR;' which I read back; with an emphasis on the '200'. The FO (PF) selected vertical speed mode after I set 7;200 ft. in the altitude preselector and called '7;200 ft. set!'. The published altitude at KANTR is 7;500 feet; which is located above terrain at 5;851 ft. We leveled at 7;200 ft. and she called for Flaps 18; and we joined the final approach course with the runway; and the terrain below in sight since descending out of 9;000 ft. Just then the GPWS System chimed in with 'Terrain! Pull Up!'. The FO dutifully disconnected the autopilot and I told her NOT to go around; as we were on a published segment of the final approach in good VMC (ELP was reporting 10 SM Vis) and I had the terrain in sight the whole time. We were not descending; and we had been level for some time. We landed without incident and taxied to our gate. Upon docking; I asked Ground for the phone number to the folks at approach control. The fellow who answered offered that he was indeed the Controller. I told him what had happened and he said that it was not at all uncommon; and that 7;200 ft. was their Minimum Vectoring Altitude in that sector. I told him that I would be filing a report with respect to the incident; for his own information.If there are other similar incidents here a communique should be distributed to the pilot group.
column125: Air carrier Captain reported GPWS Terrain warning while following ATC clearance at Minimum Vectoring Altitude during approach to ELP airport.

column121: Significant freezing rain event the day of this flight led to 1/4 to 1/2 inch clear ice covering the entire aircraft. There was no attempt to de-ice the aircraft prior to the crew arriving for preflight. The engine inlets needed to be de-iced prior to block out so that we could start the engines after block out. This de-icing of the inlets took a considerable amount of time due to the significant accumulation of ice in the bottom of the fan section of both engines. By the time we were able to block out (2h 39min late) and taxi to the remote de-ice pad A; a short distance from our ramp; the de-ice trucks had run out of fluid and trucks needed to also be refueled. Another significant delay ensued. Almost an hour after block out; de-icing began. The entire airplane was de-iced with Type I fluid since there was no precipitation falling. Aircraft was fully de-iced and inspected by the de-ice team. We then proceeded to our departure runway and prepared for takeoff. The reason for this safety report became clear as soon as we began the initial climb segment immediately after takeoff. We began shedding ice from the entire fuselage and this shedding continued through 12;000 ft.; approximately 7-10 minutes after takeoff. All four crew members could hear the ice departing the aircraft and felt the airframe vibrations as large chunks of ice tumbled down the length of the fuselage. All four crew members each have 20-30 years of aviation experience; and no one had ever experienced anything like it. In my 30 plus years of heavy transport category aircraft operation I have never experienced this kind of ice shedding event. I believe that the de-ice procedure was completely ineffective for this amount of clear ice that covered the entire aircraft. With that amount ice being shed from the aircraft for that long; we had a significant amount of Ice still adhering to the airframe when we took off. The engine vibration was well within limits even during the climb out and so the crew chose to continue the flight. I was concerned about airframe damage from that amount of ice departing the aircraft; and because of that concern; I recorded an AML entry asking that the aircraft be inspected for damage after arrival in ZZZZ. [Cause was] inadequate de-icing for the amount of clear ice that was adhering to the airframe. Also the de-ice crew was possibly unable to see the ice after de-icing; since it was clear ice and fully covering the aircraft; and the airplane was still wet from the de-icing fluid used. [Suggest] re-evaluate the process of de-icing when so much clear ice is adhering to the airframe.
column125: Air Carrier Captain reported inadequate deicing procedures resulted in departure with significant airframe icing.

column121: Upon completion of work on the aircraft; we boxed up our three pieces of tooling with no HAZMAT to return with us on the first ZZZ1 flight.  We attached the SLI (Shipper's Letter of Instructions) labels as required and moved them to the far left of the baggage cart that we were provided. We then moved the three hard containers with visible HAZMAT labels and no return paperwork on them to the far right of the baggage cart. We then asked her if we needed to move the cart to a secure area and she said to leave it where it was.  We again; reiterated the importance of making sure the HAZMAT items were not shipped with our tooling; and asked her to make sure and leave a turnover if she was not going to be available in the morning. We still had to scan paperwork to Maintenance Control; and I failed to give her a copy of step 3A after confirmation from Maintenance Control that they received all documents.  After going through security in the morning we asked the Operations Agent on the ZZZ1 flight to confirm that our three boxes of tooling and only our three boxes of tooling were on the plane.  Due to TSA requirements; we are unable to go down to the ramp to confirm or review shipping procedures once we have been screened.
