column121: Upon pushback from ZZZ Gate 1; it was soon apparent the Pushback Crew was experiencing a problem. They said nothing but it was increasingly clear the Tug was sliding as well as the aircraft not proceeding in a direction I would expect. I tried asking the Driver if there was a problem but did not receive an answer via wireless headset. When his Tug was starting to jackknife; I decided to use my brakes to stop the aircraft. By this time; the Tug came very close to impacting the aircraft on my side. I later learned that his headset was working; but he was trying to talk to the other Ramp Agents instead and not me. I also believe he was cognitively overwhelmed with the unexpected situation as that same phenomena (not responding to me) continued later when we attempted to another push after re-attaching the tow bar/Tug. The First Officer was also adding his input; which was not helping the situation with communication. It was a communications mess. We called the station to inform them of the situation and eventually a Ramp Supervisor came out and took over. We then discussed the option of attempting to move the aircraft to another part of the ramp where it was known to be less than nil braking. Going back to the same gate would only have been to an area of known poor/nil control. We eventually got to an area where the Ramp Agents could safely walk and feel that the ramp was in better condition and where other aircraft were not experiencing any problems.When I landed approximately an hour prior in a different aircraft; my taxi to Gate 2 took me to an area where I lost all steering and braking control for about five seconds. We immediately notified this on Ops frequency; and at least one other Crew stated they experienced the same. Luckily; we slid to an area where I regained control and then carefully proceeded to the gate when the aircraft performed adequately. I then called Dispatch via my cell phone immediately after block in. He said he would pass it on to the supervisor; but I did not hear any apparent immediate concern. Instead; he said I needed to alert the Station; as it is their job to manage that info (I was really puzzled that our Dispatch gave me that answer). I eventually found the Ops Agent and wanted to make sure the Station had this information; as I was very concerned that others could experience worse.Q1: What does it take for a Pilot to state before any real concern is expressed by those managing our operation? Was poor or nil braking not a big enough concern?Q2: Why had nothing been done to correct the situation or at least alert other Crews that some areas were okay but others were NIL? Or stop the operation?Q3: Why would a Push Crew try to fix this problem without getting any other assistance or guidance? I could see they were guessing and even willing to just leave us there as they told us to try to taxi out of it. They even tried to tow us forward on the re-attempt with our engines running. They were completely overwhelmed; which gave me even greater concern.Q4: As Crews; we have no accurate resources (ZZZ is a joke as it is often old and/or inaccurate) to tell us real time conditions on other parts of the airport other than asking Ground Control (which I did). I was concerned that everything was starting to freeze over; and I did not want to the PIREP stating I was in NIL or off the taxiway later on. Without having routine freezing rain experience; how can I know how quickly conditions can go from good to bad?Q5: What does it take for a pause or stop in our operation? Damage? Injury? Taxiway departure? It seems like we just continue pushing with no apparent oversight. That is not a comforting feeling nor does it give me much confidence our system has mechanisms to protect me before getting in a terrible spot.I would appreciate answers to these questions and would like to know if anyone in Headquarters feels this situation was acceptable or not?

column121: Pushed away from gate. Started taxing in ZZZ alley when I got a call from #1 Flight Attendant; (FA); that there were First Class; FC; passengers that were not wearing face coverings after being told to wear them by the FAs. Stopped the aircraft and made a very 'To the point' PA that any non-compliance with Flight Attendant instructions; particularly pertaining to facial coverings; would have 'un-favorable' consequences. I had already made it clear that facial coverings were required while on-board during my 'welcome aboard' PA. Conferred with FAs that my second PA was successful; and we continued taxi and takeoff. Once established in cruise; the FAs informed me that they were having problems with FC passengers willfully being non-compliant regarding wearing a facial covering after being advised as such multiple times by at least 2 different FAs. My FAs had even switched working positions in order to try to de-escalate the situation and convince the passengers to comply. I commenced communication with Dispatch and relayed the situation with advisement to contact customer representatives. Shortly thereafter; due not only to non-mask wearing; but also; disruptive behavior by passengers requested to be re-seated in Main Cabin. I further relayed this information to Dispatch. It was at this point the FAs gave the notification of passenger misconduct warning. Shortly thereafter passenger started harassing my FAs with constant cornering them in the FC galley and demanding trivial items. At this point; even after a tremendous amount of patience; de-escalation attempts and warnings by the FAs; and with building harassment and aggressiveness being demonstrated by passengers; I notified Dispatch that we would be diverting to ZZZ1. We landed at ZZZ1 non-eventfully; without being overweight and without declaring an emergency. Passengers were removed from the aircraft. We departed ZZZ1 and arrived in ZZZZ uneventfully. Please allow me to acknowledge my FAs for their display of 'Consummate Professionalism' during this flight. They were tireless in their attempts to de-escalate the situation in hopes of precluding a diversion. I would also like to acknowledge the support of Dispatch and company as reflective of the number of communications that were made prior to our diversion. And last; but certainly not least; I would like to acknowledge the expert airmanship demonstrated by my First Officer during our extremely busy diversion as well as throughout the rest of a very long day. Should you need additional information from me regarding this diversion; please don't hesitate to contact me.

column121: A321 TOGA (takeoff/go-around switch) takeoff with APU on. Pouring rain. While climbing through approx 18;000 ft; first one; then other flight attendants called to say they smelled a burning rubber smell in cabin but could not see smoke. Passengers were also complaining. We smelled deice fluid in cockpit (plane had flown from ZZZ1 to ZZZ); but otherwise we kept talking with them to see if it would dissipate. While still discussing a return to ZZZ; first one; then two passengers had trouble breathing and the flight attendants made a PA for a doctor on board. At this point we felt we needed to return to ZZZ for an overweight landing. We notified and coordinated with ATC; Dispatch; and ZZZ OPS to return and have paramedics at the gate. The cause was unknown; but aircraft did have an MEL for avionics cooling extract fan that required it to remain in override. Perhaps this could have contributed to burning smell or a different load on air conditioning.
column123: The Captain (CA) and I noticed a smell in the flight deck while in the climb; roughly around 10;000 feet.  The FAs (flight attendants) called climbing through flight level 180 stating they smell an odor in the cabin.  The FAs also stated some passengers were complaining about the odor.   The Captain requested the flight attendants to call back in 10 minutes and state if the smell is dissipating.  The FAs call back shortly stating several passengers are having difficulty breathing.  At that time the Captain made the decision to return to the ZZZ.  I took over as Pilot Flying and ATC communications. I requested to return to the ZZZ and notified ATC for an overweight landing.  At that time the aircraft weighed roughly 180;000 lbs.  The CA took over Pilot Flying on the arrival shortly before joining the approach to runway.  The aircraft weighed approximately 177;000 lbs on landing.  When we arrived at the gate paramedics attended to several passengers who were having difficulties breathing. [Possible cause or related issue]; we were relatively heavy; had a slight tailwind and the runway was wet.  The TPS (takeoff performance system) called for config 2; TOGO; APU OFF.  As a measure of safety the CA decided to leave the APU and APU bleeds on.  I concurred.  The aircraft's extract fan was also MEL'd (MEL 21-05a).  The CA and I both felt the odor mostly resembled anti-icing fluid.  Though we also discussed the possibly the inoperative extract fan or the APU usage on takeoff was the cause of the odor.  But mostly we thought it was anti-icing fluid.  Once we realized passengers and the cabin crew were being affected the decision was made to return to ZZZ which resulted in an overweight landing.

column121: At 800 feet AGL; clicked autopilot off for a visual landing. At 500 ft.; FO called 'Stable; cleared to land Runway XX Center.' I replied 'Landing.' Between 500 and 400 feet AGL tried to make small lateral correction with aileron but aileron movement was limited. Used a touch of rudder for correction. Clicked autopilot button again and crossed checked then confirmed that 'Flight Director' was displayed in PFD. Landed uneventfully but elevator movement was very heavy in flare. After landing at taxi speed; I tried to move the yoke left and right and there was very limited movement. The First Officer tried as well with the same result. We checked the Flight Control and Hydraulic Displays and both were normal.I considered a go-around but quickly [determined] a go around would be extremely difficult with big power changes and limited flight control capability. The flight path was set up to touch down in the landing zone on speed so I elected to land.Unsure what caused the flight controls to be limited. After landing; I debriefed Maintenance in the cockpit and put a detailed write up in the logbook.

column121: On initial climbout of ZZZ off Runway XXC we experienced loss of power shortly after passing 400 feet and received the 'Landing gear' aural warning. I double checked the gear handle and verified gear position; then verified N1 rollback; momentarily thinking we had dual engine failure. FO exclaimed startle; I replied 'fly the plane'. FO disconnected auto throttle; brought the thrust back up to takeoff position. We momentarily lost altitude and airspeed as Startle and surprise delayed our recognition slightly. Timing of the event was before flap retraction so we were near flap over speed during recognition and recovery; I said 'watch the speed pitch up pitch up' until flaps were retracted. FO later indicated his flight director was not giving correct indications for phase of flight. FO was able to recognize and manually control the aircraft; resuming normal climb out. Once the aircraft was under control; auto pilot and auto throttle engaged normally and no further anomalies were experienced.Unknown; weather was stormy; with moderate turbulence and lightning flashes in vicinity; in full IMC.We teach hand on thrust levers at all times during arrival and landing phase; but not during takeoff...had the FO had physical contact with the thrust levers during the climb; the AT retarding would have been instantly detected. I recommend the same procedure is taught for takeoff as is for landing...one hand on the thrust levers.
column123: After checking everything was normal we lined up on runway XXC in ZZZ. We verified our automation was in the correct mode including TO; ROLL; and FLCH were verified on our FMA as well as the crosshair flight director was up. As I advanced thrust the auto throttles took and the captain confirmed that ATTCS armed and we had normal TO thrust. at 80 knots while verifying the speed I saw the AT were in their normal HOLD mode. At this point everything was completely normal. When I went to rotate and was transitioning in the instruments I noticed that the FD had switched during the roll to the diamond mode which is supposed to happen at 1000'AGL. (Latter the captain confirmed that there's was normal). I had a normal rotation and pitched towards a normal takeoff attitude disregarding the flight director. At approximately 400 AGL the auto throttles commanded idle thrust suddenly. The startle and surprise nature of this took a second to process where we lost approximately 50 feet. At this point I disconnected the auto throttles and set climb power. The automation was still not working correctly including the flight director. Once we climbed through sterile we turned on the auto-throttles and they worked throughout the flight but we watched them very carefully and called Maintenance writing up the experience on the ground. The cause is unknown. before Takeoff we both verified we were in the correct automation modes. Once in cruise flight we verified all out take-off date and departure limits were set correctly and they were. Contributing factors to the loss of altitude was the thunderstorms in the vicinity; night; and moderate turbulence. More effective startle and surprise training in the sims. We are taught to keep both hands on the yoke throughout departure I think at 400 feet though 10;000 we should be guarding the thrust levers like we do on approach to landing.

column121: Upon arrival at ZZZ Maintenance notified us that there were multiple damaged fan blades in the number 1 engine. While we do not know when or how this occurred; we can only guess that it was due to snow/ice ingestion on takeoff roll; improper de-icing and inspection of engine inlets prior to engine start; or de-icing prior to takeoff. While there was no active precipitation; upon arrival at the aircraft; the crew noted snow and ice on the aircraft to include in the engine inlets. Per [company] procedures; after the doors were closed; before blockout; the crew call Ramp to have engines cleared. The clearing crew showed up. The Tug Driver noted them moving around the aircraft and appeared to be clearing engines. They left shortly thereafter; and we confirmed with Ramp Tower that the clearing and inspection had been logged complete. After push back onto taxi; we noted that the taxi lane had not been completely plowed. There was a large snow berm; approximately 2 ft. high about 10 ft. left of centerline; which converged toward centerline all the way until Taxiway XX. After some discussion with Tower and the Pushback Crew; we opted to have plows come and clear an area in front of us; that they could pull us to clear of the berm before engine start to avoid ingestion. Engine start was slow; even for Pratt & Whitney; but no starter or engine limitations were exceeded. N1 started around 20-25%; well below the 40% limit. After engine start anti-ice was turned on due to temp/dew point spread. We taxied on cleared pavement to the de-ice area. The taxi took less than 15 minutes so no engine clearing was used. During de-ice we noticed B777 push back out of a gate on [taxiway XX]. It was pushed back through a berm of snow and ice. After de-ice we taxied and took off after this B777. It is possible that the B777 had some snow/ice on its trucks that was deposited on the runway on takeoff. From de-ice; we taxied to Runway XX. The turn from Taxiway XY onto Taxiway XZ could have been cleared of snow better; but the turn was made using minimal thrust. It is possible that some compact snow or ice was ingested here; however; once cleared for takeoff; we did a 30 second engine clearing procedure and all engine instruments appeared normal. After takeoff; the Captain mentioned a rumble; which sounded like it was coming from a pack. It was faint enough; that we didn't feel it was an issue; as all packs checked out normal. Later on climb out the number 3 engine EVM fluctuated up to 5.0; then back down to normal ranges only slightly above the other two engines. The captain sent a message to [Operations} asking about engine telemetry; and we were advised it was good; so we decided to press on.

column121: This safety concern occurred on two flights. Same aircraft and same exact routing and runways for departure (7L) and arrival (24R). The routing was the 7L.KEENS2.MESSI ESTWD.HLYWD1.24R. The First Officer briefed all of the points; speeds; and altitudes on the SID via the FMC CDU and I confirmed them on my EFB. We completed the Before Start Origination checklist; received performance takeoff data; and completed the Before Push checklist with no issues. After pushback and engine start; we started to taxi away and when I placed the LEGS Page up on my CDU there was now a discontinuity after the first departure point; and the next point. We corrected the situation by re-selecting the SID; transition; and departure Runway 7L; which removed the discontinuity. That situation by itself would be a little unusual; but as we flew back later on and the same issue occurred yet again it appears that there is a performance software issue that needs to be looked at. The Cost Index was 15 on Flight X and 5 on Flight Y. I unfortunately did not reference the FMC software version. We had no discontinuity on our flight; so the issue could be departure related; the SID related; or performance software related. Bottom line is that there is an issue that might cause pilots to take off and soon afterward encounter a discontinuity on the route; causing a potential navigation error.Flight Ops needs to work with Dispatch and Maintenance to determine if certain weights; Cost Indexes; FMC software versions; SIDS; airports; etc; are causing a discontinuity after receiving performance takeoff data in this fleet or solely this particular aircraft.

We decided to level out at 6;000 feet MSL while we confirmed the situation and attempted to cycle the gear. Tower provided vectors and a climb to 9;000 feet; we initiated a go around over the threshold per ATC instructions and cleaned up the aircraft per SOP. The autoflight was re-engaged after the go around. During this time after the failure of subsequent attempts to cycle the gear and with the lever still down; we eventually got the L/G GEAR NOT DOWNLOCKED ECAM. The ECAM was run according to SOP by Captain [Name] while I flew the aircraft and handled radio calls. We [received priority]; stated our intention to return to land on Runway XYR and requested CFR (Crash Fire Rescue Equipment). Gravity extension was successful and we were vectored to the approach. Approach and landing were normal with the exception of the gear doors remaining open. We landed with 8000 lbs. of fuel. We stopped on the runway and Operations was standing by to tow the aircraft back to the gate.

column121: While on final approach the PF was having difficulty slowing the aircraft and continuing the descent. The headwind we had been fighting quickly turned to a crosswind. The PF elected to re-bug and use flaps 40 well above 1;000 feet. As the PF I selected the new flap setting in the FMC and verbally called out the Vref and target speeds. As we were slowing past our previous target speed the PF called for flaps 40. We had no amber band visible for flaps 40 placard speed; so I verified the placard; 162 knots; and selected the flaps seeing 158 knots and slowing on my tape. As I verified the speed brake was armed he again called for 40. The flaps were still at 30. At this point we were now below 1;000 feet but above 500 feet. We discussed the non-movement and load alleviation. As the PM; I suggested; pitch up and slow; the flaps moved to 40 as we suspected they would. The checklist was completed and we were able to be stable by 500 feet AGL; so we continued the landing. We did not observe any limitations being exceeded on the flaps or in procedure as the PM was able to manage the approach prior to the 500 foot gate.In discussing this event during our debrief we believe that we did meet our approach gate criteria. We were in our first 'heavy' approach in many months as the flight was full. The weight may have contributed. The wind was also a contributing factor as it shifted down the final enough that by the time we departed the traffic flow had reversed.Neither of us were averse to going around but it did not seem necessary in the moment as it seemed we met our criteria to continue. Having said that I'm certain eyes further from the instrument panel may have captured data we missed but I believe we trapped and corrected the situation.
column123: While on final approach I; PF; called for final landing flap (flaps 40) and flaps did not move to commanded position (they were at 30); despite being slower than max speed for flaps 40. Since we were within a few knots of max flaps 40 speed; I slowed further and flaps extended to commanded position. I believe the flap extension occurred right around 500 feet.  The final approach speed was within stabilized approach criteria and the outcome of the approach and landing were not in doubt. Landing was uneventful.We have been flying mostly empty airplanes for almost a year and this flight was almost completely full. I believe the higher landing weight coupled with a significant loss of headwind on final contributed to the airplane taking a while to slow down to an acceptable speed for final flaps. When I called for final flaps; we were 3-4 knots below the max flaps speed and I believe the aircraft's safety system was restricting flap movement until I was a little slower. As we return to Pre-COVID passenger loads; I will have to adjust lead time for decelerating the jet. Today was a good reminder.

column123: We commenced the boarding and Flight Attendant #2 and I walked to aft galley and both smelled a noxious odor. I called the Flight Attendant 1; three times and she in turn told the Captain. He said 'it is probably a leaky trash bag or rotten food.' Flight Attendant 2 called the Captain directly and he again blew us off. We had a deadheading pilot also go to cockpit to relay information and when he got back; he said the 'theory is that it is a leaky trash bag'. We had been on the aircraft for 4 hours prior to this event as we brought the aircraft in from ZZZ. The fumes were coming out of air vents in galley and aft lavs and was going into c zone. 33 minutes after we first notified Captain; at the end of boarding; he came to the back and said 'I don't smell anything; we are going to ZZZ1'. With that; he turned and walked back to the front. Yes; the fumes had just dissipated by that point; 33 minutes later. There was no interaction; NONE. He obviously did not care about the noxious fumes in the aft section of aircraft. For 33 minutes; he continued to disregard every attempt to tell him what was happening in the back. He's a Check Airman; really? He's supposed to be the best of the best. I felt like my safety was jeopardized and I would never feel safe flying with him again. What if I reported smoke; would he say it is stale cigarette smell on someone's shirt? The one important bit of information he might need might come from the most junior Flight Attendant or even a new hire. In this case he had 4 very senior Flight Attendants and disregarded all of us when we made 5 attempts to get his help in telling him about the noxious odors. Captain obviously needs some intense CRM training. Maybe giving a check ride to another pilot and trying to manage fume events are just too much for him. It obviously was.

column121: Aircraft X was an air return back into ZZZ; for the standby display cool fan malfunction causing the display screens to overheat. This aircraft was ferrying to ZZZ1 for a repair. During troubleshooting it was decided that the problem could be relays K7HK and K11HK in JB2. The relays were replaced per the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) CH24/ESPM (Electrical Standard Practices Manual) and did not fix the problem. The next likely part was the avionics cooling control panel; it was replaced per AMM CH21 and did fix the problem. Because I had removed JB2; a retest had to be performed per the AMM CH24. The first half of this complex task was done in the hangar. The second half requires the engines to be ran. Everything was checking out good per the AMM; until the final engine start. During the start sequence on the LH (Left Hand) engine everything seemed to be normal; then I received an APU Overtemp red warning message which distracted me from watching the LH engine parameters. After the APU Overtemp message cleared I noticed the LH engine ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) at 998 degrees. I immediately put the LH thrust lever to fuel cutoff and motored the engine until the ITT was below 120 degrees. The MDC (Maintenance Diagnostic Computer) engine exceedance history showed the LH engine to be at 1110 degrees for 10.6 seconds. This is the first time I have ever encountered 2 overtemp events or 2 red warning indications at the same time while working one of our aircraft. I was working hard to get this task done so the crew could move the aircraft yet that day; as they were standing by in the hangar to depart after repairs were completed. I must admit I did feel pressured and hurried; however I did complete the retest task per the AMM; with everything checking satisfactory. As for the engine hot start event; I really regret it happening. It seems like it was one of those situations that does not occur together all that often. I felt I was distracted and was task overloaded for maybe a second or two which played a factor in this unfortunate event.

column121: On the morning of an international departure that was scheduled to depart later that evening; the Captain emailed and informed both FOs of how the flight would be conducted in regard to face masks.  During the pre-flight phase; the #2 FO challenged the decision and said he was walking off the trip unless the Captain agreed to wear a mask whenever he was on the Flight Deck.  In an effort to maximize safety and also to address the #2 FO's concerns; the Captain offered the solution that he would wear a mask during cruise; whenever the #2 was performing his relief duties; but; with safety concerns about glasses fogging and hindered communications during critical phases of flight; said that #2 could sit in the cabin rest seat during those phases if it would make him more comfortable (since masks would not be worn).  The Captain believed this was 'legal;' since an #2 actually wasn't required by the FARs on the planned 6 hour and XX minutes flight and was also the safest option since; if the #2 dropped the trip; the flight would likely be sent un-augmented with zero inflight rest periods then available to the 'flying' pilots. The #2 agreed with this solution and the flight departed.Prior to the later descent; the #2 stated that he believed that an FAR's had been violated by him not being in the cockpit for takeoff.  He said that he would be in the cockpit for descent and Captain said he was welcome to be there but reiterated that masks would not be worn during critical phases of flight.  The #2 did then come up for the descent and landing.After the aircraft was parked and debrief conducted; #2 said he would be submitting a report over his belief that an FAR was violated by him not being in the cockpit for takeoff and departure.The Captain and #1 FO are not aware of any 'violations' of FAR's in this instance but decided to report the incident in case there's something they are not aware of.

column121: Dispatch notified us that the release was not signed at cruise.   I immediately realized he was correct.  I added 2000 pounds operational fuel on the way to the airport and discussed this with the crew.  I planned on signing the release and talking with the Dispatch in Operations (Ops); because this is one of the last places internationally that we still go to Ops.  The van takes us through security then to Ops then to the bottom of the jetbridge.  All 3 of us had done this recently and knew of no change and in fact the 10-7 page states that we are not allowed to go through the terminal.  However; upon reaching the airport the driver brings us to the terminal; stating that this is the new procedure.  We verified on our iPads and even called Ops to verify this change.  Indeed; due to COVID; we go through the terminal.  The security was extensive; overly extensive and time consuming.  The walk to the gate is long and although we hustled; we still arrived at the jet later than desired.  I called Dispatch for the brief once arriving to the cockpit and received a standard brief which included a new release; release 2 due to ZFW increase.  I agree that was okay; but after the call; we realized the 2000 pounds I had added via app was not added; so I called the Dispatch back.  The Fueler arrived during this call and he agreed to add the extra 2000 pounds for us and I told Dispatch it was done so no new paperwork was needed.   I wondered why the Dispatcher had not included the 2000 pounds. In retrospect I should have realized something was amiss; for example; the release not being signed.  We then had discussions with Ops regarding the extra 2000 pounds; but it was all resolved.  During this time; the FO saw the dispatch release; stated it was #2; but neither of us noticed it said 'not signed' at the top; only noted that it was release 2 and that we were all fit for duty.  We had the Oceanic checklist out and looked through it; but missed the dispatch release on it.  I have been signing the release lately enroute from the hotel to the airport since we never go to Ops anymore due to COVID; except today; since this is one of the few places that we do go to Ops.  However; apparently; we don't.  A note in the 10-7; an Ops alert; or something stating this would have been helpful.

column121: Normal takeoff and climb out. We went to FL400 for cruise altitude. We got to cruise; made our PA turned off the seatbelt sign. I was Pilot Monitoring. FO (First Officer) said;'uh oh we have a light on the HYD overhead.' I looked up and ENG2 engine driven pump said low pressure. I canceled the master caution and got out the QRH. Simple checklist; select the HYD pump switch to off. End of checklist. We pulled up the hydraulic display on the center screen. B system 106%; normal pressure. We started a what if dialogue. We agreed it was OK to continue with present condition. We looked up Loss of System B in QRH; and discussed it. We looked at flight plan divert circles and discussed scenarios. After 5-10 min the system B quantity started to decrease; slowly at first. I asked ATC for a descent to FL 320. Now the System B started to decrease rapidly. We knew we were about to loose Hyd Sys B. We selected Autopilot A to fly the aircraft; still descending; we were now over Location X but before ZZZZZ fix. We texted Dispatch we were going to lose System B and wanted to confer if we should divert or continue; Note-Loss of SYS B checklist did not say land at nearest suitable airport. We were almost to FL 320 and the ELEC 1 low pressure light illuminated; as the system quantity reached 0 and system pressure was 0;pump switch off per checklist. We got a few more lights and confirmed we had a complete loss of system B. Unbelievably we now got an ENG 1 hyd low pressure light illuminate; pump switch off per checklist. ELEC 2 HYD pump only hydraulic pump now functioning. It held autopilot A. We looked at each other and said lets head to ZZZ1; we had previously talked about divert points and where to go if the situation had gotten worse which it did. During this time we noticed A HYD quantity decreasing from 90+% to low 80's(we thought we might loose A too)I requested a descent and a turn direct to ZZZ1 from Center for a hydraulic loss. He gave us a different heading and said to expect to hold for sequence. We were now clearer to the controller and requested priority handling. The lead FA dinged us and asked if everything was OK; I told her no; type of situation; and to prepare the cabin for a divert to ZZZ1; I asked her to have the cabin ready in 10 minutes; no evac prep necessary. We got direct from ZZZZ Center; reprogramed the FMC and let dispatch know we were diverting. We started in on the loss of System B checklist as we were making a dive for ZZZ1. We ended up taking a vector to lose altitude. We completed the loss of system B to the ALT Flap extension. I then called back to the FA confirmed TEST; no evac; trucks would be standing by; we might seem like we were landing faster. I made a PA to the passengers. The FO did an excellent job of flying the airplane first; great CRM working with me on the checklists; with ATC ; keeping me in the loop where we were when we were being pulled from so many directions (We were getting pulled from ATC; Dispatch; FA; PAX; checklists...). We completed the ALT Flap extension and then landing checklist. The landing was normal for a flaps 15 landing.After the parking checklist; we debriefed. ZZZ1 station manager entered the aircraft and said they might have an aircraft swap if we could fly to ZZZ2. Sent Maintenance report. I talked to the FO and cabin crew and they all wanted to continue and fly to ZZZ2. We called dispatch and he elaborated on the possibility of us flying to ZZZ2. All the crew members wanted to finish the flight to ZZZ2; so we started in on this plan. I spoke with the Operations Manager and the ZZZ2 Chief Pilot for clearance for all of us to continue to ZZZ2. We did have to also fill out a simple report and give copies of our licensed to the [local] authorities. We informed the passengers. The plan did come together and we did an aircraft swap and an uneventful continuation to ZZZ2.
column123: In cruise; the System B Engine Pump 'Low Pressure' light illuminated. The Captain (non-flying pilot) accomplished the QRH checklist and the pump switch was deselected. Hydraulic quantity in the 'B' system was over 100%. Approximately 5 minutes later the 'B' system quantity starts to rapidly drop to zero. After reaching zero; the 'B' system Electric Hydraulic Pump unexpectedly illuminates 'Low Pressure.' We also receive the associated caution light for the flight control system. While the Captain was completing 'Loss of System B' checklist and we were discussing our options (ZZZ1 vs ZZZ2); we received another caution light for System 'A' Engine Pump 'Low Pressure.'We immediately decide to divert to ZZZ1. The Captain advised ATC; and notified the Dispatcher over ACARS. We completed the checklists; notified the Flight Attendants; and informed the passengers. There was a very clear division in the flight deck workload. The Captain worked the problems; communications with the company; and in cabin communications. I flew the aircraft and communicated with ATC. This workload division not only works well in the simulator but also in real life.We completed the 'Loss of System B' deferred items and Alternate Flap Extension procedure. We shot the ILS in ZZZ1 and landed without incident. Clearing the runway we taxied to the gate. The System 'A' Electric Pump continued to function and we fortunately had no other problems.This whole situation was extremely similar a recurrent training scenario that we had not that long ago. Having 'seen it before' was strangely reassuring.

column121: During our approach briefing we planned to exit the runway at Taxiway V near the far end of the runway to facilitate our taxi to parking. After landing on Runway 31R I followed the green leadoff lights to exit the runway at what I thought was Taxiway V and was already committed to continue onto the taxiway when Tower told us to exit at Taxiway V join [Taxiways] B and S to the ramp. The First Officer noticed that we had exited at Taxiway WW and asked the Tower if okay to exit there. The Tower then advised us that [Taxiway] WW was closed but no problem. We noticed that a couple of low and narrow snow berms across the taxiway that were left over from snowplows and we continued forward without any problem. I also noticed at the time that there were other aircraft tire tracks through the snow and did not appear to affect our progress. The taxi to parking was uneventful. During the landing rollout I tried to locate our position on the moving map airport diagram which I pre-positioned as much as possible at Taxiway V area; but could not ascertain exactly our current position. I saw the green leadoff lights; and thinking that we were at [Taxiway] V continued to follow them onto the taxiway. There was also another aircraft on short final behind us and it was my intention to exit the runway expeditiously so as not to complicate its arrival. I did not see a taxiway sign prior to the taxiway and determined that we must be exiting at [Taxiway] V. The Tower Controller did not seem to be phased by our encroachment onto a closed taxiway. We were already committed to Taxiway WW and there was no way to stop the aircraft and safely make a 180-degree turn to get back on the runway to exit at Taxiway V. There were not any cones or barricades with caution lights across Taxiway WW; and as it was not a construction area I felt that we could safely exit on [Taxiway] WW. To complicate matters; taxiway signage in that area is not sufficient as I did not see a WW sign prior to the taxiway - only the sign on the right side of the taxiway after entering [Taxiway] WW. Also of concern is that the green leadoff lights were illuminated allowing aircraft to taxi off the runway onto a closed taxiway. The lights should have been extinguished. I did not see any green leadoff lights at Taxiway V.

column121: We were flying; from ZZZ to QRO (Queretaro; MX). During preflight inspection; the FMC database was current as well as both pilots' Electronic Flight Kits. While in-flight; the weather was reporting clouds at 1;200 feet 5 mile visibility and light winds. The runway in use was [Runway] 09. While in cruise flight; Mexico Center informed us to expect VOR DME 2 for RWY (Runway) 09 approach in QRO. The aircraft was set up; and the Pilot Flying (Captain) completed all briefings. While in cruise flight; Mexico Center gave us a late descent clearance which is very common on this flight that required LVL/CHG mode and speedbrakes to get back on path. While we were descending to our first cleared altitude (around 14;000 feet MSL); Mexico switched us to QRO Approach. Upon contact with QRO Approach about 15-20 miles out; they advised of a traffic on a ten mile final; and informed us to now expect the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 Approach. We were recleared direct to QRO VOR; provided another descent; and then shortly thereafter; Approach cleared us for the approach. The First Officer went into the FMC and configured it to fly direct to QRO VOR. After the aircraft was established on course to the VOR; the First Officer selected the QRO VOR fix in the FMC and inserted the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 approach after verification with the Captain. Because of the angle the aircraft was approaching the VOR (straight in Runway 09); and relative to the approach procedure (an outbound heading 292 followed by a left procedure turn inbound); an additional procedure turn was required just to begin the approach. The procedure turn would normally be done at the VOR. Due to the FMC not having a procedure turn at the VOR to begin the approach for arrivals from the west; it immediately started auto-sequencing fixes to fly the aircraft directly to the outbound procedure turn DME 10 from the QRO VOR. The First Officer had to re-enter the VOR into Direct To and build a holding pattern into the FMC. There was a missed approach holding pattern depicted on the approach chart; therefore; the First Officer built a hold based on the holding pattern published. The First Officer informed ATC that a procedure turn was required at the VOR and also notified approach that the aircraft would enter holding as published to begin the approach. ATC advised us to descend to 11;000 feet and cleared for the approach. ATC seemed confused as to what we were doing. It appears that they were expecting the aircraft to make a hard left after crossing the VOR (almost a 180 degree turn) into unprotected airspace that contained mountainous terrain. The minimum safe altitude for that sector is 12;800 feet and if the aircraft would have flown that; there could have been a CFIT event. Once the aircraft entered the holding pattern; making a procedure turn to enter the crew selected IMM EXIT and the aircraft completed the current holding pattern; just a procedure turn; and exited the hold to fly the entire approach as planned and expected. There seems to be an issue regarding the Jeppesen Charts; and FMC database for this specific approach. The FMC did not contain any proper procedure to join the approach legally. Also the FMC sequencing the approach could have presented multiple issues including CFIT; TCAS; or lost of Situational Awareness.
column123: We were heading to MMQT to shoot the VOR 1 approach from the west. We were headed direct to the VOR with the approach loaded after that. Approximately 9 miles prior to the VOR the airplane started a left turn to join the outbound portion of the approach. This was not appropriate or legal. We turned the airplane back towards the VOR and realized there was nothing loaded to turn the airplane around to join the approach legally. There is also no procedure turn depicted on the chart. There was a holding pattern at the VOR and a missed approach procedure associated with the approach. We decided to enter the holding pattern at the proper altitude and told the controller we were doing that. That allowed the airplane to turn around and we were able to join and commence the approach that way. The rest of the approach was uneventful

column121: After an uneventful approach and touchdown with Captain as Pilot Flying; the aircraft was decelerating normally with speed brakes and reversers deployed. The crew accomplished a normal exit of the runway when smoke could be seen in the flight deck and sirens sounded in the cabin. Purser was immediately contacted and told flight crew that there was smoke in the cabin and detectors going off. The Purser was asked to assess the situation in the cabin as simultaneous contact was made with the Tower. Cabin was asked for any signs of a fire or source of smoke and none were present. The Tower advised crew that a runway treatment had been used two days prior and that upon crew request no signs of smoke or fire were visible coming from aircraft. Crew determined it was safe to exit the runway taxiway due to smoke being from possible ingestion into the packs or reversers from chemicals in the runway area and proceed to the ramp with constant contact with the cabin to ensure no escalation or fire warnings.A short time later an evacuation message and siren was triggered in the flight deck. Once again we verified with cabin crew that no fire or source of smoke could be assessed. We requested that the emergency equipment be available and accompany the aircraft to the gate out of an abundance of caution and increasing warnings in the flight deck. A normal shut down was accomplished and the flight mechanic entered the flight deck and informed crew that he had inadvertently set off the evacuate warning while trying to cancel the smoke detectors in the cabin.Crew was met by local airport authorities and emergency personnel. During the interaction with crew we were informed that two compounds 'Sodium Formate' a liquid treatment and 'Potassium Acetate' mixed in with 'aviation grade sand' had been used two days prior and could possibly have been ingested by reverser system and packs leading to smoke. A giant smoke cloud could also be seen at the midpoint of the runway at least 200 feet tall but centered in one location; the possible site where chemicals interacted with the aircraft. Crew taking over the flight was briefed on the situation and Maintenance was in the process of examining the aircraft. By all logic with no indications of a fire and smoke being generated inside the aircraft an external source was deemed the most likely cause. The pebble sized compound that may have been present along runway edge and some portions of runway; even though runway appeared perfectly clean and clear were brought by airports OPS Crew after an inspection of touchdown and mid runway areas.With the compounds mentioned not being familiar to crews not much comment can be given; I would suggest familiarizing crews with this event to help discern an actual fire with a foreign contaminant causing indications of smoke and fire. I would also point out that procedures need to be followed in regards to on board mechanics response to dealing with abnormalities; rather than helping in trying to cancel an alarm after it was deemed non-threatening the issue was compounded which could have forced an evacuation had flight deck and cabin crew had poorer communication.

column121: We landed in BTR. We were instructed to roll out to the end of the runway and exit left onto Taxiway Foxtrot. I remember seeing a NOTAM that B between Alpha and 4R was closed. Foxtrot was on the opposite side so we confirmed that Tower wanted us to exit left onto Foxtrot. They said affirmative left on Foxtrot and we complied. The CA (Captain) slowly steered us off Runway 13 and onto Taxiway Foxtrot. He was on centerline the entire time. At this point; I was getting the flaps up; clock started; APU started; and the rest of the after landing flow. Immediately after this; I called up ground for further taxi instructions. I felt a slight dip in the left side and we were unsure of the cause. The Captain said he added some power and the airplane continued to roll forward taxiing. I was focused on getting some complex taxi instructions from ground that were abnormal and a bit confusing. It took several calls for me to clarify the taxi instructions. When we parked at the gate; I went out to do my post flight walk around. The ground crew was already taking pictures and I could see dirt on the left side wheels. That's when it clicked that the left wheel had gone into the grass. I informed the Captain of the left wheel; and he called maintenance as well as informed Dispatch.Tower advised us to 'exit left at the end on taxiway Foxtrot' and to contact ground when off. We complied with their instructions. There is no mention of wingspan restrictions or weight limits for Taxiway Foxtrot. The company documentation does not make mention of any restrictions to Taxiway Foxtrot either. column121: Flight was all normal until we were cleared for a visual approach. Approach vectored us about 2 miles outside of the Final Approach Fix. When cleared for the a visual approach the First Officer turned inside of the Final Approach Fix. We had briefed the towers and their height and had them visually. The First Officer turned off the flight directors and turned directly towards the runway; about 20 degrees angle.  At 1;000 feet Tower called and asked if we had the towers in sight and said he had gotten an altitude alert.  At that point we were still visual with the towers and a half dot low on the glide slope. I directed the First Officer to come left and get on final. We continued the approach and landed. Found out afterwards this was the First Officer's first time to this airport and that he really didn't have a good visual on the runway. I felt his turning off the flight directors added to his lack of situational awareness. We discussed this approach afterwards and he felt I should have directed a go around. I believe he was waiting for me but I was in the green.  I didn't know he was lost. I explained to the First Officer that there is a reason we brief instrument approaches at night; to use them.  I shouldn't have allowed him to make the turn directly towards the runway but told him to intercept closer to the Final Approach Fix. The First Officer needed to communicate he wasn't in the green and execute a go around if he felt it was needed.
column123: Cleared visual approach after I stated to the Captain that I had the beacon in sight. I turned toward the airfield and began my descent referencing the glideslope. I only saw the beacon; not the runway. Tower issued a low altitude alert as I flew too close to the towers west of the field. I had the towers in sight and the Captain gave me verbal commands to help me orient the runway. The landing and rollout were uneventful. I accepted a visual approach based on the beacon alone. I was also distracted by the airspeed going below the hook for reasons I didn't understand. After landing; the Captain and I thoroughly debriefed the approach and landing.

column121: Arriving at the aircraft and checking the logbook; I noticed that the last crew had written that the Takeoff Configuration light and horn activated on takeoff (speed of activation was not noted). I surmised that the crew rejected the takeoff and subsequently swapped out of the aircraft after returning to the gate and the aircraft was not flown afterwards. The corrective action was a check of the Takeoff Configuration Warning System with no faults noted. Since nothing was actually corrected; the Captain and I discussed the possibility of it activating again on our takeoff. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the Forward Cargo Bin C. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. We were relatively full on this flight and our V1/VR speeds for Flaps 1 on Runway XXR were 125/135. The engine start and taxi out were uneventful with the throttle burst yielding no takeoff warning. On the takeoff roll at approximately 130 knot (5 knot after V1) the takeoff warning horn and light activated. We elected to continue the takeoff. The initial climb was normal and we discussed that we would be writing this up in ZZZ1. The Captain called for 'flaps up' at the appropriate speed and I moved the flap lever to UP. We had a few distractions from ATC due to hold-down altitude that was cancelled. Before I moved the landing gear handle to OFF; I checked the flap indicator and noticed that the flaps were still at 1 with the LE FLAP EXT green light illuminated. After confirming that the flap handle was up; I told the Captain the issue and that we need to keep our airspeed below 250 kts. and level off to handle the problem.After notifying ATC that we would need to level off; they gave us vectors for terrain while we ran the QRH for Trailing Edge Flap Disagree. Since the QRH doesn't really address the disagreement when attempting to RETRACT the flaps and only deals with setting the flaps for landing; we turned our attention to coordinating the air return. Dispatch was advised of the return as well as Station Ops in ZZZ. Our current gross weight was a little over 130;000 pounds so we extended the gear to add drag and burn off excess fuel for landing. The F/As (Flight Attendants) and passengers were notified of the return. Since this was a flight control issue; we [received priority handling] and notified ATC that we were requesting [Runway] XYL but would need time to reduce our landing weight to 128;000 pounds. We felt this was the safe option as time was not an issue. We then ran the QRH; ran the performance calculation for the Trailing Edge Flap Disagree QRH; and then the brake cooling module. The flaps extended normally with the Alternate Flap system to 15 degrees. The only slight issue was although I read the section directing the flap lever to be moved to the final flap position (15); we were sidetracked by discussing slowing during the extension and this was not done until after the QRH was completed. This allowed us to see our Flaps 15 maneuvering speed. After the delay vectors were complete and we were below the maximum landing weight; we made an uneventful landing on [Runway] XYL. Brake cooling allowed us to take right to the gate and the ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) trucks followed. No other issues occurred. We swapped into another aircraft and continued the pairing.
column123: The aircraft was an originator. The previous day a takeoff had been rejected because of a spurious Takeoff Config Warning and the maintenance resolution was no faults noted. The F/O (First Officer) and I discussed possible reasons for a false warning lasting a few seconds; which refreshed our memories of the warning system and thankfully prepared us for a repeat occurrence. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the forward cargo bin. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. On takeoff; approximately two seconds after the F/O's V1 call; the configuration light illuminated and the warning horn sounded. The F/O called VR; and we lifted off. The light went out and the horn stopped about the time the wheels left the ground. The F/O's performance and adhering to procedure during this event was flawless; which combined with our earlier discussion allowed the situation to be handled easily. We briefly mentioned writing the issue up again in ZZZ1. I called for Flaps Up; from their takeoff '1' setting. F/O moved the flap lever to Up; and then moments later told me the flaps didn't go up; and instructed me not to go over 250 [kts.]. We were still at about 200 knots; so no airspeed issues. I told F/O to tell ATC we needed to level off and maintain low airspeed. Initially we told ATC we would follow the SID and get back to them. ATC gave us a terrain clearance altitude. We confirmed the flaps were not up. I called for the QRH and we agreed that 'Flap Disagree' was the appropriate checklist. The checklist starts off by saying 'to prepare for landing' so we paused the checklist; agreed we were not going to ZZZ1 with flaps out; and I messaged Dispatch we were returning to ZZZ; told ATC; and received clearance to return to ZZZ. I notified the F/A (Flight Attendants) and told the passengers we were returning to ZZZ. We ran the QRH for Flaps Disagree; the procedure went mostly uneventfully. We were at 130;000 pounds; so we took delaying vectors to burn fuel to 128;000 [lbs.]. We checked the brake cooling for Autobrake 3; no issues. We did [receive priority handling]. We landed Flaps 15 and taxied to the gate. Positive takeaways. The CQT training from (year)?; (year)? that emphasized flap malfunctions prepared us well to handle the stuck flaps. Negative takeaways. The QRH for Flap Disagree was obviously written with a failure occurring during approach in mind. For our situation of failure on takeoff; the procedure kept us with the flap handle up until we had returned to ZZZ and were preparing to land; which meant we had flaps out; but no maneuvering speed. We know that Flaps 1 speed is 180 knots approximately; but it would have been one more item in our favor if we had moved the flap handle to match the flaps to give us the normal sight picture on the displays. While we were extending the flaps with the alternate switch; between watching the flap gauge and calls from ATC; we momentarily missed the instruction in the QRH to move the flap handle with the flap movement. We followed proper flap speeds as flaps were extending; but that that was because of our experience; not the display. The QRH should have the instruction to move flap handle with flaps before the actual instruction to move the flaps so that crews can discuss the handle in advance. We ran the brake cooling for Autobrake 3; and then tried to run again for Autobrake 2. The brake cooling module did not work the second time. We recalled a recent (Company communication piece) about Dispatch doing something to mess up performance calculation results; which could be rectified by requesting landing data again; but that did not work. Something in the performance calculations needs to be corrected so that brake cooling can be run more than once. Brake cooling was not an issue; even with Autobrake 3; so this was a small nuisance. Based on passenger comments; F/As did a great job. F/O's performance was excellent; our teamwork together allowed the situation to be handled easily.

column121: During the approach we were cleared direct down to 8000 feet from 12000 feet. During the descent Autopilot was engaged and following LNAV and VS we were encountering continuous light to moderate turbulence throughout the descent. As we passed through approximately 12000 feet and beginning to slow; we experienced severe turbulence mixed with continuous moderate [turbulence]. When we initially encountered the severe turbulence; the Autopilot disengaged; the aircraft was changing altitude and air speeds abruptly with several hundred feet of altitude change and at least plus or minus 20 to 30 knots airspeed changes. The Captain was thrown hard enough to hit the overhead panel with his head and we received a report one of our Flight Attendants had been hurt and several passengers had hit their heads. I as the Pilot Flying took manual control of the aircraft and flew the remainder of the descent and approach. The aircraft was extremely hard to control throughout most of the descent and approach as we continued to encounter continuous turbulence; strong crosswinds and wind shear. During the ensuing descent and approach the aircraft was extremely hard to control as we continued to experience moderate to severe turbulence; strong crosswind and wind shear throughout the approach. Once established inbound and cleared for the approach we were pushed several degrees off course and had some airspeed fluctuations of plus or minus 20 knots. We quickly discussed missed approach but prior to reaching 1000 feet we had regained the course; were on glide path and stabilized (properly configured) to continue the approach. We continued the approach while receiving some lower wind shear of plus or minus 10 knots down to approximately the 500 foot call. At 500 feet we were still stabilized and continued the approach to landing without further issue. Throughout the approach and landing; we had airspeed; altitude variations and heading deviations that were extremely hard to control due to the turbulence and wind shear events we were experiencing. I do not believe at any point we had any exceedances or violations; however; it was a very task saturated environment. There were no reports of the severity of the turbulence ahead of us and it was a very unexpected event.This was an example of good Crew Resource Management as the Captain and I maintained good communication throughout the event and helped to cross monitor the aircraft systems and instruments. As the pilot flying; I was entirely focused with aircraft control and the Captain doing the pilot monitoring was ensuring all the descent and approach tasks were completed. We kept good crew communication with what was happening with aircraft control and situational awareness. A recommendation is for pilots to ensure they continue to practice hand flying skills for situations like this. The autopilot was unusable; and I was thankful I constantly practice hand flying the airplane. It helped me with confidence to control the airplane to the best of my ability in a situation where the aircraft is being tossed around by turbulence.

column121: Earlier in the day I wrote up the airplane for a pack 2 overheat. We were flying an airplane with an MEL on pack 2. We were cruising at FL250 about 90 miles north of our destination when we got a red 'bleed 1 leak' warning message on EICAS. I notified ATC that I wanted an immediate descent to 10;000 ft. for a bleed leak. The FO (First Officer) handed me the QRH and we began the descent and notified the FA (Flight Attendant) to take her seat because hot air was going somewhere it shouldn't and that we would call her back. I began to run the QRH. ATC gave us FL200 as the initial descent. He asked if I was requesting priority handling; I said YES. He asked for clarification on what a bleed leak meant for us and gave us 10;000 ft. subsequently. Our initial descent rate was about ~3500 fpm; faster than normal; to get out of the icing conditions and closer to a safer pressure altitude. I ran the QRH as written until I reached END. Once I finished running the QRH and put it back in the storage cubby; we began to breathe a sigh of relief that things are probably going to be okay. I directed the FO to slow the descent rate to ~1000 fpm. We were at about 16;000 ft. by this point. The FO then pointed out to me that cabin pressure dropping as indicated by the amber boxed Cabin Alt reading on the EICAS. Cabin altitude was at roughly 9;800 ft. and climbing. We elected to keep pace down to 10;000 ft. in order to get in front of the reducing cabin pressurization. The checklist list was not written with a pack 2 MEL in mind. I began to realize the ramifications of what I had just done by turning off Bleed 1; Pack 1; and closing the cross-bleed switch.The priority handling request with ATC and the events we had just gone through had my mind racing from adrenaline. I decided that 'worrying' about the pressurization system wasn't necessary. We were at 12;000 ft. and descending and if I recall correctly cabin pressure differential was about 2.2 psid. I decided to press dump on the cabin pressurization controller after looking over at the FO and mentioning that pressing the dump button wouldn't harm anything and that we weren't in dangerous territory as far as what happens if I press it. We felt a minor pressurization change as the airplane equalized. In hindsight; this was entirely unnecessary. I should have simply let the airplane depressurize on its own.I then began to evaluate how much fuel our descent to 10;000 ft. would burn instead of being at FL250. It took a minute for the FMS to catch up to the descent we had done. The initial fuel numbers it gave us led me to believe we would be very close to divert. I gave it some time and the numbers got more accurate for fuel calculations. I determined we had no need to divert on account of fuel. I notified dispatch; ATC; and the FA that the urgency was over and we would continue to our destination.Next; the airplane began to get hot and stuffy. One consideration was diverting to the nearest airfield. I didn't want to have a heat casualty in the back. The other was to get air into pack 1 so that it was useful in cooling the cabin. I looked at the overhead panel and discussed with my FO the notion of starting the APU to feed pack 1. This was a risky decision because if the leak was closer to pack 1 then feeding APU bleed air into the system would induce basically the same situation. I figured that I could simply turn the APU back off if that turned out to be the case. I figured the air and pressure coming from the number 2 bleed was hotter and higher pressure than the APU. The checklist had given me the steps to solve the problem perfectly if only my number 2 pack weren't MEL'd. I had a short mental struggle with my decision to do something that contradicted what the checklist had just made me do a few minutes earlier and really felt strange using Captain's authority to bypass it. I pride myself on checklist discipline and following the books as best I possibly can. In hindsight; I think alittle thermal discomfort and more rigidity with regards to the checklist would have been wise.I selected auto on the cross-bleed switch and turned on the APU and fed the number 1 pack. The airplane cooled down inside. I spoke with the flight attendant once more to ask about the faces of the passengers and if anyone knew about what just happened. She said they didn't have any idea and that we would keep it that way. We shot an ILS approach and landed normally.This situation was a learning experience of the highest caliber for me. I have since re-learned how the cross-bleed switch logic works. I have studied the layout and function of the bleed and pneumatic systems and learned much more about airplane pressurization. Pressing dump was not the right decision and I wouldn't do it that way again. Selecting the recirc fan off to bring in fresher air would have been a better choice than turning on the APU.

column121: I was in command of Aircraft X schedule service from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We departed normally and were climbing to our assigned altitude of 32;000 ft. when just prior to level off our Flight Attendant called us in the cockpit to report that she had a smell of smoke in the cabin. We maintained communication with her as she said it seemed to be coming from Row 4 emanating from the lighting valance on the aircraft left side. We told her to monitor the situation and let us know if there was any sparking visible. She told us that she physically checked the valance and PSU's and they were very hot to the touch and that the smoke and heat was migrating rearward now from Rows 4 thru 10. I told the FA to get the PBE [Protective Breathing Equipment] out along with the fire extinguisher and prepare to fight a fire if one erupted. I then told the FO (First Officer) to notify ATC of our situation and that we needed to return to ZZZ. We were then cleared to return and given a decent clearance to 24;000 ft. Still not sure what type of smoke we had in the cabin I asked the FA to come forward so we could have the FO check the smoke for type of odor (electrical or engine based). FO advised me that the smoke odor seemed to have been not electrical. I then had him get the QRH out and run the procedure for SMOKE IN THE CABIN procedure. We accomplished the memory items and in coordination with ATC requested priority handling and were given an unrestricted decent to 8;000 ft. and vectors to a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. The ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) trucks were standing by for our arrival. The QRH procedure was completed and the smoke seemed to dissipate a little according to the FA. We landed without incident and upon initiation of communication with the ARFF commander we were told there was no smoke evidence on the exterior of the aircraft. Since it appeared the internal situation was under control we decided to taxi to the gate for normal deplaning. Fire Dept. followed us to the gate and upon arrival ; they boarded the aircraft and I advised the commander of what had happened and where it had been located. The ARFF members then checked the aircraft over with their thermal heat locater and found no heat source in the Valance or PSU. They then left the aircraft. Dispatch and MX were notified of the situation. Aircraft passengers were deplaned without incident.

column121: When arriving at new aircraft; the ground power was connected. The temperature in the back of the plane was stifling - it had to be 95 degrees Fahrenheit in the plane. I told my forward Flight Attendant (FA) and we reported to Captain. Passengers were allowed to board and they immediately began taking off as many clothing layers as possible. FAA and company regulations still require everyone to wear masks; despite CDC warnings that masks should be removed when overheated. As the AFT FA; I am responsible for making announcements in a mask; which is laborious and requires many more breathing pauses than usual. Saying the announcements with a mask; in ridiculous heat is more; exhausting; distracting; and physically concerning. My only focus was being able to breathe and the health of my passengers. I walked to the front of aircraft to get some air; but also to get water for the poor passengers. Thankfully; the plane did cool off in the air; but it was still extremely uncomfortable.Extreme heat conditions on the airplane combined with mandatory mask compliance for passengers and crew caused this event.  Crews can be terminated/lose benefits if removing masks on board the aircraft in front of passengers. Until recently; FA's were not required to wear masks while making announcements. Passengers can be fined/lose flight privileges for removing masks. The threat of the FAA fines and penalties under the new federal mask mandate appears to supersede common sense safety practices and concern and care for crews and passengers.Masks; may help prevent viral spread (there is much data to refute those claims); but prevents the passengers and crew to breathe much needed fresh oxygen. The effects of not getting enough oxygen and the potential for hypoxia were ingrained into me during FA training. I am greatly concerned that airlines and the FAA are continuing to put the safety of passengers and crew at risk with mandatory mandates that restrict fresh oxygen; which can cloud judgement and critical thinking abilities. Heat exhaustion and the need for fresh oxygen when wearing masks was acknowledged by the CDC. Of course; the CDC recommended spacing of self 6 feet away; but plane passengers and crew do not have the luxury of a 6 foot distance. Mandatory mask mandates on planes should also come with the ability to tell passengers and crew to remove masks when feeling anxious or stressed or when breathing is compromised. If one feels sick or faint because of heat and a mask; the ability to lower a mask on a plane should be allowed. FAs should be empowered to use their common sense when enforcing masks in extreme heat conditions. The 'appearance of safety' seems to be aviation's new standard of practice rather than 'actual safety' of anyone on board an aircraft. This is a very serious shift in thought for the FAA and airlines.  The unintended consequences of these 'appearance of safety' standards are frightening.

I can't smell alcohol; smoke; or even jet fuel when wearing a mask; which is required of me at all times - especially in my jump seat.The ability to do my job as a safety professional on an aircraft is greatly reduced thanks to these mask mandates. column121: I; the First Officer; executed the charted Visual Approach. Landing was uneventful and rolled to taxiway Tango before passing controls to the Captain to taxi to gate. As we exited the runway Tower gave taxi instructions to the gate. and to '... stay with me'. I read back the taxi instructions and the Captain repeated them as he commenced taxi from the runway and stated 'flaps up'. I then commenced my after landing flow; raised the flaps; checked speed brakes stowed; autobrakes off; flight directors off; wing lights off; steady and strobe to steady; trimmed to 5 units; check weather radar off; cycled ramp (though not needed) to active in VHF2; and started removing flight pertinent printer strips. By this time we were somewhere near the Bravo; Golf; Sierra taxiway junction. I briefly looked up as Captain stated; 'There's Golf'. I don't remember what I heard exactly that caused me to look up again; some reference to Golf taxiway perhaps. But when I looked up I did not recognize where we were. I saw lighted taxi signs for Sierra; Golf; and Bravo in the distance to the left. I could see blue taxiway edge lights all around but nothing in front of us. The blue taxi edge lights were very disorienting especially without a lit taxi center line. Our taxi and turnoff lights were so dim that they were essentially useless. The moon was providing more light than they were. On my IPAD I could see our own ship; we were on Golf but heading the wrong way. The Captain had turned right instead of left. At that point he turned left in an attempt to get back to Alpha taxiway; I assume. He did make me aware that he was concerned about accidentally crossing on to the runway. Due to the very poor lighting and the sea of blue taxi edge lights; taxiway was difficult to discern from anything else. All you could see was directional taxi signs in the darkness and blue taxi lights scattered about. The Captain turned left until there was a break in the blue lights with the Bravo sign visible just a little further away so it did appear as though we were turning on taxiway Bravo though I could see no yellow line. I told him I didn't see the taxiway; I think we're going in to no man's land; and Captain said; no; we're on Golf; there's the sign for Bravo. I was confused about the blue lights; they didn't seem to be oriented right and the our ship was sort of on Golf but pivoting so I allowed the events to progress thinking maybe I was just disoriented. When we proceeded ahead the ground before us was just dark. Really no discernible features except for blue taxi lights up ahead that seemed to mark the edge of Bravo. I said I think we're off the taxiway. Captain stopped. We exchanged thoughts on the best way to proceed from that point. We called tower to confess. Tower took a look; said we were just near Bravo; or Golf; I can't remember exactly but he was not concerned which taxiway we ended up needing to get to the gate. I thought we might not be on prepared surface but the Captain was sure we were still on the taxiway just facing the wrong direction. So I told him clear to the right; let's turn all the way back around and take Bravo. The Captain turned tight right and proceeded back the way we came. The jet stopped and thinking it was an incline the Captain added power and we rolled back on taxiway center; turned left on Bravo; took Foxtrot then Alpha to the gate; tower then stated; 'Not a problem guys; the snow plows do more damage than you'. No other occurrences from then on. We did discuss the possibility that we may have left the taxiway. The Captain was confident we had not and I was inclined to believe him since I could not see the ground beneath us; we were just avoiding taxi edge lights. I told him I would check and do an external walk around once we shut down. During deplaning maintenance met me before walking out. She asked me if the landing was rough and I said; actually; no; the landing was great... WHY? She showed me a shot on her cell phone of our nose strut and this is your nose gear. It was covered with dirt. I went down to look at it and it was dirty but both tires were still intact at that point and I saw no evidence of anything else on the mains or the engines. The mains were spotless; engines were clean. I came back up; told the Captain the mains were covered in dirt on the tires and on the lowermost part of the strut. I then stepped out of the cockpit while he talked to maintenance. We turned the plane over to maintenance; they said they would check out the gear and clean it off and we left; still not sure we actually left the taxiway. The wind was blowing in excess of 30 knots and dirt was blowing all over. We chalked it up to that.It was dark; really dark on that end of the airport. The taxiways are a conglomeration that looks more like spaghetti. The whole area is labeled HS1; for good reason. They are difficult enough to navigate in daylight; much less at night with no centerline lighting; a plethora of edge lights all outlining various 'islands' on the field; taxiway ID and directional signs for every taxiway that intersects in HS1 and a useless taxi light. That is a lot of scattered lights with no reliable taxi light to help gauge distance. The Captain was disoriented. Golf taxiway is constructed right on the curve at a 45 degree angle. The directional sign at night can make the left turn on Golf easy to miss especially with the opposite direction of Golf being directly in front of you. I; the First Officer was task distracted. I was performing after landing flow and cockpit cleanup. The Captain had told me during this trip that he was once based in [the area] and was very familiar with this airport; not to mention he was a check airman. My guard was down and I was not as diligent as I normally am during the taxi operation. Being tired and expectation bias. It was night; the end of the day in serious winds. The Captain and I were exhausted most of our mental energy on planning the approach and landing given the conditions that night. The approach was not exactly a standard one we do all the time; and we were not landing on the usual runway you get at this airport. A better taxi light would have alleviated much of the confusion. The lights are not adequate. Neither of us was really sure that we ever left the taxiway. Taxiway centerline lights. There are many islands outlined in blue and no green center lights to actually show the trail through the maze of them. Distance judging is difficult in the dark and it was dark for us. Those lights would have helped. I should have stayed more engaged in the taxi phase to back up my Captain. Getting lost is going to happen and there are two of us for a reason. I allowed myself to get disoriented as well.
column123: Landed Runway 31 LGA. Cleared at taxiway T. ATC gave us T;B;G;A to gate. Turned right on Taxiway G instead of left. The area around taxiway G is confusing; especially at night. The area is not marked well and very dark making it extremely hard to find correct taxiway. Light up the area better. Better taxiway designations. Area should be redesigned.
