column121: There were storms in the area; and we were given a reroute by ATC; to go south to the coast; and then follow the coast west to IAH. The FO (First Officer; Pilot Monitoring) had made a passenger announcement telling them that we were expecting storms along the route of flight; and that we were anticipating a bumpy ride. I; the CP (Captain; Pilot Flying); had advised the FA that it was going to be bumpy. In the climb out; we encountered light turbulence. Upon reaching cruising altitude of FL280; it was smooth; so we briefly let the passengers up. Upon reaching the coast; ATC advised us of multiple storms and cells along our route of flight; and had mentioned that several aircraft ahead of us had gone south of these storms; had stayed within 50 NM of the coast; and had reported nothing worse than light turbulence; and advised we do the same. After discussing with the FO; we agreed that flying south of our route; and staying within 50 NM of the coast; was our best option. At this time; I had my radar up; and the FO had his terrain map up. We advised the passengers and the FA to expect a few bumps; turned the seat belt sign back on; and to remain seated. We also decided to slow to turbulence penetration speed. We were painting multiple red and magenta cells which we were staying south of; and had a lot of green all over the radar. We were dodging and avoiding the cells to the north; while staying within the 50 NM range of the coast. We then must have hit an embedded cell that the radar did not pick up; as it was only reading green. Almost instantly; we went into severe turbulence; and lost approximately 400 feet. The aircraft did not go into any unusual or upset attitudes; and the Auto-Pilot remained on. During this turbulence; we also had a suspected lightning strike - we saw a flash of light all around us; heard a bang; and smelt the 'fireworks' smell that you usually smell associated with lightning. After being struck; we got a Stall Protection System advanced master caution message appear. It disappeared within 5 seconds of it showing. As quick as the severe turbulence hit us; it disappeared. ATC queried us regarding our loss of altitude; at which point the FO reported the severe turbulence and suspected lightning strike. ATC asked if we needed further assistance; to which we replied no. As previously mentioned; this happened very quickly. All in all; I would say it lasted no longer than 30 seconds; and closer to 20 seconds. Once we were back at FL280; we had completely exited all weather (which we had been in for a majority of the time upon reaching the coast); and were in clear blue skies. I spoke to the FA; and asked if she was OK; to which she replied she was. She then asked if it was OK for her to check on the passengers; which she did. There were no injuries; and the only thing she mentioned is that the passengers were staring at her wide eyed. ATC asked if there were any injuries onboard; we replied with none. The flight continued with no further incidents. Upon landing; both pilots thoroughly inspected the outside of the plane on the walk around; noting a black mark on the right side of the nose which may be the entry point to the suspected lightning strike; but with no damage seen. I wrote up the plane with 3 write ups - Severe turbulence; Lightning strike; and Lock out/Tag out installed.CRM was effectively utilized during this event; with the PF using the radar; and the PM using the terrain. With the information available to us at the time; with ATC advising us of going south of the cells; as opposed to north; the decision; at the time; to go south was the correct one. That being said; I think it would have been smarter to go north of the cells; but we did not have that information. Utilizing the radar was key during this event; by staying out of the red and magenta cells. However; the radar has its limitation; especially considering they are older pieces of equipment; and can not 100% accurately paint embedded cells; of which we hit. After the event; ATC began recommending to other aircraft to go north of the cells. Ultimately; I would say the crew were stuck between a rock and a hard place - staying within the 50 NM boundary of the coast; but staying as far south as possible of the mega cells to the north. Additionally; I would like to mention the extraordinary job that the company did after the incident. Upon reaching the gate; multiple members of both [safety teams] reached out to me and the crew; checking that we were OK; and that the passengers were OK. I feel our company truly encompassed themselves with the company values; of which we stand for; and has made me thoroughly proud and joyful to be a part of.

column121: Turning final ZZZZ fully configured at 150 knots I armed the Localizer first than the Approach mode. First Officer inquired and received the landing clearance. I noticed that the glide slope didn't capture and that we were going above the path. I tried to descend in Vertical Speed; but it didn't come active; so it wouldn't work. Approach mode light still on. I disconnected the Autopilot; lowered the nose and started a descend using the VGSI (Visual Glideslope) path indicator and the outside PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator). During the descent we tried to reset the Approach/Glideslope unsuccessfully. The approach was pretty bumpy with some good downdrafts. The aircraft went below the glide slope and I started to correct back when the pull up warning came on then stopped right away. Then the glide slope warning followed. I was just under the path recovering and had 3 red lights and 1 white on the PAPI. Speed around 10 knots above Vref and decreasing toward Vref. I was very focused on the approach and continued to an uneventful normal landing.We were configured early; ready for approach; but the Glideslope not capturing and the uncertainty concerning the landing clearance created a distraction that put me behind the aircraft and I developed some tunnel vision trying to remedy the approach. I became fixated and continued when I should have discontinued the approach and gone around. After landing the First Officer said to me that she had mentioned going around; but it hadn't registered with me during the approach. I tell First Officers that there is no mission; but today I didn't follow my own advice. It's easy to become over focused without realizing it. When in doubt; go-around.
column123: The event began while beginning the ILS Approach. The company notes on the approach dictate not to arm the ILS until reaching a certain position because of the possibility of false localizer signals. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and I was the Pilot Monitoring.  I remember thinking that the Pilot Flying armed the approach later than I would have since we were well beyond the designated point. My best guess on what happened is that because of the delay the localizer armed but the glideslope never captured because we were already too high. Whatever the reason for the automation not doing what we had expected; the result was that we realized that the Glideslope never captured and were trying to get the aircraft to come down.Not only were we distracted with being above the intended glide path; but we were handed over to tower late and I was busy with getting clearance to land while the Pilot Flying was flying the plane trying to get back to a stabilized approach. As the aircraft was getting back to a normal glide path (3 red; 1 white on PAPI) around the 500 foot mark I gave my stabilized approach callout and realizing we were slightly above speed and correcting; but the vertical speed exceeded what is acceptable. At this point I said 'I think we should go around'. I can't remember if it was just before or after I said this that we got a 'PULL UP' alert. The Captain elected to continue the landing. Later after discussion; I learned he may have had tunnel vision to the point where my go around call didn't register with him.My unfamiliarity with ZZZZ did not help our situational awareness as well as being distracted with getting switched over to tower (late) and attempting to get landing clearance around the same time we realized the automation did not perform as expected. As a FO/PM not being assertive enough when a go-around was needed.Abiding by company SOP to the letter. No matter what; at 500 feet if stabilized approach criteria aren't met; it's an automatic and firm 'GO AROUND'.

Be more deliberate in accomplishing checklist especially at the gate before airborne when stress and task demand is low.
column123: Departing ZZZZ at 1;500 feet power did not reduce to climb power. The Captain checked the takeoff pg X for altitudes; they were correct. He engaged VNAV and I called for flap retraction on schedule.Cause - Recency in right seat. Monitoring. Refrain from staying heads down in the checklist. Confirm selected items.

column121: Once established in descent just below FL180; we received a call from the Flight Attendants that there was an odor in the vicinity of row X. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil; but not a burning or acrid smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row X; to whom it was very noticeable; which was also confirmed by FA 'B'; but only when they walked up to row X. There was no visible plume anywhere in the airplane. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.The FO was flying the airplane (PF) so they took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. The comment about a fuel smell drove the pilots to suspect a fuel leak; but after running through the fuel leak checklist; no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing; both engine fuel flow rates equivalent; quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable; but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector; while we requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However; after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course; we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority; which ATC quickly accommodated; clearing other aircraft from our path. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit [Runway] XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon exit at Taxiway 1; we were cleared to cross runway XXL; and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of runway. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities; we taxied to the gate; making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution; we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake; we immediately shut down (left-hand-side) engine #1; confirmed good/stable AC external power connection; then shut down (right-hand-side) engine #2. Prior to departure from ZZZ; we were sprayed with both Type I 'Deice' and Type IV 'Anti-Ice' fluid; with engines running; at the X Pad.After landing; FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. FO also said that after landing they briefly noticed an odor.We could have [advised ATC] earlier on in the event. This would have allowed us traffic priority earlier in the descent (and speeds above 250 KIAS once below 10;000); getting us on the ground sooner and reducing the overall time of pax/FA exposure to fumes.We flew the same airplane the following day; and the airplane was cleared by Maintenance with no defects found. Nothing was wrong with the airplane itself. Fumes remaining localized in a certain area of the cabin suggests internal point source emission rather than external ingestion or airplane system malfunction. However; at time of writing; we still do not know; definitively; what caused the fumes.The FAs are commended for their prompt notification and accurate description of the nature and extent of the fumes. FO is commended for flying the aircraft while coordinating with ATC and requesting ARFF; while the CA ran checklists and coordinated with the FAs; then flying the approach almost to minimums. Working together seamlessly is key in these situations; and the CA commends the crew for a job well done.
column123: Prior to departure from ZZZ; we were sprayed with both Type I and Type IV fluid; with engines running; at the South De-Ice Pad.Once established in descent just below FL180; we received a call from the FA's. I (the FO) assumed it was the FA's notification that they were seated. Instead; they communicated to the CA that there was an odor in the vicinity of row x. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil; but not a burning smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row x; to whom it was very noticeable. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.I (the FO) was flying the airplane (PF) so I took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. Since the CA was communicating with the FA's; I trusted his lead on necessary checklists to run; as he had the first hand information on the situation in the cabin. During this time; we had entered IMC conditions; and I was flying the airplane and working the radios; receiving several heading; altitude and speed changes during this time.The comment about a fuel smell drove us to suspect a fuel leak; but after running through the fuel leak checklist; no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing; both engine fuel flow rates equivalent; quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable; but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector; during which I requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However; after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course; we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority; which ATC quickly accommodated. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon landing; I cracked the Thrust Reversers (TRs); and briefly noticed a smell in the flight deck. I then decided that the use of TRs may not be the safest procedure; as it was still unclear what was causing this smell. Thus; I immediately stowed the TRs and decelerated using only the brakes (long runway; good braking action).Upon exit at Taxiway 1; we were cleared to cross runway XXL; and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of XXL. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities; we taxied to the gate; making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution; we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake; we immediately shut down engine #1; confirmed good/stable AC external power connection; then shut down engine #2.After landing; FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. This was my 2nd precautionary ARFF event on 2 consecutive workdays (though separated by a period of leave). Having had the time to reflect upon the first event; I felt calmer and more prepared this time. I focused on making a successful approach (almost down to minimums).One error I made was to start configuring and thus slowing down too early. Due to several heading changes and an ATC request for us to slow down while the aircraft in front of us on the approach sped up to best forward speed; I had felt momentarily disoriented regarding our distance to the ZZZ1. Luckily; my brain was about 5 miles ahead of the airplane. Once I realized my error; I paused further configuration (which was gear down flaps 3 at that time) until closer to the ZZZ1.Considerations that were made were items for fire and emergency evacuation; should a fire develop after landing. Luckily; this was not the case.To my knowledge; it is still unclear what caused the smell. If it would have been more severe (filling the entire cabin and flight deck); then the checklist for smoke/fumes would have been appropriate.Overall; I feel that this event was handled well by everyone involved.

column121: We were cleared to FL 230. Passing through 17;500 feet; #1 engine rolled back to approximately 30%N1.  The N1 and EGT had flashing red and yellow arcs and the lower section had a red flashing box around both engine indications. Our initial analysis was engine failure.  We requested to level at FL 180; communicated to ATC our situation and requested vectors to return to ZZZ.  Upon further analysis of the engine condition; the Captain (Pilot Flying) stated the engine was still running but noted the indications were not normal. We also saw the EEC in ALTN mode.  Captain continued to fly and directed me into the QRH for the EEC ALT MODE checklist since the engine was running and not surging; stalling; or any indications dictating complete failure or the need to shutdown.  We completed the QRH for the EEC ALT MODE according to our situation and indications.  We discussed and agreed to also reference and ran the QRH [for] One Engine Inoperative Landing.  I continued communications with ATC; while the Captain communicated with F/A's and made a PA to passengers. I computed [landing] data and set up the FMC. Captain flew the approach and landing; taxiing clear of the runway to a safe location.  Autobrakes were used and no manual braking activated until slowed (approximately 50 knots) and prior to the exit of the runway.  Based on our weight and configuration [calculations] prior to landing required the use of autobrakes and brake cooling calculations.  I calculated the [landing data] for Non-Normal One engine Inop with 15 Flaps landing.   Brake Cooling calculations returned a 58 minute cooling period; which we accomplished at the turnout abeam runway.  Emergency Rescue Crews communicated to us no visible smoke from brakes and heat signature negative. After the 58 minute cool down; we were given clearance to taxi and proceeded to our gate.
column123: When we arrived at the gate; Maintenance was working on the #1 engine. The previous crew that had the aircraft had returned to the gate. When they started the number one engine they got the Engine Control light. Maintenance cleaned the cannon plugs did an engine run and returned the aircraft to service. Our engine start and initial climb were all normal. We were on radar vectors for our route and climbing through 17;500 feet or so when the #1 N1 Gauge flashed yellow twice. We both saw it; then the #1 engine rolled back to 31% on the N1 but the engine didn't quit. We leveled at FL 180 and requested vectors back to ZZZ. We ran the EEC ALT Mode Checklist and the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist from the QRH. Landed Flaps 15; autobrakes 3. We ran the brake cooling calculation prior to landing. We had a 58 minutes of break cooling.

column121: We were level 5;000 feet 250 knots approaching ZZZ VOR on the ZZZZZ2 Star. Approach gave a heading 280 and slow to 180 and asked if we had the field in sight.  We were heading 330 and I was thinking a turn to 350 was coming so 280 heading caught me a little off guard. I (FO) was pilot flying. The sun was just above the horizon as I looked west and across the cockpit for the field.  Simultaneously I was looking cross-cockpit and programing the speed and heading change into the FMC. I could make out the field so I said to the Captain (PM); 'I can see the field; you can call it in sight.'  I noticed another aircraft on TCAS at our altitude on TCAS and then saw them visually less than ten miles away; also headed west toward ZZZ [Airport]; I noted the  paint scheme and relayed to the PM all that information and that they were probably headed to the north side of the airport.  In my head I was thinking that our airplane was not slowing down as fast as I would like when the PM said 'where is that airplane; I think we need to turn.' I pushed the localizer button on the FMC but the airplane did not turn so I turned the autopilot off and manually turned to intercept final for [Runway] XXR. As I did; we received at TCAS TA then a few seconds later a TCAS RA to climb.  The ADI showed a red boxed area from level flight down (I was descending) so I just leveled off until we heard 'clear of conflict.'   Then Approach gave us a 180 heading; paused; and then said 'you guys can't do that;' and switched us to Tower.  I was able to correct the high energy level of the airplane using gear; flaps; and speed brakes and continued the approach and landed uneventfully.Fast close to the airfield; sun in eyes; failure on my part to use automation.Something from ATC that I was going to turn towards the runway instead of downwind in the [Runway] XXR pattern or an advisory where we were in the sequence.  My recency of experience led to not arming the localizer; while I did brief that at the start of the first leg I could have reemphasized it during the approach brief.

The Captain checked the left engine oil quantity on the MFD and it indicated 2 quarts. I started the Low Oil Pressure checklist which lead to the Precautionary Engine Shutdown checklist. We secured the engine; [advised ATC] and headed back ZZZ. I called Flight Attendant and told her what the situation was; made a PA; and we continued to land safely in ZZZ. I cannot answer this as I am not a mechanic and do not know why the engine lost oil. I feel like we took all appropriate actions in a timely manner. If this happens in the future; I would maybe try to slow down a bit and delay the flaps 22 extension to short final as we were heavy and airplane wouldn't hold altitude after we extended the gear down/flaps 22. We retracted the flaps back up to 9 to be able to hold altitude which worked well; and then re extended the flaps to 22 on short final. column121: Intended to land flaps 30 in windy conditions with add speed of 14 knots.  Visual approach on Visual Approach Slope indicator and slightly below ILS glide slope. We received a Ground Proximity Warning alert for 'too low terrain'. Rechecked landing gear was down and landed. We realized on very short final that flaps were actually set to 25 instead of 30. We did not select flaps to 30 since we were so low. With the extra speed we had added for the gusty winds; I felt we were safer to leave them set at 25 and land.
column123: While on final approach  we experienced a Ground Proximity Warning 'Too Low Terrain' aural warnings. Knowing that we were on glide slope and Precision Approach Path Indicator and the runway was in sight in VFR conditions; we decided to continue the landing. We ensured that the landing gear was down and that we were free of terrain; however; on short final the Captain noticed we were at flaps 25 instead of 30. It was decided to safely complete the landing since we were stable on speed and path. We already had built in a 14 knot wind additive for the windy conditions. The entire approach was stable including at the 500 foot 'Stable' call out point. I take responsibility for misreading the flap gauge; and will certainly give it more focus in the future. One potential factor; not an excuse; is there was the distraction of balloons going by our aircraft around the time of the landing checklist. I reported the balloons to Tampa Tower.

column121: On the ZZZZZ X arrival into ZZZ; we were given a descent to FL230.  As PF; I re-cruised for FL230.  Prior to ZZZZZ1 we were told to descend via the arrival.  I dialed in 6;000 feet for the Runway XXL approach.  Initially the descent point was visible and looked normal.  After flying several more minutes it became clear that we were past the descent point.  It was about this time that the descent point disappeared from the ND.  We started an immediate Open Descent with full speed brakes.  We were unable to get relief from the altitude/airspeed requirement at ZZZZZ2 (250/110) due to radio congestion.  We were given a frequency change and got relief from ZZZ Approach who gave us a descent to 6;000 feet which we accomplished.  The rest of the approach and landing was uneventful.  When the PF re-cruised he inadvertently typed in '320' instead of '230'.  There was not an immediate erroneous depiction on the ND.  Everything looked normal; however we continued past the descent point.  Just as we realized there was something wrong; the ND descent point disappeared.  The PF has been on reserve and has flown very little in the last two months.  The next two flights went well with no problems.The two pilots were on the first leg of the trip.  It was the first time they'd flow together.  They were working well together and both were attempting to follow policies/procedures.  This was a dumb mistake by one pilot that was not caught by the other.  By re-cruising; the goal was to have the ND provide usable descent point information.  I listed this as a 'Moderate' risk rating because we easily received relief from ATC.  If they had not assisted us; the risk would have been higher.

column121: Sat in ZZZ for hours for a delayed flight coming from ZZZ1. During the swap; the outgoing Captain informed me that the Crew that brought the aircraft into ZZZ1 said that upon landing the right thrust reverser malfunctioned. The delay was due to Contract Maintenance MEL'ing the right thrust reverser. During pre-flight I checked the logbook; Release; and stickers as well as looked up the MEL on my EFB. During this time the 'A' Flight Attendant informed me that a passenger was refusing to wear their mask and creating a scene and that the CSR had been called. Eventually the passenger was removed and an updated report was sent to the aircraft. During the distraction I neglected to click on the hyperlink in the MEL in the Maintenance portion labeled MEL SP#XX Thrust Reverser System. If I had I would have noticed on that a Circuit Breaker for the #2 Engine should have been pulled and collared. Upon landing in ZZZ2 I informed the outgoing Captain of the MEL. During my commute home I received a text from said Captain that he found the wrong CB had been collared and that he had written it up and ZZZ2 Maintenance was fixing the issue. Upon reviewing the SP#XX I can only assume that the CB for the #1 Engine had been pulled instead.
column123: Inbound Captain advised that they had received the aircraft late in ZZZ due to Thrust Reverser MEL applied in ZZZ1 on previous flight and then further delayed on their flight due to a Passenger refusing to comply with mask requirements.In reviewing the logbook I found that the MEL sticker in the front of the logbook was not completed. The MEL number was not entered; the Special procedures performed were not entered and the circuit breakers pulled and collared were not entered.   When I reviewed the logbook entry; the special procedures were references SP-XX.  I also observed C/B's  #2 Engine TR Sync Lock and #2 Engine TR INTLK pulled and collared.I then reviewed the MEL and SP-XX and discovered the following errors.1. SP XX calls for the #2 Engine TR Sync Lock c/b and the #2 Engine TR Control c/b to be pulled and collared.  the Control C/B was NOT collared as prescribed in SP XXnd the INTLK c/b WAS collared contrary to SP XX2. There was no MEL sticker placed on the Inoperative TR lever.3. There was no MEL sticker placed above the respected N1 gauge.I contacted Maintenance Control to confirm my understanding of the MEL regarding the incorrect Circuit Breakers and they confirmed the wrong circuit breaker had been pulled.  Notified ZZZ2 Maintenance and entered the discrepancy in the logbook. ZZZ2 Maintenance arrived and corrected the circuit breaker configuration and signed off the discrepancy I had entered. Missing information on the logbook sticker was also corrected.I have long felt that our MEL is VERY inadequate when it comes to circuit breaker identification.  In this particular instance the nomenclature is correct and was just applied incorrectly by the Mechanic; but if the C/B locations were included  it would have been much more apparent to the Mechanic as well as flight crew that the two C/B would not be immediately adjacent to each other.  I have brought this to the attention of Flight Ops previously with regards to other MEL's and have been advised that changes are slated for a future revision that has been delayed due to aircraft out of service returns; COVID and other issues. I also feel it should be reinforced to flight crews that MEL compliance is not solely the responsibility of the Maintenance department and that we should always verify (to the limits of our abilities) those aspects of MEL compliance which we have ready access to on each airplane we accept regardless of previous crews acceptance of the aircraft.

column121: About XX minutes after we reached our cruise altitude; my FO (First Officer) and I observed the level on our #2 Oil Qty gauge go from 11 to Y then Z; then blank rather quickly.  It had been normal up until then; we just caught the decrease at 11. After checking the QRC and QRH for Low Oil Qty to no avail; we noticed our #2 Oil Pressure dropping. It stabilized at 29 psi but fluctuated from XX to XY with 29 being the median amber band.  This continued for the remainder of the flight until TOD (Top of Descent).  I referenced the Engine Low Oil Pressure Checklist in the QRH on Page X.XX.  It states that if the oil pressure is at or below the redline: Go to the Engine Failure or Shutdown checklist on Page X.XY. The oil pressure never reached the redline; so the checklist stops there.  All other engine parameters were normal with no vibration.  My FO (First Officer) continued to fly and talk with ATC while I set up a phone patch with our Dispatcher as I decided that there was too much information to use ACARS.  I told them what was going on and that we were continuing on to ZZZ but we were also prepared to divert if need be later on.  They were in agreement as there was no need or requirement at this time to shut the engine down or divert.  I talked with the Flight Attendants and we had a good discussion about the situation.  I told them that our aircraft was operating just fine and that it seems that we have an indication issue and that I was not going to make a PA.  I also asked them if they could discretely look at the aft portion of the right hand engine to see if they saw any oil.  My FO (First Officer) and Flight Attendants did a great job along with our Dispatcher and Maintenance Control.  Later in the flight; our Dispatcher gave us single engine landing data for ZZZ.  Descending into ZZZ when the thrust levers were slowly retarded to idle; the oil pressure and qty actually increased.  By the time we were on final approach; the said indications were normal.

column121: We conducted the ZZZZZ4 arrival and joined the ILS XX approach from ZZZZZ [Intersection] as briefed. When the Captain contacted the Tower; the Controller cleared us to land XX Right. The Captain read back the clearance. I said; 'Can you confirm Controller wants us to land on the right? We're on the ILS XX Left.' The Captain confirmed with the Controller cleared to land on the right. The Controller responded 'Affirmative. XX Right; Cleared to land.' At the time; we were well above 1;000 feet in visual conditions with the runway in sight and; so I had no objection. I clicked off the autopilot and side-stepped to XX Right and we landed. No issues arose with ATC or any other traffic. The next day; the Captain reached out to me and we spoke over the phone. Captain learned that we had actually been cleared for the ILS XX Right approach and Captain intended to file a report. A couple of days later I was finally able to confirm that this was correct. We aren't able to determine if it was being read back correctly or incorrectly; but there was never a clarification type of response from ZZZ Approach. It's also important to bring up that the Captain was wearing a face mask throughout the flight operations which did contribute to difficulties in communication with myself and with ATC at various times during the trip. This likely was a contributing factor to our deviation. Another contributing factor was the violation of sterile cockpit below 18;000 feet by the Captain and myself. Personally; I was distracted by our conversation as well as the fact that Captain was wearing a mask during the flight.Complacency is also a factor as the ZZZZZ4 Arrival usually results in the ILS or visual to XX Left.I think our company needs to take a harder stance on mask-wearing during flight operations in the flight deck.  I recommend that the company forbids the use of masks by pilots during flight operations to ensure that communications are clear and effective. In this case; it can be assumed that the Captain was repeating the clearance saying 'XX Left' but the Controller did not hear it clearly and assumed Captain was saying XX Right. Therefore; Captain was never corrected and we continued with what we had expected in our heads. There were multiple points throughout our trip that ATC did not understand the Captain and asked who was calling or needed clarification on what Captain was saying because it was difficult to understand with the mask. I thought on several occasions throughout our trip that it was the Captain's choice to wear it but if we have an emergency situation that I really hope Captain would take it off so that effective communication could be established and maintained. An emergency situation did not occur; but clearly an issue did arise with our approach to our destination.
column123: ZZZ had a broken layer at 1;700 feet and we were expecting to do an approach. Descending into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ4 arrival we had set up for the ILS [Runway] XXL. We were assigned to join the ILS [Runway] XXR at ZZZZZ [Intersection] and then later cleared for the ILS XXR approach. We did not fly the ILS XXR. We flew the XXL approach and when we were on with Tower; we told them we were inbound on the ILS XXL. Tower cleared us to land XXR. By the time we contacted Tower we were out of the clouds and could see the runway. We verified two times that we were cleared to land XXR and not XXL. And Tower confirmed that we were to land XXR. Since we had visual on the runway; we side stepped and landed on XXR. We were probably at 1;500-1;600 feet AFE when we side stepped. We were confused as to why they had changed runways on us; but we knew that XXR was longer than XXL and that the landing speeds were the same and we were familiar with the airport. As we side stepped; I programmed in the ILS XXR so that we had a backup source even though we visually had the airport in sight. Later in the evening it still didn't sit right with me that we had a runway change that late; especially since we had been on an IFR approach. I realized we had in fact been assigned ILS XXR all the way back on with Approach. They never corrected me. So; I either read it back correctly but we were really hearing what we wanted to hear (ILS XXL) or they never corrected me and we all missed it. The approach was stable all the way through for XXL and the sidestep was done in a safe manner.I attribute not being sterile in the descent as a factor even though we were assigned to join ILS XXR at ZZZZZ prior to FL180. I would say complacency and expectancy were the primary factors. XXL wasn't closed and we were set that we would be doing the ILS XXL. It was also the last leg on the last day of our trip and we had had a long day. I had been up since 8 or 9am and we had flown 4 legs. This flight landed around XApm.I can say that I once again am reminded how serious our jobs are and that miss hearing a simple 'L' vs 'R' can be life changing. I can only say that I am thankful that this took place during a low traffic period and that we were able to maintain a safe condition. I'm honestly not too sure how to avoid this situation. I believe that writing down my clearances would assist in allowing me to verify and that maybe I need to make sure to turn my headset up so that I won't miss ATC.

column121: Captain advised we had a maintenance issue to have checked out before boarding our return flight to ZZZ. I believe pilots saw something had leaked under the engine; observed by FO walk around. Mechanic looked for AC left engine fuel leak suspected by pilots; after a period of time (I do not recall) mechanic could not find leak; he signed off on logbook. Pax began boarding; entry door was closed; on push back; FA's were doing safety demo when FA 4 was called over by passenger sitting in right window seat a few rows aft of the wing. Passenger stated something was dripping from wing. Demo was almost complete; FA 4 continued with demo then looked out to see pax concern. Upon seeing fluid dripping from several places along the underside of the wing; she went to get another FA to see the issue. FA 4 took FA 3 to see the dripping. FA 4 and 3 went to the forward entry area to inform FA 1; I was working FA 4 and standing next to FA 1 so I was also informed at this time. FA 1 called Captain (CA) to advise. Several minutes later we were notified by CA that we were going back to gate and need to disarm doors. Same mechanic (only one I saw) returned. Passengers remained onboard while he checked the issue further. It is my understanding he reported he still found no leak. Sometime later CA advised crew and passengers via PA that we would be starting engines at the gate to further troubleshoot the problem; he advised passengers to remain seated. I was told this test was done at the Captain's request; not the instruction of this mechanic. Engine test was completed; seat belt sign turned off; more time passed and it was decided to deplane passengers. While crew waited on the AC for info from the company as to our schedule and whether this plane was going to be able to be repaired; our FO showed CA a video of the fuel leak while the engine test was running. I saw this video; fuel was pouring from the engine like a running garden hose. CA stated he had no confidence in this mechanics ability to perform his job as he appeared that he had no idea how to handle it. While I was discussing this with CA he told me he asked the mechanic earlier to call Company Maintenance base for instruction. The mechanic told CA yes he did call Company. CA told me he was angry with this mechanic because he himself called Company and was told mechanic did not contact them.  Aircraft was taken out of service hours later.
column123: Upon arrival at Gate 1 in ZZZ; ground personnel connected to headset after engine shutdown to report a fluid leaking from number 1 (left) engine. He smelled his fingers; reported that it smelled like fuel; and asked me to investigate the fluid. The First Officer and I both investigated; and felt; to the best of our knowledge; that the fluid smelled like fuel. At that point; there was a puddle under the #1 engine; 3 feet in diameter; and fuel was dripping at a rate of 2-3 drips per second. As we stood there discussing; the dripping reduced to 1 drip every 4-5 seconds. The FO and I agreed that we were unfamiliar with any allowable drips on the 737 MAX LEAP engines; and I proceeded to the cockpit to make an entry in the aircraft logbook; dispatch a code in ACARS; and call the Maintenance Control to coordinate for a maintenance technician. The technician arrived and we conferred on the above information; and he proceeded to investigate and coordinate with the maintenance team in Company (my assumptions; although I did hear his telephone conversation at one point). After his investigation; he returned to the cockpit to inform me that he had opened the engine cowl; performed his checks; and found all valves ready for service. He signed off the write up and dispatched the aircraft for service. We boarded the passengers and pushed from the gate at XA:40. Push back was normal; engine start on engine #2 was normal. After push back was complete; we started engine #1. After engine start; and after the push crew had disconnected and given me a salute; ground personnel came back; pointing to the #1 engine. At the same time; the Cabin Crew called to alert me to a passenger that was reporting fluid leaking from the RIGHT side of the aircraft; and a Flight Attendant confirmed that we were leaking fluid. The report that fluid was leaking from the right was incongruous; and caused the FO and I a couple minutes to confer and investigate what that could be. We later found out the leak was in fact from the LEFT side; and was from the #1 engine. I did note in my investigation; that the #1 main tank fuel quantity differed from the #2 main tank fuel quantity by nearly 400 lbs; a discrepancy that didn't exist before pushback as I had noted the fuel during the Before Start checklist. By this time; the same ground coordinator who had reported the previous leak connected to headset and reported that we were again leaking fuel from the #1 engine. His report was that fuel was gushing out from under the engine cowl. The FO and I coordinated and elected to taxi back to the gate to expedite arrival and engine shutdown. The ground crew quickly assembled and we returned to the gate at approximately XA:48; and shut down both engines. I made another logbook entry and called Maintenance Control to inform them that we had returned to the gate and required the maintenance technician to perform more checks before we could depart. The maintenance technician returned; and we performed an engine run at the gate on the #1 engine; which resulted in identifying a large fuel leak; with the technician recording video. At this point the aircraft was taken out of service; and I began coordinating with station personnel and Crew Scheduling for subsequent actions.

column121: During single-engine taxi out; the A FA called the cockpit; informing us of passengers' non-compliance with the facemask policy.  The decision was made to return to the gate. As we taxied back toward the Ramp; I coordinated with the Captain; advising that I felt it was appropriate to perform an After Landing flow prior to returning to the gate. Captain agreed; and I accomplished the flow.  While holding for a gate; and on the apron with the parking brake set; the A FA called back to the cockpit; advising that the passengers were now willing to comply and that the three FAs were comfortable with continuing the flight.At this point we re-accomplished a Before Taxi flow (as appropriate for our single engine taxi configuration); then ran a Before Taxi Checklist.  We then coordinated with ATC to proceed with a taxi clearance for departure. The Number 1 engine was started and the rest of the taxi and takeoff proceeded uneventfully.  Once airborne; I noticed that we had departed with the autobrake selector in the OFF position. As I thought about the sequence of events leading to that I thought of two things:  placing that switch to RTO takes place in the Captain's Before Start flow.  I also recalled that when I performed the After Start flow (following the Passenger incident); I placed the Window Heat switches to ON; another item that is normally accomplished in the Captain's Before Start flow.Clearly; in our unique situation; a Before Taxi flow; followed by a Before Taxi Checklist was insufficient to reposition all switches to their appropriate positions prior to taxi and takeoff. Of note; neither of us felt rushed; and we both felt that we used good CRM to methodically think through our situation before continuing; yet in the end; something was missing. I've referenced the manuals; looking for a procedure that would have trapped our errors; but am still left wondering.  Since we started the original taxi single engine and never shutdown that engine; the procedure in Flight Ops Manual never entered our minds; yet that guidance probably would've caught the error.Non-standard Ops lead to inadvertent takeoff with auto brakes selected off.
column123: On taxi out; the A FA called to tell me that there was a family being non-compliant regarding the face mask policy. I made the decision to taxi back to the gate. I asked the FO to complete the After Landing Checklist. While we were waiting for a gate; the FA called to tell us; 'Never mind; the issue is resolved.' At that point; we completed the Before Taxi Checklist and taxied to the runway. After takeoff; the FO pointed out that RTO switch was not re-selected to 'armed.' Our unique situation made it impossible for autobrake re-selection to occur.In this situation; our normal checklist does not catch the error. I should have triple checked everything because our routine taxi out was interrupted.RTO reengage missed during a taxi back to the gate and subsequent cancellation of that.

column121: DFW has an odd system of ground-frequency assignment for the east side of the airport; that has long concerned pilots for the very reason this incident highlighted. Outbounds from the remote; E Terminal spots of XX to YY are often assigned the discrete Ground frequency of 121.80; even though all other east-side operations for the apt are issued 121.65. However; those of us assigned 121.80 are never switched to the 'main' frequency of .65 that everyone else is operating on.On this day; as we taxied out we were assigned 121.80; but the First Officer; to his credit; decided to take the initiative to also pull up 121.65 on the other radio; so we could hear what was being said to and by the other aircraft operating in the same area and taxiways and the same controller. Northbound on Taxiway K approaching Taxiway Z there was a B737 waiting to pull out. Ground issued instructions to them over 121.65 to pull out ahead of us; and then transmitted to us on the same frequency to give way. The only reason we were aware of these transmissions was because we were monitoring both frequencies. We gave way to the B737 without incident and everyone went on their way none the wiser; except us. Had we not been monitoring 121.65 but just on our assigned frequency of 121.80; there's every reason to believe both aircraft would have gotten much closer together before the ground controller might have discovered his error; and ultimately; it was not his error but the assignment of two; discrete frequencies to different aircraft taxiing on the same taxiway.

The FO (First Officer) was Pilot Flying and while he was flying the approach I noticed what I thought were two birds just to the right of the aircraft at around 9 o'clock but outside the course. I made the FO aware of this and continued to keep scanning for more birds in the area since the first one I saw was well clear of our course. However at 2;300 ft. and 0.5NM past ELREN on the ILS 4 the two objects were actually drones that past off our right hand side that were the size of two big birds. I noticed the two were indeed drones because I saw the propellers on two of them and they had a shiny black finish on them. I also checked the TCAS to see if they were there; but it didn't show them on the screen. I relayed this information to HOU tower and told them what altitude and where they were. Upon landing and taxing off the runway and contacting ground; I was given a phone number to call the tower to give them more information on the description of the drones; and where I spotted them on the approach.My suggestion is to always keep scanning the area for any hazards while flying even if the TCAS system doesn't show anything in the area.

column121: Pushback was delayed due to catering (and vehicles impeding the catering truck from approaching the aircraft).  Following push clearance; the tug began the push but we came to a stop after approx. 15 sec. I thought perhaps something crossed behind us and we would resume the push.  But; after a few more seconds; the tug driver said that a catering truck wasn't moving.  That seemed odd; and the Captain and I wondered why a catering truck wouldn't clear a moving aircraft.  That's when the Captain looked through his side window; over his shoulder and told me; 'THAT'S why the truck isn't moving - it's sitting under our wingtip!' We hadn't felt anything and the tug driver was asked if we were touching.  He said that he couldn't tell.  A crowd gathered.  I informed ramp of our situation and our intent to remain in position to investigate. A maintenance rep came on interphone and let us know it was difficult to determine how close the wingtip was to the roof of the truck.  It was judged safe to set brakes. After some time; it was decided to let air out of the truck's tires.  Personnel climbed atop the truck and after getting a closer look; the truck was moved.  No visible contact/damage was noted but the possibility was mentioned that the winds were moving the aircraft slightly and the wingtip may have bounced off the roof and that may have not been enough to show damage but that an inspection would be the best course of action.  We were cleared to be pulled forward to the gate and the aircraft was taken out of service and the crew and passengers deplaned to the aircraft at the adjoining gate.  The remainder of the flight was uneventful.Since we were being pushed straight back; we did not see the events leading up to the potential contact.  It would seem that a combination of catering truck driver and wing walker inattention may have contributed.[Suggest] Company communications to [the catering company] and maintenance re-iterating the need to be vigilant.
column123: About 60 feet into a routine pushback; the aircraft stopped.  The Tow Driver told us a 'catering truck driver is refusing to move.'  I asked if I should set the Parking Brake.  The Tow Driver said 'No.'  I looked out the left window and saw a catering truck with no driver in the cab.  I called Ramp Control on the radio to report the situation.     I looked out the window again to see a Maintenance Technician on the catering truck's over-the-cab loading platform.  He was leaning on the railing to look toward the aft-right side of the truck.  I opened the aircraft L2 Window to get a better view.  I saw the Left Wing apparently resting on the middle; top-right of the back portion of the catering truck.  I saw numerous Ground Crew and Maintenance personnel walking around the catering truck gesturing at the apparent contact point.     A Maintenance Supervisor saw me looking out the window and got on the Ground Interphone to tell me what was going on.  She said they thought there was actually no contact with the catering truck but couldn't be sure until they employed an operable hydraulic work lift - the first one they tried was inoperative.  I asked how big/small the gap was.  She thought the wing was about an inch from touching the truck; but the wind was causing the aircraft to gently rock; possibly bouncing the wing off the top of the truck.     After many minutes; a plan emerged to deflate the tires of the catering truck and tow it out of the way; preventing any possible further contact with the wing as the wind blew.  After the catering truck was clear; the Maintenance Supervisor got back on the Ground Interphone to tell us the aircraft was being taken out of service as a precaution and a replacement Ground Crew would tow us back to the gate for deplaning.  We were not to set the parking brake until safely at the gate.  Company Operations and Maintenance coordinated a different aircraft for us to continue the flight.     The tow was uneventful.  Once parked; we ran the Shutdown Checklist.  Maintenance Technicians boarded and asked us to not shut down the aircraft.  They also invited the First Officer and me to go outside and get on the work lift to inspect the wing.  To my eye; there was absolutely no indication of any kind that the wing had contacted the catering truck; however; I know that painted panels of modern materials can deform; return to shape; and not show outward signs of damage.  Not that it was my decision; but I concurred with Maintenance in taking the aircraft out of service.     Passengers and crew boarded the new aircraft and departed uneventfully.Cause Unknown.  I would only be speculating on events that occurred out of my view.I can only speculate how this event occurred; so I cannot provide prevention suggestions.

column121: Very light 757; 16.7 on the fuel; almost empty payload; operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1; daytime VMC. High winds in effect. Vref was 111; Vapp is 126. I was PF (Pilot Flying); and decided to fly faster on final since we were in a light 757; and my limited experience with this situation led to this. Missed approach procedures were reviewed multiple times as other jets had to go around several times. Runway was dry; over XX;000 feet long; plenty of distance. I decided to fly a new Vapp of 135; as the jet was having problems controlling the airspeed since the winds were about 060/22G30. Our divert was ZZZ1; and we knew that several aircraft attempting to land had to execute missed approaches. All this into account; I decided to fly around 135 KIAS; as this felt like a more stable approach. The airspeed wouldn't stabilize safely below this number; as it was all over the place and I had to fight with the autothrottles to maintain within 15 kts of the initial Vapp of 126--it just wouldn't stabilize at a speed below 135. My reasoning is that since I was light; in a 757; long runway; daytime VMC; and super gusty winds; I had plenty of room to stop safely without encountering hot brakes or running out of concrete. We landed uneventfully; although long; as I touched down past the touchdown zone--this was the only cost of flying faster; and I felt it was worth it; all things considered. We landed and were able to taxi clear on taxiway; no problem.  If I was in a 767 or a heavier 757; I wouldn't have even thought of this; and we would have flown the Vapp given; for better or worse.  Were we technically unstable? Yes; I believe we were. Were we safer; in my eyes; flying a more stable approach with the winds we had? Yes; I also believe this to be the case. We never had a windshear warning; and we never felt unsafe; but looking back; I was in the wrong; even though I felt more stable; which led to a safer approach. However; the AOM procedures don't allow for this; so I was technically in the wrong; even though the airplane flew better and safer; in my opinion. Next time; I will fly the Vapp given; and if we have to divert; then so be it.

column121: Since COVID; these particular international schedules have been in a lot of flux. Most sequences; up until now; have been 'rockets' where we only get to rest a relatively short amount of time during the day after an all-night flight; and then fly back all night. I have written about this before; and this is to reiterate: these sequences are sub-optimal in terms of safety due to the limited rest. The threat on these sequences is NOT a virus; it's the cumulative fatigue after being up for two straight nights. There is no reason not to make ALL these flights have a longer sleep opportunity with a 30 plus hour layover.  Three times in the last 2 months we lined up for the wrong runway in ZZZ after the double all-nighter. Fortunately; someone caught the error before it was critical; but it is reflective of the fact that the three of us are sleep-deprived. In this aircraft category; you have an older pilot group to begin with. Give us the opportunity to get enough rest.Upon arrival in ZZZ; I was extremely tired; and felt my ability to monitor was degraded.Schedule all these international trips as longer layovers. It's a safety issue; pure and simple.

column121: On SID's; when assigned climb via clearances; and when the top altitude is higher than the flies altitude; it is expected to climb to the restriction; top of SID. This particular SID says in the top altitude box; FL230 is the top. Upon further reading; it should say FL230 or filed altitude; whichever is lower; as the SID says in the textual description. Perhaps this is an issue with Jeppesen charts.  Once past the 10;000 foot hold down at MUGBE; the Captain set FL230 as the expected clearance. Just before passing FL200; Captain queried ATC to confirm FL230; but received a response approaching FL220. A clearance was given to descend FL200; and we complied. It was then that we reviewed the textual part of the chart and noticed our error. The expectation that other SID's do not include this exception is biggest cause. Also; not detailed re-reading lengthy textual descriptions on SID's every single use; contributes. ATC clearances can include 'climb via; except maintain...'. This clearance would easily eliminate this oversight and airports like DEN; should have knowledge of the departures to aid in this. Also; Jeppesen charts should include these little nuances in the top altitude box on the SID; since this isn't true of all SID's.

column121: Normal departure and flight enroute to ZZZ with thunderstorm approaching ZZZ airport on arrival from the west. Radar vectors for ILS XXL for approach; multiple speed adjustments from ATC on approach and no reports of wind gusts on initial arrival from ATC with winds 180/6 from ATIS. Storm had moved over field when on approach. On short final there was an RVR (Runway Visual Range) update from recall of greater than 5;000 RVR and moderate to heavy rain but no winds passed from recall. VMC around 1;100 feet and could see right and center runway but then went into torrential rain downpour around 400-500 feet on short final where Captain made an EFIS lights call and then I shortly after picked up runway lights and landing environment just prior to minimums and was a little high but was adjusting in close. Around 30-40 feet we had an instantaneous airspeed loss of around 10kts and at that time I had decided to go-around but with the airspeed loss and instantaneous loss of lift we touched down as go-around decision was made. We had a semi-hard landing and bounced and go-around selected all simultaneously. We were slow to put the speed brake back in after touching down but did eventually secure it and maintained attitude as we executed go around. Go-around procedures were completed airborne. Vectored back around by ATC for uneventful approach; landing and taxi in. The Captain and I both did a walk around of the aircraft post flight to ensure integrity of aircraft and check tail skid as a precaution but didn't notice the skid was ground down as we later were informed from the Director of Operations and Maintenance. We debriefed the event. Windshear/airspeed loss at low altitude while simultaneously executing go-around and didn't maintain proper go-around pitch once touching down as indicated from tail skid damage. Quicker reaction from crew with go-around with instantaneous airspeed loss and loss of lift and maintain proper attitude of aircraft on touchdown when executing go-around. Follow rules to live by; do not make large control inputs when in flare/go-around close to ground.

column121: Climbing through 16;000 feet to FL 200 we experienced a high whistle sound from the front of the airplane. I felt pressure on my ears; nose; and head and had the air pushed out of my lungs. We identified a cabin depressurization and I reached for my O2 mask. I took a long inhale from the oxygen and then proceeded with additional memory items. The Captain began an priority descent. I reached for the Pax oxygen switch with my right hand and the PA button with my left hand. I communicated with the Captain that I was going off comms to tell Pax to put on oxygen masks. The Captain stated 'Wait. They are going to be fine here in 2-3 seconds and I don't want to replace the masks.' This occurred around 13;500 feet. So I did not complete memory items per the Captain's instruction. I contacted ATC and advised we were on an priority descent because of depressurization. We received a new assigned altitude of 10;000 feet. The Cabin started to repressurize around 11;000. ATC asked if we wished to declare priority handling and the Captain declined. We were able to continue to ZZZ without incident.There were several deviations from our normal operating procedures that concern me. First the disregard from memory items on the checklist. Second; the captain did not have his O2 mask plugged in. He believed he could plug it in fast enough if needed and that he doesn't plug it in because he forgets to unplug it after a flight. This caused a delay in performing a memory item. The Captain was able to plug his oxygen mask in but never donned it during controlled handling decent. Also; we did not formally ask for priority handling with ATC. We could not diagnose the problem for the rapid depressurization so we were unaware of what triggered it. I suggested declaring priority handling to cover our bases if anything else occurred. This flight had already been abnormal with the priority descent. The Captain disagreed saying the problem is over. Lastly; I do not believe the cockpit acceptance was completed for this flight. It is typical that the FO (First Officer) does the walk around and security check while the Captain is completing the acceptance. While doing the walk around it is very apparent that the shaker pusher test is being tested from outside the airplane. You can hear the shaking on the horizontal stabilizer. I did not hear it that morning. Also upon startup; the Captain found a popped circuit breaker on his side for De-Ice. I'm not sure when the circuit breaker popped but no de-icing equipment was on so I assume it was before startup. This is another missed item on the acceptance checklist. Now; these deviations did not cause the priority handling to occur but they could have added on to make the event worse.

column121: We were at FL350 in cruise between ZZZ and ZZZ1. ATC had given us left and right deviations and ZZZ1 when able. The radar was not painting much at the time but we were trying to deviate around what we saw on the radar. At the time everything was obscured and we were in the clouds. We did pop out just a little before the front and could make our way around a couple of the darker areas but it was not possible to get around all of it. As we crossed the front we started to get some shear in the winds that caused the airspeed to start to go up and down quite a bit. The autopilot then kicked off so my FO (First Officer) took manual control and the airspeed and altitude varied a lot as he flew the aircraft. The turbulence only got to a moderate level at most of the time but the downdrafts and updrafts made it difficult to keep any specific altitude or airspeed. Soon we hit a downdraft that was much worse than the rest and we were unable to maintain altitude even in climb power. I took control of the aircraft and told him to tell ATC we were descending because we were unable to maintain altitude at the time. We ended up descending about 1;000 feet and were able to level off at FL340 once we were through it. At the time I was just worried about keeping airspeed and not stalling the aircraft. Once we were clear ATC cleared us down to FL330 and we continued on to ZZZ2. At the time of the initial shear we were talking and did not detect the variations in airspeed that were the telling signs of the shear coming. At the time I did not declare an emergency but looking back at it I would now because we were unable to maintain altitude at the time.
column123: While enroute we were navigating around some weather that was obscured. We were communicating with ATC about the best route to take around the weather. We were not painting much if any precipitation at all angles on the radar. We were on left and right deviations and ZZZ when able. Just after passing the ZZZ1 VOR at FL350. We started to experience some light turbulence which continued to worsen. I turned on continuous ignition and continued to maneuver around the weather the best we could. The VSI (Vertical Speed Indicator) started a small trend of 120 FPM down. column121: I completed a thorough walk around and told the Captain there was a lot of ice on the aircraft and we were going to need to deice. I also recommended we take off with full Anti-ice on and the Captain agreed after a minute. We did a full deice type 1 and 4 everything went as planned. I ran the cold weather cold soaked check list to prepare for deicing. Once Deicing was completed I received all the pertinent information from iceman and wrote it down on a TOLD card. I then completed the deicing check list and we called ground for taxi. I made sure all the deice check list was completed and we taxied out for departure. Myself and the Captain talked about leaving the flaps and slats up or down while taxiing and due to having such a long hold over time we chose to lower flaps to proper flap setting for takeoff knowing that our hold over time would be reduced by 50%. As we pulled onto the runway and did our final configuration check we had a no take off and the Captain adjusted the FMS info for takeoff and the neck check was good to go. We were cleared for takeoff and I did all my flows and the before takeoff check list. Power was set and we began to roll and immediately the Captain was going left and right on the runway due to the winds being so strong and at this point I put my feet on the pedals getting ready to help the Captain. We reached V1 and I called out V1 then rotate. As soon as we rotated next thing I know is we are going left of the runway due to the winds being so strong at this point I don't remember if I called out positive rate and this allowing the Captain to call gear up. The next thing I remember is calling out acceleration and the Captain calling out flight level change and auto pilot on. At this point we are getting bumped all around due to the severe weather.  The Captain then says flaps and I raise them watching the airspeed as we are bumped around.  I call out speed since we are getting close to the speed warning and the Captain does not have time to get the nose up higher to stop this warning from happening then we notice all of a sudden we have a packs off message and the Captain says the packs are off and I state they are on.  He resets them but to no avail.  They continue to show off.  At this time the Captain says the gear is down and raises it while we are being thrown all around. I ask ATC if we can level off at 11;000 and they clear us to level off at 11;000.  We are still getting pounded and unable to maintain 11;000.  I reach for the QRH as the Captain calls for the QRH between 11;000 and 13;000 the packs off warning message goes away and due to already being at 13;000; ATC asks if we would like to continue to climb and I state yes after looking over at the Captain and he nodded his head to say yes. I then ask about the weather and they state the weather will calm down above 20;000. We are then cleared to climb to 23;000 and I say to the Captain when we are above 20;000 I'm sorry I don't recall if I called out positive rate allowing the Captain to call for gear up and the Captain responds that he did call for gear up and he always does. But I don't recall any call out for gear up. I would really like to hear the recording just to see what all was said while we were being battered around. Everything ended up normal from this point on.  Once we landed our flight attendant stated the passengers were not happy with the take off and were screaming.Unfortunately; there is not much we could have done on this take off that we did not already do. We had already talked to ground to see if other aircraft had taken off and they said everything was fine with the first 3 departures. We checked the winds with ACARS including gusts and ACARS showed the take off to all be within tolerances. I wish I remembered if I had called out positive rate and had heard gear up but I did not and don't remember.

column121: We were approaching BZN; planning RNAV RNP 30 Approach. When we checked in with Big Sky Approach they assigned us the RNAV A Approach and cleared us direct SURPE. I typed it in manually and we proceeded direct. In my search in the FMS for that approach; it was not in the database. We had it in the Jeppessen FD Pro; but not in the database. Prior to reaching SURPE we became VFR; called the field and completed a visual approach. Having it in the Jeppessen charts and not in the database in the FMS is not cool. Leads one down a path to red. ATIS is not digital so our awareness of what approach is being used was late; late; late in the flight.  Brought us into the red. Into the red at an incredibly critical phase of flight is also not cool. Set up a liaison to make the airports like this aware of our fleet capabilities. Example: we have charts in the Jeppessen; but not in the FMS database so don't assign said approach.
column123: We were inbound to BZN VOR expecting vectors to the final portion of RNAV (RNP) Runway 30.  We were planning to request direct JAPER intersection for the balance of the approach.   The airport was reporting VFR conditions but we were still IMC in the descent.  We were handed off to Big Sky Approach about 20 DME from the airport.  Without given a chance to request JAPER we were directed to proceed to SURPE intersection on the RNAV (GPS)-A. That's when our situational awareness went red.   We accepted the approach as it was listed in our FD Pro.  I manually put SURPE in the legs page and descended to 10;000 feet as directed.  The First Officer tried to pull up the RNAV (GPS) - A in the FMC but it was not there.  Luckily we broke out into VMC approaching SURPE and completed a visual approach.I can think of three. First; the controllers need to be aware of which approaches they can and cannot assign.  Secondly; if an approach is published in FD Pro but not available in the FMC that discrepancy should be clearly spelled out. Finally; I made an assumption that if a procedure is in the FD Pro it would also be in the FMC.Big Sky needs to know which of their approaches are not in our FMC's.  This would help them immensely to plan for our arrivals.  We also need to complete an internal audit of all airports we serve to either remove or annotate in the  pages which FD Pro approaches are not found in the FMC.  I will now compare each approach in FD Pro to the FMC when arriving at a unfamiliar airport as I never want to be trapped in this situation again.

column121: During boarding there were 2 JS riders; plus nonrevs with seats; plus working crew in the aft galley which I attempted to work around to complete duties. There was some impediment. During MX (Maintenance) delay a NONREV from Cabin C came to aft galley and argued with me about why it was not OK for her to charge her cell phone with the vacuum outlet in the galley. I advised her of the safety policy regarding that. After demo I was in aft galley when I smelled strong oil and oil exhaust smell that extended a few rows into the cabin past Row 31; including lav. It seemed to dissipate after several minutes with forward movement of plane which is common so did not report then. During cruise a pax (passenger) from Row 33 came aft to complain of nausea and headache asking for water and pain med and denied having symptoms prior to flight and complained of fumes bothering him. I smelled oil in the aft galley area intermittently throughout flight; and was experiencing some mild symptoms myself but still did not write report on paper prior to calling CA (Captain) to keep him informed. All 3 MC crew were in galley when pax complained. FA (Flight Attendant) 4 provided water and med to pax. FA3 and FA4 both went forward for pilot breaks and cabin surveillance AFTER I called the FD about this issue so I assumed FA1 would be informed by someone else including the CA; but he was not. My mistake which I apologized to him for. During cruise we were experiencing turbulence in the aft so I waited several minutes before calling the FD to notify we were experiencing turbulence in the aft and to request SB (seat belt) sign on if they felt it was appropriate. During cruise I went forward to provide CDW about aft lav to FA1 but he was in the lav for an extended period of time and I had MC duties to attend to so I slipped the form under the FD door and called the FD to tell them same. At gate arrival a stronger smell of oil entered the aft galley area and cabin and lav so I called the FD; for a 4th time; with out calling FA1 first; to confirm AFT doors showed unarmed; asking to vent aft galley and report the very strong fumes of oil. He asked me to fill out the info on paper and to see him to debrief together and asked who all was involved. I tried to do an ALLCALL from the aft but was unsuccessful in reaching the entire crew with one call so tried to do individual calls. I was only able to reach FA3 and FA1 who began to yell at me about my poor CRM and said he only found out when the FD door opened and the CA said something about it. Both the CA and FA1 said I did not follow CRM procedures and said only the FA1 is to call the FD on cabin issues. I was unaware that was the case even for safety situations; including turbulence in the aft; that I was primarily aware of and apologized. FA1 accused me of intentionally creating conflict and of having a pattern of same. Each of the last 3 times I have flown with him he asks me what I want to be when I grow- up in front of passengers; another time we flew together he yelled at me for making a PA about the seatbelt sign prior to XA:00 as FA2 because he thought the IFM said XB:00 not XC:00 and people were sleeping; and only the FA1 makes announcements. I suppose this factored into why I was directly calling the FD and not using the loud interphone to call FA1 as well. And why I did not opt to make the turbulence without seat belt sign on announcement instead. I can't speak to why no one else told him about fumes and pax complaint. There was an opportunity during the crew briefing to establish cabin to FD flow that I think was missed. With multiple employee pre-boards and a full flight we were all highly tasked during the pre-boarding and boarding processes I have experienced both FD wanting only to speak with FA1 and stating such and also being invited to call with any safety concerns regardless of position in cabin. In my main concern and focus for safety of flight I unintentionally possibly violated CRM flowon this flight.

column121: During cruise; 3 hours in the flight; I heard a loud noise that sounded like a stall/chug. I was near L1 door. I asked the A FA (Flight Attendant); he heard it but he didn't. Later on; I went to the back of the plane. Aft galley & told the C FA what I felt and she told me she felt something 'unusual' on the floor of the aft galley; probably about the same time I was in the fwd galley. We decided to call the pilots (called them twice) but they didn't pick up. We would try again a few minutes later; figured they were busy with the sound but just then; they called for a lavatory break. We ended up forgetting to notify them. During decent; wheels down; the C FA & I felt the aft of the aircraft chug a few times and make the strange popping sounds. We both looked at each other and decided to talk about it upon landing. When we landed; we both agreed it was 'abnormal' so we called the pilots when we were disarmed and at the gate. After calling the pilots and explaining to them; the Captain told us to go to the flight deck and close the flight deck door. He ended up explaining to us that they did feel the abnormal chugs and thought it was a bird strike and didn't know until we were on the ground that the engine had failed (showed us on the monitor a red icon on the engine) but didn't really explain other wise. Myself and the rest of the crew didn't feel that great about the debrief. The A & C were able to go but the D and I had to continue on to ZZZ. That night; going to bed; I realized how serious the situation was and made me feel uneasy. On date; after landing in ZZZ1; a different Captain was talking about the incident because earlier in the day; there was an emergency landing by another airline and the [type aircraft]. Anyhow; when he realized I was on the ETOPS flight; he mentioned that we were lucky to be alive. He did an amazing job explaining that our situation was a 'compressor failure' and many things can cause that but the biggest concern was that after leaving ZZZ2 ; the engine was sending pings to maintenance notifying of the engine overheating...the pilots decided to continue on to ZZZ3. Knowing that bit of information; and then to experience the compressor failure and no good CRM; I am frustrated; annoyed and somewhat uneasy flying to ZZZ2 now after hearing unfamiliar sounds about three hours into flight (the C FA heard these sounds as well); I called the pilots at about 3 hours into flight but didn't get a hold of them. I then forgot until the next set of sounds were heard at gear down. Upon parking at the gate; I called the pilots and I was instructed to talk to them with the door shut when I go to the front. After all guests were off the plane; I explained to the pilots again what sounds we heard and the Captain told me (then the rest of the crew) that the sounds heard were those in line of what is heard of a 'bird strike'. He then mention something to the fact that the engine went off line (he said this because I pointed out that the engine symbol on the instrument panel had a red square on it) about two times and we all were then confused and he said we shouldn't worry about it.  Better CRM and think about the whole ready; safe; go action plan. There should have been a way better debrief by the pilots. After an event like this; I shouldn't be the one pushing for answers when I felt uneasy.

column121: I was seated on the jumpseat on flight deck and the First Officer demanded I wear a face mask after pushback per policy; while they both (Pilot Crew Members) did not; which is inconsistent with Safety and general communication requirements requested of a Jumpseat Crew Member. Here is why:To ride on the jumpseat we must be a current licensed pilot; with current medical license and fit to perform duties.1. We are consistently asked to be a second set of eyes. Because I wear glasses where I wear my face mask my glasses fog up. I'm unable to see instruments and other traffic.2.The face masks impedes verbal communication with the other Crew Members if needing to intervene because the Crew is wearing headsets; jet noise and unable to effectively hear or read lips. This is well documented in studies.3.  The time to useful consciousness is limited. Having glasses and face mask impedes putting on O2 mask on in the event of a Rapid Decompression. The flight deck door is locked; we have NO rubber jungle that falls and I'm solely responsible for my own Safety to get my mask on. This is an impediment to Safety as a Jumpseater. I am not treated the same as the operating Crew Members; even though I'm asked to be a Safety Observer.
