column121: Out of an abundance of caution and to the best of my memory I can recall that shortly after the initial climb and in a clean configuration the Captain alerted me that he had some difficulty with the electric trim on his control yoke. I observed that it was indeed intermittent. After I completed the Climb Checklist we tried some trouble-shooting with both autopilots and my trim switch. With no caution lights; I referred to the QRH to help diagnose the issue with the proper checklist. During this time the Captain was contacting Dispatch and Maintenance for assistance while I talked to ATC. At some point in this process we were able to notice that my autopilot would engage and I became the Pilot Flying. We stopped the climb and slowed the aircraft. The Captain proceeded with the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative Checklist which calls to cutout both stab trim cutout switches and manually trim the aircraft. As I flew manually we elected to advise ATC and return to ZZZ. The Captain informed the Company; ATC; flight attendants and passengers and offered his assistance to me. I vaguely recall that during the descent a Speed Trim Fail light illuminated as a result from the cutout switches being selected to cutout. There was some discussion that we may or may not be over the max landing weight upon arrival and therefore an AML entry was entered after landing along with a Speed Trim Fail; Stabilizer Trim Failure; and inoperative autopilots entries. I performed a safe Flaps 15 landing [and] all passengers and crew deplaned safely with no injuries. I can attest that the training I have received was very beneficial to the successful outcome from this event. I believe as a crew we worked the problem out very well with the strategy and am thankful for the Captain's knowledge; professional conduct; and reassurance to everyone for a safe outcome. The mechanic did state that perhaps the event may have been caused by a software issue.
column123: During climbout and after cleanup; I noticed that the electric stabilizer trim was intermittent. Then it became unresponsive. At this point the Speed Trim system appeared to actuate for about half a second and never actuated again. We attempted to engage the A autopilot. It wouldn't engage. The B autopilot did engage and I passed control of the aircraft to the FO (First Officer). We conducted the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' checklist. Within about 5 minutes of engaging the B; it disengaged itself and the FO hand flew the aircraft for the remainder of the flight. We advised ATC and returned to ZZZ. We selected Runway XX and requested a 15 mile final to get fully configured and trimmed as well as possible. The FO was able to manually trim the aircraft without difficulty. During the descent; at about 12;000-15;000 feet; the 'Speed Trim Fail' light illuminated. We conducted a Flaps 15 landing and taxied back to the gate. I made an AML entry for the Stab Trim; Speed Trim Fail light and for possible overweight landing.I think the focus of the MAX simulator session was helpful in dealing with this situation.
column124: Reporter stated they were unable to manually trim the aircraft until the trim cutout switches were engaged. Post flight; it was learned that the electric stabilizer trim  failure was possibly due to a relay which had failed.

column121: VNAV (vertical navigation) would not arm before takeoff. Because I was flying the Max for the first time I considered this may be something different or weird about the new airplane. After writing this up on the ground the mechanics did a reboot of the airplane and these problems seemed to go away but now we experienced the failure of the Captain's FMC multiple times.  Upon arrival at the airplane that morning I found the FMC switch in the 'R' position instead of the normal 'BOTH.' During preflight; with the FMC programmed; I engaged LNAV (lateral navigation) and VNAV with the Master on my (First Officer) side. A few minutes later I noticed VNAV disengaged. I reengaged it. A few minutes later I noticed it disengaged again. This time I told the Captain and he said he noticed it as well. This was my first flight in the Max so I chalked it up as a Max-ism. I thought it would 'fix itself' airborne. The Captain and I discussed it and decided to just proceed and attempt to engage it airborne after multiple attempts on the ground to keep it engaged. This was the only discrepancy I noticed on the ground. Once airborne we did attempt to engage VNAV but it would disengage within a couple seconds. I climbed out in LVL CHG (level change mode) all the way to FLXXX when ALT HLD (altitude hold) engaged. After a few minutes at cruise the Captain decided we should try switching everything to his side so we switched to CMD A and engaged VNAV. After this we had no further issues with VNAV. We agreed I would continue to be pilot flying utilizing the A autopilot and the master on his side.  During cruise shortly after engaging VNAV as previously discussed I began noticing weird things on my ND (navigation display) and PFD. On the PFD on my speed tape the minimum and maximum maneuvering amber bars would simultaneously shoot out.  The minimum would jump up about 8 knots while the maximum would simultaneously shoot down about 2 knots and then immediately retract. Also the ND would ratchet instead of making smooth movements. This was especially noticeable in turns. Lastly we noticed ANP (actual navigation performance) going as high as 1.3. By the end of the flight I would say it was back in the normal range; less than 0.1. I flew the STAR in LNAV/VNAV to the bottom and performed a visual [approach] with no other issues. We wrote this up on the ground doing our best to explain this to Maintenance. The Captain and I decided if we set up the box and selected the master on my side and engaged VNAV and it stayed engaged we would be satisfied and then switch everything to his side. After boarding was complete and we were just about to shut the door both FMC's blanked with a MAP and VTK (vertical track) on Captain's PFD. We called Maintenance back out for another 'reset'. We then closed the door and pushed back. As I began to start the engine we had the same failure again on the FMC. Captain called Maintenance and they told us to return to gate.  By this point the Captain and I agreed we would not be taking this airplane. With its previous history that we learned about in previous log pages; along with the multiple issues we experienced; combined with the complicated process involving an MEL for both FMCs and an early wake up we agreed it would not be the safest course of action. Hindsight is 20/20 and looking back armed with the information I have now I would have never left the gate in ZZZ.
column123: During my preflight I noticed the FO (First Officer) engaging VNAV and it disengaging a few minutes later. He tried a couple of times and it would not stay engaged.  He told me he found the FMC switch in the Both on R and switched it back to normal. We discussed waiting for final numbers and trying again.  It continued not to engage after final numbers and I decided to push back and start and try again on taxi.  A couple times during taxi we tried to engage it and would only last seconds. We discussed departing old school bug up N1 flaps 1 and try again airborne knowing the jet can fly without VNAV.  We both were comfortable with that decision. It was his leg and the F/D (flight director) was on his side.  There were no other discrepancies. As we rolled out on the runway and were cleared for take off I engage VNAV and it stayed on until 500 feet and disconnected. I am guessing it held on with TOGA (takeoff/go-around). We tried engaging VNAV a couple times in climb and after level off at FLXXX with no success.  We were on autopilot CMD B (command B). At that point I selected CMD A and then engaged VNAV and it stayed on. We decided to leave it on CMD A.  The remainder of the flight VNAV remained engaged. It was the FO's first time in the Max and my second leg so he remained the pilot flying using CMD A. About the same time we were switching sides we noticed on his speed tape the minimum and maximum amber bars would jump up from the bottom about 5 knots and down from the top about 2-3 knots. Also the ND (navigation display) would glitch from left to right 5-7 degrees. Both of those continued the entire flight; the ND would glitch more in a turn. All 3 airspeeds were matched the entire flight and Captain's side had no issues of glitching and we received no cautions about airspeed.  A little while later we received a scratch pad message that I don't remember exact wording but was about FMC position when I looked at all latitude and longitudes FMC; IRSL (left inertial reference system); IRSR; GPSL (GPS left); GPSR were normal within a couple of decimal points looking normal to me. I then noticed the ANP was 1.3 and bouncing between 1.2 and 1.3.  I monitored that and it started to decrease back to normal around .03; .02 but it took 20 to 30 minutes and would move between .02 and .11.  Towards the end of the flight it seemed to be more steady around .03; .02. No other scratch pad messages and the flight had no other issues. We landed [and] I wrote up the problems and we both talked to the 3 maintenance technicians to relay as much info as we could. I know that they powered down the aircraft and did operation tests that all passed and signed off the aircraft. We boarded the passengers for [our next] flight.  We discussed that we would check both sides for VNAV engagement; also monitor all speed tapes and ND's for any glitching before takeoff.  As we were about to close the door both FMC's blanked out and Map flag; VTK flag; and no runway flag on my side only appeared. No FMC prompt on either FMC screens only ACARS; ACMS (aircraft condition monitoring system); SAT (satellite).  I called Maintenance and they came out and talked about that they had Captain's FMC history. I asked about it and we looked it up in the previous logbook; first I had heard about that. I was thinking new airplane I did not realize that there was an entire logbook already used below the current logbook.  They then switched the FMC switch to both on R and the flags on my side went away and FMC prompts returned. I told them I cannot takeoff like that.  They called Maintenance Control I believe and they did a circuit breaker reset which fixed the flags and returned the FMC prompts and the FMC switch back to normal. We closed the door and started the pushback. As the FO was about to start engine 2 the same flags returned on my side and no FMC prompts on both sides. Maintenance Control told us to return to the gate because he could not MEL it. We returned to the gate and Maintenance again did the circuit breaker reset that only lasted a few minutes before the flags returned. They decided to MEL the FMC with my approval. The FO and I did not want to continue with this aircraft because of our history with it and that it had only been powered down and 2 circuit breaker resets.  We now would be manually setting bugs and thrust for the entire flight in an aircraft we both had very little time in and had an early morning show to start the day and it was now late afternoon.

column121: I was thanking passengers as they disembarked onto the jet-bridge in ZZZ; and I was trying to call rows to deplane on the PA. The cleaning crew were at the front door (1Left) trying to get on the plane while the passengers were leaving; and the pilots were also trying to gather their bags and leave. This made the situation very chaotic. I was not aware of it being a 'quick-turn'; as I am always happy to try and help out with the quick-turn cleaning.The cleaners slipped on a few at a time; in between passengers leaving. I saw the two aft crewmembers with their luggage; and moving forward through the cabin; towards me. The cleaners were already onboard; cleaning throughout the plane. I said; 'last but not least!' to the final passenger; thanked her and gathered my belongings. I looked back and only saw the cleaners; and my crew who were almost to me. I didn't see any more passengers and thought we were done. I double-checked my doors and the forward lavatory and stepped off the plane. When the aft crew stepped off; there was a male passenger with them who had been mixed in with the cleaners. He did not have his boarding pass with him. He said he wouldn't leave without it; and that his seat was XX6. He wanted to go look for it himself; but crew went to look. His boarding card was found under his seat.A contributing factor is having so many people onboard/in jetbridge and the cleaning crew coming onboard (sometimes in just sweatshirts; hoodies; jackets; hats; masks; etc.) and mixing in with disembarking passengers; and vice versa.  Flights are more full now; and anyone can be mistaken for a cleaner.Other factors: double-checking the passengers haven't lowered or removed their masks; as they often do now; as they are coming down the aisle towards me and the boarding door. The passengers are trying to look down the aisle and gauge how far we've gotten with the row announcements to deplane. Also; 2-3 pilots using the lavatory; gathering bags and leaving; while passengers are disembarking causes more confusion. All of this; and the extra amount of ground-staff/cleaners onboard and in the jet-bridge in civilian clothing; causes more confusion; multitasking/load at the boarding/deplaning door.I assumed the last passenger I saw; and said goodbye to; was our final passenger onboard.I would not have stepped off the plane had I known there was still one passenger onboard.I will also alert corporate security to this incident; and the added potential for this confusion during disembarkation.

column121: We were flying the VALLY2 SID out of MIA.  The SID note states; 'SPEED RESTRICTION...Turbojet aircraft accelerate to 250 knots; if unable; advise ATC.' I was the PF (Pilot Flying) and at 10;000 feet; I asked the Captain for Economy Climb.  We accelerated to ECON CLB.  Shortly after reaching this speed; ATC instructed us to fly 250 knots and stated something like...Aircraft X; maintain 250 knots; Center will give you a higher speed; you've already accelerated.  (Not verbatim; I cannot remember the exact phraseology). It gave us the impression that we missed a published speed restriction.  After rereading the SID note; we are both confident that this is not a speed restriction.  We are also confident that we did not miss an ATC assigned speed restriction. If however our interpretation of this SID note is incorrect; it is not written as it should be. The Jeppesen Chart Legends publication has a section written about speed restrictions.  It clearly states that 'speed restrictions vary widely within individual procedures.' If we unintentionally violated a speed restriction in this case; perhaps this 'wide variation' in depicted speed restrictions needs to be better address from a human factors perspective; since the VALLY2 SID does not clearly depict a 250 knot speed restriction with terminology such as 'maintain 250 until advised by ATC' or 'do not exceed 250 knots etc.

He came up to the flight deck to report this about the same time the smell and smoke were noticed in the flight deck.  The CA (Captain) left his seat briefly and upon seeing the smoke in the ceiling area; came back up and notified ATC.  I noted to the CA and ACM that they should immediately pull all the galley circuit breakers; that we didn't need that equipment and likely the cause of the problem.  The ACM did this immediately.  As the PF (pilot flying); I continued to fly expeditiously to the airport while the CA (Pilot Monitoring) accomplished the smoke/fire/fumes checklist.  My O2 mask was pulled but not donned.  Shortly after the galley CB's were pulled the smoke and fumes began to dissipate.  The CA notified ATC that the situation was improving but we still requested priority handling.  We were already on final and visual with [runway] XXR and cleared to land.  Landing was uneventful and we exited the runway; taxiing to our ramp followed by fire and rescue equipment.  After shutdown; the CA went to disarm and open doors for personnel with he found that the cabin doors would not open electrically.  That was when he noticed the ground service bus CB was popped.  Maintenance was contacted via interphone and notified that we could not open doors electrically.  Rather than blow the door open pneumatically we chose to wait for Maintenance to get the door open.  (There was no evidence at this point that smoke/fire was a threat).  Maintenance personnel were able to mechanically open the door.  Fire personnel came up and we described the above situation.    Quick action by our ACM and expeditious handling by ATC and all crew members brought this to a successful conclusion.

column121: I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) on our flight to ZZZ. We departed the runway and flew the ZZZZZ departure. All was well through 10;000 feet and shortly thereafter; the A/P was coupled. We were VMC and it was a normal; 270 knot climb. Approximately 8 miles before ZZZZZ; maybe climbing through 14;000 feet; the aircraft began an uncommanded; soft turn to the right of course. It then increased to a more abrupt banking turn to the right; accompanied with about 4-5 degrees of nose-down pitch attitude. The turn to the right was approximately 40-50 degrees total. The airspeed quickly increased and I saw airspeed tape up to; but not into; the barber pole. I don't recall any aural warning and the EICAS was clear. This evolution was quick. The CA (Captain) and I exchanged a few words as he detected the error; followed by an A/P disconnect and a manual recovery; which began with a pitch input and throttle adjustment. I was talking to Center as this began and was queried immediately. I replied that we experienced a perceived autopilot anomaly; but were correcting. We were instructed to rejoin the departure at ZZZZZ and continue from there. The CA and I discussed the event; and once back on profile; we re-engaged A/P and continued the flight in normal fashion.I'm still not sure what happened. The DP (Departure Procedure) was loaded directly from the FMS data base; with no modifications. We were climbing VIA; in magenta FLCH. When the aircraft began to stray; the A/P was following the flight director cue the whole time. The pitch down was concerning and both of us suspected a trim runaway at first; but as the yoke was pushing forward from the A/P; the CA quickly de-coupled the A/P and recovered back on course. Looking back; we performed normally and programmed the FMS normally. I have no explanation for this event; but I am grateful we were VMC at the time and that we recovered in a timely manner. The CA did further consulting once we landed in ZZZ.

column121: During cruise STAB OUT OF TRIM light illuminated intermittently.  Complied with STAB OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure.  Maintenance notified via ACARS. Descending with autopilot and autothrottle on; aircraft did not level off at the preselected 4;000 feet.  I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle and began to return to 4;000 feet.  I tried the electric trim and found it to be inoperative.  I notified the Captain of the inoperative electric trim.  The Captain tried his electric trim and also found it to be inoperative. Captain conferred with me about disconnecting the STAB TRIM CUT OUT switches.  I agreed and the STAB TRIM CUT OUT switches were disconnected.  Captain opened the QRH and we complied with the STAB OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure.  The STAB OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure directed us to the STABILIZER TRIM INOPERATIVE procedure; which we complied with.  I tried to operate the manual trim with my left hand could not move the trim wheel through a full rotation.  I notified the Captain of this and he tried the manual trim.  Captain seem to require both hands to operate the manual trim.  Captain notified ATC and we requested delay vectors. We requested the longer Runway of XXR.  We performed a flaps 15 landing on XXR. column123: This report is being submitted to cover the altitude deviation on approach into ZZZ. The altitude deviation was a direct result of a malfunction of the stabilizer/stabilizer trim system. The other required category reports will be covered in a separate irregularity report.Approximately two hours after departure and level at FL350; the STAB OUT OF TRIM (amber) light illuminated. We ran the STABILIZER OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure. Autopilot B was engaged and remained engaged while the light was eliminated; the aircraft maintained altitude and airspeed in light mountain wave and light chop conditions. Since the auto pilot appeared to be trimming the aircraft normally and in accordance with QRH; we continued normal operation. We notified maintenance control and Dispatch via ACARS and made a maintenance logbook entry for the condition. Dispatch acknowledged receiving the message. The light remained illuminated for approximately 10 mins. During this time both the first officer and myself reviewed not only the QRH; but Stabilizer Trim Inoperative QRH procedure in the event that these stabilizers stopped trimming at some subsequent point. We also reviewed be available information in both the flight handbook as well as the systems handbook.The STAB OUT OF TRIM light continued to illuminate intermittently in durations that ranged from several minutes to just a few seconds. We also climbed to FL370 with no abnormal indications and with the B autopilot remaining engaged. I observed some movement of the trim wheel at various times.During the cruise portion of the flight; the light was extinguished most of the time; but we did have the intermittent illuminations periodically. We informed dispatch and maintenance control that the light was illuminating intermittently.On the arrival into ZZZ we were given several intermediate level offs as well as crossing altitude and airspeed restrictions all of which were met with autopilot B engaged.While being vectored around some weather; for a visual approach to Runway XXL; we were kept somewhat high on the profile and were in a fairly aggressive dissent to 4;000 feet.  Autopilot B remained engaged throughout this descent. At 4;000 feet the flight directors commanded a level off but the aircraft continued to descend below 4;000 feet and did not capture the altitude; the first officer (pilot flying) immediately disengaged the auto pilot and auto throttles and began to correct The flight path; but due to the out of trim condition of the stabilizer the aircraft descended to approximately 3;500 feet before being able to level off the aircraft with considerable back pressure on the yoke.We informed ZZZ Approach that we had a stabilizer issue and were attempting to correct back to 4000 feet. They directed us to maintain 3000 feet. At about this time; the first officer informed me that 'I don't have any trim' and I saw him activate the yoke stabilizer trim switches for nose up and nose down trim with no movement of the stabilizer trim wheels. I attempted to trim the stabilizer using the yoke switches on my side with no effect as well. The first officer was holding a great deal of back pressure on the yolk and stated 'I need nose up trim' at this point with his concurrence after having verified that neither yolk could trim the stabilizer electrically; I selected both stabilizer trim cut out switches to cut out.At this point I told the first officer that he was going to continue to be the pilot flying and also have the radios while I reviewed the QRH procedures. After I verified that we had accomplished all of the steps and had been directed to the next QRH section. Well I was reviewing the QRH procedures the first officer attempted to trim the aircraft manually and stated 'I can't move the wheel'. It was at this point I believe where I [requested priority] with approach and told them that we had a stabilizer trim failure and we were attempting to trim the aircraft manually we requested and receiveda vector to do this and we reported our souls on board as well as fuel and requested ARFF assistance at the airport. At this point I attempted to trim the stabilizer nose up manually from my side but was unable to turn the stabilizer trim wheel. I directed the first officer to attempt to slow the aircraft to clean maneuver speed in an attempt to unload the stabilizer so that we could trim the aircraft manually. At some point approaching clean maneuver speed I was able to begin moving the trim wheel nose up but it was still quite difficult and required a significant two-handed effort to move the wheel at all. I managed to get several turn nose up trim and the first officer said 'that's good'. At this point; we were in a more or less in trim condition at clean maneuver and clean. We continue to execute QRH and requested the longer Runway (XXR). It was at about this point I believe that I informed the flight attendants of our situation and that we would be landing in about 5 to 10 minutes; to expect a normal landing but that there would be fire trucks standing by.We completed QRH and had a normal flaps 15 landing on Runway XXRWe rolled out normally and cleared the runway and informed ground control and the ARFF captain that we did not require any further assistance.We taxi to the gate and shut down the aircraft; debriefed the flight attendants; and spoke with maintenance on the ground about our situation.

column121: This flight was the first leg of a four day for the Captain and I. The Captain said he would be the pilot flying; that I would be pilot monitoring and he briefed everything up; including threats. We made each other aware of our lack of recent flying experience and lack of proficiency. I informed him that I only have a little over 700 hours on type; that most of that time was trans-cons prior to the pandemic and that I haven't flown much in the past twelve months. I also informed him to the best of my knowledge this would be my first time flying into ZZZZ [Airport]. We agreed that we would take things slow and that we were doing everything correctly. Our taxi out; take off; departure and cruise were routine and uneventful. Approximately twenty minutes prior to the Top of Descent the Captain briefed our descent and approach into ZZZZ and we ran the descent checklist. Center gave us a descent; followed by descend via the X Arrival. We were handed off to approach and told to expect the VOR [Runway] X; after ZZZZZ [Intersection] to fly present heading for a vector to the VOR approach. Prior to ZZZZZ the Captain called for flaps 1; After ZZZZZ he called flaps 5; slowed to 190 knots and approach gave us the vector and cleared us for the VOR X approach. We were at or near the final approach fix when the Captain called gear down; flaps fifteen followed by flaps 30 landing checklist. I set final approach altitude; we were VOR/LOC and VNAV descending per the approach and slowing to our vref of 156 knots. At 1000 feet we were fully configured; and I believe we were at 165 knots. I called 1000 feet; the Captain was task saturated so I said 1;000 feet; set missed approach altitude and said cleared to land. I noticed VNAV had kicked off; I verbalized it and re-selected VNAV; I thought it went to VNAV PTH; but in our debrief I learned it went to VNAV SPD. Between 1;000 and 500 feet the fastest speed I saw was 170 knots. At 500 feet I called 500 feet and saw 171 knots and almost called a go-around. I called 15 knots fast; the Captain said correcting and I saw the speed slowly begin to decrease. I was focused on airspeed as we were at the limit for a stabilized approach and I was looking at the runway as I was concerned; we were going to be high. We continued our approach and I was beginning to become uncomfortable; at approximately 200 feet I noticed we were at 170 knots (it may have been a couple knots faster) but 170 is what I recall.  At approximately 200 feet I called that we were high and fast; the Captain said correcting and I saw the speed slowly begin to decrease and he pitched down to correct. At approximately 100 feet I wanted to call for a go-around as we were fast; 170 knots or faster; however I was unable to verbalize it. We touched down hard and flat; we may have had a small bounce; but I don't believe that we did. The Captain deployed the reverser's and we made a normal exit onto taxiway and proceeded to parking. Upon parking; we debriefed this event; we both conducted thorough post flight inspections of the exterior. To the best of our knowledge the aircraft was nott damaged. The Captain contacted Maintenance and they wrote up the hard landing. The Captain also called the Duty Manager.Factors that led to this event were both of our lack of recent flying experience; unfamiliar airport; night operation; Runway X PAPI out of service; the change from VNAV PTH to VNAV SPD and I did not call for a go-around.I have learned from this event and will call for a go-around if I become uncomfortable or we become unstable in the future.
column123: We were flying into ZZZZ [Airport] on the VOR [Runway] X approach at night. I had not flown for a year. Currency was a factor.  While on approach I configured on time and landing checklist was called for and completed.  At 500 feet we were 15 knots fast (171 knots) and the FO said we are fast. I said correcting. At 200 feet I was 17 knots (173 knots) fast the FO said we are fast; I tried to correct.  Also; at 200 feet the FO called out high. I over corrected and landed abruptly from 50 feet to touch down. I do not believe this was a bounced landing but may have been. Our pitch was flat; and we landed main gear first. Our descent rate from 50 feet to 0 feet was extreme.  The failure of myself or as a crew to not call a Go Around was the primary mitigating factor.  Also executing an off center VOR approach with a PAPI OTS at night was a factor. I felt I was not high but in reality; it was due to lack of visible surroundings. Furthermore; the VOR approach only gave guidance to 1;054 feet MSL. To further complicate issues the VNAV disconnected. So; in essence we were left minimal visual guidance. Winds were 20 knots reported and was another factor. My FO stated he was about to call for go-around at 500 feet and 200 feet; but neither of us did. After landing we taxied in normally. We both did several post flight inspections. I also notified Maintenance and the Duty Pilot of the events. This was the first leg of a 4 day with an FO I've never flown with. All briefings were completed. The FO and I discussed before departure how infrequently we have flown due to the pandemic. He had never been to ZZZ [Airport]. I had not been in 2 years. All approach briefings were concluded in a timely manner. The STAR in use was the X arrival. After ZZZZZ [Intersection] we were instructed to fly present heading for radar vectors to join the VOR X LOC. The VOR approach X is a very tricky approach. It is offset with limited visual guidance. Flaps 1 was initiated prior to ZZZZZ. Flaps 5 was initiated after ZZZZZ. Best to our knowledge we were configured by the FAF. The FMA was showing VOR/LOC and VNAV path commencement to approach; at some point we lost VNAV path and went to VNAV speed. I accomplished a LAVS check but did not add 2 and 4 mile rings. I may have gotten very close to exceeding flaps 30 speed. I also believe my flare was minimal at best. Having a PAPI would have been beneficial.

We were cleared to land by Tower and continued the approach at 170 kts. Spacing was holding at 3 miles; but as we approached the marker I noticed our spacing was closing faster than normal. At about 2.5 outside the marker I made the decision to start slowing to avoid going around. (Full disclosure; I have been in the exact situation before and had to go around twice on this approach.) What I misjudged was how fast the 737-700 slows down. We were at approach speed too early and the Tower asked our speed and instructions. We made the aircraft behind us go around from my error in speed control.

column121: We had returned to the gate 2 times for passenger related issues. We then taxied out to the hold short line. We sat there awaiting the final closeout for ten minutes or so. When the close out came; there was no performance uplink; so I went to change ZFW and CG to match the latest closeout. I then verified that the V-speeds matched the takeoff performance page and we departed. The flight plan had us filed for FL380; but the VNAV page capped us at FL370.  We then leveled off at FL360.  After some discussion given our light weight and nearly standard day temperatures; we began looking for the reason for the low Maximum Altitude. We found that I had entered the ZFW incorrectly from the final closeout.Causal factors could include feeling a little rushed to get going after the half hour delay. Another factor could have been the lack of an uplink that led me to manually enter data.  Additionally; while I have been to training recently and am fully current; there is no smoothness or rhythm to my flying due to a lack of consistent time in the aircraft.  Hopefully having a regular line in Month will improve my proficiency.
column123: After returning to the gate for a passenger issue; we were running slightly behind schedule.  Original closeout deleted and after starting the second pushback; we had a new closeout (Rev 01) with good numbers which were accepted by the FMS.  During the second pushback; we were directed to tow back to the gate for a baggage issue.  Finally pushed back a third time and during taxi for departure; we received an ACARS message that closeout had been deleted and to wait for new numbers.  Received revision 02 (one pax less) of the closeout.  Did not get the prompt to accept new numbers.  Got another message of a deleted closeout and to wait for new numbers.  As we were getting more behind schedule; we ran through the numbers with the latest closeout (Rev 02) and confirmed the numbers as OK for a Flaps 10 degree; 10 knot tailwind TPS; with a plan to then cover the changes (if any) in the next closeout revision.  Waited approximately 20 more minutes at the end of the runway; number one for departure and finally got Revision 03 of the closeout; which was unchanged from Revision 02.  No prompt to accept the new numbers; so we manually updated them.  After I had checked the PERF page TOW numbers with the latest closeout numbers; the First Officer noticed that the ZFW was slightly off and updated it; but entered XYZ.X instead of correct number XAZ.X.  (Unnoticed at the time) Original number had been XAB.C.   V-speeds did not delete from the FMS; and with a slightly lighter TOW than the plan; I figured we were good to go.  V-speeds did not need to be changed; so we didn't.  We then completed all items of the Before Takeoff checklist and took off normally.  During the climbout; VNAV showed a max altitude of only FL360 instead of the planned FL380.  I found this odd; as we were lighter than the original planned weight and the temp at altitude was normal.  When we leveled off at FL360; I looked again at the closeout and compared it to the FMS perf page and then discovered the ZFW entry error.  Corrected it then and the VNAV max altitude fixed itself.  Remainder of flight uneventful.Because we were late and at the end of the runway; I may have rushed the FO to enter the ZFW data too quickly; which resulted in wrong data in the FMS. column121: The NIITZ 1 RNAV Departure from Runway 8L depicts FLAAR as prior to the lake.  The E/O (Engine Out) Page for 8L shows it as past the lake. I realize that DP1 is an altitude (3;500 feet - 6;000 feet) but the diagram does not match up. I expressed my concerns to a Check Airman friend and he did a better job of analyzing the problem. He noted the brown arc on the E/O (MSA circle we assume) shows FLAAR to be at 25 NM. I used the FIX Page of the FMC and put the LAS/12.7 arc and it lands on top of FLAAR. So; I see two problems. The 'terrain' and the omission of 'Not to Scale' could create confusion when you are trying to build a visual model of the E/O. Also; I'm not sure we recognize the hold at FLAAR is really only 12.7 NM from LAS; not 25 where it may seem less threatening to following traffic.My friends words: I agree that if you were trying to create a mental image of what you were doing in case you lost an engine; then the engine out diagram (picture) would lead you astray. The dilemma arises from the 12.7 ring and FLAAR being almost coincident. It gets worse; because 12.7 and FLAAR have nothing to do with one another. 12.7 only matters if you are below 3;500 feet. And FLAAR only matters if you are above 3;500 feet. So we are mixing altitudes with rings with fixes with terrain features with no warning that the drawing is not to scale! The disturbing part to me is that the E/O has the standard 25 NM MSA ring (at least that's what I think it is; and it is at 25 NM); which lends credence to FLAAR being 25 NM out (not about 13). So you are totally right! The written text is fine; but the diagram is very misleading.  I think we need to put 'NOT TO SCALE'. Or get rid of the terrain features. But the mixing and matching just leads to confusion (at the worst time).

column121: After the addition of thrust for T/O (takeoff) and selection of TO/GA (takeoff go-around) and N1 attaining T/O power; the aircraft was already rolling and had achieved approximately 15 knots of forward motion.  At that point we heard a very loud bang followed by a hard left yawing motion. The PF (Pilot Flying) immediately retarded the throttles to idle; and applied smooth breaking; which brought us to a complete stop.  We were angled left by about 30-40 degrees in relation to the center line of Runway 4; just prior to taxiway. I immediately informed ATC that we had stopped on the runway; the PF informed the PAX (passengers) to stay seated.  At that point we began to assess the situation. Initially we thought it was a blown tire or nose wheel steering issue. In that moment of assessing I noticed the #1 Engine Fail Caution illuminate in the #1 EGT Gauge. I informed the PF of the indication. It was the only indication we saw. No fire; no red lines only the engine failure alert caution. We reviewed the Rejected Takeoff Procedure; completed the QRH for Engine Failure. We then assessed the rolling and breaking capability of the aircraft and we found it to be normal.  We got clearance to exit the runway and return to the gate. As we pulled in to the gate; we remembered that we had not run an After Landing Checklist and quickly completed that; followed by the Parking Checklist. Then; the jetbridge malfunctioned and we had to wait until Airport Ops came to fix it. Once the jetbridge was attached I exited the aircraft to inspect Engine #1. I found the N1 fan blades and the stators directly behind them to be in a normal appearance. When I looked into the tailpipe of the turbine section; I found metal debris from the engine and both the aft fan blades and stators in front of them to be damaged and missing pieces. I hustled back to the Flight Deck to inform Ground Control that they needed to do a FOD check of the runway as we had; had and engine failure and that they needed to check for small engine parts.

He called for gear; however; I was unable to extend the gear because we were not at the appropriate speed. We were switched to Tower. The Captain continued the descent all the while attempting to reduce speed. Best guess we were at approximately a 7 mile final. We received an EGPWS 'TERRAIN TERRAIN'. column121: All preflight items complete INCLUDING Main Electric STAB TRIM CUTOUT switch with normal results. Student Captain was Pilot flying for this leg. Shortly after Takeoff the PF commented that his electric trim switch was not working and asked me to try mine; which also did not work. I asked him if the elevator was working and he replied that it was and felt normal. We asked ATC to level off at 12;000 ft to work on a flight control issue and was approved. We did not ask for priority handling at this time...we engaged the A Autopilot successfully but shortly after the 'STAB OUT OF TRIM' light came on. As we began to look up the appropriate Non-normal; the PF disengaged the autopilot and tried to manually trim the stabilizer. Although he was successful it looked like it was difficult to rotate so I asked to give it a shot to feel the force required to rotate. The force required to rotate was abnormally high but did provide results and we were flying a trimmed aircraft at 240 knots. By now I was considering that a Jammed Flight Control (the stabilizer in this case) was the source of our STAB OUT OF TRIM  problem. So the first checklist we addressed was the Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls Non-normal and also the Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls procedure (the script/expanded explanation). Around this time we requested priority handling with ATC because checklist called for landing at nearest suitable airport. We were hoping that we might get electric trim back when moving STAB TRIM switch on pedestal to OVERRIDE. Did not happen. Called Dispatch with Maintenance Control on the line hoping for some systems expertise. Ended call with where we started. We began to discuss possible value of running STAB OUT OF TRIM checklist. We did. But before doing so we noted the hazard of running multiple checklists and capped our STAB TRIM OVERRIDE switch to normal. The Jammed Flight Control non normal resulted in moving both STAB  TRIM switches to CUTOUT but also called for landing at nearest suitable with Flaps 15. About this time we got on radio again with Maintenance Control; Dispatch and also the Flight Operations. Our hope was that Flight Operations might be able to get a Hydraulics of Flight Controls Maintenance expert on with us. We discussed both checklists and Flight Operations talked about the potential effect of slower speeds. This call ended with general consensus we were on the best track and we discussed whether to land sooner or burn down to below Max landing weight. Because we felt the aircraft was stable and our condition was not likely to get worse we chose to burn fuel. I talked to PF and told him it would be prudent for me to do landing since that would be his first one from left seat in aircraft. We briefed our arrival plan which included our trim plan as we reduced airspeed and extended gear and flaps. As we descended and slowed we reminded ATC of need for priority handling equipment. Only significant thing to report was that by the time we had fully configured and slowed to final approach speed it was extremely difficult to trim manually. In fact; with one pilot exerting maximum effort; you could maybe get the manual strection about a quarter turn. All of this led us to believe that the Stabilizer was DEFINITELY jammed. Landed uneventfully; had equipment check us out then taxied to gate. Flight Attendants were given TEST brief and told there was no need to prepare for evacuation.
column123: All systems checked ok at gate; but after rotation we discovered our electric stabilizer trim was inop. column121: I was a passenger on a flight to Spokane. I was sitting in seat X. I was traveling with my spouse who was seated on the opposite side of the aircraft in seat Y. The flight enroute was uneventful. On descent; we were again in VMC conditions. A visual approach would be likely as there were no clouds between our position and the airport. The active runway was 21. As an airline pilot I have done the visual arrival into GEG Runway 21 many times from the south and am aware of the several high towers that are southeast of the airport and directly in line with the arrival into Spokane. Two of the towers are nearly 950 high; so this is a significant threat to arrival aircraft; especially if pilots are heads down and not noticing the towers. If pilots are only focused on clearing the terrain by 1;000 ft. that will clearly put the aircraft in near contact with one of these two towers since the towers themselves are nearly 1;000 ft. above ground. Having been a commuter for much of my career; I have flown over these towers as a passenger no less than 100 times. I know what the normal proximity is to those towers should be and look like from both within the cabin and flight deck on this visual approach. From my vantage point in seat 2A; our vertical proximity to the towers southeast of GEG was not normal and appeared to be dangerously close. We appeared to be much lower over the towers than I had ever seen before in nearly two decades of flying into the airport. I was definitely uncomfortable with what I was seeing and even a bit shaken by what appeared to be a 'close call'. Our arrival into Spokane was mostly normal after that event. The landing appeared to be a bit long; perhaps even out of the touchdown; but nothing of great significance. Upon arrival at the gate; my spouse and I deplaned. Once inside the terminal; my spouse asked me 'Did you see that arrival?' I said 'You mean; how close we were to those towers?' My spouse said;'YES! My God I have never seen those towers so close in my life- that wasn't right.' My spouse is also an airline pilot and commutes so he too is a valid witness to what occurred on that flight. We discussed whether or not to say something as we understand that events can happen from time to time. Because of the seriousness of what we saw; we felt it was appropriate to contact ALPA in an effort to highlight this real threat to all airlines and general aviation regarding the visual arrival into GEG. Over the years I have seen certain deviations from standard that were noteworthy but nothing that alarmed me the way this did. My hope is that additional training can be provided to all airline pilots regarding the towers in proximity to GEG. Perhaps a greater emphasis on arrival procedures. Maybe even a bigger emphasis on the Jeppesen chart itself. I also think the arrival gate coming into GEG from the south should not be allowed over the towers; either VMC or IMC. They are a threat in either scenario. Lastly; a possible change to ATC protocol would be for Approach to require visual confirmation of the towers to arriving aircraft when a visual approach is expected.

column121: On final approach into ZZZ I was Pilot Flying. After calling for gear down we received a BRK RH FAULT advisory message. We finished configuring for landing and I called for the Quick Reference Handbook(QRH). The QRH procedure had us run the 'Landing Gear/Brake malfunction landing checklist'. At this point I called for a go around so we may accomplish the necessary items and let ATC know. After the go around I made a PA advising the passengers we had a faulty brake indication and had to go-around to run the checklist. I spoke to the Flight Attendants and told them I would update them; shortly but we should be landing in the next 5 to 10 minutes. Immediately after; I sent a free text to Dispatch advising them we had a brake fault and were executing a go around and running the procedure. I do not recall receiving a response from Dispatch.The First Officer completed the procedure as I prepared the aircraft for landing. The procedure called for a flaps full landing and longer roll out. At this point I decided it would be best to [receive priority from ATC] and have the fire equipment standing by as this was a brake issue which would cause asymmetric braking. I also requested ATC to switch our landing runway to a runway that was longer than our planned runway. After the procedure was complete I called the Flight Attendants and told them we had [an urgent situation]; we will be landing in 5 minutes; expect emergency equipment and we will not be bracing. I then made another PA to let our passengers now we had an issue with one of our brakes and out of an abundance of caution I have requested the airport to deploy its safety equipment but I did expect the landing to be normal with an extended roll out. My voice remained calm and I made no mention of an emergency during the PA. At this point ATC vectored us to final and we configured and ran the appropriate landing checklist. We touched down and I used reverse thrust and very gently applied brakes.I immediately felt the right hand brake was not biting. I had to mainly use the left brake with right rudder to maintain centerline. Once the plane slowed below 60 knots I was able to slow with both brakes and used the tiller for directional control. The right brake was working but did not feel as effective. We exited the runway and were able to taxi normal; albeit at a slow speed. At this point I noticed on the STATUS page the right outboard brake temperature did not rise leading to the conclusion that it was indeed that brake which had failed. I elected to taxi with both engines to reduce asymmetric thrust. Parking at the gate was normal. I entered the discrepancy in the logbook; called Maintenance and headed to our overnight.In hindsight I do believe [advising ATC] was the right call even if the issue did not end up being serious. I was worried about asymmetric braking and was also not sure if the brake had failed released or with full pressure. I felt it was best to declare and have the trucks standing by and not need them. The only thing I would have done differently would have been to call Dispatch before talking to Maintenance. After discussing the event with the company it seems Dispatch was not aware of the issue until after the plane arrived at the gate. I usually call them first when we have maintenance issues but In this case since the flight was terminating I figured it would be best to go directly to Maintenance but I can see how the lack of communication can cause confusion with Dispatch.

column121: While being radar vectored to the visual final for Runway XX at ZZZ; Approach Control issued a descent to 6;000 feet MSL. We read back the clearance and proceeded to descend to 6;000 feet MSL. The Captain did observe that we seemed closer to some radio Towers on a hill than what would appear normal; but we received no GPWS Alerts. We continued on vectors and flew an uneventful approach and landing. After a call from Tower a few hours later; it was explained that the descent clearance to 6;000 feet was issued to a (other carrier X) whose readback was on a different Approach Control frequency. Our readback to that clearance as Company A (very similar sounding call sign) must have occurred at the same moment as (other carrier's) reply. Since the (other carrier X) aircraft had been on a different approach frequency; we had yet to hear any other communications to or from that aircraft; and ATC had not issued a caution for the similar sounding call signs. Additionally; ATC did not issue a low altitude warning if we had gone below the Minimum Vector Altitude in the sector we were within.When managing multiple frequencies; ATC should ensure that aircraft with similar call signs are alerted to possible miss interpretations. Furthermore; ATC should minimize the use of simulcasting on multiple Approach frequencies and consolidate traffic to one radio frequency.
column123: We were being vectored for the visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ from the east. ZZZ Approach Control issued a clearance to 6;000 feet MSL. We were later contacted that the clearance was for (other carrier) X; on another frequency and not for Company A. The clearance apparently took us below the MVA for that sector. The Controller was controlling multiple frequencies (he was busy) and never advised us of similar sounding call signs. We did not receive any terrain cautions from the aircraft or Controller.  The subsequent approach and landing were uneventful.Listening during communications is always the most important.  Being advised of similar sounding call signs is an important step to help alleviate threats and for Crews to be more vigilant.

column121: Only upon my meeting with the chief pilot was I aware that I had a close range encounter with terrain.  We never received any type of warning.  The Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS) did not notify us nor did we get a terrain alert from ATC.  A previous report was submitted regarding this flight due to other reasons.  I viewed the flight path in question as a go around (not anything to hide).  The following is what I recall.  We planned and briefed a Localizer Approach.  When transferred to Approach we were informed the Localizer Approach was not available.  We were left with the RNAV Approach. I requested the First Officer to brief the approach.The RNAV Approach was showing in the FMS. Approach gave us a clearance to a fix; the First Officer responded; but I did not understand the fix.  A fix I was expecting to hear was not what I heard.  I asked the First Officer to request the fix again.  Approach replied and again I could not understand what was said.  I am not seeing anything on the approach plate nor FMS what I am hearing.  Approach mentioned that the fix is on the approach plate then spells it out. Now I understood and knew where to go.  We are heading to ZZZZZ and at ZZZZZ I notice the aircraft is not turning.  The FMS had a discontinuity then direct to ZZZZZ.  I turned off the auto pilot and hand fly to get back on track.From ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 the course was centering. Inside ZZZZZ1 was going IMC I wanted to go missed [approach].  Somewhere during this time; the flight in which I was following shifted.  The First Officer tried twice to call Approach for a heading and altitude. No answer.  I transferred the controls and called Approach.  Approach responded.  Approach said something about not to continue the descent and gave an altitude and heading.  The second time around we landed. In reviewing the flight; I can see many errors.  I allowed to many little errors become a larger error.  With the little errors I allowed myself to become distracted.

column121: We were assigned an aircraft to take from ZZZ to ZZZ1 that had the BLEED 1 system on MEL. The FO and I discussed before departure in our threat based briefing about how the BLEED 2 system would have a hard time pressurizing the entire aircraft all the way up to our cruise altitude of FL XX0 and how we should make the climb as shallow as we could without exceeding VMO or any airspeed restrictions in order to help the BLEED 2 system pressurize the aircraft.After takeoff the aircraft was pressurizing normally but then somewhere around approximately 7;000 feet on the climb we noticed that the cabin altitude was increasing at about the same rate as our actual altitude and there was only about a 2;500 foot difference between the two. Knowing that only one bleed system was trying to pressurize the aircraft we continued with the hopes that it would catch up and pressurize normally.At 12;500 we got the Cabin Press warning so we leveled off and asked ATC for the lowest altitude they could give us; we were over the [name] Mountains at this time so the lowest altitude they could give us was 12;000 feet. At 12;000 feet the cabin pressure was holding steady at about 9;500 feet but wasn't increasing or decreasing any further.The FO and I discussed running and looked at the pressurization fail checklist but both agreed that the checklist was designed for a 2 bleed operating system and that this was a unique situation.At this point I called Dispatch and Maintenance to discuss the best plan of action; after some discussion Dispatch told us that we needed to return to ZZZ because we didn't have drift down performance for our route of flight at 12;000 feet. By the time this was decided we were almost on the other side of the mountains and I could see the town of [name] about 30 miles to the southeast of our position. My decision was to not turn around and cross the mountain range again at 12;000 feet without drift down performance. When Dispatch became aware of our position we both decided that the best plan of action was to continue to ZZZ1.We landed in ZZZ1 without any further incidents.In hindsight there are two things I wish I would have done differently. The first thing I should have done was to not continue over the [name] mountains with the pressurization not adequately pressurizing the aircraft. I think my continuation was due to the fact that I was unfamiliar with how the pressurization of the aircraft performed with only one bleed system operative and it was my first time operating the aircraft with that particular MEL. If I had it to do over again I would have asked for delay vectors while we waited to see if the pressurization would catch up with our altitude and that way I could have avoided crossing the mountains at an altitude without drift down performance and just returned to ZZZ.The second thing I would have done was to at least run the unpressurized flight checklist; it was a short flight with a very high workload and even though we were still partially pressurized it would have been a good checklist to run just to see if there was anything else we were missing.
column123: Bleed 1 was consistently giving a #1 bleed hot caution on previous flights. Therefore; the bleed 1 source was placed on MEL. The only guidance from the MEL was that we shall not turn on the affected bleed valve. Climbing out of ZZZ; we were filed too FLXX0. Bleed 2 was on bleed 1 was off. Upon reaching 12;000 feet the cabin press master warning light appeared. We leveled off and descended to 10;000 feet. We contacted Maintenance Control and Dispatch. I took the radios and was already PF. Due to not having drift down performance and already being pass the mountains Dispatch and the pilots agreed that it was best to continue to ZZZ1 as we had a lot of fuel.   We noticed the aircraft was very slow at pressurizing during the climb we attempted to help the system by reducing the rate of climb. This seemed to have little affect. It was almost expected by us that the master warning would go off. Once it went off we noticed the aircraft was at 12;000 feet. But the cabin pressure was at 10;000 feet. So there was a small pressure differential. We therefore decided that we would not put the masks on as this would make commutation more difficult with each other and there was no need for an emergency descent. We descend to 10;000 feet as soon as possible this allowed the cabin to descent to 8;000 feet which was much more normal. We contacted Maintenance Control first as we knew what caused the problem. They advised us to call Dispatch. Drift down performance was not available for our altitude so by the time we contacted Dispatch we had passed the mountains and we agreed with Dispatch that it was safest to continue to ZZZ1. Due to the aircraft not pressuring and knowing the issue causing the problem we did not run the cabin press checklist as this would have advised us to turn on bleed 1 which is specifically what we were told not to do in the MEL. By descending down to 10;000 the master warning went away. We continued to ZZZ1 with no further issues.1) It's important to continually monitor the pressurization panel. 2) Maybe contact [Dispatch during preflight for other options]. 3) Knowing that if the bleed source is on MEL; we should expect the aircraft to not pressurize.4) I would not feel comfortable flying an aircraft with this MEL again unless we were filed below 10;000 feet know the system would not pressurize.5) The MEL was not clear on what to expect with this system inop.

column121: During the approach briefing for the ILS approach to Runway 15 at LCH; the First Officer (Pilot Flying); informed the Captain that he had problems with the Runway 15 localizer on two previous flights for this runway. The FO (First Officer) said that on both previous flights; the Runway 15 localizer did not stay centered. The FO explained the Localizer Course Deviation Indicator (CDI) had swung left and right of course. After discussing this; the Captain and FO agreed that the FO would remain on GPS guidance while the Captain would monitor on the localizer radio guidance. After being cleared for the approach; The FO intercepted the inbound course on GPS guidance. The Captain's localizer guidance initially appeared stable. Approximately three miles prior to the final approach fix; FIDGA; the FO switched his course guidance to the localizer. The approach guidance was stable. We passed FIDGA; intercepted the glide slope; and began our final descent. At approximately 1;300 feet MSL; the localizer began deviating left and right of course. The autopilot was engaged. The FO disengaged the autopilot and we immediately descended below the cloud ceiling; which was approximately 1;100 feet MSL or 1;200 feet MSL. The Captain and FO both sighted the runway at 1;100 feet MSL. At some point below 1;000 feet MSL; the localizer appeared to be stable. The remainder of the approach was uneventful. During the approach; the winds were 40 knots from approximately 200 degrees; prior to the FAF. After clearing the runway; we reported the problem to the Control Tower. The FO informed the Tower Controller he had problems with the Runway 15 localizer on two previous occasions. The Tower Controller said he had not received any other notifications about problems with the localizer from any other aircrews. At no point was the approach unstable. [Request] inspection of the localizer antenna. A query to the LCH Control Tower to determine if other aircrews have experienced the same problem. A notification in the daily read warning aircrews they might encounter the same problem.

column121: Flight ZZZZ - ZZZ1 (all nighter). Runway XXL departure IMC conditions with TS (thunderstorms) in terminal area. Crew briefed to remain seated due to expected turbulence on departure. Passengers briefed in welcome aboard announcement that the Flight Attendants would remain seated due to rain showers and bumps on departure. Performance for A/C weight of 145k; Flaps [set]; Runway XXL bleeds on reduced thrust T/O. Normal T/O executed with a climb to cleared altitude FL230 commenced. Passing approximately 11;000 [ft.; high elevation airport]. Cabin Alt Red warning light illuminated and horn sounded. Horn silenced - pressurization panel checked - and confirmed correct positioning of switches as terrain noted and communication coordinated with ATC for 'safe' altitude and significant weather avoidance required. Aircraft climbing at normal rate and leveling at 11;000 [ft.] was not an option. O2 masks donned and immediate action items of QRC executed. Remainder of checklist executed as Flying Pilot coordinated deviation with ATC and Captain with regard to safe altitude and course for primarily terrain avoidance and significant weather avoidance as a secondary threat. 17;000 ft. deemed to be safest altitude based on position of aircraft. Requested and set. Executed checklist items concurrently with NO resolution to regaining aircraft pressurization. All indications were normal; but obvious that aircraft was not pressuring at all. Plan determined by flight crew to coordinate safe corridor passage through the 'valley' - again based on terrain primary and weather secondary. Coordination with FAs indicated that passenger O2 had deployed automatically (and of note was deployed manually too during procedure); and that crew and passengers were 'safe'. ACARS NO COMM was illuminated likely due to A/C altitude and mountains blocking signals. Crew coordinated for lower altitudes as safe MORA (Minimum Off-Route Altitude) conditions permitted to account for passenger O2 eventually being depleted. Initially 15;000 [ft.]; then 12;000 [ft.] coordinated to attempt to get cabin altitude below 10;000 [ft.]. At 12;000 ft. with the pack switches selected to high - crew was able to get the cabin altitude to below 10;000 ft. On initial communication with the cabin crew - communication with the forward cabin was nearly impossible due to loud noise by door 1L (our apparent source of no pressurization). Crew communication conducted via aft galley inter phone to determine crew and passenger status. Cockpit crew determined return to ZZZZ not best course of action due to terrain; weather; heavy weight of aircraft and passenger O2 depletion. ACARS comm with Dispatch established as determination for diversion and potential diversionary airports weighed. Both ZZZZ1 and ZZZZ2 considered. ZZZZ1 determined to have more threats due to lack of familiarity; time and rising terrain by the airport. ZZZZ2 considered and subsequently determined (in coordination with Dispatch) due to familiarity; the fact that we have been routinely using it as an alternate for ZZZZ flights; safe passage from our current location to airport at 12;000 ft. and relatively easy weather avoidance to get to airport. Aircraft integrity was addressed and deemed not to be an issue to choose the more distant diversionary airport. Coordination with ATC-1 and ATC-2 Control completed to receive priority handling (even though very few aircraft were in the sector). Coordination with Dispatch continued throughout with updated runway data; weather and ZZZZ2 [company] ground operations taken care of. Clearance given to descend for the ILS [Runway] XXR approach to ZZZZ2. Crew understood and briefed overweight landing procedures for ZZZZ2 having previously agreed that the threat of landing at 133;000 lbs outweighed the threat of remaining airborne for another 45 min to burn down below max landing weight. Of note; on descent through 7;000 ft. a loud sound [was] heard in [the] cockpit - aircraft integrity deemed safewith no abnormal engine indications. Aircraft executed a normal approach and landing to Runway XYR in ZZZZ2. Upon arrival maintenance items entered for O2 deployed; aircraft pressurization; and overweight landing. Upon post flight it was determined the aircraft had at least two bird strikes which were also entered in maintenance log book. Maintenance quickly determined that door 1L had failed to seat properly but had given a closed condition indication (never any door indication illumination in the cockpit). Challenges existed in ZZZZ2 for both crew and passengers due to aircraft flight originating in [foreign country] with current COVID restrictions in place and requiring adherence.

We ended the day with 11.8 hours duty and approximately 8 hours flight time after factoring in a maintenance test run prior to our turn. On the arrival we were assigned delay vectors for Runway XXC due to ZZZ airport's wind shear concerns. We continued to plan accordingly. Visual conditions in the ZZZ terminal area; current speed was 220 knots; approach cleared us down to 3;000 feet and 030 heading. Shortly after they asked if we had the field in sight. We confirmed; then they cleared us for the visual approach Runway XXC and gave additional instruction to slow down to 160 knots. The PF called for Flaps 8 and then Flaps 20 at appropriate speeds. As we continued to slow down; he contemplated a need for flaps 30. Due to it being almost XA PM; the flight deck was dark; so I grabbed the speed cards and turned on my chart holder light to verify if we needed flaps 30 to stay above maneuvering speed. I noted flaps 20 provided a 4 knot buffer above slowest maneuvering speed; however; the flight conditions caused some light turbulence stemming from gusty wind conditions. The PF called for flaps 30 to provide a bigger margin of safety above Va. Unfortunately; as I got distracted with our Va and speed cards previously mentioned; I failed to notice that the APPR mode was not armed. As result; staying in HDG mode and distracted we flew through the Localizer. Approach called and queried us on our flight path. The PF disengaged the autopilot and corrected back without delay while I responded to ATC that we're correcting. The PF landed the aircraft shortly after without any further irregularities. Despite a warranted concern to make sure we're at a safe speed for the given aircraft configuration; I let myself become distracted with said task and should have done better dividing my attention. As soon as the words 'cleared for the approach' are broadcasted; focus should shift to the FMA by both pilots for confirmation that APPR Mode is armed.

column121: This covers two flights in the same airplane.I was doing a Captain OE flight with a Check Airman for both legs.The airplane had come from the hangar to try to address an MEL. The FO's audio control panel inoperative.The procedure in the MEL was used to recover the audio channel on the affected side.However; doing this rendered the following systems inoperative.The FO's side stick Push To Talk (PTT) would not work.The ACARS would not work.We failed to write up the above items since we knew the cause was the audio switching panel issue.If we had written up the ACARS as not working; we would have seen MEL #### which has some Dispatch procedures and operational procedures on our part. One of which is to monitor company communications thru SELCAL or voice on appropriate VHF/HF frequencies.However; the FOM enroute/communications section states that flights will continuously monitor ACARS; SELCAL; and/or appropriate VHF/HF frequencies (121.5 does not transmit SELCAL). Although ACARS is the primary means of maintaining this watch domestically; foreign coverage is limited. If ACARS is inoperative or in an area without ACARS coverage; establish a SELCAL or monitor the appropriate voice frequency. The Company must be able to immediately communicate with the aircraft at all times.We both failed to do this on both legs of the day.Although I finished training on Date; my first OE trip started approximately 3 weeks later. This was my second OE trip. There have been huge time gaps in my training and I was still feeling very much in the yellow on this airplane. My inexperience with the airplane and domestic flying kept me very firmly in the yellow while flying those legs. It wasn't until I was able to decompress from those flights the next morning that it occurred to me that we didn't adhere to the above referenced FOM.Even though I am flying with a Check Airman and said Check Airman has signed for the airplane; I still need to be in command and take my time to check all of my available references. Even if this means the flight goes out late or we refuse the airplane.

column121: Climbing through 34;000 feet we encountered a noise and grinding sound with a significant vibration through the plane. I noticed an odor and told the Captain and at that exact time the flight attendants called up saying that there was smoke in the cabin. We looked at the instruments and noticed both engines were erratic in their readings and a high vibration occurring on the number 2 engine. All of these events were happened at the same time.  I flew the aircraft the Captain worked the checklist and requested priority handling.  We shutdown the number 2 engine. An airport was right in front of us and we decided to divert there. Captain took care of the passenger PAs and flight attendants while I controlled the aircraft and flew.  After completing all the checklists and on downwind Captain took the aircraft and landed the plane. Fire Department was on scene and looked over the plane after we landed. They didn't noticed any leaks or fires so we taxied to the gate with them following us.  We had paramedics meet us at the gate to treat any passengers or crew members in case they needed assistance.After we made it to the gate and the passengers deplaned we inspected the number 2 engine.  There was damage to the nose cone and fan blades and inner engine cowling.  Something happened in flight for the parts to become damaged.  We were at FL340 so I doubt there were any birds or anything we hit; not sure why this happened.
column123: Climbing through 34;000 feet at climb power we encountered a cyclic; significant vibration through the airframe. The First Officer then noticed a toxic odor which I then noticed. This was immediately followed by a call from the flight attendants advising that the cabin was filling with smoke accompanied by a toxic odor.  This all happened over a period of about 15 seconds. We then looked at the engine instruments and noticed erratic engine indications along with reduced thrust and high engine vibration on the number 2 engine. The First Officer continued flying the aircraft and I communicated the situation to ATC with a call and a request for lower altitude. I completed the engine severe damage/separation checklist resulting in a precautionary shutdown of the number 2 engine. I then advised ATC we would be diverting for landing.After that I called the flight attendants to check on the status of the cabin. They told me the smoke and smell were dissipating rapidly. I advised them of the situation and that we would be making a precautionary landing  and would be landing in about 25 minutes. I then advised Dispatch through the ACARS message of our situation. After checking in with the First Officer on the status of the diversion I made a PA to the passengers advising them that we were having problems with one of our engines and that we were going to make a precautionary landing.  I also told them that in an abundance of caution they may see some safety equipment inspecting us after landing. Through the descent I made several more calls to the cabin to check on the status and made another PA to reassure the passengers. I also completed the one engine inoperative checklist along with the non routine landing checklist. I elected to assume control of the aircraft for landing and took the controls after we briefed the approach and after landing considerations. After landing without incident; we cleared the runway on a high speed taxi way and stopped so that the Fire Department could make an inspection of our aircraft. After Fire Department told us they saw no abnormalities I elected to taxi to the gate.The FO and I made a visual inspection of the number 2 engine and saw damage to two compressor blades along with damage to the spinner and the inner engine cowling. I was surprised at the small amount of damage considering the effects to engine performance and the smoke and fumes in the cabin.  I'd like to add that the First Officer did a great job in his duties which allowed me to focus on my duties. His calmness; superior airmanship and advice were instrumental in the smooth handling of our situation. I'd also like to commend the flight attendants especially the number 1; on their calmness; communication and professionalism in a very stressful situation.

I believe sometime around this thrust reduction is when the banging and shuddering stopped. In total; I believe we experienced approximately 5 to 7 distinct; noticeable bangs and shudders but I cannot say for sure. I did not see any overtemp or excessive vibration indications.Some time during the compressor stall sequence; ATC told us that they observed the number 3 engine smoking during our takeoff and climb. I don't remember exactly when ATC called us during the sequence. At this point; we got clearance to level off at 4;000 feet while we ran the compressor stall QRH and decided to return to ZZZ shortly thereafter.  Due to our high takeoff weight; we coordinated with ATC to facilitate a planned fuel dump. ATC cleared us to hold and climbed us up to 12;000 feet for our dump.  We dumped approximately XX;000 lbs of fuel in about 15 minutes.  Once our dump was complete and we landed uneventfully and taxied back to the ramp. We did not request emergency services however; they were in place awaiting our arrival anyways and they followed us to the ramp.Since neither of the remaining 2 engines exhibited any problems at all; I do not know what lead to the one engine's condition.  Since all three engines were exposed to the same operating conditions; I am at a loss for why only the one engine had problems during the conditions that all three engines were exposed to. I believe my manual thrust reduction action may have been when the stall sequence stopped but; I cannot say for certain.
column123: Passing approximately 1;000 feet MSL on departure from Runway XX and ZZZ we heard several (4-5) loud bangs and felt aircraft vibration. The First Officer (FO) was flying and he noticed fluctuation of the number 3 engine N1 and a slight; momentary yaw to the right. Departure control then informed us that the tower had seen 'black smoke' coming from our right engine. The FO reduced thrust on all engines as we transitioned the climb thrust altitude. We experienced no further abnormal engine indications for the remainder of the flight. We coordinated with ATC to return and made a quick call to Operations to appraise them of our situation and ask them to relay that information to maintenance. We ran the ENGINE COMPRESSOR STALL checklist in the QRH. Although the engine operation appeared normal; we opted to increase bleed air demand on all engines as a precaution. Furthermore; even though the engine operation appeared normal; we decided that it would not be prudent to remain airborne for 3 to 4 hours burning fuel.  We therefore asked ATC for fuel dump instructions. The controller instructed us to climb to 12;000 feet and to prepare to hold.During a slow climb to altitude; being careful not to approach the thrust level that existed at the time of the compressor stall; we [advised ATC]; reviewed the FUEL DUMP checklist and sent a diversion ACARS message to Dispatch. Shortly after level off ATC cleared us to commence dumping fuel while proceeding to the holding pattern. We dumped roughly XX;000 lbs over the next 15 minutes during which time we thoroughly discussed our situation; reviewed contingencies; and built and briefed an ILS approach to Runway XY. The Captain flew an uneventful approach and landing with Autocontrols off inside 1;000 feet. We exited the runway; waved off the responding emergency vehicles and taxied to our ramp. Due to lack of parking; we blocked in on the ramp main taxi line; checked in with Maintenance on the intercom; shut down the engines; made Maintenance Log entries; contacted the Duty Officer then scurried to the recovery bird.
