column121: During departure and approach phases; FMS switched to ROLL-GA (Go Around) modes without pilot command. On takeoff from ZZZ; performing the ZZZZZ1 departure from runway XX in HDG (heading) mode; PF (Pilot Flying) called for and PM (Pilot Monitoring) confirmed PITCH mode at acceleration altitude. Cleared from base leg for descent to 7000'; given vector to intercept localizer for ILS XXR; and cleared for visual approach; PF selected VS mode to begin descent and assigned heading in HDG mode with LNAV pre-selected for intercept. Autopilot was engaged. Again; spontaneously and uncommanded; FMS switched to ROLL-GA modes. Autopilot initiated climb. PF recognized the malfunction; switched off the autopilot; arrested climb; re-trimmed; and hand flew approach to landing. PM selected CRUISE thrust. (GA mode climbed aircraft from about 7400' MSL to about 7600' MSL before recovery and pilot resumption of descent.) PM attempted several times to re-sequence approach in FMS; FMS kept returning to ROLL-GA mode. Additionally; attempts to turn off distracting Flight Director and use raw green needle LOC/GS data for visual approach were unsuccessful. PF landed visually. After arrival at gate and aircraft shutdown; malfunction was entered into maintenance logbook and Maintenance control was contacted.

column121: Aircraft X was arriving into the ZZZ1 area from ZZZ before XA:00 pm in night conditions with fair visibility; with one FA (Flight Attendant) and no PAX (passengers) aboard. At perhaps 12 miles southwest of ZZZ2; descending out of 10;000 feet; cleared to 8;000 ft. with the FO (First Officer) as Flying Pilot; several instruments suffered anomalies. The Captain's MFD (DU 2) and FO's PFD (DU 5) became blank; both RMUs (Radio Management Units) displayed all dashes except for Comm indications; and EICAS presented one CAS (Crew-Alerting System) message that I recall - RA 2 (amber). ZZZ1 Approach Control was issuing vectors toward the east and cleared the flight to 7;000 feet and then requested our altitude as they were no longer receiving the Mode C altimeter report. The CA (Captain) advised ATC of our electrical issues. The FP (Flying Pilot) selected PFD on his reversionary panel MFD switch to restore flight instruments for view on his operating DU 4; although the navigation info was unusable with a red X. The CA indicated he could see ZZZZZ; the final approach fix; on his PFD. The CA attempted to find an applicable QRH malfunction but the crew was not presented with an obvious CAS message to troubleshoot. The crew discussed what might be at issue and the CA checked the circuit breakers. Although DC Bus 2 was suspected there was nothing positive to confirm it. The FP accepted a clearance to 5;000 feet while stating to the CA that the aircraft was now clear of the mountains. However the autopilot failed to capture the altitude so the FO disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the remainder of a visual approach to a successful night landing at ZZZ2 runway XXC. At some point south of ZZZZZ the CA advised that we should land the aircraft and figure out the problem on the ground and so we proceeded to configure normally and complete all checklists. The CA concluded that Generator 2 might be at fault and so reset it. His MFD began to restore just prior to landing; and the FO's DU 5 did so during taxi in to the hangar. Maintenance personnel met the aircraft and the possibility of a GCU fault was discussed. Normally a failed generator should be compensated for by the EDL to prevent the loss of flight instruments or displays. The aircraft was handed over to Maintenance for further investigation. This event allowed the crew to demonstrate excellent CRM through coordinated effort; superb communications; and teamwork under the direction of the CA. This approach provided for a calmly executed arrival to the destination. Curiously both crew members had just completed Annual Equipment Exams on the same day sit in ZZZ3. The preparation and study for the review was clearly an advantage to the crew and proved the value of the training.Submitted respectfully;NAMEFirst Officer

At that time; Tower came on the radio and said; 'Aircraft X; exit the highspeed [Taxiway] 2X or the reverse.' We understood the reverse to be Taxiway 1. My First Officer than switched to Ground; who told us to 'Taxi to the gate via Taxiway 2 and 3; cross [Runway] YYL; C and [Taxiway] 4;' to which my First Officer acknowledged.Ground Control then came on shortly thereafter with us on Taxiway 2 and told us that he really needed us on Taxiway 2X to exit; 'not' the reverse. We then realized that with everything going on in the cockpit during a typical ZZZ landing; stopping the aircraft; etc.; Tower probably told us to 'Exit the high speed [Taxiway] 2X; not the reverse.' Instead; we heard that to be 'Exit the high speed [Taxiway] 2X or the reverse.' The speed of the speech to which the clearance was given by the Tower also made the clearance difficult to understand; plus the radio sounded a bit muffled (Tower controllers wear masks while working). To note; there were no conflicts and no aircraft on Taxiway 2 upon exiting.After taxiing into the gate; I called the Tower directly and spoke with one of the controllers (but not the one who gave us that clearance). After explaining what I felt we heard the clearance to be; he responded that since they wear masks in the Tower; sometimes it's difficult to discern exact language with short bursts of words and hence the confusion between words like 'or' and 'not' when used in a quick clearance as was done in this situation. He said that most likely Tower was trying to get us off more quickly by using the high speed [Taxiway] 2X (instead of the reverse at Taxiway 1) in order to get a departing aircraft off before the next arrival.He told us 'no problem' and 'I'm sure the Tower Controller was not upset at all because I haven't heard about it.' So; most likely; it was simply a sequencing issue with Tower in order to expedite their flow. If the Controller had anticipated what he wanted and told us that clearance on final rather on during the last part of the landing roll after I positioned the aircraft into a left turn off onto Taxiway 1; that might have helped him. I also believe the mask that the Controller was wearing and the speed of his speech in which he delivered his clearance muffled the word 'not' that we heard as 'or.'

column121: No violation occurred. We found a potential issue with an arrival and approach into Las Vegas. We were descending via the RNDRZ 1 Arrival into LAS. The bottom altitude at ROAMN is 8;000 ft. Prior to reaching ROAMN; we were cleared to join the localizer for the ILS1L after ROAMN. This approach has a ROAMN as the IAF/transition. When we closed the discontinuity to hook up ROAMN (common waypoint on the STAR and approach); the hard altitude of 8;000 ft. (per the STAR) dropped from the flight plan. The VNAV recalculated the descent; which would have left us about 600 ft. high over ROAMN. I pointed this out to the Captain (PF( Pilot Flying)) who then reprogrammed the FMS and added 8;000 ft. back as a hard altitude at ROAMN. I looked at several other STAR/approach combinations that all have common waypoints. For each one I found; both the STAR and the approach list the common way-point with the same hard altitude. The 1L ILS does not list ROAMN with a hard altitude of 8;000 ft. even though it is on the STAR. Does this need to be updated ? If not; when cleared for the approach prior to the IAF; are you relieved of the hard altitude on the STAR if the IAF isn't listed with one as is the case here?

column121: In cruise I told the CA (Captain) I needed to use the lavatory. We called back to the FA's (Flight Attendants) who said they were finishing up service and would come up when they could. When they called up; they gave the code word as normal. I did a positive exchange of controls to the Captain since it was my PF (Pilot Flying) leg. He took controls as normal. Door unlocked and the crew swap went normal. Upon finishing in the lavatory the B FA called up to begin the next crew exchange. She informed me that the CA wanted to use the lavatory too. I was waiting in the galley expecting the A FA to come out so we could do the normal process of me sitting down; getting controls back; getting any flight updates; and then having the FA's call back up so the CA could use the lav. Instead; the flight deck door opened and out walked the CA. No one was at the controls; the A FA was in the process of moving from my seat to the CA seat. I immediately said 'she's supposed to come out first; no one is at the controls'. The CA responded 'oh; right' or something along those lines. The B FA and myself expressed our concerns over the incorrect lavatory exchange procedure. He then proceeded to open the lavatory door. Not go back into the flight deck. I rushed into the flight deck; sat down; got myself situated and locked the door since there was no pilot. I got the aviate; navigate done and now wanted to communicate. I asked the A FA what happened and she said 'I don't really know; he told me to switch seats with him so we squeezed past each other'. I told her that's not normal and that I needed to talk to the CA. The B FA called up; said the code word; and the CA came back in. I talked to him about what happened and he said something like 'oh right; that did seem strange'. I talked to him about the correct procedure which he; I assume; did not know. I told him we had no one at the controls and how dangerous that is. Upon getting to the hotel the FA's asked me if I was going to fill out a report. I called the Pilot Union Professional Standards to get their opinion on the situation. I used this as a teaching moment; however; the whole event should never have happened.

Included with the brief was a request to maintain good communication with the flight crew on any matters. Further; instruction was given to the Lead F/A to step back from any passenger problems while at the gate and engage the Gate Agent to handle the passenger problem.b. Near the completion of boarding the Lead F/A came to the flight deck to inform the crew that two passengers boarded the aircraft with alcohol. Passengers were engaged by another flight attendant; not the Lead; and denied that they had alcohol. Lead F/A advised that the alcohol beverages had spilled. Flight crew and Lead F/A agreed to a plan to resolve the matter. Passengers complied with instructions and remained onboard.2) During Push Back from Gate Xa. Flight crew worked through preflight preparations; including a review of performance data for [Runways] 18C and 18L. During FMC programming flight crew determined that a new [set of performance data] had been generated removing data for 18L; the most probable runway for departure. New performance data was updated via ACARS for 18L and was reviewed by the flight crew and programmed into the FMC. MEL XX-XX was reviewed. All other preflight preparations were completed per company policies; procedures and flows. Load close-out was received at the gateb. Flight crew called Ramp [name] for a clearance from Gate X and received clearance to push back. Ground crew declined to push the aircraft from Gate X due to conflict with aircraft in the ramp alley. First Officer discussed the push clearance with Ramp [name] and was assured the clearance to push was valid and that aircraft were not in conflict as the other aircraft were from the adjacent concourse. Ground crew was advised and still refused to push the aircraft. Another inquiry was made to Ramp [name] and push clearance was rescinded.c. Conflict aircraft from adjacent concourse departed the ramp. Ramp [name] re-cleared the aircraft to push from [Gate] X. Ground crew complied with the push back clearance. Two engines were started in the ramp alley. Ground crew received a wave off/salute. After start flows and checklist were accomplished. Out time XB:31 local/XA:31 UTC. d. Captain and First Officer used headsets and discussed abnormally high side tone volume on the INT function with MIC selected. Various adjustments were made to set appropriate communication volume3) Taxi from Gate X to Runway 18La. First Officer issued a request to taxi. Ramp [name] issued a multiple part clearance. (Taxi south line; Spot XXS; caution for pushback on [neighboring gate]; contact Ramp East 129.225 at Spot XXS). The clearance from Ramp [name] clearance was given rapidly and muffled. A second request was made for a taxi clearance/confirmation. Clearance was heard and understood by both crew members. Aircraft proceeded to XXS.b. Approaching XXS; First Officer contacted Ramp [name2]. Ramp [name 2] responded with a clearance to taxi to [Spot] XXS and contact Ground at  [spot] XXS. Captain verbally reviewed triggers with First Officer for Before Take Off Flow and advised that a flight control check would commence on Taxiway C. Approaching [spot]  XXS Ground Control issued a clearance to taxi [Taxiways] Mike; Charlie; hold short C10 for [Runway] 18L. First Officer replied to Ground Control and Captain responded to the First Officer repeating the clearance with emphasis to Hold Short of C10. The taxi route was continuous without stops or delays. Numerous aircraft were on Taxiway C and positioned at various ramp location spots adjacent and parallel too Taxiway C. Two aircraft were positioned facing south at Spot XYE. The aft positioned aircraft at XYE had its landing/taxi lights illuminated while stationary.c. Flight control checks were initiated on Taxiway C prior to C10. During the initiation of the elevator check as the First Officer was verbalizing elevator position; Ground Control re-issued the taxi clearance to hold short of [Taxiway] C11. Flight control checks were discontinued; the taxi clearance was accepted and responded too by the First Officer. The Captain repeated and verbalized the clearance to the First Officer with emphasis to hold short of C11. Flight Control checks were re-initiated by the Captain. At full aft elevator the First Officer verbalized the elevator position simultaneously as Ground Control re-issued a clearance to continue to [Runway] 18L. The First Officer read back the clearance. The Captain repeated the clearance to the First Officer. The Captain maintained full aft elevator during the communication with Ground Control and the First Officer.d. Flight control checks re-initiated from the beginning of the Before Take Off Flow and the remaining flow items were completed. The taxi/landing lights from the aft aircraft at [Spot] XYE were obscuring the view on Taxiway C. The Captain stopped the aircraft in a position on Taxiway C that used the forward aircraft's wing at Spot XYE to block the glare from the aft aircraft at Spot XYE. The Captain gave a courtesy flash of the taxi light to alert the crew of the aircraft on XYE of their landing/taxi light illumination. The First Officer verbalized and switched Radio One to the Tower Control frequency. The parking brake was set. The Captain called for the Before Take Off checklist. Task Loading increased due to a reduced time factor in the task/time equation. Flight crew members were in the green area of the [threat mode]; however external factors were compressing the time component and additional time elements would be required to remain out of the yellow and in the green area of the threat mode paradigm.e. As the Before Take Off checklist was being accomplished the aircraft on [Taxiway] C12 was cleared on to [Runway] 18L; however no clearance was heard on the radio. At this time both the Captain and the First Officer deduced that an incorrect frequency was selected on Radio One. The error was trapped and corrected. The flight crew was now in the yellow area of the threat mode paradigm due to a high task load environment.f. Upon tuning of the Tower frequency; the crew re-initiated the Before Take Off Checklist. Simultaneously the Tower Controller issued a clearance to proceed onto the runaway. The Tower Controller's voice conveyed a tone of agitation; immediacy; anger and frustration. Additionally; the Tower Controllers diction was rapid; difficult to hear and understand. For reasons of safety; the crew declined the clearance. The flight crew again attempted to complete the Before Take Off Checklist. The Tower Controller responded with agitation and another clearance that was rapid and difficult to understand with a demand to expedite taxi onto the runway and in some manner exit the runway. We advised the Tower we would need 30 seconds and we would be ready for departure. The Tower Controller responded again with agitation and anger and demanded we taxi onto the active runway in an expedited manner; with a rapid diction pattern and clearance that we were unable to understand while an aircraft was approaching the runway for landing as we were being lambasted by the Tower Controller regarding other traffic waiting to depart.g. At this point the demands from the Tower Controller had compromised the safe operation of the aircraft as the issued clearances appeared too no longer be operationally motivated. The Captain momentarily took over radio communication and advised the tower that we were unable to accept the clearance. Our decision to not move the aircraft was driven by safety concerns and based on the threat mode model. The true safest course of action was to keep the aircraft stationary until the task loading paradigm could be shifted to normal operational expectations.h. The Tower Controller remained agitated and instructed the crew to copy a telephone number and demanded a call tothe number. The Tower Controller read the number; we advised that we received the number and the Tower Controller re-read the number a second time and got a digit incorrect in the second reading and self-corrected their error of the telephone number. We confirmed receipt. The Before Take Off Checklist was completed; and we advised the Tower Controller we were ready for departure.The CLT airport during this bank of flights and the previous bank of flights was a chaotic mess; as is the case with CLT with all banks of flights. Aircraft crew transiting into an out of the 1 and 2 concourse are subject to extraordinary delays and the resultant increase in stress as are the Ramp Controllers and local ATC controllers. This high level of stress with too many aircraft movements in too small of space is a significant negative factor in the safety equation. The attempts by airlines to operate in this manner is a contributing factor to the degradation of safety and the stress applied to all personnel is a concrete byproduct of this poor planning and management. Further; the manifest stress is evident in the voice; demeanor and diction of ATC and other personnel which results in a degrade performance profile.Reduce access and aircraft movements in the 1 and 2 concourses to better manage traffic flow. Properly staff and monitor ATC positions and personnel for signs of stress. Review and stream line CLT Ramp operations and coordination with ATC Ground Control.

column121: During walk-around; [the] FO (First Officer) found a dent in [the] aircraft; aft left side; near lavatory service. [The case was] entered into [the] AML and [we] informed Maintenance. Contract Maintenance took pictures; detailed measurements; and notes for submittal to ZZZ2 Maintenance Control. After approximately an hour; it was determined that [the] aircraft was good to go; item was deferred; and the paperwork was completed. Flight was uneventful to ZZZ1. At the gate in ZZZ1; a Mechanic came out to the aircraft with some ACARS paper that was requested inbound. We mentioned the dent; so he said he would go take a look. During this time; [the] aircraft was serviced; passengers were boarded; and the flight was 'ready' for departure. The door was actually closed when the Crew Chief informed us that we were on a maintenance hold. The same Mechanic returned and told us that the dent was very significant and the aircraft should be taken out of service for repairs. He mentioned that the aircraft shouldn't have flown and was a 'blowout' waiting to happen. A Maintenance Supervisor came out; evaluated the situation; and the aircraft was subsequently taken out of service. Why and how was it determined that the aircraft was 'good to go' at an outstation; but when the plane gets to a hub it's taken out of service? I understand a forward-leaning mentality when it comes to serving our passengers but this should never be at the expense of safety. We were informed by the Maintenance Supervisor that the discrepancy was deferred in ZZZ but the aircraft was to undergo further evaluation when it arrived in ZZZ1. This sounds plausible; except; the only reason the discrepancy was 'further evaluated' was because we needed ACARS paper and happened to mention the dent to an experienced and highly trained Mechanic; who applied the brakes to this situation. Mistakes can happen; but in situations where there is doubt regarding airworthiness; it is better to err on the side of caution.

column121: At initial entry into the flight deck; a large amount of coffee was spilled on the aft; center; pedestal of our Airbus A319. Despite an immediate clean up with a large number of paper towels; the first noted impact may have been the failure of the ACARS printer; as indicated by an MCDU message; and the failure of the 'Slew' button to advance any paper. We then began a long series of phone calls with our dispatcher and Maintenance Control (conferenced in) to both attempt a reset of the printer or secure an MEL entry. The total time on the phone was likely over 30 minutes; after which we had an ACARS printer MEL. During our extensive time on hold; I began to suspect that some of the coffee may have also entered other components; such as the Flap/Slat and Spoiler control modules; all near the ACARS printer. After advising Maintenance Control of this; their guidance was to cycle the various components at the gate to see if they worked; we did so; but that generated a FLT/C ECAM Slat Sys error message. Maintenance Control suggested that we try the tests again; once both engines were running; which we did. Both systems appeared to operate nominally so we dismissed our push crew for taxi out. Within 2 to 4 minutes of commencing taxi; I noted an electrical odor; followed soon thereafter by visible whiffs of electrical smoke coming from the ACARS printer area. I directed the First Officer to immediately pulled the ACARS printer Circuit Breaker (as we knew from our earlier Maintenance Control-directed troubleshooting); but found it had already popped. We returned to the gate after consulting with Maintenance Control and local operations; whereupon our aircraft was eventually removed from service.This was arguably the greatest failure of my entire aviation career; I am aghast that we allowed this situation to progress as far is it did; particularly in light of the 'What If's?' We almost took off in an aircraft with grossly uncertain airworthiness. An after-the-fact Google search reveals a long history of potentially catastrophic aviation emergencies and incidents from cockpit fluid spills; we would have added to this list if the ACARS printer had happened to begin smoking a few minutes later; or if the spoilers or flaps/slats had had an uncommanded movement; or if the Engine Master Control(s) had detected a false 'Off' signal...all from a stray drop of coffee migrating to the wrong place at the worst time.While there are many parties to this series of mistakes; I feel that Maintenance Control guidance in this matter was woefully incorrect and caused a serious; negative; impact on our flight's safety. Furthermore; our own flight training has been deficient; we should have known to ground the aircraft. Had we been correctly trained on this threat; we would have never left the gate. Prior to this event; I had little understanding of the potential damage from fluid spills; now I know better; particularly after seeing the coffee stains near the cannon plugs and wiring of essential items inside the center pedestal. Lastly; we were not the first; nor will we be the last; to spill something on the flight deck: the FAA and other aviation authorities should quickly establish Technical Standard Orders for all equipment in 'spill zones' so as to prevent potentially catastrophic outcomes going forward.

column121: Flight was scheduled to depart ZZZ. We arrived in the flight deck and performed all the normal procedures we have for a normal push back. Captain did the preflight walk around and I loaded the FMC. We agreed the OFP (Operational Flight Plan) looked good and the rest of the flight plan looked sufficient for a potentially bumpy ride to ZZZ1. Captain advised to Flight Attendants to stay seated out of ZZZ until we knew the ride would allow for their safe duties. I was the flying pilot and after Captain did his first flight of the day and PM (Pilot Monitoring) duty brief; I briefed the SID. We planned for a normal pushback with 2 engine start for a quick taxi for departure. We performed the BEFORE TAKEOFF CHECKLIST on taxi out down the ramp for takeoff on runway XX.While we were taxiing down to runway XX; I noticed there was a split between the L and R duct pressure. I made note of it to Captain and we briefly discussed these splits we have seen before in this aircraft and recall it being a known normal occurrence. I cycled the L PACK (Left) switch to OFF and back to AUTO as well as the ISOLATION VALVE switch to OPEN and AUTO and saw the duct pressure needles sync together. We decided it would be a safe action to depart and noted we would keep an eye on the duct pressure and pressurization.We departed runway XX and CLIMBED VIA THE SID. I hand flew the departure to the mid 20s and then turned the autopilot on. I noted Captain mentioned 2 different times that the aircraft was pressurizing normally though the duct pressure still was split. The ride was mostly good and the flight attendants were up but the seat belt was still on. As we approached our level off altitude of FL340 the CABIN ALTITUDE horn and the MASTER WARNING lights illuminated. We verified the CABIN ALTITUDE was high on the pressurization panel and performed the Immediate Action items for CABIN ALTITUDE WARNING OR RAPID DEPRESSURIZATION/EMERGENCY DESCENT. The CABIN ALTITUDE was not controllable; and we continued with the descent. There was a definite issue with immediate communication over the inter-phone with the masks on and all the noise. Getting the mask on and the audio panel correct to be able to speak and hear over the speaker poses a threat in this airplane if not practiced. We were able to communicate with each other and ATC but it was challenging with all the noise and distractions.Captain identified as a priority flight with ZZZ Center and we began the initial descent over the mountains. I initially turned off the AUTOPILOT to pitch over and begin the procedure. Once we were established in a descent; I turned the AUTOPILOT back on and descended to FL190 with the high terrain in mind. We saw an aircraft below us on the TCAS and had to shallow the descent initially before we were cleared lower. Captain proceeded with completing the checklist and communicating with the Flight attendants; passengers; and dispatch. Descending through approximately 16;000 feet I noticed the CABIN ALTITUDE was in a normal range of around 7;000 feet and we took off the oxygen masks. We leveled off at 11000 in the vicinity of ZZZ2. Initially we were planning on diverting to ZZZ2 because we were so close; but Captain's experience and familiarity with ZZZ3. This led to the decision to divert and there was difficulty communicating with dispatch possibly due to our low altitude so we opted to landing in ZZZ3. The flight attendants and passengers were all briefed for the diversion to ZZZ3. I left the AUTOPILOT on and we flew the RNAV (GPS) Runway XY 29 approach and landing. All checklists were completed before ZZZZZ intersection and the landing was normal. CFR ( Aircraft Rescue & Firefighting) was there upon arrival.We were parked at the hard stand in ZZZ3 and the ramp personnel brought over the ramp to allow the passengers to vacate the aircraft. Operations were there to help while we figured out the plan of action for the passengers. Captain discussed the situation with the ChiefPilot; Dispatch; and Maintenance and I aided the flight attendants with passengers. I walked to the OUTFLOW VALVE and noted a mesh substance blocking the OUTFLOW VALVE from fully closing. Captain manually opened and closed the valve and I videoed the movement.

column121: On Departure out of ZZZ the crew experienced significant audio distortions on COMM 1. Switched to COMM 2. In the vicinity of ZZZ1 contact was lost with ATC for a period of approximately 10 minutes. ACARS was also lost at this time. Upon reestablishing contact ATC was able to hear the crew loud and clear but on board the ability to receive ATC transmissions was significantly degraded and there was significant static and noise on both frequencies. As the flight progressed the quality of the reception continued to degrade and COMM 1 became completely unusable. The QRH was run and the MEL; FOM and AOM (Aircraft Operation Manual) were utilized. The decision was made to Identify as an emergency and continue to the planned destination. Due to the inability to contact the company; ATC was requested to tell the company of the communication issue. As the flight progressed the quality of the reception continued to degrade on COMM 2 until it was barely usable. Upon entering the approach segment of the flight NAV 1 and 2 provided unreliable lateral and vertical information. The flight concluded safely at the destination. Flight crew that handed off the aircraft noted issues with the ACARS no other pertinent information was provided by the crew as they departed. ACARS was usable for the preflight and initial departure portion of the flight.The cause of the radio communications failure is not known by this crew member at this point in time.Air traffic control was very professional and they were immensely helpful and indispensable throughout the event.
column123: While departing ZZZ; on climb out and then more noticeable as we neared ZZZ1; static / screeching distortions were noted on COMM 1. At least three times; we asked ATC how they heard us; and the reply was 5x5. We could hear ATC at a 2 or 3. We advised ATC of this. Conditions deteriorated throughout the flight; causing us to utilize COMM 2 as primary.After a short period; COMM 2 began a degradation similar to COMM 1. All flight instrumentation; engine gauges; etc. showed normal parameters. QRH / FOM checked; Captain and I monitored and with COMM 2 not improving; and notification updated information to ATC; Identified as an emergency. Plan and back up plans were made by crew; flight attendants briefed; company notified. Flight continued with no further issues. It should be noted that during a period of time; no COMMS were heard; and we queried ATC to make sure we had not lost all communication. Additionally on approach (visual conditions) both lateral and vertical guidance was observed unreliable. Furthermore upon accepting the aircraft from the previous crew; the Captain noted issues with the 'ACARS' noting we may have to reset the ACARS.The cause of the action is outside of the scope of this crew member. ATC was outstanding. Helpful professional and went above and beyond.

column121: Pushed back from the ZZZ gate X; during push back; we received the okay from ground crew personnel that we can start engine 1. During engine start of the number one engine; it was noted that we had a hung start as the N2 gauge only got up to about 31 percent. Once the Captain and I noticed the indications; we went into shutdown procedures of the number 1 engine. We did note the engine 1 ITT temperature rapidly increase; before it decreased. After shutting down the engine to prepare to restart; ground crew personnel attempted to notify us that there was a fire. However; due to faulty headsets of ground personnel; this information was hard to make sense of. At this point to confirm a potential fire; we contacted the flight attendants to check the rear of the aircraft and look out the windows to confirm the fire potential. The flight attendants did not see any flames or smoke. The decision was made to open the main cabin door; to allow the pilot in command to visually verify there was a fire threat. After the pilot in command visually inspected the area; he was able to confirm that there was a fire and we promptly called for an aircraft evacuation of the passengers and crew. Fire units were notified promptly by ground crew and notification to ZZZ Ground Control of evacuation of passengers on the ramp. The Captain and myself (First Officer) continued to do the Engine Fire (on the ground) Emergency Procedure Checklist and the Passenger Evacuation Procedure Checklist.
column123: Pushing back we were cleared to start the number one engine. While starting the engine we noticed the engine went to 30 percent N2 and N1 was hanging at 6 to 7 percent. When we were doing the shutdown procedure we noticed the ITT gauge started going up rapidly then went down to zero after we shut down the engine and had no other messages appear on the aircraft. After we shut down the engine the rampers were trying to tell us something; but their radio had a lot of static and I could not understand them. I thought they said fire; but I was not sure because of all the static on the radio. We had no indication on the EICAS of an engine fire. I had my First Officer call the Flight Attendant and check to see if there was a fire. They called back and said they could not see anything. Still unable to understand what ramp was saying; I decided to open the cabin door to visually check; and there was a fire on the number 1 engine. I ran back inside and told the Flight Attendants to evacuate the aircraft. The First Officer and I ran the Engine Fire (on the ground) Emergency Procedure Checklist. After we finished the checklist I shut off the aircraft and made sure everyone was off the aircraft.

column121: We were flying back to ZZZ on a clear dark night; arriving on day four. It was my leg (Captain); PF (Pilot Flying). About 20 miles out we were given a vector to ZZZZZ which is about 6 miles south of ZZZZZ1; the final approach fix for runway XXL. The controller asked us to keep our speed up to 210 or better until final as she had other inbound aircraft that she was sequencing in. We switched to green needles and sequenced the approach according to our normal procedures. When we were about 10 miles from ZZZZZ; approximately abeam ZZZZZ1; we called the field in sight. The controller gave us a heading of 080; cleared us for the approach and switched us to tower. She noted that the other aircraft would be following us and to keep 170 or better to final. At this point we were about 5 miles from ZZZZZ1 at about 90 degrees intercept. The heading the controller gave us would take us inside the final approach fix before we intercepted the final bearing. Seeing this; the FO (First Officer) noted that we had not begun our decent to final approach fix altitude yet. I called for the descent; flaps 20 as we slowed to final approach speed. As PF; I noted that the flight guidance would not give us a good intercept because the intercept was too great. At this moment; the autopilot began the turn to final too soon. I turned off the auto pilot and began hand flying. As we began the turn to final I called for flaps 30; and then flaps 45 as we neared the final bearing. As we were completing the turn; the FO (Pilot Monitoring) noted that we were still high and that we should increase our rate of decent; we were about 2000 MSL; I steepened our decent and he selected 1000 fpm as we rolled out. I called for and we completed the landing checklist. Tower came up and checked us in. We had not called at the FAP (Final Approach Path) as we were busy flying. At this point; we were about 4 miles from the end of the runway at about 1800 MSL. The tower gave us landing clearance and noted that we were low as the PF I called for us to stop our decent; and I leveled the aircraft at about 1500 MSL. I noted that I had not completed the turn correctly and we were not quite on final bearing. I corrected and called for zero VSI (Vertical Speed Indicator) and adjusted to get on final. The FO complied and we continued inbound. At about 3 miles from the runway on final bearing our GPWS alarm went off; PULL UP. As PF; I called for a climb and began a climb at about 5 degrees nose up. As we began our climb; the GPWS alarm went off again; saying PULL UP; I increased the climb; and we climbed about 200ft; as we were very close to glideslope. I was about to call for a missed approach; when I noted that the climb had put us on glideslope; and the PAPI's confirmed us on glideslope. Seeing this; I reestablished our decent and the FO called stabilized at about 3 miles. We landed normally; completed our checklists and shut down the aircraft in accordance with our normal procedures. We have procedures and training guidance that should have prevented this. In this case; there were several errors I made on this approach. As PF; I should not have accepted the vector inside the final approach fix with such a large intercept heading. As Captain; I knew that the flight guidance would be unable to make the turn correctly and we would need more room to make the turn to final. I should have asked to continue our course and give the controller other options. This likely would have prevented the whole series of errors. I should have started my decent to FAF altitude sooner. We were at 3;000 feet; 5 miles from ZZZZZ1 as we turned; and I delayed our decent to 2;400 ft. for several seconds as I turned off the flight guidance and began the turn. If we had been at 2;400 MSL we would not have required a large decent in the turn to final. When the tower checked us in at 4 miles and noted that we were low; I should have called for and established a climb back to glideslope instead of just leveling out. We were very close to glideslope and we should have re-intercepted it first. When the GPWS alarm went off; I should have immediately called for a Missed Approach. We were low (hence the alarm) and there is no space or time for altitude errors on final. Any delay calling for a Missed Approach puts safety at risk. Finally; there was probably some 'get-home-itis' in our minds as we were flying. Arriving late at night; at home field on day four; we were tired and wanted the trip to be over. Going missed would have delayed our landing. Also; we were also trying to satisfy the controller who was sequencing us in front of another aircraft. We needed to focus on our flight; not her decisions or problems.

The Ground Controller then stated to give way and that he meant to tell us the plane at XX1 was going the opposite direction on Kilo to join Lima to XXR. Neither of us were aware of that when it occurred. We never should have been cleared to taxi until the traffic from spot XX had cleared us going the opposite direction; or our clearance to taxi should have included to give way to opposite direction traffic from spot XX1."
column123: We were positioned at ZZZ ramp spot XX. An aircraft at spot XX1 was cleared to taxi to [runway] XXR; but I wasn't paying attention to his routing. I thought I heard via 'Kilo.' Immediately after that; we were cleared to [runway] XXR via Kilo; and told an airplane on Kilo to our right waits on us. The airplane at spot XX1 began taxiing and I began my taxi so as to be in front of the airplane on our right that was taxiing; but waiting on us. I can't be positive; and it may have been just my expectation; but I thought I saw the airplane from spot XX1 (on our left now) start a left turn on Kilo. With him safely in front of us (I thought); I briefly looked down at the FMC then to my right to make sure we were clear of the airplane on Kilo. The First Officer then said; stop; stop; stop." The aircraft from spot XX1 had turned to the right not left; and was now right in front of us. He had been cleared to the runway via Kilo; K5; Lima. We had not been moving very fast since we had just left spot XX; but I applied the brakes quickly to ensure safe separation. This; I learned later; had caused our number one Flight Attendant; who I did not know was standing; to lose her balance and fall against the galley area. Ground Control then apologized for not letting us know; or to give way. We continued to the runway and I spoke with the crew to make sure they were okay; our number one especially. They all said they were okay and that they were good to continue to ZZZ1. In flight; the number one Flight Attendant told me she wanted to file an injury on duty report. I was very concerned for her at that point; but she said she was just a little sore; she could perform all her duties; and we would be okay to continue. I concurred with her that it would be safe to continue to ZZZ1. We were scheduled to turn around and fly back to ZZZ.I was still very concerned; so I asked the number one to coordinate with her supervisor and get guidance since she wanted to also fly back to ZZZ. I called safety to get guidance as well. Our Flight Attendant stated she was fine to fly back and could perform any and all her duties. After observing; and speaking with her; the First Officer and I both concurred with her assessment that it was safe and reasonable to continue. We landed uneventfully in ZZZ and a team member met the airplane for our number one."

column121: We were holding short of XXL on Sierra and another aircraft; was holding (arriving earlier).  Somewhat unexpectedly; we were cleared for takeoff.  I pushed the Attend button; and slowly crept toward the runway to keep the operational flow going.  After a long delay; and now approaching the runway; I pushed the Attend button again; with no immediate response.  I continued onto the runway. A FA then called us to state they were enforcing a passenger failure to wear a mask issue (this was also an issue during boarding). I directed the FO to ask Tower for a 30 second delay on runway; which was granted. The FA then communicated to me (the exact words I do not recall); that the situation was corrected.  I was fully under the impression that they were ready for departure.  We then executed the takeoff; but as it turns out; a forward FA was still standing in the isle of the cabin and had to take a seat in the aft galley. Once at level-off; we discussed the situation. column123: As the A FA; I was conducting my final walkthrough. I was at the last row of seats. A child that was seated in the last row with her sister and mother was not wearing her mask. The mask was in the mothers bag. This issue had been addressed earlier upon boarding. The CA dinged us for departure.  I called the CA from the AFT galley to let him know the same family was not in mask compliance. I asked if I could call him back and he replied with we are on the runway. Finally got the child in compliance so I asked the D FA to call the CA to let him know the mask was on. 2 rows in front of the mask compliance issue was an elderly lady whom refused to stow her large bag on the floor nor in an overhead bin. I had a bin open to try and coax her into letting me stow the bag for her when we took off so I took the nearest jumpseat for takeoff.

column121: First Officer; Pilot Monitoring. Captain; Pilot Flying. 3;000 feet MSL inbound to AWLEE 210 KIAS or greater assigned. Cleared for a visual approach approximately 5 miles from AWLEE 170 or greater to 5 mile final assigned. Continue on heading; allow spacing for visual approach at 210 KIAS. Abeam CRDNL given 080 heading and still cleared for visual and switched to Tower. 080 heading gave a perpendicular intercept course for final. Captain armed approach mode. Aircraft began an early turn to final simultaneously the Captain input a command that caused the plane to enter into pitch mode. I called out pitch mode and he turned autopilot off. I advised the Captain that he needed to begin a descent since we were inside the final approach fix and were 600 feet high. I entered vertical speed mode and put in a thousand ft per min rate of descent and dialed in a 45 degree intercept into the heading. Captain began slowing down and called for gear down; flaps 30; and flaps 45 at appropriate speeds I called for level off when I realized we were at 1;500 feet MSL (acceleration altitude). Simultaneously we received a call from Tower advising us that we were low for our area. I informed Tower that we were leveling and continuing our visual approach. At this point I went outside the cockpit and became focused on looking for towers that would pose a danger to our flight. I didn't recognize any threats. I thought that we could maintain this altitude and intercept the glideslope without issue. We then received a call of terrain. I said we needed to climb. No climb was initiated. We then received the audio alert of woop woop terrain. Pull up. At this point I stated we needed to climb. I began pulling back pressure and a climb was initiated. The audible signals ceased and we continued to intercept the glide slope. Once established on glide slope and on course I called out 1;000 feet stabilized and we completed the approach to a landing.  As soon as we were at 1;500 MSL I should have called for a go around. I knew the Captain was disoriented and was confident that I could act as a back stop to get him onto final. I didn't call for a go around after we stopped getting the audible warnings because we were at that point established within the safe and standard parameters of the approach. However; a go-around may have been the pertinent thing to do to increase everyone's situational awareness.

At this time the PM had called Departure Control and we were issued a climb to 4;000. The PM set 4;000; I confirmed verbally and then commanded VNAV. I continued to manually fly since we were assigned a heading. I had briefed a speed of 200 knots due to being below Class B Airspace and now came to the realization that I had just commanded the aircraft to speed up while we probably weren't high enough yet to legally accelerate. As I held the pitch to hold the airspeed; the altitude alert went off at 4;300 feet. I then clicked off the autothrottle; pulled the thrust to idle and pitched to return to 4;000 feet as the Controller called to remind us to maintain 4;000 feet. We reached 4;500 feet before descending. Flight proceeded without further incident.I had not flown much recently. Reserve lines in my home town had recently materialized and I was enjoying the absence of commuting. I hadn't flown since February with the exception of a PT and upset training in March. I felt that hand flying would be good to help regain proficiency. Our clearance was to fly runway heading for vectors; so I thought this would be a great opportunity. In hindsight I should have waited for a little less busy environment to ease back into it. The FO had flown out of ZZZ1 before and was aware that things could get busy. I should have taken this as a bit of a warning. I could have also thought about how to handle this departure a little more thoroughly. FLCH would have been the better choice in this situation. It would have held 200 knots and commanded a 500 FPM climb. Far more manageable.
column123: I was PM. The Captain was PF. Our initial clearance was 3;000 feet and runway heading. The Captain briefed a low altitude capture using 200 knots as we were under the Class B shelf and relatively light. He briefed the intention to hand fly until we were given the intercept to the initial fix on the departure. The initial level off went well and according to the brief with the Captain hand flying. Were quickly given a new heading and a climb to 4;000; which I read back to ATC and set. The Captain confirmed the altitude and called for VNAV. I watched to confirm the start of the climb; then turned to switch my iPad view to the chart page. I heard the altitude alert; looked back to see the airplane pitched higher than the flight director and realized we were climbing past 4;000. At the same time the Captain disengaged the autothrottles; reduced thrust and pitched to return to 4;000 feet. At this time the Controller called us to tell us she needed us back at 4;000 feet. The altitude was about 4;500 feet. The PF corrected back to 4;000; then were soon given another climb.  Upon debrief we both realized that FLC would have been the better mode to engage as the VNAV reverted to the programmed speed that was too fast for what we were trying to do. The Captain mentioned he increased the pitch to control the speed and that caused us to climb thru the assigned altitude.As we were still in a critical phase of flight; I should have been more vigilant in monitoring the rate of climb; the speed and the vertical mode. If I had; I could of called it out to help the Captain arrest the acceleration and rate of climb in time to avoid the overshoot. I suggest that more emphasis be placed on the use of FLC and also VS mode. We seem to minimize their use as we rely on VNAV so heavily. The call to engage VNAV becomes a reflex. In this scenario; FLC or VS would of been a better mode that would of prevented the increase of speed that in turn contributed to the overshoot.

column121: Takeoff and climb to cruise was uneventful. At cruise FL260; received ATC reroute to avoid weather. Reroute was ZZZ1 then back onto the ZZZZZ arrival. About 50 miles north of ZZZ1; we were cruising at 280 kts in IMC conditions at +2 degrees TAT with engine anti-ice on. The Captain was flying. We then noticed the airspeed start to go way down then go way back up. It indicated maybe 40 kts to 300 kts (unsure exactly). 'Airspeed low' kept announcing as well. The Captain turned off the autopilot and autothrottle and set 4 degrees nose high and told me to set power. I pulled the power to 70% N1 and we compared PFDs. My airspeed indications would indicate properly for a few seconds then jump up or down. The Captain's was constantly moving up and down so we transferred control to the First Officer. I called for the QRC and the Captain read and accomplished the steps (we had missed flight directors off). We had climbed a couple hundred feet during this and I asked the Captain to notify ATC and I turned the airplane eastbound in an attempt to exit IMC. It worked and a couple minutes later we exited IMC and started a descent to warmer air. While the Captain ran the QRH for unreliable airspeed and informed ATC/dispatch; I continued to fly. As the air warmed and as we exited IMC; airspeed indications returned to normal. We reviewed pitch and power setting in the QRH to make sure the airspeeds were accurate. The rest of the descent and arrival to ZZZ was uneventful. My guess is we accumulated ice on the probes enough to make the airspeed indications go unreliable. I didn't see abnormal icing on the windshield wipers nor was icing reported. Being in IMC at +2 degrees was about perfect conditions for it. After landing; the Captain and I talked about how we were thankful for 737 MAX simulator training we had both recently completed. The training prepared us so well for this and I am thankful to our check airmen in the sims. I felt well prepared for this as described above thanks to 737 MAX training.

column123: Shortly after takeoff we noticed our number 2 oil quantity had dropped to 1 quart indicated by an amber '1'. column121: On Date there was an unfortunate damage to the Right Horizontal Stabilizer of Aircraft X. This damage drove Safety Bulletin on Date 1; which suggested a breakdown in communication as the root cause of the damage. However; most technicians (and supervisors) believe the real root cause of this damage was caused by the inability to use the correct equipment to accomplish the task at hand due to [the] Stores Department using both sides of this bay as staging and storage for their various equipment and items (tires; crates of all types and sizes; stacked at heights of over 10 feet in some instances). The work to be accomplished was on the right hand wing tip but because of all the equipment on the ground a small 35 feet JLG or widebody lift could not be used; instead a much larger JLG was necessary; positioned much further away; resulting in contact/damage to the right horizontal stabilizer. If this was a one off; the technicians probably would not have as much heartburn but this issue of stores using Bay 3; one of our prime widebody aircraft bays; as a storage has been going on for years and has resulted in other aircraft damages in the past.  This has been a well-documented and hot topic of discussion in ZZZ meetings; crew briefings; safety team raising it with messages; every level of management has been made aware of this over the years.  Sadly; the situation is getting worse instead of better.At our latest ZZZ meeting Date 1; a supervisor questioned the findings of the investigation stating that in his experience working the service center; he felt the stores equipment was more of a causation factor than the loss of communication. The reply from another member of management 'I am not aware of this being an issue'. Another participant suggested there was a lot of documentation but was told 'we can look into it and maybe build a case to get the stores equipment moved'. Since the damage; this stores equipment problem has been highlighted at the daily crew briefings and what is glaring to most techs since this damage is the fact that not only has nothing been done to mitigate the issue; it has actually gotten worse since the latest damage. This aircraft has been out of service now for almost 3 weeks; (if we are to believe the finance people when they tell us that a wide body generates X money on average a day); that's a costly stores area; just looking at it from that perspective!The unfortunate reality is in the event of a damage the technician is grilled in the investigation; sent for drug and alcohol testing; always made to feel at fault; always told it was self-induced pressure; and of course have their records pulled showing they signed off a specific training course; maintenance & engineering bulletin; awareness class etc. I have examples of this from many investigation reports.  I'm filing this report because the front-line mechanics don't want to for fear of repercussions if they did.  Sure; there are many human factors that come into play when incidents like this happen but when you look at it; this is not complacency on the part of the mechanics. There are real pressures to get these aircraft in and worked in BAY 3 and we crutch the system on a daily basis because of these pressures.  My question; how is Company living up to their values of safety always being #1 when this issue has been ignored for years despite the attention and spotlight?What is staggering to most; weeks after the latest very costly damage the situation is actually worse. The only answer could be; if you investigate and find the root cause that suits; then of course it will be impossible to mitigate and address the real root cause! I won't gain any friends for pointing this out but this issue needs to be addressed. It is our responsibility; from safety; to Management; coworkers etc.; to do the right thing; provide a safe work environment; which helps keep us all safe from injury and our assets from being damaged. We owe it to each other and ourcustomers. At this juncture this needs to be a priority from senior leadership because constant suggestions and concern from the floor have hit a brick wall and frankly we on the front line don't have the authority to fix the problem.

Unfortunately; after re-calulating our new flight plan and fuel; we noticed that due to our reroute we would be landing at ZZZ1 with minimum fuel. Letting them know that if we continued to fly to the ZZZ2 VOR that we would be landing with min fuel. We were given 'deviations as necessary direct ZZZ1 when able'. Our radar showed two storm cells about 3-5 miles in diameter. We decided to deviate around these cells and proceed direct ZZZ1 once clear of the storm. While navigating around these storms we began to experience updrafts and downdrafts. During our course of route the autopilot was engaged and suddenly began to deviate from FL290 by +800/-300 ft. The VSI (Vertical Speed Indicator) showed a climb and descent of +/-4;000 feet per min and the cockpit windows became fogged. During this time the airplane did not feel like it was pitching this extreme and did not exceed +5/-2 degrees. Altitude miscompare flags appeared on our PFD'S (Primary Flight Display) and the VSI had a RED X for less than 5 seconds. I began to run the QRH. ATC contacted us about our altitude and asked if we were having a rough ride. We responded and advised of the situation and were cleared to descend to FL240 at pilot's discretion. After the airplane was stable at FL290 we descended to FL240 and landed at ZZZ1 with 2;400 pounds of fuel and no further incidents.

column121: While on initial descent into SFO; I obtained a METAR and D-ATIS for the airport prior to my briefing. On this particular day; the wind was from the west and quite gusty between 35 to 40 knots. I wanted to ensure the crosswind component was within my limitations as a First Officer. At the time; I noticed a discrepancy between the METAR wind direction and that of the ATIS. METARs provide wind direction in reference to true north whereas ATIS and D-ATIS provide in reference to magnetic north. At SFO; the magnetic variation is 14E; meaning we would subject that amount the direction in reference to true north to get the wind direction in magnetic north. For simplicity; I will round to 20 degrees. At the time; the wind on the METAR was 280 degrees but that on the ATIS was 300 degrees. Both reports had the same reported time and date and the rest of the information including peak wind was exactly the same on both reports. There seems to be a large discrepancy between the two since if the METAR says the wind is 280; then in magnetic that is 260 and not the 300 that was advertised by the ATIS. This 40 degree difference is quite large. I was curious and began to observe the ATIS and METARs over the next couple days and found that SFO is consistently reporting; on the ATIS; a value that is 20 degrees greater than the METAR. Possibly explanations for this could be that the wind information is coming from different sources; but it seems quite peculiar that the wind direction on the ATIS is consistently 20 degrees greater than the METAR.  Any pilot would use the METAR; subtract 10 or 20 degrees; and get a wind direction of 270 or 280 degrees magnetic. The ATIS is reporting it as 310 degrees. This discrepancy can be large enough to cause confusion with crosswind landing limitations for the aircraft and pilot. I have noticed this issue prior to this flight; but did not think much of it until I noticed it consistently wrong over the past few days. If you view the METAR and ATIS for OAK and SJC; the ATIS for both reports a wind direction that is 10 degrees less than that of the METAR. This is as expected. SFO; however; reports 20 degrees greater. I addressed SFO Tower about this directly; to which they responded that they do not control this data as it comes from the 'weather people downstairs.' I am just curious if this is intentional or if this is; in fact; an error. Perhaps SFO Tower quality assurance can take a look?

During the brief of the arrival we had noticed that the crossing restriction at the first fix (DARAN) on the arrival (DARAN1A) was incorrect as compared between the approach plate and the arrival selected out of the FMC. The DARAN1A arrival is FL210 to FL230 at the DARAN; the altitude from the FMC showed FL250 to FL280 (DARAN1B). At this point we both cross checked the date on the approach and discussed when we had both done our last update. We concluded that we had both updated just before the flight and the dates were correct on the approach chart. We then had thought that maybe we had incorrectly loaded the wrong arrival into the FMC. We proceeded to monitor each other as we reloaded the landing runway approach and the correct arrival. After reloading the FMC with the landing runway approach and the DARAN1A for arrival we noticed that the crossing restriction at DARAN remain the same FL250 to FL280. Due to congestion in Mexico City our flight and another flight were told to hold 20 miles north of DARAN. When told to continue our plan was to question the crossing restriction at DARAN; but we were descended in the hold to FL210. After arriving at FL210 we were cleared to DARAN and the rest of the arrival landing on Runway 5R [was] uneventful. I have previously been into Mexico City and number of times and the DARAN1A crossing restriction at DARAN has been correct as depicted compared to the FMC. NOTE: All other fixes and crossing restrictions on the DARAN1A were correct except DARAN at FL250 to FL280. The FMC loaded DARAN1A is incorrect. Please check the FMC database is correct to make sure the DARAN crossing restriction between FL210 toFL230 is correct.

column121: On a day; VFR approach to RNO just to the north of waypoint URATE as depicted on the RNAV (RNP) Y to 16L; EGPWS alerted 'Caution; obstacle.'  The FO as pilot flying altered his flight path; yet we then received 'Obstacle; pull-up!' which the FO did.  Both the hill and obstacle at 5;101 feet MSL were in sight the entire time.  We then continued for a normal uneventful landing.  Enroute; we had discussed extensively the challenges of RNO; including terrain; single runway; engine failure considerations; and higher than typical descent rates and true airspeeds; and were comfortable with our position and closure rate with the hill and tower.Cause - EGWPS will alert for terrain or obstacles for either proximity or closure rate sooner than I expected.  By being carefully studied on the terrain and obstacles in the vicinity of RNO prior to arrival; we were well aware of the tower and hill located at the location of the EGPWS alert.Suggestions - Give a wider avoidance to high terrain or obstacles both horizontally; vertically; and with respect to closure rate.
column123: Cleared visual approach 16L RNO. Turned to intercept extended final near FAP WORTH. Had briefed and set up for RNAV (RNP) Y 16L and using it as backup to visual. Dialed in 6;400 and began descent to FAP altitude turning base to final. EGPWS alerted 'Caution; Obstacle'. As PF I verified obstacle in site and continued turn to final away from it. Soon after alert 'Obstacle; Pull up' occurred. I disconnected the AP and initiated a climbing turn away from obstacle that we had kept in site the entire time. Alert ceased very quickly and we continued an uneventful and stable approach and landing. Approach briefing had included a good discussion on RNO hazards including single runway operations; EO considerations; mountainous terrain; high descent rates and TAS. We knew where the obstacle/ hill was on the approach and felt comfortable with our position relative to it on the visual approach.Cause - The preceding aircraft was denied the instrument approach. Visuals in mountainous terrain create unique challenges. Being cleared to follow proceeding aircraft and maintain spacing may have also caused a more square pattern than desired which brought us closer to the obstacle.Suggestions - Maintain the practice of following IAP ground track even on a visual approach if not intimately familiar with the terrain. Also; be cognizant of how EGPWS tracks descent and closure rate. The warnings certainly came quicker than we expected. I would give high terrain an even wider berth.

column121: [We were] cleared for the visual approach. Pilot in Command hand flew the visual approach. Switched to Tower and was cleared to land. During the descent to land Pilot in Command got too low. Second in Command informed Pilot in Command to climb as aircraft was too low and almost hit terrain Pilot in Command said he was good; Second in Command advised Pilot in Command to immediately climb. Pilot in Command was reluctant to climb. Tower informed us that we were too low for that sector of the approach and to Immediately climb. Pilot in Command climbed back up to 3;100 feet from 2;000 feet; then landed normally. Pilot in Command lost situational awareness during a visual approach. Pilot in Command initially did not react and did not listen to advice from Second in Command that the aircraft was too low on the Approach. It was not until the ATC Tower Controller told crew to immediately climb to 3;100 feet; did the Pilot in Command react and then climb back up to 3;100 feet. Suggest that the company discusses and better trains flight crews in performing visual approaches at day and night and to somehow incorporate improved Crew Resource Management Training so that if a Second in Command tells the Pilot in Command to climb or descend Immediately; he or she will listen and react immediately; and then ask questions later when the risk factor has been mitigated.

After completing the required items and discussing all of the impact items; I sent ATC a CPDLC message as to our loss of navigation equipment and inability to remain in RVSM airspace due to the loss of the auto pilot. column121: Once on final for [Runway] XXR; we got a TCAS RA event from what appeared to me an (other carrier) aircraft that overshot the final for XXL. We did not have the transponder in TA mode because we were never given a Traffic Advisory from ATC; and did not have the aircraft in sight as instructed by our guidance. The RA instructed us to Adjust Vertical Speed. It commanded approximately 1500 FPM descent. We were at flaps 10 and 1;500 feet AGL. As we descended per the RA we continued to configure the aircraft. We were below 1;000 feet by the time we got to flaps 30. The aural glideslope warning sounded. We knew we needed to go-around but couldn't because of the aircraft above us. When I looked at the ND (Navigation Display); I saw the red square showing the intruding aircraft right above us at +5. It was at 800 feet when we got the clear of conflict aural message and elected to go around.The (other carrier) aircraft; in my opinion; went through their intended final for XXL. A contributing factor was the lack of notification by ATC.
column123: While descending through approximately 2;000 feet AGL on the visual approach and on the ILS glideslope to Runway XXR in ZZZ; we received a TCAS RA Descend. The conflicting traffic was slightly above and behind us on Runway XXL. We believe the Descend RA extinguished at approximately 800 feet AGL (although a review of the FRM (Fault Reporting Manual) afterwards says it should be inhibited 'below approximately 1;100 feet radio altitude'). After following the Descend command and by the time the command extinguished; we were not in a stabilized position to land. We executed a go-around. We were not informed about the traffic by Approach and therefore did not meet the requirements to switch to TA Only for Runways XXL and XXR in ZZZ. We were vectored around for a normal landing on XXR. As we switched to ZZZ Tower; another aircraft in front of us also experienced a go-around for the same situation.Presumably the conflicting traffic met the requirements to switch to TA Only because they keyed up on the MIC and said they didn't overshoot and we should/can switch to TA Only. However; we didn't meet the requirements to switch to TA Only.  ATC never asked us to report them in sight; presumably because they were behind us! So; what happens to our RA resolution when the conflicting traffic is in TA Only and transgressing on us? Presumably they can't be offered an RA resolution (which would likely have been for them to climb). If they had climbed the Descend RA 'pressure' on us could have been alleviated sooner. Instead we were forced lower and lower. And all of this was close to the ground. Even though the RA inhibits reaching 'approximately 1;100 feet radio altitude' the conflict with the other aircraft still exists; and we were pretty sure we were below 1;000 feet before the RA extinguished (as evidence by being already slightly into the 1;000 feet white tape). When the RA finally went away we executed a go-around from about 600-800 feet; but the traffic conflict doesn't magically go away.This event occurred right as we were configuring to land; so we never had a chance to fully configure prior to 1;000 feet AGL; as maneuvering for the RA was taking up our attention. The time in the RA resolution mode was more than momentary. It seemed long and sustained enough that it felt like it would just RA us into the ground. As I now knew a go-around was imminent there was a slight moment in my mind I thought about going around right then and there; but the RA continued. I can see where a Crew may be spring loaded to go-around even though the Descend RA is still present.The FO recognized that the traffic showed '+500' on the MFD display. The FAA defines a Near Midair as 'an incident associated with the operation of an aircraft in which a possibility of collision occurs as a result of proximity of less than 500 feet to another aircraft...' We were likely very close to meeting that definition.There was a slight tail wind at altitude for aircraft joining final from left base to runway XXL allowing for increased potential for overshoot. Maybe a very slight overshoot by the other aircraft and the tight sequencing by ATC created this incident; but we can't be sure. It's possible ATC was sequencing aircraft too tight.

column121: The hydraulic reservoirs have a big red caution label. It reads; 'CAUTION DO NOT OVERFILL HYDRAULIC RESERVOIR. FILL TO APPROX. 2/3 BETWEEN REFILL(RFL) AND FULL (COCKPIT PANEL SHOULD READ 92% FULL) REFER AMM 12-12-00.'Below the caution label there is an ATTENTION label. It reads; 'ATTENTION Do Not Overfill the RESERVOIR. Overfill can Cause Hydraulic Fumes To Enter the Flight Deck and Passenger Cabin'Some years ago I had an air return when the cabin filled with acrid mist causing eyes to sting and some to choke. The flight attendants thought we were on fire! The Captain and I used goggles and oxygen to safely return. This event was caused by both hydraulic reservoirs being filled to capacity. I believe the cockpit panel read 107%. If I'm recall correctly this is the most that will register.Although I have not since had visible or detectable odor; I believe crew and passengers are breathing atomized hydraulic fluid whenever the reservoirs are over serviced. The leg noted in this report from ZZZ-ZZZ1; started with both reservoirs reading 100%. At shutdown they were at 92%. Where did the difference go in a three hour operation? The day before; my aircraft had 107% in system A and 92% in system B. I alerted Maintenance of the over service. The Technician proceeded to move System A to B. The result was both reservoirs at 100%.I have dealt with this issue individually before. I find a small portion of our technicians understand the significance. Sometimes I meet with great resistance.[Recommend] a notice for Aircrew to remind them of the placards and similar or more specific training for all our Maintenance Technicians and Maintenance Control.
column125: B737-800 Captain reported loss of Hydraulic Reservoir quantity when reservoir is overfilled. Reporter theorized that hydraulic fluid is being atomized resulting in harmful cabin fumes and physiological symptoms.

column121: We checked in at ZZZ for flight to ZZZ1.  Walking onto aircraft to preflight and get ready the FA's (flight attendants) commented that they smelled a strong fume odor in the rear of the cabin.  The prior crew had left the APU running and that was providing the air to the cabin.  We were not immediately sure what it was but the longer we were inside the aircraft the more it seemed to smell all over the aircraft.  One flight attendant soon commented that she had been in a fume smell diversion and that she felt it now smelled exactly like what she had experienced before. As I was contacting Dispatch and Maintenance Control; the ZZZ station without our knowledge or consent had sprayed the entire aft cabin with some kind of disinfectant spray to cover up the smell and had begun to board passengers.  When I was made aware of this I radioed them to stop spraying the aircraft; halt the boarding; and remove the passengers that were onboard.  Maintenance Control had called a contract Maintenance Tech to investigate the odor.  Meanwhile; we had shutdown the APU and connected the ground air. When the Maintenance Tech arrived; he had a bunch of paperwork for items to check; and mentioned that he was going to inspect the APU.  He did not seem to know what to check or how to check it.  Ultimately he handed me the pile of papers and ask us to run the engines.  In an effort to help we did so.  We could not specifically determine the source of the smell; but it seemed stronger with the APU providing air.  We were unable to isolate the source and could not fly the aircraft or do a maintenance ferry flight. Afterward; Maintenance Control then informed us that the residual contamination in the air ducts would have to be cleaned and tested with special equipment; and that they would have to send a road crew down from ZZZ to perform those functions.  So Maintenance Control knew from the start that this type of contamination issue required special procedures and equipment to deal with and withheld that critical information unnecessarily exposing us to who knows what kind of long term health hazards instead of just informing of this up front. After we officially could not use the airplane; it was around XA:30pm.  We were assigned to fly another aircraft for the flight now departing at XG:15pm.  We then spent the next few hours trying to get a day room so we could get a meal and away from the airport before the later flight.  Each time were verbally told we had a room from Crew Tracking; Hotel Desk; etc.; we called the hotel and were told there were no such rooms available for us.  After wasting a considerable amount of time on this effort we were finally given rooms and arrived at the hotel just after XF:00pm. I walked down the highway from the hotel to find something to eat after having nothing for several hours.  Finally sitting down to eat a sandwich; I realized that I had a dull headache from trying to determine if the fumes were no longer present in the aircraft when isolating certain ducts for Maintenance Control.  It dawned on me that I was fatigued and I reported this to Crew Tracking. The cause was Maintenance; fume smells; lack of timely day room. [Captain suggested] better communications with Maintenance and Dispatch.

column121: We departed the gate and were instructed to taxi to Runway 28 via 'D; A; A1 to the Runway 28 holding point.'  Upon glancing at the taxi diagram; referencing the our Airway Manual (AM); to verify our taxi route; I quickly realized a discrepancy between the instructions we were given and the chart -- there was no A1 taxiway that reached the runway.  Before we could inquire about these instructions; the controller gave us a 'follow the aircraft ahead' instruction.  Digging a little farther; I began to notice that this discrepancy was worth a report submittal because the 10-9 Chart for MMGL differs from the AM; and neither the 10-9 Chart nor the AM agrees with the airport in reality.  Upon your own review; you will discover that there is a difference in taxiway names between the 10-9 chart; and the AM; specifically as it relates to the A taxiway.  Additionally; in reality there is an A1 taxiway; properly signed; that parallels the A taxiway toward the approach end of Runway 28.  There is also an additional taxiway; A2; that connects the A taxiway to the runway; prior to the approach end of Runway 28 which is not charted on either chart. The airport NOTAMS reference a change in taxiway naming convention; however; the NOTAMS do not make sense with either the current charts; or with reality; and in fact lead to more confusion.  I believe that by paying attention to aircraft position with reference to the published chart; I was able to help the Captain remain in the green; and hopefully trap this threat from snaring other crews.  In deliberating whether to submit this report; I concluded that since this threat affects the broader aviation community; the report would be more appropriate for resolving this discrepancy to the benefit of everyone.
