column121: Some really troubling events unfolded on our flight; ZZZ-ZZZ1. After ground power failed and the high pressure air carts were removed to be repositioned for a gate start (APU is on MEL) the cabin environment was no longer safe or acceptable to have nearly XXX passengers onboard. I had the FO call ZZZ Operations on the radio to have them send an agent to open the cabin door and deplane the passengers. The jetway was still attached to the aircraft but nothing was being done to get the passengers safely off the jet.  I turned on my cell phone and called the ZZZ ramp manager's phone number and requested immediate assistance. After further needless delays several flight attendants came to the flight deck to tell me they could see the agents standing in the jetway but there were doing nothing; my request to begin the deplaning was being ignored. I next called the flight office and requested a Chief Pilot and a manager to come ASAP to gate XX to assist. I have attached several photos to include the air synoptic of the excessively hot cabin temperatures after the air start units were removed and the jetway power failed! It gets much worse; and I will provide the whole narrative as it unfolded.When I arrived at the gate 50 minutes or so before departure I was informed that only the first officer had arrived and was onboard. The gate agent had just received a call that the cabin was very warm and ZZZ Operations wanted us to start the APU (why did Operations not know the APU was placarded). I assured them that the FO was most likely already addressing the matter. When I arrived at the flight deck I saw the FO had the air synoptic pulled up and I noted the aft cabin temp showed 102F. The FO pointed out that the APU was placarded inoperative. Air start units were being connected at this time to power the air conditioning pacs. During the FO's walk around he had taken a picture of the way the ground crew had connected the PCA hoses. How long had the PCA even been hooked up is unknown; the jet arrived at this gate at XA:00 in the morning; but regardless; it was all to evident the PCA air was not making it into the cabin do to the improper connection. The FO joined me and we returned to the terminal; I spoke with the gate agents and told them it would be a fairly long delay waiting for the cabin to cool.  I asked them to keep the flight attendants from boarding the hot jet when they began arriving at the gate area.  After the ground crew had finished hooking up the air start carts; the FO and I went to the flight deck to check that the air conditioning was functioning. Nearing the schedule departure time we were finally getting the cabin temp to where boarding could begin. After boarding was complete and the cabin door closed the ground crew checked in and cleared us to start the right engine. I informed them that on this aircraft; per the manual; the left engine is started first with ground air start. The ground crew had positioned the air start units incorrectly to start the left engine. I told them to let me know when the left engine was clear for starting. The crew then shutdown the air start; even though they did not have a tug hooked up to reposition the equipment!  We no longer had ANY cooling airflow into the cabin. A couple of minutes later the electrical power from the jetway fails. The ground crew begins fiddling around but can't get the power restored and there are no portable power units near this gate. I later learned; after speaking with a facilities manager; that this jetway power supply had a service tag hanging from the power panel and should not have been used do to erratic 400HZ service. So with only battery power on the airplane; recirculating fans have shutdown; there is no cool air being provided; you can see [on] our air synoptic the cabin temps quickly were above 95-98 F.  In the interest of safety for the passengers it should be obvious why I requested an immediate de-planning of the passengers.  Unsatisfactory that ZZZ station was delaying opening the cabin door and safely removing the passengers.  I even resorted to threatening a ground evacuation after a repeated request for help to draw their attention to the seriousness of the issue at hand.  Passengers are wearing face coverings in a cabin approaching 100 F with all the cabin and cargo doors closed.  Still the gate agents would not open up the cabin to begin deplaning the passengers until some passenger service manager gave the go ahead; why?After the passengers had begun deplaning the ground crew finally located a portable electric unit and began reconnecting the air start carts so we could operate the air conditioning. The ramp supervisor was now on the flight deck with us with along with some other manager in tow. They were questioning why I had their ground crew shutoff the air start units and have them moved. I said that is not what I told them to do. I only stated that per this aircraft manual the left engine is to be started and to let me know when the area was clear to start the left engine. While discussing the horrible failings and going over the situation I looked up and noticed the ground power had only been restored to the PRIMARY GRD source. This aircraft requires two ground power feeds or one from the ground and the APU; our APU was still placarded INOP! There is a risk of overheating the eclectic connection the way they had provide power (see PIC). I pointed this out to the manager. I also asked him that when they provide the correct ground power and air conditioning and we can get around to re-boarding the passengers are we going to have a ground crew available so we can start and pushback as quickly as possible. The manager assured me they would have a crew there for us. He lied!  After we had closed the cabin door with our original passengers minus 20 or so that chose to not fly with us; I called the ground crew to get the go ahead to start. No ground crew at our gate!  The FO called ramp to ask where our ground crew had gone? Twenty seven minutes later a crew arrives at the nose but does not check in on the headset. I have the nose camera on so I can see them as they fiddle around with connecting a tow bar and what not. I had flashed the nose taxi light to get their attention and made many interphone GND crew alert chimes; all of these signals were ignored. When they did finally get on the headset I expressed some frustration that we could have been starting the engine while they prepared for the pushback. They were quick with the excuse that they had just arrived and were unaware of the situation. When we were cleared to start the left engine the air start units were not running in the high flow position and the duct pressure has only 16 PSI; 25 PSI is minimum to start. I asked them to check the start units were set correctly. This ground crew had no idea how to operate their equipment. The AutoStart of the left engine failed on the first start attempt. The second start attempt reached idle and stable barely.Almost three hours late and somewhere about half way to ZZZ1 from ZZZ I noticed that ZZZ1 had us arriving to gate XX; even though the APU was on placard. ZZZ1 gate XX is a tow in only gate with engines shutdown per the ZZZ1 airport pages. FO wants to send a message to dispatch right away. I say lets just give them a little more time to do the right thing and see if they get it sorted out. Sure enough about an hour from arrival we send for the changeover info for ZZZ1 and they still have us arriving gate XX! I sent dispatch a message to ask if ZZZ1 is really planning for us to use gate XX with an INOP APU? Dispatch calls ZZZ1 Operations and they finally get around to changing our arrival gate.Ground crew not following procedures and failing to correct errors.  Station management not supporting a safety culture to support flight operations in the interest of passenger safety.Attention to details in preparation for supporting an operation with a aircraft that has an MEL placard affecting normal ops; in this case the APU inoperative.  When the PIC Captain of the flight; after all the doors closed and ready for flight; calls and radios the station that the passengers need to be immediately de-planned due to safety concerns; then this decision needs to be supported and executed without delay!

column121: After intercepting the glideslope it was noted by both pilots the aircraft was not slowing down normally.  Despite lowering the gear and deploying speedbrakes we were having a difficult time getting 10 knots below the next flap speed to continue to configure a variable tailwind was noted between 5 & 10 knots which helped explain what we were seeing.  Continuing to investigate however both pilots thereafter realized we were abnormally low and the PF disconnected the AP and leveled off.  Tower called with a low altitude alert shortly after that and we acknowledged it; configured normally and were stable by 500 feet AGL.  Landing and roll out was normal.  There were multiple approach NOTAMs that day and we miscalculated the effective times on the one stating the ILS XXL was unusable.  We were an hour off and were arriving inside the last 30 minutes of the effective time.  It turns out NAVAIDs maintenance was manipulating the glide slope signal at the time; causing the glide slope to appear lower.The ILS to XXL was OTS and NAVAIDs maintenance was transmitting a lower than normal glidepath. It would have been helpful if ILS status had been repeated on the ATIS; as it normally is; but it was not.  During the low altitude call from tower they were even quick to add to the call that it 'was in the NOTAMs'.  Further investigating with my prior position with FAA Flight Inspection it is still in their guidance that NAVAIDs maintenance is not supposed to transmit a localizer signal if they are going to manipulate the glide slope signal to avoid this hazardous; misleading; information.  The localizer and glide slope both were transmitting; with a proper ID; at the time of the incident; we even crossed ZZZZZ at the appropriate altitude of 3;000 and showed on path.  It was after that when the aircraft would no longer slow; as it was chasing a depressed glide path. column121: During walk around; a ground crew man informed the Captain of need to push prior to darkness as ground crews have difficulty seeing. Pushback happened after dark due to weather delays. Initially; the tug driver wanted to drop the airplane with a minimal push which would have resulted in a max pivot turn. We felt we were unable to have wingtip to wingtip and/or tail to tail clearance so we asked the tug driver to pull us out further telling him it was too tight. He complied. The right wing walker seemed confused as he walked in front of the engine and not at the right wing-tip; the closest point of potential impact. Walking in front on an engine had no value to us as an aircrew. Once we were released from the tug; taxiing was extremely difficult due to several factors. These were narrow alleyway; very poorly unlit alleyway; at least 1 heavy jet parked on low D gates; construction on the south side of the alley way; no hazard O4 lighting for the construction fence; ramp and construction vehicles parked outside the fence on the ramp; and poor surface markings. Taxiing out was extremely slow and challenging and we notified an inbound aircraft to be careful. Poor visibility due to rain and the glare from wet added or exacerbated the taxi out difficulty. Poorly lit area; poorly marked area; new operational area; construction. Our first warning came from the ground crew when they express difficulty with completing the pushback after dark. If not for the interior lights of the terminal; I feel we would have struck the aircraft parked at gate. Our second clue was the attempted drop spot which showed us the degree of difficulty these crews were operating in. Better training for wing walkers. Better lighting in this area. Better surface markings to assure wingtip clearance in this area. Hazard lights on construction fence. Removal of all equipment and vehicles on ramp parked up against the fence. Reevaluation reflective paint stripe/J line coming from this alley. Until at least some items are addressed; all night operations should be towed to the top of the alley with lighted vehicles to protect rampers and cover far distance as wing walkers. I feel this is an aircraft damage event waiting to happen; even without the low light low visibility conditions.

column121: Winds were calm at ROA.  ATIS called Runway 24 as landing and departing using RNAV (RNP) Z RWY 24.  ATC asked us if we wanted the visual.  Given terrain and having never been to ROA I elected to stay with the RNAV approach.   ATC had us cross STEFN at 5;400 feet which had us 400 ft high.  We attained VNAV PATH and 150 KIAS approximately 3 miles after STEFN.   Since we could see the terrain and visibility was greater than 5 miles we planned to maintain 150 KIAS until 5 miles prior to the airfield.   Between DBERD and WILHE there is depicted terrain with a spot elevation 2;058 feet.  Just pass that terrain; still on LNAV and VNAV PATH at 150 KIAS Roanoke Tower gave us a low altitude warning. We verified both our altimeter settings and altitude.  We advised Tower that we could see both terrain and the airfield.  Tower acknowledged and advised us that they could see us clearly; and that they were required to announce the low altitude alert anytime it is activated.  Otherwise; the approach and landing were normal.  Of note there was no GPWS alert with flaps 20 and gear up.  After block-in; I requested a phone number to discuss the event.I spoke with [ATC] and inquired about the altitude alert call.  He indicated they sometimes get an altitude alert activation; but usually on vectors to visual Runway 24. He also indicated he was not as familiar with the Tower sector.   I asked him to look into it a bit more given that the only difference between what I flew and what I would have flown in IMC is I would have been 25 KIAS slower which would have resulted in a descent rate difference of just 133 FPM given a constant wind.  The wind in this case was a light headwind during the approach.Had I been in IMC and/or could not immediately determine by visual reference terrain clearance; the approach would have terminated with an immediate climb and terrain escape maneuver.Recommend the altitude alert system be de-conflicted to ensure aircraft on FMS glide path for the RNAV Z RWY 24 do not get erroneous alerts and/or note on company chart outlining requirements for speed on the approach or other requirements to successfully complete the approach in IMC.No deviations noted by Tower or aircrew.  The low altitude alert system may need to be adjusted or approach procedures may need to be adjusted to avoid erroneous low attitude warnings.De-conflict low altitude warning with proper approach lateral and vertical guidance.

column121: The Autopilot A was engaged. The RNAV ZZZZZ3 Arrival and the RNPZ XXL were programmed in the FMC. The  approach was not connected at ZZZZZ; as we were not cleared for the approach.  Approximately five miles prior to ZZZZZ1 [fix] we were told to expect vectors for the ILS. We selected the ILS XXL in the FMC; and upon executing the selection; we received an Autopilot Disconnect message; and an A/P Disconnect Caution light. The aircraft went into Control Wheel Pitch. I; the Pilot Flying; immediately selected Vertical Speed to keep the aircraft in a state towards the impending crossing restriction. I also reset the Altitude Alerter for X;000 feet; as we now were in Vertical Speed and needed altitude protection at ZZZZZ2 [fix].A few seconds later we passed over ZZZZZ2. The Autopilot Disconnect Caution light illuminated; and the Autopilot Lateral Mode switched to Control Wheel Steering; and the aircraft didn't turn and follow the still illuminated and displayed LNAV PATH. I immediately engaged heading mode; and turned to rejoin our intended course. Approach gave us a heading; as the minor deviation from our path was most likely noticeable.  The rest of the flight proceeded uneventfully.  We assumed we programmed the FMC incorrectly; in some way; and we needed to be more vigilant.  ZZZ to ZZZ1 [airport]; we were on the ZZZZZ2 RNAV; Autopilot B engaged; on PATH. We were given an intercept heading to join final for [Runway] XX. Heading mode was selected. The aircraft flew heading and was in VNAV. The final approach course was entered into the FMC; and upon executing; the Autopilot B Vertical mode disengaged; with the A/P Caution light and the aircraft descended in Control Wheel Pitch.  We selected a pitch mode and proceeded without further incident.My concern:  I don't know why these disconnects happened. If they are normal for the -800 MAX; I am unaware of this. I thought all of our fleet types were programmed and responded to Pilot programming the same; in this scenario.  I've never experienced [other model] aircraft revert to CWS Pitch or roll; even with faulty Pilot programming.  We both assumed that perhaps; since neither of us had flown a MAX in a few years that we missed some training; or company notice.  We assumed that the error was a Pilot programming error.   I called the Chief Pilot on Call and told him of the occurrence the first time; and he was unaware of such a thing happening normally. We confessed that we actually had more experience than him in the MAX. He indicated I should call later and talk to the MAX programming expert and he perhaps could explain why the MAX behaves in this way. That is why we flew the aircraft a second leg with the anomaly; I assumed it was Pilot programming error.  A few days later; I was contacted by a Chief Pilot; who informed me that our experience was a malfunction; and that a logbook entry and maintenance resolution should have taken place.  I assumed it was a MAX anomaly; but it was a malfunction.

column121: Severe turbulence encounter on climb after departing.  We conducted a full and normal briefing in operations prior to the flight. During that briefing we identified a threat of possible turbulence around 20;000 feet based on a PIREP. Upon arriving at the plane; I briefed the lead Flight Attendant. That briefing included a discussion on turbulence. I directed that the Flight Attendants stay seated for the departure until I call. Ground operations through takeoff and climbout were normal and uneventful. Departure cleared us to 17;000 feet. We leveled there awaiting hand off to Center and were in light turbulence. After a short delay we were cleared to climb to approximately 25;000 feet and to contact Center. I initiated the climb via VNAV. Almost immediately we encountered severe turbulence. The airspeed was fluctuating and the plane banked +-25 AOB (Angle of Bank). The autopilot remained engaged and made appropriate corrections. However; I put my hands on the controls in anticipation of needing to take control. The ride was so violent that my First Officer could not get his hands on the radio knob to change frequencies. By 18;000 feet the ride eased to moderate turbulence. When I deemed it safe; I then picked up the PA and asked 'Flight Attendants check in.' They checked the cabin and reported all passenger; crew and plane were safe. The First Officer made the check in with Center; reported the severe turbulence.At an appropriate time; I notified dispatch of the event. He published our PIREP. Later we submitted the log entry for maintenance. Further down line ZZZ1 Station was notified and I discussed with them an appropriate response upon landing. The remainder of the flight was uneventful; not even a ripple of turbulence. Once blocked in and checklists completed; I greeted passengers in case any were still concerned. They all seemed very appreciative; and thankful. Many even commented on the smooth landing and offered thanks for a safe trip. Customer Service; Maintenance and Flight Operations and met us at the gate. I provided full debriefs to each. The flight operations manager said we did a great job but also advised we submit a safety report. I want to offer that I believe the system; Standard Operating Procedures; and tools made available work. While I could not foresee the severity of the turbulence that awaited us; we knew a rough ride would be encountered in that area and took precaution. The result was no injuries to crew or passengers or damage to the plane. I offer this report mostly to help improve the system. And I am happy to answer any questions if necessary.
column123: WSI (Weather Service International) indicated a narrow band of turbulence on our route from roughly 17;000 to 20;000 feet due to shear below a jet stream.  Larger jets reported moderate (PIREP symbols) turbulence on WSI so the Captain had the flight attendants remain seated after takeoff until we called them.  At the time of the event the seat belt sign was ON and everyone on the plane was seated.  As we climbed through 17;000 feet the turbulence worsened from moderate to severe.  Large and rapid airspeed deviations of +/- 25 knots and sharp rolling moments of roughly 25 to 30 degrees occurred for roughly 2 minutes; all estimates.  As Pilot Monitoring it took me awhile to tune the ATC radios for a frequency change as I couldn't grab the tuning knobs in the turbulence.  I believe ATC instructed us to climb from 17;000 to 19;000 feet and that put us into the worst of the turbulence.  Once we were cleared to climb higher (above 19;000 feet) the ride improved quickly.  I believe a hand off from TRACON to Center caused much of the delay but I am not certain.Again; the seat belt sign was on and all flight attendants were seated per the briefing.  No injuries and no damage.  We did not make the 'be seated immediately' announcements as everyone was still seated since takeoff.  We were focused on getting a higher altitude and a better ride. Once we were clear of the turbulence we asked the flight attendants to 'check in' per our turbulence training.  We filed a PIREP with ATC and notified Dispatch.

column121: Upon departure from Runway XXR; just as we reached acceleration altitude I received an emergency PA from the flight attendant informing me there was smoke in the cabin. I immediately shut off the gasper fan; the recirc fan; the packs; and the APU bleed. I inquired as to the severity and was told 'it's bad.' My First Officer and myself did not see or smell anything resembling smoke. I immediately informed ATC we would like priority handling and requested vectors for an approach back into ZZZ. I asked the flight attendant if the passengers were in danger and if I needed to drop the oxygen masks. I was told at this point 'no' and was informed that the smoke had stopped. I asked the flight attendant to remain on the PA and to inform me the instant any more signs of smoke appeared.We were given vectors around to shoot the ILS to Runway XXR. I told the flight attendant we would be landing soon and to plan for a normal landing and taxi back assuming the smoke remained stopped. After a successful overweight landing; we exited the runway and taxied into the ramp. We had fire trucks follow us into our gate. They informed us they saw no heat signatures on our aircraft. The aircraft was successfully deplaned without injury or incident. Contract maintenance arrived a short while later and found a panel light in above seat X had shorted out and burned through the contact casing.Hindsight 20/20 I wouldn't have requested priority handling. In the moment; given the information I had to work with; I made a decision based on the fact that I thought there was a fire in the cabin and wanted to get the aircraft on the ground as quickly and as safely as possible. Crew Resource Management was almost nonexistent during this event. There was a very big language barrier between myself and my First Officer. During normal operations I often struggled to understand what he was saying. I took the lead on the radios; navigating; the communication with the flight attendant; and piloting the aircraft.

column121: Coming into IAD the errors started when we were intercepting the localizer for Runway 1R. I was the pilot monitoring and the FO (First Officer) was the pilot flying. Approach cleared us to intercept when we were basically already crossing the final approach course so we had to navigate back to the localizer on our own. At the same time we had been getting hit with some minor wake turbulence from the airplane ahead of us which Approach informed us was a Boeing 777. We were then cleared for the visual approach and advised of the caution for wake turbulence and to maintain 170 kts. until 5 miles out. At this time we configured gear down flaps 20. I had just recently had training in the sim for wake turbulence and remembered how dangerous it could be so I advised my FO to use caution and I believe I recommended maybe staying above their path since we had already hit a small portion of their wake prior when we were on downwind. He elected to turn the autopilot off and hand fly slightly above their glide path. We then continued down and around 100 ft. got a terrain warning. Our first reaction was this was because we weren't on glide path and the FO called out; 'visual; landing.' around 50 ft. we got another aural message stating 'too low terrain'; at this point I realized something was wrong and quickly scanned and noticed we were still at flaps 20. At this point I immediately called for a balked landing. The FO restated in a question; balked landing? I said yes and he immediately executed the maneuver. We advised ATC of the go around and they asked for the reasoning and I stated we were unstable. We continued the go around and came back to land on [Runway] 1R after some vectoring without further incident. To add to this and to summarize; we did not complete a landing checklist; we were not fully configured and were at gear down flaps 20 degrees; and our speed bug was still at 170 kts. We received a terrain aural warning that we misinterpreted followed by a second aural warning and executed a balked landing at a medium energy state with lower power setting but high airspeed. Our attention started deviating from standard starting with the poor intercept angle of the localizer. I further complicated the situation by over concentrating on the wake turbulence from the 777 and focusing too much on the FO's glide path and what I would call tunnel focusing on his flying. I believe my statements to him about the wake turbulence also led to distracting him from normal flight operations as well. He was talking through his thought process on staying a half dot high on the glide path and I was responding with statements like I agree; not necessarily breaking sterile cockpit but also causing more distraction on both of our parts. This was the first time that I had not completed a landing checklist. It has made me realize that while being aware of threats like wake turbulence is important; it's even more important to maintain a greater situational awareness and take a step back and not tunnel focus on one threat while other threats could arise. While I am glad we did not try to force a landing. This is a mistake I never thought would be possible or would happen to me. I have definitely learned a lot from this experience.

column121: Operating flight ZZZ-ZZZ1. Myself and other Flight Attendant during taxi noticed a musty like fume smell moments after pilots turned on the engines. Followed by extremely hot temperatures in the cabin which overtook the cabin. Immediately we noticed the majority of the customers reaching for their air vents and received multiple comments about the aircraft blowing 'hot air'. We walked through the cabin and were able to identify the fumes were coming from the Air supply vents towards the FWD of the Cabin. The intensity was Level 2 Moderate. Flight Deck was notified immediately. The moment the engines turned on I immediately felt a sudden rush of heat and immediate chest pain/tightness; nausea; and the air felt very thick making it slightly harder to breath. Ones the Flight Deck was notified they immediately responded and shut off the engines. I gradually began to feel better and my symptoms eventually went away. We returned to gate and deplaned the aircraft. Maintenance requested details of the Fume Event which we provided. Maintenance deferred the P.A.C.K. located in the FWD of the aircraft which stopped the Fumes. We re-boarded and departed from ZZZ -ZZZ1.These fume events are happening more than it is being reported. The company procedure for these events are misleading crew members into reporting to the company as an ODOR (Smell) event vs Fumes event so that they don't have to report it properly. Out of fear of retaliation crew member choose to not report and ignore symptoms. These too common mechanical issues are exposing us to harmful chemical exposures and causing us to get sick at the moment and then experience more severe symptoms later. Myself and many crew members. If we can enforce and install Carbon Monoxide sensors on the aircraft which is something we have in our own homes and is not costly; we can prevent and attend to these fume events in a timely manner and prevent Crews/Customers from getting sick or worse situations that can cause a more severe safety incident.

column121: I was the First Officer and Pilot Monitoring for our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After an uneventful departure and climb we established our cruise at FL360. Approximately 15 minutes into our cruise the Captain noticed a bright light near the top of his side view window. He brought my attention to the window heat unit which was glowing. From my vantage point I initially thought the unit itself was aflame but after several seconds it became apparent that a short existed which was contained within the window panes. A glowing line similar to a light bulb's filament began snaking downwards from the heat unit between the window panes. The Captain tapped the window several times which managed to briefly extinguish the light. We both acknowledged the need to descend as soon as possible and I requested a lower altitude with ATC. ATC mentioned traffic directly in front of us and stated he would try to give us a descent after the traffic passed. During this time; around 10 seconds after the Captain tapped the glass; the short reignited and continued to grow. The Captain noted an acrid smell; unusually high heat emanating from his window; and again expressed the need to descend. I pointed out the traffic; now visible to us; at our 12 o'clock and stated that we can descend shorty after they passed underneath us. For a third time I requested a lower altitude with ATC. The window failed shortly thereafter. The Captain's side view window let out a loud bang and fractures spider-webbed its entirety. For the first time since this incident began we received a L WSHIELD HEAT EICAS message followed by another L WINDOW HEAT EICAS message.Considering the potential for smoke/fumes and loss of cabin pressure we both immediately donned our oxygen masks; ensured they were at 100%; and established communications between ourselves and ATC. As I was donning the mask I saw the previously mentioned traffic pass safely below us. I relayed this to the Captain who began an emergency descent and told me to notify ATC. I [advised ATC] and let the controller know we were beginning a descent. As the Captain was flying our descent I sent an ACARS to Dispatch notifying them of the L WINDOW failure and that we would need a diversion. The Captain noted that we were close to ZZZ2. I plugged ZZZ2 into the fixes page; identifying that we were 55 miles away and subsequently plugged ZZZ3 into the fixes page; identifying us to be 90 miles away. Our first thought was to proceed to ZZZ2 as it was so close. I requested a heading from ATC as the airplane was about to turn north towards ZZZ1 along our original route and that we would likely be diverting to ZZZ2 but were still weighing our options. ATC gave us a heading which we accepted. As we were established in our descent I told the Captain I'd notify the flight attendants. He continued to fly the airplane as I called the FAs. I provided them a brief note of what had happened; that we were diverting; and that we would make an announcement to the passengers when we knew where we were going. They were professional and calm throughout the notification. The Captain handed control of the airplane to me so he could run the QRC and QRH. I accepted the aircraft and he quickly and effectively ran both checklists to their completion. By the end of his checklists we received a message from dispatch identifying ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 as good diversions. We were closer to ZZZ2 but still in the flight levels. We discussed our options. Considering ZZZ3 was a crew base; maintenance base; and nearly perfect to descend to from our present position we elected to proceed to ZZZ3. After establishing ourselves at 10;000 feet we removed the oxygen masks and donned our normal headsets for easier communication. The Captain gave the flight attendants a full briefing and updated the passengers on what had happened and why we were going to ZZZ3. I flew the airplane with autopilot engaged; managed ATC communications; notified dispatch that we were an [priority] aircraft and going to ZZZ3; and proceeded to obtain ZZZ3 weather; performance numbers; and set up the approach in the FMS. By the time the Captain completed his duties we were at 5;000 feet and on delaying vectors for Runway XXL into ZZZ3. We discussed what both of us had done ensuring we had not missed any items seeking immediate attention. Satisfied; he briefed the approach; we ran the descent checklist; I transferred the aircraft controls back to him; and I notified ATC that we were ready to proceed to the airport. The rest of the flight continued uneventfully. I called Ops to ensure we had a gate; we shot the approach; several emergency vehicles followed us after landing; and we canceled [with ATC] while taxiing in.The Captain detected a light in his peripheral vision. He discovered a short working its way through the window pane.Repeated cycling of the windshield heat in a prior checklist revision likely led to the unit's failure and short. We knew it was likely a matter of time until the window failed. We immediately began planning our descent and diversion choices.I was surprised at how challenging it was to hear ATC and/or the FAs with the oxygen masks on. Our breathing was very loud over the intercom/speaker which made it very hard to hear other voices. It might be worth noting in sim sessions.

column121: As Pilot Flying; at approximately 1;050 feet AGL on the ZZZZZ3 departure; we experienced a rapid succession of three bursts. At the same time; I was reducing the thrust levers to CLB mode. The gear was already up and the Captain; Pilot Monitoring; was just checking in with departure. Both of us weren't sure if we had hit a bird or something else. We had another rapid succession of three bursts with associated ECAM that almost instantaneously cleared the screen. The Captain quickly recognized the right engine (#2) indications were 'rolling back' and stated so clearly. He then ensure positive aircraft control by verbally stating; 'Your aircraft'. I responded with 'My aircraft'. The right engine ECAM message went away just as quickly as it displayed. The right engine then showed normal parameters and 'parallel' with the left engine. The Captain reviewed the Quick Reference Card and determined no action from the QRC required. He [advised] ATC while I simultaneously flew the aircraft on crosswind and turned downwind. The thrust levelers remained at CLB setting and flaps 1 on downwind with no other associated engine indications at approximately 2;500 feet MSL. We both agreed the best resolution was to land the aircraft ASAP. Our current weight was below max landing weight. I very quickly briefed a visual approach to Rwy XXR while the Captain loaded an approach in the FMGC. With gear down; I made the right turn on a base leg. I pushed the SPD button for managed speed as I thought we were in APPR Mode however; I quickly pulled the SPD button for selected speed once I noticed the engines were increase thrust for a higher speed. At this point we experienced one more rapid succession from the right engine which quickly resided again with speed now selected and winding back to approach speed. We configured final flap setting to 3 and briefed our potential go-around if required. The Captain successfully ensured our Descent and Before Landing checklist were completed with clearance to land. Upon a successful landing; the Captain ensured the passengers and crew were informed to remain seated while we taxied to the gate. ARFF did a complete review and temperature check of the engines with nothing significant to report. Noteworthy items...the aircraft was hand flown until downwind. Auto pilot was engaged briefly once at 2;500 feet MSL. The autopilot was disengaged when turning base leg and hand flown for the visual approach.Definitely a startle factor; particularly since it happened just above 1;000 feet AGL while thrust levels are normally set to CLB mode. Additionally; the initial confusion as to whether we had hit something (bird?) since the ECAM did not display an action. Furthermore; once the ECAM action did display it was nearly instantaneously gone as the engine continued to attempt to resolve the problem.Since ENG Stall isn't on the Checklist; this scenario could be used in future training events to increase awareness and action based on a low altitude scenario during take-off phase.

column121: The Captain and I were scheduled to depart ZZZZ in a 737 MAX. The flight was full and we knew we had max takeoff weight issues for runway limit. The outside temperature was 16 degrees C and winds were variable for Runway XXR. On our first pushback; we did not have our load closeout and we pushed from gate and began to taxi; even while seeing potential overweight issues. After calling ZZZZ Operations; we received our load closeout and ran the numbers. The temperature increased to 18 degrees C and that significantly degraded engine performance at our weight and required configuration. We noticed that we would be overweight by about 1;100 pounds. We discontinued taxi; messaged Dispatch via ACARS and coordinated a return to gate for overall reevaluation. Dispatch and the flight planning team determined we needed to offload passengers and associated bags and that would fix the problem.Now; enough time elapsed that we needed more fuel and needed a new ATC flight plan clearance. ZZZZ Clearance informed us that we had no clearance in the system and we needed to contact Dispatch. We did that via ACARS as well as through ZZZZ Operations. This disconnect with the clearance occurred more than 10 times over a 4 hour period before they finally got a clearance through ZZZZ ATC. We were told that the issue was that ZZZZ ATC did not like something in the clearance request that ZZZ1 Dispatch submitted. However; ZZZZ ATC would not talk to ZZZ1 Dispatch; nor tell them what was wrong with their submission. ZZZZ ATC would only work through ZZZZ Operations; who does not submit flight plan clearance requests and had no idea what is required. We; the aircrew; decided to not push back until we had our clearance and a valid load closeout. It began to rain during our delay and I requested approximately XX different updates based on new weights; temperatures and runway conditions. Also during this 4 hour delay; Dispatch and the flight planning team repeatedly pulled off many passengers and bags. This required continuous updates for accuracy. The passengers were told to deplane after X hours and were given a time to be back at the gate for departure. We got everyone back on board; received our flight plan clearance; a valid load closeout and departed via ZZZZ Runway XXR. The flight was uneventful and we landed safely in ZZZ2.The main issue on this flight was planning and execution by the company. The company tried to leverage the 737 MAX in an environment where it does not need to be flying with full loads and the flight planning team tried to execute an inherently flawed plan. In ZZZZ; rain is constant; but the temperatures and winds that day were very moderate compared to what routinely occurs in the summer months. Even at 18 degrees C; the 737 MAX is extremely weight limited at this airport's altitude. The 737 MAX should not be flying in ZZZZ during even moderate temperature months with full passenger and cargo loads. The ATC flight plan clearance issue is a procedural or communication issue between the company and ZZZZ ATC. ZZZZ Operations should be able to intercede in these situations and fix any issues that come up; but training and awareness is required. Ultimately; this was a non-issue due to the more time-consuming weight issues associated with this flight. Our flight planning departments must continue to gather data related to the 737 MAX during normal operations at all airports throughout the year. This data will lead to an executable annual route schedule for the 737 MAX and ensure smooth operational tempo while maintaining appropriate safety margins.

column121: During TO out of ZZZ thrust levers anomaly- TO thrust setting as I remember was 84.6; however; when First Officer selected TOGA the thrust increased to over 90% N1 before reducing. Discussed with First Officer after climb out after verifying First Officer had as I expected acted properly (setting thrust) continued to ZZZ1. Executed the visual approach to Runway XX at less than 50 feet thrust lever(auto throttle) anomaly - executed go around. ATC cleared us to 2;000 - during the Go Around I feel it's safe to say we were in the yellow and mitigating any transition into the red by both actively flying/monitoring aircraft instrumentation and following SOPs and yes very deliberately. There was a surprise effect from the aircraft not acting as directed (thrust levers/ auto throttle) as the approach itself was stable. Then we were vectored in visual conditions back around for a second approach to Runway 31. After parking at the gate in ZZZ1 Maintenance was notified of the irregularities with thrust levers (auto throttle).The aircraft was removed from service by Maintenance.Thrust lever / auto throttle anomaly that added a startle effect and divided attention or required additional attention. We could have after the missed approach disconnected the A/T but felt better about closely monitoring/ guarding the thrust levers.
column123: On the take off from ZZZ when I pressed the TOGA button; the throttles rapidly advanced to near full forward; and then slowly retarded to the selected takeoff thrust as we were rolling down the runway.  The throttles came forward very rapidly and went further forward then I would expect.  We were set for a 22K takeoff with an assumed temperature reduction. After takeoff the Captain and I discussed the anomaly.  It was very unusual. The rest of the flight; up to the landing flare; was normal.  I was flying the new visual approach. The approach was loaded into the FMS. The autopilot was engaged. I think I remember disengaging the autopilot if the final turn to final.  In the flare; below 50 feet the throttles began to advance by themselves. I remember being right on speed prior to this. I felt the throttles move forward; and I remember trying to hold them back.  I think the autothrottles were attempting to go around.  I felt the aircraft 'ballooning' and I saw that I was now going to fast (I remember seeing 155 knots). At this point I said go around and pressed the go around button. We climbed out and tower gave us a visual downwind to return. The go around was a normal go around. After cleaning up; I went right back to flaps 1 for the downwind. I was trying to process what just happened and the Captain and I discussed it. We were both surprised by the auto throttle. While turning base; the auto throttles were doing a poor job of holding command bug. They were very slow to respond. I turned off my flight director and visually flew a visual pattern (I had no lateral guidance from the FMS; the approach had not been resequenced. I know the airport very well could see where I needed to go.  I left the auto throttles engaged but I had a firm hand on the throttles. While on base; the air speed got 5 knots slow and I manually pushed the throttles up to speed up. I completed a visual approach and normal flaps 40 landing with flight director off and auto throttles engaged. The auto throttles functioned normal after I had manually pushed them up; but in retrospect I should have disconnected them and flown manually. They were definitely suspect at this point. The flaps 40 approach and landing was normal and smooth. The auto throttles worked as they should.  We had a mechanic at ZZZ1 meet us and we wrote up what had happened. The next morning while eating breakfast; I was 'bothered' by what had happened and I called Name to discuss the anomaly.  We discussed the anomaly in detail. He didn't have any answers either; but said he would keep an eye on the aircraft; X. Additional note; the approach was stable prior to the auto throttle anomaly. We were following an [aircraft] that was going very slow. We were minimal space behind them so we were right on speed throughout the approach to flare. I believe the autopilot was engaged until the turn to final.I am not sure if this was a fault with the airplane auto throttle; a 737 Max anomaly or a coding issue with the new visual approach? Thinking about what had happened on the takeoff; I suspect something was wrong with the auto throttles. I am fairly new to the Max. [No suggestions]; however in retrospect I should have turned off the auto throttles when it became clear they were not working correctly after the go around.

column121: This was the second leg of an OE for the First Officer who was returning to the line after more than one year on leave. We had planned and briefed a Single Engine Taxi (SET). I asked the Pushback Crew to push the aircraft 'towards ZZZ' to better align us for SET Ops. As we were pushing; I noticed a Company aircraft on the adjacent gate was also getting ready to push and commented to the First Officer that we might have to start both engines to safely taxi away. I then realized we could make a left 270 to make our turn towards the east; to taxi to the planned runway. The Pushback Crew asked for me to set the brakes and I complied; then asked me to set the brakes as they were pulling away. This caused a chuckle from both he and I as he got jumbled with his scripted words. The First Officer had completed the #2 engine start and started his flow. He got to the Air Conditioning panel and asked if it was set correctly.I reached up and turned the #2 engine bleed on and commented that the pack was now being powered. Between the chuckle with the Pushback Crew and the First Officer query; I lost my focus and didn't notice the FO did not complete his flow and callout. I was also concerned with getting the aircraft moving in the left 270 before Company pushed. The FO called for taxi and we proceeded down CS and Mike. After being cleared onto Mike and seeing there was no line for Runway XX; I called for #1 engine to be started. The FO started it and did his After Start Flow; noticing and announcing that we hadn't set the flaps. I verified this; stopped the aircraft and commanded flaps 1; Before Taxi Checklist. These items were accomplished; we continued with normal operations and took off and flew to ZZZ1 without further incident.Don't get distracted during critical phases of flight; specifically when very specific cues are used to command flaps and run checklists.
column123: During the Crew brief; and prior to pushing back in ZZZ; the Captain briefed a single-engine taxi (SET). The Captain requested from the Tug Operator that the pushback be angled toward the turnout direction; to facilitate an easier SET break away to begin taxi.  When the pushback was complete; we discussed whether or not to start the remaining #1 engine; and abandon the SET plan; because the Pushback Crew had not pushed the aircraft in the position instructed. Ultimately; we decided to request; from the Ramp Controller; a turn in the opposite direction and continue with the SET plan.  Being on the second leg of OE; and getting familiar with the switch positions of the pressurization panel; I had stopped my after start flow at that panel; to ask the Captain a question. Inadvertently and after that interruption; I neglected to continue the flow to its completion.  Subsequently; we began our taxi without setting the flaps; which helps to trigger the Before Taxi Checklist.  When we eventually started the #1 engine during taxi out; I noticed that the flaps had not been set; as I usually re-check the items on an after start flow.  We stopped the aircraft; set the flaps; and completed the Before Taxi Checklist.  The flight continued as normal.I think that getting further comfortable with the pressurization panel; and that particular flow; will increase situational awareness and become less of a distraction.

Noticed that the attitude pitch did not match the flight director command followed by a Level Two 'STAB out of trim' alert.  We then made the decision for an air turn back; notified ATC; transferred control of the jet to the me (Pilot Monitoring) and advised ATC of the need to dump fuel (gross weight-600K LBS.) with a request for a holding pattern at a block altitude of 6;000-7;000 feet. ATC denied the hold and elected to vector us over the water in their radar holding pattern. The QRH was consulted for stabilizer out of trim which led us to a non abnormal alert 'Stabilizer Inop. We then noticed that the stabilizer trim had not moved from the takeoff setting of 8.0 degrees. Fuel dump continued in the radar hold until 522K gross weight; then the cross feed relays failed and forced the dump command to stop. We flew in the radar pattern for about another 50 minutes within about 35nm from ZZZZ until our bingo fuel of 32K; with now a runway change to XXL. ATC was advised of the need for a 20nm final approach and a request of no traffic in front of us. We discussed the go around possibilities; configured on schedule early of the slats/flaps and gear. Aircraft control was then transferred to the Captain and the autopilot disconnected with noticeable pitch down; landed uneventfully. Failure of trim gear fuse pin."

column121: I was Pilot Flying.  The right thrust reverser was inoperative and disabled by maintenance; the left thrust reverser was available for use.  After touching down and derotating; I deployed the left thrust reverser.  When I attempted to move the thrust lever backward from idle reverse to increase reverse thrust I found that the thrust lever would not move and my hand position somehow felt different from usual.  In that same moment I realized that instead of lifting the thrust reverser unlock lever I had lifted the shutoff lock and moved the thrust lever into shutoff; shutting down the left engine.  I called out the problem to the Captain and told him I would be using only brakes to stop the aircraft.  There was plenty of runway remaining and heavy braking was not required.  We taxied to the gate using normal single engine taxi procedures.After performing several thousand landings in this aircraft I have a well developed muscle memory for engaging reverse thrust.  I also have a well developed muscle memory for shutting down the left engine during taxi.  With the right thrust reverser disabled; thrust reverser use required touching and moving only the left thrust lever instead of both thrust levers.  I am fairly certain that this interaction with only the left thrust lever subconsciously triggered the muscle memory motions for a left engine shutdown instead of those for activating the thrust reverser(s) which usually involves moving both thrust levers.  I had landed the same aircraft the day before with the same inoperative right thrust reverser and properly deployed only the left thrust reverser.  I have no other explanation for how I managed to perform the motions for an engine shutdown instead.I will be much more aware of this possibility for inadvertent incorrect hand motions possibly caused by muscle memory triggers when operating an aircraft with a deferred thrust reverser.

column121: Arriving in San Diego; we had been cleared for the RNAV Z Runway 27 approach. We checked in with the Tower and were cleared to land. I heard Tower instruct a [heavy jet] to; 'Line up and wait; traffic on an 8 mile final'. Checklists and callouts may have masked additional communications on the frequency because I can't recall whether the [heavy jet] flight was cleared for takeoff; or not. We broke out of IMC at approximately 1400 feet. The Pilot Monitoring called 'Runway in Sight - Landing'. Shortly thereafter; the First Officer said; 'Is that an airplane on the runway? I looked closer and honestly could not tell. The navigation and beacon lights were blending into the approach lights and it was difficult to distinguish the aircraft. We had to get closer before the actual structure of the airplane was apparent. We had already determined that a go-around/missed approach was necessary; but before we could communicate that to the Tower Controller; she issued the go-around instruction; 'Fly the published Missed Approach; and contact Departure'. I had observed that the offending aircraft was stationary on the runway; and not in the midst of a takeoff roll; so I knew that the published missed approach or runway heading was appropriate; and that a sidestep departure for spacing was not necessary. So we complied as instructed. We had already determined our BINGO fuel enroute and knew that we could accept one more approach before diverting to our alternate; so we accepted vectors back for another approach. The subsequent approach and landing was uneventful. The [heavy jet] had been removed from the runway and was still holding short when we landed. No mention of the reason for the go-around was given by the Tower; nor did we ask. Because we knew. There was an airplane on the runway.     Cause: [The] decision to work a Maintenance Irregularity while on an active runway. The Tower's decision to put the [heavy jet] on the runway when they were not ready to depart; and then forgetting about them. And our loss of situational awareness based on the radio communications that were; or were not; taking place on the Tower Frequency.In the future; if the First Officer questions the security of the runway; or the landing clearance; I will instruct them to simply; and without delay; to ask the Tower. This would NOT have prevented the necessity to go-around; but perhaps would have initiated the maneuver a little sooner."
column123: While on the RNAV Z 27; we were handed off to Tower and were cleared to land. This occurred at approximately SAYAE intersection. The approach continued normally and we broke out about 1;400 feet and then called 'runway in sight'; 'runway in sight landing'. Sometime after the 1;000 feet stabilized cleared to land call; I noticed what appeared to be an airplane on the displaced threshold of Runway 27 and said; 'Is that an airplane on the runway? The darkness of the displaced threshold area against the runway lights and the fact that the aircraft was in position pointed away from us made it difficult to tell. However; by the times the words were spoken; we were close enough to see. At the very same moment we began our go-around; the Tower issued instructions to go around and fly the published missed approach; which we did since the aircraft on the runway did not appear to be moving. We proceeded with a normal go-around and returned for a normal landing since we had sufficient fuel. In the simplest terms; we executed a normal go around due to an aircraft on the runway. Why was there an aircraft on the runway? I am not sure. Shortly after we were cleared to land; we heard the tower instruct [another aircraft] to line up and wait; traffic 8 mile final. I honestly don't recall hearing a take-off clearance; perhaps due our being engaged with our tasks and callouts during the approach. We did see the aircraft short of the runway when we returned. It wasn't until later that we read that they had a mechanical issue.Maintaining better awareness of traffic utilizing the runway particularly when we can't see it yet. Better awareness would have allowed us to question if the runway was indeed clear. That may not have prevented the go around this time; it would've depended on how soon we became aware."

column121: I have written the main cabin door on this airplane up four times. The Flight Attendant can't open it with anywhere close to normal force. I had the First Officer and Flight Attendant film the force required to open the door and they couldn't do it. It only opened after I put IMMENSE force on the handle. This is a safety hazard because the door is the primary exit in the event of an emergency. Of the four times this door was forced open after it was written up; two of the write-ups were done with our own aircraft maintenance personnel on board and two I personally forced the door open with almost all of my strength and leverage.The airplane should be ferry flown to a maintenance base and undergo flight testing to determine what is causing the main cabin door to jam itself shut after flight.

column121: I reviewed the maintenance log when I arrived at the aircraft for the first flight of the day. It had just been released from maintenance. It had previously been written up for a strong smell coming from the lavatory. The corrective action stated that the lavatory had been leaking into the cargo bay. It had been repaired the same day and I was the first to fly the aircraft. I included this information with my crew brief.During the descent to ZZZ1; sometime prior to FL180 because the descent checklist had yet to be completed; the FO (First Officer) and I heard what sounded like an extra loud flushing noise from the FWD LAV (Forward Lavatory); but then developed into a loud sound similar to an engine spooling down; immediately followed by a strange; slightly chemical odor. We both looked at each other and confirmed what we heard and smelled. I called the A F/A (Flight Attendant) to verify if anyone had just flushed the toilet. She said someone was in the lavatory; had just flushed; and it smelled strongly like excrement.The odor quickly subsided. We discussed the possible sources. The LAV was a different style from most of our aircraft so it could have just been a sound [different] than what we were used to. The LAV had just been repaired so the odor could have been related. Since there odor was gone and there were no other indications of abnormality we continued to ZZZ1 but I had the FO start reviewing synoptic pages for any clues and I started reviewing possible diversion airports. We made a list of airports closest to our position as we got closer to ZZZ1; ZZZ2; then ZZZ3; then ZZZ4.During descent after passing through FL180; I started to hear and feel the aircraft surging. It sounded like it was coming from the engines. I de-cluttered the EICAS to check for vibration. There was a notable difference in engine vibration; but they were still in the green and there were no other indications on the EICAS.At approximately 13;000 ft. the FO and I both noticed a strong acrid odor. I called the A F/A who confirmed the LAV was not in use. I then called for the Smoke; Fire; Fumes QRC (Quick Reference Checklist). We donned our oxygen masks and the FO started through the QRC. We were almost exactly on top of ZZZ3; which we had already decided as a suitable airport; so when the FO [read the steps related to ATC] of the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook) I told him to [request priority handling] and ask to land at ZZZ3 immediately.ATC assigned an ALT of 9;000 ft. As I started to descend; the aircraft began shaking violently. ATC continued to vector and assign lower altitudes. When the FO turned off the RECIRC fans per the QRH; I asked him to put the checklist down and set up the aircraft for landing. We were very close to the airport and descending quickly. I decided the priority was for the FO to get our landing numbers and set up the approach while coordinating with ATC and the FA's. I could not help because I suspected external damage to the control surfaces so I did not want to take my attention away from maintaining positive control of the aircraft.Somewhere around the 9;000 ft. mark or lower we received an EICAS PACK 1 FAIL. This was the first time the EICAS provided any kind of indication of an abnormality. We had experienced a loud noise; strong odors; violent shaking; and now a PACK 1 FAIL. It felt as if the aircraft had suffered major damage and safe completion of the flight was at serious risk. ATC had placed us on a downwind for the ILS but; fearing we may be losing more systems and controllability; I told the FO we were turning immediately to final. As we slowed to approach speeds the shaking reduced. The FO contacted the FA's to go over [procedures]. I did not order a brace and I did not intend to evacuate. The aircraft was stabilizing and there weren't any smoke or fire indications in the cabin or flight deck. I landed and stopped on the runway. I requested an inspection by the fire trucks to make sure the aircraft wasn't on fire and we were safe to taxi. I made an announcement for everyone to remain seated and that we had landed due to a maintenance issue; but that the aircraft was safe and we were taxiing to a gate.In our judgement; due to the order and severity of events; we thought the aircraft may be in serious jeopardy. An immediate landing was the safest option available. I have often conducted a very similar scenario with FO's on long flights out of the area and near ZZZ3; during cruise. The scenario is a fume event. The reason this is important is because the QRH for fumes is very long and involves a lot of system isolation for troubleshooting. It would take 20-30 minutes for us to review the QRH in a relaxed; stable environment. Only at the end of the QRH do you see just how much runway would be required if you're heavy and have taken a lot of performance penalties due to the QRH troubleshooting process. Because we were so close to the airport and descending quickly; I prioritized performance and navigation over completing the QRH. There simply was not enough time for the full checklist.Parked at the gate; I called Dispatch and explained what was going on. They weren't aware of the diversion. The FO had asked ATC to notify our company during descent. I was getting bounced around a lot between Dispatch and [Administration] with Maintenance talking to them in the background; but Maintenance immediately insisted that it was a simple air system failure and that the aircraft was safe. Both the FO and I conducted a walk-around. I said the aircraft was not safe to fly. I wouldn't have landed in ZZZ3 if I thought the aircraft was safe. This aircraft needs a full maintenance inspection based on the severity of conditions we had just experienced. [In the past] I've had a hydraulic line rupture at FL200; I've had a brake failure on landing; I've had a full system failure. This was like nothing I had experienced and felt far more severe at the time than just a simple air system failure. It was serious enough that I didn't know if we would make the runway. This aircraft had a recent history of fluids leaking into the cargo bay. How much unseen damage was caused by these fluids? Why wouldn't an inspection be required if the maintenance department is saying 'oh yeah the smell and shaking is from the system blowing out'? As I'm trying to convince Dispatch and Maintenance that an inspection needs to be conducted; this is already approaching about 2 hours after landing; the adrenaline started to fade and the fatigue settled in. The entire crew was exhausted to the point that even the FA's were fatigued. Having drilled this scenario; I believe I acted appropriately given the circumstances. QRH calls for system isolation to identify the source but with odor being cause of the [diversion] and no EICAS indications there is no way to verify the source without taking the O2 mask off; which is extremely dangerous. We were so close and working with so little time that getting on the ground immediately became the top priority.

column121: There was a momentary unreliable airspeed followed by a brief failure of the PF's (Pilot Flying) PFD. Once the PFD was restored; airspeed was still momentarily unreliable.While operating the flight from ZZZ to ZZZZ; I was the pilot flying. After deviating for weather; we were proceeding directly to ZZZZZ to perform the VOR DME 2 [approach to] Runway XX at ZZZZ. Approximately 20nm from ZZZZZ and descending; we encountered IMC and light precipitation and light turbulence which gradually increased to moderate turbulence. We were partially configured at flaps 1 and gear was down at 200 kts and beginning our turn for the arc when my airspeed began having deviations of +/- 15 kts; I attributed this to the increasing turbulence and precipitation we had encountered. While banked and descending; the PLIs (Pitch Limit Indicator) presented and I had a loss of airspeed below the green dot and a gain of airspeed that presented amber digits. At this point my airspeed completely went away; as if I was on the ground; a grey box was present where the digits would be but there was no V-Speed information. Shortly after this occurred; my PFD went black for a moment; but never reverted to a different display. Once this happened; I transitioned to the IESS (Integrated Electronic Standby System); rolled the wings level; advanced the thrust levers; climbed to ensure terrain clearance; and we returned to VMC.Nearly immediately after establishing the climb; the PFD and all information on it returned; although there were errors with the airspeed. Initially; the airspeed showed faster than we were; as if we had been repositioned in the simulator; and we received one aural 'High-speed' until the airspeed settled back to what the IESS was showing. Our altitude at this point was approximately between 17;000 ft. and 16;000 ft. with a high peak around 9827 ft. in our vicinity. From our descent; I knew I could find VMC around 19;000 ft. so I directed the pilot not flying to tell ATC we would be present heading and climbing to 20;000 ft.I did not direct the PNF (Pilot Not Flying) to declare an emergency as we were busy figuring out what just happened and coordinating a plan between each other. In the climb; we cleaned the aircraft up and ran an after takeoff checklist. Once we were in VMC; we worked with each other to determine that all of our instruments matched and were reliable. We also determined that we could remain mostly VMC by performing the approach from ZZZZZ1 and asked to proceed directly to ZZZZZ1. We successfully performed the approach and landing at ZZZZ. Upon exiting the runway; we received both AFCS (Automated Flight Control System) Fault; and ADS Probe 1 Fail messages. We felt that we could have been struck by lightning; but we could not find any strike points on the aircraft; and all static wicks that were visible to us were found intact. We entered both messages above in the AML as well as an AML entry for a possible lightning strike.I feel my actions were appropriate given that we were not in radar contact any longer. I was unsure if I could trust any pitot or static instruments and I knew where I could find visual conditions away from terrain. I should have declared an emergency but at the time I felt that doing so with the language barrier would have broken down my communication with my First Officer when we needed to focus on flying the aircraft. Additionally; he was able to secure a clearance for the same heading up to 20;000 ft. as soon as I asked him to do so.

column121: Aircraft was directed to taxi from gate 1 to Runway XXL via Taxiways 1; 2; 3; 4. While on Taxiway 3; turning right to join Taxiway 4; both crew members noted an aircraft that appeared to have just been pushed back from gate 2. It was also agreed by both crew members that the tail of the aircraft appeared to be just inside the ramp boundary line. Approaching the aircraft at gate 2; the FO noted that the right wingtip was on the boundary line. The Captain then stated that he was going to deviate left of the taxiway centerline for additional clearance and the FO acknowledged. Approaching the aircraft; the FO was monitoring the right wingtip. From the cockpit angle the wingtip appeared to have approximately five feet of clearance and this was communicated to the Captain. The FO continued to monitor the wingtip until it appeared to initially pass the tail of the other aircraft outside of gate 2 and then announced it was clear to the Captain. It was at this time the right winglet struck the horizontal stabilizer. (Aircraft  speed was approximately 5 knots.)  The FO then called out to stop multiple times. The Captain stopped the aircraft and made an announcement for the Flight Attendants and Passengers to remain in their seats. The Captain verified with the Flight Attendants that everyone was OK. The crew then coordinated with Ground Control and Operations to return to gate 3. An ACARS message was also sent to Dispatch while waiting for a gate assignment. It is the FO's initial assessment that the wingtip must have started to pass on the opposite side of the horizontal stabilizer of the aircraft outside of gate 2; but incorrectly determined that it was on the near side based off the cockpit angle and understanding that the Captain had deviated left of the taxiway for more clearance. There were no distractions and the crew communicated clearly.  Actions that could have prevented this incident would have been if the crew had stopped on Taxiway 4 and waited for the aircraft at gate 2 to move and provide more clearance. Additionally; the FO could have better assessed the wingtip spacing.
column123: We were cleared to taxi from [gate] 1 to [Runway] XXL via [taxiways] 2; 3 and 4. As we were joining 4; I noticed an aircraft facing terminal at [gate] 2; which appeared to be just inside of the movement area line. I mistakenly assumed it was an aircraft that had just pushed and that he was waiting to taxi. My expectation bias was that he would not have been pushed deep enough to interfere with Taxiway 4. As we were NE bound on [Taxiway] 4; I steered aircraft left of taxi; centerline to give more clearance around other aircraft. I asked FO how we looked on wingtip clearance. The FO stated; 'We are clear by 5 to 10 feet.' As we were passing behind the aircraft I felt that a main tire hit a pothole. As I asked what that was; I felt another 'bump'. The FO stated 'Stop. Stop.' I brought the aircraft to a stop and the FO told me we struck the other aircraft. I would estimate we were at a speed of 7 to 8 knots when the contact occurred. We began our taxi on #2 engine. I believe the second engine start was complete prior to contact. There was a typical level of chatter on ZZZ Ground frequency; which was busy. After the contact; I stopped the aircraft on Taxiway 4 and set the parking brake. We reported the incident to Ground Control. While I made a PA to the cabin to remain seated; the FO notified operations to coordinate a gate return and contact Maintenance. We returned to Gate 3 without further incident.Task Loading - I did a poor job of managing task loading. ZZZ is very busy and congested on the ground. With multiple aircraft moving in a densely packed area; I should not have opted for Single Engine Taxi (SET).  This would have reduced the workload on both crew members and perhaps allowed for better situational awareness as we were moving towards the departure runway. Risk Management- I did not properly balance the risk of aircraft contact with continuing on the taxiway. Had I stopped and waited on the other aircraft to move well clear of taxiway; I would not have assumed that unnecessary risk. This also relates to rushing and trying not to clog up a taxiway. I should have set the brakes and not moved forward until aircraft in question was well clear.
