column121: Upon finishing my three-day paring in ZZZ1 at (time/date) I received a phone call from Scheduling; as I was leaving the aircraft. They told me they had added on to my schedule; they needed me to deadhead to ZZZ; then ferry an aircraft back to ZZZ1. I was concerned because I had already flown quite a bit that day and was afraid that I would not be legal for it. The Scheduler assured me that I was legal and that it was all okay. I asked them to look into it again because I had my doubts. I then asked if they could provide a hotel for rest at the end of the turn as I would be extremely tired. She claimed she would pass it on to the hotel desk. Upon contacting the hotel desk they said they could only provide a room if there was an unused ZZZ1 overnight room; which there was not.I proceeded onto the gate for the first leg of the ZZZ turn. Inside 30 minutes to departure there was no crew or other deadheading crewmember present at the aircraft. The flight to ZZZ was scheduled completely empty except for the Operating Crew; myself and one other deadheader. Again; I was concerned that I would time out before we could complete the turn so took it upon myself to prepare the aircraft for departure and set up the cockpit for the Operating Crew; in order to expedite our departure. We eventually departed 18 minutes later than planned. Upon reaching ZZZ; the operating First Officer left to recover a diverted aircraft back to ZZZ1 and I quickly prepared our aircraft for our return to ZZZ1. Unfortunately; once again; our aircraft experienced multiple delays due to random unexplainable maintenance locks; issues with load and balance calculation and performance. As we sat on the ramp at ZZZ I could tell that I would soon be in danger of timing out and verified my legalities. It showed a Table B Limit of XX42C without extension. At roughly XXX25CI called Crew Scheduling and notified them I was within 20 minutes of reaching the latest takeoff limit; and asked them what their plan was. The Scheduler on the line said that there was someone looking into my legalities and that they would call me back. That call never came. Shortly thereafter the aircraft issues were resolved and we were able to depart at XX37CF; just five minutes before the XX42C takeoff limit. With the aid of computer program and the printed crew legalities sheet; it appeared we had taken off within limits and were completely legal to fly the flight.Upon landing at ZZZ1 at XX04C; we were told that there were no gates available we would have to hold on the pad until one became available. Shortly after parking in the pad; we received an ACARS message referencing my employee number and requesting a flight delay extension. It showed several times; but those times did not match any times on the calculator on computer program. It was confusing and seemed to be in error. Since we were parked in the pad with the parking brake set; the Captain took the radios and I called Crew Scheduling. I explained we were on the ground waiting for a gate; I told them I had received the ACARS message and that it did not make sense - I asked for clarification and the implications of accepting or rejecting. They placed me on a brief hold but when they came back they were not able to answer any of my questions and essentially didn't seem too concerned since we were on the ground in ZZZ1. Since Crew Scheduling was not able to explain the ACARS message I neither accepted nor rejected the extension. Once again I asked for a hotel room; and they said they were not able to accommodate.A gate finally opened; we terminated the aircraft and I left the gate. As I was walking away I got a call from Crew Scheduling; a different Scheduler was on the line telling me that I had violated the limits. I explained to him that I had taken off five minutes before the limit time and that I should have been legal to fly the flight. The Scheduler explained that even though that was true I had violated the 'Last Block In' time of XX15C. I told him that I was not aware of any Last Block In Time; it is not a number that is published or provided to us in the cockpit; either by the Crew legalities sheet or the computer calculator. I also explained that I had called Crew Scheduling multiple times this evening to voice my concern over my proximity to the limits and not once during any of those calls did any member of Crew Scheduling even bother to mention a 'Last Block In' time limitation. The Scheduler tried to explain that it was all okay as long I say I was aware of it and that I was in acceptance. I countered that no; I was not aware of the limit despite my multiple requests to Crew Scheduling to evaluate my limits; and no; I was not aware I had exceeded any limit; yet when I called for an explanation of the ACARS message; it would have been the perfect time to tell me; and finally no; I did not accept the extension; nor did I reject it because nobody at Crew Scheduling could explain it to me. However; by default; a lack of acceptance should be considered a rejection. This was obviously not what the Scheduler wanted to hear; so he told me that he would forward it to a Supervisor; who would subsequently call my Chief Pilot. I said that was fine; asked that he have the Supervisor call me as well and we ended the call.This experience has taught me that Company does not have either the capability or the desire to adequately protect its pilots from exceeding FAR Part 117 Flight Duty Limitations and Rest Requirement restrictions. I understand that FAR 117 responsibilities are shared between the certificate holder (Company) and the pilot (myself). In this case; however; the pilot had expressed concern about the limits three times; asked for clarification from the certificate holder; yet was repeatedly stonewalled with evasive or non-existent guidance in order to complete the operation. Finally; after successfully and safely completing that operation the pilot was criticized for exceeding a limit the he was never provided; warned of; or explained ahead of time. Then finally the certificate holder attempted to coerce the pilot into accepting the extension after the fact.Resolution of this issue and prevention in the future should include: 1. Provide pilots with the latest block-in time on the crew legalities sheet and computer in additions to latest takeoff times for every flight. This allows pilots to clearly understand all limits of the flight. 2. Better and/or more extensive training of Crew Schedulers on FAR Part 117 duty restrictions. 3. Clearer and more proactive communication from Crew Scheduling to pilots about approaching limits. 4. Make available crew rest accommodations; on request; to a pilot that has been flown to the extent of or over the flight limits on the last day of a paring. Accident prevention should extend beyond the confines of the cockpit. After working 13 hours and 48 minutes on duty operating aircraft; nobody should be behind the wheel of a motor vehicle late at night.
column123: This event involves a potential exceedance of the Part 117 Maximum Block In (MBI) time for the First Officer at the end of a long duty day that included a re-route (involuntary assignment). It has already been reported by the First Officer; and I agree with and support his report. Rather than repeat his whole narrative; I will highlight important points and add one or two additional observations.In ZZZ; we experienced multiple unexplained maintenance locks which prevented us from receiving takeoff data. (Unknown if this malfunction was due to the new maintenance software; or ZZZ Ops not entering our actual fuel on board - which was tankered in and approximately 3;000 pounds more than expected on the release.) After about 30 minutes; we were able to resolve the situation by correcting fuel on board on a new release (and new takeoff reference number.) Feeling pressure to simultaneously deal with First Officer's legality issue while resolving the maintenance lock issue was a distraction and threat that (unlike weather; passenger issues; or aircraft malfunctions) is created by the system. In other words; although Part 117 is intended to help improve safety; the way it's applied ends up being an unhelpful distraction and a threat to safety.The First Officer tried to raise legality questions on the original call. Later; during the re-assignment; the First Officer called Scheduling at least three times to try to discuss the situation. Although I could not hear the other end of the conversations; it sounded like each time he was told they were aware of it and 'working on it.'The First Officer had accepted an extension the previous night. This caused him / us to wonder whether he was even legal for an extension on a 2nd consecutive night? He attempted to bring this up to Scheduling but never got a good answer from them. (Like everything else in Part 117; it's not as easy to answer as it should be. It certainly isn't a yes/no answer.)Once on the ground in ZZZ1 and holding in the pad for a gate to become available; we received an automated ACARS message asking to accept or reject an extension. This was done at the very last minute; when the only realistic options were: accept the extension; or violate Part 117. That doesn't really give the pilot any option to reject the extension. As previously stated; he had already been trying to work with Scheduling prior to this. And; he also (unsuccessfully) attempted to clarify his block in time and options with Scheduling after the ACARS message. When there was still time to address the issue; Scheduling would only give him a 'we're working on it.' It seems like the only option Scheduling would consider was strong-arming him into accepting the extension 'or else.' As we approach what looks to be a very busy summer flying schedule; with the strong possibility that the pilots being brought back in July from extended time off will arrive on the line too late to fill the gaps; Scheduling and Dispatch might consider being more proactive looking for other solutions (offering more premium open time trips; not diverting aircraft into airports where we only have one scheduled flight per day; etc.) versus pushing so hard and flirting with legality issues. In the interest of fatigue management and safety; I don't think it's reasonable to assume that a pilot who has been involuntarily reassigned more flying at the end of a long trip will automatically desire to voluntarily accept an extension to his flight duty limits. The discussion needs to happen much earlier; and not through an automated message giving the false appearance the pilot has an actual choice in the matter.

column121: Denver airport is becoming hazardous to fly into due to non-specific ATIS; poor communication between DEN Center and DEN Approach; and the normalization of multiple arrivals and approaches being programmed during a normal arrival into Denver. This has increased substantially in the last few months and is resulting in aircrews being nearly continuously heads down reprogramming and briefing arrivals/transitions; approaches; taxi plan; getting appropriate landing data; briefing such changes; reviewing NOTAMs associated with these changes...etc. This is usually done while dodging weather; and mitigating turbulence; while descending into high terrain and congested traffic into an airport with multiple; parallel; similarly named runways. I feel there are three root causes. 1) ATIS is not very useful. Basically; a direction of traffic flow and a listing of all available approaches DEN has. 2) There seems to be a system now where approach tells Center what runway transition to assign aircraft. This transition frequently doesn't make sense and was not anticipated; programmed and briefed. Then; upon handoff to approach; the transition to another runway is often assigned. Then when the actual runway and approach is assigned; it frequently results in another reprogramming. This is acceptable during rapidly changing weather...it is commonplace all the time; however. On Aircraft X we programmed and briefed the FLATI 2 RNAV; RWY26 transition; RNAV Z Runway 26 approach. (Winds were 25024G34.) After starting the descent; we were given direct BYYKE; for the LONGS RNAV arrival. We programmed the LONGS arrival; Runway 26 transition; Runway 26 RNAV Z approach. We told Center that we were requesting Runway 26. Center directed us to fly the Runway 16R transition. (even though we were planning not to accept this approach). They said they are directed by DEN approach what transition to assign). We reprogrammed the ILS R16 transition and approach (we are now well along in the descent...moderate turbulence; and a VNAV discontinuity resulting from the reprogramming not being executable because of an approach transition altitude in-congruence) This was resolved quickly and safely and flown uneventfully with a 25 knot crosswind landing. The forecast approach winds were spot on; the ATIS hadn't changed substantially in an hour (Though there were about 5 or 6 of them). The point is; there was no significant change in weather driving this. I could have written the same report the last time I arrived to DEN on my last [arrival] from the east. On the flight today; we planned and briefed two different arrivals; one of the arrivals changing the transitions twice; two different RNAV Z approaches; an ILS approach and two different runways/performance numbers; NOTAMs; engine failure procedures taxi plans etc. I wouldn't spend time filing this report if it was a 'one off' It is becoming the norm and accepted scenario into Denver. It is also a contributing factor with DEN historically having issues with RNAVs. Each of these arrivals is complicated with at least 5-10 different altitude or speed constraints associated with them.

column121: Approach control cleared us direct to WESEN for ILS [Runway] 08 [approach] at SJU. Captain was Pilot Flying; First Officer was Pilot Monitoring. This was the second leg of the night for this three day pairing of a long duty day. Level at 3;000 ft. (pilot selected) then cleared descent to 2;500 ft. (pilot selected) accomplished in vertical speed. Aircraft pilot selected speed was 180 kts. Controller assigned heading 110 to intercept and then cleared us for ILS [Runway] 08 approach. Approach/Land was armed and 'Land Armed' was displayed on PFD. The localizer remained identified and aircraft turned to intercept inbound course. Glide slope was above. Halfway through the intercept; the aircraft made an abrupt pitch-up followed by a thrust increase. This was very unusual as I have never experienced or seen an aircraft climb to capture a glide slope. While this was happening the aircraft exited approach/land mode and reverted to heading mode and solid bow tie altitude (2;500 ft.) All FMAs were 'white'. During the automation the aircraft pitched up and altitude was approximately 3;000 ft. in an attempt to capture the glide slope. The FO made a quick analysis and quick calls to the pilot flying while I was simultaneously disconnecting the autopilot and manually retarding the throttles to correct this anomaly. The aircraft was stabilized and a hand flown ILS was accomplished without autopilot assistance. This aircraft was scheduled for an 'auto land' for currency requirements and subsequently not accomplished. The First Officer monitoring that was accomplished and the verbal inputs from the FO were timely and appropriate; solid CRM. A note in our company aircrew briefing guide notes: Safety Alert Runway 08 Intermittent Glideslope Weak or intermittent glideslope signals have been reported when using ILS Runway 08. Exercise caution and intercept glideslope at the altitude depicted on the approach chart to guard against following a false glide slope signal. If the crew experiences any anomalies while conducting the approach; report the incident to tower and file an event report.

column121: After being cleared for takeoff on Runway 1 in DCA; the Captain transferred the controls to me. Shortly after the '80' knot callout and my response; I noticed Aircraft Y approaching an intersection ahead and it appeared they were moving faster than if they planned to hold short of the runway we were departing. I focused on flying the aircraft while closely monitoring Aircraft Y. Just as I was considering taking action; the aircraft came to a quick stop short of the runway. Around the exact same time the Tower Controller transmitted 'Aircraft X!' with no further instructions. We continued the takeoff uneventfully and Tower gave us their phone number to call upon landing in ZZZ; assuring us we were not in trouble or at fault but wanted to hear our side of the situation. The Captain asked me if I saw the aircraft and after a brief discussion it was obvious we both saw the same situation unfold.I am unaware of Aircraft Y's communication with ATC. With that said; I'm assuming it was either a lack of situational awareness on their part or ATC giving incorrect instructions.I do believe the system in place will normally prevent these occurrences. Maintaining situational awareness. Verifying clearance prior to crossing an active runway. Both pilots being heads-up. Physically checking the runway for aircraft should be the last barrier.
column123: We were cleared for takeoff on Runway 01. I turned control of the aircraft over to the First Officer (FO); and after he applied takeoff power I took control of the throttles. Several seconds later I made the '80' call; which the FO acknowledged. About this time I noticed an aircraft (Aircraft Y; I think) up ahead approaching Runway 01 perpendicularly on a taxiway (probably Taxiway G; but maybe M) at a fairly rapid taxi speed. I focused on the aircraft and began to wonder if it was going to stop as it got closer to the runway environment with no sign of slowing. At this point I mentally prepared for performing a rejected takeoff. Just as the aircraft reached the point where I was thinking I would reject the takeoff I noticed the aircraft stop with a pronounced 'dipping of the nose' from hard braking. At this point I knew the aircraft had stopped and takeoff could continue. I estimate our speed to be about 120-130 knots at this point. A second or two later the Tower Controller made a somewhat excited call; 'Aircraft X!...no further transmission'. As we passed the other aircraft I looked over and couldn't determine if it was over the hold short lines; but could tell it was very close. We continued the takeoff and shortly after getting airborne; the Tower Controller asked us if we had the number to call the tower when reaching destination. After retracting gear and flaps I asked the FO 'Did you see that other aircraft?' He replied he did and after further discussion I determined he saw basically the same things I did (aircraft approaching the runway; considering a rejected takeoff; 'dipping of the nose' with hard braking; knowing the aircraft had indeed stopped and comfortable continuing the takeoff). I called the tower when reaching ZZZ. The Controller taking my call informed me the other aircraft had entered the runway environment and asked if we noticed anything. I replied we did; but continued the takeoff because we knew the aircraft had completely stopped and we couldn't determine if it was over line or just very close. The person taking the call also mentioned the Tower Controller started to issue a rejected takeoff command to us but didn't finish because the Ground Controller confirmed the encroaching aircraft had stopped; hence the 'Aircraft X...'SMGCS lighting installed at DCA and used in all weather conditions; not just low visibility. Red lights are very effective in reminding pilots they are not cleared to cross/enter a runway.

column121: In cruise flight FL3XY; we received a yellow EICAS Left Hydraulic Quantity (L HYD QTY) message. We opened the QRH and followed the checklist for L HYD QTY message which had us turn off the associated Left hydraulic pumps in order to conserve (if able) quantity in the system. We had the status page up and noticed it was approximate .47 on the Quantity listed; and then also noticed it continued to slowly drop in number as we continued to complete the checklist. The checklist had us reference Hydraulic System Pressure -Left (only) checklist to see affected subsystems (extensive list and checklist). When referencing this and seeing the involvement with degraded flight control systems (spoilers; nose wheel steering; thrust reversers; etc.) and looking at ZZZ's current and forecast wind (strong steady and gusty crosswinds); Captain transferred controls and ATC communication to me and began consultation with Company on best options for us. The quantity during his conversation with Company continued to drop and I (with his agreement) slowed the cruise speed in case we elected to divert based off of possible flight control degradation based on the conditions in ZZZ. We both discussed the nice conditions back in ZZZ1 and long runway for a potential flaps 20 landing with other degraded flight control systems. As the discussion with Dispatch/Maintenance Control/ Chief Pilot continued; the hydraulic quantity continued to drop and then stabilized around .17 (where the standpipe sits in the reservoir?). Hydraulic pressure continued steady at approximately XY00 with some slight fluctuations and we agreed (temporarily) that ZZZ would still be viable based off of the Power Transfer Unit (PTU) input to the Left Hydraulic system.As the conversation with the Company continued; the Hydraulic pressure then started to fluctuate and eventually went to zero along with the quantity. At that moment; the status message POWER TRANSFER UNIT popped up. The captain relayed to Company this information and with the concurrence of all; the election to divert back to ZZZ1 was made based off of all the available information of system degradation; weather conditions in ZZZ and time to complete the extensive HYDRAULIC SYSESTEM  PRESSURE - Left (Only) checklist. With concurrence; I advised ATC our wishes to divert to ZZZ1 and [request] for priority handling. Shortly after receiving revised clearance; ATC coordination and required information for them; we reprogrammed the box and began our diversion back to ZZZ1. Within a few minutes; we received an ACARS message from Dispatch that ZZZ2 was reporting good conditions with a favorable runway alignment for the winds. Captain and I evaluated runway XY (RWY XY) and agreed ZZZ2 was a good option at only 233NM from our current position (plenty of time to reprogram; complete the involved checklist and land safely with a direct headwind on RWY XY).At the moment of agreement; we then asked for diversion to ZZZ2 for RWY XY under emergency authority with full fire equipment standing by for precautionary purposes. We were then given revised clearance to ZZZ2 and completed the flight without further incident after completing the checklist.Being that the nose wheel steering was inoperative; we stopped the aircraft on the runway after landing on the centerline and waited for evaluation by fire/rescue and awaited tow-in to gate from the runway to the gate from a supertug. Supertug tow was delayed for several minutes after evaluation from fire/rescue and their report of significant fluid leakage from the aircraft right wheel well pertaining to the system malfunction.

column121: I was called to assist in an aircraft spill situation on an A300 aircraft. I arrived as the First Responder was finishing up. I initiated the spill form and another AMT (Aircraft Maintenance Technician) documented the spill in the aircraft logbook. The aircraft had been in ZZZ since about midday and the spill was reported by the unload crew. The aircraft arrived with no containers in the aft lower compartment where the spill was located so a determination as to the source of origin for the spill would not be possible. The aircraft had operated [two] previous flight legs. The spill affected all areas of both the LH side and RH side outboard positions 5 through position 6. The responder said the spill was a 'mild' alkali and that he had used gray spill pads to try to absorb and clean up the unknown material. He said that a sample should be sent out to positively identify the substance. I documented this on the spill form which I completed down to the corrective action field. I inquired as to obtaining an [reference number] but there seemed to be a hesitancy to issue one and the spill form seemed to be met with the same response. The responder showed me the reference material that he used and stated that sodium bicarbonate could be used to clean up the unidentified spill. I informed both him and several on site Supervisors that since it had been identified as an alkali; the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) Chapter 5 procedures (as per the GMM) would take precedence for any cleanup actions. It appeared that they wanted to load the aircraft but sometime later; the aircraft was ultimately removed from service. I later spoke briefly to the incoming supervisor prior to my leaving my shift for the day and mentioned the spill form which needed the [reference number] and remaining entries after corrective actions were completed. The following day I pulled the history and saw that the log item had been cleared and noted that there was no deferral for a spill on the aircraft. Since I had initiated the spill form; I was concerned and called Company and asked if they had a copy of the completed form. They controller looked but could not find one. I reached out to the [records department] who had the applicable log page but no attached spill form. I inquired as to whether the form had possibly already been scanned and the log page was there but the spill form was not to be found. I informed my Supervisor of my concerns. I understand the GMM (General Maintenance Manual) procedure directs that once the area has been cleaned and a visual inspection accomplished by the AMT; no further action is required but there is more to that procedure. GMM spill response procedures cover roughly two pages and are fairly specific regarding spills determined to be an alkali; a spill that does not have a known source and the requirement for a deferral for a reinspect of the spill area at a later date. The GMM also provides guidance for the disposition of the aircraft spill form. I went upstairs to my manager's office and asked the questions regarding this procedure with the GMM in hand. The response that I got was that the spill was cleaned up by a [company name] vendor that we pay good money for (cleanup service) and at that point; the aircraft spill form is no longer necessary and that is the end of it as far as I was to be concerned. I mentioned that his answer is not in line with what the GMM says. My ultimate concern is for the aircraft and for the AMT's who signed the logbook if any part of this process was misrepresented to them in the name of getting the aircraft back into service. Hopefully this is not the case. The ZZZ Aircraft Hazardous Material Spill Flow Chart; the GMM and the Aircraft Substance Spill Form are very specific with the responsibilities for spill events such as this. It seems like every spill event in ZZZ is like the first time with decisions being made on the fly.

column121: On Aircraft X we received an ENOTOC (Electronic NOTOC) from Load Control. While we reviewed the ENOTOC   I noticed that there was no UN HAZMAT number and pointed it out to Captain as something I believed was supposed to be on the ENOTOC. Having flown cargo at multiple previous jobs I am very familiar with the HAZMAT paperwork requirements. However; as the ENOTOC is fairly new and the printout is overly confusing to read and decipher Captain contacted Load Control to get further clarification on the matter and to insure that we were in compliance with the procedure and regulations. Load Control assured us that everything was in order and correct for the flight. I do not recall whether we sent to NOTOC acknowledgment before or after we contacted Load Control for clarification. Apparently my initial intuition that something wasn't right with the paperwork was correct and we should have requested new paperwork be sent. Even today I have no idea what HAZMAT was actually on our aircraft. I believe the primary cause of this error is the cumbersome layout of the ENOTOC format to begin with. Every time we receive an ENOTOC it's like trying to decipher a sudoku puzzle. The columns (location; weight; UN number) don't seem to align with what is being listed for the HAZMAT. Even figuring out the location of the HAZMAT requires finding a number on the form and then referring to the bottom of the form for the actual position (at least I think that's what we do because it's a form that is in such disorder that I'm not even sure if I'm looking at a position number or a weight). To compound this ENOTOC issue was the fact that when we inquired with Load Control they assured us that the paperwork was correct and everything was in compliance with procedure. Where the error occurred is unknown; but more awareness from everybody involved could have easily prevented this error.  I [suggest] a reevaluation of the ENOTOC procedure and paperwork is in order. The ACARS printout needs to be simpler and easier to read. If it can't; then we should return to the previous procedure with a hard copy of the NOTOC paperwork.

column121: At ZZZ we were notified by the maintenance technician as part of the maintenance briefing that the autoland system was 'still' deferred and that a part was to be installed when the airplane returned in a few days. We noted that the previous crew had performed an autoland to Cat II standards; and had not written up the airplane with an items. An inspection of the logbook showed multiple issues with the First Officer (FO) raw data glideslope (G/S) indication and other failures over the last few landing cycles. During the flight we received messages from dispatch asking us to perform an autoland in ZZZZ1 to recertify the autoland system as that is how the airplane was deferred; i.e. the aircraft could be recertified by a satisfactory autoland being performed. We thought this strange as the previous crew performed an autoland to cat II standards and did not write anything up. The captain needed a landing for currency anyway; so a few messages were exchanged to that effect with dispatch; which led us to be directed to do an autoland in ZZZZ because the weather at the destination that the airplane would be flying were cat III. We said we would and performed the autoland. On approach we had a no land 3 message on the EICAS and a status message cue. The airplane then indicated the CAT II only on the PFD. We also saw that; as per multiple write ups; the FO's side G/S indication for the raw data portion was not in view. At about 1500 feet above the ground; the FO side glideslope came into view; but the aircraft showed slightly high on glide slope according to the raw data indication (note very slightly high; not out of any parameters; but still a bit unusual for the indication while on autopilot). Atmospheric conditions were VFR and the runway was in sight during the whole approach sequence. At about the time that the FO's raw data for the G/S reappeared; the Captain's side G/S raw data indication disappeared from view; though there was no indication of fault noted on EICAS with either of these issues. We continued the approach and the captain let the airplane land and it landed normally and tracked the centerline normally. The autoland was written up as unsatisfactory due to the loss of both raw data indications during the approach; the FO side data came back; the Captain side never did once it was gone. It appears to me that the autoland system deferral perhaps was not deferred properly as multiple failures over weeks of time suggested a problem with the system; and in the case of our monitoring of the autoland during our flight resulted in the same G/S issues on the FO side as well as a new failure on the Captain side of the raw data indications.

column121: We had been cruising at FL370 for almost an hour. We were with Jacksonville Center on frequency 135.62. At the same time; Jacksonville Center told 'Aircraft Y [we were Aircraft X] to turn 50 degrees right. We were already performing the TCAS RA maneuver as this call came in. Clear of conflict came about 37;700 and we smoothly transitioned back to FL370. Jacksonville pointed out additional traffic above us to our left as we transitioned back to our assigned altitude and cleared us back to direct CAMJO. Jacksonville was told on the radio of us responding to a TCAS RA.  Dispatch was contacted by ACARS to report the event. ATC doing more with less during the pandemic.Controllers should only work a single frequency.

column121: After diverting to ZZZ we arrived at ZZZ1 a few hours late. Upon arriving at the departure gate for our next leg we discovered the flight had already been boarded an hour or so early. The ground service bus was connected and the battery switch and emergency exit lights were off. We discovered there were two open write ups in the book which were a LAV water heater issue and a pack issue. We called maintenance to let them know about the write ups. A little bit later we were told the aircraft was being taken out of service. A replacement aircraft was eventually found. During preflight I called Dispatch to discuss ZZZ2 operations during late night tower closure procedures. About ten minutes later I received a call from Dispatch that the runway lights were NOTAM'ed out that night and we were not going to be able to go. He was; however; going to call ZZZ2 and ask if they could keep the lights on. The  Concourse Manager and the tower came up with a 'plan' to depart and if I couldn't get into ZZZ2; due to no runway lights; to divert to ZZZ3 and they would bus the pax to ZZZ2. This was not a plan I was in favor of to say the least. ZZZ2 equipment maintenance agreed to delay the runway light not/closure till after our arrival; which was approximately XA:30PST. About an hour from arrival we received a GPS 1 and 2 message with an accompanying TERR POS message which was the result of a [name] NOTAM regarding jamming. We discussed the situation of a late night RNAV arrival into mountainous terrain with a tower closure and no GPS and terrain warning. Just prior to descent the GPS returned. Reporter stated the cause of the late departure was maintenance deciding to take the aircraft out of service after it had been on the ground for three hours. Boarding a flight an hour before aircrew showing up and the ground service bus as the only power source. The emergency exit lights were not on as well as the battery. The decision by non pilots to fly to a 'special airport due to terrain' not knowing if the runway lights would be working only to divert to another airport. [name of area] jamming and the loss of GPS and terrain warnings.Operations management needs to change from reactive to proactive.

column121: Aircraft was dispatched with the RT INNER fuel quantity indicating system inop. Per the MEL; the RT INNER fuel tank quantity would have to be verified by an alternate means. Arrived at the aircraft; fueling was complete and the fuel service form had been signed but the alternate verification had not been recorded in the system. Called Maintenance and they said it was in progress and would be signed off shortly. First Officer (FO) confirmed that they were dripping the tank while he was on his pre-flight walk around.Received an ACARS alert that the system had changed; verified the MEL signoff and it confirmed 6;600 pounds in the right inner verified by Magnetic Level Indicator 2.Fuel Service form showed block in fuel of 19.2 lbs. and that 11.0 lbs. of fuel had been added to bring us up to a total 30.2 lbs.Climbing out of ZZZ got RT INNER FUEL tank pump fault. As Pilot Monitoring (PM) complied with ECAM and turned the pump off and consulted the QRH. When I brought the FUEL page back onto the ECAM I noticed the RT OUTER tank was burning and we had a fuel split of 1000 lbs between the RT and LT outer tanks. The working pump in the right inner tank showed a green line which I took to mean fuel pressure from the RT inner tank but the RT outer was burning down.I put the crossfeed valve in line so that LT inner tank was feeding the #2 Engine. Fuel stopped burning from the RT outer tank at that time. After a minute or two closed the crossfeed valve to see if the RT inner tank would now burn. Fuel started burning out of the RT outer again. Put crossfeed back in line to manually manage the fuel burn and to minimize the imbalance between outer tanks.FO and I discussed what we thought was going on. At this point I believed there was no fuel in the RT inner tank. We both agreed that we could not continue on to ZZZ1 and talked of possible diverts. We discussed returning to ZZZ but I believed there was no fuel in the RT outer tank and if that was the case; we already had an almost 7000 lb split between left and right sides.At this point we were about 50 miles to the west ZZZ2 and decided that was our best divert option. FO continued flying and worked with ATC to change destination and begin descending. I tried to contact ZZZ2 Ramp on VHF 2 but got no response. Informed operations via ACARS of a fuel discrepancy and that we were diverting to ZZZ2. He acknowledged and sent us routing and new numbers. Coordinated arrival with ZZZ Center and ZZZ2 Approach and shot a visual approach and landing to RWY XXR ZZZ2. Left inner tank was empty by the time we started the approach and were burning tank to engine on both engines.Once in the chocks we discussed what had happened and ran numbers on how much fuel we should have and how much we actually had. We blocked out with 29.2 and as per the fuel burn indicators had burned just a little over 10;000 lbs. We should have had 19;200 lbs. RT inner tank; inop FQIS; showed 5;900 lbs; but was empty. LT outer showed 7.4 and RT outer showed 6.0 for a total for a total of 13.4.ZZZ2 Maintenance verified fuel on board with MIL sticks. LT outer 7.7; LT inner 0.0; RT inner 0.0; RT outer 6.0 for a total of 13.7.A failure in the system ensuring required fuel is on board when dealing with a Fuel System MEL.
column123: Aircraft assigned had MEL for RT Inner fuel tank quantity indicator inoperative. When we got to aircraft and I began my walk around; I noticed maintenance moving a ladder over to the right wing inboard of the engine. As I got around to pre-flight the right main gear I asked the maintainer if they were checking the fuel quantity and he confirmed they were. This struck me as a bit odd since the system indicated Flight Ready when we were in ops. I finished my pre-flight and when I got to the cockpit I mentioned to the Captain they were checking the tank on pre-flight; but we both agreed there was no record of the check in the maintenance history. He called Maintenance and they said it was in work. We received an ACARS informing us the aircraft status changed to not flight ready. Shortly after we then received a Flight Ready ACARS notification. I then confirmed the fuel added from the previous flight block in and the fuel slip using the APS. The APS; fuel slip and fuel page all were within +/- 200-300 lbs of total quantity. We blocked out and departed on Runway XXR. After getting a turn east and a climb; ECAM indicated a RT Inner tank pump fault. The Captain began handling ECAM and QRH as Pilot Monitoring (PM). As Pilot Flying (PF); I was not head's down much but I did notice we had approximately a thousand pound split between the LT and RT outer tanks. The fuel page also showed the left pump in the RT inner tank still operational with a green line leading to the right engine. The RT inner showed approximately 5.7. The Captain informed me he was going to place the cross feed valve in-line to feed the right engine from left inner tank. When he did that the RT outer tank burn stopped. After a few minutes he closed the cross feed and again the RT outer tank quantity began decreasing after monitoring it for a minute or two. We then paced the valve back inline to manage imbalance. At this point we were leveling off and we began discussing what was taking place in the fuel system. Despite what the fuel system was indicating; we both came to the conclusion that there was no fuel remaining in RT Inner tank. Based on where we were; and the headwind we would have turning around to ZZZ; we elected to inform Center that we needed to land at ZZZ2. As PF; I took over ATC comms and FMS management to get a descent and set up for approach to ZZZ2 while the Captain attempted contacting operations via ACARS to tell them our situation and plan as well as call ZZZ2 Ramp. We descended and landed at ZZZ2 uneventfully. Once we were blocked in we discussed what we blocked out with-29.2 and had burned-10.0 per the fuel consumption gauges for each engine. The aircraft showed we had 19.2 onboard. We discussed this with Maintenance and they did the manual verification of the tanks confirming that the left and right inner tanks were empty and the actual fuel onboard was 13.7.Unsure other than a discrepancy between what amount of fuel was added and what reading was taken to manually verify RT inner tank quantity.I do not know what took place during the fueling / manual verification timeline to offer feedback on how to prevent future occurrences

column121: While checking the fuel slip and comparing it with the previous flight block in fuel; FO (First Officer) discovered a 6;500-lb. discrepancy. We called Maintenance and asked about another fuel ticket. Maintenance advised us that they could not find one but assumed that fuel was added to the aircraft because of an Inner Tank Fuel MEL was worked on and cleared. I asked if they were going to make the appropriate AML write-up and look for paperwork and they advised that they would and would get back with us. After about 15 minutes; we had not heard from them; so we called and was told that they couldn't find the fuel slip but they were going to come out and check our fuel quantity using the magnetic level indicators. I went downstairs to check on the progress and was informed by Maintenance that they had checked the levels but were going to stick the tanks to recheck. I went back to the cockpit and a several minutes later was informed by an AMT that the Right Inner Tank only had around 4;000 lb. of fuel in it versus the 10;500 lb. that was reading on the Fuel Quantity Indicator. Fuel was uplifted; the tank quantity rechecked; and the previous MEL that was cleared was reinstated.The aircraft had the Inner Tank MEL for several flights prior to being worked on. Not sure if part that was replaced failed or what could have happened. Comparing fuel slips with previous flight block-in fuel is a good check; and my FO made a good catch. Maybe this should be a policy for anyone who fuels; de-fuels our aircraft. Additional training of this would be beneficial during ground school and/or tri-annual training.

column121: It was the first flight of the morning and also the first flight of the trip for me. I just met the crew; me and the FO [First Officer] never flew with each other as well as being new. Also; we never had been to this airport before. Everything was normal as far as boarding; we started both engines at the gate because the end of the runway was very close to the ramp. The FO called for taxi and ATC says taxi to Runway 27. While taxing I was telling the FO about the hydraulic procedure and asking him when he turned the hydraulic switches from on to auto. During that brief conversation I passed [Taxiway] A5 and was told by ATC to stop and do a 180 back to [Taxiway] A5. (Which is the beginning of the runway) and given the Tower number. I called them when we landed in ZZZ1 and he said it was common (it happens about once a week) and they will soon be posting that area as a hotspot. The rest of the flight was normal ops.Causal factors: It was the first flight of the morning and it always seems rushed; combined with the new weight and balance and a new crew; it felt like I was trying to catch up. Also; it was a new unfamiliar airport with the runway about 100 yards away; combined with a somewhat vague restricted area on the other side of the field. I believe this was the subtle chain of events along with a brief disruption in my situational awareness that was the direct cause.I believe I should have looked a lot closer (zoomed in) at the airport diagram; and should have briefed the FO exactly where the runway entrance was at [Taxiway] A5 and where the restricted area boundaries were. Also; as I mentioned before; and ATC also told me; they need to revise this chart and put that area as a hotspot because it's so easy to pass if you're not completely focused. Also; I should have waited to ask the FO about the hydraulic procedure till later. Also; as far as the chart goes; not only should this area be a hotspot but it should be magnified in the corner of the chart as well as having a description on the 10-7 pages that covers both sides of the airport where the boundary is.

column121: Please accept this report; as this is the first opportunity I've had to file this report. I FA #1 boarded Aircraft X and when the #2 Flight Attendant boarded the aircraft she mentioned to me if I smelled the oily smell coming from the air vents (gaspers) in the forward galley. I did smell the oily smell coming from the gaspers. She mentioned it to the Captain and he stated that they had just brought the aircraft in from ZZZ and that the Flight Attendants has not mentioned anything. During the initial boarding I the #1 FA mentioned the continued smell to the Pilot. it also smelled like 'dirty socks'. The boarding process eventually was completed; seated and stowed and the final souls on board count was given to the Captain; closure of the Forward 1L door closure was granted by Captain; door was closed; PA was done to arm doors and cross check ; crosschecks were completed by all Flight Attendants; an 'all call' was performed by me #1 FA to ensure all Flight Attendants had armed doors and cross checked; final cabin secure given to Pilot prior to closing cockpit door. Safety demo was performed; and safely checks were completed by all FAs prior to take-off. During the flight I the #1 started to experience a huge headache; felt nauseated; felt like passing out; had a terrible stomach ache and felt dizzy. the other Flight attendants #2; #3; and #4 also complained about having headaches; felling nauseated; feeling dizzy; feeling tingling in fingers; and having upset stomach. All of us did not feel right; and felt ill. I called the Captain with our concerns and told him I would call him with an update. I called him again and he said to for each of us to fill out a report which we did; and he collected all of them. I eventually called him back and told him we needed to have the paramedics meet the plane upon landing at ZZZZ1 and that all the Flight Attendants #1;#2;#3;#4 need to go to the hospital. Once on the ground the paramedics met the plane but stated that all four of us could not be transported in the only ambulance that showed up to take us to the hospital after telling us all to get into the ambulance. we had to get out and go back up the stairs from the ramp and back into the terminal and wait on the logistics to be figured out on how they were going to transport us to the hospital.  I had reported that 'All' four Flight Attendants need to go to the hospital. That lack of preparation on the ground to transport us to the hospital became quiet the debacle; and took a long while.  Once back inside the terminal we contacted medical company to report our illnesses. The paramedics left then had to be called back to come get us; I was told that they were on another call and that they would come back. Eventually they did; they took some basic vital signs; were missing some medical equipment (CO2 monitor)and worked with the ground personnel to figure out how to get us to the hospital. after at least of over 2 hours after landing In ZZZZ1 they finally took us to Hospital X in City which is 45 minutes from the airport to be seen in and Emergency Department. We were  never given oxygen as a basic  medical resource after complaining of possibly being in a 'Fume  Event' by the paramedics. At the Hospital X we were given  [medical treatment]. No blood work was ever done; again; oxygen was never administered to any of the Flight Attendants. I had an X-ray done because I was complaining about my lungs hurting. The x-ray report came back normal; after being read by a regular doctor; but a specialist said after he reviewed it that I  had fluid in my right lung. We finally were released from the emergency room after they secured payment by Air Carrier name ; as they told us we could not leave until the bill was paid. I had to use my own credit card to pay for  all the Flight Attendant prescriptions; as the pharmacy  was off site. We were transported back to the hotel and checked in for our overnight. We were grounded by medical. We were given  instructions to go to another hospital the next day which was in their network Hospital Y. We complied with this request and we received IV therapy; were given prescriptions; and blood work was done which showed a lot of our levels out of normal range. We remained at the hotel for 5 days under the care of Medical until we were released to fly to our home base of ZZZ2. Once back in the United States we were contacted by Company; [Air Carrier] employee medical provider and were told to go to a US hospital to get checked out and have test done.  I was seen at Trauma Center in City where I reside with the approval of Company.  My final diagnosis was- lung injury. I am still taking prescriptions; and I am still on my inhaler. I continue to experience pain in my lungs and I am still under the care of Company. I want to be contacted by the FAA about this report. - [F/A Name; Employee No.]
column123: Please accept this report; as this is the first opportunity I've had  to file this report.  As soon as I stepped onto the aircraft; I noticed a dirty sock smell- an oil smell. It was strong to me. I mentioned this to the #1 and #3. I then stepped into the cockpit to introduce myself. After a few cordial words; I asked 'Do you guys smell that?' The Captain said 'What?'- I said 'it's like an oil; fume or dirty sock smell'. The Captain said 'no; we just brought this aircraft in from ZZZ and had no problems; and the other crew (other flight attendants); never mentioned anything'. I went back to the back galley where I was working. We started boarding; and then departed. I did walk back up to the front during boarding and the smell CLEARLY a dirty sock smell; which we all know only comes from oil; was still lingering.  Approximately an hour and twenty minutes into the flight; (maybe and hour and thirty) the number 1 came back to the back galley where the rest of us flight attendants were sitting. I said to all of them 'Hey; I just want you all to know I have a mad headache and I don't feel right and I know it's from that smell I smelled before boarding'. Each flight attendant then shared that they too had headaches; and the number #3 said his fingers were tingling; the #4 said she felt dizzy and had vertigo; and the #1 said he felt like he was going to pass out; was nauseous; and had a bad stomach ache. The #1 called the Captain; and he went through the cabin fume event checklist. He asked each of us several questions. We had a few different conversations with the Captain and the #1 had called the Captain several times. At one point in my conversation with the Captain he said something about why we didn't say anything; and I said 'wait a minute- I did say something and you told me you brought this aircraft in from ZZZ and there was no problems and the other flight attendants never mentioned anything'. The Captain replied; 'Yes; you did; I dropped the ball'. As the flight progressed to ZZZZ1; the cabin crew felt worse. The Captain was informed that we wanted the paramedics to meet the flight AND that we ALL needed to go to the hospital. We landed in ZZZZ1; deplaned the passengers and walked up the jetway; we had to wait about 5 minutes for the paramedics. We immediately called Medical to inform them of our situation and our symptoms. Medical wanted to go into grave detail about our information and the crew was getting more and more anxious and feeling worse. One of us finally said 'Please; can you just get us on the way to the hospital and we can call you on the ride to give this information?'  We all sat in wheelchairs. The medics took our blood pressures; however; were lacking in any other medical equipment. They used my SPO2 monitor to complete our initial vitals. Never were we placed on O2.  The lack of ground logistics for the transportation to take us all to the hospital was a huge fiasco. We sat for over two hours before getting transportation that took ONE HOUR to get to the hospital. We had repeatedly stated we wanted to go to the hospital and the delay of care was unacceptable. At one point we were all brought down the stairs to the bottom of the aircraft where an ambulance was waiting. We all got in the ambulance; and then about 20 minutes later were told to get out as the paramedics would not take all 4 of us. Back up into the airport we went. Not to mention that it was about 90 degrees outside and we were in full uniform. I then began to feel like I was going to pass out. We were placed back in the wheelchairs. Finally a van was procured for our transportation to The Hospital X. This took over an hour. Name was an agent for Air Carrier in ZZZZ1 and went with us to the hospital. She was extremely helpful. We arrived at the hospital and eventually were all placed in separate rooms; examined; were given IV medication and then prescriptions to go back to the hotel with. NO X-RAYS; EKG's or other tests were taken at this hospital. Not one of us were given oxygen therapy. No blood work was taken. We were cleared to leave after about 4 hours HOWEVER we were not allowed to leave because the hospital had not received any payment! It took several phone calls with Medical; and the company to get the bill paid. This part is unclear as most was spoken in  [local language]; but from what I gathered; Name (our liaison) was given a credit card to pay the bill. Furthermore our #1 took ALL of our prescriptions across the street and paid for them out of his pocket!!! After another hour long drive back to the hotel; the crew checked in; changed clothes and barely made it down to the restaurant to eat before it closed for the night. The next morning Medical called to check in on us and determined we all needed to be checked out again. This was after Medical questioned WHY we went to THAT hospital last night. I've never been to this Destination before and it's not like any of us picked a hospital. Medical set it up for us. Well Friday morning; Medical said that wasn't the hospital they are affiliated with and we need to go to Hospital Y. This was about XA:00 am local time. It was XD:00 local when we got into a van to take us to the hospital. This was another huge fiasco; there should be measures in place to easily get medical attention when needed! The company (daily Ops) had told the #1 to take an ride hailing service!!!! He informed the person on the phone of the dangers of ZZZZ1; and that you do not take a ride hailing service as kidnapping is a serious threat. But I digress. We finally arrived at the second hospital an hour later and there we proceeded to get another IV placement with medication for our individual symptoms; X-rays; blood work; & EKG's. We were also given different prescriptions to take with us. This time it was all covered and the scripts were filled right then and there. We were not medically cleared to fly out of ZZZZ1 until Date. We landed in ZZZ2 and were met by each of our supervisors. We talked with them for awhile. We each eventually went on our way home. I then called Company because I wanted to get checked out in [domicile]. Finally on [following day] I was contacted and was given instructions to go to the hospital as now my symptoms included a chest tightness; a continued head ache and just a feeling of being 'off'. I went to General Hospital Z on Date & Time I gave the doctor there my union provided card that explains aircraft fume event procedures and what I was exposed to. My doctor at the ED decided he wanted to contact his colleague who was an infectious disease specialist.  I was given IV medication; a 12 lead EKG; chest X-rays; oxygen therapy for 1 hour; and several vials of blood work; some of which were repeated after an hour. The doctor determined that the symptoms I was having were in line with inhaling a toxin. He advised me to follow up with my primary care doctor; to get plenty of rest and to take it easy. As I am writing this report; my head aches are managed by Motrin; I still have a chest heaviness and feel my heart racing at times and have had two episodes of feeling like I am going to pass out. I have finished the prescription medication I was prescribed. I am worried about the long term repercussions of this fume event. I am also worried about losing time and pay away from work. I want to be contacted by the FAA about this incident.

column121: This was the first time flying into RIC for both crew members. Captain was PF and FO was PM. Crew planned to fly the SPIDR 4 RNAV Arrival and to connect to the RNAV (RNP) Y Runway 16 (RIC was landing Runways 16 and 20). Crew requested and was approved by Potomac Approach to fly the RNAV (RNP) Y to Runway 16 from DEEER (Potomac directed crossing DEEER at 4;000 feet MSL). We received the approach clearance around REDNG. FMC had given ALERT MESSAGES all flight long there was a steep descent after HEMME waypoint (280 KIAS/11;000 feet - 12;000 feet crossing restriction). FMC was correctly programmed. After passing HEMME; the aircraft began to deviate from the RNAV path by getting high. It became very clear; pilots had to intervene substantially in order to correct the aircraft back onto the VNAV PATH to successfully fly the RNAV (RNP) Y Runway 16 Approach. PF used maximum inflight speedbrake; elected not to use extending flaps. Aircraft airspeed was restricted to 250 KIAS or less as aircraft was transitioning to below 10;000 feet MSL. The only technique to slow the aircraft and attempt to re-establish the RNAV vertical path was to extend the landing gear about 30 miles from the field. Crew was able to correct aircraft back to RNAV path and complete the approach + landing. If this was another crew with little or no experience flying this RNAV Arrival to RNAV (RNP) Approach into RIC with actual weather; there is a high probability they would not successfully complete the approach and landing (would have to go missed approach; other altitude/speed deviations and/or compromise safety).

I believe the cause of this was; the autobrake selector in the MAX is in a different position than the NexGen aircraft; specifically in the center console rather than next to the landing gear selector lever. When we accomplished the Before Start Checklist; of course one of the items is 'AUTOBRAKE' with a response of 'RTO'. I responded with the appropriate call of 'RTO' purely by rote memory without actually looking at the autobrake selector. I recall looking towards the landing gear lever where I expected to see the autobrake selector and for some reason was convinced I saw it and it was set properly to RTO. We taxied out and departed uneventfully. It was only upon accomplishing the clean-up items after flap retraction that we noticed the autobrake selector was in the off position. The rest of the flight continued uneventfully.

I also think that supervisors should make an announcement in the department shortly after a new shift starts to let them know of the issue. Multiple screen printer messages I think would also help. column121: At start of shift; we were informed that NOTAMs had not been available since approximately XA:00z due to damage to the FAA servers.  Several messages sent by [the] domestic manager to get NOTAMs by calling Airport Operations at our airports to obtain NOTAM information.  However; this wouldn't work with many international airports due to language barrier (later resolved when international NOTAM access was restored;) and even with domestic airports; the information is only good until the phone call would be terminated because without new NOTAMs coming in; we would have no way of knowing if a new NOTAM was added later.  Additionally; Center; FIR and FDC NOTAMs were not being updated either; so that information also not available as required by FAR and FOM.Consequently; I elected not to release any of my flights until the NOTAM system came back up.  I attempted to have the flights all prepped so they could be sent immediately when the NOTAM system started coming back; but I fell behind even doing that; and all 13 flights on my desk released late and took the associated delays.  Contributing to the late releases were thunderstorms approaching ZZZ during the inbound and having to focus my attention on those rather than getting flight plans prepped.  My purpose with this report is to both self-disclose the fact that I sent releases later than specified by the manual but also to raise concerns about management's solution to 'mitigate' the NOTAM issue.  The manual is clear about our requirement to check ALL NOTAMs; and merely calling airport operations does not ensure that all NOTAMs are received.  Some NOTAMS; like runway closures; taxiway closures; approach light outages; etc; may come from Airport Operations; but others may be issued by the FAA NOTAM office (FDC NOTAMs;) others are issued by the ATC centers.  It's simply unrealistic and imposes too much of a workload on both international and domestic dispatchers to be expected to call dozens of airports (9 alone on one of my ETOPS flights;) along with multiple centers to try and get NOTAM information while also dealing with thunderstorms and all of our other flight following duties.It seemed very much that the overriding concern was getting releases out regardless of whether it was legal or prudent to do so. Apparently; the FAA puts the NOTAM servers on the top floor of one of their building.  When thunderstorms moved through; the roof leaked and allowed water to soak all of the servers. Better server placement by the FAA would be a good start along with a robust backup system in a completely different location along with the necessary programming and bandwidth so that failing over to the backup system is a near-instant process rather than requiring hours.

column121: On left base for visual Runway (RWY) XX; slowing to full configuration and turning final; flaps were extended to 45 degrees while flight spoilers where deployed at 1;500 feet. Speed trend vector was decreasing although thrust setting was at expected thrust setting for approach. Captain called for increased power and crew realized that the flight spoilers were not fully retracted while turning final. The aircraft speed was approx. 150 knots which was below the SOP maneuvering speed of ref + 17 knots with spoilers deployed. At this time the stick shaker activated for approx. 2 seconds and the angle of attack was lowered. The flight spoilers were immediately retracted and the stick shaker stopped. Continued to join the localizer and were on a stabilized approach by 1;000 feet and landed without any incident.While slowing to configure for final approach; Pilot Flying (PF) believed the flight spoilers were fully retracted and called for flaps 8 and 20 at 200 knots. Then the call for gear down and flaps 30 at 180 knots. PF was approaching the localizer course; called flaps 45 at 160 knots. To reduce automation workload the autopilot was disconnected and was preparing to make a left turn to intercept the localizer and glide slope. The stick shaker activated at this time because the flight computer detected a pending stall with the flight spoilers deployed. Immediately after the flight spoilers were fully retracted; the stick shaker stopped and the aircraft was on speed with flaps at 45 degrees. A left turn was made intercepting the localizer and the aircraft was on a stable approach by 1;000 feet.ATC gave direct to the final approach fix for the visual to RWY XX while still descending out of 6;000 and needing to slow to configure for landing. PF could have anticipated needing more distance to reduce airspeed; possibly without flight spoilers; and fully configure the aircraft by 3 miles of the final approach fix by descending sooner and leveling off earlier. This would have reduced pilot workload and automation management allowing for a more thorough scan of the aircraft and its systems before deploying flaps and slowing to final approach speed.

I felt that was the safer course of action. First Officer agreed. We landed. I had instructed the flight attendants to inform me if the conditions worsened otherwise we would taxi to a gate. [Airport response] services followed us to the gate and inspected the interior with an infrared camera and didn't find any sources of heat. Due to no airflow onboard and the temperature rising in the cabin we deplaned. All passengers were grateful for a safe return.As a crew we worked together; kept each other calm and controlled. column121: Arrived at aircraft. I reviewed the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) to verify what I had already reviewed on my IPAD. I told the technician that I did not put the discrepancy in the AML; and if he wanted me to; I would get the AML from the other maintenance technicians and make an appropriate entry. He said; it's okay. We then pressed on with the other issues. I never made a HYD B low" entry into the AML. I made an AML entry and called Maintenance Control regarding the issue. I then left the aircraft and debriefed the oncoming Captain on all of the above issues. I later called the oncoming Captain and was told that during trouble shooting in ZZZ1; a hydraulic leak was discovered in one of the wings.With the many MEL's and the newly discovered maintenance issues; I failed to make an AML entry regarding the low system B hydraulic quantity prior to having it serviced. I also allowed it to be serviced without an AML entry.Suggestions: Maintenance could clear MEL's on overnights and service low fluid quantities. They could also investigate low fluid quantities that are out of the ordinary."

column121: Upon landing; we were advised by Ramp control that our gate was occupied and to have Ground Control hold us off of the gate.  Ground Control cleared us to taxi north on [taxiway] 1 from 2; make a u-turn in the pad; and then hold short of 3 on 4.  We did so and were the third aircraft in line.  A B737 was first and an E-175 was second.  After a while; the E-175 was cleared to his gate and made a hard right to get out of line and proceeded to his gate.  Because the Captain was on the radio with Operations and I was on the radio with Ramp Control; we did not immediately move away to close the gap left by the departing E-175.  Upon completion of our radio calls; the Captain dropped the parking brake and began slowly moving forward to close the gap between us and the B737 that was now the first aircraft in line.  I noticed Aircraft Y coming from my right at a higher than normal rate of speed but was initially convinced that he was cutting through the pad and would be turning south on taxiway 5 to form a second line of aircraft holding short of 3.Both the Captain and I realized at the same time that the Captain of Aircraft Y was trying to squeeze between us and the B737 ahead. The Captain hit the brakes hard enough to make the aircraft stutter to a stop. Had we not noticed Aircraft Y and the Captain of my aircraft not hit the brakes; it is possible that the left wingtip of Aircraft Y that was rapidly cutting in line might have come across our flight deck window.  We were both stunned.  No clearance had been given for that aircraft to squeeze between us and the aircraft ahead of us.  No heads up had been given on either the Ground Control frequency or the ramp frequency to alert us that he was going to try and squeeze in ahead of us.  In my over 20 years of flying for an airline; I have never before seen such a reckless move and it is the closest I have ever come to an aircraft accident. I have thought about this for the past 22 hours and cannot for the life of me think of anything that would cause a pilot to think that taxiing in this manner was safe; a good idea; or in the best interest of anything I know about the safe operation of an aircraft and the protection of the passengers in one's care. I cannot speak for the mindset of the Captain in Aircraft Y.  I cannot think of anything that would cause me to operate an aircraft in this manner and therefore have no idea what to suggest.
column123: Our gate was occupied; so we were instructed to get in line on the taxiway behind a company aircraft. During this time; the line began to move and I taxied forward. Another company Aircraft Y approached at a fairly high taxi speed and cut in front of us. I was able to stop in time after realizing where they were planning to go. If I had not seen them; their wing would of hit the front of our aircraft. We had switched off ground frequency to get an update on our gate. I returned to the frequency and asked what that was. I believe Aircraft Y answered that there was no room at the end of the line (the reason for cutting in front of us). Later; I asked the Ground Controller  what their flight number was; and I was told 'Snitches get stitches'.  I asked the Controller if I heard them right and Controller responded that it was a joke. I responded that I didn't think it was funny; I took it as a threat; and asked for the Tower phone number. I believe Aircraft Y taxied in front of us not knowing with certainty that we would see them. They did something that could of potentially damaged aircraft or injured persons. I can't speak for the crew of flight Aircraft Y or why they thought that was good practice and safe to do.  As far as my crew; I don't believe there was anything we could of done to change the outcome.  As far as the Ground Controller; I believe by what Controller said; Controller saw what had happened and didn't intervene. This created the possibility of two aircraft colliding on the ground. Instead; I believe; Controller thought the best course of action was to make a joke out of the situation.

column121: First Officer's landing. After touchdown and roll out to the end; we were issued taxi instructions while still on the runway and during transfer of control from FO to Captain for taxi. I heard taxi Alpha to the gate which I read back. As we turned across the hard stand for gate X from Alpha the controller informed us we had been instructed to taxi Alpha Fox. [The cause was] Task saturation. Controllers should not issue taxi instructions until clear of runway. Busy airports should have a standard and understood initial taxi route so that you have time to clear the runway and listen to further instructions. Maybe they could be depicted on the approach plate or in the airport diagram or the controller could issue with landing clearance.
column123: On the landing roll out while we were transferring controls we were issued a taxi clearance to gate X. The Captain still had the radios as we were decelerating through about 80 knots. He responded to the radio call and I can clearly remember him saying taxi to the gate via Alpha. There was no correction from ATC so we taxied to the gate. As we crossed the ramp area the Controller advised us the instructions were Alpha Echo Foxtrot. We apologize and proceeded to the gate with no further issues.The inability to hear the controllers instructions clearly at a busy time in the landing roll out combined with the lack of correction by ATC when our read back was incorrect. In the future I will restate the instructions from ATC once I have the radios on the ground after the roll out is complete. I will also plan not to respond the ATC during task saturation like this.
