column121: On arrival at ZZZ; winds were variable and began to favor Runway XX for landing. We were set up for landing on Runway XY. I; acting as Pilot Monitoring for this leg due to special qualification airport; suggested to Captain that we swap our planned arrival runway due to winds and additional available landing distance (approximately 500 feet) for landing on Runway XX. The FMC was reprogrammed correctly; briefed; and we accepted a heading to intercept final Runway XX. With approximately a 30 degree intercept; approach control cleared us for the ILS XX. Captain selected approach mode early. This caused the aircraft to capture a false glideslope and the aircraft began a descent prior to capturing the localizer. I called this to the Captain's attention; of which he was also aware.Prior to localizer capture I recommended a discontinued approach. Altitude was well above Minimum Safe Altitude and the approach was salvageable but due to my experience level in the jet; I suggested a soft go-around. The Captain elected to continue; to which I agreed and remarked that our subsequent protected altitude would be 2;600 feet; which we were currently above; and that I would monitor. The Captain; slightly flustered about the false glideslope capture began to fiddle with Auto Pilot disconnect; Flight Director reset; and approach mode was re-armed. The new capture mode now is LOC but with a failed Glideslope. The aircraft has defaulted into the current vertical speed. I call slightly below glideslope; Captain again resets Auto pilot; Flight Director; and re-arms the approach mode. Localizer captures; Glideslope has been armed; and we are currently in a 700 to 800 FPM descent; very slightly low on Glideslope; at a safe speed; and safe altitude.I call attention to our protected Final Approach Fix altitude and glideslope intercept at ZZZZZ 2238 feet. If I remember correctly; we were approximately 3 miles from ZZZZZ when I remarked that at our current Flight Path Angle would have us slightly below our target altitude without any correction at ZZZZZ. Let me be clear; the aircraft was; based on our current descent rate; projected to be only slightly below 2;300 feet at the Final Approach Fix. A minor correction would have rectified the approach path angle and captured the glideslope. I called our altitude to the Captains attention once more approximately 1 to 2 miles prior to ZZZZZ; where we had now reached 2;300 feet; the charted approach value. Right as I was going to call for the Go Around at ZZZZZ; the tower controller issued a Low Altitude Alert; the Go Around was called and initiated; and the aircraft was at approximately 2;100 feet; a little less than 200 feet low at the charted glideslope intercept altitude; as well as above 1;000 feet above ground.The Go-Around was accomplished without error and a subsequent ILS was flown to Runway XX without any additional complications. Upon debrief; I became aware that the Captain was unaware that he had not captured the Glideslope. I re-framed the situation for us to consider alternate action and explained my reasoning for a requested discontinued approach prior to localizer capture. I am still low time and in consolidation. I had no reason to expect that we could not become stable with glideslope capture prior to Final Approach Fix. Hindsight is exactly that and this event began and ended all within 4 miles. The Go-round was completed to qual standards with safety and stable approach criteria in mind.False glideslopes capture prior to localizer capture due to not allowing the aircraft to capture in LOC or LNAV prior to arming the approach mode. Again; I believe I was very clear about our impending altitude deviation; however I don't believe I heard any response from the Captain from 3 miles(my initial call) and 1 to 2 miles(my second que). I could be wrong. The whole event spanned a time frame of less than 3 minutes from 'looks good' to 'doesn't look so good' so I could NOT have fit many more altitude callouts in that span. Due to my low experience in the jet; I incorrectly expected a correction that I did not receive. The go around was initiated at or just seconds after the Final Approach Fix. An assumption of understanding is not the greatest way to handle approaching a go around. I do not believe I was hinting and hoping but I will be more aggressive with my descent planning awareness callouts so as not to enter into a [undesirable situation] in the future. However; the correct decision was made concerning the safe operation of the aircraft and the proper response was executed.
column123: Trip was third leg of the day.  Landed from second leg at around XA:40 local and got to sleep room at XB:10L.  Awakened 30 early of show time at approximately XB:40L.  Weather was marginal regionally and at ZZZ. ZZZ1 was filed alternate but also monitored weather at ZZZ2 for second option.  First Officer has less than 75 hours and ZZZ is Special Qual field. Identified the CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) hazard; short runway; marginal weather; etc.  Pre briefed the ILS XY enroute as winds were favoring that runway.  Also talked about EFVS (Enhanced Flight Vision Systems) and auto land contingencies.  Upon contacting ZZZ approach; they asked if we wanted ILS XX due to a wind shift.  Initially decided to stick with XY but reversed the decision seconds later due to shorter usable runway on XY due to displaced threshold and winds favoring XX slightly.I was flying the approach while the First Officer set up and briefed the ILS XX.  We re-accomplished the approach checklist and accepted a clearance direct to the Final Approach Fix to cross at 2;600 feet and maintain until established; cleared for the ILS.  We put the 2;600 foot hard restriction at the Final Approach Fix and were navigating LNAV/VNAV.  Just prior to Final Approach Fix I mistakenly selected the approach mode.  The aircraft immediately intercepted what I believe was a false glide slope and begun to descend before intended.  I turned off both flight directors and attempted to get the aircraft out of approach mode. The aircraft stayed in approach mode because I did not disengage the autopilot.  So; after re-engaging the aircraft tracked the localizer in LOC mode and Vertical Speed with Glideslope Flight Mode Annunciation struck through as a failed mode.  Realizing the error; I disconnected both flight directors and autopilot and immediately re-engaged and re-automated.  At this point I believe the aircraft momentarily intercepted a glide path; and almost immediately and simultaneously with the Tower Controller realized we were about 250 feet low of the glide slope intercept altitude.  We immediately performed a discontinued approach and climbed to 3;000 feet.  We received vectors for another ILS XX and auto landed uneventfully.Fatigue was undeniably a root cause although not the only issue here.  Flying two legs and then getting only 30 minutes opportunity to nap between legs was just a little too much for me despite 'feeling pretty good' ahead of the flight involved. In retrospect I should have used LNAV/VNAV to get solidly on the ILS final before selecting approach mode.  And; also; I should have and will in the future decide to discontinue an approach as soon as any serious mode switching starts happening on the final approach. In the light of day and after a nap I know this solidly; but it is much more difficult with a foggy brain at XF:00.  So; in the future; I'm going to use LNAV/VNAV more and not use APP until later in the approach. Revision of the flight pairing to allow for more rest time...even an hour nap; would help.  Also; making sure to use LNAV/VNAV and protect GSIA (Glide Slope Intercept Altitude) at 1 NM prior to the intermediate fix.

column121: After seeing my flight was delayed; I called Maintenance Control and they said they weren't able to service the hydraulic system I had written up the night before. The local maintenance didn't have the correct parts or fluid. The technician told me they were flying out the parts; fluid; and mechanics from ZZZ. I asked if hydraulic fluid was allowed to fly and they said it was fine. After the aircraft arrived and the mechanics finished servicing the aircraft; I arrived and began my preflight duties. The mechanics said they had one sealed can of hydraulic fluid and the pump tool they used to service the system. I called the on Duty Pilot and he told me it was fine as long as it was sealed and the partially used can was being left. This didn't sit right with me so I tried to find information about it in the manual. Hydraulic fluid wasn't listed but there also wasn't a phone number for the company HAZMAT specialist. I escalated the issue to the Union and they were able to find a reference in the Dangerous Goods Manual (DGM) appendix about hidden hazards. I also googled the hydraulic fluid (Mobile HyJet IV-Aplus) and found the safety data sheet listed the fluid as a Class 9 Dangerous Good. After leaving a voicemail with the Duty Pilot saying I was going to deny boarding to the fluid and equipment; the duty manager called me and asked why I was going to leave the items and that it was going to cost a lot of money to get it back to ZZZ. I referenced the DGM and they said I was good to depart.This [Hazmat violation] was either caused by ignorance of our DG policies or was negligent behavior on the part of operations. I've been told before from them that hydraulic fluid is Hazmat. They once drove 3-4 hours to another airport because of this same issue. Either way; this was a significant safety violation. A comprehensive review of DG policies and the quality of training need to happen. Either they actually didn't know or they disregarded safety policy for the sake of operational convenience. Either is scary in a 121 airline.

column121: The flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 was the third leg of our day. We had landed at XA00Z which was an hour advance of planned passenger's arrival. Our passengers soon notified us of late arrival upon which I checked to ensure we would not be affected by EDCT (Estimated Departure Time Clearance) and that weather wouldn't be a factor. I then obtained our flight clearance which included a full route meaning we weren't getting our shorter overwater route. That route would also avoid any of the approaching weather by a wide margin. I re-ran our flight plan to ensure we had adequate fuel as the new one was 110 NM longer and would slightly change winds. The original route required 3;570 lbs total including enroute burn; 45 min reserve; and alternate based on cruise altitude of FL400. No alternate was required though as destination weather was > 5000/5 for the entire day and projected to remain so. Still; we plan and carry alternate fuel anytime we have the ability to do so. I had rounded the final fuel load up to 4;000 lbs total as it's all too common flying in or out of ZZZ3 airspace and suddenly getting significantly different routing or held down below cruise altitude for a bit. That decision would prove critical in preventing a divert later in flight. We boarded passengers at XB30Z and were given taxi clearance to 30. Upon nearing the runway; we were told to taxi to the holding area and would start taxi again at XB50Z for a XB54Z release. Approaching XC00Z; we were cleared to taxi and then into position and hold where we sat for approximately 3 minutes before being cleared for takeoff. Shortly after checking in with departure; we were given a 250 kt speed restriction and then given multiple vectors 90 degrees off of route. During most of this we were held below 15;000 ft. After being cleared back onto our flight plan; we were step climbed 6 times until we reached FL 330 about 30 minutes into the flight. During this time we also had to request deviations for weather. A slight left deviation would've allowed us to safely clear all the weather even at the lower altitude; but all aircraft were being directed that right was the only choice. Based on what traffic we had directly in view and on TCAS; it didn't make sense as it looked clear with all possible conflicts being to the west. We attempted to work right but even with significant deviations directly westward we were going to be boxed in by cells. Both NEXRAD and our onboard radar indicated yellow to red echoes well above our current altitude. We and other aircraft at higher altitudes continued to request eastward deviations and were denied. We also repeatedly requested higher as that would've been a satisfactory way of being able to comply with what they needed; but again were denied. At this point; I told the ZZZ3 Center controller that we had no choice but to go left as there was no place we could safely penetrate the weather. They finally relented and after a short deviation that was within 2-3 NM east of the course line; we were around it and back on flight plan. I was prepared to declare pilot authority to deviate for safety of aircraft; passengers and crew had they not. Between the additional ground time; ATC vectors; deviations; and hold down; we had eaten significantly into the additional fuel and were showing below a 45 min reserve if we remained at the lower altitude. This was even after seeing the deteriorating fuel state early and slowing down significantly from cruise speed to M.65. After again requesting further climb and being denied; I declared minimum fuel. Instead of the controller acknowledging; we were shifted to the next controller. Upon checking in; we were still held down and told to expect some time before climb. I again interjected on the radio that we were minimum fuel which was acknowledged by the new controller by him stating; 'uh..ah...well; ok.' He then stated we wouldn't get any further climb until with ZZZ4 Center. By that time we would be over State andstill at FL330 just over an hour into flight. The PM and I evaluated the fuel state and knowing the potential ATC delays we could face in ZZZ1 area airspace despite the great weather that we may be facing a divert. I kept our home base of ZZZ5 and ZZZ6 in mind should that be required. We set 1;000 lbs as an acceptable; safe fuel state needed to both put us above minimum fuel and give us some additional in the event of further delays. After ensuring ZZZ4 Center knew of our fuel state; we were held down for nearly another 10 minutes and then stepped 4 times from FL330 to FL400. After reaching FL400; we pulled back to M.67 and finally saw 1;100 lbs overhead destination and decided to continue. I considered requesting FL430; but based on less tailwind and the increased burn to climb I decided it wouldn't be beneficial. Fuel state improved to 1;280 lbs as the winds shifted and thanks to a small shortcut by Center. During decent with ZZZ4 Center; we were turned roughly 120 degrees off the arrival and it wasn't until questioning the controller if he knew that we had declared that he stated no and turned us back towards ZZZ1. Even though I had never rescinded the previous declaration; it apparently had not been passed to some of the subsequent ATC sectors. I told the controller that we were currently above min fuel but would not continue to be with continued vectors away from destination. We were shortly passed off to the approach controller and landed uneventfully from the RNAV XX. Final fuel state at shutdown was 1;145 lbs.Our passengers being on time might have alleviated some of this as weather had not moved onto our route at that time. More fuel would've have also created more pad; but the additional alternate fuel that wasn't required by regulation or the situation plus additional contingency fuel should've been more than sufficient to prevent it. Getting held down well below planned cruise altitude until almost halfway through a 2.5hr flight is pretty uncommon but played the biggest role in this.

column121: After departing we were flying the ZZZZZ departure.  At around ZZZZZ1 intersection on the departure; at approximately 18;000 feet; the Captain (Pilot Flying) called the transition; followed by ATC giving us a frequency change. As I (Pilot Monitoring) looked down on the aisle stand to change the radio frequency; I heard the Captain say something while there was a sharp right rolling movement of the aircraft.  I looked up and saw a red AUTOPILOT disconnect EICAS message; and the Captain with his hands on the control wheel.  I had assumed that we had experienced wind shear; being in the terrain that we were located.  After the Captain appeared to have the situation under control; I asked the Captain if he wanted me to report the incident; to which he replied yes.  I reported to the controller that we had hit a strong gust on departure; which he acknowledged.  The Captain then said something along the lines of did you see that?  We almost hit a glider.  He had disconnected the autopilot and rolled the aircraft to avoid the glider.I believe I said; is that what happened; to which he said yes.  I can't remember my verbiage; but I believe I then reported to ATC that we had almost hit a glider. ATC acknowledged; and then passed along to the aircraft behind us the information.  At no point did we receive any type of TCAS alert; nor any warning from ATC about a target in the vicinity.  After that last transmission to ATC during which the incident happened; we switched frequencies and continued on with the flight uneventfully.  Later when we were over the ZZZ track; we spoke to the aircraft behind us but they said they had not seen the glider.  Looking back with hindsight; I should have reported the incident to the controller by saying; 'I wish to report a near-midair collision.'  I cannot say enough about Captain's quick thinking and airmanship to bank away from that glider and avoid what would have potentially been an air disaster.
column123: During climbout from ZZZ on the ZZZZZ departure at an altitude of about 17;500 feet we encountered a glider. The Pilot Flying turned off the autopilot and banked right to avoid a possible collision. This event occurred just as we were given a frequency change to Departure Control. At no time during this event was there any traffic depicted on the TCAS nor was there any traffic alerts given by ATC. The Pilot Monitoring passed this information to the controller before switching to our new frequency.

column121: Departing Munich; we were given a push clearance that said; after the crossing Medium Transport aircraft; cleared to push to face north. This was relayed to the push-crew and acknowledged. Push commenced shortly thereafter. We couldn't see; but assumed the Medium Transport passed. A brief time later; Apron control asked us to stop our push; which was relayed to me and the me to the push-crew (there was the lift tug driver and another person on the headphones). I allowed a reasonable amount of time to transfer the stop; but they kept on pushing. I asked them again to STOP the push. The person on the headset seemed confused. I again told them to stop the push; stop the push. The push slowed but never stopped and then began to pick up pace. I then with louder; more stern voice told them to STOP; HALT THE PUSH; figuring the German stop command might do the trick. Nope; the push just continued. After we came to a stop on the start spot; I asked him if he understood what STOP meant - he was flustered. I overheard the FO talking to apron trying to convince them that we had told the push crew to stop multiple times. They mentioned it was a reportable event; hence the filing. This is very rare for Munich or any German airport. I am convinced; this was purely a language issue and the gentleman on the headset did not understand the bigger picture. The tug driver was also dependent on what he told him and I don't think he was aware of what was going on either.
column123: Upon receiving our push clearance Ramp control instructed us to wait for an aircraft to taxi by; then push.  This was relayed to the push-crew; and they immediately began to push.  Ramp control instructed us to stop; as the aircraft we were supposed to wait for had not yet passed by.  The Captain instructed the push-crew to stop and had to tell them several times; before they would stop.  When they did stop; they just paused and began to push again.  This happened; I recall about 3 times; and ramp control kept instructing us to stop; but we could not get the push-crew to do so. The push-crew eventually just pushed us all the way back; contrary to our instructions to 'halt.'  No explanation was given; as to why they would not stop. column121: Departed ZZZ 4L in windy gusty conditions with a normal takeoff. Passing approximately 500 feet; a Rudder Ratio EICAS caution message appeared. I followed the QRH procedure after doing the 'after takeoff' checklist. This procedure stated: Above 160 knots avoid large or abrupt rudder inputs; Crosswind limit is 15 knots; Do not autoland. I made a maintenance write up and we continued. Climb was in IMC with light chop since there was a weather system moving into the east coast.Approximately an hour and half into the flight at FL340 received a Cabin Alt EICAS warning along with Cabin Altitude light and aural warning. We performed the immediate actions: Donned the oxygen masks and established crew communication. I followed the Cabin Altitude checklist and when I came to the decision tree: Cabin altitude is controllable (I switched to the other alt controller without any change) or Cabin altitude is uncontrollable; I felt that I was in between the two since the cabin was slightly above 10;000 feet and HOLDING STEADY. I advised ATC and asked for a lower altitude to the mid 20;000 feet thinking the cabin would decrease below 10;000 feet. I was also reluctant to go any lower because there was weather and turbulence below us. I called the purser and asked if the cabin oxygen masks had dropped and she informed that they had not confirming that cabin altitude never got above 14;000 feet. The cabin altitude decreased below 10;000 but the EICAS message was still illuminated so I asked for lower again. Passing 20;000 feet the Cabin Alt warning went out and the cabin showed approximately 6;000 feet so I elected to stop at FL190. This kept us right above the weather with the FO deviating around the tops.I informed the purser of the situation and made a preliminary PA. Contact with Dispatch was next with Maintenance Control on the line. Maintenance Control was not able to rectify our situation so the Dispatcher and I started looking for a divert airport. Due to the weather and the cross-wind limit of 15 knots due to the Rudder Ratio issue I was very limited in airport selection since the cross winds were in excess of 15 knots in ZZZ1; ZZZ2; ZZZ3; ZZZ; ZZZ4. ZZZ5 was the only option with calm winds; 400 Feet broken; 3 MI visibility and rain.I made the decision to divert to ZZZ5 with dispatch concurrence. I informed the purser and made another PA.We began planning for landing into ZZZ5 and was told of moderate turbulence ahead. I seated the flight attendants. Approaching the IAF for [Runway] XXL ATC informed us of an aircraft ahead of us Going Around since they were unable to see the runway at mins. I inquired about XXR and was told there was another aircraft on approach for that runway. That aircraft landed and we proceeded to a normal landing. Fire and rescue greeted us and after getting the all OK we taxied uneventfully to the gate.

column121: Planned fuel was 6;040 and got fueled to 6;200. We took off with roughly 6;000 pounds of fuel and minimum fuel was 5;564. So we left with well above minimum required fuel according to release. We were enroute and about halfway to 2/3 of the way through as I monitored our fuel burn. I noticed based on current conditions at that time (winds aloft were greater than planned and ATC requested Mach .77 or greater while .76 is planned); that we would be about 700 pounds under planned landing fuel. So as a crew we quickly setup for long range cruise and contacted ATC that we needed to slowdown even though they insisted we maintain a high speed. So we slowed to Mach .63 for long range cruise and then ATC descended us to 27;000 feet from 31;000 feet starting down early because we were slower than surrounding traffic.Then we get instructions shortly after to change arrivals keeping us away from other traffic. Once we finally got situated with the changes; dispatch beat me to notifying them and sent us an ACARS asking about the route changes and fuel. So we told them current plan and situation and based on the information back from dispatch; we had sufficient fuel as long as we maintained LRC (Long Range Cruise speed) to ZZZ allowing us to land with just 100 pounds of fuel more than planned and dispatch had us landing at roughly 1;850 pounds. At some point ATC also queried us asking about why we would be taking off with less fuel than we need to do the flight; even though we didn't. We actually took off with more fuel than planned. ATC was actually being unprofessional about the whole thing and giving us a hard time; because we asked to slow down to conserve fuel as stated over the radios in order to avoid getting into a bad fuel situation later or having to declare minimum fuel; and then he put us on different arrival and etc. It just created more workload and pressure by his attitude and questions as if it was our fault than it needed to be and ATC did not help with that even though they're there to help us.He made us sound bad on the radio as if we didn't know what we were doing about our fuel. Then sometime later while setting up for new arrival; ZZZ does a runway change as well after we got our LDR (Landing Distance Required) and brief; so that added more workload trying to update everything and re-brief in addition to ACARS taking longer than usual to respond. During all of that; Center then instructs us to level at 19;000 feet after getting the first descend via due to VFR traffic at 17;500 feet!  After traffic passes Center then gives us descend via again with immediate handoff to Approach in the same transmission. So First Officer does the handoff while I'm assessing and starting down seeing how quick we need to descend.  I saw we needed to do 6;000 feet or more a minute in order to meet the crossing restriction. I knew that wasn't going to happen so right as I was going to tell First Officer to let ATC know we can't make the restriction because of the level off earlier due to traffic as he was checking on; Approach immediately on initial contact asked if we would make the crossing restriction and we said no.He immediately then got upset and asked if we told the previous controller who would be Center and we said no because we didn't have time as we literally just switched and got the clearance at the same time and literally a few seconds later discovered we couldn't make it work. So we explained that to Approach but he wasn't accepting that and blamed us for not making the restriction or notifying Center before talking with Approach. But we literally had no time between the clearance and handoff at the same time and during the frequency switch that's when we noticed the issue and first transmission with Approach we weren't given the time to tell him that before he asked and queried us. So Approach then gives us two small delay vectors and rejoin arrival. But Approach said we should've told them early on we couldn't make itbut again we explained the situation and that we were not given that chance to do so. So we then continued on after that with no further issues.Insufficient fuel planning on release as it never reflects the actual fuel burn since release doesn't account for delay vectors or vectors on approach. The issues with ATC and last second changes to arrival and runways were a result of not having enough fuel at normal cruise followed by slow ACARS affected our ability to fly the planned arrival causing a higher workload for us and ATC which then caused the hiccup with crossing restrictions and with crossing traffic as well.  For fuel; we slowed for LRC and got a couple shortcuts once on the banker arrival. We were able to gain most of our fuel back because of LRC and landed with 2;200 pounds. For the crossing restriction; we just explained the situation to ATC and along with Center; Approach gave us a hard time and we notified them we couldn't do it; then we carried on with no further issues after that.For fuel planning and fuel contingency; we should be doing a minimum of like 500 pounds and 750-1;000 pounds extra on IFR days. Also for holding fuel; that should be 600 pounds minimum as we realistically burn more than 400 pounds on a go-around on a VFR day. As far as ATC goes after discussing with my First Officer as the situation that unfolded after another as a result; we maybe should have declared Minimum fuel early on knowing we wouldn't have enough unless we slowed down. But because of LRC and little to no delay vectors we determined to have enough hence why we never declared. However; if we declared min fuel early on that would've maybe given ATC more understanding even as frustrating as it may be; and allow us priority to slow and not have to descend via and etc. And that maybe would've avoided the issue with crossing at ZZZZZ1 and etc. One thing led to another; so next time maybe declare min fuel and decline a descend via to stay up high longer and to reduce workload. It was a good learning experience except for lack of professionalism and help from ATC.

column121: On approach to land in LAS from vectors; and cleared for the visual my Captain had just turned final at approximately 3;800 feet and was on a stable descent to land. At about 1;150 feet our RA dinged 'traffic' which indicated about 200 feet below us. We couldn't see the traffic. At 940 feet to land (3;000 AGL); we had an RA warning go off due to a helicopter. The warning was to our right. We still couldn't see the traffic; but the warning soon turned into an announcement from our aircraft systems to 'pull up' at 940 feet on the RA. This particular situation was out of our control to avoid. We don't generally have issues with helicopter traffic; and in this situation at such a busy airspace; we could not disregard the RA instructions so low to the ground and at such a critical phase of flight. column121: When I got to Aircraft X; it had a writeup for (paraphrasing) '#4 tire worn'. We were scheduled to take aircraft from ZZZ to ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 to ZZZ to ZZZ3. On our second pass through ZZZ with about five minutes to push the Ops Agent informed us of a Maintenance lock on the Release. About that same time we got an ACARS message from Dispatch saying the same thing and that it was something about a tire change. I called Dispatch and the guy answering the phone said he had tried to call Maintenance and no one answered so he would try again and let me know. I called back seven minutes later and asked to be transferred to Maintenance Control to talk to them directly. Maintenance Control said the tire was allowed only three cycles and the aircraft was 'dead' until it was changed; that it was supposed to be done the first time we went through ZZZ but somehow it didn't happen. This is five minutes before push with no one in sight to change the tire. Five minutes or so after scheduled push; a crew came out to change the tire. The guy that changed the tire took the logbook and came back about 45 minutes later with it saying we were good to go.(As an aside; I informed Maintenance Control the aircraft was coming back to ZZZ for the night and could they change it then. Maintenance said it was only good for three (3) cycles. In 15 years I've never seen a tire written up that wasn't changed immediately and the first I've ever heard that a 'worn' tire is good for only three cycles. This information would have allowed us as a crew to be more proactive to get the tire changed the first time we went through ZZZ or at least set up for the next pass through. This could have prevented over an hour delay.I looked at the logbook and saw in the lower right corner 'MTO W/O Closed' with the 'YES' circled. I didn't look for any narrative in the pink Maintenance part. That is my bad but I took MTO W/O Closed to mean the work was done. We did the 'Before Start Originating' checklist and departed without incident. I noticed a missed call and a text from the succeeding Captain about the logbook having a problem. Being out of the aircraft and in the hotel room by then; I have no way of knowing what the problem was for the logbook but apparently the Captain had to call Contract Maintenance to verify the #4 tire was changed and enter it in the logbook. The long and short of it is I may have flown an aircraft with an open writeup because of improper documentation and my ignorance in seeing that.

column121: During our taxi-out and takeoff role; the Captain and I noted a Number 1 Fuel Filter Bypass Master Caution Light.  We both felt this was part of a MEL condition entered into the aircraft's ELB; but feel the MEL procedure to be both ambiguous and poorly written.  The condition should not be available for ER [Extended Range] operations.During our pre-flight planning activities; the Captain and I noted a defect of 'Repeat. LH Fuel Filter Bypass warning light was on for 5 minutes' written up on the Electronic Log Maintenance Logbook (ELB).  Maintenance indicated that 'Fuel Filter Signal Disagree' on EEC #1 was the actual issue causing this light to indicate. Maintenance deferred the fault by placing the #1 Fuel Filter Bypass Light on MEL 7304A.The ELB indicated that maintenance replaced the #1 engine fuel filter; did an engine idle run; and noted no gross contamination of the fuel in the filter.  No further CDU faults were noted by maintenance.  The number #1 engine 'Fuel Filter Bypass Light' was placarded.  Upon referencing the 737NG MEL; as far as we could tell; this is all the maintenance action items that need to be completed.As for the flight crew actions to be completed for MEL 7304A; we must only assure that the:1. 'Remaining fuel filter pressure warning system must operate normally.'2. 'Maintenance is required to verify malfunction is in fuel filter bypass warning system on initial deferral.'We noted that the flight crew actions for this MEL are rather sparse: Our normal pre-flight activities would ensure that the #2 Fuel Filter Bypass Light was extinguished and maintenance indicated they performed step 2.During our pre-flight briefing the Captain and I discussed this MEL; verified that the system was not needed for ER operations - as our flight to Destination would; of course; fall under this category.  Unfortunately; a complete discussion and briefing about this item may have fallen slightly short as we became mildly distracted with a separate and unrelated new maintenance fault in the parking brake accumulator system that was noted during our flight deck pre-flight activities.  In turn; our flight became delayed at the gate in ZZZ as the parking brake system needed to be deferred using another MEL.  Additionally; we waited for connecting passengers from an inbound ZZZ1 flight.We pushed back from the gate in ZZZ started to taxi out for a departure on Runway XXR.  During a turn on our taxi to the runway; we both noted that the Master Caution light illuminated for the Number 1 Fuel Filter Bypass Master Caution Light.  I canceled the light and the Captain decided he wanted to stop in a safe area to deal with the possible issue. I agreed and ground control in ZZZ allowed us to stop on Taxiway 1.As the Captain stopped and set the parking brake; we both stated how confused we were about the fuel filter bypass light illuminating.  I checked the 737QRH for this light and it only indicated that 'erratic engine operation' may occur 'in flight'.The Captain and I discussed how it was extinguished after engine start; and only illuminated momentarily on taxi out; during a turn; and it was now extinguished again.  We referenced MEL 7304A again from the 737NG MEL.  Nowhere could we find whether the 'inoperative/placarded' light should remain illuminated; extinguished; or momentarily indicate.  We discussed that most MELs similar to this deferral would explain to the flight crew that a caution light may illuminate.  (See example MEL 78030: 'NOTE: The 'Master Caution' and 'ENG' MAY illuminate when performing master caution recall.')The Captain decided to call Dispatch and conference in maintenance while stopped on the taxiway.  We told our Dispatcher about our issue and he brought in Maintenance on the phone line.  The initial maintenance personnel transferred us to the 'Specific area.'  The 'Specific area' advisor told us that this momentarily illumination was normal and part of the MEL; the write-up was already in the ELB; and that it is 'OK to continue.'During our conversation the Captain; Maintenance; Dispatch; and I came to the conclusion:1. There is no maintenance procedure to deactivate this light.2. The issue is already indicated in the ELB.3. Maintenance stated that was a normal and 'very common' occurrence on the 737 fleet and we are OK to continue.After finishing our conversation with maintenance and dispatch; the Captain and I amended our takeoff briefing to be prepared for this light to illuminate during the takeoff roll.  I; as the PNF; would indicate it was this light; cancel the alert; and the takeoff would continue in both the low speed and high-speed regimes.During the takeoff roll; at approximately 120 kts (at least 20 kts below V1); the Number 1 Fuel Filter Bypass Master Caution Light did illuminate.  I called out that the fault adding 'expected!'; canceled the Master Caution Light; and we continued the takeoff.  The light extinguished itself shortly thereafter.  The light never illuminated again throughout the rest of the flight.  The flight continued uneventfully to ZZZ2.
column123: The maintenance release had an open write up for the 'fuel filter differential pressure warning system'.  We read both the maintenance release and the MEL (7304A). Not much information other than the other system must be operative and if you do get the other filter bypass light; you should assume both engine filters have an impending bypass condition. Startup was normal. On taxi out; we got the left fuel filter bypass light; the side that was written up. It caught us off guard; because no where did it say that the light might come on. We pulled over and got a phone patch to Maintenance Control to discuss the light. Maintenance Control said it was normal with the problem and we were OK to continue. The light went and we taxied for takeoff. At approximately 120 knots; the light illuminated again. We continued the takeoff and the light went out shortly after we were airborne. The light did not illuminate again until taxi in.

column121: On the arrival into the ZZZ area; ATC kept us high due to departing IFR traffic. We heard the departing traffic calling ATC on the radio after departure; but got no response. Because we were getting very close to the airport; we elected to reduce speed in order to make the impending descent easier to manage. We were monitoring both the ATC Center frequency and the CTAF frequency at ZZZ. There was a significant amount of General Aviation traffic operating in the vicinity of the ZZZ airport. As the speed was reduced below 200 knots; the First Officer; who was the PF; asked for Flaps 8 and 20. I verified that the speed was below 200 knots and selected Flaps 8 and 20. As soon as I selected Flaps 20 I realized we were still at 16;000 ft.; and said; 'We can't do that yet;' and immediately retracted the Flaps back to 0.  At this point we were only six or seven miles from the airport; still at 16;000 ft. We had identified the traffic threats on TCAS. In order to initiate our descent to the airport; we canceled IFR. After descending through 15;000 feet the First Officer again asked for Flaps 8 and 20. Because we had extended the flaps earlier above 16;000 feet; I was focused on the altitude. Due to the fact that we had slowed to below 200 knots the first time we extended the flaps; I failed to look at the airspeed indicator; thinking we were still below 200 knots. We were discussing the maneuver we would need to make to circle around and descend to the airport at the time. ATC and CTAF radio traffic was also heavy at the time. As soon as the flaps were selected the overspeed clacker started up. I looked at the airspeed indicator; saw that we were above 200 knots; and reached for the flap lever with the intent of retracting the flaps. At this point I'm unclear what EXACTLY happened next.  There was some turbulence; we were beginning our turn; and there was a lot of radio traffic.  We were also focused on the traffic displayed on the TCAS. All of this created a great deal of distraction. My hand was on the flap lever at the time; with the intent of retracting the flaps. Whether it was because of turbulence causing me to inadvertently move the lever; or me simply moving it the wrong way because of the distractions; I did; in fact; move the flap lever to 45. The overspeed clacker; interestingly enough; added to the momentary confusion. In fact; at one point I believe the First Officer said; 'What the hell is going on?' I was mortified to see the indication that the flaps were at 45; because there was no intent; plan; or call for further flap extensions. It was simply a mistake. I immediately retracted the flaps to zero. We did not receive any message associated with a flap problem; i.e. 'Flaps Fail'; etc. After everything calmed down and things were back in order; we continued the approach; which ended up resulting in a go-around because a general aviation aircraft cut us off on short final. After landing and proceeding to the gate; I wrote up the flap limitation exceedance. Maintenance arrived later; inspected the flaps; performed functional checks; found no irregularities; and returned the aircraft to service.In my opinion there were several factors contributing to the event. Distraction was probably the primary cause. We were distracted by all the radio traffic on the CTAF frequency. Sometimes it was difficult to differentiate between the CTAF traffic and the Center traffic. Also; being left so high so late on the arrival created a self-imposed sense of immediacy...'We need to get down'. Interesting to note that this urgency was never 'real'; but rather something we imposed on ourselves. Assumption was another contributing factor. Because we had originally slowed to below 200 knots; I assumed we were still at that airspeed when flaps were requested the second time. This assumption caused me to neglect the airspeed indicator before selecting the flaps because I was more concerned about the altitude.This is primarily an exercise in self-discipline and patience. The training and procedures are all in place to help prevent these types of events from occurring. It simply becomes incumbent on each pilot to be disciplined enough to not allow external factors to get in the way of simple; straight-forward procedures that can and will keep the aircraft; passengers; and crew safe.

Because the winds were calm; the runway was clear and dry; and I knew a safe landing could be accomplished; I elected to continue the approach. I still landed softly and safely in the touchdown area; and stopped in the usual amount of runway required. It was an uneventful landing.When we taxied clear of the runway; I asked Tower and asked about the frequency and asked the FO to pull up the current ATIS to see if there was a NOTAM about the ILS frequency; and sure enough; it was OTS. In hindsight; I'm not sure how I missed that on the ATIS; but I should have read it more carefully and I could have avoided this situation altogether.

I then queried the Approach Controller about whether or not they would like me to call our base leg for Runway 26L.  The Controller replied that our base leg would be visible on their radar; and that a call was not necessary. Not realizing that there was INDEED a transition from the BERBN intersection to HUXAR on the ILS 26L; we proceeded turn north whilst descending to intercept the Runway 26L localizer just outside of RELIN intersection (D7.2 IRLE) Runway 26L.Shortly thereafter; we were told by the Approach Controller that we had initiated the turn too soon; and we were given a heading to the East in order to avoid traffic (other carrier) that was already established on final for Runway 26L.  We did receive a TCAS TA (no RA); and after completing the turn to the East; the TCAS TA was resolved. After the turn to the East; and with proper separation between our aircraft and Aircraft Y; Approach Control vectored us back to the north to join the localizer and clear us for the visual to LAS Runway 26L. We were then handed-off to LAS Tower. Landing was uneventful. After landing; we were provided a phone number to call LAS TRACON. The COKTL 1 Arrival and the latest ILS 26L charts for LAS are dated (date). I can tell you that I was certainly not familiar; nor had I ever been assigned the ILS 26L from the COKTL 1 Approach (I wasn't even aware that there was a transition from BERBN intersection; as that transition is located on the new ILS 26L Approach chart). My apologies to the LAS Approach Controller for our misunderstanding.As an added measure; I would prefer to see more information added to the COKTL 1 Arrival; like a ball note referring Pilots to the BERBN transition on the ILS 26L LAS.  An added note within our company pages may help bring attention to this transition as well.

column121: Aircraft was dispatched with an inoperative Pack #2 due to a regulator fault and [the flight] was in full compliance with the MEL at departure. Flight was completely full in the cabin. Due to Pack #2 being inoperative it was difficult to cool the main cabin temp using only Pack #1. Using only Pack #1 at FL370 we were able to maintain 72 degrees in the cabin using max cold and high flow. Approximately 200 nm west of ZZZ at FL370 we received an ECAM AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT. ATC was notified and [priority handling was requested]. Upon checking the pressurization and bleed air page; it appeared that Pack #1 was overheating showing an output temperature in amber yet we never received a Pack 1 OVHT ECAM. The cabin altitude was still under control. A descent to 10;000 ft. was initiated without exceeding the cabin altitude before we complied with the ECAM to turn off Pack #1 leaving us unpressurized. Contact was made with Dispatch and Maintenance Control to discuss the situation resulting in a diversion to ZZZ.
column123: Approximately 240 nm from ZZZ; at a cruise altitude of FL350 and while in communication with Center; an ECAM aural and Master Caution sounded for AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT. The CA (Captain) said he noted a momentary amber overheat temp in Pack 1; but it did not trigger the PACK 1 OVHT caution. I (Pilot Monitoring) did not see this indication that had subsequently returned to a green inlet temperature. Pack 2 was previously secured and turned off per the MEL deferral on our 2nd release. Pack 1 showed a fault light. The AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT ECAM directed us to secure Pack 1; descend to 10;000 ft. MSL or MEA and then turn on the RAM Air when the pressure differential was less than 1.0. Even though Pack 1 had a fault light in the overhead panel; it appeared to be partially functioning; the cabin pressure holding and the cabin altimeter only increasing at a very slight rate. A flight crew decision was made to begin an immediate normal descent to 10;000 ft. without the use of oxygen while closely monitoring the pressurization page to ascertain the true nature of the Pack 1 malfunction. The CA directed me to assume pilot flying duties and ATC responsibilities while he coordinated with Operations; Dispatch; flight attendants and the passengers. We began a coordinated 1500-2000 fpm rate of descent via two ATC-assigned step down altitudes of FL300 and FL200 before ultimately reaching 10;000 ft. The aircraft was lowered in a steady continual descent with no pauses which I believe helped our situation. Cabin pressure held steady around 8;000 ft. during the normal descent. Upon reaching 10;000 ft.; Pack 1 was secured; differential pressure reached less than 1.0; RAM AIR was selected on and the cabin altimeter climbed from approximately 8;000 to 10;000 ft. as expected. We completed all remaining ECAM items until the screens were normal. The rate of fuel burn at 10;000 ft. MSL made reaching our initial destination of ZZZ1 impossible; and it was decided that ZZZ was a suitable diversion while 200nm away and with 11;600 pounds of fuel aboard along with the best Maintenance; aircraft and passenger accommodation options. We informed ATC; Dispatch; Operations; and proceeded accordingly. We switched to the next Center and the Captain [requested priority handling] and returned to the pilot flying role while we coordinated an uneventful arrival via the ZZZZZ to Visual XX approach at ZZZ and ultimately parking at gate XY. We were then met by the ZZZ Chief Pilot at the gate and proceeded to fill out a risk mitigation form following the event. We then accepted a new aircraft and release at gate XZ and ultimately brought the same passengers to ZZZ1 two hours later than originally planned.In totality; I felt the event was handled safely and professionally. The CRM skills taught and utilized allowed both the CA and First Officer to properly divide duties while ensuring sufficient cross checks and communication. At no time did I feel rushed or stressed. I believe the deliberate delay in securing the faulty Pack 1 that appeared to be functioning along with the continual scanning of the pressurization page allowed us to avoid an unnecessary priority descent; use of pilot oxygen; or the deployment of passenger oxygen that might have accompanied a rapid depressurization. All in all; I felt the CA was composed and handled the event in line with Company desires. While I regret the delay the passengers experienced; I believe we handled the event in a safe and caring manner.

column121: I was the PF (Pilot Flying) on this flight from ZZZZ1 to ZZZZ. On arrival into the ZZZZ terminal area; we were cleared direct to ZZZZZ and cleared for the ILS XXL approach. Weather at ZZZZ was reporting winds 280 at 12; few clouds at 3;000 ft.; altimeter 29.62; and no other significant weather. The initial approach was uneventful and we were fully configured and stable by about 1200 ft. AGL. At approximately 800 ft.; I turned off the autopilot and began hand flying. Then at approximately 700 ft. we received an audible wind shear warning that lasted for 3-4 seconds. This caught us both by surprise as there were no other conditions that would be associated with wind shear. There was no convective activity in the area; the weather was good; and the wind readout showed stable at 12 kts. The aircraft showed no airspeed fluctuation nor an increasing or decreasing trend vector; the thrust setting was normal; pitch attitude and vertical path were stable. During the alert; the weather radar showed a lot of red radar return that wasn't previously there; and did not correlate with what we were seeing visually out the windscreen. We both assessed the situation; and agreed that the alert was erroneous. At this point we were at about 300 ft. AGL; and the Captain told me to continue. I agreed with this assessment and decision; and continued to land normally. Not once did we receive any other indication that wind shear was present; it wasn't even 'choppy'. It was smooth all the way through landing. After reflecting on the event; I still believe that the alert we received was false. With that being said; as a crew; we probably should have discussed making a logbook entry and discussing the alert with the mechanic once we were parked at the gate in ZZZZ. Going forward if I encounter something like this again; I will handle it differently for a couple of reasons. First; the FOM does state that if a wind shear warning is received; to follow wind shear escape maneuver or to execute a normal go around. Secondly; I do not want to get into a habit of second guessing the warning systems on board the aircraft. Regardless of a suspected error; and as long as safety is not compromised; follow procedure then once at the gate; make a logbook entry for a suspected error.
column123: We were operating this flight from ZZZZ1 to ZZZZ arriving approximately XA:30 UTC. Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring) and FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying). We were set up for the ZZZZZ1 RNAV arrival for the ILS XXL. The aircraft (a B767) was empty and our landing weight was 198;100 lbs. VApp was calculated at 122 and VRef at 117. The weather was VFR. There was no convective activity; a few clouds at 3000 ft.; winds 280 at 12 reported on the field; and altimeter at 29.62. We were cleared to the fix ZZZZZ to begin the ILSZ XXL at 4000 ft. We intercepted the localizer and armed the APPCH. We continued to configure the aircraft for landing maintaining VFR conditions. With the aircraft fully configured for landing (Stabilized Approach criteria met) at approximately 700 ft. AGL we received a wind shear alert. The weather was VFR; and the winds at our altitude were showing stable at 12 knots. There was no airspeed fluctuation (including the airspeed trend line); the throttle position did not change; the thrust setting did not change; and the aircraft pitch attitude did not change. As PM; I did not elect to call 'Go Around' as the aircraft was fully stabilized; fully configured for landing and we were passing through approximately 300 ft. AGL with the PF hand-flying the aircraft. Given the situation with all of the present conditions and the state of the aircraft; I believed the alert was erroneous. I should have made a logbook write up on the EPGWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) to check for errors. There were no reports of any wind shear activity in the area and the weather conditions were VFR. Also given the location and state the aircraft was in; I thought it would create an unnecessary 'non-normal' situation that could have potentially caused more problems than just continuing the approach and landing the aircraft. As I stated above; the aircraft exhibited no indications for us to believe that there were any type of wind shear occurrences at the present time or in the immediate time prior to landing.

FO barely flared during a visual approach at Runway XXL in ZZZ that ended up causing a hard landing situation.[Reporter recommends] possibly rotate brand new FO's and make them fly more often. We advised ATC we had no such fix. They had us go to ZZZZ regardless.  They then asked to confirm the route we were flying. The route we had loaded from Dispatch was NOT the route ATC had on file. But it was the route that was originally in FD Pro for [us].  ATC then had us fly that earliest FD Pro flight plan to ZZZ. We were asked later during our flight to call BOS Center once on the ground. I did. They wanted to figure out what might have been the reason our flight plans did not match up. I stated to him I had loaded the revised flight plan from our Dispatcher and that I accepted the PDC flight plan clearance message as it appeared to match our revised flight plan.  I called our assigned Dispatcher and informed him of the problem. He thinks PDC did not load the revision but he should have gotten some kind of rejection notification if it was kicked back. Which he did not. So we do not know why ATC did not get the revised route that we flew. I would suggest that if the ATC PDC message that acknowledges our clearance was a complete route; not 'as filed'; I would have caught the discrepancy in the flight plans. It was unique in that both flight plans began with the ZZZZZ. It worked out in our favor that ATC gave us a short cut before we left the ZZZZZ. If not; somewhere after the ZZZZZ we would have deviated off the ATC filed route. The route that Dispatch sent us matched the route in [our] flight plan. column121: The incident happened during our descent on the ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ. As far as I remember; we had been cleared by the previous Controller and told to do the XXL transition. I had already programmed the FMS for that specific arrival and pre-loaded the ILS XXL. The weather was not an issue with a clear sky and great visibility. I briefed a visual approach for XXL; backed up with the routing of the ILS for that same runway; and made sure we had the discontinuity between the last point on the arrival - ZZZZZ1 and the first point on the approach - ZZZZZ1. We were then told to contact the next Controller and assigned different altitudes on the arrival while maintaining the routing. For some reason; at one point; I thought/assumed we were cleared for the visual and got rid of the discontinuity by linking the first point on the approach with the last point on the arrival - ZZZZZ1. I turned to the Captain to ask him to 'confirm' and proceeded by removing the discontinuity. Because we were not cleared for the approach yet; the aircraft proceeded past ZZZZZ1 on a XXX as expected; but because it was now programmed to fly the approach it started turning at ZZZZZ2. The Controller asked us if we were flying the RNAV; we responded that we were doing the XXL transition and as the Captain said these words we realized we had made a mistake by leaving the XXX. The Controller kindly reminded us what we were expected to do and gave us a heading to intercept the localizer for the visual XXL. What led to this mistake is mostly my fault. I was fixated on flying the visual; and I forgot to actually make sure we had been given the clearance before getting off the arrival. My mind was too focused on the preconceived idea of what was expected rather than what we had actually been cleared for that I failed to properly communicate with my Captain. I was complacent; and this led to confusion in the cockpit and with the Controller.
column123: During our descent on ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ; we were cleared to descend via ZZZZZ ; XXL transition. We programmed the FMS for that particular arrival and transition and preloaded the ILS XXL. The weather was good with clear sky and great visibility. Pilot Flying; briefed the visual approach XXL back it up by ILS. We made sure the discontinuity between the last point on the arrival ZZZZZ1 and the first point on the approach ZZZZZ1. We were told to contact the next Controller and assigned us different altitude on the arrival while maintaining the routing. I contacted the next Controller and for some reason we thought; we were cleared for visual via ZZZZZ1 transition. As we past ZZZZZ1; we continue to fly heading XXX as we approached ZZZZZ2 the plane was about to transition to the new fix. At this point ATC assigned us a heading 350 and asked us if we are flying the RNV transition? Which responded yes and I realized the error. At this point he assigned us 310 heading to intercept the localizer and cleared us for visual to XXL.We were both fixated and our mind was set on the preconceived idea of what was expected rather than what we had actually been cleared for; especially when the proceeding traffic receives that clearance. I (we) failed to confirm and communicate with each other and ATC. I got complacent and side tracked; the combination of these two led to the confusion in the cockpit and with the Controller.As a (Captain/Pilot Monitoring) I should have communicated and confirmed that we are both on the same page and understood the clearance and when in doubt ask the ATC for clarification. I want to make sure and get the confirmation before removing the discontinuity and not to rush. Do not assume if previous aircraft receives particular clearance we will get the same and avoid complacency. I will emphasize this on my future arrival briefings to ensure this doesn't happen again; FOOLISH ASSUMPTION/MISTAKE.

column121: During the pre-start check; the crew confirmed that all three altimeters were set properly.  I have a clear memory of personally checking all 3 altimeters.  As Pilot Flying I was hand flying a vectored departure and given a clearance to climb and maintain 10;000 ft.  Approximately 200 ft prior; as I was leveling off; I was given a new clearance to climb and maintain 16;000 ft.  I continued to hand fly and completed a smooth level off at 16;000.  As I was doing so; ATC gave us a notification of opposite direction traffic 1;000 feet above us which we had on TCAS and immediately saw visually.  All appeared normal and I believed ATC was simply letting us know why we had not been cleared higher and was giving a normal notification of traffic.  The transmission was partially garbled; and the Pilot Monitoring (PM) requested that ATC repeat it.  ATC simply responded with 'maintain 16;000' which the PM acknowledged.  The PM then noticed that our altimeters did not agree and informed me that my altimeter was set at 29.92 instead of the local altimeter setting.  I reset the altimeter and discovered that I was actually at 16;180 ft; which likely had prompted the call from ATC.  We were just short of 200 ft high.  I descended and was at 16;000 before passing under the opposite direction traffic.  We did not receive a TCAS TA or RA.  I have no memory of resetting my altimeter to 29.92 but surmise that I must have done so as it would be very difficult to have hit the button accidentally.  While allowed to set 29.92 once assigned a climb above 18;000 ft; my normal practice is to wait until the altimeter setting flashes approaching 18;000 ft to reset it.  Normal practice meaning I don't recall ever doing it differently.  I cannot explain when I reset it to standard; except that it was after the pre-start check and prior to leveling at 16;000.  My best guess is that I did so at 10;000 for some reason; as that was the only altitude I passed that I would have considered significant; although I was on profile in a 250 knot climb both before and after 10;000 ft.  In this case; the local altimeter setting was close enough to standard that I did not exceed the 300 feet limit for a flight violation or cause a traffic conflict.  This was just luck however.  Had the altimeter been significantly different from standard; I don't believe I would have been more likely to notice the error and could have been responsible for a conflict.I'm not sure what the cause was except that I simply made an error.  Why; how; or when escapes me.  However; I did have to call in fatigued that morning as we were on a late in the day pairing but had been delayed overnight to a morning departure two time zones to the east.  When I called in fatigued unable to fall asleep early; I was given my 10 hours and a later show time; though to make the later show time I still needed to get out of bed two hours prior to when I was accustomed.  After I woke up to my alarm; I was notified that the aircraft was still in maintenance and was given an even later show time; and I took a short nap.  In the end; the error happened during a time I'd normally be awake; but I did not get my normal sleep routine.  I had legal rest and did not feel particularly fatigued; but I can't discount that fatigue very well could have contributed to such an unusual error.  I utilized the Fatigue Risk Management Plan (FRMP) to the extent I felt necessary and neither Crew Scheduling nor the company pressured me in any way to fly fatigued.  Perhaps I should have insisted on an even later show time.  My feeling of responsibility to our customers who had already been delayed over 12 hours was a factor in making a show time that was earlier than normal for me; considering time zones; but again; I didn't feel overly tired at the time. Obviously; having made this error for the first time; I'll be more cognizant of when I hit the button to bring the altimeter to standard going forward.  As far as the possible fatigueaspect; our promise to our customers to transport them to their destination at the time we say can sometimes conflicts with our promise to transport them as safely as possible.  I have availed myself of the risk management plan several times in the last year and have never received any negative feedback or pressure to fly fatigued.  There are times when I feel the probability of losing pay has pressured other pilots to fly with less rest than they needed; but in this case pay was not a factor as I was the only pilot available to fly this leg to an outstation serviced only once per day.  So; I was going to be paid for the leg no matter when I flew it.  Therefore; I can't recommend any changes to the risk management plan.  I simply need to do a better job of anticipating and assessing my own fatigue level.
column123: Climbing out we were assigned to maintain 16;000 ft. First Officer (FO) was pilot flying. Altitude was verified at '1;000 to go' call. As we went through 15;000 feet; I said 15;000 climbing 16;000. FO was hand flying; as we near 16;000 (about 100ft to go) I noticed he wasn't slowing down the climb rate. I looked over and his altimeter was set to 29.92 instead of the altimeter we've gotten when I checked in of 30.16. As I looked over ATC asked if we had the 16;000 ft altitude assigned which I replied affirmatively. As I was done talking to ATC I told the FO he had the wrong altimeter setting; and that our Altimeter was 30.16. FO did level off at 16;000 ft but he had a wrong altimeter setting. FO may have pushed the standard 29.92 altimeter inadvertently at some point after initial departure. As the altimeter were set and cross checked for departure on the ground. We had checked our level off altitude on the 1;000 to go call. But I didn't notice at that time he had a wrong altimeter setting. I think on the 1;000 feet to go call we should have notice this discrepancy; but I was looking at my PFD and not his. FO should have mentioned that his altitude did not match with mine at the 1;000 to go call.

column121: We received a request to go direct to ZZZZZ. Dispatch had filed us on a southerly track to avoid significant weather on the H-track. The only options given were to accept or standby. We were not going to accept the re-route so we hit standby. The standby was accepted. We sent a message that we could climb instead of a re-route and ATC gave us a climb.Sometime later; the re-route request showed up again but this time the only option we were given was to accept. We ignored the request but that left the ATC icon up on the Upper DU [Display Unit] (so future ATC alerts may not be noticed).This annoyed me so after crossing ZZZZZ1 we noted that accepting the persistent direct routing request would only bypass our next waypoint by about 10 NM. I accepted the ATC routing but waited for a reply from ATC before proceeding. ATC responded with ROGER. So; we went direct ZZZZZ per the clearance. ATC then sent a message asking us to confirm request. We never sent any request so we followed up with a direct message stating we were accepting the previous direct routing from ATC. Shortly thereafter we asked to call ZZZ Center.I talked with the controller and explained the situation. He closed it out on his end with no action but quality control will still review.With CPDLC; ATC cannot ask a question but only provide one answer (accept). That leaves us with an open request.
column123: There should be a CPDLC option to accept; reject; or standby. Not just accept or standby. If you don't accept; the message stays open; and the ATC alert never extinguishes. This could cause a future message to be missed.

column121: This was a maintenance reposition flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was flying as the PIC with a Captain in the right seat. Pushing back from the gate; we had a zero fuel weight (ZFW) of 52;000 lbs. The gross weight on the performance was off by over 4;000 lbs from the data received; and we were out of balance. The aircraft had no passengers; no flight attendants; no baggage; just 14;700 lbs of fuel and two pilots and all galley carts.  We called the Dispatcher to inform her that we were out of balance. She told me on the phone that she was [gone] the previous week when we were transitioning to 5 zone weight and balance and she didn't know what was going on; and literally just handed me off to the pilot on duty to figure out. This was totally unacceptable. She is the dispatcher of record; has equal legal responsibility for the planning of this flight and upon being informed that we're out of balance and had our ZFW change by thousands of pounds in a few minutes time; she just hands me off to an unrecorded phone line with the pilot on duty?! My head is still spinning.  At the gate; our ZFW was 52;000 lbs. Now we are being told to put numbers in the box for ballast but I have no idea what it means 1.0 2.0 3.0 etc; what does that correspond to? We are not actually moving any ballast anywhere etc. The pilot on duty and some other manager on with him; and myself went back and forth for a good amount of time trying to figure out what the accurate zero fuel weight was; what an accurate gross take off weight was; and my main concern; if our stab trim; and V speeds were accurate and safe. I want to reiterate; this was a total and complete debacle. There was so much confusion on the phone as to how we got these numbers from computer and what they meant; and if they were accurate. I had to ask the pilot on duty and manager point blank on the phone; are you telling me these numbers are accurate; and safe for us to depart; before I would continue this flight any further. This 5 zone weight and balance makes no sense how we could be out of balance with only fuel on board. It does not seem like this 5 zone system was well thought out; or that ferry / reposition flights were accounted for. How this got approved by the FAA is beyond me. Additionally; our FOM states that 'the amount to be considered unusable shall be noted on the dispatch release and be considered as unusable by the flight crew'; no such comment on this release is present. If were using fuel for ballast for CG limits which is totally news to me seeing as we never had a problem with CG on 3 zone weight and balance; then the PIC must be notified because if that fuel is used; an in flight emergency would have to be declared because the aircraft would no longer be within CG limits.

column121: On arrival into EDF we were on ANC Approach. After initial contact; ANC asked what approach we wanted at EDF. The Pilot Monitoring replied the Visual 34. ANC instructed us to turn left heading 260 and descend and maintain 8;000 (we were at 13;000.) While rolling out on a 260 heading and still descending; ANC came back and said they were going to take us the other way and to turn back right heading 330. We rolled out on 330 still descending. At around 9;000 descending; ANC asked us if we wanted Runway 16 and that the winds were 330 at 5. Taking into account our position and high altitude relative to EDF Runway 34 and our weight; I decided that this would be acceptable; but wanted the IRO to double check the numbers before accepting this change. I said 'standby' and the Pilot Monitoring transmitted 'standby' to ANC. ANC immediately instructed us to descend and maintain 3;000. At the same time of ANC transmission; we were leveling at 8;000; and I was asking the IRO to run the numbers for 16. The Pilot Monitoring replied '3;000; Aircraft X'. I reset the altitude selector to 3;000; verified the altitude with the Pilot Monitoring; engaged FLC; set speed and we began to descend. This clearance seemed logical considering we were clearing terrain; there was no traffic on TCAS; no terrain indicating on the HSI (I was in terrain mode) and we needed to lose altitude to make the airport. There was no further contact with ANC ATC until they instructed us to maintain 8;000.Descending through approximately 6;700; ANC contacted us and instructed us to maintain 8;000; low alt alert and that the MVA in that area was 8;000. After landing and block in; I was notified by EDF Tower (via the military) that ANC TRACON wanted me to give them a call (which I did after speaking to the Chief Pilot.) They took my info and said he would be forwarding to quality control (assurance?) and they may contact me as they were looking into it. There was either an error by ANC Approach or we mistook instructions for another aircraft. After the flight while discussing with the crew; myself and the Pilot Monitoring thought we heard the same instructions. Considering we may have accepted a clearance for another aircraft on frequency; I later looked at the flights in and out of ANC at the same time. There was another flight that arrived in ANC shortly after we landed. It is possible that the instruction were meant for them. It is also possible instructions were meant for an entirely different aircraft and we mistook it for us. There was high workload at the time while considering a runway change; configuring the aircraft and checking landing data.The Pilot Monitoring immediately replied to maintain 8;000. I rolled the altitude selector back to 8;000; clicked off the autopilot; added power and hand flew the airplane back to 8;000 and then reengaged the autopilot. If in fact we did accept a clearance from a different aircraft; caution must be used when similar flight numbers are on the same transmitting frequency; especially during high work loads. Unfortunately; we were unaware of the other aircraft at the time of the event.

column121: Upon arrival to the aircraft; an ACARS message from our dispatcher was already on the printer asking if we had Revision X to our flight release.  I opened and downloaded the flight release to my iPad.  The release was indeed Revision X.  We replied to the Dispatcher telling him that we did have Rev X onboard.  I never saw the original Rev Y.  When uploading the flight plan to the FMC; the route that loaded was consistent with Rev X.  This route was: BLZZR4 BLZZR BAF Q480 CANDR RAV J64 [...].  I logged into the CPDLC and we received the clearance via CPDLC.  The CPDLC clearance was: 'CLEARED TO ZZZ ARPT BLZZR4 THEN AS FILED. [...]' We accepted the clearance.  From this point the flight progressed normally.  After departure while flying the BLZZR4 departure we were talking to Center; we had not yet reached the BAF waypoint.  The controller gave us a shortcut and cleared us directly to TRIBS intersection.  We couldn't find that fix on the legs page and replied that we were not showing TRIBS on our route.  The controller inquired as to what our route was and I replied with the route that was on our release (noted above).  Controller replied that they had a new route for us and cleared us from our present position direct to TRIBS Q406 BWZ J6 HVQ J78 FAM SGF [...] to ZZZ. We accepted the new clearance; entered it into the FMC; then notified Dispatch via ACARS of our new route.  Later in the flight; while talking to the next Center; the controller notified us of a possible pilot route deviation and gave us a phone number to call Center upon arrival in ZZZ.  The flight continued uneventfully to ZZZ.  Enroute to ZZZ; the Captain and I discussed what possible route deviation could have occurred.  We could only speculate that there was a difference between the flight plan on our Rev 01 Flight Release and the route that Center had cleared us via CPDLC and expected us to fly.  We were confident; however; that we were never off course since both the CPDLC clearance and Rev X flight plan had us flying the BLZZR4 departure; and the shortcut and subsequent reroute issued by Center occurred while we were still on the departure route.  At BAF (Barnes VOR) is where Q480 & Q406 diverge).After the Captain called Center from ZZZ; we suspected that the cause of the problem was that the Rev 01 route wasn't processed by BOS prior to issuing us our CPDLC clearance.  Since both the Rev X route; and the original route that BOS expected us to fly both began with the BLZZR4 departure; we had no idea from the CPDLC clearance of 'CLEARED TO ZZZ ARPT BLZZR4 THEN AS FILED.' that there was any discrepancy.  We are unsure why the updated route wasn't processed by BOS prior to issuing our CPDLC clearance.   Perhaps there is a cut-off time where changes are no longer accepted or processed. Even when being issued a 'Cleared As Filed' CPDLC; listing the entire filed route at the end of the message would be another way to confirm that the ATC facility has the same route as the crew does on their flight release.  In addition; being able to print the entire CPDLC message would also be helpful to not only have a hard copy of the clearance; but also to avoid having to step through multiple pages on the FMC and potentially miss something.  This would be especially helpful when there is an unexpected reroute as part of the CPDLC clearance.
