column121: Showed up to the gate at XA am from being assigned trips off reserve; met the Captain and the gate agent where we learned from the Gate Agent we had 2 non rev maintenance guys coming along with us. Went down to the aircraft where I started doing my checks and setting up my stuff; I came round from my walk around and started doing my 1st flight of the day checks. In the middle of while I was doing my 1st flight of the day flows the maintenance person asked me if he could bring his stuff up to the aircraft instead of the cargo bay I said sure (I heard him say tools and something else) as he walked out the jet bridge I paused for a minute and the Captain walked into the cockpit; he asked me where the maintenance guy was going. I told the Captain he went to get his tools and I think he said something about hydraulic fluid; I told the Captain I haven't read DG (Dangerous Goods) in a while but don't know if we can take it he agreed and went outside to tell the maintenance personnel to hold on for a second; he came back in sat in his seat pulled out the FOM and searched [but] could not find anything specific so decided to ring the duty pilot; at this point I carried on with my first flight of the day flows over hearing the conversation the Captain was having on the phone with the duty pilot; I heard something along of the line as it being explained as a hydraulic pump by hand in a little crate basically a little hand pump; and Captain was assured we are not taking any hydraulic fluid it's been emptied out might have a drop or two that was missed with a paper towel that's all... Captain looked at me and said don't know if you heard most of that which I replied I have he assured me we are not taking any hydraulic fluid and if I was comfortable going in which I told him in that case I have no issue going to fly. Well I believe we did everything that could have been done to ensure we were following SOP and company policy and procedure but there was a breakdown in communication between duty pilot / Maintenance Control and base Maintenance Manager where they forget to tell us we're taking canisters of hydraulic fluid.
column123: I was given Aircraft X on my first day of a four day reserve stretch. When I arrived at the gate I was informed that this was a maintenance (MX) reposition flight for an aircraft in ZZZ1. The two mechanics were sitting in the gate area and I went over to speak to them. I was informed the aircraft in ZZZ1 had issues with its hydraulic 2 quantity and that they had to head over and look at the system. I went back to the gate and got the paperwork; met my First Officer (FO); [Name]; and went down to the aircraft. As we began doing our first flight of day items and loading the flight plan; I told [name] that I would go upstairs and inform the gate agent he could let the mechanics board. Unfortunately the agent was having issues with scanning the mechanics on; so I called our Dispatcher so we could have them put on the release and they could come down. On the jet-bridge with the mechanics one of them told me he wanted to go check if they had got the tools out to the aircraft yet and that he wanted to also 'make sure the pump would not be leaking'. I immediately asked him if he was referring to a hydraulic pump and he confirmed he was. I told him I had to contact the Operations Controller because there should be no hydraulic fluid on the airplane; especially not any that could be leaking. at XA:01am I called the Operations phone tree and connected myself to the Chief Pilot; [Name 2]. I told [Name 2] that Maintenance told me they were worried about a hydraulic pump that could leak in the cargo compartment and needed to know exactly what was going on with this reposition and the equipment I was bringing. [Name 2] agreed with me that no hydraulic fluid was allowed to be transported and we went through the FOM looking for any guidance on hydraulic pumps and transporting that type of equipment. Our joint search of the FOM was in [the] chapter under the Hazardous Materials and Dangerous Goods section. This call lasted 13 minutes and 7 seconds and we agreed that there was no exceptions about equipment such as a hydraulic pump and [Name 2] told me he was going to talk to the Maintenance Head in the Operations. at XA:18 am I missed a call from [Name 2] and he left a message saying 'I just got a little more info on that hydraulic pump so to speak on your guys repo flight. Apparently it's a ground servicing pump; basically a tool we are bringing down there for maintenance.' I called back at XA:19am and he explained to me that we were bringing a pump that Maintenance would use on the ground to pump fluid into a hydraulic system on the other aircraft. He told me that Maintenance confirmed it was washed out and did not contain any hydraulic fluid.  I then went back and spoke to the mechanics to confirm this was the correct information. They said yes; the pump was indeed a servicing pump and it had been cleaned thoroughly prior to transport. With this information I and the conversation with Maintenance and the Operations Controller I decided that this was indeed a legal fight with cargo that was permitted in accordance with our FOM. On Date 2; I received a call from [Name 3] from the safety committee. He informed me that a Captain on the return flight for the broken aircraft was being asked to transport canisters of hydraulic fluid from ZZZ1 back to ZZZ and asked me if I knew anything about how they got there. I told [Name 3] that I had not transported any canisters from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and was under the impression that the pump and two tool kits were the only items aboard my aircraft. [Name 3] told me he would investigate further and call me back. [Name 3] called me back and informed me that we had unknowingly transported 2 canisters of Hy-Jet IV-A+ to ZZZ1 and informed me to fill out an ASAP with all pertinent details. Two Canisters of Hy-Jet IV-A+ were brought aboard Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1 without knowledge to the flight crew. There was clear confusion and either misinformation or lack of information between the flight crew; Operations; and Maintenance. In the future on maintenance reposition flights; or any flight requiring equipment to be flown for maintenance; an itemized list of equipment that is being transported should be signed my maintenance personnel; one copy should go into records and the other copy should go to the flight deck to be reviewed by the flight crew. This way there is a clear paper trail of evidence and accountability in the event that anything like this should ever happen again.

column121: Just prior to the EEP(ETOPS Entry Point) on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we received an ACARS message from Dispatch informing us that a possible 'hoverboard' might have been loaded in the cargo area. It should not have been and with the dual concurrence of us and Dispatch it was decided that the safest course of action was an air return back to ZZZ. We discussed with Dispatch if they wanted us to burn down to a normal landing weight or land overweight. It was decided to land overweight and that Maintenance would met us at the gate and conduct the overweight inspection. We requested and received Runway 8L for landing due to its length and to minimize brake heating. The landing was normal and the overweight inspection was successfully accomplished and the 'hoverboard' was removed. Clearly; there was a breakdown somewhere that allowed an item of non approved Hazmat to be placed onboard the aircraft. How and why this happened is beyond the limited facts that I have available but I think a in-depth review of our processes and procedures with regards to these items would be warranted.
column123: Prior to reaching the ETOPS Entry Point and Oceanic Airspace; we received a message from Dispatch informing us of a safety of flight issue regarding some luggage onboard. A Hoverboard (non-permitted item) had somehow passed through TSA screening and had potentially been loaded in a cargo compartment. In conjunction with Dispatch; we felt the safest decision was to return to our departure airport of ZZZ. This required an overweight landing and maintenance inspection. Not only was the item found on our aircraft; but apparently two Hoverboards were found. More extensive checks or passenger questioning during the check-in and security phase. Passengers need to also be made aware of the seriousness of having such Hazmat items onboard a plane.

column123: Initially set up and briefed for the ILS XX. New ATIS was obtained with runway change to XYR just prior to runway transition point on the ZZZZZ Arrival.  Re briefed and set up for ILS XYR. column121: Pushed off of gate X - ramp told us to taxi to spot X.  Taxing out of alley from [gate] X - there are ZERO taxi lines.  Paint has been removed. Passing by spot Y; there was a plane coming in spot B blocking me from A.  There were ZERO taxi lines to be able to get around aircraft at spot B that started taxing. I told ramp that there were no taxi lines for me to get around other jet.  He asked me if I had my charts - which I did. He said it was construction.  Nothing in Jeppesen showed any 'alternate' taxi procedures.  There was a dashed yellow-black line to the North of standard taxi lines; but it went no where.  Later I could not find any mention of what a dashed yellow-black line meant in the AIM.  This was the first time I have taxied from X concourse to spot Z.CLT ramp just wants to move metal.  Having to switch to 3 different frequencies to get from one side of the ramp to the other is distracting.  Having ramp ask me if I have my charts or that due to construction I can taxi where I want is an accident waiting to happen.  There are ZERO lines to follow.  For us at night; unfamiliar - WITH our current charts out giving ZERO guidance and getting no help from ramp was was very uncomfortable. We stopped several times to make sure we had wing clearance with other aircraft taxiing.Publish and mark standard taxi lines during construction.

column123: Air return to ZZZ due to L FADEC caution during climb out. Dispatch and Maintenance notified and agreed. QRH completed; no emergency declared; return to ZZZ without incident. column121: On the departure; the First Officer (FO) had requested Heading Mode (HDG); Flight Level Change (FLCH) during the climb out as we were given a heading.  It was bumpy and he was trying to comply with the SID instructions to speed up to 250 KIAS while hand flying in bumpy air.  As we approached the 5;000 foot altitude restriction; he started to slow his climb for the level off; but didn't pull back on the thrust levers. The autothrottles were on; but we were not quite close enough to the altitude for the flight director to switch to 'ASEL' on the FMA and begin capturing. In a climb; the auto throttles remain at full thrust in green FLCH until ASEL is annunciated; and since the FO was hand flying and beginning the level off before the Altitude Select (ASEL) annunciation; the speed began to pick up.  As pilot monitoring; I noticed the airspeed at 255 KIAS with an increasing trend and I called out 'airspeed' to alert him to the airspeed.  He seemed confused and did not make any corrections. I then called for him to 'pitch up' which he did slightly; but he mentioned the level off altitude that was approaching.  I said to 'pull the thrust back' and he seemed confused again and replied that the auto throttles should do that.  I then pulled the thrust levers back myself to slow the aircraft down as the speed was starting to go past 260 KIAS.  ATC gave us a 'climb and maintain 7000' and a direct to one of the fixes.  The FO pitched up for the climb and I was able to let go of the thrust levers as the speed was again under control.  As we were climbing; ATC instructed us to climb to 16;000 and the FO called for 'Autopilot On' prior to the next level off so there were no further issues.  I reminded him that there is no speed protection in the level off for the FLCH mode if he is hand flying it and levels off early.   ATC didn't seem to notice the increased airspeed;  and the flight continued without further incident.The FO said that he finished IOE and for the next month was unable to get any flying from crew scheduling.  He had less than 30 hours on the aircraft.   The following month; he had to be in Country to check on family due to the COVID pandemic.  He said that he had flown earlier that day and seemed to be comfortable in the plane.  It became clear that he was rusty on the details concerning the FLCH mode.  After I spoke with him about what happened; he said he understood and he did not make the same mistake on his flight the following day. Any time a pilot has less than 100 hours (consolidation) on an aircraft; and doesn't fly for more than 30 days; they should be given a trip with an IOE instructor both to give them recency of experience and to refresh any forgotten material.
column123: During take off climbing to the assigned altitude of 5;000 in flight level change plane accelerated to 250K; during last 1;000 ft I shallowed the pitch as climb was getting a bit bumpy due to builds up around [the] area and I was trying to avoid flying through a cloud straight ahead. Captain advised me of speed increasing and passing 250 and I assumed the auto-throttle would have compensated for that as it was engaged. Leveling off to 5;000 speed past 260 and the Captain reached out the thrust lever decreasing power avoiding further deviation. Soon after cleared to 7;000 climb and flight continued with no further deviation. After IOE I was put on reserve and didn't fly for about a month; I then was able to pick up a line and fly just one sequence as a tragic event forced me to drop the rest of the month and travel overseas; as a result in 2 months I only flew 19 hours and that was my first day flying after a long stop. As newly typed on a new airplane I didn't immediately recalled the different ways the autothrottle responds; however soon after the event my Captain explained [to] me what happened and refreshed my memory on it. After IOE it would be good to assign some extra flight to help consolidate; maybe assigning more frequent flights and not letting more than 2 weeks without flying would avoid skills deterioration until the first 100 hours are reached.

column121: The following narrative is due to a complete lack of threat and error management and operation performance.   This was the first leg of a 4 day trip and I would be flying with a First Officer for the first time.   We were heavily delayed to start our day and weather was terrible.   High winds and windshear were reported throughout the whole Company system with several crews diverting.   Yet my release for this flight indicated nothing other than I should evaluate the use of Runway XX for ZZZ departure.   When the aircraft arrived I met the arriving Captain and he explained to me the auto pilot master warning EICAS message occurred at 1;000 feet on the coupled ILS approach into ZZZ.  The Captain stated maintenance refused to take the write ups as it was going to ZZZ1 and they would casually look at it there.   I immediately called maintenance and asked why they wouldn't take write ups and said from what it sounded like a write up was not warranted.   The maintenance controller asked if I wished to MEL the autopilot and I stated how can I?  At this point I should have immediately refused the plane; but at Company; refusing to fly gets us an immediate phone call from the Chief Pilot office.   We Were now operating in the red of the threat and error management philosophy.   On the way to ZZZ1 we experienced moderate turbulence as expected and when we turned base for Runway XY the field was surrounded by virga.  The FO and I briefed a go around and the windshear escape maneuver once more.   On final at about 1;200 feet the Autopilot Fail master warning EICAS  message appeared and the Autopilot disconnected.  I continued to hand fly the aircraft and remained stable to about 300 feet where I encountered increasing performance and the approach became unstable.   A normal go-around was executed and we called positive rate gear up; we received the windshear caution.   Immediately after we hit severe turbulence.  We diverted to ZZZ without further incident.  The remainder of the flight was performed without the autopilot.Company maintenance did not take a write up from a Captain. I wrote up the AP failure and the encounter with severe turbulence. All write-ups must be taken by maintenance.

column121: After completion of pushback and after receiving salute I flashed the landing light.  The push lead and a wing walker were observed walking away as the tug backed away from the aircraft.  Approximately 10-15 meters off the nose a small bag which apparently contained the push headset fell out of the tug cab where the bag and the headset fell apart laying on the ramp.  The tug driver saw it fall out his side of the cab and stopped.  As the tug driver stepped out of tug it began to roll towards our aircraft with the tow bar still mounted on the front like a battering ram.  The tug driver immediately jumped back in the cab and stopped the tug and manipulated some controls.  The cab driver was the only one in tug and rest of pushback crew was oblivious as they walked back to gate area.  I don't know if the tug has a parking brake but the tug driver again stepped out of the tug while it idled away from the aircraft towards the terminal.  The unmanned tug continued towards the terminal at a walking pace while the tug driver scooped the headset into the bag and then he jogged back and jumped in the moving tug.  The tug now under manned control continued back to the gate are and we taxied out for departure.I don't know if it was complacency or rushing to get out of our way or both but I would like to think push tugs both have a park position as well as a park brake both if which should have been used in this case in my opinion. Emphasize safety to ramp members to protect persons and property.

column121: All events through pushback were accomplished without note. During pushback; a puddle on the ramp aft of the normal oil spot was noticed behind the #2 engine. Puddle was not present on the walkaround. A stream of drops along the ramp was also noticed while the #2 engine was run. After five minutes the fuel leak had not stopped and we towed back to a gate. Maintenance was called; ran several tests; and two engine runs. The leak dissipated as the tests were completed. No fuel appeared to be leaking while engines were running; except for one within limits from the heat exchanger. Forms were completed to indicate it. Aircraft pushed and started again. No leaks were noted.Shortly after takeoff/cleanup; Captain announced a split in the thrust levers. Autothrottles were used for takeoff with VNAV (climb page 2L adjusted for 202 knots at 1;000 feet AGL). Looking at the engine instruments; I noticed the #2 thrust lever about three knob widths ahead of the #1. #1 N1 was at commanded power with the #2 N1 showing the white commanded power bar of about 95%; but the engine only producing about 88-89%. Further advancement of the throttle lever produced no increase in power. Vertical Speed was selected and we reduced our climb rate to bring the power back. As the power came back; the throttle synced and power matched. VNAV was reselected and as the power returned to full climb; the split reappeared with the #2 indicating a commanded increase without the engine delivering the power.As this was being discussed; the center tank fuel pumps were turned on (750 pounds in the center tank). Immediately after the pumps were turned on; the power matched and all indication were normal. As soon as the center tank fuel was exhausted; the split returned. Crew leveled at FL 270 and elected to return to ZZZ. As power was less than full climb at cruise/descent; and no abnormal indication were present during these flight conditions; no QRH Checklists were run. The rest of the return to ZZZ was completed without note. Engine performed as expected from level off to shutdown.Contract Maintenance expressed an increased level of calls from aircraft coming from the paint shop; fuel leaks were common with these aircraft.  Would recommend a Maintenance individual check and run engines prior to returning the aircraft to the line.
column123: Origination flight on an aircraft that had just come out of the paint shop. Preflight was uneventful with no fuel drips or puddles noted. We pushed five minutes early. On push back #2 was dripping fuel and did not stop after a short time and engine was shutdown. After consultation with Maintenance Control; we returned to the gate and called Contract Maintenance. Contract Maintenance did four motoring tests as directed by [company's] Maintenance. With each test; the dripping became improved. Then an engine run was completed with decreased dripping; but not to a small enough level to allow Dispatch. Contract Maintenance then opened the cowl and did an engine run to determine location of drip. After that run; the component dripping was identified and the dripping had decreased to an amount that allowed MEL. MEL was completed. This was about a 2.5 hour process. Ground Ops and Operations were very helpful with accommodating the Passengers as well as they could. I had given periodic in-person updates to the passengers. Finally; we pushed-back and the engine starts were uneventful without any drips. Uneventful taxi. We took off on Runway XX with a headwind 20G30. On push up of thrust; #2 lagged a bit and I pushed the thrust lever up to get closer to match and continued my crosscheck.  As we approached V1/VR I noticed #2 still lagging by a few percent and pushed up the throttle some more. Normal on centerline liftoff and climbout. After liftoff; I informed the F/O  (First Officer) that we had a split throttle situation. We cleaned up on schedule and began to evaluate the situation (again the aircraft had no adverse flight characteristics). With the aircraft cleaned up and climb power set; we observed that although the #2 demand pointer was correct; the #2 N1 lagged approximately 2-5% N1. Once our climb rate was reduced in Vertical Speed and at a slightly lower climb thrust setting; the engine was normal and tracked normally with the demand pointers and thrust lever position. To this point we had continued to follow ATC instructions to keep it simple. We found that the engine reacted the same with the autothrottle On or Off. Also we had 750 pounds of fuel in the center tank; so once established in the climb we turned the pumps on and immediately #2 N1 returned to normal operation at full climb power. When center tank was empty and pumps turned off; the malfunction returned. With this information we leveled off and informed ATC that we would probably need to return to the airport. While level we reconfirmed no other abnormal conditions or switches out of place. Also at level flight in this situation there were no conditions that warranted a QRH Checklist although it was discussed. F/O and I discussed the situation and decided that without the aircraft able to achieve full climb thrust on Main Fuel pumps only; the safest choice was to return to the airport. F/O flew and talked to ATC; while I informed flight attendants and passengers of need to return to the airport for safety reasons and gave them our ETA. I called Station Ops on VHF and informed them of our need to return; get a gate; and asked them to contact Dispatch. We also confirmed via ACARS with Dispatch the need to return due to engine unable to achieve full climb power (or something like that). The F/O did a very good job and stayed ahead of the aircraft preparing for the briefings; descent; and Approach Checklist. We referenced the Diversion Checklist to ensure we had covered the suggested items. We accomplished a normal descent and asked for a long visual approach to increase probability of a stable approach and landing without the need for a thrust needful go-around. F/O flew stable approach and landing with normal braking. No emergency was declared; no special handling requested; and a normal weight landing occurred. Uneventful taxi-in and shutdown. Flight was canceled and the passengers accommodated as best as Ops could. Debrief with the flight attendants yielded that although disappointed in their flight being cancelled; they were appreciative of the Safety of turning back. Immediate notification with XXXXXX was done after engine shutdown with Dispatch; Supervisor; Maintenance; and Chief Pilot.The Location X crews both above the wing and below the wing were very familiar with the Maintenance trouble shooting of engine drips on starts because they have seen it more the once from aircraft coming out of the paint shop.  An engine run after paint shop would have found this problem before a revenue flight was disrupted.  Maybe this may be a prudent practice--an ounce or prevention may have saved a pound of Customer frustration.  Perhaps a faster crosscheck by myself might have allowed a reject option in the 70-90 knot range; but even then there was no decrease in power and I perceived the N2 engine thrust close-enough to N1 engine thrust to ensure a safer option than a medium speed reject.

column121: We finished the first leg of three on the last day of a three-day trip. We pulled into the gate at LAS with a scheduled plane swap. After completing the Parking Checklist and other post-flight duties; I cleared the FO to head out while I stayed with the aircraft while passengers deplaned. Ground power was connected initially but air was not. As deplaning commenced; I asked the agent to call for ground air. It was 106F OAT and I was concerned about cabin temp. I understood from the agent that the aircraft would be on the ground for some time. After all passengers were off; I went outside and asked Ramp to connect ground air. A few minutes later one of the guys came to the cockpit and informed me that ground air was inop. In the meantime; one of the new FAs (flight attendants) came onboard saying she came down early because the terminal was very crowded. As the situation progressed I decided to leave the APU on for cabin cooling; informed the FA and agent and went on to my new aircraft. At the time I didn't give it a second thought. It wasn't until I got to the new aircraft; finished preflight duties and had a few minutes to reflect that I realized my error. Sick feeling. I told the FO that I would be back and hustled back to the previous gate to remedy my mistake. Probably 30 minutes or so had elapsed since I had left it. By the time I got back to the gate The new crew was onboard and passengers were boarding.I must say that I didn't feel any type of particular time pressure or any major distraction. I'm not sure why my thought process went so awry. While this situation is not common; I'm sure it's not unheard of and I should know better than to leave the APU running and Terminating Checklist incomplete. I certainly could have stayed with the aircraft until the new Crew arrived.I am sure that I hadn't reviewed FOM in some time so unless I'm the only one who has messed up this way; adding that to our training profile may raise awareness to this issue and prevent someone else from making the same mistake.

The gate was unusual for (Company) operations; and we had to deal with broken jetway stairs and ground power that was disconnected during boarding. These were both stress inducers; and we should have recognized that we were being pushed into the Yellow before we even left the gate. The Captain was unfamiliar with the airport. I could have done a better job walking him through the taxi procedures. I should have realized this would cause a distraction while starting the second engine. We were on a MAX departing for an ETOPS flight; and fuel is almost always a consideration during taxi out. We chose to delay APU start at the gate and single engine taxi to conserve as much as possible. We even briefed the earlier start because of lengthy MAX engine motoring; but it still wasn't early enough to be complete before crossing [Runway] XXL. We should have started the engine earlier so I could concentrate on one thing at a time. Both the Captain and I were new to ETOPS flying. We were in and out of the Yellow during preflight as we worked through the extra preflight procedures. We should have given ourselves more time to complete these tasks.

column121: The event happened at night on taxi out from gate to Runway XXL. column123: We had been reassigned after a long weather delay and misconnect out of ZZZ.  We had to consult with dispatch to confirm our clearance and routing. column121: We were operating our flight ZZZ to ZZZ1. This flight operates at close to if not at its max weight where maximum performance from the aircraft and crew are required due to the short runways. Headwind operations; or more importantly; absence of any tailwinds; should be the main concern of ATC and pilots when utilizing this airport when such performance is required.In the hours prior to this flight ZZZ was running a south operation; departing RWY XX; as one would expect with a reasonable headwind (180/7kts). Approximately 20 minutes before departure; they switched to a north operation; now departing RWY XY. This change seemed illogical as it now was using a runway that had a 7 knot tailwind for takeoff. With this change our flight was unable to depart as we were too heavy due to a tailwind weight penalty of 9;030 lbs from our runway limit.I asked ZZZ Ground/Tower Control why they had changed to a north operation. The answer we received was that arriving aircraft on the XXXXX Visual were encountering a tailwind at altitude and therefore the change. This puzzled me. Is this an official procedure that the FAA ATC has at ZZZ or shouldn't runway selection for takeoff and landing be based on surface winds?We had no choice but to wait for an opening for RWY XX; which caused a significant delay to our companies reliability operation; not to mention putting other aircraft in an awkward position of either compromising safety margins or accepting lengthy delays. Switching runways around based on winds at altitude rather than safety of landing and departing on short runways with tailwinds; puts the pilots in the position as the last line of defense for safety.  Just FYI; we also only had one reverser. Although RTO does not include the reversers in its stopping distance calculations; it was still a consideration to us.ATC changing runways from a headwind to a strong tailwind. Putting pilots in a less optimal position to operate their aircraft.The additional work load and max performance requirements when utilizing a short runway with a tailwind should be avoided as much as possible especially at ZZZ. Every foot of runway concrete is paramount to operating safely at this airport. Therefore every knot of tailwind compromises that safety margin.

column121: I was Pilot Flying. I triggered a stick shaker/pusher at the Final Approach Fix. I recovered per SOP.[There was] a northbound squall line west of the field. A last minute wind shift caused us to switch runways. Although it was fast; we were able to set up and brief before intercepting course. ATC forgot to turn [us] on the ILS; so we went through the localizer course. This led to reactionary vectors and the aircraft doing S turns until we passed the final approach fix. At this point we were flaps 30 with the power reduced. I called for the go-around; but when I pressed the autopilot disconnect button; I became fixated on the lack of a missed approach course. (I didn't press the TO-GA button.) While troubleshooting; the airspeed continued to decrease leading to a simultaneous stick shaker and pusher. I lowered the nose and recovered per the training; paying special attention to the radar altimeter. I briefly oversped flaps 8 on recovery.Stall recovery training works. I was able to accomplish the recovery quickly without having to think about it. However; it shouldn't have gotten that far. It was my first go-around since OE. I was task saturated and in the moment couldn't remember where the TO-GA button was. We were able to handle weather; ATC error; runway changes and an instrument approach at the same time. However; because our go around was triggered at a relatively untrained aircraft state/position; I missed a critical aspect of the maneuver. I don't believe this is a common problem; but incorporating go-arounds during recurrent in various positions may be beneficial.

column121: While taxiing into [spot]; it was raining with lowered visibility. The ramp agents were standing in position with the exception of the marshaller. The Safedock system was in operation; and I saw an agent by the controls. I followed the line clearly marked [spot]; which was between both wing walkers. Directly in front of this line; which was angled to the left; was the door marked [spot]. I had line of sight to Safedock. As a newer Captain; I did not have any reason to doubt that this was my 'J' line to follow. As I approached and passed the large [spot] painted on the ground; I realized that it was a dashed line; rather than a solid. Just as I noticed this; a marshaller appeared to my left. The marshaller then waved his flags at me and pointed to my left. I then realized that there was another [spot] line; and that I was in the wrong one.The marshaller emphatically waved his batons to my left; and I believed he was directing me left to exit the ramp. I had my FO [First Officer] call Ramp Control and got clearance to turn left and swing back around for the correct 'J' line. I received that approval. I conducted the turn after the marshaller again waved me to the left.I was able to gain clear sight of the vehicles on both sides and noticed no impediment to my progress. I turned around on the taxi lane and entered the straight in 'J' line using Safedock.My FO said that he then saw some markings for the slanted line that indicated it might be for an B737.I was approached by a Ramp Supervisor upon exiting the aircraft. He stated that I had 'jet blasted' his rampers during my exit turn. I explained my perspective; given that I believed I was following the ramper's direction. He told me that 'Next time; call for a tug.' I told him that I understood his concerns; expressly apologized for my confusion during the parking; and that I would heed his advice in the future.[Causes]1) My inexperience as a Captain2) The addition of 'J' lines for B737 aircraft that lined up with safe dock; were labeled exactly the same as the ones for Airline aircraft3) Rain and visibility issues4) Last leg of a day that began [early]5) Confusing and very late directions given by marshaller[Suggestions]1) Use this as a learning tool with respect to ground operations2) Given the human factors present in this event; I believe there needs to be changes to the paint for B737 'J' lines.3) More focus in inclement weather4) Recognize that fatigue can play a role at every stage of a flight; including taxiing to park5) Use my own judgment when given instructions that don't seem to be correct/ safe.

column121: While in cruise at FL400; I noticed cabin altitude display illuminate Amber on upper EICAS showing cabin altitude of 8300 feet and rising at 300-400 ft/min.  Aircraft was dispatched with one pack deferred; two operating. I brought up the ECS schematic to verify Packs 2 and 3 were both supplying pressure and in High Flow. They appeared to be operating normally; but I then noticed a Status message with a Pack 2 fault; cabin altitude was already 9;000 ft. and still climbing. At this point I requested a descent from ATC to FL 360.  They gave us a vector for descent.  A minute later; with Cabin altitude of 9300 ft.; I informed ATC we had a pressurization issue and needed to descend.  We were given FL390 and then a few minutes later; FL360.  Pressurization stabilized at 8;500 ft.; but began to climb again at 100-200 ft/min. We requested and were given FL 320.  I notified Operations Control via ACARS (SATCOM inop); that we had a Pack 2 issue and that we had descended as cabin altitude had been increasing. They were given our fuel and told I would keep them advised. We were at FL 280; where cabin altitude at stabilized; but showing slight increase. I recommended to divert to ZZZ along our route of flight; but they informed me they wanted the airplane in ZZZ1.  I informed ATC that we needed to change our destination for 'maintenance' from ZZZ2 to ZZZ1.  We were given proceed direct ZZZ1; about 350 miles away; where we landed uneventfully.Cruise flight when cabin altitude appeared amber on Upper EICAS.Strictly a maintenance issue with the aircraft. We had Pack 1 deferred and any issue with the remaining Packs was going to cause pressurization issues.To assess the situation; attempt to bring pressurization under control; and descend as necessary to reduce cabin altitude.  QRH was utilized to validate what pressurization reading we should have at the various altitudes.Aircraft was dispatched to pick up freight in ZZZ2; and then proceed with a Pack deferred.
column123: Pushback; taxi; takeoff and climb were completely normal. Weather on departure were calm winds and decent VFR in the terminal area. The weather became more marginal upon leveling at cruise. On this leg I myself was the First Officer and Flying Pilot. The Captain was the Pilot Not flying. We also had a Relief Pilot on board and loadmaster.  The event began somewhat early in cruise at FL400 when the Captain noticed a cabin altitude display Amber on the Upper EICAS display. He then immediately selected the ECS page and we both were made aware of a 8;300 foot cabin and rising at 300-400 fpm. The aircraft was dispatched with Pack #1 deferred; therefore packs 2 and 3 operating normally. After diagnosing the situation via the ECS page; both packs 2 and 3 appeared to be supplying pressure and in High Flow as designed when one pack is selected off.  However on the Lower EICAS we both noticed a Status message with a Pack 2 fault. Cabin altitude was still climbing and at this point showing 9;000 feet and still climbing. At this point we agreed to suggest a decent to FL360 and were given a vector for decent. About a minute later with Cabin Altitude of 9;300 feet the Captain informed ATC that we had a pressurization issue and needed to descend now; we first were given a decent to FL390 and shortly after to FL360. At FL360 we observed the cabin initially stabilizing at 8;500 feet; but shortly afterwards began again climbing at a lower rate than previously of 100-200 FPM.  We again agreed to request a lower altitude of FL320 and ATC cleared us to FL320. The Captain then notified Operations Control of the situation via ACARS (SATCOM Inop) that we had a PACK 2 issue and we were descending with a cabin altitude still slowly increasing. The Captain requested further decent to FL280 and ATC complied. At FL280 we experienced a cabin altitude almost stable at around 8;000 feet but still trying to climb at a slow interment 100 FPM. The Captain notified the rest of the crew including the Relief Pilot and load master. The Relief Pilot was taking his rest but immediately returned to the cockpit to help in CRM and dealing with the situation. I suggested the Relief Pilot pull up the cabin altitude chart showing what the cabin altitude should be for our current altitude so we would know how far off from normal we were.  All 3 crew members talked about possible diversion airports and relayed our ideas to Operations Control. After communication between Operations Control and us it was decided by Operations Control to divert to ZZZ2 to address and fix the situation. The Captain immediately requested to divert to ZZZ2 and informed ATC as to why; and I put us on a course to ZZZ2 via ATC instructions. At this point we were about 350 miles north of ZZZ2 with plenty of fuel and sufficient weather for landing. It was agreed that the F/O would disregard the pitch guidance until the instrumentation issue could be corrected. Captain continued running through the checklist from the QRH; it was determined that the F/O's instrumentation was valid; and the Captain selected the right side Air Data Compute (ADC). From that point forward; as we slowed to 250 knots; the airplane essentially flew normally. F/O continued to manually hand fly the descent and approach to an uneventful landing. After inspection; the aircraft was taxied back normally. column121: Taxi clearance: taxi from ramp position XX;  right turn onto W3; left turn EW; right turn S7A; then S7; hold short S7C.    As a crew; we were a little bit tired from our 1st leg in the middle of the night; our scheduled ground stop time plus the delay as maintenance took care of a Pressure Regulating Valve issue.    In any case; if you take a look at the VVNB Airport Moving Map (AMM) taxi chart; it appears as though EW is a separate taxiway. The color differentiation of light gray versus the ramp coloration of dark gray gives the impression we would be taxiing from the ramp onto a separate; defined taxiway; not onto a yellow line that is at the outer edge of a parking ramp. In addition; S1 (the taxiway that is adjacent and parallel to EW) had green lights illuminated; again giving the impression S1 was the active taxiway EW. So as we taxied via W3; EW looks like it's part of the ramp. In other words it does not appear to be EW taxiway. S1 appears to be EW. The poor signage does not help as well. Clearly the main issue here is that we had never been to Hanoi and never experienced this. That said; as we taxied out and entered S6A; the intersection between EW and S1; my copilot notified me we had passed EW. We stopped there. We advise ground we missed EW and needed to take S1. Ground control gave us S1; routed us back onto EW; then S7A; S7 and then our takeoff. That said; no conflict with any traffic; only one maybe two other aircraft moving on the airport at that time. Ultimately it was a non critical event.    To help prevent this from happening in the future; a caution note regarding taxiing at any time (i.e. taxing in or taxing out) when given EW would be helpful.
column123: After setting up the cockpit for the ZZZZ1-ZZZZ leg; we sat in the back to rest while Maintenance was working with an MEL item.  The aircraft was one hour later than schedule to allow extra time for maintenance.  Fatigue was now starting to show after two 18-24hr overnights in lockdown.    After final setup and brief; we received our taxi clearance; from spot XX; E3.EW.S7A.S7.S7C hold short [Runway] 11L.  We discussed the route that appeared clearly marked on the Airport Moving Map (AMM) page and began taxiing.  We realized we had crossed beyond the centerline of EW and were unable to make the turn and stopped.  After calling the controller of our position; he gave us S1.S6A.EW....the rest was normal.    Looking back; the green taxi lights were lit on S1.S6A.EW and FD Pro AMM page in dark mode makes EW look very different from the ramp area.  Expectation bias may have played a role in how controllers have started using follow the greens (used in SIN but not in HAN) and what we interpret as a clearance.  I will personally pay closer attention to where we are in the future.

column121: The crew flew the RNAV X RWY to 34R at RNO in day clear weather with winds reported at 260/26G31. During the flare; the crew executed a go around due to a strong gust destabilizing the approach. During climb out; the Tower Controller called the winds stronger out of the West and suggested a visual approach to Runway 25. Although having reviewed the 10-7 Special Considerations page earlier in the flight; the crew did not recall the takeoff and landing restriction on Runway 25.The crew configured for a 5 mile visual approach to Runway 25; then briefed and commenced the approached. Descending on the approach with the terrain visible and safely below the aircraft; it became apparent that the terrain east of the airport would not allow a safe approach. At approximately the same time; our descent rate in combination with the terrain resulted in a brief 'Terrain' warning; the pilot flying adjusted the aircraft flight path and then executed a go-around. The crew then flew and landed from the RNAV X to RWY 34R. I believe rushing and a false sense of familiarity with the airport led to an incomplete recognition of all the information in the 10-7 pages. I have operated into RNO regularly but not often and always to light winds down the primary runway. Arrivals and approaches are briefed extensively and flown according to standards. The day of the event; we conducted a thorough briefing for the approach; to include reviewing the operating manual about the exact procedures for executing the EO (Engine out) SIDs at RNO and which RNAV approaches we were authorized to fly.Despite my review; to include Special Considerations/Restrictions; I did not refresh the [Runway] 7/25 restriction in my mind and in the moment I did not recall the critical restriction. Additionally at the time; I did not feel like we rushed the visual approach. However; I now realize that I was focused too much on flying a stable visual approach and landing into the wind and not taking the time to truly review the approach and missed approach. Take the time to thoroughly familiarize yourself with all the applicable notes during your airport review and briefings.
column123: RNAV X 34R to RNO in day VMC; reported winds were very close to limits (260/26 G31). Due to an extremely strong gust which destabilized our approach we executed a go around. After max effort go around and stabilized climbing clean; Tower suggested we use Runway 25. Even though we had both reviewed the 10-7 pages earlier in the flight; at that particular moment we did not recall the prohibition to landing on that Runway. After agreeing that we would look at it; I as Pilot Monitoring set up the box for a visual by extending a 3 degree GS to an extended 5 mile Center Line to give us VTI.The Pilot Flying double checked the 10-9A page and the landing app. While still considering this option; we maneuvered towards the extended Center Line and set and then descended to an altitude above the depicted altitude in that area. Our rate of descent combined with rising terrain triggered the EPGWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) to a 'TERRAIN' call. The Pilot Flying immediately altered his flight path and the terrain remained visible and well below us. It became abundantly clear that a stable approach would not be possible and we abandoned this option. We opted for another attempt at the RNAV 34R; and despite strong gusty crosswinds were able to maintain a stable condition to touchdown and landing.Things I have taken away from this event: The winds Tower reports may not be the winds you experience at the Runway. By sticking to a ridged stable approach and associated Standard Operating Procedure's mantra we kept from bending metal; violating a FAR; exceeding a limit or attempting something really stupid. And although RNO is a complex city and we review the notes every time we go there; the [Runway] 25 note was momentarily forgotten. We reviewed the 10-9a pages but somehow forgot to review the 10-7 pages in that situation. A mistake I (or my First Officer) will never make again.I firmly believe that this is a onetime incident. A few moments either way and we would have missed the gust and landed uneventfully. And I have a hard time imagining that another crew; or me again; would ever forget the 10-7 notes in a complex city. But again thanks to our training department's dogma regarding stable approaches; we are self-reporting not something far worse.

The aircraft showed a little high on the path but was correcting and it showed very close to the speed restriction of 230 kts.  I sat back down and verified the restrictions on my tablet. There was a lot of foreign language chatter on the radio. Upon crossing the fix; Shanghai issued a clearance direct to MPI which was the IAF for the approach to [Runway] 16L.  It wasn't until after we landed that the PF and PM were talking about being high over the PD230 fix however they agreed they were on speed.Understanding which arrival they were trying to issue took more time than necessary.  The pronunciation of the arrival was very hard to understand. This complicated things more than usual and it cost time. The frequency congestion in a foreign language complicated things when trying to get them to repeat the clearance.  On a side note this was the first time I've ever heard an approach clearance to a runway with a Left designator as 'Cleared for 16 Lima' ...the PM was corrected to say 16 Lima after she responded with 16 Left.  it didn't make sense.  When passed on to the Tower Controller; they correctly said 16 Left.My only suggestion is if you look high on a path; Flight Level Change works pretty good to hustle down to the altitude.  I can't say for sure if this descent was done in PATH or FLC.  The language barrier is what it is and probably won't change much.

column121: At approximately XA:30 hours; just moments prior to boarding; I smelled a very strong; musty; wet dog like odor inside the cabin. I immediately called out to the lead F/A and asked her to come back to observe what I was smelling. [Lead F/A] stated she could also smell the odor. Accordingly; I immediately made my way to the cockpit. The odor became so strong that my throat started to burn; and I began coughing. I told the Captain that we were being fumed and that I was going to notify the boarding agent to immediately stop boarding in order to prevent further issues (i.e. passenger exposure.) The Captain stated that he was notifying maintenance and agreed to hold boarding. I left the aircraft (no passengers were onboard). While making my way up the jet bridge to notify the agent; customers were beginning to walk down the jet bridge since boarding had commenced. I was able to stop the passengers and advised them to stop; turn around and go back into the terminal since we were having maintenance come to the aircraft. I did not advise them why. I entered into the terminal and advised the agent in a discreet manner to stop boarding as we were experiencing an aircraft fume event. I then returned to the aircraft briefly to advise the Captain that the agent was notified. The crew exited the aircraft and we remained in the jet bridge area for a few moments until maintenance arrived. We collected our belongings and exited the jet bridge into the terminal to gain better air quality. I continued to experience a burning throat and my cough continued. At that time; it was prudent to seek medical attention; therefore; I contacted Medical to seek advisement. I was given a clinic appointment at [medical name] and was seen by a doctor accordingly.Improper aircraft maintenance was the cause.Recommendations  - Contacting numerous departments; is too much following an incident like this. One call should automatically provide the needed support; guidance and direction that we require during events like this. Because this is my 3rd fume event; I was able to more quickly identify the inherent risks; take appropriate action to limit passenger exposure; and limit extended exposure; however; it was still medically concerning and we should have less calls to make following these dangerous occurrences.
column123: During the preflight the ground air was not sufficient to cool the aircraft.  I had the ground crew turn off the ground air and the CA started the APU. column121: As this report is not timely; it is to the best of my recollection. Approach phase of the flight to DEN. Briefed and installed the SSKII 2 RNAV/ILS 16R. On arrival we a received multiple speed and heading changes but we were back on course and LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. At some point prior to CLIFF; for whatever reason ATC changed clearance to RNAV 16R for us and the Aircraft (AC) behind us. I was Pilot Not Flying (PNF) so I installed the approach/transition. The AC ahead of us was in sight and was on the arrival but still assigned the ILS 16R. The approach was verified by both the First Officer (FO) and myself. LNAV/VNAV were still engaged and the speed window was open as ATC had already been assigning speed changes. The FO located the Approach briefing guide for the RNAV/RNP approach and RNP values for the approach were line selected and installed. All altitudes for the approach were verified.  I made the comment that 'Since ATC has been messing with our speed so much; the speed window is already open'. So far the approach was flawless and the aircraft (AC) was on the vertical and lateral profile.Upon reaching CLIFF the AC began a descent as it should have. TDZ had been set and VNAV Path was engaged. As we approached CEPEE the MCP/FMA's had not changed SPD/LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. The magenta track depicted CLIFF;CEPEE;AAGEE;JABRO;JETSN; RW 16R; as it should. It was upon arrival at CEPEE that the event occurred. The AC continued to descend and VNAV path remained engaged. But; the AC continued to track straight ahead. CEPEE had not become active and the vector leg out of CLIFF was still engaged. I had been so concerned with the vertical profile that I failed to notice CEPEE was not active. Realizing what had happened I went to the FMC to LS AAGEE; but ATC noticed at the same time and assigned us either a 080 or 090 heading. ATC also canceled the RNAV approach clearance for the AC behind us. We landed without further issue. Once inside the terminal; still pissed that I allowed this to happen; I located the Captain of the AC that landed behind us to apologize. He informed us that ATC had mistakenly given him the # to call. I took the number (#) and called immediately. After a conversation with the supervisor I was informed that there was no safety issue; no loss of separation; and no need to file a report.Looking back; how this could have been avoided... first of all; I could have just said 'unable' when ATC switched us to the RNAV RNP 16R. Although not a big deal at the time...after flying all night; briefing and installing one arrival and approach then; at the last minute being reassigned to a RNAV/ RNP approach which requires lots of briefing and changes; and programming; was probably not the thing to do. What else could I have done...I allowed myself to get distracted. I should have continually monitored the lateral path to insure the AC was doing what we thought it was going to do. It was very clear and it was easy to look outside to follow traffic. It was also the FO's first Pilot Flying leg so there was instruction taking place and attention was diverting to multiple places.The FO did a great job when we were reassigned to the RNAV RNP Z 16R. He did not miss a checklist; procedure; or setting.I'm disgusted that I allowed this to happen. I am unfortunately or fortunately very familiar with the airspace and lateral/ vertical deviation issues in the area. I'm not the first and sure won't be the last; but I know what I will and won't do next time.
column123: During the SSKII 2 RNAV Arrival phase; we were advised by ATC to expect the ILS 16R approach. A few minutes prior to CLFFF; the last point on the SSKII 2 arrival; we were assigned the RNAV (RNP) Z R16R approach. We were on a northerly heading in HDG mode at this time for vectors for the previously expected ILS. The Captain; as Pilot Monitoring (PM); selected the correct RNAV Z 16R approach as well as the correct transition (CLFFF transition) in the FMC. I verified the selected approach and transition after he did so. I then set up the approach per all steps of the Approach Briefing Guide and briefed the approach. We were then given direct CLFFF and selected LNAV. We were cleared for the RNAV RNP Z R16R approach shortly before arriving at CLFFF. Upon arriving at CLFFF; I verified that the CLFFF waypoint sequenced in the FMC to ensure we were now on a published segment of the approach. I selected LNAV; VNAV; opened the speed window for the appropriate speed; requested the PM set touchdown zone elevation (which he did); and verified that the ENGAGED FMA's were in green LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft began a descent per the VPATH glide slope. I ran through the items again to verify that the approach was proceeding correctly. I verified again that the FMA's showed an engaged green LNAV and engaged green VPATH. The approach was proceeding as expected. At the CEPEE waypoint; the aircraft should have begun a right turn towards the AAGEE as part of the track towards the final approach point and final approach course. The aircraft did not turn and continued in a straight course after passing CEPEE. I immediately checked the FMA's again to ensure it did not revert to HDG mode. The FMA's were still in green; engaged LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft was also still in an expected VPATH descent to the TDZE. Within a few seconds; and before we could figure out why the aircraft did not turn; ATC called to cancel the RNAV approach and gave us a right turn for a visual approach to runway 16R and gave clearance for the visual approach. We proceeded uneventfully for the visual approach and landing. After arriving at the gate and leaving the aircraft; a pilot from another aircraft that was behind us during the arrival and approach advised us that he was mistakenly given a phone number by ATC to call regarding the RNAV Z 16R turning issue that we actually experienced. We got the phone number from him and the Captain called. The ATC supervisor said that no report would be required; there was no loss of separation; there was no safety issue; and how just wanted to know what happened. The Captain and I reviewed everything we did in setting up; preparing; and executing that approach and could not figure any reason why the aircraft did not initiate a turn at CEPEE and continued straight while engaged in LNAV with the proper approach waypoints; altitudes; and sequencing verified in the FMC.

column121: Flight was cleared for approach into Runway XX at ZZZ. After noticing the approach was too high; the flight crew executed a go-around and missed approach. The flight crew then tried to re-establish contact with ATC but was not successful. After reaching missed approach altitude the flight crew decided to turn and make left hand traffic for Runway XX; where we made a visual approach and landing while making position reports on the local CTAF frequency. After landing; it was realized that the flight crew could have potentially violated the proper missed approach procedure or additional approach clearances into ZZZ after not being able to contact ATC. After parking at gate; Captain called ATC via phone to cancel IFR.One possible cause could be the relatively rare experience of flying into an uncontrolled field at night and the procedures that are associated with that. There was also some confusion about the type of approach the flight was cleared to execute; in this case; RNAV or visual approach into Runway XX. We believed we were cleared for the visual approach. However; being unable to contact ATC added confusion and doubt to the situation after landing. Flight delays most likely added stress as well.The first suggestion for future experiences would be to be more mindful and diligent about confirming the type of approach we are cleared to execute. This would have clarified the proper procedure when executing a go-around. A second potential solution would have been to gain altitude in order to try and contact ATC. As for the approach; the flight crew could have requested vectors to leave and then rejoin the approach when the aircraft was at a more appropriate altitude before needing to execute the go-around.
column123: After executing the go around; [we] climbed to pattern altitude to make a left traffic pattern instead of executing the published missed approach. column121: Upon accepting Aircraft X; the inbound Captain; told me details about an MEL for Bulk Fuel Temp. He stated that there was an associated CAS MISCOMP" (Crew Alerting System Miscomparison) status message and that this was relayed to him by the previous Captain. They had no issues on their flight. We accept aircraft and depart ZZZ1. Not long after reaching cruise about 60 miles SE of ZZZ we lost our left fuel tank quantity indication along with our total fuel quantity indication. I had also recently updated the fuel in the FMS after reaching cruise altitude. Due to the MEL; we had been monitoring the fuel system for any possible errors and we had additional fuel after reaching altitude than planned. Right before we lost our left fuel indication both tanks were even. We did not receive any cautions; nor any indication on the fuel EICAS page of a "Fuel Channel Fail" status or caution like you are supposed to. After approximately 3 minutes of no left tank fuel quantity indication; we referred to the QRH for "Fuel CH 1/2 FAIL" for guidance and equalized our fuel flow between engines. In this circumstance; in addition to another aspect of already have a MEL on the "BULK FUEL TEMP"; along with not receiving EICAS indications like the system is designed to; we decided to divert to ZZZ. At some point during the beginning half of our descent to ZZZ; our left fuel quantity indication came back but my decision to divert was already made. We didn't have any fuel indication for approximately 8-12 minutes. We followed all procedures as far as alerting Dispatch; Flight Attendant; ATC; made a PA to passengers; In range to the line; followed by below the line and ensured we would not be overweight. We did not declare an emergency at that time. Upon getting vectors to final approach for runway; we intercepted the localizer below the glide slope. Approx 7-8 mile final when I called for 'Gear Down; Flaps 30;' but the gear did not move. Shortly after we received a "GEAR DISAGREE" master warning. We were at approx 3;400 ft flying the glide slope and not yet past [the] FAF so instead of calling for a go around; I disconnected the autopilot and asked for delay vectors to troubleshoot. We received an altitude assignment of 3;000 ft; heading 190; which required a descent.We then ran the QRH for "GEAR DISAGREE"; and after multiple attempts using the gear handle we used the alternate gear extension as called for in the QRH. All three gear came down and were indicating green. At this point I let ATC know we were ready to return for landing and we requested priority and to have trucks ready just in case. We also followed procedures to inform company of the [situation] and informed the flight attendants (FAs) of new situation. We also told the FAs to perform a "BRACE" command just in case due to the QRH stating directional control on the runway might be difficult. We ran through all the proper procedures except for the Go Around checklist. Looking back; we should have even though we did not miss any items. At the time; I did not consider the vectors as a go around due to being 6 miles out and having to descend to the assigned altitude. Upon touchdown; we received a "STEERING INOP" caution and I noticed directional control required more rudder than normal. Runway XXL does not have any high speed exits so we stopped on the runway; coordinated with airport command; and waited for buses to deplane the passengers.We did not use a tug to be pulled off the runway because I was unsure if the alternate gear extension was applying pressure to the nosewheel similar to nosewheel steering. I talked to Maintenance and they were also unsure. We did our best to keep the passengers up to date while waiting for the buses to deplane the passengers. We did not evacuate as there was no imminent danger after landing and the runway being closed. Unrelated to the gear; I should not have assumed and trusted another persons word that a CAS MISCOMP (Crew Alerting System Miscomparison) status message was in association to an MEL without verify the MEL procedure; and not just reviewing the MEL. We should have written that up at the gate in ZZZ1 although it may be completely unassociated to all our issues. I should have called for the go-around checklist to reconfirm we completed all the items even though we did not do a go-around maneuver."

column121: We were taking off from ELP on Runway 22 and had an initial clearance for the TDOWN3 RNAV Departure.  Tower cleared us for takeoff with revised clearance to turn left to 200 and climb to 17;000 [feet].  I was the flying pilot manually flying.  As we were accelerating and getting the aircraft to a clean configuration we were issued a frequency change to Departure.  Upon checking in we were immediately given further instructions which included a right turn after reaching 6;200 feet to 060.  Both of us misunderstood the turn right part of the clearance.  The FO (First Officer) read back 'passing 6;200 heading 060' and had no response from the controller.  We climbed through 6;200 and turned left. We were about half way through the left turn when the controller saw the mistake and told us it was a right turn; but then told us to continue the left turn.  He later asked us to call them for possible pilot certificate action. There are several causal factors [due to direction of turn by flight crew].  First; having a clearance for an RNAV departure that has a left turn from Runway 22 sets you up to expect a left turn out for protected airspace even after receiving a last minute change to the departure plan using radar vectors.  Because the radar vectors are given last minute the old departure stays in the FMC showing the original route on our map displaying that left turn; so even though we were not following the route displayed it probably influenced our thought pattern.  There is no published departures turning out to the right from Runway 22 due to mountainous terrain if you are departing east.  Secondly; we also had prebriefed the engine failure procedures that have you turn out to the left for the same reason.  Third; from a 200 heading to turn right to 060 is counter intuitive because it is more than 180 degree turn. All of these factors I think caused expectation bias to turn left and not hear the right turn instruction.  Fourth; the controllers failure to emphasize the right turn part when it is more than 180 from current heading and his not ensuring the read back was correct. Controllers need to emphasize the direction of turn especially if it's more than 180 degrees and ensure they get a correct read back.  On the phone the controller said this was normal to avoid traffic from Mexico.  If this is a common procedure to use radar vectors to turn us out an opposite direction of our assigned clearance then there needs to be some notes somewhere in our charts so we can prepare for that ahead of time.  This non published procedure could cause conflicts with terrain in the event of an engine failure.
column123: The missed approach and takeoff engine failure profiles for Runway 22 tell you to turn left.  The TDOWN 3 SID; we were assigned; tells you to turn left off of Runway 22.  The reason all of the departures turn left on Runway 22 at El Paso is because there is high terrain if you turn right.  On takeoff; we were told to climb to 17;000 feet and turn left to heading 200.  When we contacted Departure; the controller quickly blurted out a long; involved clearance.  I responded; 'Passing 6.2; turn to 060.'  He did not respond back to my radio call.  On a heading of 200; the heading of 060 is to the left.  As we entered the left turn to 060; the controller informed us that he had told us to turn right to 060; he also told us to expedite our left turn and continue to a heading of 010.  When we rolled out on the heading; he told us to call a phone number because of a potential violation.  I read the phone number back to him and asked him to verify.  He did not respond because he was working two frequencies; and was talking to another aircraft on the other frequency. When we called the phone number for El Paso Departure Control; they told us that left turns off Runway 22 often conflict with traffic at a Mexican airport.  So; they often vector you to the right.  The Captain and I have both been in and out of El Paso numerous times; and have never gotten a right turn off Runway 22.  None of our guidance for El Paso says to expect a right hand turn.  Expectation bias caused us to hear 'turn to 060' instead of 'turn right to 060.'  Also; the Departure Controller was working two frequencies and did not catch that we said 'turn to 060.'  Here is what he blurted at us at 1;000 feet AGL while we were retracting the flaps; '[company name]; radar contact; turn right to 060 and climb to 17;000.'  He also had a thick; Hispanic accent.  If the keyword was 'right'; it didn't help that he placed it in the middle of a sentence with no emphasis or follow up. If left departures off Runway 22 conflict with Mexican air traffic; perhaps they need an updated departure procedure.  The ATKNN 5 Departure off Runway 22 turns right; but it continues west bound.  There are no departure procedures for Runway 22 that turn right initially; and then continue to the east.  Also; none of our guidance tells us to expect a right turn off of Runway 22.

column123: Landing 10L in FLL. Approach briefed thoroughly. Stable approach the whole way. Captain completed the landing checklist at appropriate time.
