column121: Last day of 3 day trip.  Started both Engines and joined the long line of departures.  Had a closeout; completed all the checklists and taxied J; K7 short of Y.  We also requested numbers for tailwind takeoff (10 knots). Somewhere in between we received an ACARS that closeout had been deleted.  Holding short of Y; Ground told us we were next to taxi to W and hold short of 9L.  At that point we questioned ourselves if we had the closeout (it had been a 40 minutes or so since out).  We realized that no numbers had been sent since the message of closeout deleted.  The First Officer (FO) notified Ground and then Ground instructed us to turn right on Y and hold short of Approach End.  Ground told us to next time to tell them sooner; since there were many behind us. I made the turn to Y immediately to get out of the way and was looking for any signs that designated the Hold Short Point.  I must have missed it or went past it while turning into Y. Since they were landing on 9R and taking off 9L my brain went into looking for any hold short point (not as familiar with PHL as I would like to be). I was thinking 9R.  The next point I saw was the ILS sign short of P.   We stopped short of it. We were told that when able to call a number.  When I talked to them they said that they were concerned since they have been told that there are no signs or poor signs around K; Y and that approach end.  The main reason they wanted us short was to avoid damage from aircraft taking off.  [Contributing factors include] communications; sense of urgency; heavy workload; poor markings; no approaches to 9L; wrong picture in brain.  For PHL; do not instruct pilots to turn K onto Y and hold short of Approach End; there isn't enough room to complete the turn and hold short.  The aircraft will be blocking K anyway if holding short.  Also; hold the critiques of not notifying them of closeout until we are stopped.  Next time I will do what I have done for XX years; make sure I know the entire route (taxiing) on the chart instead of turning immediately and looking for signs.

column121: On Date; I was assigned as the Captain of Aircraft X; an Company flight with scheduled service from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The aircraft was Aircraft X. At the time of this flight; I had already flown two previous legs and was fit for duty to conduct the round trip flight to ZZZ1.As I settled into the flight deck to perform my preflight routine; I noted that the left side window of the aircraft was suffering from de-lamination. At the time I estimated that the de-lamination was approximately 4 inches tall and 18 inches wide on the bottom side of the window. After speaking with my First Officer; I consulted the Company standard operating procedure manual for the CRJ 700 aircraft. The SOPM states de-lamination and/or cracking is allowed two inches from the edge of the windshield around the entire periphery with four inches of penetration in the corners. Later on I was able to take pictures of the de-lamination and I used a takeoff and landing data card as a measuring tool and determined the de-lamination was approximately 3.75 Inches tall. The width of the de-lamination was approximately 18 inches but was not measured. I checked the maintenance log for the aircraft and found multiple previous write ups by Captains who had believed that the de-lamination exceeded standards. In each instance I found that Maintenance had signed off the window as being within standards and not a problem. I phoned ZZZ Maintenance Supervisor Name and told him that I would have no choice but to write up the window again. He said that was not a problem and they would come out and sign off on the window. When Maintenance arrived the A&P looked at the window from the jet bridge and began the process of returning the aircraft to service without taking any measurements or further inspecting the damaged area. I was standing in the jet bridge at the time an observed a copy and paste from a previous write up stating that the window was still within limits per CRJ700 CMM 56-11-02. At that time; I was not satisfied with the return to service an asked to see they see CRJ700 CMM 56-11-02. When Maintenance pulled up the section it had a picture that exactly described what is in the standard operating procedure manual for the CRJ 700. It clearly states that the limit on de-lamination is 2 inches from the bottom of the window which we already knew had been exceeded. At that point Maintenance agreed with me that the aircraft could not be returned to service and called his supervisor. Name1 from ZZZ Maintenance came out to the aircraft and showed me in what I was told is the PPG windows manual a section that states the following.'Allowable de-lamination is two inches from the edge of the daylight opening around the entire print and four inches in the corners. Localized areas of de-lamination are allowed to exceed the continuous peripheral limit as long as pilot visibility is not impaired'. Name1 told me that localized is any one side of the window. Believing that localized should be a defined term I asked for any documentation on what exactly localized means in that statement but was unable to get a written answer from any available manual. At that point we reached an impasse where I along with my First Officer was not willing to take the aircraft in an un-airworthy status and outside of the limits of the standard operating procedure for the CRJ 700. Name1 stated that they would find another crew.I contacted my dispatcher for the flight and told him that I would be unable to accept the aircraft as airworthy and would need a replacement aircraft. Around that time Maintenance was communicating with someone in ZZZ2 that the aircraft was airworthywhich further complicated the situation where a flight crew was saying it is not and maintenance is saying that it is airworthy.Approximately 2 hours later with the same aircraft still assigned to the flight I was removed as the Captain due to my refusal to take it and the fact that I was now up against duty limitations. I was replaced by another reserve Captain. At that point I was still sitting next to my First Officer who was not comfortable either taking the aircraft. He called crew support and informed them he could not take the aircraft and was then transferred to the OCC Coordinator. I overheard during the conversation that the coordinator told him that in 25 years with the company she had never had a crew refuse an aircraft due to window de-lamination.Shortly after that a new aircraft was found to complete the flight with the remaining crew members.When I completed my drive home; I looked at the flow board and found that the aircraft had been returned to service and was now completing a flight to ZZZ3 with an entirely different crew.In conclusion despite every attempt at talking with Maintenance and getting a satisfactory resolution or answer on why the aircraft was airworthy my entire crew ended up believing that the aircraft was not airworthy. I also had a major financial incentive to complete the flight as it would have paid 150% had I completed it. Despite the pressure that I received from maintenance and the financial loss from refusing the flight I simply could not determine the airworthiness at that time.Most of the things that we find wrong with an aircraft are either deferrable or are not deferrable. Very few things have ambiguous statements like it's okay if it's localized even though it's outside of the standard operating procedures manual for the CRJ 700.Most of the things that we find wrong with an aircraft are either deferrable or are not deferrable. Very few things have ambiguous statements like it's okay if it's localized even though it's outside of the standard operating procedures manual for the CRJ 700.It goes against the safety culture of this airline to make attempts to bully a flight crew into flying an aircraft that is not airworthy. It is my belief that Maintenance has become accustomed to signing off de-lamination that is outside of standards despite not being able to clearly define what localized means. This is known as the normalization of deviance and has resulted in numerous fatal accidents in aviation.

column121: On descent into ZZZ; we set up for the visual to XX backed up by the ILS. I was the pilot flying. We were given a runway change from Runway XX to XY. We made the necessary changes and briefed them. The ILS frequency for XX and XY at ZZZ are the same. After we were not receiving a good signal on approach to XY; we asked Approach if they had switched from XX to XY. He responded roger and sent us to Tower. He sounded busy and both the Captain and I agreed that he had not really processed the question.Once with Tower; we asked the same thing and they advised us to let them know if we ever got a good signal while on approach. We didn't have good ILS guidance and the Captain suggested I click off the autopilot and hand-fly it down. I did so and was working to maneuver myself on final. I overshot final while continuing to descend. I was worried that this would trigger a GPWS warning as I could see that I was near high terrain to the south of the field. I adjusted my vertical speed as I corrected toward final; but still got a GPWS warning. I responded to the warning as I continued correcting back to runway centerline.We were immediately out of the GPWS threat and elected to continue the visual approach but we were left high after the response. It was here that I should have seen we were not in a good position to continue and should have gone around. As we continued down final; we were at idle thrust and flight spoilers were out as we continued to configure the aircraft. I don't believe that we were fully configured below 1000 ft.; which was outside of stabilized approach criteria; and we still had the flight spoilers extended - which; after review; was against company limitation. By 500 ft. we were fully configured but still fast and slightly high. Another opportunity to conduct a go-around. The power remained in idle for almost the entire approach. We landed on Runway XY.Due to poor maneuvering to final while on visual approach; an overshooting final resulted in a terrain warning. Rather than make the decision to terminate the approach there; we continued; which resulted in an unstabilized approach that continued to a landing. [The cause was also] failure to call a go-around when that was the appropriate course of action. When you think you should go around; go around. Don't wait for someone else to call it and don't continue an approach that isn't stable. Follow SOP and your training.
column123: GPWS warning followed by an unstable approach into Runway XY in ZZZ. We were descending into ZZZ and were set up for Runway XX. Approach advised that winds had shifted and asked if we would like Runway XY. We accepted and began to set up for XY. When we had the airport in sight; we were cleared for the visual. As we armed the approach for the autopilot; we were told by Approach that the localizer and glideslope may not be working. My First Officer turned off the autopilot and began hand-flying the visual. He became distracted by configuring the airplane and was flying through the localizer when I informed him he needed to start his turn. As he began the turn he started descending; which caused a GPWS warning for a couple seconds due to terrain. We were confident of terrain clearance but leveled off until we were back on the localizer. Once we were on the localizer; we were high. We began our descent and continued configuring. We weren't fully configured until about 800 ft. AGL. We proceeded with the landing without further event.I think fatigue played a factor in our poor decision-making to continue the approach. We had a [before-dawn] wake-up call that morning and this was our 4th leg of the day. We had been dealing with thunderstorms and delays all day long.

column121: Captain and FO (First Officer) experienced multiple additive conditions/factors that led to not completing checklists fully [and] briefing; that led to taxiing without selecting takeoff flaps. For example; use of opposite flow runway for takeoff; bleeds-off takeoff requirement; MEL that appeared to be corrected; ATOG and minimum required fuel to include MAX warm-up requirements; bleeds-off takeoff requirement; possible delay of 45 minutes for Ground to coordinate opposite direction takeoff from taxi call; i.e.; fuel concerns; trying to make push time; [and] single-engine taxi necessity. These additive conditions took us out of our normal flow and led to us taxiing without selecting takeoff flaps or running the Before-Taxi Checklist.We captured the error and threat during the Captain's Before-Takeoff Flow; with the Configuration Warning horn. We had not crossed the hold-short line; but the time it took us to run the QRH; correct the aircraft configuration; and then run the Before-Taxi and -Takeoff Checklists; Tower canceled our takeoff clearance; due to opposite direction requirement. We were shortly thereafter cleared for takeoff. We thoroughly debriefed what happened and how it happened; as we are both very experienced operators.
column123: Due to multiple distractions and additive factors - opposite direction; full-length takeoff on XXL and coordination involved with fuel issues - an MEL I spent too much time getting an explanation from Maintenance; discussions managing minimum takeoff fuel and ATOG requirement; bleeds-off takeoff discussions; being fairly new to ETOPS and not fully in sync with my ETOPS flow; and allowing myself to get rushed to make push time; took us away from our normal flows and mistakes were made; culminating in a taxi without takeoff flaps set.Our error was captured with the before-takeoff flow throttle burst; as Tower cleared us for takeoff. We got the horn; and that put us in the yellow. We ran the QRH; reset the flaps; and ran the Before-Taxi and Before-Takeoff Checklist to ensure we didn't miss anything; and got back in the green. As we taxied toward the hold-short line; Tower cancelled our takeoff clearance. Tower re-cleared us for takeoff shortly thereafter. The rest of the flight was solidly in the green.

column121: We were flying ZZZ1 to ZZZ; a XA00 report in ZZZ1. It was the First Officer's (FO) initial trip back from a 10-month furlough. We were on the ZZZZZ RNAV arrival from the northeast. I was the PF. ZZZ was landing north. ZZZ airport had an overcast layer obscuring the airport. At the appropriate time; I briefed the ILS XXR approach. We set up the FMS and tuned/identified the NAV radios for XXR; the normal approach for this arrival. When we checked in with ZZZ Approach; we were advised to expect the ILS XXL. I briefed the approach and we tuned/identified the NAV radios. We were being vectored to intercept the localizer. It looked like we overshot the localizer on the NAV display; so I turned to intercept. ATC advised us; 'It looks like you are lining up for the wrong runway;' and turned us off of the approach. There were no conflicts with any other aircraft. They then told us to expect the ILS XXR. We flew that approach successfully to a landing. While we were setting up for the XXR approach; we discovered we never set up the FMS for the ILS to XXL. [I believe the cause was] early sign-in. Overcast skies obscuring airport. [It was also the] FO's first trip after furlough. [I suggest] verification that both the NAV radios are tuned and identified and the FMS is set for the proper runway/approach.
column123: Planned and briefed approach for ILS Runway XXR and was given ILS Runway XXL. The CA (Captain) set up and briefed new approach. I verified the frequencies and inbound course but neither of us set the new approach into the FMS. Was getting vectors to the ILS XXL [and] we had the correct ID for the ILS. When the CA looked at the ND and saw himself flying through the course for what was ILS XXR; the wrong approach; he corrected the heading to go back to intercept the course on the ND. The Controller said you are turning to line up for wrong approach and told us to go around.I have not flown since [last year]. I also do not have much experience in the aircraft. Was first flight since furlough. [I plan on] getting more flying in and becoming more comfortable in the aircraft; getting back into the rhythm of the flights.

column121: On approach into [Runway] [27C] in Chicago it was by all accounts a normal day. A storm had passed about 2 hours prior giving way to the benign conditions usually experienced after the passing of a storm. The wind was hardly noticeable I had nearly no crosswind correction in on the approach. As we approached the final approach fix Tower cleared a 777 to cross our landing runway. We continued; the aircraft was fully across the runway by the time we reached 1;000 feet AGL and parked on Taxiway TT. I assume he was waiting for a clearance from Ground to continue further. We continued on the approach and right as I was bringing the thrust levers back to idle a sudden jolt of firm left aileron and right rudder were needed to continue a safe ground track and land the aircraft. I am not sure exactly what bank angle was achieved but the proximity to the ground made it seem like quite a lot. My guess is around 10-12 degrees of bank at 10 feet off the ground. Some comments from passengers sounding the alarm that things where not correct when they got off the airplane make me think things where perhaps worse than I know due to the speed at which this all happened. The incident all happened approximately 10 ft AGL. Due to the suddenness and nature of the incident the best course of action was to land the aircraft. I had plenty of runway available to safely execute a full stop landing. Had the event happened at say 50 or 100 feet; a go-around would have certainly been necessary. The landing overall was completed without further incident. We taxied to gate; deplaned. And other than a few comments from Flight Attendants and passengers it was a normal operation. The cause of this sudden change and necessity for rudder and aileron was due to the 777 parked on Taxiway TT attempting to taxi right as I was landing. He was headed out for takeoff so I assume he was all loaded up and needed a lot of thrust to get moving. This is what caused such a dramatic necessity for correction very close to the ground. I hope out of this pilots and Controllers are made aware of the possibility of incidents like this in the future if we're not operationally prepared in some way. The cause of the event was the new taxi procedures and runway configuration due to the addition of 27C in Chicago. When cargo carriers taxi on TT they're putting anyone landing at risk of jet blast. At least a note could be added to our company pages alerting pilots about the possibility of this happening. But maybe even a change in how Chicago does taxi operations.
column123: There is a significant safety threat to aircraft landing on Runway 27C in ORD; due to jet blast from aircraft crossing 27C on taxiway TT.  This taxiway is approximately 1;100 - 1;200 feet from the departure end; so it is perfectly situated to impact aircraft in the landing flare.  To make matters worse; aircraft that cross 27C are instructed to contact Ground on TT and are therefore not on frequency when given an instruction to continue their taxi. In this particular case; a 777 had crossed 27C; then stopped on TT; presumably awaiting further taxi instructions from Ground.  They were not on our frequency.  At under 10 feet we were hit with a really bad amount of jet blast from the 777.  The First Officer did a fantastic job of getting the roll event back under control for a safe touchdown.  We advised Tower of the event. Something with regard to the above needs to change.  Either; aircraft should cross somewhere else; Controllers should advise aircraft crossing 27C at TT to use minimal power when resuming taxi; Controllers advise pilots of the jet blast potential; or at the very least; there should be a note on a chart.

column121: This was a FFOD flight. While completing the hydraulic test; Hydraulic Pump 3B would not work. While writing this up; cabin boarding commenced. The associated circuit breaker 1A2 remained set in. Because of this problem; along with the emergency lights not working; and in consultation with Maintenance Control; it was determined that the airplane would be deplaned because it was unknown how long the flight would be delayed in getting maintenance personnel to the airplane to resolve the maintenance issues with the aircraft. I left the aircraft; still prior to the original departure time; and notified the ramp agents and gate agents. The passenger gate checked bags were brought back on the cart to the front of the plane so passengers would be able to have their things in the terminal. I made the announcement to the passengers face-to-face via the Flight Attendant's (FA) inter-phone explaining that we would be deplaning due to the aircraft needing maintenance and the time required for them to complete their job to ensure the airplane was safe for flight. It was also due to the hot temperatures making it uncomfortable in the cabin of the aircraft.As the passengers deplaned; there were a number of passengers saying that they would rather be late; but fly in a safe airplane. I kept assuring them their safety is our top priority. A couple expressed discontentment due to the strain placed on their travel plans and possibility missing their connections. I told them I that I apologized for the inconvenience; but that I needed to make sure they were completely safe on our flight and directed them to the gate agent to see what could be done to help them. I did not see anyone making a video or taking pictures with their phone. There were a couple of people talking on the phone.While I was greeting the passengers as they deplaned; the first officer notified me that the R PACK HI TEMP caution message came on and shut the PACK down by itself. This was then written up in the ELB.During the approximately 1 hour and 55 minutes delay; I made several trips into the terminal (about every 15-20 minutes) to make announcements to the passengers providing up-to-date information regarding the time frame of the delay; the status of the maintenance process; and to express sympathy for the inconvenience and disruption to their travel; but that their safety is our first priority.Maintenance came out to the airplane and resolved the hydraulic pump issue and verified the emergency lights had been charged long enough by the APU and the R PACK was deferred.By the time Maintenance had completed their items; several passengers had rebooked to a flight leaving for ZZZ just an hour or two later. Some that were just flying to ZZZ opted to drive instead saying the trip would be quicker. Again; I did not see anyone appearing to be making a scene or social media post; video; or taking photos. There was one man who expressed his displeasure at not making his connection in ZZZ. I expressed my apologies for his inconvenience; but told him that his safety was our top priority.As Maintenance had returned the airplane to service on their part; we elected to board the airplane while waiting for Dispatch to return the airplane to service. I made the announcement in the terminal that the maintenance issues had been resolved; again expressing apologies for the inconvenience; but telling them that their safety is our top priority. At that point; boarding commenced. I called Dispatch and verified that I had the the amended release; with its associated limitations on the cruise altitude. They then returned the airplane to service; which we saw verified in the ELB.After boarding; the flight deck crew and cabin crew complied with all procedures and we pushed out of the gate for taxi. After contacting ATC; we had a 5 minute wait for our flow time at the end of the runway. After waiting; we departed climbing on departure; with me acting as Pilot Flying (PF).As we climbed throughabout 7;000 feet; the L PACK HI TEMP caution message illuminated. A couple seconds later; the PACK fault light illuminated and the cabin depressurized slowly. I told my First Officer that we were going to level off at 9;000 feet; which we did.I verbalized that this was an unanticipated threat and that I was flying the airplane. I stated that there were no QRC procedures or memory items. I then told him that I was going to have him fly the airplane; holding a general orbit over the airport within the confines of the airport. I made the radio call at that point to ATC that we were leveling off at 9;000 feet and would be making turns over the top of the ZZZ1 airport for what I approximated to be about 15 minutes. ATC asked if we were declaring an emergency. I declined declaring an emergency and told him that when I got back with Center; that I would want vectors back for the approach. Center responded with 'roger.'I then proceeded with the QRH abnormal L PACK HI TEMP (Bleed source is engine) procedure. The procedure did not resolve the problem and the caution message remained illuminated. Because I did not have any operative PACKS that negated the ability to transfer the bleeds from the engines to the APU.I contacted Ops on COM 2 and notified them of the problem and that we would be coming back to the airport. They responded and understood. I called the Flight Attendant and notified her of the problem; but that this was not an emergency; just to clean up the cabin and configure for landing. I told her that she had 10 minutes.I then made a PA announcement that we had lost pressure in the cabin and that we would be returning to ZZZ1 after I had completed a couple of procedures. I expressed my apologies of the continued problems and the inconvenience to them.Because of the slow depressurization of the aircraft; the CABIN ALT caution message came on while I was running the L PACK HI TEMP QRH procedure. This was expected and I ran the abnormal QRH procedure for CABIN ALT after finishing the procedure for the L PACK HI TEMP. The CABIN ALT caution message persisted; as expected. My next procedure to run was the abnormal QRH for Unpressurized Flight Procedure (PACKs off). I completed this procedure; confirming the guarded switches with my First Officer. During this entire time; my First Officer had been making CTAF radio position calls. Another airplane had flown up underneath us and was staying 1;000 feet below us. Because of this; the other airplane would get within 800-900 feet below us and kept tripping TCAS traffic alerts. My previous instructions to my First Officer were to orbit the airport; which he was doing. I had to stop the QRH procedures and redirect where to put the airplane to avoid the continued TAs. I changed my instructions to him that he could outline the geographic exterior of the valley to avoid the other airplane. We never heard any radio calls on CTAF from the other airplane of what they were doing or any intentions. These radio calls are not required in the ZZZ1 area.I finished the QRH procedures.I called the passengers again and attempted to assure them that; although we had lost pressure; the airplane was still flying fine and the flight crew was working to get the airplane on the ground safely and we should be on the ground within 10 minutes.I contacted ATC and they told me that unless I could climb higher than 10;000 feet; I would not be able to get vectors. Because the weather visibility was virtually unlimited and there were no clouds; I called the airport insight and cancelled IFR. In hindsight; I should not have canceled IFR; but I was still given traffic advisories from Center until we were clear of the conflicting targets.I directed the FO to fly east over the desert area that had lower terrain obstacles that would allow us to descend to land on Runway XX.I explained to my First Officer that we didn't have cabin pressure and that we would need to plan a slow descent rate.I heard the FA's jumpseat click and I called her to verify that she had been able to complete her duties; which she affirmed. I then made a PA announcement attempting to assure the passengers that the procedures were complete and we would be landing in about 5 or so minutes. I went on to explain that because the airplane was not compensating for the lack of pressure that they would feel the pressure change in their ears.Inside the airplane; it did get very hot. Even with the RAM AIR open; we were not able to cool it off. I did have concern about some of the elderly passengers we had onboard. The ECS page said the cabin temperature was 34 degrees C; but it felt hotter. The QRH procedure talks about keeping the speed up to 250 knots for cabin cooling; but that was not possible due to landing and having to keep the airplane confined in the valley and maneuvering for landing.We landed normally; besides the pressure; and taxied into parking at the terminal. We opened the door; which immediately allowed cooler air into the cabin; and I made another passenger announcement; again expressing apologies for the problems and that they could talk to the gate agent to make further arrangements.I wrote up the L PACK HI TEMP caution message in the ELB; called maintenance control and finished up with them. Operations then wanted to move the airplane to an adjacent FBO to open up gate space for flights expected later. Maintenance Control made a note in their record of the location of the airplane being moved to the FBO and stated that they were fine with the airplane being relocated.As passengers deplaned; they were frustrated with the return of the flight.After everyone was deplaned and safe in the terminal; the plane was pushed back and we repositioned it to the FBO. I called Dispatch and had them close out the ELB; as the program had locked me out from being able to close out myself. Old equipment on a hot day.I cannot entirely control the effectiveness or reliability of an airplane or its systems.
column123: The Captain was flying out of ZZZ1 on the ZZZZZ departure; Runway XX. With the right pack deferred already; we received a left pack hi temp on the right; climbing turn. Upon receiving the caution message; we established a benign flight regime at 200kts; 9;000 feet in a right-hand orbit atop ZZZ1. The Captain then assigned duties amongst the crew per [company guidelines]; specifically I flew the aircraft and the captain ran the appropriate checklists and assumed pilot monitoring duties. Concurrently; we notified ZZZ Center; ZZZ1 OPS and Dispatch of our situation and intentions. While completing checklists we received a traffic advisory from ZZZ Center and TCAS advisory. We were able to visually acquire the other aircraft quickly and adjust our flight path to continue our response to the situation. After completing all required checklists; we notified the FA and passengers about the situation and reengaged with ZZZ Center about our intentions to return into ZZZ1. We conducted a standard descent/approach briefing; set up a left-hand intercept onto the final approach course and established a slow; deliberate descent profile on the approach [Runway] XX into ZZZ1 and landed/taxied to the terminal without incident. The left pack hi temp caution message caused the crew to conduct the actions as described in the narrative.Issues with aircraft cannot be completely avoided; the crew acted and responded to the situation in compliance with our directives and in a safe manner.

column121: Pushing off gate/listening to Ground. There was a lot going on with weather approaching the field; certain departure gates shut off and others open. We took a minute to discuss how we got there and knowing we had been distracted; 'reset' ourselves and continued with the Before Taxi Flow and Checklist.[Suggest] Self awareness during high workload that things can unknowingly be skipped.
column123: Pushed back and disconnected from tug. Only started one engine for departure delays due to weather at the field. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed our plan to taxi off ramp and wait for weather to pass. After that; I must have believed that he did the after-start flow and we did the Before Taxi Checklist. However; I was wrong. We cleared left and right and I started to move the aircraft; but immediately I knew the aircraft was not configured properly for taxi. I stopped the aircraft and started the after-push procedures again. The distraction of the weather delays got me out of my normal routine; as well as the FO's. Neither one of us trapped the errors until too late. We ended up with a return-to-gate event.While we start engines routinely and do Before Taxi Checklists several times a day; we can get distracted by outside factors. I should have delayed the discussion about weather or anything else until after the start flow and Before Taxi Checklist was complete.

column121: We were making a visual approach to Runway XXR in ZZZ. The airport was is sight; while the downwind leg and convective activity was present south and west of the airport. After receiving landing clearance from Tower; a wind check was issued and landing speeds adjusted accordingly. The First Officer (FO) was flying and called for landing Flaps 30. The Before Landing Checklist was accomplished and I did a second wind check. We discussed the new speeds and continued the approach. Shortly thereafter; we received a Too Low Flaps Warning. Upon inspection I discovered that the flaps were in the 25 detention. The flaps were moved to position 30. I considered a go-around; but elected to continue the approach as we were on speed and path and a go-around would have been into the convective activity.Obviously; this was a failure to read and verify the checklist items. While debriefing the event with the FO; we both agreed that the monitoring of the wind/ weather was a factor as we considered our performance on final. Also being in a MAX 8 was a factor as the location of the flap gauge is different than the NG; possibly affecting the visual flow of the checklist items. Other factors were the weather deviations on arrival and non-standard arrival into a visual from the north side of the airport and terrain monitoring. Passenger issues requiring Dispatch coordination and the aircraft being met by Law Enforcement at the gate. It was a very busy flight at the end of a long day.

column121: I was the Line Captain in the First Officer's seat. After numerous delaying vectors which cut into our planned landing fuel; we were finally cleared for the ILS Runway 35L. Passing through 9;000 feet we noticed an aircraft approaching our aircraft from the east at 8;000 feet. As we descended on the glideslope; passing 8400 feet; the TCAS generated an RA on the aircraft; which was still at 8;000 feet. We came within 400 feet. of merging with this aircraft! We circled back for another approach; cleaned up to conserve fuel; and advised Approach that we were now at a minimum fuel state. We circled back for another ILS to Runway 35L; which we completed normally. I called the TRACON Supervisor on my cell phone after parking. He said the other aircraft was supposed to intercept the final for Runway 35R but neglected to do so; which resulted in a rather severe loss of separation. According to the TRACON Supervisor; the other pilot blamed his automation for not capturing the 35R localizer.
column123: Working Final Radar. Because of weather; it was necessary for me to use the ILS approach for my runway; 35L. The parallel final for Runway 35R was able to use visual approaches. I had cleared Aircraft X for the ILS to Runway 35L at Denver International. I switched communications to Tower. A few seconds later; the pilot of Aircraft X called on my frequency that he was responding to a TCAS RA and climbing. Aircraft Y was cleared for a visual approach to Runway 35R at 8000 ft. but was crossing his localizer. Aircraft Y ended up turning virtually underneath Aircraft X before heading back northeast to Runway 35R. Aircraft Y was at 8000 ft.; Aircraft X was indicating 8400 ft. and climbing. I cancelled the approach clearance for Aircraft X; turned west; and climbed to 9000 ft. Aircraft X was re-sequenced and landed safely on Runway 35L.North landing configuration is the preferred operation. This morning; the wind was out of the south at 8 to 12 kt. Although pilots were complaining about tailwinds; we maintained the north operation. In addition; convective weather was south of the airport; sitting on the final approaches. This affected [the] pilots' ability to see the airport. The only other weather in the airspace was a small area east of the airport that had no impact. In a north configuration; the runways; 35L/35R; are direct parallel runways. If we had landed south; as the wind and weather favored; we would have used a widely spaced configuration and landed on runways 16R and 17R. We also could have easily used visual approaches and the aircraft would have been in clear weather all the way to the airport and had a headwind. Landing north unnecessarily was a major contributing factor in this event. Also; the parallel final for Runway 35R was training and the Developmental forgot to turn Aircraft Y in a timely manner resulting in the overshoot. This could have also been avoided in a south operation because of much more spacing between the runways.

column121: Very interesting set of circumstances led our flight today to take the clearance to 'Line Up and Wait' that was meant for another aircraft in ZZZ [airport].  After we pushed off our gate; we were cleared to taxi to Runway XXR at [taxiway] 1 from our ramp via taxiways 2; 3 and 4.We were all done with our taxi out procedures and checklist by the time we were number 1 aircraft at the hold short line of taxiway 1 for XXR. Traffic was moving steadily; so the Captain taxied right up to just prior to the 'Hold Short' line.  This is where the weird circumstances happened for this event:The first thing that happened is the 737 MAX RAAS (Runway Awareness and Advisory System) EGPWS Aural Callout announced our approach to Runway XXR as it is intended to do so.  Also; at the exact same time; the Tower Controller gave a clearance for an aircraft to; 'At XX Right; 1; line up and wait.'  What happened is that the two voices; of the RAAS; and the Controller; most likely blocked each other out to us; the crew.Since I was working the radio; I made the assumption that the Controller was calling us since we heard tail end of; 'XX Right; at 1.'  I repeated back exactly; 'Line up and wait Runway XX Right; at 1; [call sign].'  After that we did not hear anything from the Controller as the Captain taxied into position for the hold.  As we were taxiing onto the runway; I noticed from the opposite side of the runway at Taxiway 5; Aircraft Y taxiing what looked like across the runway to me. As the Captain rounded out the turn to line us up with the runway; we hear the Controller say; 'Well; that's interesting.'  He then proceeded to tell us that we had taken the clearance for Aircraft Y to line up and wait.  I then proceeded to apologize; but that I had also read back to him the clearance.Since Aircraft Y was behind us on the runway; the Controller just told us to hold position; and he proceeded to re-shuffle the order; and was able to let us go first in front of Aircraft Y.  We got a clearance for takeoff and had a non-eventful departure.  As the Controller handed us over to Departure Frequency; he stated; 'Upon further review; I think I screwed that up; no worries; contact Departure.'At that point we started formulating a theory on what may have happened and the Captain and I started to debrief it in late climb out; and cruise flight.What I believe happened; is that when the RAAS created the aural warning that we were approaching runway XXR at intersection 4X; was the exact time where the Controller called Aircraft Y to line up and wait. BUT; upon further review of the audio of ATC; the Controller gave out the wrong taxi way intersection to Aircraft Y. What we both heard right after the RAAS had completed its aural callout; is the tail end of the clearance.  Even though Aircraft Y was on taxiway 5; Tower gave out the incorrect clearance of 'Aircraft Y; Runway XXR at 4X; line up and wait.'At this point; I believe either both the Aircraft Y pilot and I probably keyed the mic at the same time; and repeated back the same clearance since we assumed we heard the tail end of the clearance as 'XXR; at 4X; line up and wait.' Or; maybe I read back the clearance first and the Aircraft Y pilot also assumed since he heard me take the clearance that it may have been for us only? That I don't really know.
column123: I was taxiing to Runway XXR at [taxiway] 4X.  I was approaching the runway hold short line as Aircraft Y in front of us received their takeoff clearance.  I kept the aircraft rolling and was applying the brakes to stop just short of the hold short line when the MAX aircraft that we were in gave us the [aural alert] 'Approaching Runway XXR'...at the same time Tower gave the clearance to line up and wait.  The [aural alert] 'Approaching Runway 28R' occurred simultaneously with the call sign when Tower said '[Call sign]; XXR at 4X; line up and wait.'  The First Officer read back the instructions.  Tower did not correct the read back.  We were the only aircraft in position to take the runway at XXR at 4X.  I continued taxiing onto XXR at 4X and as I was turning onto the center line; Tower said 'Oh isn't that interesting'; and then '[Call sign]; you took Aircraft Y's clearance.' I had seen Aircraft Y on the other side of the runway; farther east; at [taxiway] 5.  And he was actively stopping short of XXR at 5.The Controller basically said 'that is ok; Aircraft X will go first.' He advised us to hold in position; he then cleared us for takeoff.  After takeoff he said that 'upon further review; it looks like I messed up.'

column121: We departed ZZZ for ZZZ1. The climb mode was set to E-CLB. At approx 12;000 feet; I decided to engage max con thrust to climb over weather. Soon after; a pop or bang was felt / heard and the aircraft yawed to the left. The EICAS indicated ENG 1 OUT. Both me and the First Officer (FO) acknowledged the message and I called for the QRH. I received priority from ATC and requested to level off. I maintained the current heading and slowed so that me and the FO could assess the situation. Soon after; we requested a turn back to ZZZ with ATC. As we descended toward ZZZ; we ran the ENG OUT QRH and; after making sure all indications were green; we attempted an APU assisted restart. N2 did not rise above zero. Restart was abandoned and we secured the inop engine and prepared for a one engine inop landing. I spoke to the Flight Attendant (FA); explaining that we had suffered an engine failure and that we would be landing in approx 7 to 10 minutes back in ZZZ and to prepare for a normal landing. I also made an announcement to the pax with the same information. At 5;000 feet; a few miles south west and visual with the airport; we entered a visual hold; maintaining separation from a few weather cells in the vicinity; to finalize setup; checklists and briefs for a visual approach backed up by an RNAV to RWY XX. When ready; we asked for direct-to the final approach fix and executed the visual app. Once on the runway; emergency vehicles followed us to check for smoke or flames. I spoke to the FA to make sure everyone was OK. Both me and the FO made announcements letting the pax know what was happening. After it was ascertained that there was no fire threat; we organized a gate with ops and taxied to it.

column121: During climbout from ZZZ passing through approximately FL190 #2 HYD ISO VLV; #2 ENG HYD PUMP; and #2 RUD HYD Master Cautions illuminated in sequence with approx. 10 seconds between each annunciation. I (Captain; Check Pilot; Pilot Flying) identified; verbalized and canceled the Master Cautions after First Officer (Pilot Monitoring) acknowledged each Master Caution. Crew acknowledged that the #2 HYD QTY was approx. 10%; and #2 HYD PRESS was 0 psi. With all 3 Master Cautions illuminated I called for the #2 HYD PUMP caution checklist first. First Officer (FO) began E&A checklist and I took radios. I informed ATC of hydraulic system malfunction; return to field with vectors requested; informed number of souls and fuel onboard; [received priority handling] and advised we would be running checklists and would inform ATC when completed. After we completed the #2 HYD PUMP; and during the hydraulic systems failure checklist; when it states to complete descent and approach checklists; I informed FO to pause there so I could communicate to Dispatch and inform of situation; and have operational control congruency in plan to return to ZZZ. Amendment to Release to return to ZZZ was recorded at XA12Z via phone with Dispatcher Name. I then requested patch through to Maintenance (MX) Control and informed of situation; malfunction; and hydraulics system indications. Aircraft was flying with normal controllability.Flight Attendant (FA) brief was made to include normal landing in ZZZ at approximately XB50lcl. PAX were informed of system indication that required us to return to ZZZ; and to please pay close attention to FAs instructions as they prepare cabin for arrival; and as a standard precautionary measure Fire Department would be standing by with lights flashing. I informed FO of landing weight; FO derived landing bugs from E&A checklist. We completed the descent and approach procedures and checklist; planning RNAV Y RWY XXR; and proceeded with completion of hydraulic system failure landing checklist; followed by alternate gear extension checklist with no operational airspeed exceedance. FAs reported back cabin secure for landing; FO and Captain in agreement informed ATC aircraft was ready for return to land; and that it would be a slower than normal RWY exit and taxi due to inoperative nosewheel steering requiring taxiing with differential power and braking. After normal landing; ATC was informed that Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting (ARFF) [were] no longer needed. FO informed ZZZ OPS to chock main gear also due to emergency/park brake accumulator pressure only available. Taxi to spot was performed with shutdown. AML entry was made with communication with MX CONTROL.

column121: During boarding; all of a sudden Flight Attendant 1 (FA-1) and Flight Attendant 3 (FA-3); in the front galley; [and] I smelled like a scorched cloth smell when you turn on an oxygen bottle; or a burnt crayon smell. The smell spread in the first-class cabin. I experienced this smell before and knew right away that it was a fumes/cabin odor event. Most likely; the aircraft has an oil leak in or close to the engine. I informed the Captain immediately; and he smelled it; too. After a few minutes; my throat became scratchy; and I started getting lightheaded. When I turned my head; I felt as if my eyes caught up with my head with a slight delay. (said she smelled it; but that she was OK. I went on the jetway as the smell was really getting to me. My heartbeat became faster; and my speech even became slurred: my words were not coming out as fast as they were usually. I started losing the ability to function; almost. Name FA-3 kind of took over and made some announcements or was listening to the Captain; when he was calling me. The Captain reported the fumes/odor; and a mechanic came onboard. The boarding was complete; but the Captain notified the agents of the problem. I needed some fresh air; so I went to the jet way door; opened it; and took a few breaths; but a customer service supervisor; I think; told me to close the door immediately; as in a few minutes some machine was going to be turned on; 2 gates away from ours; and the smell would have come to the jet way from the open door. I did not smell anything outside; but I closed the door immediately; as I was instructed; well before the machine 2 gates away; was turned on; so there was no way that any smell/fumes could have come in through the door. The Captain made an announcement that the passengers needed to deplane; and everybody deplaned. We deplaned as well. I immediately went to sit down; as I felt dizzy. I took a bottle of water with me; to keep me hydrated. After the flight kept being delayed further and further; it was finally delayed until the next morning; to allow the mechanics to work on the plane. The Captains were given the name of the hotel where they were going to layover; but it took over an hour for the Hotels and Limo department to work on our hotel stay. We waited and waited and finally decided to go with the Captains; hoping that Company would put us in the same hotel. When we went outside; still not knowing where we were staying; a van driver flagged us and told us we were going to stay at the hotel with the Captains. As we were driving; I received a phone call from ZZZ Flight Service; Name; confirming that we were staying at the hotel. After a good night sleep; the next morning; I felt much better; however; both of my hands were shaking; and; when I put my contacts back on; I realized that they were foggy. The driver who took us to the airport told us that the plane was fixed by the mechanics. The plane we boarded was; in fact; the same plane we had the day before. When I looked in the logbook; I read that the mechanics could not reproduce the problem; and that; therefore; nothing was done to the plane. They wrote that it could have been a smell/fumes coming from outside and reaching the plane from a door left open. As I described above; the fumes/odor started on the plane long before anybody operated any machine or equipment outside. There were no fumes/smoke/smells outside. In the morning; though; I did not smell the smell from the day prior. However; I felt the presence of the fumes; as by the time we were taking off my throat became scratchy again. Name FA-3 didn't look that good; either. As soon as she came onboard; she did not have the energy she displayed the day prior and sat down immediately in a first class seat. I asked her if she was feeling OK; and she said she felt tired. She did not feel like herself. She said she could not sleep well; as she felt heaviness on her chest. She thought that maybe she ate too much food during the flight; but that now she realized that it was not what she ate. I told her that it could definitely be an increase in blood pressure or other symptom related to the fumes. As the flight progressed; she went to the back. I continued to serve in first class; and; twice; I couldn't even speak; as my throat became really scratchy. I went to the galley to drink some water and felt better. When we arrived in ZZZ; I felt better; but; at night; I had headache; so I had to call sick for the trip I had the next day. After a good night sleep; I felt much better. I thank the Captain for reporting the problem; however; I don't think that the plane is fixed. The problem was not fumes or smell coming from outside but something wrong with the plane; probably an oil leak causing toxic fumes and odor to come in the cabin. It would be nice if they could check and try to find the leak. I do not feel safe flying on this airplane. As far as the operations went; there was a lot of confusion with our hotel accommodations and with communication from the Company to us. The next day; there was also a lot of confusion regarding the new departure time; as the flight info on our tablet; Company; and the information the Captain's had showed all different departure times. Communication between the Company and the crews really needs to improve. Scheduling should contact us directly; instead of relying on automated methods of communication.

column121: This aircraft just came out of long term storage. It needed a full thrust takeoff; ETOPS verification for hi-altitude APU start and an Autoland update. Two separate Maintenance write-ups occurred after door close but prior to push back. This resulted in delays and multiple MRD updates. Both pilots reviewed and verified FMC load was normal after each anomaly corrected. On takeoff the FO (Flying Pilot) called for 'Autothrottles.' EPR mode engaged normally but throttles were slow to advance and left throttle lagged approximately 1 knob width. At 'check thrust' call FO commented to check left engine throttle. I had noticed the slow movement and manually moved both throttles to the commanded full thrust EPR setting. When passing 3;000 ft. the aircraft speed bug would not accelerate above CMS (approximately). We set 250 manually and each time we tried to engage VNAV or FLCH the command bug retreated to approximately CMS. We also noticed the command EPR was indicating CON thrust. I tried to engage CLB on TMSP panel but had no effect. At this point I said we'll wait until above 10;000 ft. to troubleshoot further. Above 10;000 ft I noticed that the VNAV CLB page appeared normal; but there was an 'ALL ENG' prompt at 5L which I'd never seen. After selecting the ALL ENG prompt the airplane returned to normal CLB mode. At no point during ground operations did either pilot ever select the CLB EO prompt or the subsequent Execute key. After landing and debriefing with Maintenance and the next leg's Captain; this Pilot stated she had also previously seen a 'split throttles on takeoff result in the aircraft believing it was in a single-engine situation and engaging the EO CLB mode. A Maintenance write up for Autothrottles was written up and Maintenance debriefed. (Autothrottles worked normal for remainder of our flight).

column121: BHM ATIS advised runways 6 and 36 were active; with visual and RNAV approaches in use to both. Conditions were VMC with good visibility. Upon initial contact with BHM Approach; we were advised to expect Runway 6. The First Officer briefed a visual approach to be backed up with the RNAV Runway 6. As we approached the terminal area; we observed a single heavy rain shower cell located directly on the final approach course for Runway 6; very near the final approach fix. This cell was approximately 5 NM wide and ATC had advised two other aircraft that this weather contained 'light to heavy' precipitation. It seemed to us that if we were to continue to pursue the approach for Runway 6; we would most likely fly through this weather.After brief discussion; the First Officer and I determined that an approach and landing to Runway 36 would keep us clear of that weather. BHM Approach agreed and vectored us for an RNAV approach to Runway 36. The First Officer briefed the RNAV 36 approach and I entered the landing data for Runway 36; including current ATIS reported winds - 110 at 6 kt. The approach proceeded normally with the aircraft configured normally for landing and in a stable condition. The First Officer had switched off the autopilot at just below 1;000 ft. and maintained the proper glide path with the 'snowflake' showing on glide path. At some point just below DDA; 1;530 ft.; and MDA; 1;480 ft.; very near the ridge just south of the airport; we received a terrain caution with [a] 'too low terrain' audible message. The First Officer adjusted pitch and we went very slightly above glide path momentarily. We received no additional warnings or cautions and the First Officer readjusted pitch to resume normal glide path. Touchdown on Runway 36 was normal and within the touchdown zone. At no time did we receive any 'pull up' or 'obstacle pull up' alerts; only the one 'too low terrain' alert. At the time of alert; the FO (First Officer) responded in accordance with the note in [the] POH Bulletin XX-XX; X.X.X. Conditions during the event were day VMC with good visibility; 10 SM.I believe this terrain caution could have been avoided by not performing an approach to Runway 36 in the first place and by maintaining a profile slightly above glide path. I did not observe us ever being below glide path. In thinking about the event afterwards; I realize that while the charted procedure guarantees obstacle clearance down to the MDA; it is the pilot's responsibility to maintain visual clearance from terrain and obstacles once below MDA. In the case of this particular approach; doing that requires one to fly a profile above a normal glide path. I had always known about the ridge and antennas south of the airport; but had never flown an approach to Runway 36 in BHM. Despite it being a charted procedure which is permissible in day VFR conditions; I'm not convinced that it is an approach that I would use in the future - due to the need to maintain a higher than normal glide path in order to avoid the terrain alert. In my opinion; flying a steeper approach could potentially lead to other issues such as landing long or past the touchdown zone if not managed very carefully. In the future; I would likely only use Runway 36 if in an emergency if Runway 6/24 was not available.

column121: We arrived at ZZZ Gate at approximately XA:30. Upon arriving at the gate there were no ramp personnel in the area. We parked as directed by the DGS system; shut down the engines; and performed the Shutdown Checklist (including 'Brakes Set'). After a few minutes; (indicated by the cargo doors opening on the ECAM) ground personnel approached the aircraft to perform their duties. I left my seat to use the lavatory and to assure the #1 Flight Attendant (FA) and our First Class passengers that we were diligently trying to find someone to open the door. Approximately 10-15 minutes later; the agent opened the door. I returned to the flight deck to gather my belongings before saying goodbye to the passengers at the door. We never received the 'chocks in' hand signal and had no ground power connected despite our efforts to get it done. In the mean time; shortly after main cabin door opening; a maintenance tech came up to the flight deck and gathered some pins from the gear pin stowage compartment; for what he indicated was some sort of inspection. I was called the next morning and informed by the ZZZ1 Director of Flight that while we were on the flight deck we had an aircraft rollback causing damage to the jet bridge. Not one person on or near the aircraft indicated that we had any aircraft movement and First Officer (FO) and I were totally unaware of the rollback. Often we arrive at the gate and there are no ramp personnel to chock the airplane. In addition; very shortly after door opening; there is a maintenance technician present to perform required operational inspections. As the flight deck crew; we performed our required post flight duties. We cannot account for the other several departments involved in the safe securing of the aircraft. As the Pilot-in-Command (PIC) of the aircraft; I sincerely believe that the parking brake was set. Given the intense scheduling practices and understaffing of the airline on the Aircraft Maintenance Department and Customer Service; along with the obvious poor training of Ground Support; I have no idea what happened.

column121: After takeoff; during gear retraction; we heard and felt 2-3 loud bangs and thuds with associated yaw and shutter of the aircraft. Initially; we considered a landing gear tire might have blown or it was retraction problem due to gear in transit timed with [another] problem. Once gear was fully retracted; a series of bangs and shutters occurred again and during our global assessment (Nothing displayed on ECAM); we noted a spike in temperature on engine 1 EGT as corresponding to the problem. [We suspected] compressor stalls. Reducing the power on engine 1 to idle eliminated the problem and the engine ran normally. We immediately [requested priority handling] with ATC requesting the ARFF equipment; as well as a box pattern back to XXR (longest runway); leveled at 4000 feet MSL; maintained configuration at 180 knots. We ran all appropriate checklists including: Engine 1 Stall in flight with Engine Parameters Normal at Idle; Non-Routine Landing; and Overweight Landing. We made an initial and landing imminent announcement to the flight attendants and passengers. During the initial series of compressor stalls and after the engine was stabilized at idle neither the flight attendants nor any passengers reported any other engine problems such as fire; smoke; vibrations; etc. Once everything was complete we flew the ILS XXC approach to a normal touchdown and landed to a full stop on the runway so that ARFF could look over the aircraft before we taxied uneventfully to the gate. Weight at touchdown was 3;000 to 4;000 pounds over the max with a 200 FPM touchdown. After shutdown; we made 2 logbook entries (Compressor stall after TO and Overweight Landing). We debriefed the Chief Pilot; Maintenance; ARFF Chief; Gate Agent; and Passengers. We saved all paper work; photos; and contact information.An Airbus Pilot jump-seater was very helpful with event CRM. Possible failure factors included heavy weight; TOGA takeoff; and a warm day stressing the engine. In addition; APU had been on MEL for 8 days adding to engine fatigue and stress with ground air and cross-bleed starts; and it was the aircraft's first flight of the day (even with ample warm-up time). Following policies; procedures; flows; and checklists all while maintaining positive aircraft control in an un-rushed manner using all available resources and thorough CRM led to a safe resolution to the engine failure on takeoff. [I recommend] better and more prompt APU maintenance; and the use of non-TOGA flex takeoffs on longer runways in hot and heavy takeoffs situations.
column123: Shortly after takeoff; during gear retraction; we noticed a loud thud or two. Initially; I thought it was a problem with landing gear retraction; since it started while the gear was still in transit. Shortly thereafter; the noise occurred again. A spike in engine temp was noted during the sounds; and the spike immediately disappeared. The EGT over-temp readings were happening too fast (and clearing so fast) that no ECAM message was triggered long enough to stay up. Once power on the #1 engine was reduced; the engine ran normally at idle. We requested priority handling and leveled off at 4;000 feet. ATC began vectoring us back for a visual approach to the longest runway; XXC. We requested ARFF to inspect the plane on landing. Flight attendants; passengers and Dispatch were advised of the situation and our intentions. All appropriate QRH procedures were complied with. Non-normal landing procedures were complied with. Overweight landing procedures and landing distance assessment were completed. A straight-out heading was requested and approved in the event of a missed. An uneventful approach and landing was conducted. After stopping on the runway; we requested ARFF to inspect the #1 engine for damage. No damage was noted and we continued to the gate. I'm not sure that this event was preventable. The only unusual thing about this aircraft was the deferral period for the APU. I think it had been deferred 8 days ago; which is quite a lot of external air start cycles and cross bleeds. Just speculation; but if this malfunction was associated in some way with a bleed air valve; the fact that the APU was deferred so long-and all the associated unusual starting procedures (perhaps external air starts) could have been a factor. It might be something to consider from a maintenance tracking perspective. I hear that we are seeing more inflight engine problems lately. I think APU deferrals should be as short as possible for a variety of reasons.I have a feeling that this event may have been associated with the APU deferral. I think emphasis should be put on deferring them for a shorter time and routing planes in need of APU work to a Maintenance facility sooner. In no case is a week deferral reasonable or necessary. (I don't think any troubleshooting had even been attempted to get the APU operating again.) TOGA Takeoff could have been another contributing factor; as we are asking a lot of the engines in hot weather.

column121: This was a routine flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1; in a B757. We had a normal push back; cross bleed start and taxi. On the takeoff roll; we rotated on speed and pitched to approximately 15 degrees. Noted the airspeed appeared to accelerate in the climb more than normal so I pitched through the flight director to stop at 20 degrees but that did not arrest the abnormal airspeed acceleration. Around 1;000 to 1;500 feet in normal configuration (flaps 5; standard takeoff power and pitched just below twenty degrees) the airspeed entered the red over-speed tape. At the same time we received multiple master warning lights and bells; master caution; clacker; and multiple failure notifications of electrical and avionics in nature (such as red OVSPD; Rudder ratio; Mach Speed Trim; ATC fault; GEN DRIVE; Left EEC; Right EEC etc.). The Captain's instruments indicated over 400 knots and over 40;000 feet of altitude. The Captain and I agreed the standby instrument appeared normal around 185 knots in a climb. I disconnected auto throttles; switched off flight director and recovered the airplane at 180 knots leveling off at 4;000 feet using standby instruments and flaps 5. The Captain noted it appeared my instruments began returning to normal to match the standby instruments. The Captain's complete instrument suite remained failed through the rest of the event. The Captain requested priority handling] and an air turn back with vectors for Runway XX. One attempt was made to re-engage the flight director and autopilot to no avail. Uneventfully; we hand flew a VFR approach to landing. We then had a normal taxi to our remote gate and released Fire Rescue vehicles from assistance.

column121: We arrived into the alley inbound to gate XXB to find [another] aircraft (737) stopped whilst approaching XXA. Ramp attempted to contact crew to direct a tow-in. The aircraft did not reply; and taxied in. I realized later that it was a MAX aircraft; with new Leap engines that allow for taxi at idle power in all but extremely heavy gross weights. I stopped to allow for the gaining of momentum as XXB gate is poorly designed with significant uphill slope. A swarm of service vehicles approaching XXA did not pay attention to marshaling crew at XXB trying to clear our path. So we lost momentum approaching gate and had to stop almost abeam gate. When it appeared that the gate area was clear; we had no lead Marshaller guiding us in. [I then] realized that the parking guidance system was on; but due to the positioning of the gate it was obscured. While still parallel to the gate; we goosed the power for momentum; went to idle; and just made it up the hill. It really should not be that hard to get into a gate.There were many issues. The SOP speaks to aircraft stopping and needing a tow-in; but what if it is a MAX that is at idle and can move at idle thrust? Additionally; training ramp personnel should include a lesson on situational awareness. [There have been] countless approaches to a gate blocked by vehicles which; in a hurry to service an aircraft; block gate access for other aircraft whilst paying no attention to marshallers. And finally; gate XXB has added a parking guidance system you cannot see until you are almost abeam the gate and committed. How does one know to approach?

column121: Aircraft X was scheduled for flight ZZZ to ZZZ1.  First Officer (FO) and I reviewed the aircraft maintenance issues prior to arriving at the airport noting MEL 27-11 and associated MELs.  At the aircraft during preflight; I reviewed the MEL procedures for 27-11 and worked with FO Name to perform the test procedures listed.  The test stated: To verify both control columns are connected; proceed as follows:  1. Hold LH control column in neutral position. 2. Try and move RH control column forward and backward. 3. If there is no relative movement between the control columns; they are connected.  While performing this test; we could see that if the LH column was moved the RH column didn't move at all; and same with the RH column.  We immediately called Maintenance Control who said that didn't sound right; and said he would call Maintenance back to the aircraft.  Note: the disconnect handle was still in place.  Once Maintenance arrived; we performed a flight control check with the hydraulics on.  At this point; it was noted the LH column only controlled the left elevator and the RH column only controlled the right elevator. No EICAS messages populated.  The only EICAS message was 'Pitch trim Disconnect' which was associated with the original MEL.  Maintenance was confused and said they had done all the control checks and that everything checked ok.  We sincerely believe that had a flight been attempted; it could have resulted in a catastrophe. Poor maintenance flight control checks.  Aircraft released to line with defective controls. I believe if maintenance had read the MEL and done the control check that was listed; they may have caught the system malfunction.

column121: After being cleared the ILS PRM Y to Runway 10R at ORD and being cleared to land; Tower issued a go-around instruction to our aircraft.  The ILS PRM Y has a 2.5 degree offset course to the runway due to the close nature of the two Runways 10R and 10C. At approximately 500 feet; we gained sight of the runway and began maneuvering to stabilize the approach on runway centerline by approximately 200 feet. The go-around command was issued at approximately 300 to 400 feet.  The go-around instructions were to climb to 2;500 feet and fly the localizer course. The CRJ-200 procedure for a go around is to TOGA; advance power and set the flap to 8 degrees and initiate a climb. This was accomplished uneventfully; however; we were already approximately 0.5-1 dot left on the localizer proceeding visually toward the runway centerline. Once the TOGA is initiated; the command bars will raise to command a climb and also capture the heading the aircraft is currently on when the button is pushed.  This all happened as we were transitioning back into IMC.  The localizer was still displayed on both displays; however due to the sensitivity of the localizer beam at that distance from the antenna; I am not certain of our actual deviation in terms of distance to the left of course.  The Tower Controller informed us we were supposed to be following the localizer course and issued a right turn to heading 140 degrees; followed by a new heading of 150 degrees.  We complied and were vectored around a radar pattern to an uneventful landing on 10R.Although we could have possibly corrected faster to the localizer course to prevent the left of course deviation; I think this is an unnecessarily complicated go-around instruction.  The 'button pushes' required; and the delays in the automation system before it appropriately reacts essentially rule out even using it; especially in low energy state while transitioning back into IMC.  Even though we had immediately pressed the NAV button after the TOGA; the command bars did not capture the course because we had been maneuvering visually and were far enough away from the localizer course so it defaulted to 'roll' mode.  This added an element of confusion and additional button pushing as we were executing the go around.  Also; I have personally never been issued a clearance to rejoin a localizer course during a go-around in my aviation career; so it was definitely unexpected.  I would recommend a non-breakout go-around clearance on a PRM be limited to something very simple like a heading and an altitude to climb to.  This would simplify the communication and lower the overall workload in the cockpit during a critical phase of flight.

column121: CONF 1 TOGA takeoff and no APU. Normal start go #1 at the gate per non-normal start; the same for the #2 start after the push back. After-start check complete; load closeout comes. We were under PTOW (Planned Takeoff Weight) and good winds and temperatures. Normal taxi and checklist to [runway] XXC. Cleared for takeoff; CA sets TOGA. Normal acceleration Vr. Shortly after Vr; heard a loud bang - CA (Captain) says; 'I think we blew a tire.' I said; 'I agree.' CA kept flying; we left the gear down. Speed was bleeding off; and then I said 'engine failure.' [Requested priority handling] with intentions to return to ZZZ. Leveled off at engine acceleration height [and] started to accelerate; thinking the gear was up. We decided to leave the flaps at 1 to return to the field and not knowing if there was any damage. [We] completed the ECAM procedure; follow-ups. CA talked to the FA's (Flight Attendant) to prepare for a precautionary landing and made a PA to the passengers; per the OD pages. ATC asked us to climb to 4;000 ft. Then; we realized the gear was still down. [We] raised the gear [and] completed the after-takeoff checklist. Did the landing approach; overweight landing; and checklist. Briefed the approach to [runway] XXC and descent checklist. Configured on schedule; landing checklist; and landed uneventfully. After stopping; the CA made a PA; talked to ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting); then taxed to the gate.[The cause was a] startle effect and the initial confusion of a tire failure or an engine failure. That played a significant role in the distraction of the landing gear. [I suggest to] do a max weight V1 in the SIMs.
column123: Flight planned for configuration 1 TOGA/max takeoff and dispatched with APU inop. Normal ground air-start on #1 engine per checklist. After pushback [was] complete; normal cross-bleed start #2 per checklist. After-start checklist called for and completed. Load closeout received and we were under planned takeoff weight. Normal taxi out with all checklists complete; we were cleared to line up and wait runway XXC. Subsequently cleared for takeoff and selected TOGA. Acceleration was normal and rotated at Vr.Shortly thereafter; heard a thump. I stated; 'I think we blew a tire.' Thought about not raising the gear and continued flying the aircraft and noticed rapid degradation of speed. FO (First Officer) stated; 'Engine failure.' Immediately lowered the nose and started trimming based on rudder trim to level the wings and center the rudder. Aircraft performance was very degraded but assumed it was due to heavy 321; [I] don't ever remember flying the simulator engine out near max takeoff weight or we had severe damage to the wing. [Requested priority handling] and stated intentions to return to ZZZ; thinking the landing gear was up. Elected to leave flaps at 1 and return to the field as expeditiously as possible as we were down to 1 engine and 1 generator. Completed Engine Failure ECAM procedure; ECAM follow ups; notified the Flight Attendants to prepare for a precautionary landing; and made a PA as per the OD pages. ATC asked if we could climb to 4;000 feet and said we were unable due to weight. At this point I realized the gear was still down. Raised the gear [and] completed [the] after-takeoff checklists. Accomplished the landing data for overweight landing and checklist; briefed the approach to [runway] XXC; and completed descent checklist. We were then cleared for the ILS XXC approach configured on schedule; performed the landing checklist; and landed uneventfully. After stopping; made a PA; ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting) checked out the aircraft; and we taxied to the gate.[The cause was a] startle effect and initial confusion of tire failure versus engine failure played a significant role in distraction from raising the landing gear. As pilot flying; my attention was completely absorbed with flying the aircraft with assumed degraded performance and didn't allow for transfer of aircraft control. Additionally; lack of experience on the fleet and as a new Captain also played a significant role. Departing over max landing weight with no APU was probably not a good decision. Additionally; I think a max weight takeoff V1 cut should be added to our training. Crew coordination with the flight attendant and ATC was excellent.
