column121: During Cruise we received an ACARS message from the company [Dispatch] that they had left 1768kg (initial message said 1768lbs but was later corrected) of Dry Ice off the DG manifest.  We began to send follow up messages back and forth to confirm the location and total quantity of the dry ice.  It was determined that the total quantity was 1884kg vs the DG manifest value of 166kg.  Basically; 2 cans worth of Dry Ice had not be accounted for on the DG manifest.  The crew deployed the Drager CO2 monitoring system immediately and was also directed to do this from the company.  We also ran the QRH for this event.  Upon further review; it was determined by crew and Dispatch that the dry ice quantity on board not only exceeded normal FOM limits; but was over the supplemental limits in the FOM.  I began a conference call with the Dispatcher; DO; and Flight Operations.  Based on all the information; they recommended we deploy the CO2 monitoring system and keep a close eye out for any elevated CO2 levels; but that we should be able to continue safely to our destination which was another 8 or so hours away.  We knew if the levels were elevated we could follow the QRH and use oxygen to breathe safely and divert if needed.  We also knew that we were flying right over ZZZ1 in about an hour which we could just divert to immediately to remedy the problem.  This would give us time to get ready for the divert and allow us to burn enough fuel to get below maximum landing weight.  So basically our options were 1) continue or 2) divert.  We woke up the Captain to provide him all of the data so he could make the decision.  With all the data and the opinions of the crew; he decided we should continue.  The decision was supported by the crew and Dispatch.  The rest of the flight was uneventful.  Obviously; undocumented hazardous materials is a big deal and could have serious safety concerns.  Luckily everything worked out here.  Once the issue was identified; Dispatch was a little slow to get us all the info and to provide input.  I believe this was because the Dispatchers had a shift change.  I think this led to information slowly being provided to all parties. The cause was someone [erred] in the chain of [custody] during loading; documenting; and manifesting must have made an error which led to this dry ice not being manifested.
column123: Approximately 20 minutes into flight; we received a message via ACARS from Dispatch that 1768lbs of dry ice went on the aircraft unmanifested and to please use supplemental dry ice procedures. At that time the RFO was in the jump seat and he retrieved; turned on and distributed a Drager monitor to each crew member. Once established in cruise; CA proceeded to the CRM as planned/briefed and RFO took the left seat. Subsequently we received message that the unmanifested dry ice was 1768kg; not lbs. We confirmed with  that the 1768kg was on the main deck along with the 116kg that was manifested ; for a total of 1884kg of dry ice on the main deck. The main deck limit is 1814kg. DO stated that he and dispatch agreed; that with all systems on the aircraft functioning properly and with FOM 10.37 DRY ICE SUPPLEMENTAL PROCEDURES in place; we were OK to continue to destination; however; if Captain desired to divert that would be appropriate as well given the over-limit situation. At that time; we had just passed the east coast of [State]. Diverting to a [company name] base at that time would have required dumping fuel in order to land under MAXLGW. FO and RFO discussed and determined that we would arrive overhead ZZZ1 on current flight planned route at MAXLGW and that if a divert decision was made; ZZZ1 was the most appropriate divert base. One hour prior to arriving overhead ZZZ1; FO awakened the CA in the CRM and informed him of the situation and [Dispatch's] deferral to him on a divert decision. CA agreed that continuing on  was appropriate. FO/RFO informed [Dispatch] via ACARS of decision to continue to [our destination] using dry ice supplemental procedures. Rest of flight was uneventful. A [contributing] cause was it had something to do with this being a chartered/non standard flight.

column121: While on our first attempt to land at COD we were vectored onto the RNAV to Runway 4 visual conditions prevailed and we were using the RNAV primarily for additional terrain clearance continuous moderate turbulence and windshear persisted on the arrival. ATC vectors and my attempts to maintain an airspeed that buffered against the rapid ups and downs of the green line and the rapid fluctuations of the indicated airspeed left us high and fast on our first attempt so we initiated a go-around missed approach. There was a significant tailwind down the valley that sheared to a headwind at the surface this contributed to us being high and fast.While we were climbing out we were instructed to climb and maintain 15;000 feet and were given vectors back to TOCUD. Approaching TAKBE the Captain requested a turn direct to TAKBE from ATC. Being at 15;000 [feet] we couldn't lower the flaps [so] the Captain instructed me to set 12;200 [feet] for TAKBE and start down. I complied with these instructions and as we dropped below 15;000 [feet] we began lowering the flaps and configuring.Shortly after starting our descent ATC issued a low altitude alert and stated that his minimum vectoring altitude was 15;000 [feet]. We were visual with both the mountains and airport in sight but failed to get proper approval from ATC for the visual approach before descending. As a side note we were being shook pretty good by the continuous moderate turbulence and I was really having to work the thrust levers to maintain a safe airspeed. We informed ATC that we were visual and we were cleared for the approach to Runway 4. We successfully landed on our second attempt. At no time was the safety of the fight or terrain clearance an issue and no EGPWS cautions or warnings were issued.Confusion on my part of the Captains instruction to 'sneak / start down'. It was the last leg of long hot sweaty day with multiple Captain swaps delays and MX issues; heat fatigue and dehydration were setting in and the turbulence and windshear created a very challenging flight environment.Once we goofed up and should have made sure that we were cleared for the visual prior to initiating a descent from a clearance altitude. The clearance to turn direct to TAKBE was not a clearance to descend even though we were visual. Mountain airports and strong winds are a difficult mix and other than adopting overly restrictive limits these difficult approaches will continue to be part of the job.

I was taxiing at 15 kt. on the straightaway; brought the thrust levers to idle; and began braking to slow down for the 1st turn. The 1st turn is about a 30-degree angle. When I started the turn; we were at about 12 kt. and slowing; [and] then began hydroplaning; I had no nose wheel steering or braking. I continued to turn the nose wheel to the right hoping to gain traction and [to also] keep the airplane on the taxiway. After that turn; the airplane gained traction and the nose wheel steering was able to steer the plane to the right. However; I still did not have braking available. I was able to steer the plane back to the centerline and [to] stay on the taxiway.
column123: We were taxiing in from landing on Runway XXL in ZZZ. During the approach there was moderate rainfall. Our taxi instructions were to taxi via Taxiway XY; Taxiway XZ; Taxiway XA; Taxiway XX; hold short of Runway XXC at Taxiway XX. As we turned onto Taxiway XX from Taxiway XA; the moderate rain had started to subside. The Captain was taxiing slower than usual due to the contaminated taxiway conditions - standing water. [At] the first bend on Taxiway XX as it turns from a south to a southwest heading; the aircraft almost completely lost traction. The nose wheel understeered and the aircraft continued straight ahead even as the taxiway turned. The Captain applied braking and the main tires also lost traction immediately. I also applied the brakes on the First Officer's side because I thought we were going to depart the taxiway. The aircraft skidded approximately 15 feet and nearly departed the prepared surface. At the last second; the aircraft slowed enough to allow the nose wheel to regain some effectiveness. The Captain was able to steer the aircraft back toward the centerline. There was a short; but secondary loss of traction [and] as we overshot the taxiway centerline; the aircraft was still in a partial skid.I have never seen an aircraft moving that slowly lose traction on a wet taxiway. I estimate the aircraft was moving at 15 kt. when the turn began. Both the Captain and I agree that this was something neither of us expected or have ever seen in our combined experience on the 737. I do believe any prudent pilot would have taken the turn at the same speed considering the conditions. It's my feeling that there was some issue with drainage or that [that] stretch of pavement is unusually slick during rainy conditions. I notified the Ground Controller of the event and reported braking action as fair to poor. I asked them to inform other aircraft of the slippery conditions on Taxiway XX between Runway XXL and XXC.

column123: Flight ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. Level FL370 for about 10-15 minutes just short of ZZZ3.  Pressure page came up on lower ECAM and we saw that cabin pressure was rising quickly above 8;000 PSI. Cabin pressure was climbing as we descended; so that as we descended through 16;000 ft the cabin pressure reached 14;000 feet and the cabin oxygen masks deployed. CA requested single frequency approach and I requested AARF. We made normal visual (ILS back up) approach into ZZZ. Landed and stopped on RWY XXC.  AARF looked for indications of fire/smoke.  There were none.  We taxied to gate X and AARF followed.  All passengers were deplaned and firefighters boarded to check for fire indications. column121: There had been a ground stop for passing storms to the east; which were now 1/3 of the way between ZZZ and ZZZ1. The Captain gave a briefing and asked the Flight Attendants to remain seated the entire flight due to the cells we'd be flying around and the potential for turbulence. He also made this part of his welcome aboard announcement.We took off and were given a 090 heading; transitioning north of the group of cells. This group of cells gave us a small option north toward ZZZ2 VOR and a small option south between cells. Neither path had a significant advantage over the other.Once we were abeam the northern track; ATC gave us a hole they depicted on their radar to our 1 o'clock position. We opted to continue straight; but ATC said straight looked worse to them. We conversed back and forth with them and the hole appeared to our right and clear skies on the back side. We maneuvered right; then left to make a perpendicular path through the hole. The bottom of the hole was higher than our altitude and we were given a climb from 17;000 to FL210. We tried to establish this climb at 250 kts. to stay slow for possible turbulence. This was made difficult by the fact we had an MEL for the speed bug. The speed bug jumped from the upper 200s into the lower 300s; back and forth throughout the flight. It was distracting and was the first time either of us had experienced this particular anomaly in nearly four years. Just prior to penetration; we could see heavy lightning coming from the cells immediately left of our path; extending toward the area we were originally going toward.As we climbed to FL210; we penetrated the lower portion of the hole and into IMC. Throughout the encounter; we had moderate turbulence and heavy to extreme rain. Our ice detection caution message activated; as well.We estimate the pass took 30 to 45 seconds to transition. I tried to transmit to ATC not to send anyone behind us; but never received a response.Once in clear air; I tried ATC again and they said they'd been trying to reach us to say the hole had closed up on their scope. We never their transmission either.In discussion after passing into clear air; neither of us felt we'd encountered hail. The sound of the rain striking the window and body of the aircraft were consistent with heavy to extreme rain.I checked on the Flight Attendants to make sure they were ok and to make sure the passengers were ok; and everyone was. We landed without incident and discovered damage during the walk around.The first area I noticed was the radome. There were extensive areas where the paint had been removed and the composite material underneath was exposed. There were three areas where horizontal slices in the composite material were visible. There was at least one area where a circular area was compromised. Most of the damaged paint and material were on the upper half of the radome. There was one hole that was previously covered during the preflight inspection that was now exposed due to speed tape coming off the aircraft. We conducted numerous; slow and methodical visual inspections of the exterior of the aircraft over the course of the next two hours. The only other damage was an unidentified antenna on the top of the aircraft. It was located aft of the VHF 1 antenna and forward of the upper beacon. POH and PRM (Pilot's Reference Manual) searches failed to produce an identity to this antenna; and might possibly be a wifi antenna installed after manufacturer documents were printed.The Captain notified [Maintenance Control]; the Chief Pilots; and Dispatch and briefed them on the incident and the status of the aircraft. Our Contract Maintenance arrived about an hour later and began making an evaluation of the damage. Our return flight was eventually cancelled and we rode the brakes for Ground Personnel while they repositioned the aircraft. We left the aircraft with Maintenance and proceeded to the hotel. After the flight; the Captain and I debriefed our flight and the incident. The flight attendants and the passengers were secured at the time due to crew briefings and the announcement that the seat belt sign would stay on and the flight attendants would remain seated throughout the flight. As previously noted; we had north and south options that were basically equal. Since our radar conflicted somewhat with ATC; we applied their observations into our decision making process in accordance with good CRM procedures. We had convection on our left and right sides and clear blue skies ahead. At that time; we were within a few miles from ZZZZZ and just about to level off at 3;000 feet. The Autopilot Mode Control panel was in Vertical Speed (Altitude Acquire) and LNAV to ZZZZZ. I was anticipating going to ZZZZZ1 and was ready to change the altitude to 2;800 feet in MCP for the autopilot. We were then cleared on a 160 degree heading to join the final approach course of 128; and cleared for the approach. I didn't hear the Controller say 'maintain 3;000 feet until established.' I selected VOR/LOC and dialed 2;800 feet into the autopilot Mode Control Panel. Because we were in a descent and in Altitude Acquire; the autopilot continued to descend towards 2;800 feet.My First Officer said we were supposed to maintain 3;000 feet. I had missed that part of the clearance so I dialed 3;000 feet into the Mode Control Panel; but by that point the aircraft had descended below 3;000 feet and was continuing to descend and would not ever capture 3;000 feet. I was also trying to slow the aircraft and get it to capture the localizer. Seeing that we weren't going to level off; I tried to use Vertical Speed to make the aircraft climb back to 3;000 feet; but it was continuing to descend. Our descent was exacerbated by the fact that I still had the speedbrakes deployed almost to the flight [descent]. ZZZ TRACON (Approach Control) said he he had a low altitude alert and his MVA [Min Vector Altitude] was 2;800 feet. We were now at about 2;300 feet. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles; started a climb and we decided to go missed approach. I finally stowed the speedbrakes; climbed to our clearance altitude and we then got re-vectored by ZZZ TRACON for another approach to Runway XXR and landed safely.
column123: We were being vectored around some weather coming into ZZZ and were given a descent to 3;000 feet and direct ZZZZZ outside of ZZZZZ1 on the ILS XXX. After a pause; as I pondered his meaning; I responded that we were IMC. At the time; I didn't think we were high; so I assumed he meant visually. Just a couple miles outside of ZZZZZ; Captain asked for a turn to ZZZZZ1. I paused because I was anticipating a vector shortly to intercept the final approach course. Because it all got really busy; I didn't see that Captain dialed in 2;800 feet. So; I don't think it acquired 3;000 feet and was now descending below it. Then I think 3;000 feet was reset into the MCP and yet the aircraft was still descending. All of this was happening while I was replying to ATC and I didn't realize what happened until after we talked about it later. We triggered a low altitude alert; and ATC informed us that we were to maintain 3;000 feet until established. I responded that we were correcting. Captain was climbing back up to 3;000 feet and we were slightly south of the localizer. I figured by the time we got back to 3;000 feet; we would then be high for the approach and not being established on the localizer; I said we should go-around. Captain agreed; and we did. column121: New Captain was PM; LCA (Line Check Airman) was flying from right seat on arrival into IAH. Approach kept us so high the entire time we had to get approval to miss the altitudes. Aircraft on other arrivals were holding and we were expecting the same. We were cleared to descend via the GUSHR arrival; and had to use full speed brakes the whole time but we made 10;000 at 250kts; and were able to make the bottom altitude at GUSHR at 6000 and 210 kts. Big rain shower at 15 miles out on the final of 8L. By the time we went by the rain shower it was mostly north of our course but there was rain and lightning coming out of the shower. TCAS showed traffic on 8R behind and above us. We could see him out of our window.  We were told to hold 200 knots till about 10 mile final. At this time; traffic somewhere; behind us we think; said they needed to go around because of rain and lightning. Approach gave us a frequency and switched us to tower and told us to tell them our speed.  We switched to the Tower frequency but must have put it in wrong; and when we tried to check on to what we thought was tower; another approach told us it was the wrong frequency. To go to the Tower; we looked up on the Jepp chart and the Tower frequency for 8L was 120.725. We called Tower on 120.725 and they cleared us to land. On final after that; a monitor came on and told us to change to 119.82. We switched to 119.82 and it was the same Tower Controller as 120.725 and she cleared us to land a second time. After landing we were told to contact ATC for possible pilot deviation. We had no idea why. We contacted the ATC Ops Manager who said there was a possible conflict with the traffic on 8R as that traffic was so close that had he not seen the airport and been given a visual we would have been too close and had a separation issue.1. We were cleared for an ILS. There was no PRM operations being used or advertised.2. The tower frequency they were using; 119.82 is nowhere on the IAH 70-9 page; dated 16APR21; effective 22APR21. ATC Ops Manager said Houston has been using frequency 119.82 as Tower for a few weeks because coverage was poor on the other frequency in some areas; but that frequency (119.82) is not published anywhere. 3. After talking with ATC Ops Manager; we verified in the NOTAMs there was nothing about 119.82 being used anywhere.4. Why is approach cramming the planes on approach so close that a momentary loss of communication results in loss of separation?

column121: As Captain; I was the Pilot Monitoring and the First Officer was the Pilot Flying for this flight. On the take off roll at approximately 90 to 100kts; I hear the First Officer make the comment 'There seems to be a lot of airflow through this window'. I glanced over and to see from my point of view that the window appears to be closed. I shift my eyes back to the runway centerline; airspeed and engine instruments while thinking about what he said. At approximately 110kts; it becomes loud with high airflow into the flight deck. The First Officer shouts 'My window is open'. I quickly glance over to his side to see he has his left hand on the control wheel and is holding the R 2 flight deck window closed by the window lock lever with his right hand. I immediately took the controls. At this time we are approximately 120kts just prior to V1 (129). I took a quick glance at my First Officer and back to my instruments; I saw that we were Vr + 8 to 9kts. I then rotated. I saw a positive rate of climb and shout 'gear up'. The First Officer assumed pilot monitoring and raised the landing gear. I shouted 'Can you crank the window closed at all?' He responded 'No; it won't close'. At this point; Tower had advised us to contact Departure. I selected the Center Autopilot; VNAV & Heading Select with a heading of 360 as assigned. I opened the speed window and remained at Flaps 5 to prevent the airplane from accelerating. I figured the faster we would go; the louder the flight deck would be and the more the First Officer would struggle to hold the window in position. The First Officer shouts 'I can't hear anything from ATC.' Around 3;400 ft. I contacted Departure and informed them that we need to stop climb and return to the airport because we have a flight deck window opened. We were given a left heading of 270 and to maintain 4;000. We performed the after takeoff checklist. My First Officer states 'I can't hear anything from ATC but what do you need from me?' I responded 'ATC is giving us vectors back to ILS RWY XX. If you can; get flight deck performance for Runway XX and set us up for the ILS RWY XX; I'll do a quick brief; then we will do our Descent and Approach checklist.' With one hand still on the window crank; the First Officer did just that and along with his flow. ATC gave us another vector and asked if we need more time. I told ATC that we were not ready and asked to continue heading at 270 and 4;000. Once we were set up; briefings and checklist were complete; I advised ATC we were ready for the approach. Since I was flying while doing the radios myself and the First Officer with only one free hand available; I decided it would not be prudent to be heads down and message Dispatch through ACARS. I felt the priority was to fly the plane and get us safely on the ground. I informed ATC 'We [request priority]; 2 souls on board and approximately 4 and half hours fuel on board'. ATC asked the nature of the [situation] and I replied 'We have a flight window cracked'. I meant to say cracked open; however; the noise from the airflow was a little distracting. ATC gives us an intercept heading of 100 and clears us for the approach. We were stable; fully configured; and all checklists were complete prior to the final approach fix. At 800 feet AGL we broke out of the clouds. I had the airport in sight and disengaged the autopilot. A normal landing was made at approximately 265;000 lb. We informed Tower that we did not need assistance and taxied to parking. Upon taxi in; I do not know if the First Officer closed the window or left it in its previous condition from flight; opened. Perhaps he left it alone so that Maintenance could inspect. I wrote up that the First Officer R2 flight deck window opened on takeoff/climb and I waited for them to inspect. There was no damage or defects noted.I honestly do not know if it was a Flight Deck Window malfunction or if it was ever truly locked. Both of us had opened our Flight Deck Windows on the ground during preflight because the APU was off and the temperature was in the 70's. About 30 minutes prior to block out; I started the APU and we closed our windows. In the Before Start portion of the checklist; I verified my flight window was closed and locked with strut at a 90 degree position. I heard the First Officer respond 'Closed and locked'. I could see his Window Lock Lever was in the forward and locked position; however; I could not verify if his decal showed 'CLOSED' nor if the strut was at a 90 angle simply because of the angle from where I was sitting in the Captain's seatI think that in the moment; the First Officer did a great job of prioritizing aircraft control in such a critical phase of flight. To be in the high speed regime of takeoff; so close to V1 and to keep 'aviating' while a huge startling distraction occurred was commendable. He also; kept his head in the game and jumped to the pilot monitoring duties without delay. He prompted me for the after takeoff checklist as we were about to level off at 4;000. If I could have done one thing over; I would have shouted 'My controls' in a louder voice. I didn't take into consideration that the First Officer could not hear well at that point.I'm also appreciative of our Company training video made by Boeing of a flight with the flight deck window opened. I'm glad that I was shown to me during my 767 upgrade training. I never thought I would be in that situation but thankfully I had some idea of what to expect. The plane will be extremely loud and distracting but it will safely fly.
column123: During takeoff my window opened immediately after the CA (Captain) called '80 knots; thrust set.' I was PF and saw the window rolling aft. I grabbed the window handle with my right hand while continuing to fly. I maintained runway centerline and described what happened by shouting cross cockpit to allow the CA to have the information and make an appropriate reject decision. About 10 knots before V1 the CA took the aircraft. I couldn't hear him verbally call V1 due to the cockpit noise and open window. Perhaps I didn't hear him call V1 because he had already taken the aircraft. Regardless it was loud and my audio panel wasn't set up to compensate for the noise.When the aircraft rotated I immediately assumed the role of Pilot Monitoring. He shouted to raise the landing gear and I did. The CA flew and took the radios because I had shouted cross cockpit that I couldn't hear ATC well enough to communicate. Both of us had to compensate because of the noise. The CA selected heading select and turned left to our assigned heading of 360 and elected to select VNAV and Center Autopilot Command almost simultaneously.The CA requested to stop climb around 5;100 MSL and informed me that we would return to ZZZ. Around this time I had determined that as long as I held the window with a good amount of strength it wouldn't roll open. I adjusted my interphone and ATC freq to Max volume so that I could hear. I then asked the CA if he was ready to run the After Takeoff Checklist and we did. Everything from that point forward was standard and in order except that the CA had to turn the Standby Attitude Indicator to ILS mode because I had one hand holding the window; the CA [advised ATC]; and did the radios. After we landed all roles were normal and the taxi in was standard.This situation is dynamic. I think perhaps a better verbal transfer of aircraft control on takeoff roll but we effectively handled the situation. I thought the CA was going to reject the takeoff. By the time he processed what was going on he decided it was safer to continue the takeoff. It was loud and we coordinated the best we could in this situation.

column121: We had coordinated on a ZZZ to ZZZ1 out and back for extra gas so we wouldn't have to shut down the engine at ZZZ1. We had a quick turn and the APU was INOP.  After taxiing into the gate without incident; we shut down the left engine and left the right engine running. I got our new release and it said we needed 7.8k gate/6.1k min fuel. We had 6.8k on board and Dispatch gave us a ton extra for holding. I called Dispatch and asked just to take the fuel we had on board and they agreed and sent us a new fuel plan via ACARs. Simultaneously; I had the First Officer go out and tell the ramp we didn't want fuel or external power. He came back and said in informed the Ramp Supervisor. AC power was not applied to the aircraft. We deboarded and boarded without incident. Then about 20 minutes after getting into the gate; while briefing the takeoff; I noticed the AUTO XFLOW INHIBIT message and saw we were taking on fuel. It was less than 300 lbs at that time. I immediately jumped up and opened the galley door and shouted to the fueler to stop because the Right engine was running. It took him approximately a minute to understand what I was saying and he stopped fueling. We took on about 1000 lbs total. I contacted the ramp and he said that they were Other Company and not under his direct control. I informed him I would write up the incident. Rest of the flight was without incident.Have a notice to the pilots and to stations directed specifically at the rampers and fuelers that aircraft cannot Hot refuel. This seems to be more of we're finally busy and COVID is over so we're rusty and rushed. I had a second incident at ZZZ on the return flight. We arrived at the gate in ZZZ without incident. I shut down the left engine while leaving the right one running since we had no APU. The ground crew had trouble hooking up power and before I shut down the second engine; I saw the AUTO XFLOW INHIBIT status message. I had the First Officer immediately head to the galley door to have ramp stop fueling which was just starting. I was mostly deplaned and power was coming up so I killed the engine. The First Officer got the fueler to stop and we took on less than 100 lbs. I discussed with ramp personal reminding them not to start fueling until the engines are shut down. Nothing further of note happened after that.Unrelated; but distracting; update the APU start checklist and remove all items that are duplicates and will be handled under another checklist (told data; doors; trim; fuel check value test; etc.).

column121: Original clearance was to fly the ORKA5 departure with LAS transition. FO was flying. At or near COOPP intersection Center gave us instructions that we understood to be 'fly heading 070 degrees and expect ORCKA and then the BEALE transition'. We set up our FMS for this new transition. Shortly afterward we both heard what we thought was 'cleared direct ORCKA and fly the BEALE transition' and the CA read exactly that back.  A few minutes after we had established course to ORCKA center called another flight and directed a stop climb at FL190. We were passing through FL200 for FL230 when we noticed another aircraft on TCAS at 10-15 miles range reach 300 feet below our altitude before descending back down to FL 190. Center then called out that we were off course. CA replied we were direct ORCKA then BEALE Transition as directed. Controller then stated 'No you were cleared ARCUS and the BEALE transition'. ARCUS is the next fix after ORCKA on the ORKA5/BEALE SID and sounds very similar to ORCKA on a VHF radio. No TCAS alerts were initiated and no conflict occurred.The primary factor is the fact that ORCKA and ARCUS; two consecutive points along the ORKA5 SID sound similar over the VHF radio.  So similar; in fact; that both pilots heard it wrong when the clearance was first issued and the ATC controller heard it wrong when we read it back.Two suggestions: 1. I recommend that Jeppesen change either ORCKA or ARCUS naming on the SID.  2. When waypoints on a SID sound so clearly similar ATC should phonetically spell out the fix cleared to.

column123: While being vectored for ILS approach to RWY XXL at ZZZZ; the Pilot Flying momentarily began an early descent through required altitude of 2;600 feet.  I; the pilot not flying; and the jumpseat pilot gave immediate verbal corrections. Aircraft descended to approximately 2;420 feet as the Pilot Flying regained situational awareness and applied corrective action to include resetting the MCP altitude; and then reverting to manual control.  The recovery was smooth and controlled.  As the aircraft was returning to 2;600 feet; ZZZZ Radar Control called to direct climb to 2;600 feet.  I responded to ATC while the Pilot Flying completed the recovery.  Approach and landing were completed uneventfully.   This was the final segment of a 2 leg international flying pairing nearing 17 hours of duty.  All crew members were not at their best state of alertness.  Original arrival setup was for a STAR coupled to an ILS approach.  Flown arrival was very non standard. The aircraft was vectored off arrival path and given clearance to disregard many published mandatory altitudes.  This complicated arrival descent planning and may have led to the Pilot Flying losing some situational awareness.  ATC Traffic on approach ahead was a potential conflict.  This diverted my attention during the approach.Delays in positive corrective action which could have lessened/prevented the altitude deviation were potentially caused by distraction due to traffic call; lessened cognitive performance due to overnight/long duty period; lack of urgency due to VMC weather with runway in view.

column121: Early descent and low speed condition resulting in go-around. I was the Pilot Flying. Very short flight. Visual approach to RWY 15 at CHS. I was expecting the ILS approach. I missed that the GS for RWY 15 was out of service. We had briefed the OSPRI7 STAR. ATC recleared us direct to the airport and eventually direct MAMAE intersection to join the localizer for [Runway] 15 at 3;000 [feet] ft. Airport was in sight and we were cleared for a visual approach. I armed the approach and when we went into altitude capture at 3;000 [feet] I incorrectly set an altitude below 3;000 [feet] to allow the descent to continue in order to join the glide slope. I then realized we were not receiving the glide slope and were below the FAF crossing altitude at 1000ft. I disconnected the autopilot and stopped the descent. Unfortunately I did not also call for the flight directors off initially. I am relatively new to the equipment. Since we were in landing configuration of course the speed dropped rapidly. We were in landing configuration with the airport and PAPI's in sight but since the approach was unstable I decided to go around. We then flew the RWY 15 RNAV (GPS)Y to a normal landing. It was the third leg of a busy day with thunderstorm avoidance on the first two flights. It is my practice to carefully review the NOTAMs but somehow I missed the GS OTS. I haven't been into CHS as yet and the flight is very short and our ATC clearance had us high from the top of descent.Direct to a new airport on a time compressed flight for a visual at night is never in my opinion a pleasant way to conclude a long day of flying. Upon honest reflection I fully acknowledge I had a strong expectation bias for the ILS to 15. The lack of the GS and the unexpected consequences placed us in a reactionary position which is unacceptable.Our training is clear on how to capture and correct erroneous situations should they occur and we did our best to stop and correct an inadvertently entered unstable position. This was a clear example of the value and necessity of our human factors training. I know these things have happened before and I consider it my professional responsibility to not allow it to happen to me. And yet it did. Recognizing; and fully appreciating how higher than expected workload situations can present themselves is an essential aspect to our work. An increased diligence regarding the review of NOTAMs is a resounding suggestion I'm making to myself for one. Also; the need for particularly increased vigilance when in situations such as this is something I'll never forget.

column121: Inadvertent switching off of IR1 mode selector which deactivated that associated ADIRU. ADR and IR data not available. This occurred during flight one of day two of an initial Captain upgrade. The trainee came off the B777. He has been with our company for many years. The three legs of day one was extraordinarily busy. It was immediately clear to me during those three legs he had studied hard during training and had mastered much of the material. On the first two legs of day one I had a LCA (Line Check Airman) in-training watching me conduct the line check as part of that LCA's upgrade training. I commented to the new LCA not all trainees will be so well prepared as this one.This flight was leg four of the IOE and the first flight of day two. Our transportation to the airport was 15 minutes late and there was a detour so we arrived at the aircraft about 30 minutes prior to departure. Normally; I introduce myself to all the FAs (Flight Attendant). However; because we were on IOE; [we] were somewhat late to the aircraft and on Release 6. I only introduced myself to the FM. I felt I did not have time go to the back to introduce myself to the FAs assigned to the rear of the aircraft.We had been in the seat for approximately 3 hours. The upgrade Captain requested I ask the FM to prepare the meals and that we would then take a restroom break when the meals were ready. I did so. The FM called us about 25 minutes later to state the meals were ready. The upgrade Captain offered me the opportunity to use the Lav first. I declined and said he should go first and I would then go. The door chime rang and then I heard a knock. That knock is not standard. However; it occurs occasionally with legacy Company 2 flight attendants. We put on our masks. I saw the upgrade Captain move to get out of his seat; stand up; and let the FA in while he then left the cockpit. I noticed nothing odd about his movement out of the seat and to the rear of the cockpit. I saw out of the corner of my eye the FA was standing near the rear of the cockpit just behind and to the right of the Captain's seat; a normal position for a relief FA.My concentration then focused on something else. I think it was because we were getting ready to enter a large area of convective activity. I might have been looking at WSI and comparing that to what I was seeing on the weather radar. Why my gaze was generally focused forward and right I am not sure; but it was. I planned to brief the relief FA about this weather and its possible effect on their service in a few minutes. It was at that point; maybe 30-45 seconds after the upgrade Captain had left the cockpit; that for lack of a better description; 'all hell broke loose.' The cockpit went from a completely benign environment to one of confusion. The startle effect was in full force. The first warning was a continuous repetitive chime and the warning lights flashing. I immediately looked at the E/WD (Engine/Warning Display) and noted about 4-5 ECAMs listed; primary secondary and independent failures in both red and amber. I silenced the CRC (Continuous Repetitive Chime) by pushing [the] master warning light. That silenced the CRC. However; there still was an aural alert going off that I could not silence; which created a fair bit of consternation on my part. I look at my PFD and saw the FMAs were wrong. I then saw the AP (Autopilot) was off and that there was nothing where I expected to see the AT (Autothrottle) condition. I noted the aircraft climbing slightly and corrected that. I knew the AP disengaged for some reason but didn't know why. I thought about engaging AP 2 but then thought that may create new problems; so I elected to hand-fly until the ECAMs were sorted out. I saw we were no longer in NAV but again; wasn't sure why. I did see that the aircraft didn't diverge much from the 'green line' so lateral stick inputs weren't necessary. At this point ATC called to ask us something about recycling the transponder. We wereon speaker at that time; I responded we had a problem and to standby.I then noted the airspeed increasing and pulled the TLs (Thrust Lever) back; I didn't want to add an over-speed to our problems. This silenced another aural sound. I do not recall seeing a Thrust Locked ECAM or FMA which I thought would have been the source of the alert I couldn't silence. I glanced at the Captain PFD (Primary Flight Display) and ND (Navigation Display) and saw they didn't look right.The aircraft was reasonably stabilized now but; in my mind; because the ECAMs were displayed; the situation wasn't. I then told the FA to recall the trainee Captain to the cockpit. He opened the door; looked and then closed it; and said he was in the bathroom. I told the FA I knew that and I wanted him back in the cockpit now. He then had the FM knock on the Lav door. The trainee Captain returned to the cockpit and the relief FA left. The trainee Captain was incredulous when he looked at the E/WD. I told him I was hand-flying; had the aircraft and radios; and that he was to handle the ECAMs. It was at this point I noted we were about 20 knot slow; well within flying speed but slow for planned speed. I had overcompensated for my worry of overspending the aircraft. I pushed the power back up. Airspeed had fallen out of my cross-check. The trainee Captain methodically and correctly went through the ECAMs. As I recall the first several ECAMs had no action items; one ECAM had us switch the air data switch to three. At some point during this; ATC stated they now had data on us and asked if we needed assistance. We told him we were completing a procedure and to standby. Once the status messages were read and the ECAM procedure completed; I reached up to engage AP two. It did so. I armed the AT and then moved the TLs to the climb detent to engage it. Our ATC clearance was to proceed direct to a fix so we reinserted that. I don't recall having to pull or push to capture our assigned altitude but I can't be sure.It was now maybe 4-5 minutes after the initial event where I could take a breath. I recalled the ECAM and saw the ADR 1 fault. I then looked over to the ADIRS panel and saw IR mode selector one was in the OFF position. It; of course; was on for the flight up until some point in [the] last few minutes. I asked the trainee Captain if he recalls hitting the switch with his head or back as he left his seat. He said no. I then thought perhaps the switch was defective. This aircraft came to us as a through flight. We did not have to turn them on so we had no knowledge of how that switch felt by turning it on. We again discussed it and he stated he didn't recall even touching the overhead panel while leaving the seat.Because I didn't introduce myself to the FAs at the rear of the aircraft prior to the flight; I wasn't sure which FA came to the cockpit during our break. I asked the FM to ask the FA who came to the cockpit to call us on the interphone. That FA did and I asked him if he recalled touching anything on the overhead panel; he stated he did not. What I found unusual was that during the event; the FA seemed very nonplussed by the cacophony of sounds in the cockpit. I would have expected a FA to at least ask what was going on; but maybe he was somewhat shocked by what he saw and heard during his short time in the cockpit.The trainee Captain and I discussed that I would write up the ECAM and then conference Dispatch and Technical Support Maintenance Control to provide further details of what we thought may have occurred. I wanted the switch looked at but also didn't want Maintenance to search for a problem which might not exist. I ACARS'd Dispatch with the request and he set up the conference call. The communications with Technical Support Maintenance Control were reasonably good and he captured exactly what I wanted him to know and he appended it to our write-up. Since the Captain's displays were significantly degraded; we switched PF/PM roles. Fromthat point we continually deviated for weather; were put in holding; and changed our alternate three times. We over-burned by almost 5500 lb on this flight; more than on any flight I have been on in [an] Airbus. It was an understatement to say this was a busy flight. I don't know how this happened. The final flight of the day was a termination. As the trainee ran that checklist and turned off the IRUs; he stated he couldn't believe how he accidentally managed to switch that style of switch - pull and turn - off by getting out of the cockpit.I am disappointed in myself for not more thoroughly reviewing the flight manual for ADR 1 fault after things had settled down. We did not have a GPWS TERR FAULT light and no ECAM direction to switch it off so it remained on. We discussed that threat in that we were now the aircraft's GPWS system and to be cognizant of the terrain. We also discussed changing the transponder to position 2 but did not do so because there was no ECAM direction to [do] so and ATC noted no anomalies in our reporting. Also; once I saw the IR mode selector switch in the off position; I should have considered reviewing the NAV IR fault non-normal even though we didn't have that ECAM. I did not do a word search in the flight manual for ADR. Had I done so; I would have seen that there may be RVSM limitations associated with its failure and should have gone to the FOM for further information. I recall many years ago; our Line Manager at the time; wrote up in his weekly update a similar event. As I recall he wrote the trainee somehow managed to hook the window shade into that same switch and turned it off. That of course didn't happen here.

column121: We were descending on the arrival into ZZZ. We were descending at a high speed programmed into the FMC. I have over 10;000 hours flying the Next Gens and am comfortable with that descent profile. This was my first MAX flight. Somewhere in the descent the FMA changed without warning to MCP SPD (Mode Control Panel Speed). It went unnoticed. I have witnessed many Next Gens revert to VNV SPD (Vnav Speed); but never MCP SPD. There is a significant difference; in that MCP SPD gives no altitude protection. I have never seen anything like this. Somewhere around ZZZZZ/11000; we received a radio call and became distracted as the aircraft descended through 11000. I did not catch the deviation until 10;000 and momentum and recovery took us to about 9;500 feet. I disconnect all automation and hand flew the recovery as I tried to figure out what had just happened. We reported the deviation to ATC and continued to ZZZ without incident.I do not know why this happened. I can only guess that somehow LVL CHG (Level Change) was inadvertently selected. Another theory is that VNV could not keep up and reverted to MCP SPD. This happens sometimes in the Next Gens; but it always reverts to VNV SPD; which is much safer.

column121: While at cruise at 35;000 feet in Cairo control airspace; we began to receive a series of Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting messages- ATC Fault; Unable RNP and Terrain Position.  We referenced the Quick Reference Handbook for each message but were unable to clear the faults. We asked ATC if they saw any issue with our transponder and they replied that they saw no problems. Shortly after crossing from Amman control to Jeddah on airway Y415; we received the FMC message 'Verify position'. We saw that we were off the airway to the left and ATC asked if we were on the airway. The First Officer and I put our range scales to 5 miles and noted that the left side showed us approximately 3 to 5 miles left of course; First Officer side showed the same distance to the right of course.We checked the FMC position reference pages and saw that GPS position was blank and substantial errors on the other positions - FMC; IRS and Radio. We advised ATC of the GPS failure and could not determine which source was accurate. ATC said we were showing right of course. I selected GPS off then on; selected HDG (heading) select to manually steer to course. Reselected LNAV. Nothing seemed to be working. I asked for direct to a fix further down the airway. No VORs were on this airway to use for navigation. I repeated switching heading to LNAV but the aircraft symbol did not move closer to the course line as if it was frozen. We were continually advising ATC and monitoring position reference as GPS was now intermittent and RNP-ANP errors were constantly changing. Eventually GPS began to work and we were able to get back on course.  This entire time we never received any EICAS or FMA indications of any faults such as 'GPS'; 'IRS Nav Only'; 'LNAV'.  ATC passed the information to subsequent ATC and they offered vectors if needed. After position MOGON; navigation functions all appeared normal for the remainder for the flight.

column121: During cruise flight; the Master Caution light illuminated with the #2 engine driven B hydraulic system light. We ran the QRH and turned the pump off; and also noted that the B system indicated approximately 3000 psi but zero quantity. We discussed the possibility that although technically the conditions were not yet met per the QRH; there was a strong possibility that entire B system had likely failed or was failing and notified Dispatch via ACARS that it was a possibility. We ran the weight data for landing in ZZZ with the B system inop; and came up with approximately 1;300 feet of stopping margin with max manual braking. We let Dispatch know that even with a hypothetical total loss of the B system; ZZZ was still acceptable and they concurred with our stopping margin calculation.  The B system held steady with approximately 3000 psi until we started our descent into ZZZ with approximately 120 miles to go.  As we were descending; the psi of the B system quickly dropped to near zero and the ELEC 1 B pump Low Pressure light illuminated; along with the Flight Control B Low Pressure light. We ran the QRH for Loss of System B and calculated brake cooling; which advised staying off the gate for 30 minutes.We advised Approach of the situation and asked for delay vectors for checklists and CFR (Crash Fire Rescue)  trucks to be present at the end of the runway to check brake temps and condition after landing. We landed on the runway at the end and shut down engines at the request of CFR. CFR noted that hydraulic fluid was leaking from number 2 engine and brake temps were above 500 C. They were also concerned about hydraulic fluid on the hot section of #2 engine aerosolizing and advised we wait for cooler temps for ramp safety. CFR advised that although the brakes had cooled acceptably they were still concerned about the possible aerosolizing of hydraulic fluid from #2 engine hot section and advised we wait another 10 minutes. This all led to a lengthy ground delay but we did the best we could to keep the flight attendants and Passengers informed. In our judgement it was the safest course of action to follow CFR recommendations.

column121: I knew it was going to be a struggle getting out of ZZZ with all passengers on board when I saw the take-off performance. At 40C the margin between PTOW (Planned Take-off Weight) and MTOW was 1100 lbs. My First Officer (FO) was terrific; but it was his first trip since IOE; he had 18 hours on the airplane at the start of the sequence; and had not flown prior to training for about 8 months. In addition; it was only my second time flying the ZZZZZ departure; which has three at or above altitudes on it; which is a new thing in ZZZ.  I live in ZZZ; and consequently fly out of there a great deal.  All previous RNAV departures used to have at or below altitudes on them (to keep clear of inbound aircraft); so it never used to be an issue worrying about making altitudes on the SID.  At the aircraft; I was already concerned about two things: brake temps and having to bump passengers.  I asked my FO to pull us up numbers for 41 and 42C; just in case it got hotter; as it was likely to. In addition; I believe the winds were swinging around - runway XXR had a tailwind component at one point; so I was also looking for numbers for XYL; but due to terrain; the only runway that worked at all was XXR.  I noticed that we would be unable to make the restrictions and asked the FO to ask for altitude relief on the SID as soon as he contacted ground.  In my experience; asking for altitude relief at other airports was never an issue; so I was not overly concerned. We pushed back; and naturally were over PTOW.  I asked the FO to request a new take-off performance for 41 and 42C.  We eventually landed on a Flaps 1 take-off performance requiring thrust bump which got us legal for takeoff.  All this occurred during the short taxi from the terminal to runway XXR.By the time we reached number 1 holding short of the runway; I realized we had forgotten to ask for the altitude relief on the SID. I asked the FO to do so as we were taking the runway.  The controller; upon hearing the request; told us to taxi clear and get a new clearance.  By this time there were 6-8 aircraft in a queue for takeoff; and our brake temps were over 150 degrees.  My main concern was that if we had to leave the runway; it would get too hot to accommodate the load; and by the time we taxied for another 30 minutes; the brakes would be too hot for takeoff.  So; glancing down at the FMS; which showed that we would miss the altitude restrictions by 5-700 feet; I knew that if we delayed cleanup; we could easily make those restrictions.  I told the controller that we could manage the departure; and he again cleared us for takeoff.  I told my FO that since we were at the max performance envelope of the airplane; he should rotate very gently.  As we were rolling down the runway; my attention was fixed on the EGT; as I had not done a bump takeoff before; and the engines were exactly on the edge of the red.  He did as I asked; and as a result; we were very fast on the initial climb segment.  As we climbed out; I was fixated on the altitude.  Once it became clear that the 5;000 ft altitude (I think around 4;500 feet MSL) I relaxed a bit and told him we could clean up.  He set climb power (which was a much greater reduction than normal due to the thrust bump) and I reached for the flap lever and set flaps up.  At this time we were still wings level.  I was so fixated on the altitude; and our airspeed shortly after takeoff was so much higher than usual that I didn't take a good look at the airspeed indicator.  I believe that I retracted the flaps very early. VLS (lowest selectable speed) jumped by perhaps 40 knots; and we ended up about 20 knots below VLS.  Naturally; we were now facing rapidly rising terrain; and the SID commanded a right turn.  My FO started to turn; and now instead of being below VLS; we were in alpha floor.  I instructed my FO to lower the nose; but it wasn't happening quickly enough; so I grabbed the side stick and pushed the nose over; at the same time requesting him to let go.  There was a momentary DUAL INPUT" annunciation and a momentary noticeable low speed buffet which lasted perhaps a second.  We lost perhaps 300 feet of altitude as I got the airspeed back.  We were able to make all of the altitude restrictions and I don't believe there were any deviations from the SID.  Once we recovered; the only other item remaining was how to get the auto throttles out of alpha floor.  Eventually; we turned them off (match and mash) and back on again and that got the system back to normal.I was using my knowledge of past experience flying the old SIDs.  They didn't have airspeed or at or above altitudes; and my experience in the past that asking for altitude relief on a SID was not a big deal.  In addition; I was flying with a brand new (very sharp) but inexperienced FO; who was relying entirely on my experience.  I was also pushing to accommodate the load without having to remove passengers and/or cargo; and was worried about the brake temp issues; causing me to push to get off the ground as soon as possible.I made several errors.  The first one was not notifying clearance delivery early of our inability to make the altitude and/or airspeed restrictions on the SID.  In the past; ZZZ used to have a procedure for A321 aircraft to delay climb power/flap retraction to 3;000 AGL.  I think if we had used that procedure; we probably would have been able to make the altitude and speed restrictions on the SID.  That procedure is gone.  Second; when we finally did request relief on the SID (by this time we were on the runway) and the controller told us to clear the runway and get a new clearance; I should have done so; even if it had caused us further problems with brake temp and/or takeoff weight.  Third; having taken the decision to take off because I was certain we could delay cleanup; thus making us legal for the SID; I should have taken over flying duties.  This would have alleviated my FO's task saturation; as I was far more experienced in the airplane.  This would still have been sub-optimal; but I am confident the takeoff would have been uneventful.   Fourth; once I retracted the flaps and we were below VLS; I should have put the flaps back to Config 1.  So; there were many errors on my part; but an early intervention with clearance delivery would have solved everything.  I believe there should be a warning to the A320 Fleet about the new SIDS; and that at high temperatures careful note should be taken of the danger of not being able to make altitude restrictions on any SID with at or above altitudes; especially early in the SID; and that relief should be requested at the gate with clearance delivery. Also to note: green dot speed (min maneuver) was 245 with flaps up; so the only way to maintain 230 knot speed at ZZZZZ waypoint is at config 1.  Again; the old requirement to clean up at 3000 AGL would have solved this."

column121: We went through a fume event on Aircraft X. It only affected F/A's [Flight Attendant] #1 and #3. The fume felt like a severe piercing acrid; mentholated winter-fresh smell. It started slowly and it rapidly increase to the point in which our eyes started watering; and our throats; and noses became irritated. Initially we both thought either of us was chewing on a winter fresh gum for our breaths. We then asked each other: 'Are you chewing gum?' we both said 'NO!' At that moment the odor/fume got excruciatingly pungent. The fume event lasted for about 5 minutes. We both complaint of having a growing headache. After landing; we both spoke to the Captain about our symptoms. The Captain wrote a mechanical report on the aircraft; and he will follow it up with another report.I am however; requesting for both F/A's to get checked medically through airline protocols; to see if we are fit to continue on our sequence.I am strongly advising for the two F/A's affected on this incident to get check out by medical staff.

column121: After landing at MDW around XA:30L; we were taxiing from Taxiway Y to T. At the end of Concourse XX; a 737 was being pushed back. Ground did not warn us of this aircraft. The First Officer (F/O) was calling Company Ops (Ground Ops) at that moment to verify the gate assignment. Ground Ops gave us the gate assignment and proceeded to give details that I needed to call Crew Scheduling upon parking. Meanwhile; I could see that the other 737 had been pushed back farther than it should have; causing me to hit the brakes to avoid a collision. At the same time; monitoring the Company frequency and the First officer's communication to Ground Ops; I was also suddenly distracted with the thought that Crew Scheduling had an unscheduled assignment for me and that I was on the hook to call them upon parking. To me; this was a clear violation of FAR 121.542; which outlines sterile cockpit requirements; it wasn't a violation on our part; rather the Company violated this regulation. I told the F/O that I was deviating to the right of the taxiway centerline; which leaves little room to the right; to avoid the pushed 737 off my left. I slowly and carefully taxied past; ensuring we had distance. I estimate we had only 15' distance from our wingtip to theirs. Thereafter; I taxied to the gate; still distracted and frustrated that I had been tagged to call Crew Scheduling. This distracted me from the primary task of safely taxiing the aircraft. Notification to contact Crew Scheduling has no place in the sterile cockpit environment. FAR 121.152 says; 'No certificate holder shall require; nor may any Flight Crew Member perform any duties during a critical phase of flight except those duties required for the safe operation of the aircraft. Duties such as Company required calls made for non-safety related purposes as ordering galley supplies and confirming Passenger connections; announcements made to Passengers promoting the air carrier or pointing out sights of interest and filling out Company payroll and related records are not required for the safe operation of the aircraft. Ground Ops generally has no idea what Crew Scheduling is doing or needs; they're not involved in the function of who flies what and where. In this case; I believe Crew Scheduling must have deliberately contacted MDW Ground Ops ahead of time and specifically instructed them to notify us during taxi-in. If they did this; this was willful on their part; it is beyond egregious; and it cannot be tolerated. Highly recommend that the FAA issue a notice to Air Carriers and their Ground Ops and Crew Scheduling departments; explaining what sterile cockpit rules are and when Crew Scheduling assignments cannot be allowed (i.e.; during aircraft taxi). I also recommend that the FAA review our FOM and Ground Ops Manual; and specifically include verbiage prohibiting messages from Crew Scheduling during critical phases of flight and sterile cockpit.

column121: I; the CA (Captain); was PM (Pilot Monitoring); the FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying). During the climb-out phase in level flight in mildly hazy VMC at 17;000 MSL at 290 KIAS with Autopilot B engaged the Master Caution; the 'FLT CONT' item on the CA-side SAP ('6-pack'); and the right half only of the 'STAB OUT OF TRIM' light illuminated. Press-to-test of the 'Stab out of trim' light showed both bulbs operable. After establishing that FO was actively remaining the PF; I performed 'Stabilizer Out of Trim' QRH procedure with the result that the autopilot electric trim and both pilot yokes trim switches were inoperative in both directions. I notified ATC that we had a mechanical problem that would eventually result in [requesting priority] and landing at a nearby airport; probably ZZZ; but for now we were content to remain at 17;000 slowly outbound from ZZZ while we worked the problem. Knowing we were also over landing weight; nicely under control; and still had a lot of checklists to run; I had no desire to rush into diving towards some final approach fix before we were ready to land. I performed the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' QRH procedure with the result that manual hand-cranked trimming was possible in either direction; albeit against unusually high resistance and with a 'cogging' feel as if pushing against a powered but stalled electric motor. This was true even when the aircraft was in-trim. One pilot could move the trim using one arm; but two pilots using one arm each worked much better for anything more than a couple turns of the trim wheel. We found that one pilot could both hand-fly and crank the trim; but tended to make unwanted aileron inputs while doing so. So it was doable in a pinch but not smooth. The forces required to turn the trim wheel did not appreciably reduce as we later slowed & configured. In the course of reading & discussing or doing the 'deferred items' section of the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' QRH I started to activate the GPWS Flap inhibit switch.  The FO stopped me saying we were above the 250 KIAS speed limit at that time.  That sounded familiar to me; but no such limitation is stated at that point in the QRH.  Nevertheless; we chose to delay activating the GPWS flap inhibit until we had slowed to first configuration speed around 220KIAS. Discussed with [the] FO whether ZZZ was the best divert option and which runway to use. ZZZ & longer Runway XXL was the unanimous choice. By that time we were a few miles south of [the] VOR on a south-southwesterly course for ZZZZZ; roughly 100nm from ZZZ.I then performed the 'Non-routine Landing' QRH procedure; alerting ATC for a return to ZZZ XXL with ARFF (Airport Rescue Firefighting) standing by. Coordinated with ATC for return via direct arrival for ILS XXL. Asked Company explicitly to alert ZZZ Approach & Tower of the intended non-standard XXL landing. Notified Dispatch via ACARS report. Briefed FAs via intercom; and passengers via PA on the situation; my expectations; and their roles.  We selected the non-standard landing Runway XXL based on that runway being much longer than the more typical landing Runway XXR.  That was a minor miscue; because I/we had not considered the effect of the large displaced threshold. Which I now consider insignificant.  For landings eastbound the difference is 2500 feet and would be significant. Lesson learned: the big runway length number on the 10-9 page can be significantly misleading; take the time to dig into the 10-9A details page. The fact that was our takeoff runway and within Jepp FDPro I'd used the green highlighter to extend the highlighting all the way to the takeoff threshold didn't help.  What had been useful to help direct my taxi to the correct threshold for takeoff became mildly misleading when evaluating which runway to land on. Which was not a side effect I noticed at the time or had considered previously. Still working as PM I performed normal divert preparations and top-of-descentprocedures: Reconfigured FMS & ACARS for ZZZ arrival; obtained ATIS; set up radios and performed approach brief; landing assessment; etc. Notified ZZZ Ops of our return by direct radio call to obtain a gate assignment.We discussed that we'd be a little above the normal max landing weight; but the already requested priority covers for that administrative requirement; and the runway available was nearly double what the QRH procedure's performance chart said was required. Performed descent checklist and before landing checklists and flows as normal.  Throughout the evolution the FO kept us neatly in control; tight on the FD despite sometimes having to hand-crank the trim himself; caught a few radio calls I missed; and demonstrated overall high situational awareness and excellent systems knowledge. This is especially impressive for someone fairly new to the airplane who is just back from 6 months of furlough. During descent below 10;000 ft approaching downwind we changed control to CA as PF w FO as PM. We sighted the field while on base. During the turn-on to final I was using visual lookout primary; backed up by the LNAV purple line and the ILS. There was a moment of confusion as the ILS and LNAV came together before I was aligned with what I had thought was the landing runway.  Having landed on XXR dozens (hundreds?) of times over the decades; that habit was unhelpful for a few seconds before we got fully established pointing at the correct runway. We then realized that Runway XXR is concrete and very easy to see in mildly hazy conditions while Runway XXL is asphalt and much harder to see. In fact XXL was invisible until we got closer in following the LNAV & LOC. My general habit on any landing involving parallel runways is to verbalize seeing all the relevant runways by name and explicitly saying which one I'm aligning / aligned with. E.g. 'I see XXL and XXR. I'm aligning with XXL.'  For whatever reason that verbalization didn't occur; with sorta predictable results.Intercepted final outside intermediate fix in level flight at 3;000 ft. Configured to flaps 15 early and slowed gradually to Vapp of approximately 160KIAS before glideslope intercept at final approach fix. FO kept the airplane nicely in trim on my requests.Made a flaps 15 slightly overweight (approx. 148K#) approach and landing to a smooth touchdown on ZZZ Runway XXL just shy of the 2000ft marker. Upon stopping made a PA to reassure the passengers & remind them the safety vehicles would be seen around the airplane. ATC gave us an alternate frequency to contact ARFF on. Which surprised both of us a bit. Once we were communicating with ARFF I requested they inspect us for hot brakes or damaged tires.  ARFF found normal brake temps and no tire damage. At ARFF's request I released them at that point and we taxied normally to [the] gate.Following shutdown the FO attempted to manually crank the trim to the usual post-shutdown 5 units from the 8-9 units we'd used at touchdown.  At zero airspeed the trim was still 'cogging' and almost as difficult to move as it had been in flight. So we left the trim at the landing setting for Maintenance's edification. Which point we discussed with the Chief Pilot who met the flight and again later with the maintenance folks who also met the flight. I made appropriate aircraft maintenance log book entries for the stab trim failure and for the overweight landing. Spoke with Dispatch by phone before leaving aircraft per FOM. The next morning I filed the required report. In all I think this event worked out pretty close to textbook; minus the small glitches identified above.The main electric trim failing was the causal factor. Everything else is just details.1.	 Subsequent research on the ground shows that activating the GPWS Flap Inhibit switch is called for in 11 different QRH procedures; and in the Flaps 15 landing procedure.  Only the 'One Engine Inoperative' QRH procedure and the 'Flaps 15 Landing' procedures mention that limit; the other 10 QRH procedures do not.I do not know whether those differences are deliberate or an oversight. Suggest someone on the 737 fleet team look into this. If the difference is deliberate there probably ought to some verbiage available in QRH or [procedures] to explain the rationale so others don't mistakenly apply a remembered restriction where it's not intended. 2.	 We were both surprised to see that only half of the 'Stab out of trim' annunciator illuminated.  Which left us wondering at first if we had a warning system malfunction or a trim malfunction.  I surmise now that the right bulb is connected to FCC (Flight Control Computer)  B and the left is connected to FCC A.  And that had the Captain been PF; we'd have seen the left half illuminate instead.However it works; the details of left & right are not documented in [manual] where the annunciator is described. At a minimum there should be a statement like 'Only half of the annunciator may illuminate. That is still a valid indication of an out-of-trim condition.'3.	Overall; from the 'Stab out of trim' annunciator illuminating to touchdown was about 30 minutes.  From reviewing the ACARS logs I know it was at least 28 minutes and less than 35.  As the CA / PM / QRH operator I was working quickly and diligently almost the entire time to accomplish all the non-routine and normal procedures in full without hurrying.  Had we turned back even a couple minutes earlier the airplane would have been approaching the airport before we were fully caught up and mentally transitioned from handling an [urgent inflight situation] to performing a normal low-stress; albeit flaps 15; landing.Given the reality that following all the procedures fully takes nearly 30 minutes; I believe we do a disservice to pilots in the sim; rushing around the traffic pattern with an engine out. That encourages hurrying; doing QRH steps without really thinking them and their implications through; etc. We fight how we train; and we're training to hurry. I question the wisdom of that.Further I question the wisdom of planned arrival fuels that only allow for approximately 30 minutes to flameout at traffic pattern altitudes.  The so-called FAR '45 minute reserve' is 45 minutes at cruise; not 45 minutes at traffic pattern altitude with e.g. flaps stuck partly extended. I now conclude that performing a major QRH evolution discovered in the arrival traffic pattern while down near Company planned arrival fuels would necessitate skipping a lot of steps or giving them at best a lick and a promise.I believe it is unwise to plan arrival fuels that tightly. Yes; we commonly have additional hold and / or Dispatch fuels.  But each of those may legitimately be burned in delays encountered before the [urgent situation] appears.  This saves Company a lot of money on the many flights that don't turn out worst-case. But it really sucks to be the pilot who draws that short straw; and is faced with either doing a rushed job of handling the [situation] or running out of fuel.That's planning; in extremis; to fail. An industry-leading FAR 121 carrier should not be planning to fail. In extremis or otherwise.
column123: At a level off of 17;000 ft we noticed stab out of trim light. I was the PF so it was my aircraft. The Captain ran the stab out of trim QRH checklist which lead to the QRH stab trim inoperative checklist. We did not regain electric trim. Manual trim was what we were left with. Then the non-routine QRH checklist was performed. The manual trim wheel was difficult to work for both us even when the plane was near an in trim condition. Speed was slowed to about 270kts from about 290kts then. [ATC was advised] and we planned and set up for an arrival back to ZZZ.  I flew the aircraft and worked the manual trim while the CA performed checklists; set up for the arrival and approach; and the briefings. Manual trim did not become much easier until on approach when aircraft was slowed to approach speed; however even then it was difficult. The CA took the aircraft and I became the PM. The landing was nice and smooth. Once on the ground using the manual trim wheel to reset the stab trim to 5 units was still very difficult.

column121: We [were] on the Vanze 2 Arrival into MEM and I was flying. After reviewing the arrival and expecting a south landing; we got a new ATIS with the airport now landing to the north. This required a change of FASOP Intersection to 10;000 and 230 knots. I put this in the FMS. I also read the North arrival on the RNAV approach to the FO. When we got to the top of descent; we had not been given a descent yet; so we requested lower. The FMS showed us high as we continued to ask for lower altitudes to make the crossing restriction. Eventually the controller gave us direct to FASOP Intersection. I told the FO we were already going there. Then the FO realized that we were not going to FASOP Intersection; but were going to FASON Intersection. We realized that I had put the crossing restriction in the FMS at FASON Intersection; and not FASOP Intersection!! This was the reason the FMS showed us high. This error was because there are two almost identically named intersections on the arrival; With the change of runway from South to North and having already verified the points; the names being so close in spelling make the error one that could easily be repeated by other crews. Once we corrected the crossing restrictions to the correct FASOP Intersection; we were very low and we slowed our rate of descent.Because we had already verified the points on the arrival; when we got the runway change; we verbally reviewed the changes and the need to insert the crossing restriction in the FASOP Intersection.  It was night and when I looked at the FMS; the first point that came up was FASON; which I mistook for FASOP.  Both the FO and I did not catch it.  We did not realize the mistake until we were given direct FASOP because we were requesting a descent because we thought we were high and were not going to make the crossing restriction.  I did mention the two intersection name similarities to the Controller; and told him it was a potential problem.  He said he agreed; but the fix was above his pay grade.The names of FASOP and FASON need to be changed; especially when there is a crossing restriction that needs to be entered in to the FMS. With both names so similar; it is easily to put the crossing restriction at the wrong point like we did. The runway change was the key here; as we were already set up to land to the South. Then the runway changed to land North; prompting the change to put the crossing restriction in the FMS.

column121: ATC advised we would be following a heavy aircraft on approach into ORD. While on short final; I observed the aircraft we were following on Taxiway P; headed eastbound. We continued on the approach and did not experience any effects of wake turbulence. I heard ATC instruct the aircraft to turn left onto Taxiway EE and taxi onto Runway 28R; which requires a turn of more than 90 degrees to complete. As the heavy aircraft negotiated the turn; I was just beginning to flare for the landing. I suddenly experienced what seemed to be a heavy crosswind from the right (much heavier that what was being reported); associated with a higher than normal pitch attitude to arrest the descent rate just before touchdown. Approximately 1-2 seconds before touchdown; the stick-shaker activated until the main landing gear made contact with the runway. A normal touchdown and roll-out was performed and we taxied to the gate without incident. The First Officer and I both agreed during the debrief that the approach and landing was stable and on proper speed throughout.I believe the cause of this event was a result of ATC giving the instruction to the heavy aircraft to make the left turn; causing its jet blast to cross directly over the approach end of Runway 28C. It appeared to create a crosswind/tailwind from the 5 o'clock position of our aircraft. I believe this is what contributed to the higher than expected crosswind from the right and the stick-shaker to activate just before touchdown. If ATC would have had the heavy aircraft hold short until the turn could be made in between arrivals; I believe this situation could have been avoided.
