column121: While preparing for departure we noticed we would not make the departure crossing restrictions on the ZZZZZ1 departure. Our plan was to bring this to the attention of ground so departure could be made aware. They seemed unwilling to help as did clearance and our overworked dispatcher. We went back and forth and finally were given a 'modified' ZZZZZ2 departure and proceed to ZZZZZ. While doing this departure we stayed in NAV and the plane turned east towards ZZZZZ. ATC gave us headings and informed us that it was not correct. Had we reviewed the departure closer we would have noted the headings and briefed better. Also; that departure is not in the FMS database.[The causes are] a long list. First cause is [the company] operating an airplane under conditions that it should not. An Airbus 321 weighing 192;000 lbs. in 38 Celsius temperature should not be allowed. The plane barely makes it off the ground and we have to climb out in unfamiliar configurations to get climb performance. I do not believe we will have an acceptable outcome if we ever lose an engine. 90+ Fahrenheit cockpit temps doesn't help and cabin temps of mid 80's are a distraction. Constant interruptions by FA's (flight attendants) due to pax getting up is a threat while attempting to find an acceptable departure. Uncooperative ground and clearance controllers who seemed irritated to even interact with us. Overloaded dispatcher which seemed to be the norm lately and was confirmed to me by 2 dispatchers riding the jump seat. Incorrect verbiage in the performance manual regarding the IAE (International Aero Engine) bump feature which was unfamiliar procedure to me. That was a distraction because it was a green B next to the EPR gauge; not a blue B next to the N1. Missing SID from our database (that would have prevented this event). Operating an aircraft under conditions that are borderline unsafe and expected to do so. The climb was so poor the aircraft started a 1;000 - 1;200 RPM descent upon flap retraction because of the temps and lack of power. Good CRM and PIC experience was our biggest asset managing the aircraft. Of course weather close to the airport was yet another factor. Make sure bump description is correct in the performance manual. Use of A321 under heavy and hot situations need to be reviewed out of ZZZ. Continue training emphasis for CRM because it made ATC and aircraft management seem minor.

column121: Company Aircraft X; ZZZ to ZZZ1 departed at XA:00. We took off from Runway XX with right turn radar vector to a heading of 270.  I was the pilot flying and my Captain was the monitoring pilot. We were in a normal climb and around 5;000 feet we got an advisory message; cyan color in the EICAS. The message we received said 'PACK 1 VLV CLSD.' Captain pulled the QRH; which indicated to reset the associated pack by pressing and then depressing the pack 1 button. The Captain did so and the message went away.  We kept climbing and the same message then came back; she ran QRH again but I suggested to press the PACK 1 button; give it a few seconds; and then depress it again. The message went away. Passing 18;000 cleared to climb to FL330; the same message came back. At this time I felt like I was getting unusually hot even though we were flying against the sun. However; I checked the ECS and it showed 29 degrees Celsius in the cockpit and about 19 in the back. Captain did the QRH again and it told us to maintain FL250 and so Captain requested FL250 due to Pack issues. Captain then immediately looked for the cabin altitude in the EICAS and verified it in the QRH. QRH suggested a cabin altitude of 2700 and the EICAS showed a cabin altitude of 2900 and climbing. At that point Captain asked the FO (First Officer) to initiate an emergency descent immediately. Memory items were then performed by the FO while Captain asked ATC for an altitude descent to 10;000 feet. ATC asked to confirm the clearance descent to 10;000 and whether we were requesting priority. The Captain responded affirmative to both. The Captain then coordinated with the Flight Attendant for an emergency descent. We did the emergency descent QRH. Once we were in a stable descent at a rate of approximately 5;500 feet per minute while descending and keeping 245 to 250 kts for landing gear limitation; FO and Captain asked each other if they were ok and the answer was yes. Passing 15;000 feet; FO started reducing the rate of descent to 3;000 feet per minute and kept reducing the rate of descent gradually to 1;000 feet per minute by the time we got to 11;000. At 10;000 feet FO changed the plane to a clean configuration; we then requested radar vectors back to ZZZ and proceeded with normal flight. Aircraft X landed back in ZZZ with no further issues or incident.

column121: My First Officer (Pilot Monitoring) and I (Pilot flying) flew to Bogota; Columbia (BOG).  This was the first time for either of us to fly into Bogota.  During our 3+ hour transit to BOG; the FO (First Officer) and I had a very long discussion about the specifics of the airport.  About an hour from landing; ATC said that BOG was using Runways 13L/13R ILS approaches; which we were happy to hear; because we had a few questions explained below about the non-ILS approaches for Runways 31L/31R.  No ILS approaches were available for Runway 31. Once we checked in with Bogota; we were told to fly the ISVAT 3W Arrival for Runway 31L; which surprised us because we had been told to expect Runway 13.  The Jeppesen approach charts have 5 approaches for Runway 31L; although 3 of those approaches (RNP Z/Y/X Rwy 31L (AR)) are specifically not allowed to be flown by [our aircraft type].  Of the two remaining approaches listed in the Jeppesen; pages; only one;'RNP Visual Flight Proc RNP C Rwy 31L'; was available to us in the FMS (Flight Management System).  So our primary question was is the 'RNP Visual Flight Proc RNP C Rwy 31L' an instrument approach; or is it a visual approach?  Based on a simulator training event several years ago; I distinctly remember a Check Airman telling me that [company] pilots are not allowed to fly visual approaches at night.  I searched the Flight Operations Manual (FOM) for 'night visual approaches' and found nothing.  While on the arrival; a search for just 'visual approaches' yielded 28 results; a daunting number; given we were two pilots who had never been to BOG; it was late at night and we were descending on the arrival into mountainous terrain to a field at 8;400 foot elevation.  In an effort to decide whether IMC or Visual Approach rules applied; I decided that this had to be classified as a visual approach; not an instrument approach; since page 10-7B-1 lists our only available approach to 31L under the category of Visual Approach Procedures.  Finally; in the FOM; I found a one-sentence reference to visual approaches at night which states: 'At night; since obstacles may not be visible; do not accept or request visual approaches unless the airport is clearly in sight and the flight crew is certain of remaining clear of obstacles and terrain while maneuvering for landing.'  During the time we were flying the arrival; we were above an overcast and the field was not in sight; so we quickly discussed the possibility of having to divert. At some point well after we transitioned from the arrival to the approach at AMVES; the runway environment came into sight.  At that point I thought we could continue the approach; as we were down in the valley and could maintain sight of the field.  As we approached the 31L Final Approach Fix (BO480); we were fully configured for landing and Tower asked us if we would prefer to land on Runway 31R.  We said no; since we were already set up for Runway 31L.  Then Tower told us that Runway 31L was 'now closed' (and the runway edge lights and centerline lights were turned off) and that we had to land on Runway 31R.  My concern now was that we would no longer be on the coded purple FMS path to landing because we couldn't reprogram the FMS in such a short time; and I was unfamiliar with the terrain in the area.  The FO and I quickly referenced the terrain on our cockpit displays and decided that we would be clear of any terrain while I transitioned to 31R.  So I disconnected the autopilot and flew over to the 31R center line.  Another challenge was that we were initially on the PAPI glide path for 31L; and once we transitioned to 31R PAPI; were instantly high because 31R is offset about 4;000 feet closer to us than 31L.  But I was able to get the airplane stabilized on PAPI glide path before we reached 1;000 feet AGL; and we landed successfully on 31R.Of the many lessons learned from this flight; two things stand out to me. First; the 10-7 pages need a better discussion of visual approaches at night.  The fact that the title of the approach is 'RNP Visual Flight Proc RNP C Rwy 31L' (which sounds like an RNAV approach since RNP is listed twice in the title).  Second; the actions of Bogota Tower to close 31L Runway at such a late stage in our approach was totally unnecessary and inexcusable. Insufficient discussion in 10-7 pages regarding Runway 31 visual approaches at night.  Also; why Bogota Tower closed Runway 31L and shut off runway lights when we were in vicinity of Final Approach Fix and required us to transition to Runway 31R. Improve discussion regarding night visual approaches in 10-7 pages and query Bogota Tower why they closed the runway on us passing Final Approach Fix; requiring us to deviate from coded FMS path in mountainous terrain.

Once done with that; the Captain called for gear down flaps 30 in order to get configured. Shortly after I put the gear handle down; there was an aural warning and a caution/warning message. I believe it was nose door open; gear disagree and hyd 3 lo press. We both looked at the messages and the Captain called for a go around. We went through the go around procedure rather smoothly and got the autopilot on and continued a climb to 15;000 ft. MSL. As we were climbing we read the messages and the Captain called for me to [advise ATC] and that we were diverting to ZZZ2. Once we were established in the climb; the Captain transferred the aircraft controls to me so he could run the QRH. The Captain kept the entire crew and passengers informed throughout this entire flight. There was contact made with appropriate personnel; including Dispatch; ATC; Maintenance and the Company. I relayed information to ATC while the Captain ran the QRH. I believe he ran the QRH for the gear disagree message first. That cleared the disagree message and we were left with hyd 3 lo press. There was 0% fluid in hyd 3 reservoir. We continued to ZZZ2 at 15000 as directed by ATC; they eventually handed us off to Approach where we asked for a hold over ZZZ2 VOR. This helped us with time management so the QRH could be ran properly. After going through all the steps in the QRH; we finally got the gear down with three green indicators. Fuel was being monitored this whole time and there was more than enough fuel to make it to ZZZ2 and hold for an appropriate amount of time. Once the gear was down and the QRH ran we; asked for the RNAV 27 into ZZZ2. We descended in the hold and then continued to approach as normal. Eventually the approach became a visual and we landed safely following the QRH procedure. We made a complete stop on the runway and made the decision to be 'tugged' off of the runway due to lack of steering. There was a large puddle of hydraulic fluid under the nose when parked and inspection was completed.  I believe that this was an outstanding crew and a phenomenal job was accomplished by the entire crew and all personnel involved. Required actions were accomplished in a; safe; timely and professional manner.

Once we reached PLADE; I asked my FO (First Officer) to set 7;100 ft. in the mode control panel which is the minimum altitude at CI28 and started a VNAV descent with the intention to arm the ILS just prior to CI28. At approximately 7;600 ft. we received a warning 'too low terrain'. We could visually see the terrain and started to level off; then; very quickly received 'terrain; pull up' with amber showing on the terrain display.  I immediately complied by going into the CFIT recovery procedure. We climbed to approximately 8;000 ft. and leveled off seeing that we were well clear of all terrain (no more warning and terrain indicator showed us to be clear). We then reassessed. At that time; we were very close to CI28 and had plenty of light from the city and a very bright moon. We were also in a good position to continue to the airport; so I continued to an uneventful landing.
column123: We were landing Runway 28 in Guadalajara. Night VMC conditions with moonlight provided adequate visual references. We were set up to land Runway 28 using the ILS DME2 or localizer Runway 28 with the transition for the ILS DME 2 with the IKBAN transition. At the last minute; Control told us to descend via the LIVRI 1D arrival. After changing to this arrival in the FMS; we realized that we needed to descend quickly. To complicate matters; Control give us directions to go direct to PLADE. I estimate Control shortened our arrival by 40 to 50 miles in giving us the arrival change and direct PLADE which greatly compounded our decent plan. This caused us to have to execute an expedited decent while having to re-program the FMS and plan for this new routing. I verbalized terrain that was to our right as we were turning direct PLADE and both the CA (Captain) and I correlated this to what we were seeing on our terrain displays. Prior to reaching PLADE; Control cleared us for the ILS Zulu Runway 28. However; we heard cleared for the ILS Two. I attribute this miscommunication to language barriers. CA asked me to set 7;100 ft.; which would've been correct for ILS 2 but 7;700 ft would've been correct for ILS Z. We got the 'too low; terrain' oral warning followed by the 'terrain; pull up'. CA commanded auto pilot off; stow speed brake (Even though they weren't in use); pitched up and added full thrust. We had the terrain in sight the whole time; as well as the Runway environment. We climbed approximately 500 ft before determining that we could safely continue the approach without incident. We landed on Runway 28 without incident.

Since it was nighttime; and since Runway 22 in Evansville has no VASI or PAPI; I believe my sight picture was incorrect; and I judged the aircraft to be higher than it was. I corrected pitch and power and returned to the glide slope for a normal landing. I believe I can do a better job of scanning the flight and navigation instruments while on approach; especially to an airport with no VASI or PAPI.

Pressure zero; temp 35C; both hydraulic 3 pumps off; system in auto. Referenced QRH; stabilized situation. Complied with QRH; requested priority handling with ZZZ Tower; manually lowered the landing gear and proceeded to land uneventfully on runway XXR. AP2; flaps 35; no auto brakes; 400K landing weight. Restrictions for PW (Pratt Whitney) engine thrust reverser inop and limitations for turning right. As expeditiously and safely as possible we taxied clear of the north runway complex so other aircraft could land. column121: During initial descent into ZZZ noted slide [slight] odor near last 10 rows of main cabin while accomplishing landing safety compliance check.  Thought it strange but was still not sure of its origin or validity. It was not until Flight Attendant #2 stated; 'Do you smell that...?' I acknowledge the unusual odor -- about XA:58. I left my jump seat and proceeded into main cabin walking as far as the over wing exit seats.  As I approached the mid-cabin; the odor was strongest and clearly recognizable...; Category A (musty/dirty sock) odor.  I witnessed a couple of passengers wave their hand under their nose and questioned; 'Pew; what is that smell?' I returned to my jump seat and confirmed the odor with Flight Attendant #2 who then attempted to contact the flight deck (both a routine and emergency call) ...; neither call was answered.  A few minutes later; flight attendant #1 came to the aft section and explained the Captain was too busy with the approach and would call us back after landing about the odor.  The odor diminished somewhat after landing.  As the aircraft taxied to the gate; the Captain called to explained he believed it was due to a 'cold soaked aircraft'; much to do with humidity etc.  As he continued his explanation; I witnessed a significant amount of mist/condensation being expelled through the lower side panel vents.   I noted a slight minor burning sensation in my nose which dissipated a few minutes after landing.  Due to another delayed inbound flight; our aircraft was required to wait 1hour and 12 minutes before reaching the parking area.  I collected my luggage to deplane the aircraft and noted the odor of musty/dirty socks was still significantly prevalent towards the middle section of the aircraft.  I brought this to the Captain's attention; and he too noted the odor. He further explained how it could also be from a 'mildewed filter' (shaped like a sock) which simply needs to be changed on this aircraft.'  However; he further stated that it had 'nothing to do with Turbine Oil.'   We deplaned the aircraft without further incident.  I advised the outbound crew (while walking to the terminal) about the odor event which had transpired during the inbound flight.  [A] report and notification to [union name] also submitted.
column123: We were getting ready to prepare the cabin during the descent into ZZZ and I noticed a musty odor in the aft galley. I briefly uncovered my nose to get a better sense of the smell and determined it was a very distinct stinky sock odor. The #4 [Flight Attendant] came to the aft galley about 1-2 minutes after I first noticed the odor. I asked 'do you smell that?' and told me that he did as well. He then did a walk through in main cabin. He said the odor was even stronger around the exit row area and that he noticed a couple of passengers waving their hands over their face. Because we were well into the descent; I made the decision to immediately contact the Captain to inform him of the situation. I called the flight deck once with a routine call and then an emergency call; but neither were answered. The #1 came to the back galley and told us 'The Captain knows about the situation but is too busy on the approach right now.' The #4 pulled up his manual and we both agreed it was a Category A Odor. After landing the odor dissipated somewhat; but was still noticeable. I had tingling/burning sensations in my nose and felt light headed for about 5-10 minutes. The Captain called us after we came to a stop and said 'Sometimes that odor appears when descending into a humid environment.' We waited to deplane for over an hour and the smell was still noticeable; although not as strong as when I initially noticed it on the descent. After deplaning the captain walked through the cabin and agreed that the odor was prevalent; but specifically said 'It's not from an oil leak.' He explained that's there's a filter that's literally shaped like a sock that could become dirty and can cause the cabin to smell like a dirty sock. We deplaned the aircraft and I notified one of the inbound crew members of the smell when passing by.

I noticed this; as I prepared to place the Landing Gear lever to OFF and autobrakes to OFF. The TE Flap gauge showed a slight split in the needles; with the R needle slightly retracted from flaps 1 and the L needle at flaps 1. I considered both Flap Asymmetry and Flap Disagree Checklists; and we decided the Asymmetry Checklist was more correct; despite the flap lever being UP. The PF did indicate very slight anomalous roll indications; prior to engaging the AP (Autopilot). I then informed the Passengers of our issue; briefed the FAs (Flight Attendants) that we would hold and work the problem and that we would be diverting to either ZZZ1 or ZZZ. Dispatch was very helpful in getting the Company Operations Center involved and suggesting ZZZ; editing the Release and giving us fuel and weight and balance data for worst case scenario. We began the QRH; holding at the deferred items for descent and landing. I then coordinated for the RNAV Z XXR Approach; briefed the Passengers of our decision to return to ZZZ; and briefed the FAs on the ETA and after landing plans. We briefed and commenced the approach; completed the QRH; ran brake cooling and reviewed the plan one last time. The PF flew a very nice approach at Vref 40 + 30 to a smooth flaps 1 landing with AB3 required and selected. On rollout I suggested he quickly disarm the AB and let the aircraft roll out at max reverse thrust to allow for more brake cooling. The data indicated 18 minutes of cooling at the gate so we taxied to the gate; shut the aircraft down and coordinated with Operations and [Maintenance Control]. Training and Company operational priorities had us well-prepared and allowed us to handle the issue safely and with ease.

column121: When we arrived at the airplane the flight deck was around 34 degrees; but it soon cooled to around 28. Everything else was normal until the Captain stepped out to use the restroom. As soon as he sat down the ground crew pulled the ground power; but we had not yet switched over to the APU; so everything shut down. The Captain switched to the APU; but the right FMC did not start back up; and we got a R FMC FAIL status message. After about five minutes it did come back on without incident. We pushed back and started normally; but after about two seconds after I selected the status page on the lower EICAS we got a PACK 1 status message. The Captain reviewed the procedures; but because we had already blocked out and did not get any EICAS messages we continued. After starting up with the packs all off the flight deck warmed up quickly; but we knew as soon as we took off it should start cooling. At around 1;000 ft. the Tower gave us the Departure frequency and I checked in successfully. By the time we reached 5;000 ft. we were concerned by how little airflow there was; and the observer pilot asked for the ECS page to verify that the airplane was pressurizing. It seemed to be normal; and we monitored the air; but still figured as we climbed the flow would increase. Around FL180 Departure called us on guard and said; 'Aircraft X; if you can hear this transmission contact...' The Captain and I agreed that she hadn't called prior to that and I dialed in the frequency. I couldn't reach them; so I asked for another frequency. I didn't realize how much the heat was affecting me; but on the third frequency I asked the Captain to attempt to call. When he transmitted; I could hear that his call wasn't going out; and I finally recognized that we had lost the left comms. I didn't want to change the right radio from guard; because that seemed to be the only way they could reach us; so I used the center radio and was able to reach ZZZZ Control. Shortly after that we got an EQUIP COOLING EICAS message; and the third seat pilot began to run the checklist; and I asked for a level off altitude of FL300. ATC came back with FL290; but we were at FL288 and empty; so I said we would do our best. We ended up climbing to FL295 before we could get level; and promptly descended back to FL290. At this point we began to discuss returning when we noticed that the secondary attitude indicator was leaning to the right; but our wings were level; so we all agreed we should return. We told ATC we needed to return and explained that we were having equipment cooling issues. They assigned us the arrival and Runway XXR; but the workload was continuing to accelerate; and we were all sweating profusely; and told them we would like to get vectors to the ILS for XXR. I gave them the fuel remaining; souls on board; and tried to explain that we were safe; but needed to return soon. We completed all checklists; and uneventfully landed; taxied; and parked the airplane. I didn't realize until we were on the ground how much the heat in the flight deck was affecting me. Even with the lack of traffic in the vicinity; I am surprised how long it took me to recognize the radio failure. In the future I will be more cognizant of the heat and it's affects not only in seeming to increase workload; but also decreasing focus and clarity.
column123: I had gone to the lavatory on the ground prior to departure. Before I returned to my seat; the external power was pulled without my permission; and the power to the aircraft was interrupted; as I sat back down; I selected the APU power source and after waiting a bit; the R FMC would not come back. We called Maintenance up and the FMC returned to normal. We ensured all of the data that we had input was correct and then continued onward to push. The aircraft was extremely hot; and we know that they had just established air as we were arriving at the aircraft. The interior cabin was at 36 Celsius and we agreed that the aircraft should cool after takeoff. After starting we noticed a Pack 1 status message; but there was never an associated EICAS message. We followed our checklists and proceeded with taxi. After takeoff; the airflow never increased and the FO (First Officer) selected the EICAS page as we all were wondering if we were even pressurizing. The gaspers were blowing at about 5%; but cool air was coming out. It was still extremely hot in the aircraft; and the 3rd observer seat first officer said that he had hardly to no air coming out of his gasper. At around FL250; we began receiving radio calls on 121.5 and it was at this time with trying to transmit out; and different frequencies that we realized the radios were not working; except for the center. The Pilot Monitoring was able to get the right radio to work intermittent; and immediately we got the Equip cooling EICAS caution message. I continued to fly the aircraft while the crew ran the QRH and attempted to maintain contact with ZZZZ. At this point; we all agreed the best course of action was to return to ZZZZ. We were given a level off to FL290 after an initial climb clearance. We were given this rapidly; as were already in a climb; but I arrested the climb and descended back from FL295 to FL290. We were given vectors and further descent. At this point with descent power; there was almost no airflow. We [received priority] to get on the ground as safely and quickly as possible. My standby instruments were also showing erroneous. We landed in ZZZZ without further incident. After touchdown; the airflow suddenly increased to normal. Maintenance was briefed with the logbook; but I was not given the nature of the aircraft's issues before we headed back in to rest.

column121: This was a fumes event. On takeoff; we noticed an oily odor. I thought this was something transient and continued takeoff. At about 4;000 feet the smell was not going away. I said we need to return to ZZZ. We [requested ATC priority handling for an air return] and put our O2 masks on. I called the Flight Attendants (FA's) and asked if they smelled anything. I asked the Tower to send paramedics to Gate. I began the fumes checklist on the QRC. Once those initial actions were complete I stopped because we were getting close to a landing. When we arrived at the gate; Maintenance was powering hydraulic systems and testing reversers. When we got to the gate; I told the passengers to exit out the forward door quickly. After a couple of minutes of securing the flight deck; I opened the door and no one had gotten off. There was a fireman testing the air just inside the aircraft door.
column123: SOF Event during departure with an immediate return to the departure airport (ZZZ). First Officer (FO) was the pilot flying. Ground Ops and taxi out to runway XXL were uneventful. As soon as the engines reached FLEX power; a slight burning metal smell began. This smell; experienced from time to time when the engines run up; normally dissipates in a matter of seconds. This time it remained throughout the entire takeoff roll. All other aircraft indications were normal during rotation and clean up. The smell persisted and a dirty sock smell was now prevalent; intensifying somewhat as we made a turn to a 230 heading with a climb up to 12;000 feet. At 4;000 feet we elected to stop the climb; don oxygen masks; and [advised ATC the need of an air return]. As a side note; it was hard to hear ATC and ICS with the loud noise of breathing with the masks on. At this point I remained the Pilot Flying and the Captain informed ATC of our intention to return for an immediate landing on runway XXL. The Captain was also made aware by the #2 Flight Attendant that the #1 Flight Attendant was on oxygen and still feeling very sick. I loaded the FMS for arrival and began a descent/vectors for the ILS runway XXL approach. At this time the Captain completed the Smoke/Avionics Smoke/Fumes QRH Quick Action procedure and informed the passengers and flight attendants of our intention to land. We were over maximum landing weight by roughly 4;000 lbs.; but elected to proceed with the descent checklist and land instead of working through the QRH procedure for Overweight Landing due to time. The approach; landing; and taxi in were uneventful.This aircraft; Aircraft X; had a birdstrike in the #1 Engine on the preceding flight. The maintenance actions were signed off. It is possible that the fume event could be related to this event. Fume events are a recurring issue across most fleets and airlines. I know there is a lot of attention from multiple organizations on this issue and that should certainly continue.

column121: On a step climb around FL300; between ZZZ and ZZZZZ; we noticed a weather cell we wanted to deviate around. The Captain had already briefed the FAs (Flight Attendants) about the en route weather; that we would most likely have some bumps; that we were keeping the seat belt sign on; and to use caution. We were in full IMC and our radar return showed that a turn to the left would be best. We requested an initial left turn of 20 degrees but almost immediately we encountered heavy and extreme precipitation and ultimately had to turn 80 degrees. We were given the necessary deviations but then told to go direct ZZZZZ when able as well as climb to FL340. We also encountered moderate and possibly severe turbulence. We experienced both positive and negative G's. The speed tape never went into the red but the trend vector showed both rapid climbing and simultaneous descending trends that took up the entire top to bottom range of the speed tape. The plane was moving quite a bit as we were both in updrafts and then subsequent downdrafts getting bumped around. After about 5 minutes when we could actually get everything sorted out; we called back to check on the status of both the Flight Attendants and Passengers. FA1 answered and she proceeded to tell us there was an accident in the aisle and she would call us back. FA2 was about mid aircraft doing her beverage service when we encountered the worst of the turbulence. She thought she had hit her head and beverages had been thrown from the cart and some passengers tray tables into the ceiling. We consulted our FOM and made the decision we needed to contact Dispatch and make them aware to coordinate with [Maintenance Control]. We continued to keep checking on the FAs for the rest of the flight and as we got closer; FA1 called and said FA2 had requested In-Flight to meet us at the gate. Upon block in; [flight attendant representative] and member of [Company] met the aircraft. CA (Captain) called Dispatch/[Maintenance Control] to explain event and to assess if an aircraft inspection for severe turbulence was required. Based on our reading and interpretation of FOM on the definition of severe turbulence; we determined we encountered severe turbulence. However; [Maintenance Control] said because the autopilot did not disengage; that there was no 'momentary loss of aircraft control' and it was only moderate turbulence which does not require an aircraft inspection. The aircraft was not removed from service; boarding for the next flight started immediately; and [Company] took FA2 for a medical evaluation.Pilot interpretation of FOM differed from [Maintenance Control]. [Maintenance Control] did not accept our interpretation of severe turbulence. It kept them from having to inspect the aircraft and delaying the flight schedule. Any disconnection of autopilot is apparently the determining factor in deciding if aircraft control is lost. There needs to be a more clear definition of what severe versus moderate turbulence is and pilot experience should be held in account. Safety should always be the priority over schedule integrity.
column123: On final climb out from FL300 to FL340 between ZZZ and ZZZZZ intersection; we had to deviate for weather. Seat belt sign was on and FA (Flight Attendant) briefing and PA to passengers included weather/ thunderstorms in the area and to expect a bumpy ride on the climb out. We were in and out of IMC conditions as the weather radar depicted a buildup. We discussed a plan for deviations prior to the radio frequency change that we received at the same time. Originally asked for 20 degree left turn; ATC approved it and said no other traffic in the area do what we need to and cleared back direct ZZZZZ when able.Simultaneously; we encountered heavy to extreme precipitation which FA1 later said she could hear In the galley. FA1 started to clean up galley and observed FA2 in the middle of aircraft conducting beverage service. We continued the left turn to approximately a 270 degree heading due to the intensity of precipitation and increasing turbulence; while still trying to climb to FL340. In the turn and climb; we encountered moderate to potentially severe turbulence: VSI showed +/- 2000 fpm climb; ASI showed a white positive and negative trend vector for the entire range of speed tape; and we experienced zero G and positive G due to the turbulence.Once clear of the weather; we immediately called the FAs to get a status of the cabin. FA1 answered and she said there was an accident in the aisle. A few minutes later; she called back and reported that FA2 believes she hit her head on the ceiling and the surrounding passengers in the area agreed. Beverages had spilled on to passengers and were also dripping from the ceiling. Throughout the rest of the flight; we were in constant communication with the cabin on the status of FA2 and the passengers; as well as Dispatch/[Maintenance Control] via ACARS. FA1 requested that inflight meet us at the gate for FA2.Upon block in; a member from inflight and from [Company] met the aircraft. CA (Captain) called Dispatch/[Maintenance Control] to explain the event and to assess if an aircraft inspection for severe turbulence was required. Based on our reading and interpretation of FOM on the definition of severe turbulence; we determined we encountered severe turbulence. However; [Maintenance Control] said because the autopilot did not disengage; that there was no 'momentary loss of aircraft control' and it was only moderate turbulence which does not require an aircraft inspection. The aircraft was not removed from service; boarding for the next flight started immediately; and inflight took FA2 for a medical assessment.Pilot interpretation of company FOM definition and procedures differed from [Maintenance Control] definition and interpretation of company FOM defined severe turbulence [Maintenance Control] decided NOT to err on the side of safety and do a precautionary severe turbulence inspection of the aircraft due to their interpretation of the FOM severe turbulence definition; solely based on the fact that the autopilot did not disconnect during the event in order to save the integrity of the flight schedule. In the interest of safety; a severe turbulence inspection should have been conducted and a better definition of severe turbulence needs to be updated in company FOM defining what 'momentary loss of aircraft control' means. Safety should always be a priority over schedule integrity.

column121: I was assigned Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1 to reposition a plane that needed a mechanical issue fixed. Upon receiving the aircraft; I noticed the flight deck was unusually warm. The cockpit indication showed 32-33 degrees. The side window vents blew coolish-lukewarm air; and the gasper was blowing HOT air. The side vents air flow was weak and the gasper had strong air flow. I proceeded to write up the aircraft and have Maintenance look at it. After Maintenance did an inspection; they signed the aircraft ok for service with the cockpit indicator still reflecting 33 degrees and feeling unreasonably warm/hot. Surprised that it was signed 'OK for service;' I asked one of the technicians if he agreed with me the cockpit felt hot; he replied 'Yes; I would say it is warm.' I then asked if he agreed the gasper was blowing hot air; and although the side vents were slightly cool to lukewarm with weak airflow; it was not enough to cool the cockpit. He looked away without maintaining eye contact and replied '...well…we have to get this plane to ZZZ1. We don't have the parts here.' I then asked a second time why is the aircraft signed off as 'OK for service.' I received about the same reply. Eventually I was told 'it's your prerogative but it feels fine compared to outside. We are saying it's ok for service.' Shortly after; he left so I then called Maintenance Control and told them the temperature control knobs left in auto were not sufficient to cool the plane at any position; and that if you moved the knobs to manual; it was blowing out warm air immediately followed by hot air within 5 minutes. Maintenance Control replied that he didn't understand as the technician said it was 'OK for service; and only 25 degrees in the cockpit.' My statement to him was 'Absolutely not. It is right now indicating 32 degrees and nothing is fixed. Did you want me to send you a picture of the temperature?' I did not receive a reply as we talked about what the issue could be. I stated to Maintenance Control; 'I have seen this before multiple times and I think either a duct connection is loose; or there is a tear or leak somewhere; did you want me to send a picture of the cockpit temperature to show you what is indicating?' I still received no reply that he wanted evidence so I then asked him for the number I can send it to. When provided and after I sent a picture; he replied 'CABIN temperature looks pretty normal for a summer day' but mentioned absolutely nothing about the cockpit. He thought the plane was 'heat soaked' but I reminded him it had already been running for an hour and a half. I was then instructed and proceeded to run ground air inside the cabin and directly point it at the cockpit. It dropped 8 degrees from 33 to 25 in 20 minutes. I then had the ground air disconnected and within 20 minutes the cockpit heated back up to 31 degrees; and 5-10 minutes later it was again at 32. After writing it up a second time and being told from Maintenance Control it's still probably just 'heat soaked'; the same technician from before came back and I told him what we did. He replied while mumbling something about 'maybe we got some parts lined up and we'll take a look.' The First Officer and I went back inside to cool off and let Maintenance work on it. After 5-6 hours of Maintenance continuously working on the plane; I called Maintenance Control to get an update. Apparently; the technicians did in fact discover a leak(s); and were proceeding to put a sleeve(s) on. An hour later it was still not done (about 6-7 hours of continuous work since the second write up). I then was removed from Aircraft X by scheduling.Cockpit indication and hot feeling in the cockpit.Hot airplane that would not cool down without external air and feeling pressured to take a hot airplane to ZZZ1 for service.Refused the aircraft twice.The main concern is current maintenance practice. I was able to get the technician to agree that it was warm inside the cockpit even though he signed offthe aircraft as 'OK for service' because they could not find anything wrong. I will give the benefit of the doubt that maybe the technician relayed bad information to Maintenance Control and read the temperature of the cabin instead of the cockpit; however; he still told them it felt fine when clearly the temperature control knobs were not functioning properly. There was a second technician that stated the same about it being OK for service. Since the first write up; Maintenance Control had me troubleshoot it for up to 4 hours with/without the technicians. After going through 2 large bottles of water; sweating profusely; and being asked to run the ground air into the back of the aircraft instead of the front this time as it was probably still 'just heat soaked;' I said no and needed a break. Also; I mentioned that based on experience it was probably a leak or tear. Sure enough; after having the technicians look at the aircraft a second time; this is what they found and worked on for several hours. The fact I refused the aircraft twice and they 'found an issue' the second time leads me to believe they knew all along. Especially considering the fact the technician admitted to me that the cockpit would not sufficiently cool but yet signed it off and told maintenance control it was fine. A chief pilot called me to get more information and while I did not feel pressure from him directly to take it; it was clear that the company for one reason or another needed to get this plane to ZZZ1. Again; I did not feel pressure from the chief pilot directly; but I could not help but think everyone in Maintenance knew this plane could not get stuck in ZZZ. I also believe that troubleshooting for Maintenance up to 4 hours is excessive when it was clear the aircraft was not heat soaked but instead was not self-sufficient to cool on its own. I am not a maintenance technician nor one with the most experience; however; I felt undermined from the technicians signing it off and Maintenance Control having me go through the motions of 4 hours of troubleshooting and not one person taking my advice that I had seen this exact issue multiple times. More believably I was ignored and every trick was pulled just to get the aircraft to ZZZ1; i.e.; being told constantly by Maintenance Control we can get the aircraft cool enough with PC air so that we can depart but then reminding them the packs are not working properly and keep heating the plane up. Regardless; the technicians constantly tried to tie the issue to me implying that I was the problem and ultimately it was my call. If this was the case; I do not see why they would have had to work on the aircraft for several hours following my second write up.

column121: The aircraft in question was operating with MEL 27-XXX open; Spoilers #2 or #4. After engine start on both legs; an ECAM message was received regarding the spoilers but this was disregarded as a result of the MEL. Upon further reflection; these messages should have triggered further investigation on my part; as the presence of such an alert was not mentioned in the MEL. However; I had noted a write-up in the MEL about spurious messages - made by a Check Airman - which was subsequently signed off by Maintenance as essentially being unimportant. The aircraft had flown 4 legs the day prior with the MEL active. Also; at the time of this incident; I had approximately 100 hours of experience in any Airbus aircraft.The first leg of the day was flown uneventfully. Immediately after takeoff on our second leg of the day with the same plane; an ECAM caution and audio alert was triggered for a F/CTL SPLR FAULT. The message subsequently cleared itself; but then a few seconds later; would trigger again. This cycle repeated itself approximately every 20-30 seconds for about 20 minutes; until the flight reached FL270; where the message stopped cycling and instead remained. Initially; after exiting the sterile period; ACARS messages were sent and a brief exchange ensued. An emergency return to ZZZ was offered as an option; but given that we were well above maximum landing weight and the ECAM did not require us to land as soon as possible; I elected to continue the climb.Upon reaching cruise altitude; I transferred the flying duties to the FO (First Officer) and verbally contacted Dispatch and eventually Maintenance Control. Maintenance had no inflight suggestions and stated that they would look at it when the plane is on the ground. At this point; the Dispatcher and I discussed our options. Since the ECAM mentioned FUEL CONSUMPTION INCREASED and FMS PRED UNRELIABLE and we still had just under 3 hours to go on a flight planned to land with just 8;000 LBS of fuel; the decision was made to divert to ZZZ1. Dispatch changed our destination and we proceeded to an uneventful landing in ZZZ1. An emergency was not declared. While on the ground in ZZZ1; one of the responding mechanics reported to me that he discovered that the MEL procedures were not properly complied with when the item was deferred and that Spoiler Pair #2 was inadvertently deactivated instead of Pair #4. Apparently; the aircraft had flown 4 legs in this condition prior to our operating it. He mentioned to me his concern that on the [day prior]; a previous crew; the previously mentioned Check Airman had also apparently experienced a similar condition; wrote it in the logbook; only to have Maintenance simply clear the entry by writing 'info noted.' He expected that the aircraft would be taken out of service to fix the underlying issue. However; the decision was made to clear the write-up that I made and allow the deferral to continue. Based on the information that was relayed to me by this Mechanic; it appears that the initial error of deactivating the wrong spoiler pair was attempting to be covered up. This is very concerning.My relative inexperience with Airbus aircraft allowed me to be lulled into a false sense of security when it came to ECAM messages that appeared to relate to the MEL item. Seeing a write-up about spurious messages being handled the way it had been also led me to believe that there was nothing out of the ordinary; when realistically; there was a major error made by a certificated Mechanic. In retrospect; what was displayed on the F/CTL page should have alerted me to a problem; with both Spoiler Pairs #2 and #4; but I assumed that this was the same display that the mechanics and all of the other pilots who operated the aircraft before me also saw. The MEL does not give us specific guidance as to what should be displayed on this page with the MEL active; but I presume that the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) procedure referenced should tell the Mechanic whatshould have been displayed.More information in the MEL document detailing what exactly should be displayed on the SD (System Display) and what messages the crew should or shouldn't expect for a given MEL. Also; if there was indeed an attempt to cover up a maintenance error; I think this case should be used as an example as to how to properly correct an error.
column123: After takeoff we got an ECAM for flight spoiler fault that was reoccurring. We had this aircraft on the previous leg and got the ECAM and cleared it but this one kept returning. We still thought it was associated with the MEL on the Aircraft Spoiler Surface 4 INOP but Spoiler Surface 2 was also INOP. The Captain had reviewed the logbook before the previous flight and seen another crew had this happen and Maintenance had signed off [that] it was normal for the MEL. The Captain got in touch [with] Maintenance through Dispatch and they wanted us to divert to ZZZ1. We diverted and landed uneventfully.I think Maintenance improperly deferred the Spoiler Surface 4 and after a crew wrote it up; did not verify it was correct. The MEL should have had us view the Flight Control page instead of the HYD SD page for amber information of #4 Spoiler ONLY amber or #2 Spoiler ONLY.

column121: All of a sudden; the Captain stopped mid-sentence and said; 'Look at that!'  He pointed to the 1:00 right position; and we passed by a large; round; unknown object to the right at our altitude.  Based on the speed of passing; it seemed to be stationary.  It was large (much larger than a Mylar balloon); dark gray and silver/shiny; stripes (stripes of its form/shape) from top to bottom.  It seemed to have a pinch point at the bottom.  I didn't see anything attached; but the Captain said he saw a rope or something dangling behind it.  Soon after our shock; ATC gave us a handoff and we reported the object.  He was unaware of its presence. I reached out to the [nearby]  pilots to see if anyone knew anything.  One pilot responded: 'We got a message from our chief pilot this morning - balloon off SWO 100 radial 12.4nm & tethered balloon by Company.' The message the pilots in SWO received correlates with the location of our event.  I've never known of a tethered balloon at 32;000 feet.  Makes one wonder if this balloon got loose; especially given the rope the Captain saw.  If so; shouldn't ATC have been notified?  A bit more right today; and I may not have been able to write this report; along with the more than 200 people we had onboard.

column121: While reviewing the SID and release prior to departure (ABQ3 Runway 8); the First Officer and I noticed that the required climb gradient was very steep. We determined it may be difficult to meet the gradient and contacted Dispatch for guidance. I was unable to get in touch with Dispatch via phone. I then contacted a base chief pilot for guidance; who referred me to the Director of Operations. I was unable to get in contact with the Director of Operations until after departure. I then contacted another chief pilot for guidance and was referred to contact Dispatch again. I was able to talk to Dispatch and asked if we needed to run the climb analysis tool that we perform in ZZZ since this gradient was much steeper than ZZZ. Dispatch informed me that there was no need/requirement to run the analysis. I verified multiple times that this was the case; even with a steep climb gradient. Dispatch confirmed that no climb analysis was needed.I briefed the First Officer that we would need to fly a performance climb and ensure we were above 1;600 ft./min at a 200 Knot climb. After takeoff; we maintained the highest practical climb performance with E-climb; but were unable to maintain the needed vertical speed for our airspeed. We tried leaving the flaps at 9 and after that didn't work; flaps up with a climb below 200 Knots. I estimate we maxed out at 800 to 900 ft/min at 180 Knots. It was apparent that we would not be able to climb at the required rate with any configuration/speed and we made a right turn as assigned by ATC. We avoided terrain by executing the turn; but in IMC or without a quick turn crews would be in danger of CFIT. I was able to get in contact with the Director of Operations after landing to explain my concern with this departure. He pointed me to Training Bulletin XYZ; which referenced SID climb tables. This bulletin references ZZZ SIDs and it was not readily apparent (at least to me) that it would apply to other airports. After referencing the data cards; it appears that the required climb gradient of 470 Ft. per NM may not be achievable by the aircraft. While technically; there is a sentence in the training bulletin that states applicability to other airports; we have not received any training; memo; daily read; email; etc. on climb analysis at airports other than ZZZ. I was also a bit frustrated that it is recently getting harder to contact support resources by phone. I spent about 20 minutes trying to get help on a safety sensitive concern with no real available/wrong answer. While I take responsibility for this event; I followed the note on the training bulletin to contact dispatch when in doubt. I believe the company needs to issue a training; memo; etc. to make other pilots; Dispatch; and Management aware of the need for this analysis at other airports and include this on the 10-7 pages. I think this threat could result in CFIT if not corrected. While ATC would hopefully intervene; a crew could run into a situation where a GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) escape maneuver may not physically be able to clear the terrain without a non apparent turn in IMC.

column121: Preflight up through takeoff on this flight was normal ops.  I was sitting as the relief pilot with NAME being the PIC and flying pilot and NAME1 being the SIC and pilot monitoring.  During the takeoff roll and at rotation; the flying pilot rotated normally after the 'ROTATE' call and pitched up to approximately 4 to 5 degrees and then stopped rotating any further.  We were very heavy (382;094 TOW).  We had a stop margin of approximately 2;000 feet and the end of the runway was rapidly approaching.  After a moment or two; the flying pilot continued the rotation and we proceeded on normally.  After takeoff and past sterile cockpit; the flying pilot communicated to us that the airplane just didn't seem to want to fly and he held the lower pitch attitude for a moment to allow the aircraft to accelerate a bit and avoid a potential tail strike.  During cruise with my time in the seat; the flying pilot and I discussed the issue a little bit more; determined that we might be heavier than the weight and balance paperwork stated; and agreed to really check the pitch attitude on final approach at the calculated REF speed to see if that was another indication of being heavier than we thought we were.  We did find that some airspeed had to be added to the calculated REF speed to maintain the normal pitch attitude during the final approach.  Upon blocking in; we pulled out the landing REF speed chart in the QRH Inflight Performance section and found that with the additional airspeed we had to add to maintain the normal; fully configured; landing pitch attitude; it was conceivable that we may be UP to 20;000 pounds heavier than what was stated on the paperwork.  We called the Load Master up to the flight deck and he said that flight was loaded at the point of origin in ZZZZ1; he was not involved with the loading process (or maybe more accurately; he wasn't involved in the weighing of the cargo) but was just given the numbers from those that were and that we had around 20;000 LBS of cargo in the lower cargo compartments along with all of the passenger weight. The PIC placed a writeup in the logbook to alert the outbound crew (the airplane continued on to ZZZ1 with the same Passengers and cargo) and we all agreed that we needed to make someone else aware of the issue (I elected to inform the Duty Pilot) and to ensure the outbound crew knew of the situation since we wouldn't see them ourselves.  During the limo ride from ZZZ to ZZZ2; both the PIC and myself made unsuccessful attempts to reach the duty pilot through both Pilot Support and Dispatch.  During the subsequent limo ride and discussing the issue further; the PIC wondered if there was a chance that the ground crew in ZZZZ1 was using KILOS as unit of measure rather than pounds (very possible given the 20;000 LBS of cargo we reportedly had vs what the potential difference in weight we noticed with the landing REF speed).  The PIC was dropped off at the ZZZ2 airport for a commercial flight and the FO (First Officer) and I continued onto the layover hotel.  It was agreed that the PIC would continue to communicate the issue to someone in hopes of alerting the outbound crew of the situation.  I was texted later by the PIC that he did get a hold of the Fleet Captain and discuss the issue.

column121: On arrival at the departure gate; I inquired about station provision of international documents - Hawaii Reference Guide; plotting chart; and AIREP forms. Agent had no idea what I was talking about; claiming that the Hawaii flight is a domestic operation. The FOM clearly includes Hawaii operations under the flag operations description; and Hawaii is specifically addressed in the international operations sections of FOM - to include the need to use a plotting chart on random routes and the AIREP form when making non-CPDLC (Controller Pilot Datalink Communications) position reports. On this flight; the SATCOM system was placarded INOP which meant I would need to make position reports - thus; the need for an AIREP form. The Hawaii Reference Guide includes both plotting chart and AIREP forms as required paperwork to be checked prior to departure. I called Operations to ask for an AIREP form; but was told that they had no idea what I was asking for. We have been operating Hawaii and ZZZ1 flights out of ZZZ for years. If the FOM is going to require certain forms and documents; it would be very helpful to have these documents and forms available at the departure station. The same situation is now occurring in HNL as well - no international forms are being provided since they state that flights to the mainland are considered 'domestic' flying. But random routes are occasionally used and position reporting is still required. If there is no requirement for an AIREP form to be used in the CPDLC environment; the FOM and reference guides should be updated to reflect that their use is no longer required.Conflicting treatment of Hawaii operations - domestic for some purposes; international for others. Lack of clarity on what forms and documents are actually required to be used or made available for Hawaii operations. Lack of availability of international forms and documents at departure stations for international operations. If the FOM requires the use of documents and forms on international flights; it would be very helpful to have those forms actually available at the departure station. The mixed status of Hawaii operations - considered international flag operations by the FOM for some purposes but not for others - causes confusion as to which rules actually apply. This needs to be clarified.

column121: I was pilot flying; my CA (Captain) was pilot monitoring. After receiving instructions from Approach to slow down to 170 KT until a 5-mile final; we got an IDG (Integrated Drive Generator) fault message. The CA pulled out the QRH and tried to address the issue. Shortly after; we got a multitude of issues. We notified ATC and we agreed that we would be safe to land. Slat flap fail; AT/AP (Autothrottles/Autopilot) disconnect; and more. Suddenly we lost all screens and everything went black. The RAT (Ram Air Turbine) deployed and I had to continue flying using the Captains PFD (Primary Flight Display). The CA [requested priority handling] and was cleared by Approach to land and swap to Tower.CA told the FAs (Flight Attendant) we were making a precautionary landing. Tower said they had the trucks rolling and landed as best we could normally. We dropped the flaps on schedule and noticed that the Slat Flap Disagree persisted. The CA then took over the controls with ample time before the 1;000 feet call and I swapped roles to PM. We notified ATC that we could not verify [if] the gear and flaps were down. Luckily; Tower notified us that another plane verified they were down. We landed uneventfully and taxied to the gate under our own power. No passengers were hurt; only the first row or two knew something was abnormal due to the RAT vibrations; the rest of the passengers were unaware of the incident. [The cause was an] internal electrical malfunction at a time of high workload. Potentially go-around and troubleshoot If issues happen on final.

Flight was cleared to line up and wait 4L; comms normal. While in position a garbled; indistinct transmission was heard. Flight was expecting a takeoff clearance and called tower to verify they were broadcasting to us. No reply. Tower then came on and cleared flight to vacate runway; comm was loud and clear. Tower received our reply as well. Tower was then heard giving directions to a go around aircraft. The initial go around call to that flight was not heard by either pilot of our flight. Flight taxied back to departure end. Flight was cleared to line up and wait again; comms normal. Takeoff clearance was received and acknowledged. During initial takeoff roll tower came on frequency asking us if we were taking off. We replied we were and had acknowledged our takeoff clearance. Airborne tower wanted us to have our radio checked. column123: While in position for takeoff on 4L at EWR both the Captain and I did not here the takeoff clearance given by tower which resulted in a go-around for another aircraft on final.  We did hear a garbled 'takeoff;' but that was it.  We both questioned it and when the Captain tried to clarify with tower were told to hold position and then received clearance to taxi off the runway; via BB and P.   Neither the Captain or I heard the takeoff clearance or the tower directed go around of the landing aircraft; but obviously the other aircraft did.  We than taxied back into position and it took the tower at least two tries to get us the takeoff clearance.  We only heard it once.  Upon departure we verified the VHF one was working correctly with multiple ATC agencies.   Sterile cockpit  procedures were followed and there were no conversations while in position on the runway.  Neither the Captain or I heard the original T/O clearance or the wave off call to the landing aircraft. The 10-7B pages for EWR state; 'Radio shadows exist in the vicinity of the first 1800 feet of the runways.' This is true and is an obviously known issue.    Not sure what causes this; whether it is certain airplanes or position of other planes on the taxiways.  At the time of the incident there was a line of 20+ airplanes on taxiway B. This condition is unsafe and needs to be corrected.

column121: Just prior to push out of ZZZ we received and Air Bleed Message. Maintenance interrogated the system and MEL'd the message iaw MEL XX-XX. Enroute the Purser called and stated 'we have an issue; in reviewing our manual we have a Class A fume event in the forward galley. It smells like dirty gym socks.' I've had fume events in the past and I know the ramifications to the safety of the crew and passengers. We also have received good training during [Flight Attendant Training]. In the cockpit we didn't smell anything. All three flight attendants confirmed the same smell. With a Jump seat rider in the cockpit; I made the decision to take a quick bathroom break. Upon reaching the front right galley is was prevalent; mild and persistent. Upon returning to the cockpit I had the purser remain in the cockpit. I used air cell to call Dispatch and maintenance. With pilots; purser; dispatch and maintenance all on the phone call we jointly made the decision it's best to divert to a suitable airport. Over the vicinity of ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 we evaluated diversions to outstations; continue to ZZZ4 or ZZZ5. We were 570 miles from ZZZ4 and 240 from ZZZ5. Knowing ZZZ5 was just as close as spiraling down from FL380 and the aircraft would be grounded; we took into consideration passengers re-accomodation; medical response; inflight support and aircraft replacement. ZZZ5 was the best option and the joint decision was made to proceed to ZZZ5. I asked the First Officer (F/O) to [request priority] from ATC and we proceeded direct to a fix on ILS [Runway] XXR and landed and taxied to the Gate. With the jump seater being pregnant and the review of other events where fumes become hard to smell after long exposure; I requested everyone in cockpit to wear oxygen. I ran through QRC and [other procedures] multiple times to make sure we didn't miss any steps. Managing and reassessing the issue I think we did a pretty thorough job. I even turned on APU and ran bleeds to trouble shoot and nothing was working. The smell persisted in a mild to moderate amount especially in descent according to Flight Attendants (F/As). The purser had F/As rotate to mitigate one persons exposure. With a full aircraft we couldn't move anyone. Upon landing and shutting down we de-masked and opened up flight door. The first officer immediately noticed the smell and we left shortly after securing the aircraft.  I was not aware that the F/As had on the previous leg noticed any smell. They all reported after the event that the dirty socks smell was present on the previous flight. When I took over the aircraft I was again blind sided by this. The F/A in aft galley even said she replaced her socks thinking it was her feet. So my suggestion is to continue to encourage communications from the cabin and have these experiences validated and documented even if there is the slightest question to certain smells. I don't know if the Air Bleed message would have an impact on this event but if so maybe adding instructions to confirm with crew no odors prior to MEL. Having these Name (Purser) able to locate his references on his tablet was huge in assisting me with my QRH.

column121: We operated the ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight. The landing numbers were run for Runway XXL with the ATIS showing south winds at about 7 kts. and temperature about 90 degrees. Normal flaps 30 approach was flown and I used thrust reverser to about 100 kts. before getting on the brakes. Normal brake pressure was used and we took the high speed taxiway. Taxi time to the gate was about four minutes; and I released the parking brake once we were in the chocks.The Operations Agent came in and asked if we 'got on the brakes'.  I said no and he said that our Company has blown about six plugs in the last couple weeks. I received a call from the Operations and was told what happened. I also called Maintenance and answered some questions regarding the flight. Everything on this flight was normal and I believe we did not brake the aircraft down more than a normal landing.  We actually mentioned there was no reason to brake hard due to the three minute limitation on the MAX.Might consider leaving the gear down on such a short flight. Using the carbon brakes; it would be nice to have a temperature gauge for the brakes.
column123: Our first indication that there were any concerns was as the Operations Agent met us upon arrival in ZZZ. He asked if we had used heavy braking on landing because recently he had seen 6 events where the wheel fuse plugs had deflated the tires on this particular flight. The Captain immediately ensured that the parking brake had been released to allow for improved cooling. The oncoming FO (First Officer) met us after he completed his walk-around. He noted that the brakes seemed pretty warm. However; at this point the fuse plugs had not melted yet. We turned the aircraft over to the new crew and headed to the hotel. The Chief Pilot called the Captain at the hotel to inform him that the fuse plugs had melted and deflated the tires after we left. I do not believe the landing data indicated that brake cooling was required. Once at the hotel I tried to re-run the landing data to confirm that there wasn't a brake cooling message. There was not; as far as I could tell; but I could not recall the actual landing weights. I also tried to run the brake cooling module but couldn't get it to run because the release data had expired. This led me to go dig in the books for the brake cooling charts. I believe the brakes on speed was approximately 100 kts.; because I remember seeing the runway exit coming and checking the speed as I felt the increased deceleration from the Captain applying the brakes. Using this and estimated landing conditions I used the Landing Data Charts in the MAX performance manual. This indicated that no special brake cooling procedures were required. However; I noted some interesting facts in this section of the airway manual: If we had used Autobrakes 3 and VRef 145; it puts a lot of additional energy in the brakes; requiring at least 40 minutes of cooling time; and possibly into the 'Caution' for hot brakes; depending on the landing data used. The cooling time chart seems to suggest that 7.3 minutes of cooling Inflight Gear Down is equivalent to 50 minutes of cooling on the ground. The text in that section states; 'Total energy is the sum of residual energy plus energy added.' This is important to note since the previous flights of this particular aircraft had landings at high elevations on high temperature days.

column121: This report concerns the unscheduled separation of the #4 - outboard right main wheel - from the aircraft on takeoff from Runway XX in ZZZ. We began the trip receiving the aircraft from the previous crew at the gate in ZZZ1 one leg prior. There were no abnormalities on the pre-flight; no abnormalities that had not been cleared; and no major abnormalities of any kind recorded in the logbook or in the previous logbook that was in the can for the aircraft. The previous crew verbally told us that it was performing well when we received it from them. The first leg; ZZZ1 to ZZZ; operated smoothly with nothing out of the ordinary occurring. The post flight after that leg revealed no discrepancies of any kind. We pushed back from ZZZ; and our taxi route towards Runway XX included left- and right-hand turns as well as brake applications; and the aircraft continued to operate normally with no signs of any abnormality on the wheels.When we performed the takeoff; shortly after we selected the landing gear up; Tower called us and told us it looked like we lost a tire on the runway. The takeoff was so smooth that we weren't sure if we had in fact lost a tire as we had no indication in the cockpit of any system abnormalities; and the aircraft felt like it was operating normally. We knew there was construction around the runway in about the position we would have lifted off the ground at; so I thought that perhaps it was misidentified construction debris - although we hadn't seen any debris on the runway prior to takeoff. We asked them to perform a runway inspection to determine if it was our tire while we contacted Dispatch to obtain some identifying information about it; as well as to make a plan of action in case it was our tire. We contacted ZZZ Operations after some attempts; and asked them to remain at the airport to assist in identifying the tire and in case we needed to return to ZZZ.We decided not to relay to Dispatch through Operations because we initially had trouble reaching them and we believed that their Operations radio was a handheld and would not have good signal at altitude and location we would need to hold at. We decided to continue climb so that we could contact Dispatch through AIRINC. We discussed the possibility of flying by ZZZ Tower to have them identify if we were missing the tire and which one it was; but at that time we were still not sure that it was our tire and we were unsure if we would have enough fuel to do that and still proceed to ZZZ1 if that was what Dispatch wanted us to do. We made the judgement call that Dispatch would most likely have us continue to ZZZ1 due to the long runways; good emergency services; and having the finest Operations and Maintenance staff there to assist. We continued to climb along our filed route while ATC attempted to identify the tire. Shortly after that; we advised the Flight Attendant (FA) of the potential situation and that we were most likely continuing to ZZZ1; and we would wait to advise the passengers until we were sure and close to ZZZ1 to avoid panic. She said that she would take the time to review some information in her manuals. We chose to continue at a speed of long-range cruise or slower - 180 IAS being the safe speed used when structural damage is suspected - because we were unsure if there was debris on the wheel assembly that could become dislodged and damage something else; or if losing the tire had already damaged something.It took about 30 minutes to 45 minutes for us to make contact with Dispatch after that. We attempted AIRINC; Station Operations on 4 or 5 different local frequencies; relaying through company aircraft; or through another frequency. We attempted using different transmitters in case there was debris from the tire that had damaged an antenna. We were unsuccessful; so ATC attempted to call Dispatch. This took time because ATC was attempting to call using an old company number with an old area code. It was further delayed because we werebeing handed off to new controllers periodically and we had to apprise them each of the situation and have them attempt to make contact. ATC did make contact and Dispatch instructed us to continue towards ZZZ1. After that; we were advised that it was in fact our tire. We requested priority handling and continued to ZZZ1. After this determination; it took roughly 15 - 30 minutes longer for us to contact Dispatch on AIRINC.We had time with a low workload in cruise because we couldn't contact Dispatch through AIRINC yet; so we used the time to review our manuals and the QRH for the related procedures. In the QRH we decided that the Landing with Abnormal Landing Gear Procedure was the most applicable. We began to brief and discuss this procedure while trying to make contact with Dispatch through AIRINC. When we did make contact with Dispatch; [they] advised us that they thought it was the #1 wheel - the left main outboard. We told him that the procedure called to induce a fuel imbalance and to burn off as much fuel as possible before landing. We asked his opinion of going into holding on the way in to ZZZ1 to do so; and he agreed.After this determination was made; we said we would call back again and terminated the call because our radio transmitters made it very difficult to talk to ATC and Dispatch at the same time - there appeared to be interference or override between VHF 1 and 2. We began cross-feeding fuel to make the left side as light as possible and briefed the FA assuming that the #1 wheel was the one we had lost. We told the FA that there was a good chance that it would be a normal precautionary landing and that we would most likely come to a stop on the runway; or exit the runway if able; but most likely would not taxi to the gate. We decided to request for fire trucks; busses; a tug; and a GPU to be standing by. After we were done briefing the FA; we continued to discuss the procedure for approach and landing. The first step of the checklist was to notify the passengers; so we used some time to create an agreed-upon script to brief the passengers without inducing panic - which I would later administer when we were holding near ZZZ1. We noticed that this procedure appeared to be designed to cover both structural landing gear issues as well as tire and wheel problems. We were not sure if we had structural problems or not resulting from the loss of the wheel; so we briefed the procedure including several decision times - such as what we would do if the gear extended normally vs. if the gear did not extend normally vs. if we lost the hydraulic system when the gear was extended; etc. The result which did occur which we briefed was that the gear extended normally and the remaining tire; brakes; and steering operated normally for the landing.The decisions which we briefed involved in this were as follows. We left the GPWS switch in the on position because that switch's function is to silence alerts when the gear is not sensed down and locked. No fuel imbalance was established; and with our and Dispatch's agreement due to the relatively light weight of the aircraft; small practical difference the imbalance would make; and for ease of procedure application in the interest of safety. We did not pull the emergency gear extension lever due to the gear extending normally and indicating locked down by both indicating systems. Our understanding is that the emergency gear extension handle simply opens the uplock boxes; which had already been opened successfully; and that pulling the emergency gear extension handle could potentially impede us during egress if an evacuation was needed. We discussed at what time the bleeds should be selected off for approach. I had never selected the bleeds off in this aircraft in flight before; so the Captain and I had different opinions about when it should be done. We ended up selecting them off at 500 ft.; which I now agree with in hindsight. The remaining items of the checklist would be completed after we were already on the ground. We briefed that we would complete these steps if there was some kind of fire; severe damage; or loss of control evident at touchdown; but we would otherwise move slowly and discuss these steps due to the potential hazards of aircraft control involved with performing them.While we were discussing this; Dispatch called on AIRINC again and corrected that we had actually lost the #4 - outboard right main wheel - rather than the #1 as said earlier. I asked him if he was sure and made sure that Maintenance had checked the serial numbers on the wheel to be positive. After Dispatch told us this we re-briefed the Flight Attendant for the #4 wheel.After we were all thoroughly briefed; we began our delay vectors around ZZZ1 to burn down to roughly 2000 lb. as instructed by Dispatch; I gave the PA to the passengers. When we had burned enough fuel; we began the ILS to Runway XYR - the longest and most familiar runway for us in ZZZ1. The gear extended normally and we saw no abnormal flight characteristics or any system abnormalities. On touchdown; as briefed; I began using the tiller to steer the aircraft early; and we felt it pulling slightly toward the right. However; not nearly enough to warrant the emergency engine shutdown. We were able to control the aircraft throughout the rollout to maintain centerline. We chose not to try to turn off the runway as it would be a left turn-off; which would put the most weight on the right side; and we were unsure of the quality of braking that we had. We used reverse only until we were at a slow walking speed and only then used brake application to bring the aircraft to a stop on the runway centerline abeam the XX taxiway exit where the firetrucks and Operations were waiting.Tower gave us the discrete frequency to use. The firetrucks came onto the runway and asked us to shut down the #2 engine so they could inspect. We complied and they said the remaining tire seemed to be in good condition and asked us if we wanted to exit. We said no; we would like to deplane the passengers and then be tugged. While Operations was setting up to deplane the passengers; we briefed how we would manage shutting down the #1 engine in order to deplane; and requested the GPU to be connected so we could deplane with lights on without killing the batteries. When the GPU was ready; we connected; Operations pinned all 3 gears; we shut down #1; checked the after-landing and -parking checklists; called the Flight Attendant; and then began deplaning to the busses. While the passengers were deplaning; Operations connected the tug. When the passengers were clear we prepared to sit in the cockpit while Operations tugged us to Gate XX. We monitored the tug process; arrived at the gate; and began conducting the postflight inspection and filling out the logbook. I completed the logbook while the Captain called the Chief Pilot to begin debriefing.I suggest that Station Operations be provided with better radio systems; or that the ACARS system be utilized in our aircraft. It was difficult for us to establish a reliable communication with Dispatch due to a combination of poor-quality radios and not many base stations being occupied due to the time of day. A communication with Dispatch was very necessary in order for Maintenance to verify which tire was missing so that we could adjust our procedures.
