column121: On the final phase of the Visual Approach; backed up by the ILS Runway XY to ZZZ; with the intention to capture the glide path from above; the Auto Pilot (AP) and Auto Throttles were disengaged. Prevailing conditions were Good Visibility and varying Tail Winds of up to nine (9) Knots. During the final portion of the descent to touchdown; with a visual transition to the PAPI reference already established (PAPI were showing 3 RED-1 WHITE); the Aircraft descended below the referenced visual glide path; with the tendency to fly over the Runway XY overrun area at an altitude (AGL) of less than 50 ft. The moment the Captain; having the Pilot Monitoring (PM) duties; mentioned his estimation for being low on the glide path; the aircraft was overflying a point short of the RWY by about 500 feet. He consecutively called for a Go Around; which was immediately executed by the PF (Pilot Flying). Root cause is the initially higher angle of descent / rate of descent to capture the glide slope from above; that ended up to an over correction - reverse situation of flying finally lower than the projected/correct slope. column121: After takeoff at approximately 500 ft. AGL; we received an EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature) Overtemp ECAM.  We continued to thrust reduction altitude; requested priority handling; and followed the ECAM protocol which resulted in shutting down Engine #2. We completed all necessary tasks associated with an event of this nature and returned for an uneventful overweight landing at ZZZ.Contributing factors were a slight tailwind (new T/O data was obtained); heavy weight due to fuel tankering resulting in an APU bleeds on takeoff.Difficult to say; OAT was not excessive but perhaps there was an issue of some kind with the engine resulting in it exceeding EGT limits.
column123: Before departure at the gate; my Captain and I discussed possible threats prior to briefing. While the weather was nice; the two that came to mind were that while the ATIS reported wind as calm; it is not unusual to have a takeoff clearance with a tailwind; and secondly that if we had to return to field; we would be overweight for landing. As a matter of technique; I always load a return ILS into the longest runway at the departure airport in the secondary flight plan in case of a return to field; we discussed this and agreed it was a good idea.After discussing these threats; we noted that our Performance Data showed a TOGA takeoff; APU off. We requested a Performance Data with 5 kt. tailwind applied; which showed a TOGA takeoff; APU on. We entered the data for normal takeoff; but kept the we new Performance Data if needed.Upon switching to Tower upon approaching Runway XXC; we noted that the previous takeoff clearance included a tailwind. We entered the new data; ensured that flaps and APU were set appropriately; and verified that all were correct. Shortly after; we were given clearance to takeoff.The takeoff roll; takeoff; and initial climb were all normal. Somewhere around 500-800 ft.; we heard the 'ding' from the ECAM. The Captain stated 'my aircraft'; and after noting that it was not an quick action or ECAM exception; I noted it was simply an advisory ECAM with no actions; 'ENG 2 EGT High Temp'. I noted a temperature as high as 971. After thrust reduction; the ECAM then displayed the actions 'Thrust lever 2 ... idle; ENG Master 2 ... off'. We were now aware that we would be shutting down the number 2 engine. We requested priority handling and leveled at 4;000 ft. With the autopilot on; we changed controls so that I was the Pilot Flying; my Captain running the checklists; and we shut down the engine.With a maximum landing weight of 171;519 lbs.; and we were over 188;000 lbs.; we elected to slow the aircraft and deploy flaps in order to increase our fuel burn and get as light as we could before landing. My Captain completed all appropriate checklists while I coordinated with ATC. Reprogramming the MCDU for our return to field was now as simple as hitting Secondary Flight Plan and Activate Secondary. After all QRH checklists were complete and everyone was notified; my Captain asked me 'is there anything you can think of that we have missed?'; which I answered; 'No; I cannot.' We concluded with our approach briefing; with emphases on single engine and overweight procedures; completed the descent checklist; and got vectors to final. The Captain resumed control of the aircraft for approach and landing.Approach and landing were uneventful; landing at a weight of 184;400 lbs.; approximately 157 kts.; and 100 FPM descent rate or less. We came to a stop on the runway for inspection from ARFF (Airport Rescue Fire Fighting); and we immediately turned on the brake fans and monitored brake temperatures. ARFF did not note any high temperatures or leaks. We then taxied to Gate XX with ARFF following us.The takeoff clearance with a tailwind made us change from TOGA; APU off; to TOGA; APU on takeoff. This change in takeoff thrust may have been enough for the engine to overtemp shortly after takeoff. A takeoff clearance with a headwind would have been a lower thrust takeoff. In our case; the Performance Data even indicated that [Runway] XXC would have been a reduced thrust takeoff.ZZZ airport needs to be better about airport operation being in line with wind direction in order to minimize the frequency of tailwind takeoff and landing clearances.

Notified ATC of reject and needed to clear runway. Started ECAM procedures; at the same time another airline notified us over air that we had a fire on our number 2 engine. We then proceeded to extinguish fire with push button and squib. After finishing up procedure and coordination with CFR to make sure no fire was present we set up to be towed back to gate with no further incident.Apparently; Airbus is having issues with this config for takeoff. column123: Day 3 of a 3-day; early departure; last leg home.  Gate XXX; short taxi to runway XXR.  Allowed the engines to warm up for three minutes while on the ramp to get the five minutes required before takeoff.  Winds were reported 280 degrees to approx 300 degrees.  From previous experiences from flying the Airbus in and out of ZZZ; the winds can switch to a tailwind component very quickly when they use runway XXL/R for departure; so I expected a potential tailwind.We were cleared to line up and wait on runway XXR.  The aircraft was lined up with the center line and the parking break was set.  Control was then given to the FO as we awaited takeoff clearance.  Once it was received and we read it back; we immediately experienced a single chime; which normally would indicate that perhaps the airplane was not configured for takeoff.  Upon looking at the ECAM; we had an ENG 2 FAIL ECAM alert.  Normally when we encounter ENG FAILs in the simulator; we are presented with a master warning and three chimes.  This was a singular chime.  I immediately told the FO we needed to clear the runway as there was a 90 degree taxiway (1) on the right side of the runway just 50 yards or so from us.  FO advised tower we needed to clear for a warning.At this point I initially thought this might be a false warning.  There was definitely a surprise factor to all of this.  As we were clearing the runway (right turn) at taxiway 1; I glanced at the EGT and it was red.  At the same time; another airplane that was getting ready to take the active runway said he saw fire coming out of out right engine.  I stopped the aircraft on taxiway 1.  I had the FO call for the CFR vehicles.  The FO wanted to run the ECAM procedure; but I had him check the Quick Reference Card first as I remembered there was either a quick action or ECAM exception procedure that needed to be run prior to executing the ECAM procedure.  The FO started to look that up... I called back to the cabin and asked the flight attendants to check to see if there was any smoke in the cabin or any sign of fire coming from the engine.  The answer was that there was no evidence of fire or smoke; from the #3 or #4 FA.  When I returned to the FO; he said the QRC procedure he found was for an ENG FIRE on the ground.  After considering a possible evacuation; my focus shifted to getting the engine shut down.  Since we had no indication of a fire from the cockpit (other than high EGT) nor any evidence from the cabin; we ran the ECAM ENG FAIL procedure and elected to discharge a fire bottle into the #2 engine.  I made a PA to the passengers telling them we exited the runway due to an alert we received in the cockpit and to expect some emergency vehicles come around the aircraft.   The fire trucks were not present at this point; so we asked the other airplane if they could see any evidence of fire.  They couldn't see from their vantage point; so I taxied the aircraft South on taxiway 2 to taxiway 3 (50 yards?) to see if they could see any evidence of continued fire.  They still could not see; so I stopped the aircraft at taxiway 3 and waited for CFR to show up.  No fire indications in the cockpit; such as aural fire warning or ENG FIRE ECAM; other than the excessive EGT with the ENG FAIL ECAM.Once CFR arrived; communications were hampered as they were not on a dedicated frequency yet.  I queried the tower and they gave us the right frequency to be on; when they arrived.  CFR scanned the aircraft and did not find any hot spots. At this point; we had finished the ECAM procedure and were looking for any follow-up procedures (which is the next step in Airbus; non-normal methodology).  The FO couldn't find them.  They used to be in the QRH and were on [specific] paper... easy to find.  Since a previous; major QRH revision; they are no longer on [specific] pages but are found within the QRH itself.  I told the FO not to worry about finding them... that much of the material was not going to be applicable.  I redirected our focus back to the STATUS page so we could discuss the current situation of the airplane.  The big thing was that we had no nose wheel steering; so we summoned ops to get us a tug and advised CFR to follow us under tow.  It took an inordinate amount of time to get a tug out to us (maybe 30 minutes or more); but seemed like hours.  Made several PA's explaining that we were still waiting on our tug.Eventually towed back to the gate.  Maintenance met the aircraft and asked about EGTs; duration; and the fire bottle status.  I told them I remembered seeing an EGT of 669 at some point... maybe for 30 to 60 seconds.  AML entry was made indicating all of this.When all of this was occurring during a short amount of time; I originally thought that maybe this was a false alert (only a single chime).  After exiting the runway and realizing the extent of the emergency; I thought that perhaps we had the presence of flames due to a compressor stall; exacerbated by a wind that may have shifted to a tailwind.After returning to the gate; I was in contact with the Fleet Captain... who asked if the APU was ON for takeoff.  I replied that it was.  In Airbus world; you can do a Max power takeoff and run the packs from the APU; freeing-up the engines; giving you a little more power for takeoff.  That was the case this morning.  The Fleet Captain indicated that the ENG FAIL ECAM was caused by having the APU bleed ON.  Apparently; this causes back pressure on the engine bleed and is a known issue.  Tech Ops is increasing ground idle to prevent thisAfter speaking to the Fleet Captain; he mentioned that the QRC procedure (requiring completion before doing the ECAM alert) entitled ENG FIRE on GROUND is a procedure used when there is no electrical power to the aircraft.  It is a procedure that is to be used in that situation.  Perhaps I misunderstood him as our conversation occurred after the adrenaline started settling down a bit; but maybe it needs to be explained to the flight crews (the correct use of that particular QRC procedure).Also; the FO had difficulty in finding the ECAM follow-up procedures; to the point where I said we need to move to the final step of assessing the STATUS (page) of the airplane.Finally; communication from the tower on how to communicate with CFR/ARFF when they arrived could; be improved upon.  In retrospect though; we never said the word 'emergency' to them.  My instructions to the FO were to get the trucks rolling now... not very clear perhaps and maybe was a factor in the initial comm problems with CFR.Advised the Duty Chief that we were done flying for the day.  The adrenal rush was subsiding and he was very helpful in accomplishing that for us.

column121: Overloaded TakeoffPush back; engine start; fuel indications all normal. Initial taxi took additional power to move aircraft; which is unusual in a B777-200 at typical [long distance] weights. On takeoff roll; initial acceleration was sluggish even though we were TO2 max; the takeoff roll seemed longer than normal and climbout was less than usual. We were filed for initial cruise FL350; but given option of FL370 as FL350 taken; so we climbed FL370 (FMC said Max FL391). Upon level off at FL370; aircraft struggled to maintain normal cruise Mach speed .83; and I noticed amber hook was seemingly higher than normal (about 245 kts).Shortly after level off; EICAS caution 'FUEL DISAGREE'. Followed Emergency Check List and Progress Page 2 indicated totalizer about 10;000 lbs. higher than calculated. Determined no fuel leak; and followed up with QRH review of ETOPS failures; selected fuel probes synoptic display from maintenance section in FMC; and noticed many center tank fuel probes inoperative. We called Dispatch/Maintenance conference call on satcom and sent fuel maintenance display to them; all three parties agreed no fuel leak; use calculated fuel; determined it was appropriate to continue flight.We started to burn substantially above plan; and we started to suspect we were heavier than closeout. We referred to performance manual cruise pages; 1.3g maneuver data; and .84 cruise data; and our suspicions were confirmed: amber hook was indicating maneuvering speeds for approximately 50;000 lbs. heavier aircraft; also fuel flow predictions the same.We called Dispatch and Duty Pilot; asked them to contact ZZZ Station Personnel to obtain FUEL UPLIFT in gallons from fuel company. Prior procedures required us to check this information from the fuel slip. It would have caught this serious error. Initially fuel company kept sending info strictly off our aircraft gauges; but we explained to Dispatch this was not correct; due to inoperative center fuel probes; and we strongly suspected fueler had overfilled the amount required for the flight to ZZZ1.After an hour or so; Dispatch confirmed that we were approximately 50;000 lbs. (7500 gallons) heavier than planned.Our performance data/climb; cruise; descent; and landing data were invalid. The flight crew; not knowing this situation at the time of departure; could have encountered serious consequences; if an emergency such as engine failure occurred the crew may not have acted appropriately because of the unknown situation. implications for engine failure at V1 on takeoff; implications for stopping on wet runway from V1; implications for enroute engine out performance and drift down; implications for correct Vref in ZZZ1.This is an extremely serious incident in my opinion; possibly could have been caught with a simple fuel slip check.Inexperienced fuelers; lack of back up checks by the pilots; cross checking required fuel vs actual loaded fuel; possible fuel sensor failuresRecommend having someone in the crew cross check the fuel slip provided by the fueler against the master flight plan.

column121: The event occurred because Greenville-Spartanburg (GSP) is working a busy airport with one controller utilizing all three frequencies. This is a major safety of flight issue as multiple links in the safety chain were broken that day. If the sharpness of the crews from Air Carrier X and Air Carrier Y had not utilized full four ear policy and patience it could have been an issue. The actions taken by the ATC operation in GSP are uncalled for and unsafe. If this is overlooked there could be fatal consequences in the future. There are a few local airports in the area of Greenville-Spartanburg that are non-towered. If the Tower Controller delayed any further for us to be handed over to Departure; we could have had a collision or RA with an unknown aircraft all due to the unsafe actions of one controller handling a workload bound for a minimum of two personal.I was in command of Aircraft X. The Greenville Tower had one controller working all three frequencies: clearance; ground; and tower. This was a busy morning with Air Carrier Z; Air Carrier X; Air Carrier A; and us to ZZZ all departing at roughly the same time. When we called for our clearance on the delivery frequency; we noticed there was some bleed over as the controller was issuing take-off clearances. We had to repeat our request for a clearance but were given it with no issues.  I released the brakes and we called for push shortly after. Air Carrier X also called for push after us. In the middle of our push back the controller called on the ground frequency to inform Air Carrier Z of a delay for them. The two began to have a conversation on ground of a game plan to be made. As their conversation occurred our ramp crew disconnected the tow bar and gave the wave off for an all clear to a taxi. I noticed Air Carrier X had pushed off gate and we were pushed off with our nose in the direction of travel to only exit with a head on collision. We finished our 'After Start Checklist' and cleared the area to begin our taxi. I switched on our taxi and nose lights and noticed Air Carrier X did the same. With the controller and Air Carrier Z conversation occurring to what was now a clearance being given with a read back to follow there was no way for me or Air Carrier X to have confirmation one was waiting for the other. There was dense fog and low visibility on the ramp that morning. Tower does not control the ramp and a courtesy call is requested. The weather was so bad we had a take-off alternate of ZZZ1 that morning. It was a frustrating situation as Air Carrier X and I could barely make out the 2nd half of each other's aircraft; so it was a game of chicken. I tried to call over the radio and speak over the clearance being given but it did not work. Ultimately; I turned off my lights to give Air Carrier X the right of way. As we began our taxi to Runway 4 Air Carrier A called clearance to get their clearance to Houston (IAH) and that now was being broadcast over the ground frequency adding to the safety issue that no one moving on the aircraft surface could talk to each other. The Tower issued Air Carrier X their take-off clearance and told us we were next. After we got our take off clearance; we began the take-off roll with no issues. As we continued our take-off climb Carrier called the controller over the ground frequency. All we heard was the controller responding over the tower frequency meaning he was working all three frequencies still. This delayed our hand off to Departure and made us uneasy as the tower radar could not see our path beyond a certain mileage. As we checked in with GSP Departure we were given an instruction to contact Center as our time had been too long and radar services with GSP could not be utilized further.This told me the GSP airport controller took too long to hand us off and impeded the Departure Controller from doing their job properly. We did not have sufficient air traffic control separation all due to the unsafe practices of the GSP airport and Air Traffic Control operation at the airport of GSP. GSP needs to hire another controller! There must be at least one person working Ground and Delivery while another separate controller works Tower. The operation in GSP has been compromised and it is scary to think that the unsafe actions are acceptable to those working in the ATC system. If this issue were to happen again; I'm worried it could turn out like the Tenerife airport disaster with KLM and Pan Am but scraping metal on the ramp or taxing into each other.

column121: I departed ZZZ without the final dangerous goods manifest. To my knowledge; we did not receive one. I did a communications uplink review and could not find the manifest. I do not know if Load Planning failed to send the manifest. We had a communications disruption from a maintenance issue that may have cleared the communications cache before we received it. We recognized the error in flight and had Load Planning send a copy. Regardless; the responsibility is mine to depart with a final Dangerous goods (DG) manifest. I received the planned DG manifest and placed it in my usual place as a reminder to get the final version before departure. My reminder failed. This is in no way an excuse for my error. For the record; the contributing factors follow.Threats.- Distractions. A maintenance issue to resolve an Autopilot Backdrive Wheel EICAS caution and status messages; plus accompanying Bank Angle Protection inop issue had three mechanics in my flight deck for 30 minutes; including a total power down of the aircraft. The resulting flow disruption had me out of my seat and out of pre-flight flows. The mechanics stated they needed boarding stopped and passengers seated for the power down. I was preoccupied coordinating with Customer Service and Flight Attendants on passenger enplanement to assist with the maintenance issue. As part of the power down of the aircraft; the interior would go (relatively) dark. When power was restored; it took several more minutes for the lighting configuration to reset before we could continue with boarding. I was also coordinating with dispatch as the maintenance action would produce MEL items.- Perceived time compression to get the flight out as close to on time as possible. We finally departed XA41 for a scheduled XA00 out time. When the mechanics completed maintenance; we had to redo the FMC initializations and accompanying preflight items. At this point; everything else was ready and departure depended on the flight deck to finish pre-flight procedures.- Fatigue. It was close to midnight; body time. Even though I rested before the flight and managed a brief nap in the early evening; I was tired. That may have contributed towards me missing the final DG manifest.Errors.- Failure to follow standard operating procedures. I did not get the final DG manifest before pushback as required by company procedures.- Failure to execute Crew Resource Management/Threat Error Management. I did not perform effective leadership and communications during the disruption to mitigate the potential for missing the DG manifest.- Poor task management. I tried to do everything to manage pre-departure issues. This trait was identified during LOE. Management.- Delegate. I need to better involve my other crew members. In retrospect; I should have asked one of my co-pilots to manage the cabin boarding/seating issues with the Flight Attendants and Customer Service.- Communicate. Ask other crew members to help remember the final DG manifest. I only mentioned the planned DG to the 'flying' PM. The relief PM was doing the walk-around. I did not ask them to help remember.- Change habit patterns. My preflight cues to remember the final DG manifest did not work. I need to come up with a new method.- Modify leadership methods. I need to revisit the LOE observation that I take too much on to myself and develop techniques to mitigate that leadership shortcoming.

column121: This report is submitted due to concerns regarding return-to-service preparation of our long-term stored aircraft.  This aircraft had a number of issues which precluded an on-time departure and caused us to question the true airworthiness of the aircraft.  Specifically; the aircraft had massively incorrect fuel loading; such that it required ~4+ hours to move fuel to the appropriate; legal-for-flight; locations.  Second; upon the first engine start; we were surprised to see to ECAM Caution messages for 'ENG 1 (and ENG 2) REV INHIBITED.'  Thrust reverser operation was; indeed; inhibited; so we encountered another half hour+ delay while computer settings were changed to allow thrust reverser operation.  (Maintenance Control advised that these messages were likely the result of a release-from-storage checklist item being left undone/missed.)  Our total delay ended up being five hours as our Dispatcher and us concurred that additional fuel was required for our flight to ZZZ due to incoming weather; which added another 20 or 30 minutes to the delays. Our concern is that the number of time consuming and potentially unsafe items we encountered in successfully launching our aircraft suggest that either the team at ZZZ1 was rushed to accomplish these tasks; and/or given insufficient time or staff to complete them.  Another possibility is that the appropriate training and task cards were not been provided?  Regardless of the causes; with so many aircraft coming back into service; it behooves us to look into the events of this return-to-service flight so as to preclude them from occurring again; thus enhancing flight safety.  Simply suggesting an investigation or evaluation of what transpired in this return-to-service flight so as prevent compromised flight operations going forward.

column121: Aircraft X was scheduled for a XZ41 departure ZZZ-ZZZ1.  We were delayed due to being short one flight attendant.  During the preflight and logbook review; the Captain (CA) brought to my attention a previous write up from Date that the number 2 engine was shut down in flight due to an EGT over temp and that a subsequent overweight landing was made.  Both discrepancies were signed off.  The CA and I discussed this during our 'threats' briefing since we were heavy; it was hot; and we would be performing a TOGA take off with the APU ON.  It was my leg to fly.  The start; taxi; and initial take off were routine.  Prior to thrust reduction; we heard the ECAM chime and saw the Master Caution.  I stated 'my aircraft' and called for autopilot 2.  The CA advised ATC of troubleshooting a potential return to ZZZ.  We were instructed to maintain 4;000 feet and fly heading 090.  We cleaned up the aircraft on schedule; leveled off; and began the non-Normal methodology once we were stable.  The ECAM still present was ENG2 EGT OVER LIMIT.  This ECAM directed THR LVR 2 IDLE then ENG 2 MASTER OFF.  I was assigned PF/Radios and we ran the ECAM via non-normal methodology.  Once the engine was shut down; as expected; the ENG2 SHUTDOWN ECAM appeared.  We started the non-normal methodology again.  All checklists; normal and non-normal; overweight landing considerations; and briefings were complete.  ATC vectored us around and was extremely helpful while we were troubleshooting and running checklists.  Once we were ready to return to ZZZ we delivered the PAN-PAN REPORT and requested the full ILS to XXC in ZZZ.  I maintained PF duties and the CA took the PM duties.  We completed an uneventful single engine overweight landing and stopped on the runway.  Once the [airport] response crews said the airplane looked good; we [advised ATC] and taxied to park.  The fire trucks followed us to the gate.Aircraft malfunction; repeat gripe from 2 days prior.  Bore scope and engine run appeared to be the sign off.  I'm not sure that puts the aircraft in the same state that a heavy; hot take off does.Take aways/suggestions:  ATC was outstanding during our event. Next; the QRH has a section for EGT 1/2 OVERLIMIT for IAE ONLY.  We had CFMs.  I believe there may be some benefit in looking at this specific malfunction and how our current procedures address it.  If you follow the non-normal methodology; after FLYING THE AIRCRAFT; we identify the non-normal.  We check if it is a quick action or ECAM exception.  It's not. Once the duties are split; we go through the ECAM.  This particular one directs you to shut the effected engine down.  (We had the ECAM present until we accomplished the steps.) Once the engine is shut down; and you have cleaned up we do the follow up items and supplementals.  When you get to the supplementals on this non normal (attached) it discusses referencing max pointer indications prior to either reducing the thrust lever or shutting the engine down.  The problem is once you get to the supplemental; you have already shut the engine down if you followed the current procedure and strategy.  Is there logic that keeps this ECAM on with CFMs if that temp of 970 degrees C is exceeded; or does the ECAM stay on even if only 915 degrees-950 degrees is reached?  I believe this procedure as an ECAM EXCEPTION that allowed you to reference the max pointer prior to ECAM ACTION may make sense?  It may also give the crew more discretion prior to shutting an engine down.

Due to heavy traffic in the vicinity of the airport; and terrain to the southwest; ATC kept us on a vector that aligned us with a roughly 2 mile final approach to XXR. The airport was extremely difficult to obtain visually; and neither the FO nor myself had it in sight until about 4 miles out. We called the airport in sight; and were cleared for visual approach. At that time; I turned the aircraft to the right to align the aircraft for a downwind in a left hand traffic pattern; and descended the aircraft to 6;500 feet; the appropriate altitude for the 5 mile visual fix. Reaching 6;500 feet; we began to feel uneasy; as the terrain south of the airport forms a bowl; with terrain reaching 8;000 feet in places. Once at the 6;500 feet altitude; we could visually see that there wasn't any room to maneuver the aircraft in the valley to align it with the final approach course (we had about a 3 mile wide; terrain-free swath to work with). At about the same time; ATC issued us a low altitude warning; with the accompanying 'check altitude immediately' instruction. At that time; while on a heading corresponding with base leg; we executed a climb to 7;500 feet; and told tower we were aborting the approach. We overflew the airport and executed a right hand turn to set up for right traffic for XXR; a visual approach which was completed successfully. [Cause was] ATC's vector that led us into a valley not wide enough to maneuver the aircraft on approach. Poor charting of terrain on VFR maps in company publications. I'm filling out a separate safety concern report recommending an additional alert page on the company charts advising pilots of the difficulty of shooting a close-in visual approach to runway XXR from the West.
column123: ZZZ was conducting visual approaches to runways XXR and XXL at the time of the event. ZZZ Approach was descending us for arrival and told us to expect the visual approach for Runway XXR. At about 20 miles from the airport; we were told to proceed direct to the airport and report the field in sight for the visual. At this time we were also told to maintain 9;000 feet for terrain and traffic in the area. We did not obtain visual contact with the airport until about 5 miles away; at which point we informed ZZZ Approach and they cleared us for the visual and told us to contact the tower. At this point the approach controller has us on a vector to intercept approximately 2 mile final for Runway XXR. The Captain made a turn to the right and began a descent to traffic pattern altitude of 6;500 feet to maneuver the aircraft for a stable approach and landing. This turn brought us toward gradually rising terrain northeast of the airport. As we continued to maneuver the aircraft; it became apparent that there was not enough room to safely align with the runway. We initiated a climb and turned back toward the airport. At this time tower issued a low altitude warning and told us to 'check altitude immediately' (we were climbing through 7;000 feet at this time). We responded and said that we were climbing and turning back toward to the airport and that we would need to abort the approach and turn right to re-enter right traffic for XXR. A safe approach and landing was then completed without further incident.ZZZ Approach kept us high due to terrain and traffic and issued a tight vector for a visual approach that only allowed for a 2 mile final for the landing runway. Contributing factors included a busy GA traffic environment and inability to see the airport visually until about 5 miles away.A better way to conduct this approach when arriving from the west would be to join the RNAV approach from vectors or an initial approach fix (especially if this were to be conducted at night) or to vector the aircraft over the airport and down the valley to enter a right downwind for XXR.

column121: This flight was an OE [Operating Experience] with a New Hire FO [First Officer]; and double augmented crew. Normal briefings and departure preparations. Normal takeoff and climb out.I was on break at in the cabin with FO NAME (OE student). Approaching W040 at approximately XA:15 Z I was notified by one of the FAs [Flight Attendants] that I was needed on the Flight Deck.  When I arrived there; FO NAME and NAME1 told me that the 'L HYD QTY' EICAS had appeared and that they were working the HYD QTY - L (C; R) (FM 2.130.4) checklist. At that time the left hydraulic quantity was at .48 and while we were watching it dropped to .47. In accordance with the checklist; we turned off the left hydraulic pumps.We then contacted and consulted with Dispatch and Maintenance Control and made an ELB entry. Dispatch advised that the weather and winds were forecast to be favorable for our arrival in ZZZ. Dispatch said that they would contact ZZZ and advise them of the situation. Maintenance Control advised that it was likely a slow leak and that the checklist offered the best advice for the situation. After the checklist and all coordination was complete; I returned to the cabin to continue my rest. I chose not to wake FO NAME2 and to allow him to continue his rest uninterrupted so that he would be alert as PF.About 30 minutes later at XB:08 a FA woke me again and said that I was needed on the Flight Deck again. When I arrived; I was advised that the R YAW DAMPER EICAS had appeared. We completed the YAW DAMPER - L (R) (FM2.90.46) and made another ELB entry. We researched and found that the hydraulic power source for the right yaw damper is the left hydraulic system that we had just depressurized. We concluded that they were likely related. We advised Dispatch and made another ELB entry. I returned to the cabin to complete my rest period.During the approach briefing we calculated the landing distance for a normal landing; and one for the loss of the left hydraulic system. We were concerned that when we turned the pumps back on during the approach that we might lose the left system quantity completely. We initially planned to configure early for the approach; but on reflection decided to configure normally and then turn the pumps back on when fully configured. If we lost the remaining quantity at that time; we were prepared to reconfigure for a flaps 20 landing. It was agreed that FO NAME2 would make the landing if the system quantity held and that I would make the landing if it did not.On approach we turned the pumps back on after we were fully configured for landing. The pressure came up on the system and quantity held for the rest of the flight. The landing was normal and uneventful. ZZZ had CFR available for our arrival and a tug if it was needed to help us clear the runway.The cabin crew were aware of the situation; but we advised them it would be a normal operation. We choose not to advise the passengers as we fully anticipated a normal landing.One concern arose during the event. During the calculation of the landing distance there was some confusion on which line to use on the chart. With a potential loss of the L HYD system it was unclear if we were to use the line for HYD SYS PRESS L ONLY or HYD SYS PRESS R and C. The title of the column says Aircraft Config/Condition and that does not clarify which row to use. To be safe we calculated both and found that we had ample runway in either case. But it brings up the question does the row titled HYD SYS PRESS L ONLY mean that you 'only' have the left system and the other two are failed; or does it mean that 'only' the left system has failed? After looking at the landing distances; I believe the right row was indeed HYD SYS PRESS L ONLY. But it might be worth a look at this chart for crews who are managing a more critical landing distance issue without the time we had to study it.All the crew did an exceptional job during this event. FOs NAME; NAME1; and NAME2 in particular were exceptional in their handling of the event.

column121: While coming into XXX; getting close to ILS approach at 5;000ft; ATC has put us on a heading for vectors to final for Runway XXL; I started smelling burning smell; the FO smelled the same burning smell as well; at which point I told the FO to take the airplane and the radios; and called back to the flight attendants (FAs); I asked them if they smell anything and they both said they smell a burning smoke smell; I made sure with them that all the passengers were OK and they were ok as well as able to breath properly and see properly as well if there was any sign of smoke in the cabin which they said there was some in the aft of the cabin; I told them I will call back with further instructions and told the FO what the FAs told me; at which point I told him to [request expedited handling] for smoke in the cabin which I reached for the QRC which led to the [other procedures]; and the QRH; which led us to further steps of [Precautionary] Depress; Cargo off; Recerc off; and pass signs on for below 10;000ft portion of the QRH. After I performed these steps which took about I took 1.5 to 2 minutes the smell disappeared; I called the FAs back and informed them we will be making an [expedited] landing; and performed the [preparation] items; they advised me the smell and the visible smoke is not there anymore; I also told them in that case we will most likely not need to evacuate after landing but I will call them upon landing with my decision. After that I took the airplane back from the FO and he continued his PM duties. After Landing I called the FAs again to re-verify there was no smoke or smell in the cabin; as well as all the passengers and both of them were OK and once assured there wasn't any smoke or smell or any issues with the passengers; and both FAs canceled the [expedited handling] and decided to continue to the gate.
column123: Descending through 15;000 feet in ZZZ; I suddenly smelled a very strong and potent smell in the cockpit and asked my Captain if he smelled the same thing. He said yes and then immediately called the Flight Attendants. The Aft FA informed us there was smoke in the cabin and they smell the same type of odor. The Captain told them we were [requesting expedited handling]. He comes back into the interim between us and tells me he is running QRC for smoke fire fumes and my controls and radio. He tells me to [request expedited handling]. I [requested as directed] and continue our descent into the approach area. He runs QRC and QRH. Then gives the FAs the test items. Continuing the descent through 10;000 feet Captain completes the rest of the QRH procedures. He then takes back the controls and I keep the radios. Once we landed and pull off the runway; Captain calls the FAs and verifies there is no more smoke or Odor in the cabin. They said no and Captain elects to continue to the gate and cancel the [request]. We taxi to the gate and maintenance and then Dispatch was notified. Captain wrote up the log book entry and talked to one of the chief pilots who was gathering information. I completed the walk around after the chief pilot got his info. The FAs and I decided to continue to work our next flight and the Captain elected to be done for the day and continue to talk to the chief pilot.No brace was required. Aft FA said the smoke wasn't that thick but we all agree the odor was very strong and distinctive.Being 2 hours delayed on the first flight of the day and sitting around waiting. Then we get to leave late and head to ZZZ and deal with this situation during the terminal area of ZZZ was unexpected and my first in my career so far. Doing what we are trained to do in this situation the best we can and also the crew resource management. QRC/QRH was executed in a timely manner while I flew the airplane and communications was clear and concise between ATC and all crew members. I am happy with how things went and glad because it could have been worse.

column121: Aircraft X was scheduled for departure. But flight crew reported a maintenance message 'NLG UP SOL' prior to departure. The problem we encountered; No where in the AMM; GMM; or any manual were we able to find a procedure that allowed the gear handle to be cycled while passengers onboard. We were also asked by a supervisor if we can cycle the gear handle even though passengers were onboard. This supervisor was very persuasive and pushed the technicians to cycle the gear handle. We stood our ground and refused to cycle the gear handle while passengers on board.We have to address this MEL and update our manuals and procedures when we have passengers onboard. It is very critical that we have this in writing. Cycling the gear handle while passengers onboard only increases the risk of injuries.

column121: Descending through approx 12-13;000 feet for landing at ZZZZ; my FMS timed out as they occasionally do.  Gave it a few moments to catch up and then selected the FMC1 prompt in the upper left hand corner of the FMC.  Not only did it not reset; there was no standby option listed and I then noticed my First Officer's FMC had also lost all data.  On a descent into ZZZZ at about 10;000 feet I decided it would be best if I assumed control of the airplane and we did a positive transfer of control.  At about the same time I glanced over at the approach chart for ILS XXR went to the NAV page and manually entered the frequency and inbound course for ILS runway XXR.  We had a Level 1 alert to set field altitude manually and I tasked that duty to my First Officer.  I also said I had the radios at the time.  I called ATC and informed them we had lost most of our normal navigation equipment; that we would be unable to proceed directly to any fix and that I would need vectors to join the runway XXR localizer.  Passing 10;000 feet I would estimate we were approx 20-25 miles from the field.  Several times the flight director was commanding directives that did not comply with our ATC directives so I was forced to turn it off as it was a distraction.  The autothrottles also were not responding in an appropriate manner either and rather than trying to fight them I disconnected them as well.  Conditions at the field were day VMC.  On a vector and once cleared for the approach approach mode armed although I doubt it did any good I looked for the localizer to come alive and when it did I attempted to track it manually.  There were a couple S turns as I was in real time having to adjust my scan away from looking for a flight director and towards just a localizer needle and a heading and trying to bracket it.  Things became more stable as we continued down the localizer until we had the runway in sight still at many thousands of feet above the ground I transitioned to line up visually and then cross checking my localizer it showed right of course and I realized the piece of pavement many miles in front of me was the taxiway not the runway and shifted back to the left onto localizer at I would estimate 2;500-3;000 ft AGL.  We probably should have asked for a visual approach at that time but we were too busy to even think of it.  Now hand flying the airplane fully manually with no automation nor flight director assistance at around 2;000-2;500 feet I would estimate I leveled the airplane as the glide slope was approx 1 dot below us to join it.  I did not even look at the approach plate to see were intercept altitude was as we were in visual conditions and I was too focused on maintaining manual aircraft control to be distracted looking away from the panel.  ATC did ask us several times during the approach are you stabilized.  We had the situation under control so I told me First Officer tell her yes.  We were fully configured on glide slope and localizer with landing checklist complete by 1;000 feet AGL (actual more like 1;500-2;000 ft).  There was a high speed foot on the airspeed indicator but no low speed foot.  Based upon our landing weight and my prior experience in the airplane I flew the approach at 165 knots flaps 35.  The approach and landing from 1000 feet AGL to touchdown was uneventful.  This airplane had recent prior multiple flight control computer malfunctions that caused a prior crew to have a sudden pitch down moment according to the prior Captain.  My goal was to get it on the ground as soon as it was safely possible and try to separate the automation from control of the aircraft to a reasonable extent.When we lost all our navigation data from both FMS so close to the airfield and with day VMC conditions at the field and my First Officer focusing on another checklist and given the recent history of this airplane; I decided the safest course was to revert back to old school flying and not waste time trying to manage the problem through running an extended Dual FMS Loss checklist and focus our efforts on getting the airplane on the ground.The prior day I witnessed two aircraft mechanics on this same jet in conflict over whether the airplane should be returned to service or not.  One mechanic thought there was only 1 flight control computer having issues the other thought both computers were malfunctioning.  One mechanic said the airplane was AOG to me 2 times.  After that I went into the cockpit to observe their trouble shooting.  One mechanic was simply trying to clear the fault in the CFDS (Centralized Fault Display System) the other wanted to know why and wanted more time to diagnose it.  When one mechanic said to me the airplane is AOG a 3rd time I took the extraordinary step of calling the Duty Officer and telling him I was not crewing this airplane until the mechanics were given some time to troubleshoot and requested we be placed into rest.  After minimum rest we came back to the jet and I spoke with the mechanic that was objecting to the return to service the previous night and he now seemed comfortable releasing the jet to fly.I personally witnessed one mechanic trying to pressure another to push the jet back on the line and I commend the mechanic who resisted.  I don't know what happened after we left the airplane to then make him comfortable having it signed off; but I was told there would be 2 replacement flight control computers sent to this jet after I left it.  Not sure if that actually occurred.  I know we have a business to run but one of the mechanics told me at least one of the flight control computer issues was a repeat write up.  Maybe we need to give more time and attention to issues that are repeatedly written up with a common problem source.

column121: Inbound to ZZZ on ZZZZZ arrival and Level at FL330 the controller gave us descend via ZZZZZ Arrival.  FMC was Active in the Cruise page after a cruise descent earlier from FL 360 which is normal with a Top of Descent computed to start approximately 4 Miles prior to ZZZZZ to cross at or below FL320 as the VNAV is designed to do at IDLE Thrust.  We had 12;000 feet set in the MCP per normal FM 'descend via' procedures for the arrival.   Everything was set per FM procedures; light winds; Normal descent speeds.  Just prior to the Top of Descent the FMC transitioned from the Cruise page to the Descent Page and the throttles started retarding and the aircraft started descending.  Approximately 200 feet into the descent the Pitch Stagnated and shallowed and the Path indicator 'hung' and the Airspeed started bleeding off as the throttles retarded  instead of maintaining speed and descending on the path.  I saw the FMC/Autopilot was not acting correctly so I told the FO he needed to started inputting Vertical Speed down to make the restriction.   He wheeled in vertical speed and at that time the Path 'Unstuck' and dumped out showing us 400 feet high.  He wheeled in enough vertical speed to get the descent going but since the VNAV did its normal computation of TOD so close to the FIX we crossed it approximately 240 feet high as it was impossible to react fast enough to the VNAV glitch to stay on path.   The FO did everything right per the FM procedures.  So what happened here is a very common thing that I see about 20 percent of the time that should NOT be happening and started after the Planes were reconfigured to default into VNAV Speed from Path instead of honoring PATH even if it had to dive for it.  In this case a MAX.  Most of the time when it happens you are not right on top of a restriction so you have time to correct it. There is a occasional glitch in the VNAV system I believe tied to FMC software not aircraft specific that happens and I'm not sure why when the FMC transitions from Cruise Page to Descent page.  What Happens is the FMC hits top of descent and begins to retard the throttles and pitch over but for some reason the Pitch stagnates because the path incorrectly and temporarily shallows out instead of continuing to pitch over to descend and the result is the airspeed starts to bleed off.  After 5-10 seconds the FMC comes out of this Foggy zone and the path indicator then drops out to reflect where the plane should be and it Drops out of VNAV Path into VNAV Speed because when this happens the planes usually ends up 500 feet high.  When you have room to correct it you can get the plane back on PATH before hitting a restriction but in our case since it started down so close to the fix as its designed to do we did not have room to fix it.  The only thing you can do to possibly mitigate this from happening is to force the plane into the Descent page early by hitting the 'descent now' button; which is NOT Standard but not prohibited; to get it started down.  I have never seen this anomaly happen once the FMC is established in the Descent Page even when temporarily leveling off while it waits for the next TOD if an arrival has a level segment.  This is purely an issue during transition from FMC Cruise Page to Descent page and is very random as to when it happens and should be considered a known anomaly because I have seen it so many times.  Had we not been at FL330; 1000 feet above the FL320 restriction; and had we descended from a higher Altitude with more distance from the restriction we would have had time to correct the deviation in path but in this close in situation we were not.

column121: During preflight; I found an unusual wear pattern on the #3 main tire (RH inboard). Maintenance ultimately ended up issuing a deferral item for the tire; deferring replacement until later (but still flagging it for replacement).Guidance in the AOM on tire wear is unclear whether the plies are body plies or tread reinforcement plies. If they are body plies; maintenance managed to convince us to depart with an aircraft that; per the AOM guidance; had an unserviceable tire.Example photos or a more detailed diagram might provide more clarity. And while tires are expensive and the Max has indeed had a number of high-profile 'issues'; if a tire is unserviceable per our own guidance; it should be replaced; whether this is a 'known issue' or not.

column121: While in cruise flight; approximately 40NM south of ATL; we were given clearance by Atlanta Center to climb from our present assigned altitude; FL370 to FL380. Within a few seconds of initiating a climb; we received a TCAS alert for 'Traffic'. I immediately noticed an aircraft (a large amber TCAS image on the ND (Navigational Display)) at our same altitude '00'; opposite direction. I increased the rate of climb by electing CON (Max Continuous Thrust) on the N1 page of the FMC.Literally seconds later; we received an RA to 'CLIMB'. I immediately disconnected the auto-pilot and manually advanced the power to rapidly climb out of the red displayed warning area on my PFD (Primary Flight Display). At approximately FL380; the TCAS system said to 'Level Off'. At this point I was at 38100 ft. Moments later we received the aural 'Clear of conflict'. Still hand flying; I lowered the nose and descended 100 ft. back to our assigned altitude of FL380. We had just come from an area of weather over Florida and more weather was ahead beyond Atlanta.The radar was on; and I was on a 160 NM scale. In a busy area like ATL; I recalled seeing numerous aircraft on TCAS which was normal and gave no reason for concern. After the event; both of us (Us & Company) advised ATC we received an RA. The Company pilot asked ATC 'what happened back there?'. The controller replied in a broken sounding voice something like: 'I climbed them too late…'. Looking forward; I never saw the oncoming aircraft.My FO (First Officer) said the Company jet passed beneath us from the right side at a slight angle. The last TCAS altitude I recall seeing as we passed was '-02'. Perhaps; I expected that ATC would keep us safely separated at cruise altitude. At the end of the day; TCAS prevented a catastrophic event! No suggestion. I would not have responded any differently than I did.
column123: We were flying at FL370 talking to ATL Center approximately 40NM south of ATL VOR at the time of the event. ATL center gave us clearance to climb to FL380. As we got the clearance; we got a TCAS Traffic Advisory. I reached up to zoom in my ND (Navigational Display). I saw the Yellow Square and 00" next to it. During this time; the Captain had set the new altitude; and pushed the ALT intervene button. I said to the captain; 'We are going to get an RA; get ready'. As soon as I said that; we got the RA and instructions to climb. The Captain promptly disconnected the Auto Pilot and pushed the throttles up to comply with the TCAS Climb command. I saw traffic under us under the left wing. AT FL381 we got the TCAS level off command; then a few seconds later Clear of Conflict. We returned to our assigned altitude of FL380. Company later asked ATC what the reason was for getting that TCAS. The ATL controller admitted fault and said they climbed us late. The causal factor was lapse of attention regarding two aircraft nose to nose at same altitude. ATC issued a turn to avoid traffic rather than slow to happen climb instructions. ATC having more awareness in regards to aircraft in their sector that are at the same altitude."

column121: Halfway through our flight; our B-Flight Attendant asked to come into the flight deck and talk with us.  When she got to the flight deck she indicated that there was a very strong cleaning/bug spray smell in the aft galley.  And; our C-Flight Attendant was complaining of coughing and a hard time taking a deep breath because of the strong cleaning smell.  Our A-Flight Attendant didn't smell anything.  No passengers were indicating concern and; we didn't smell anything.  I informed the Flight Attendant (FA) if she was medically concerned we would patch through to medic so she could communicate her concern.  All the FAs indicated they were feeling OK and did not want to contact medic.  They just wanted someone to look at the aircraft in ZZZ2.  At that point I told her we would put the packs to high to help eliminate the strong cleaning odor.  We contacted Dispatch through ACARS to discuss the situation and see if there was an anti-microbial spray completed the night before.  Also; to inform Dispatch that they were not comfortable taking the aircraft on our next leg.  Dispatch wanted a patch through ARINC. We agreed on a patch to medic. During their discussion; Dispatch sent us an ACARS to divert to ZZZ1.  The First Officer (FO) notified ATC of our intention to divert. I notified the FAs and passengers of our intent; as well. As a precaution we accomplished the Smoke; Fire; or Fumes QRC and referenced QRH Smoke; Fire or Fumes Checklist in case the situation escalated.  Dispatch notified us the aircraft had been sprayed the night before. We communicated with our A-Flight Attendant on what to expect on landing; taxi; and at the gate.We kept in constant communication with the A-FA to constantly reassess our situation.  On our descent into ZZZ1; medic recommended the two Flight Attendants in question use the portable oxygen.  With that information I notified ATC.  We then accomplished all appropriate checklists and landed uneventfully.

column121: Another Airline's Pick up truck on ground vehicle roadway behind parked aircraft; operating at a fast velocity westbound; did not slow down or stop while I was taxing in to gate X. After I stopped the aircraft while in a 90 degree right turn; the driver of the pick up finally looked up and saw us. He then stopped the pick up but too far in to our wing's path for me to continue. Eventually he finally backed up his truck; after other people on the ground had to tell him we couldn't move until he backed up. Had I not stopped; there is a 95%+ probability he would have impacted the aircraft.Most vehicle operators at ZZZ do not comply with the basic rule that aircraft have the right away; PERIOD! This was yet another scenario of many where drivers on the ramp have cut me off and/or almost have impacted our aircraft. At ZZZ; unlike all the other airports I have operated out of over the last 30 years; it is the norm to be cut off and/or almost impacted by every type of ground vehicle; except for the fire and rescue vehicles. Quite frankly; the leaders of airport safety at ZZZ seem to find the blatant disregard for ground vehicle adherence to safety procedures as acceptable. No apologies; after the hundreds of operations I've performed parking at ZZZ gates; it is apparent that there is a serious lack of safety concern on the ramp.Better initial and continuing education and testing for all ramp personnel and ground vehicle operators. Daily observation and audits of random gate parking operations by teams of knowledgeable personnel with the authority to correct the problems. Positive incentives to follow strict safety procedures as well as writing citations to drivers for gross violations. Integrated in to this enforcement it is highly recommended to also audit and enforce strict ramp preparation after aircraft depart and before aircraft arrive to park so that the safe zone is clear of all objects AND personnel. There is no reason cones; air hoses; tow bars; etc should be within the red lines. In addition; all ground personnel should be aware of how Docking Guidance System (DGS) works and know when to pick up the wands and guide us in until the aircraft is parked. Too often; the guideman spend 50% of the time looking at the DGS so when he thinks its ok; to hand us off to the DGS with less than 75 feet to go. We don't know if the DGS is lined up properly or calibrated correctly by this time. Ive had a DGS try to get me to turn off the line in to the jet bridge because it wasn't calibrated properly from the beginning. After 10 years on this aircraft as a captain calling in these problems and writing a few reports and not seeing improvement; I am hoping these last 2 incidents and filing  reports will hopefully jumpstart a plan to get ZZZ in compliance. If all the other airports we operate in and out of can comply; I believe ZZZ can do it.

column121: During push back; the tug driver informed me that the tow bar shear pin had broken.  This had occurred in a benign and gentle manner; without any perceivable noise or vibration on the flight deck; or abnormal movement of the aircraft.   I set the parking brake and called ZZZ line maintenance.  I explained the situation; and asked if this required an inspection or logbook entry (we were on a MAX) and was told 'no' on both counts.  My first officer looked up 'tow bar breakage' in the FOM; and read to me the section that states 'an info only write up shall be made and the flight may continue as long as no aircraft damage is suspected'.  Unfortunately; that paragraph applies to the 737-NG; but not the MAX.  The aircraft should have been inspected; a discrepancy written up in the logbook; and subsequently signed off.Maybe a reminder in the form of a bulletin; for both pilots and mechanics; or a brief mention in the next quarterly CBT (Computer Based Training) to emphasize the difference in policy for the MAX.

Several hours later and done with my flying; I found the current and up to date taxiway diagram on the FAA NOS website. I downloaded the taxi chart and reviewed it. The NOS FAA chart just like the Jeppesen chart did not show an E2 nor E taxiway. I am confused why a taxiway was commissioned before it was released in charting. I did ask the Tower Controller; who was also controlling Ground; how long the E2 and E taxiway has been commissioned. And if I recall correctly; He said for 2 weeks. I would assume this is adequate time to get updated info to pilots who operate on the field. I also referenced LGB NOTAMS and there was nothing about E2 nor E. Make sure charts are available to pilots that are up to date. When a new taxiway is commissioned it should be charted or NOTAMed.

column121: We brought the aircraft in from ZZZ1 arriving at gate in ZZZ at XA:34 local. The flight from ZZZ1 was uneventful. Arriving at gate ramp personnel hooked up ground electric as well as ground air. The APU was shut down after both were connected. Approximately 15 minutes to departure I turned the APU back on. Once on line and available I deselected ground electric. Once the ground crew disconnected both ground electric and air I selected the APU bleed on. Within 30 secs of the APU bleed being selected on I noticed the odor of dirty socks indicating the presence of neurotoxic tricresyl phosphates emanating from the ventilation system. I quickly turned off the APU bleed and asked the First Officer if he noticed the smell as well; however he was unsure. I then proceeded to turn the bleed on one more time to confirm we smelled it and immediately after turning the APU bleed on the odor was back. Again I then selected the APU bleed off. We then asked operations for ground air and electric to be placed back on the aircraft while we called Maintenance Control. We also had the passengers deplane. Maintenance Control had contract maintenance come out and after conferring with Maintenance Control; Airbus Fleet Management; and [name] in the Chief Pilots Office we performed an engine run-up with contract maintenance onboard. We used a ground air cart to perform ground air start; bypassing the APU. Once the pack systems were turned on using the engine bleeds the odor was back; however at a much lighter presence. The bleeds and packs were quickly selected off and we began to shutdown and secure the aircraft. The airplane was taken out of service. Company Maintenance came in from ZZZ2 overnight and confirmed a significant oil leak from the APU. [The cause was an] APU oil leak.

column121: After a long duty day because of weather delays we finished our four day trip by taxiing into our gate in ZZZ. The ground crew guided us in to the spot and shut down the engines. When the gate agent tried to pull the bridge up to the aircraft she realized the aircraft had been stopped at the wrong spot. We were told we needed to move the aircraft a few inches forward. I made a PA and told passengers that we would have to move forward but missed mentioning to take a seat. We were told by the ground crew to release the brakes so the tug could capture the nose gear.  Because of the confusion between ground crews; gate agent driving the bridge; and us we did not realized the bridge was very close to the aircraft. At the same time the ground crew had not securely captured the aircraft and the aircraft rolled forward about two feet. We were taken by surprise as we were not expecting to move forward. As the aircraft moved forward and immediately set the parking brake but the aircraft had moved about two feet while being close to the bridge and while still having some passengers standing on the aisle. After setting the parking brake the aircraft stopped and flight attendants proceeded to make sure everyone was safely seated. The ground crew then guided the gate agent to move the bridge away from the aircraft and capture the aircraft to then move it back the correct parking spot. The bridge was reconnected and everyone deplaned without any more issues. No one was hurt and there were no damages to the aircraft. The ramp supervisor apologized and explained the ground crew was new to the job.Miscommunication between ground crew; gate agent and flight crew. Inexperience and new to the job by ground crew. Fatigue and long duty day were also factors for the flight crew. Rushing to get everyone off the aircraft. Better communication and verification by flight crews when dealing with ground crews. Understanding and self assessment of alertness and fatigue conditions. Using others to coordinate better and cross check for missed items. Take the time think and assess the situation.

column123: We were doing the ILS Z Runway XX into ZZZ. Night time; good visibility; no clouds. ATC had us at 9;500 feet; turned us to intercept final outside of ZZZZZ and cleared us for the approach. The flying pilot ( first officer) immediately disconnected auto pilot and initiated climb. We were around 8;100 feet; on the glide slope; auto pilot on when this was initiated from what we could tell. We had just passed ZZZZZ (FAF; but 17 miles out). The controller mentioned they had some glide slope problems just a week or two prior; and asked us if we were ok to proceed visually. Still being over 10 miles out; runway and PAPI in site; and glide slope still showing slightly below us; we proceeded visually with reference to PAPI and GS. The problem may have been from the auto pilot intercepting the LOC and GS at the same time and possibly overshooting the GS as it sometimes does when far out and possibly exasperated by configuration changes. This all happened about 15 to 20 miles from touchdown. Or it could have been from a faulty GS signal that they have had problems with previously.

column121: When we arrived in ZZZ to start our trip we meet with the inbound crew to discuss the inbound leg and aircraft.  There was no mention from them about any odors or problems with the aircraft.  When we boarded the aircraft we were over come by a strong smell throughout the plane. Looking back it was strange the previous crew didn't mention this. It was similar to a strong carpet cleaner smell or an odor like when you clean an oven.  There was no indication of fire or smoke much less any indications of a malfunction.  We discussed the issue with the crew and found no reasons not to continue safely.  As we boarded the aircraft several passengers started to complain especially in the rear cabin about the odor.  We discussed what the cause of the smell could be and determined that it was not a safety of flight issue since we could not isolate any problems. All systems operated normally.  We agreed to continue on the short flight to ZZZ1 hoping that at altitude the fresh air would dispute any smell.  We felt that since there was smoke all around the area from west coast wild fires that could possibly be the cause.  At cruise the smell seemed to disappear in the cockpit but as we got closer to our destination the FA'S informed us that it remained in the cabin.  There was no smoke or any indications of a malfunction. They then stated that many passengers complained that they were starting to get headaches and feel bad.  We asked if there any immediate concerns and were informed there were none.  Inbound we decided to inform maintenance control that there was an odor which seemed to be coming from the gasper vents via an MRM entry so that on arrival they could trouble shoot and see if they could remove it. After landing we started the APU and received a low oil level indication.  Not sure if this contributed to the problem or not as we accepted the aircraft in ZZZ with the APU operating and had no indications of any problems at that time.  Arriving at the gate we noticed that the smell in the cockpit remained but the cabin was stronger.   We had an hour on the ground before our next flight so felt that the problem could be resolved.  After block in we meet with maintenance and he noticed the smell as well.  His feeling is it smelled like burning oil.  We had no indications at any time of an overheat or fire on any system.  I then received a call from Name our Chief Pilot to contact Name 1 in Maintenance Control for some questions. I was asked generic questions about the entire flight to help trouble shoot the problem. As I stated everything went great expect for the strong smell.  They removed the aircraft from service and we continued our trip with another aircraft.  The entire crew handled the situation professionally and with merit.  I applaud how we worked together to assist passengers needs and answer any questions or concerns they may have had.  The flight was concluded safely and professional with our [company] principles.

column121: After pushing back on the ZZZ ramp; we went to start the engines.  During the start; the Blue Hydraulic pressure gauge came up low; just to the yellow line. Then with the rising sun coming in my side window; you could clearly see the smoke (vaporized Skydrol?)  coming out of my air vent starting to fill the cockpit.  The intensity of smoke increased with time.  We opened the windows for fresh air and shut off the packs.  Approximate about 3 - 4 minutes of chemical exposure.  We wound up taxiing back to the gate and eventually shut down the engines.  I felt a little light head; a scratchy throat; and was beginning to cough.  Captain had some similar issues.   After speaking with Chief Pilot; and self-evaluating our symptoms; we were driven to the local ER to get checked out.  At the hospital; poison control was contacted; X-ray's were taken and a breathing treatment administered before being released. Exact cause for this issue is still unknown to me...but it clearly has to do with the servicing of the Blue Hydraulic system and possible failure of aircraft parts.

column121: After landing on Runway XXL at ZZZ; we cleared off the runway at Taxiway 1 and was instructed to hold short of Runway XYL. Tower subsequently cleared us to cross Runway XXL and hold short of Runway XYR.  We proceeded to taxi to satisfy the clearance.  In an attempt to try to clear Runway XYL and also hold short of Runway XYR we encroached on Runway XYR causing a go-around of an aircraft attempting to land on Runway XYR. I believe this event was caused by an impossible clearance in combination with an attempt to comply with it. In hindsight; we should have recognized earlier that the clearance was not possible to comply with and should have communicated that to Tower.
column123: Flight was uneventful through departure; enroute; ILS Runway XXL; landing and rollout on Runway XXL; ZZZ.  Weather was VMC. Told to clear right on Taxiway 1 and hold short of Runway XYL.  Executed uneventfully.   We were then quickly given clearance to 'Cross Runway XYL on Taxiway 1 and hold short of Runway XYR.'  The Captain executed that clearance to the absolute best of his ability; set the parking brake; and turned off the taxi light short of Runway XYR.  The Captain pulled up very close to Runway XYR; in order to no longer obstruct Runway XXL.  In his estimation; the nose wheel was short of the Runway XYR hold short line; and the aircraft was only on Taxiway 1; not at all on Runway XYR; but he was trying to fit a 209 foot long B777 in a very small space.In hindsight we should have said 'Unable' to the impossible clearance; but we did not see that the space available on Taxiway 1 between the runways was insufficient until we were committed to cross Runway XYL.  The aircraft was short of Runway XYR; and to the best of his estimation was clear of Runway XYL. At this point I realized we were crossed the hold short line and saw the landing aircraft on final. I spoke up and said I think we are on the active runway for the landing traffic. Seconds after I brought that up to everyone's attention; the tower then directed the small aircraft (I believe a PC-12) on extended final to Runway XYR to go around. All crew members had taxi charts open.  Solid procedures were used.  Everyone understood the clearance.  There was no confusion at all; until we crossed Runway XYL on Taxiway 1; then I noticed we had crossed Runway XYR hold short line and saw the traffic on final.  Debriefed that we should not have accepted the clearance and should have said 'Unable' to attempting to fit a B777 on Taxiway 1 between Runway XYL and Runway XYR.Attempting to do the impossible; to meet a clearance to fully cross Runway XYL and hold short of Runway XYR; to fit a B777 on Taxiway1 between Runway XYL and Runway XYR at ZZZ. Also; a misunderstanding of the controllers expectation (due to local knowledge). We should have transmitted one of two things.  Best choice would have been to transmit 'unable' to the clearance and hold our original position short of Runway XYL; even though cleared to cross.  Second; once committed to cross Runway XYL; and in observance that the task was impossible to transmit; 'We are holding short of Runway XYR; but still obstructing active Runway XYL.'  We should have done this and left more room between the nose of the aircraft and Runway XYR.  Clearly; we could have been more directive in the situation.  One suggestion would be to have Tower change the comm to transmit; 'Cleared on to Runway XYL; but hold short of Runway XYR.'  That would convey the point that they understand Runway XYL will remain obstructed.  In that case; we would have not been concerned with obstructing Runway XYL and left more room between the nose and Runway XYR.  Better still; have Tower wait until such a time as they can clear a B777 across both runways at once.

column121: Halfway through our flight our B-Flight Attendant asked to come into the flight deck and talk with us. When she got to the flight deck she indicated that there was a very strong cleaning/bug spray smell in the aft galley. Additionally; our C-Flight Attendant was complaining of coughing and having a hard time taking a deep breath because of the strong cleaning smell. Our A-Flight Attendant didn't smell anything. No Passengers were indicating concern and we didn't smell anything. The Captain asked the Flight Attendant (F/A) if she was medically concerned; and if so; we would patch through to medic so she could communicate her concern. All the F/As indicated they were feeling OK and did not want to contact medic. They just wanted someone to look at the aircraft in ZZZ. At that point the Captain told her we would put the packs to high to help eliminate the strong cleaning odor. We also contacted Dispatch through ACARS to discuss the situation and see if there was an anti-microbial spray completed the night before. Dispatch wanted a patch through ARINC to get F/As; operations and medic on the line for a conference call.  During their discussion; Dispatch sent us an ACARS message to divert to ZZZ1. The Captain notified the F/As and Passengers of our intent; as well.As a precaution we accomplished the Smoke; Fire; or Fumes QRC and referenced QRH Smoke; Fire or Fumes Checklist in case the situation escalated. Dispatch notified us the aircraft had been sprayed the night before with antimicrobial spray. We communicated with our A-Flight Attendant on what to expect on landing; taxi; and at the gate. We kept in constant communication with the A F/A to constantly reassess our situation. On our descent into ZZZ1 medic recommended the two Flight Attendants having issues breathing use the portable oxygen. With that information; we [advised] ATC to have Medical Personnel standing by. We then accomplished all appropriate checklists and landed uneventfully.The anti-microbial spray the night before was a bit much. That needs to be more regulated. I think the call to divert was a good call; but happened very fast. Our Crew day also ended up being super long with this diversion on our first leg. We were OK to continue after the diversion; but that kind of day; with what we went through; is probably not completely safe.
