column121: I began this trip with my flying First Officer (FO) starting leg 3 of his transition operating experience from the Airbus; one International Relief Officer (IRO) relatively new to the fleet and still not yet consolidated; while the other IRO was a seasoned FO on the 777 fleet.We pushed back from gate.  After the left engine start was complete we noticed a strange and unfamiliar odor that wasn't readily identifiable.  A brief discussion took place on the flight deck about the possibilities of the odor origin and all agreed it was not an electrical smell so we continued with the right engine start procedure.  Within seconds of the right engine start completion; smoke was noticeable in the cockpit along with a very strong and identifiable electrical burning odor.  We noticed flashing switch lighting on the overhead panel; specifically the window heat switches but no EICAS warnings had appeared.  Thoughts of Swiss Air flight 111 many years ago instantly entered my mind and rather than execute a lengthy non-normal procedure; I made the decision based on being on the ground that we would be better off in the long run to remove power immediately from the aircraft.  I elected to shutdown both engines at that point and have one of my IROs open the door and check in the back with the purser and check if the cabin had smoke as we were assessing whether to initiate an evacuation or not at this point.  There was a lot of ground traffic around us in all directions; both automotive and aircraft; and I was wanting information as to just how bad things were in the cabin before committing to an evacuation. XXXXXX reacted above and beyond any expectations I had and promptly reported back with the following information:Door 1R Flight Attendant (FA) had seen smoke coming from the floor area around the jumpseat as well as the seat 1L floor area.  The customer in seat X was relocated away from the smoke area.  I was told there was some smoke in the galley and forward seats but that was it and that it appeared to cease escalating and that the floor was not hot. XXXXXX had also opened up the electronics (EE) compartment door and performed a visual inspection that revealed a scorched panel with no visible fire.  He mentioned; that while the scorched panel was warm; it was not hot and felt certain that whatever had precipitated the event had stabilized and all we had was smoke at this point with electrical odor. With that firsthand information and no further comments from the FAs; I made a PA informing the customers and inflight crew of the situation; realizing there probably were flashing lights along with some smoke in the cabin we were certain there was no further reason to suspect a fire and that we would be returning by tow back into the gate.  I would later find out from the FA and Passengers through sharing of information in the boarding lounge that it was the initial PA that was responsible for de-escalating anxiety and growing concern that would later facilitate a timely and orderly deplaning of the aircraft at the gate as well as all but 2 of our original customers re-boarding the new jet. It was  XXXXXX's 'eyes on' first hand assessment along with the purser and 1R door FA assessment that the smoke had ceased to proliferate that led to de-escalating my thoughts of evacuation onto a busy tarmac and into that of a tow back to the gate and expedited deplaning.We contacted ramp and explained our situation... 'XXX on taxiway has smoke in the cockpit with all engines shut down and requested that they facilitate a tow back to the gate right away'.  The ramp agent working the frequency appeared agitated with us and told us we would need to contact Maintenance to coordinate.  I repeated with urgency; our situation as unable to taxi and needing their help with coordination... I received no answer.  XXXXXX; my other IRO assumed the responsibilities of communicating with ramp trying to facilitate help and continued to receive a comment that 'if wecould just taxi back it sure would make things a lot easier'.  I continued to make PA to let folks know our progress and what the plan was when we got to the gate.  We had shut down all fans and other electrical items such as cabin services and entertainment.  Later we would discover that the APU had actually auto-shutdown and we were on battery only.  The smoke had gotten pretty thick in the cockpit but was now beginning to subside while we were being towed back to gate.  We requested Airport Rescue Firefighting (ARFF) be standing by should things deteriorate and instructed operations to let Ramp know that we did not want any cargo doors open for fear of possibly fueling a bad situation with large amounts of fresh air.  Once at the gate; we coordinated with airport personnel that we had no electrical power to enter a log writeup  and subsequently completed the additional paperwork for Maintenance with regard to smoke.  I was able to inspect the cabin and had noticed quite a bit of smoke during the deplaning.  I would later find out from the flight attendants; that the smoke did not actually start appearing in the aft sections of the cabin until the door was opened and passengers started deplaning.  Once off the jet; I debriefed my crew using company CRM skills; spoke with and briefed Chief Pilot as well as submitted the required incident report before making my way to the next aircraft.  I met with our inflight crew at the new aircraft and spoke with each of them to thank them for their calm and professional approach to what had potential to have been a very different outcome.  Everyone assured me that [they] were fit and ready to continue with our new jet into ZZZZ.  I did speak with one FA who waited for me outside the flight planning room.  She wanted to tell me she had experienced a headache and was removing herself from the trip. I made a PA in the boarding lounge thanking everyone for remaining calm and following their crew member instructions and proceeded to offer a very high level explanation of the event while praising the highly experienced crew I had to work with who were quick to identify and de-escalate the situation allowing us to deplane orderly and continue to ZZZZ with this new jet. We were fortunate that this happened on the ground and that we had the option of simply and quickly removing the power from the aircraft.  We all felt certain that after seeing the pictures; that had this happened in flight; we would have never had time to run a multi-page procedure hoping to isolate before something unrecoverable may have occurred within the electrical system ultimately affecting a successful outcome.A few things to note after our cockpit crew debrief:Of interest is that we elected to open the cockpit windows to vent the smoke.  I suspect that because we were on the ground; no one ever mentioned the memory item of donning the O2 mask or the thought that we might exacerbate the problem by opening the windows.  We did however consider this idea as it pertained to opening the cargo doors as we were being towed back. We train 'smoke in the cockpit/cabin' in the simulator and it can become somewhat of a spring loaded evacuation solution as we don't have any outside cues from which to assess.  In real time with real visual feedback in the moment; one gets an overwhelming reality check as to just how dangerous an evacuation of 250+ people can be on a busy tarmac if there are other options.  It may pay dividends to assess the risks and current information prior to committing to an evacuation. In retrospect; after seeing the scorched panel; it is believed that the initial odor was that of burnt dust and paint before the onset of obvious electrical smoldering.  It may also be worth a precautionary discontinuance of starting with any odor that is not readily identifiable. With both engines shut down; we were surprised to later discover the APU had also auto-shutdown contributing to some confusion as we were on battery only. Moving forward; I will now add to my before pushback ritual; the review of a telephone number for operations as we all felt strongly that we spent precious minutes trying to solicit help on the radio from ramp when we could have probably made a phone call directly to Ops to help coordinate all of the services.

column121: Crew departed late due to brake accumulator issues on previous aircraft; and a potential one on this aircraft.Ground Ops were completely normal and the FO (First Officer) had no problems deploying the flaps to 3 for takeoff.Takeoff was normal and as we were turning to an assigned heading; we reached the cleanup altitude. I called for flaps 1 and noticed that the FO had some what I felt was minor difficulty bringing the flaps up to 1. This is not unusual; a hand slips; or the lever used to move the flap handle out of the detects isn't gripped correctly for easy retraction. I thought little of it.When I called for flaps UP; the raising was again delayed; and I noticed my FO reaching around with his right hand to put both hands on the flap lever to get it up. We talked about him having trouble getting them up; and I flew the aircraft only to ensure that I did not over speed the flaps. Eventually he was able to get them up which I saw on the speed tape on the PFD and I verified on the display; and flap handle position.We discussed what had happened a bit but decided to focus on safely exiting the terminal area and getting to altitude since the aircraft was now in the safe; and proper configuration. We made a plan to contact Maintenance Control at cruise and notify them of the problem and get advice about continuing the flight.After reaching altitude; the FO told me what he had encountered and explained how difficult it was to move the lever that released the flap handle from the detent to raise the flaps.A phone patch was initiated with dispatch and Maintenance Control and we discovered that our radio 2 wasn't able to receive over long distances. We ended up substituting radio 3 for radio 2 and temporarily disabling ACARS to complete the phone patch. Maintenance Control was very helpful on the phone patch and felt like he knew what the problem was. Maintenance Control was asked if he felt the aircraft should continue to ZZZZ; and he wanted it to go to a maintenance hub. As a Captain; I agreed with that thought process and asked the Dispatcher to bring in the Ops Manager so that we could all agree on a plan of action. We could have landed the aircraft at ZZZZ if there had been a flap malfunction; but the aircraft would have been stuck there quite a while.Eventually after consideration of landing lengths; the close to overweight landing weight of the aircraft; and the potential for wet runways in ZZZ1; that the best and safest place to divert the aircraft would be ZZZ1 in case the flaps would not deploy normally. Consideration was based on the worst case; flaps up scenario.Destination was changed with ATC once the plan was agreed upon by all parties and the phone patch was terminated and ACARS restored.Maintenance Control was asked via ACARS if we should leave the flaps down after landing and they asked them to retract them as much as we could.Fortunately; the landing in ZZZ1 was uneventful. The flaps deployed normally. Upon taxi-in. The flaps were retraced to position 1; where the handle binding began to be very difficult to overcome.Upon arrival at the gate; after shutdown; I tried to move the lever that releases the flap handle from the detent and found that it was impossible to move with just one hand.
column123: We were doing a flaps 3 takeoff from [Runway] XXL. After the acceleration altitude; and above flap retraction speed; the pilot flying called for flaps to 1. I noticed; while moving the lever from 3 to 1; that the flap lever was nowhere near as smooth and free moving as it usually is; rather; it was quite difficult to move. As we accelerated through flap 1 retraction speed; it took considerable effort to get the lever out of the detent. I mentioned it to the captain who quickly made sure to raise the nose and not over speed the flaps as I used both hands to get the flap lever compressed and moved to the up position. The flaps moved as expected; with no issues; the flight control page showed normal; and the hydraulic page showed normal. We continued the climb out of ZZZ; and when reaching a safe altitude; I took the controls and radios with ATC; while the captain initiated an incredibly detailed conversation with dispatch and Maintenance Control. After exhausting every bit of information we could give; and every insight Maintenance Control had; the decision was made with dispatch and everyone in planning that they were talking to; to divert to ZZZ1 instead of potentially having a flight control issue on landing in ZZZZ; on a shorter runway; at an international station; and then leaving the plane there. We didn't [request priority] but asked approach to slow down early to get the flaps out and make sure they extended. We had planned every contingency for having to go around and then [request priority] if they didn't; and were ready to run whichever QRH abnormal procedure would have applied based on where the flaps ended up. On the approach; the flaps came down just fine and a normal landing was made. After landing; we planned; with maintenance approval; to attempt to retract the flaps but to stop if they locked again and not force anything. The lever was much less stiff from flaps full to flaps 1 than earlier; but again locked at the detent there. We left the flaps at 1 into the gate; let ramp know to tell anyone they could; and had maintenance meet us there. Sounded like they were going to replace the entire flap lever section.

column121: This event was a near midair collision in ZZZZ. On Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZZ. The new heading of 090 ended up sending us directly for another aircraft at same altitude. TCAS began with a TA then an RA. At same time controller frantically gave us a new vector. After properly executing the resolution advisory; we narrowly missed the conflict aircraft and proceeded back to ZZZZZ1 and did the RNP to Runway YY for normal landing. We never saw the conflict aircraft however they did have us in sight; and I don't recall who the conflict aircraft was. There were two jets in holding. We think the controller got our call sign confused with someone else for the 090 vector. English as a second language may have been a factor in this event. Both the F/O (First Officer) and myself remember hearing our call sign in the 090 vector. In the end it was TCAS that saved the day.

column121: I have not taken the COVID vaccine.  Because of this; I expect to lose my job in XX days or less.  I flew a scheduled trip; ZZZ to ZZZZ; on Date 1 and returned Date 2.  I am new to the [aircraft type] fleet and have XX total hours on type with XY hours towards my hours required for consolidation.In training; I was taught the importance of discussing threats before a trip with the other pilots.  My dilemma was deciding whether to tell the other pilots that I am distracted because of my upcoming termination or not to tell them.  I decided not to tell them because; having never met them before; I was concerned that this information might be perceived by them as anything from a minor annoyance with me to a possible outrage.  Prior to both flights; I addressed all my concerns and considered myself fit for duty.  Although I just recently completed training on the [aircraft type]; I am proficient in my skills.  I was convinced that should any non-normal situation occur I would be competent and able to properly perform my duties.  What I did not expect to encounter was the anxiety and inner conflict I experienced once airborne.After the flight; I was unable to go to dinner with the other pilots on the overnight because I do not have a vaccine card which is required in Country.  I felt uneasy about giving a vague reason for declining the invitation because I was uncertain about revealing the truth about my vaccination status.  While in ZZZZ; I thought about the inner-conflict that I am experiencing; anxiety about losing my job; and concern over possible discrimination by other pilots and/or cabin crew members should they become aware of my vaccination status. I was pilot flying on the return leg to ZZZ and I found it more difficult to concentrate on simple tasks especially since I am new to the aircraft.  I was also unable to sleep during my rest break and unable to eat very much due to the heightened anxiety I was experiencing.  My landing at ZZZ airport was not as good as I had hoped.  The inner tension was compounded by my uncertainty as to whether I should have confessed my vaccination status to the other pilots and what would happen to me if I made a mistake and they found out later that I did not tell them.The unexpected level of anxiety never reached a point that I would consider dangerous; but the possibility of increased errors was apparent to me.  The conflict that I experienced because I did not reveal my vaccination status at the onset of the trip was an unnecessary distraction imposed on me by the company.  In addition; I did not want to introduce an issue to the other pilots that could cause a hostile work environment.  At the end of the flight; at the gate in ZZZ; I told the other pilots that I was unvaccinated and would be losing my job soon.  I could sense their concern and as they are both true professionals; they seemed empathetic with my plight.I have not yet determined the best way to deal with my predicament and since there is no guidance from my union or the company; I will probably conceal my vaccination status on my next trip.  I would hope that there would not be any hostility directed towards me if I revealed my status at the beginning of my next trip; but considering the contentiousness of the situation I am unsure.  I believe that my training and prior experience make it easier for me to deal with these types of distractions than others.  I am very concerned for those who may be unable to effectively manage their personal problems caused by the vaccine mandate.I believe that the company's vaccine mandate has created a potentially dangerous work environment that could impact safe operations.  The divisiveness caused by the vaccine issue; the unknown side effects for those already vaccinated and the prospect of impending job terminations have culminated and become; in my opinion; an inherent risk to aviation safety.

After running the QRH and as a crew we elected to continue to ZZZZ. After planning to configure early to see if our problem would manifest into a failure we did indeed have a total HYD 1 FAIL level 2. We [requested priority handling] with ZZZZ Approach asked to continue on our current heading for 5-10 minutes and we would get back with them after we accomplished our checklists. We were given Runway XXR as an option; given that this runway was the longest we elected to utilize this option. We ran the QRH procedure and discussed potential threats and issues. Given that our nose wheel steering would be limited to the left we elected to stop on the runway and request to be towed in via a tug. We informed ZZZZ Approach of this issue and let them know souls on board and approximately how much fuel we had remaining. After being handed off to ZZZZ Tower I once again reminded them we were not going to be able to clear the runway due to our failed condition. I thought this might be important because of the restricted visibility and poor runway conditions so no one would commence a takeoff or an approach with our airplane parked on an active runway. Tower understood clearly our intentions there was no miscommunication. Our approach was normal and normal procedures were utilized in the event. The airplane performed exactly as we anticipated. After engine cool down; assuring the brakes we not too hot and we started the APU we let Tower know our engines were shut down and the aircraft was safe to approach with our company tug. As Company Maintenance personnel entered through the FWD avionics compartment and communicated with Company ground personnel via his handheld radio and would sit in the CA (Captain)'s seat while in control of the aircraft's brakes. I continued to perform Pilot Monitoring duties to obtain a taxi clearance and monitored the aircraft until we set the parking brake at Gate XX. The event overall was a well orchestrated event; [the] Captain showed excellent leadership; CRM and cockpit management skills. [The] Captain reacted calmly and confidently as I backed him up during the process. I posed questions and [a] hypothetical to ensure we had all of our bases covered and [the] Captain was very respective the few I had to offer. [The] Captain demonstrated by example exactly how a captain should react and respond to a potential dangerous situation. I would also like to note that ZZZZ Approach and Tower performed above expectations despite a slight language barrier we all had an understanding of what we needed and they were able to provide that with ease. Lastly ZZZZ Company Operations performed flawlessly we couldn't have asked for anything more. After landing in ZZZZ; Maintenance personnel identified the issue right away it was stated it was an 'auto brake controller'; that caused the #1 HYD system to leak all of its fluid and fail. I have not followed up to see if this indeed was the case after maintenance completed its final inspection and repair.

column121: While parked at spot XX on the ramp at ZZZ we were cleared to start the engines. After starting the left engine we noticed a strange smell. There were 4 crew members on the flight deck so we discussed the situation. After asking the Lead Flight Attendant if they could smell anything strange; to which they could not; we thought it could be something from the outside being sucked into the ventilation system. We decided to start the right engine and see if things cleared up. After a normal start we heard a grinding/thumping sound (hard to tell exactly; but definitely not normal). We immediately shut both engines down only to find out that the APU  had also shut down. The plane was now dark. I tried to restart the APU only to find out that nothing worked. One of the Relief pilots went down into the amp bay to see if he could find the source of the smell and now smoke. The smoke was not very thick so we had no reason to think there was a threat of fire. The FO found that a box had shorted out and burned several wire bundles. There was no further evidence of a fire so the Captain decided to have the plane towed back to the gate and the passengers removed. I included 2 threats for Flight Attendant and crew communication because after the incident we had no PA  system to communicate with the flight attendants in case an evacuation was needed. This would have slowed down the process.
column123: After push back and disconnect from the tug; the left (#1) engine was started. Upon commencement of the right (#2) engine start a very faint electrical odor was sensed. We deemed it prudent to call door 1 to inquire if the flight attendants also noticed any smell or smoke; to which they responded negative. as the right engine became stabilized after start the smell became worse and a shuddering or thumping sound was heard. No flight deck warnings occurred but there appeared to be some electrical malfunctions on the overhead panel (window heat lights flicking on and off). We decided as a crew that shutting down both engines promptly was the best move; to remediate the situation as quickly as possible. After both engines shut down; the APU failed leaving us with battery power only. At this time we noticed a small amount of smoke in the cockpit; but decided it was not dangerous enough to issue an emergency evacuation of the aircraft. The second Relief Pilot went into the cabin and stated there was smoke there as well; and he could see what appeared to be a burn mark in the amp compartment. With only one operable radio we had to switch between communication with Ramp Tower and Operations. This caused some confusion as to who we should be talking to; in order to get an expeditious return to the gate. The Ramp Tower controller did not seem to think the situation was urgent and this may have led to a delay in having a tug and ground crew called to return us to the gate. Flight attendants and passengers were briefed and there were no adverse events in the cabin. We returned to the departure gate uneventfully. Fire and police were called to be on hand and inspect the aircraft. Upon parking an exterior walk around was performed and no exterior damage noted.

column121: Received vector for initially an ILS to Runway 8R.  Intercepted LOC just outside JELLI at 5;000 feet.  Upon interception; glideslope captured aircraft autopilot began a 'substantial' descent (1;500 feet/min).  At first I didn't think anything about it. Shortly after; we were cleared a visual approach.  We were fully configured before MATON; and passing MATON I felt low on the approach; it was too shallow and looked wrong; and then I noticed our altitude was 1;200 feet MSL (1;100 feet AGL) when it should have been about 2;000 feet MSL.  Flight Director still showed us on glide path.  I immediately called out we were 800 feet low for some reason.  Suspecting an instrument issue; I disconnected the autopilot; turned off the flight director; and began hand flying.  We had been cleared a visual shortly after LOC capture and were visual; so I completed the final segment flying purely visually.  I even took the precaution of having the First Officer deselect the ILS in the nav radio tuners.  At approximately 1 mile from the runway threshold; I noticed 2 aircraft holding short on the north side of the approach end of 8R waiting clearance to cross.  A B737 was holding short on Taxiway NE; and a E-170 was holding short at NR.  It appeared those aircraft were causing interference of the glideslope signal resulting in the indications we were receiving on our instruments.  Our manual recommends backing up a visual approach with the ILS; when available.  However; good airmanship and situational awareness must always be maintained. An additional item: ATC gave us no call about our low altitude on the approach.  I couldn't find it above anywhere on this form; but I could also consider this an incident which was successfully recognized and resolved in time with no incident. I have seen aircraft waiting to cross untold number of times; but never have I seen glideslope interference such as I saw during this approach.

We took off; were in cruise; and were past the CP (Critical Point) - [middle of the flight] - when we set up for the first bathroom break. I went out first and I asked [the] First Class Flight Attendant (FA); 'If everything is all right back here.' They responded; 'Yes.' I went to the bathroom; came back up to the cockpit; and was talking to the Purser who also said everything was 'fine' as well. When the First Officer (FO) came back he then informed me that [the] FA informed him that when I had to brake to not hit the truck; she hit her right side against the forward galley wall with some of the quarter turn edging. I then called back and asked if she needed medical help in ZZZ1. She replied that she was icing it and took Tylenol and she would not need medical attention in ZZZ1." I asked the other FAs if they were all right; one stated that they didn't even feel the braking action and two others stated they felt it as they were standing but everyone else was fine. To be clear; the first time I was told something was wrong was past the CP. Before departure I briefed the FAs that if there is anything wrong or abnormal; even if we are in sterile cockpit; do not hesitate to call up and let us know. Also; during the flight; no calls to see if [there were] medical personnel on board to help with an injury were made by the FA crew.Prior to the top of descent when we set up for another bathroom break; the Purser came in and I asked him how [the] FA was doing. He said; 'She seems fine; she wants to go home; she's just a little sore.' When I went out; I asked how she was doing. She stated; 'She wanted to call in enroute injured; but then wanted to deadhead home.' I told her; 'I don't know that they will be able to deadhead her home; but if she is enroute injured please let me know and I will contact Dispatch.' She then said she was 'enroute injured.' I said; 'Do you want medical treatment in ZZZ1.' She said; 'No.'I then texted Dispatch that we had an FA who was enroute injured and would call them when we landed per the reporting requirements. I also requested priority handling and asked the paramedics to meet the aircraft to evaluate her; just to be safe. We landed without incident. When the paramedics came on board; [the] FA refused additional medical care from them and stated to the FO; 'Why did you call them out; you didn't need to do that.' Appropriate reports were made per the manual to the Dispatcher [and others]."
column123: During our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1; most of which was uneventful; we had a minor injury on taxi out of our galley Flight Attendant (FA); but we were not notified until after the CP (Critical Point); [middle of the flight]. As we came to a stop at the XX XY intersection; we at the time were more concerned about the truck that did not stop; and believed that we did not stop too abruptly for the truck but just more startled that it did not stop. Hindsight; we did not hear any clunking or hitting - and although we stopped slightly faster than normal; we did not realize that [the] FA may have been knocked off balance a little bit. We did make a call to Ground to let them know that the truck did not stop but we quickly continued our taxi not thinking too much of the incident. While the initial incident where [the] FA hit her arm may not have been that bad; it sounded like it got worse as we flew with some aching and building pain; so she let the flight crew; us; know about her sore arm and sore neck.As the flight continued; we reached radio/ACARS reception into ZZZ1 when [the] FA decided that the pain was too much and she was in flight injured and would not be able to work the return flight leg from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. As I continued to fly; the Captain (CA) coordinated with Dispatch and attempted to call ZZZ1 Operations to let them know the situation. After the CA was given all the information and was notified that she was incapacitated and unable to work the return flight; the decision was made to request priority handling [and] have paramedics meet us at the gate when we arrived to check on [the] FA.At top of descent the decision was made by [the] FA that her arm was hurt too much and after coordination with [the] FA; Dispatch; and calling Operations; we were approximately over ZZZ2 and the CA decided to request priority handling as a precaution due to an incapacitated crew member and in the best interest of the crew member's health. column121: We almost slid off a taxiway.  After landing [Runway] 27R in rain; we were cleared on C1 and proceeded southbound on Z.  At the first right turn; I heard the Captain say; 'Oh [no]' and looked up to see us slowly sliding straight for the edge lights as my CA heroically held full right tiller and popped the reverse.  We also heard a loud; sustained grinding noise from the nose wheel as we slid across its tread.  The taxiway was noticeably wet with relatively new (slick) paint markings; plus we were operating a MAX that carries extra energy while taxiing.  We informed ATC of our issue as we were able to return the airplane to the centerline.  We continued to the gate after checking with our FA and PAX (all were well).  Upon parking; my CA went outside and was able to verify that no contact was made with any lights or grass; and the airplane was undamaged.  Flight concluded uneventfully.We were vigilant regarding the weather and ready for unexpected things while flying; but our attention became divided on the ground and our senses softened.  Plus; Runway 27R is not a typically assigned runway.  Normally; a slow taxi in wet conditions; as ours was; is sufficient to keep things safe.  But in this case even that was not enough.  Additionally; we are relatively low time in the MAX (CA w X legs; FO w XXhrs); so while expecting things to be different it may also be true that our reflexes were simply not mature.We later learned from a local ORD based pilot that this corner is notorious for being very slick when wet; given the nature of the pavement; paint; and its downhill gradient.  This was news to us and would make an EXCELLENT addition to the company pages!!
column123: After clearing the Runway 27R at C1 we proceeded on to taxiway Z. At the first right turn on taxiway Z; I proceeded to make the right turn to follow the taxiway centerline but the aircraft would not turn. The nose wheel began to slide. The taxiway was wet at the time. We were in a 737 MAX at idle thrust and riding the brakes. The taxi speed was between 8 and 10 knots. I managed to keep the aircraft on the taxiway with aggressive braking. The taxiway was wet and with the strong residual thrust the aircraft nose wheel could not get enough grip on the painted surface of the centerline. It also seemed like the aircraft was tail heavy and that might have reduced the weight on the nose wheel.Go even slower when taxiing the 737 MAX with wet surface conditions.

column121: I was acting as Pilot Monitoring on Aircraft X enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We were climbing through FL270 just west of ZZZ2 when [the] Captain selected the cowl anti-ice switches to on position in response to a layer of clouds we were about to climb through. Within a few seconds of him selecting the cowl anti-ice; I noticed immediately that there was a loss of information on the Captain's side PFD (Primary Flight Display). The Captain had lost his white FMS course needle; a red RA flag appeared below the altitude tape; and on both PFD's; FMS1 in the FMA (which at the time was the active mode) had a red line through it. I called out this issue to the Captain; and he analyzed the situation to attempt to identify what information he had lost; which functionalities he still had; and which QRH checklist could be run to solve the issue. I do not recall what the active lateral mode in the FMA turned to after the Captain's side navigation information disappeared; but in troubleshooting; the Captain decided to transfer control of the aircraft over to me; as my navigation instruments were still working. We managed to arm and capture FMS2 on my side and continue flying the assigned route. We were still climbing in VS mode; now through FL280. I noticed that several functions of the FCP (Flight Control Panel) were now unavailable; including the SPD knob; and VS wheel; rendering it impossible to use any vertical mode of the autopilot. I informed the Captain that these issues may affect our ability to enter RVSM airspace; to which he agreed and informed ATC as such. ATC assigned us to descend now to maintain FL270. Unable to use any vertical modes of the autopilot; I had to disconnect the autopilot and hand fly down to FL270. I was still able to set an altitude in the altitude selector; so upon reaching FL270 I was able to reconnect the autopilot; which held altitude without issue.Meanwhile; the Captain continued to troubleshoot; looking through the QRH for what the issue might have been; and what checklist to run. He also notified the company of what components we had lost and called the flight attendants to tell them not to start any new service. At this point; ATC was aware of the situation; and an emergency had not been declared as; at the time; safe operation of the aircraft was not in question. As we were unable to identify what was causing the many failures; the Captain began suggesting a diversion to ZZZ2; which at this point we were only 25 miles east of. He began talking with ZZZ2 Maintenance and Dispatch over the radio to attempt to identify the problem and find the appropriate QRH checklist. After consulting Maintenance and Dispatch; together they were unable to identify the appropriate QRH checklist to run. The Captain and I discussed the possibility of a diversion. Given the descent and approach would need to be hand-flown on raw data (since the autopilot and flight director were rendered unusable beyond flying straight and level); all navigation information as well as RA on the Captain's side was unavailable; and there was inclement weather at ZZZ1 due to the approaching hurricane; we made the decision to divert to ZZZ2 (which at the time was VFR). Dispatch was made aware of the decision and notified ZZZ2 Ops; and told us they were prepared for our arrival into ZZZ2. We notified ATC of the decision to divert; and ATC began giving us radar vectors to ZZZ2. An emergency was still not declared as the Captain and I were still able to safely operate the aircraft in VMC and good weather conditions; and priority handling was not necessary; and ZZZ2 was not busy.Given that navigation information was only available on my side; I hand flew the rest of the flight while the captain made appropriate announcements; collected required information for landing; and set up the aircraft. We conducted a visual approach backed up by the ILS to Runway XXL at ZZZ2. The entire descent and landing was hand flown; as vertical modes were unavailable;including the ability to capture a glideslope. I was able to receive vertical and lateral information from the ILS; but the Captain's side was not; so he had to revert to cross-side information for the approach. His RA was also unavailable; so he had to make his call outs based on the information on my PFD. A normal; stable approach was conducted to a safe landing. We parked at Gate X. Maintenance came on board; and after a quick diagnostic; determined that the airplane would need to be hangared for further investigation. The passengers were deplaned and moved to a different aircraft. The cause of this event was maintenance-related. An unidentified failure occurred that resulted in a loss of multiple sources of navigation information and autopilot functions. Events like these can't always be prevented. I believe my training well prepared me for the outcomes of this event; and allowed me to return the aircraft to the ground safely.

column121: I was the Pilot Flying. The weather in ZZZ was deteriorating quickly. Thunderstorms; heavy rain and wind were moving towards the airport. On downwind we could see the airport through the spotty rain showers and were number 3 for the RNAV XX approach. The previous two aircraft reported light turbulence; heavy rain; negative windshear; and they broke out right at minimums. The weather radar depicted a large cell just to the south of the airport moving in quickly and one at the very end of the runway moving towards the airport. Lightning was also depicted on the weather radar. We broke out right at minimums with heavy rain on short final however the runway was visible and I continued with the remainder of the approach visually. At about 300 ft. I encountered a wind gust that caused the aircraft to go above the VASI glidepath slightly. I recovered by lowering the nose of the aircraft and also being cognizant of the increase descent rate that would occur. Even though there was heavy rain; the runway was still visible. With the heavy rain and wipers on max rate; it was difficult to hear anything else. My First Officer informed me that he heard an alert through the aircraft speakers that sounded like 'Don't Sink' but it could have been 'Sink Rate.' He wasn't sure. I glanced at the VSI and it was indicating about a 1;200 fpm descent rate. Speed was about 10 kts. Fast. I arrested our descent rate and got back on the VASI glidepath. I removed my headset from my ear to hear any further aural warnings. At about 100 ft. with a VSI of 850 FPM I also heard 'Don't Sink' in conjunction with the 100 ft. aural call. The descent rate had been stabilized and it was evident that a safe landing could be made within the Touchdown Zone. We were both quite certain there was no question that a safe landing could be made and also; if we initiated a go-around we would have gone directly into the thunderstorm at the end of the runway. I decided that the safest course of action at that given time was to land. I elected to land the aircraft rather than follow the Company requirement of initiating a go-around when a 'Don't Sink' Alert was received. The landing was uneventful. We touched down in the Landing Zone as briefed. Deceleration was smooth and as we were taxiing towards the gate the ensuing thunderstorms enveloped the field but the wait for our gate was not that long. We arrived at the gate a bit behind schedule. Company policy is quite clear on what is expected and required when encountering this; or any other EGPWS Alerts. I think our situation was a little precarious due to the weather; heavy rain; wipers and also a lack of direct communication as to what was heard. A prevention in this situation would be to not be in this situation. Hold; wait out the storm. Divert as necessary. Company aircraft send Aural Warnings through the speakers. There are some aircraft where the speaker volume is not that loud. Better planning and briefing would also be a factor in preventing this from happening.
column123: I was Pilot Monitoring during RNAV XX Approach to ZZZ. Last weather report from tower was 10 miles visibility and winds 150 degrees at 23 kts. gusting to 28 kts. with no reported wind shear however it was evident visually as well as on radar that a thunderstorm was rapidly approaching the field from the south.  Because of this we were vectored north of the field and cleared the approach. We discussed the published missed approach would take us toward the incoming storm and how to mitigate the risk if we had to go missed approach. At the DA; the runway was in sight (despite a quick to develop rain shower between the FAF and DA) and would remain so throughout the landing; thus we continued the approach. However; on the descent from the DA; the gusty conditions resulted in the aircraft being above glideslope and in an effort to correct glidepath; the aural 'Sink Rate' sounded on short final; followed by a sink rate call from me. The PF (Pilot Flying) made appropriate corrections; maintaining a stable airspeed despite the gusty conditions; and landed in the Touchdown Zone without incident. The post flight report noted a max sink rate of 1;215 fpm. Although the sink rate aural caution sounded; I feel the safest action was to continue the landing considering the runway remained in sight from the DA to touchdown; airspeed remained stable and a go-around would result in flying the aircraft toward the fast moving thunderstorm enveloping the airfield.

column121: While cruising at FL410 west of DEN [airport]; the Captain and I were analyzing a severe thunderstorm complex on our route of flight over NE. Our route of flight was DBL-HCT (Hayes Center)-OVR-BDF. I referenced my JeppPro app and suggested a route to the south; via HYS (Hays)-BDF. The Captain verified the routing with the dispatcher who agreed with the plan. The Captain then radioed Denver Center and requested the weather reroute by asking for 'direct Hayes Center direct Bradford'. I saw that on my JeppPro chart the VOR we wanted to fly to was 'Hayes'; but I knew I often heard 'Hayes Center' referred to on the radio so I thought to myself it was a colloquial reference to the same fix. When the Controller asked for us to repeat the request; I reminded the Captain 'Hays' but he repeated 'Hayes Center'; and I didn't speak up more forcefully again thinking it wasn't quite correct but it was colloquial reference to the same fix. I entered HYS into the FMS; verified it with the Captain and executed the turn; approximately 10 degrees right. A few minutes later we were issued a frequency change to a new Denver Center Controller who answered our check-in with; 'it looks like you're on a shortcut.' The Captain explained that we had received a new clearance due to weather from the previous Controller and said that we were 'direct hotel-yankee-sierra direct bravo-delta-foxtrot.' The Controller said something like 'I'll make sure that's updated for you' and that was the end of the discussion. At that point the Captain and I went back and reconstructed why the Controller seemed unaware of our routing and at that point I realized the Hayes vs. Hayes Center confusion - that there are two frequently-used NAVAIDs in close geographic proximity with extremely similar names.

Immediately; my PFD red flagged the following; RA; FMS1; flight director and lost my bearing pointer; I took a second to evaluate the situation and quickly realized we were going into RVSM so I notified ATC that we had lost instruments and we needed to descend which we did. We transferred controls on the FCP to the FO (First Officer) side and quickly realized we had lost all pitch modes and the vertical speed wheel. I started to look for possible failures in the QRH that may help explain what we lost and a solution with no success. I decided ZZZ3 was a good diversion airport but still was trying to figure out the problem so we slowed down. After some time looking through the QRH and trouble shooting the FCP I decided it wouldn't be safe to continue to ZZZ2 and into hurricane conditions with the instrument failures we had so I called for the diversion to ZZZ3. We were VMC the whole time so I didn't feel the need to declare an emergency. I notified the FAs (Flight Attendants) about our situation and assured them they were safe and this wasn't an emergency. I made a brief announcement to the passengers that we were diverting for loss of some of our instrumentation. We successfully landed in ZZZ3 called maintenance and did an aircraft swap. I made a passenger announcement both on the plane after landing and at the gate explaining what happened and what they could expect as well as made myself available at the new gate for questions in case anyone needed reassurance. After the plane swap we continued into ZZZ2 without incident.Unknown. Multiple equipment failures. Possible QRH for FCP failures.

column121: When we arrived at Aircraft X at spot XX; the APU was running and the other crew was deplaning. My crew; boarded the plane at gate and started to do our preflight inspections to get the flight ready. While I was doing my originating flow; the APU auto shutdown and only displayed a 'fail' light. I grabbed the E&A [Engine & APU] and ran the checklist; which only asked if there were any other lights illuminated. The answer was no so the checklist was complete. At this point it started to get warm on the plane; and we were just starting to board our specials. I allowed the APU to stay off for a few minutes; and then opted to turn the APU on again since there were no other indications of an issue. I started the APU again and it started fine; and the generator also came online fine. When I pressed the bleed air switch; the cabin and cockpit instantly started filling with heavy smoke. I instantly shut the APU down; and turned around to Flight Attendant A and told them to get the passengers off. By then; we only had about 5 passengers or so on the aircraft. After deplaning the passengers; I asked Ops to call the Fire Department to come and make sure there was nothing still burning on the airplane. They came and verified that there were no hot spots in the airplane. Maintenance was notified and the crew did a short debrief to insure we were still safe to fly. We continued our flight about an hour later.
column123: We had a plane swap; exiting crew said everything was fine; we got on. Captain was starting the APU then a [circuit] breaker blew and cabin lights went out... Captain did his checks... restarted APU... by this time we had our specials and people who needed extra time about 10 total on board. I was helping a women to her seat when I looked up and saw the end of cabin had smoke at that exact time Captain said to stop boarding. I immediately got on PA and instructed everyone to deplane.   Captain called Fire Department and Maintenance they found no hot spots. We got our bags off then went to another plane to continue into ZZZ1.  Captain was great and asked if we were both OK.   Very thankful this happened while on the ground.

column121: While climbing out of ZZZ1 enroute to ZZZ I noticed that in RVSM we were close to having a 200 ft. discrepancy between mine and the FO's (First Officer) altimeter.  We didn't go beyond 200 ft. difference and never got an ALT miscompare message.At cruise (FL350) the difference was roughly 130 ft.During descent in to ZZZ; I don't know when exactly it showed up; but I noticed at roughly FL330 during the descent we had a ALT message flashing on my altimeter.  I thought maybe the BARO knob on my side or the FO side got bumped.  I checked and saw that all three altimeters were showing STD.  Then the message went away only to show up 100-200 ft. later.  I looked at the altitudes and saw that we were either 200 or greater but not more than 220 ft. off. But then the next 100-200 ft. we were 200 ft. or less on the miscompare and the ALT message went away only for in the next 100-200 ft. for the ALT message to return and the discrepancy being 200 ft. or greater.It back and forth intermittently until roughly FL290; possibly lower; I do not recall when exactly the issue stopped.I sent an ACARS message to Dispatch to inform them and so that they could inform maintenance so that the issue could start getting worked on when we got to the gate.I also informed ZZZ Operations on the in range call what was going on and that we would need maintenance.I was looking through the QRH to see if there was a checklist for it just in case even though I was pretty sure there wasn't one.This being the first time that this has occurred to me; I unfortunately did not think to reference the standby altimeter to try to help isolate where the fault may lie; as the issue went away while I was diligently looking for a checklist and the issue was intermittent.  Also because it was intermittent and went away on its own I also did not think to inform ATC since we were already in the process of exiting RVSM.No other messages on any display unit; including the EICAS; showed while this was happening nor throughout the remainder of the flight.We landed in ZZZ without incident.I should have known that there wasn't a checklist for this issue and I need to read back up on alt miscompare procedures and how it affects RVSM and what to do.  I should have informed ATC and I should have referenced the standby altimeter to help isolate the problem.  Otherwise I think we did everything else correctly.After working with Maintenance in ZZZ it turns out the number 4 probe had failed even though we didn't get any messages other than the ALT message on the altimeters.  Maintenance said that there when they initially went through their task that there wasn't any active or logged faults with the system and that they had to do another task to isolate where to problem was; in this case the faulty probe.
column123: In ZZZ; during descent we had an ALT disagree message during descent.Upon arrival into ZZZ we had everyone deplane; had maintenance come on and do some checks.They were able to isolate the issue and ascertained it was going to be a lengthy delay.We got word that our new departure time was going to be XE:00 so we got a day room.We got back to the airport at XD:15 for the re-report time.Upon arriving at the aircraft I was informed that there was still work to do but that they just needed to tape a cover back onto the plane for one of the pitot tubes.After that they still needed to do some testing and that it would be about 30 more minutes.So; we went to the crew room to wait for the work to be done.I went back out several times to get updates and each time the return to service kept getting pushed back.Finally; once it became a return to service time of XG:00 I realized that we were going to be within an hour of our FDP (Flight Duty Period) time out in ZZZ1.So; I called scheduling and got a wheels up time of XG:55 before the pilots timed out and due to contractual issues that the main cabin door needed to be closed at XG:34. I was told that Maintenance would call ZZZ Operations who would then call me in the crew room when Maintenance was done in the flight deck and that we could go to the plane; preflight; board; and wait for the maintenance log to come back so we could hopefully get out in time.The call did not come in until roughly XG:10.We went out to the aircraft; I told the flight to not rush the preflight. I told them to take their time; not to slow down so that we didn't hit our times; but so that something wouldn't be missed; prevent mistakes; keep us legal and not on the wrong side of SOPs and Regs.We were able to accomplish our preflight in a timely matter; board in a timely matter; and we were able to get the MCD closed at XG:32. The AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) hadn't returned yet so I figured let's get the door closed so that we hit the Flight Attendant contract time and that hopefully the AML would arrive soon and could be handed to us through the flight deck window.I called Dispatch to make sure we were on the correct revision since we had a hard time getting our IFR clearance. I verified all the fuel and time values along with the correct revision. A few minutes after that a Ramp crew member came to the flight deck informing us that the fuel truck had arrived. There was apparently some confusion about fuel. I initially dismissed the fuel truck only to decide that I should make sure that wasn't any last second changes. So; I called Dispatch to re-verify our fuel numbers. There wasn't any changes and I moved on to the next step.Some time after this the AML arrived around XE:40-XE:45.After the cabin secured and we started our air start checklists due to the APU being INOP.At this point I knew that our timeline most likely wouldn't work but that it would close and that we needed to give our best effort.Right as we got to the part in the checklist to apply air to the aircraft for the air start; the FAs (Flight Attendants) called and informed us that a passenger had gotten up to use the lavatory. I told them to let me know when they had returned and were seated.I told the ground crew to apply air but that we were going to wait for the passenger to come out of the lavatory since the cabin was no longer secured. I do not know if this was the right call but I thought that it was the best call in regards to safety.After a minute or two we got a call from the FAs that there was a possible passenger removal situation going on. I asked what was going on and they informed me that the passenger was being non-compliant with the face mask and was being non-cooperative and nasty in the process.Knowing that we as a whole crew were feeling stressed; tired; and unhappy about all the delays I made sure to ask had we been on time; no maintenance; still XA:30; would this situation rise to the passenger beingremoved. They talked about for a few seconds and agreed that it wasn't. I then instructed them that since he was still being non-compliant; go back one more time and see if we can get him compliant and in line or that we would then look into removal and top report back.After a minute or two I was called back and the FAs informed that the passenger was apologetic and now being compliant and we were good to go.At this point; with the cabin re-secured; I turned back to do the air start. I glanced at the clock to check our time and it was XG:51. At this point I knew that there was no possible way to get the air start; taxi; second engine start; and wheels up at XG:55.I conferred with the FO (First Officer) if he was in agreement and if he was willing to do an extension. He gave valid reason for not doing an extension and agreed with me that there was no possible way that we could get wheels up by XG:55. The reason I asked him was just to get a second opinion and he reaffirmed everything that was already thinking. I had already decided once I saw it was XG:51 that we were done; that there was no point in starting the engines; wasting fuel; taxiing out and turning back. The most efficient and economical path was to admit defeat on there being no possible way to make it off by XG:55 for FDP limit reasons and throw in the towel.We had been fighting a losing battle; we did everything we could to safely get the plane going in time and we just had too many issues pop to delay us going out.I then informed the ramp that we had timed out and to pull the ramp back to the plane and that I would inform the Flight Attendants to do arrival procedures and that we were going to deplane.The FO and did after landing and parking flows and checklists.I then exited the flight deck to tell Flight Attendant A that we were done and to do arrival procedures and that I would inform the passengers.I wanted to be out in the cabin for the announcement to not only own the decision but to not leave our Flight Attendants hanging to deal with potentially irate passengers.I made the PA informing them what was going one; the regulations on duty limits; that we tried our best but unfortunately had timed out and that we need to deplane; that they would be taken care of inside the terminal and apologized profusely for the situation.The passengers got off; mostly understanding; some were understandably irritated; but left without incident.I called crew scheduling to let them know and it sounded like word had gotten around already.We waited with the plane until a hotel was assigned. We then shut down the aircraft; secured it; turned it over to the ramp crew; and left the airport.It was a comedy of setbacks. It was just one thing after another. If it wasn't for the passenger; or the maintenance; or the air start due to the APU being broken; take any one or two items out of the equation and we most likely would have made it. It was a losing battle from the get go; we just didn't know it until the time came were there was no possible way to get out in time.I believe we did everything safely; timely; accurately; with safety and service in mind. At no time did myself; the FO; or FAs intentionally slow down the operation for the goal of timing out. The times we slowdown was to make sure things were done safely and correctly; to catch our breaths; and move on the next step to be completed; all with safety in mind.I do not know what else we could have done. We were ready and on time until the passenger; air start; AML delay; fuel confusion came about. It just wasn't our day.That being said; in order to help speed up AML paperwork we should seriously look into getting electronic AMLs and maintenance. This has a huge potential to cut down the time it takes to get paperwork done. Plus; since we would have access to the AML on our iPads and that the AML lives in the cloud that anyone in the operation can access; we wouldn't have to wait for the AML to come back tothe aircraft. Just like in [program] we would get an alert that the AML is finished; review the changes; sign off on the review; and be on our way in a significantly shorter time.In addition to that; ZZZ is not only a base but also a place where maintenance takes place. There shouldn't be an excuse to not have parts and/or the tools necessary to get jobs done. We shouldn't be having to rely on parts and tools being flown in and we definitely shouldn't be relying on borrowing tools from [other airline] like our maintenance had to do today. I understand that it would be expensive to do all of that but is it more expensive than what we just paid for crew to stay in ZZZ in a more expensive hotel; giving 500-dollar voucher to the passenger in addition to getting them hotel rooms and food vouchers? More expensive than the domino effect that just occurred down the line. Vouchers and hotels were given to those passengers in ZZZ1 no doubt. It's more expensive to not give our Mechanics the resources to do their jobs in a timely fashion than it is to try to save money on parts and tools. Also; across all [aircraft type]; things are failing at; to me; an alarming rate. Be it in the cabin or on the flight deck; these planes are not that old and should not be having things break this much; this fast. We need to stop kicking the can down the road and actually fix things rather than defer and hope for the best. Also; we need to figure out why things are breaking so much so often so soon. This is getting embarrassing and the 3rd major delay; break; cancellation in the past week for me and in talking with other crews and ramp crews; I'm not the only one experiencing these issues. We clearly have systemic issue that we are either unable or unwilling to address and sooner than later it is going to bite us real hard and cause a serious incident or accident.

column121: Upon landing in LGA and taxi to gate instructions where; 'Taxi to gate via Sierra; Papa; Bravo; Lima; enter Ramp 9 Alpha to gate.' The blue color blends into black asphalt at night and is very difficult to see until one is right up on them. Unlit island between Spot 20 and Spot 23 can be a taxi hazard at night; especially [in] bad weather. Please coordinate with LGA Airport on either making the marker lit during night time operations; or removed for possible FOD hazard to taxi operations.

column121: Took off from TPA from Runway 19R on the ENDED Nine DP. There was a small TS cell south of the field and the Tower was calling approximately 20 kts. loss of airspeed on the climb from Runway 19L. Runway 19R looked clear to us so we didn't [think] much of it. As we were cleared to takeoff from Runway 19R; we used reduced thrust and Flaps 1. On the climb; we entered IMC and turbulent conditions as we penetrated the cell. I suddenly noticed that the vls was starting to climb up and overtake my airspeed; the vsi had a downward trend and suddenly changed to amber and the 'DON'T SINK' aural warning was triggered. I immediately pushed the thrust levers to TOGA and said 'TOGA Thrust; stow speed brakes' and executed the Windshear (WS) escape maneuver. We continued the maneuver to approximately 5;000 ft. and the Captain reported to Departure that the ENDED Nine DP is not feasible due to the presence of that TS. After 5;000 ft. MSL; we turned on course to the north en route back to ZZZ.

column121: We departed Tampa Runway 19R on ENDED9 STAR following 2 previous departures with no adverse reports. When cleared for takeoff; we observed heavy rain from a building storm about 3 to 4 miles South of field over I-275 bridge. On taxi out during the brief time when radar was pointed at weather; return displayed as a narrow band of red about 2 to 3 miles across from North to South spreading East to West well inland to East and ending over the bay to the West. We had been facing North with no view of storm for the past 10 or so minutes. Takeoff roll and climb was normal and we had penetrated the band of heavy rain by about 1000 ft MSL. Nearing S speed passing about 1;500 ft MSL; airspeed began to hesitate then decay and rate of climb turned to a descent of about 1;500 fpm down. GPWS sounded with 'DON'T SINK DON'T SINK' and First Officer (FO) reacted with TOGA and increase in pitch. The descent was arrested and climb continued. Lowest radar altitude was about 1;200 ft AGL. Total time was about 10-15 seconds and we never encountered any lateral course deviations nor any typical entry or exit parameters of windshear- just the vertical aspects. We reported the microburst encounter to Tampa Departure and advised that our flight path should be avoided by any subsequent departures.

column121: When we arrived at the plane the APU was already running.  During our preflight we were notified that we would be transporting a large quantity of dry ice and would need to use the dry ice supplementary procedures.  One of those procedures is to turn the temperature in the compartment with the dry ice to as low as it gets.  We did this.  Upon engine start we noticed that the right pack 'INOP' light was on with an associated EICAS message.  As I was going through my after start flow (flap handle; APU off; engine heats; left pack; right pack) when we got to right pack we started troubleshooting the issue.  We followed the QRH which required a 5 min wait time to see if the issue is fixed.  We proceeded to taxi while we timed the 5 min.  After the 5 min the pack reset and worked normally.  We believe that the high OAT and humidity caused the pack to freeze up and fault due to the low selected temperature.  On taxi we also had to balance some fuel due to the APU burn on the ramp.  Operations were normal to the runway.  Once we started our takeoff at 60 knots we got a right bleed off message.  Captain executed a rejected takeoff and we exited the runway.  After cleaning up the aircraft and completing the rejected takeoff QRH checklist we contacted Maintenance and trouble shot the problem.  We soon discovered that the bleed air isolation valve was open.  In troubleshooting the pack issue after start; I had not finished my flow and closed the isolation valve.  So on takeoff the air from the left engine overpowered the right and closed the right bleed valve giving us the offending message.  We re-ran our checklists and made sure our brake temp cooling was OK and departed uneventfully. Multiple non normal issues caused the flight crew to miss a flow item.

column121: L2 door was making a noise that was louder than just the whistle you usually hear. More of a medium pitched hum. Called the pilots. They said cabin pressurization looked OK on their end. I looked at seals and put my ear up to an area that looked a little looser. It was definitely louder as we explored that seal. About a minute later I started to feel lightheaded and my ability to control my breathing/focus start to feel altered. I asked the Flight Attendant 'C' in the back of she was feeling different at all. She ended up feeling weird; too. Things started to feel like it was harder to focus and spin/euphoric feelings. Harder to breathe. She said; 'We need to get out of here.' And we immediately headed to the front. I felt that I immediately needed oxygen right away and to tell the pilots that something was wrong. I felt faint-like; was grey in color; and sweat on forehead. I felt like I was having a hard time with my ability to communicate as I was speaking with the pilots. The focus/cloudy feeling in my head was unusual and anything I've ever experienced. My breathing felt shallow and also rapid at times. I was able to tell the pilots and immediately went on oxygen. It took a while for my head and body to be able to focus and for the symptoms to lessen. Used almost a full bottle of oxygen.Sat in aircraft right; inboard jumpseat for landing; with the pilot's permission; in order to stay away from L2 door.Still was feeling lightheaded; cloudy; hard to focus feeling even after we landed throughout the night. And a little lightheaded the next day; too. Was checked out by the paramedics and went to the hospital to get checked out as well. FA 'C' felt better than I did more quickly but also mentioned she had never been through that before as well... and had never felt those feelings before; either.Maybe there was an air quality issue on my side that I was more exposed to? Or slight decompression/lack of oxygen by my L2 door. I did notice it smelled like dirty socks in the back galley later when I went to the back of the plane. Sat in L2 jumpseat; aircraft right; inboard for landing to avoid sitting by the L2 door for landing. With the captain's permission.I recommend having the door and cabin area on the particular tail number monitored.

column121: While operating Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1; the flight crew noted a fuel imbalance message on the FQIS (Fuel Quantity Indicating System) display. This created a major Non-Compliance and Safety of Flight issue.

column121: After we landed in INL we had a runway excursion with a GA aircraft. While on approach we heard the GA traffic make radio calls about being inbound about 3-5 miles north of the field. We notified them of our location of about a 10-mile final for Runway 32 and they said they would wait for us to land before landing themselves. They also called us; 'In sight'. After we landed we advised on the radio we were back-taxiing; and as we were turning around we saw the GA traffic landing while we were still on the runway. They stayed well clear of us and were able to exit the runway so we could back-taxi with no issues; and no evasive maneuvering was required at any point.GA traffic apparently not being aware of the risk of landing on a runway we were still on. While he had us in sight I did not have him in sight or on TCAS; and therefore did not know exactly how close behind us he was. Construction in INL requiring back-taxiing and therefore a longer landing time than usual that the GA traffic was probably used to. Try to advise GA traffic earlier if a need to back-taxi is required.
column123: We were flying into an uncontrolled airport and made two-way radio contact with another aircraft north of the field coming into land on the same runway we were. He told us that he would let us go first since we were much faster than him and that he would follow us and be #2 to land. Normal radio calls occurred after that and we landed without incident. Because of construction there are no taxiway turn offs available on the runway and a180 degree turn and back taxi is required. After coming to almost a stop and just about to turn around I made a radio call stating that we would be back taxiing on the runway. Once we just about completed our 180 degree turn we saw the other aircraft about 50 feet off the ground at the other end of the runway in his landing flare. So we pulled as far to the side of the runway as we could just in case he made it down to us. We stayed still until he landed and pulled off on the taxiway about 2;000 feet down the runway where we needed to exit. Once the other aircraft was clear we continued our back taxi to the exit point without incident.The other aircraft stated he saw us on about a one mile final and would be number 2 to land. A contributing factor could be that he never actually saw us or he just disregarded us. Being that he was in aircraft type he might have just assumed he had plenty of runway to land and turn in before us without it being an issue on his end. Poor communication on his end as well; very few radio calls almost all of them were non standard; no tail number; no position reports at all outside of being north of the field; and simply stating 'I'll follow the jet'. A pilot with little regards to aviation safety more or less.The only thing I could think of is maybe more communication. We could have tried getting back on the radio real quick and attempting to have the other aircraft go around. By the time we saw it however; he was basically on the ground

column121: Climbing through approximately 500 ft. AGL in a right turn to 360; the departure heading selected on the MCP by the FO (First Officer) prior to takeoff; the FO's flight director; FD2; failed; the MCP (Mode Control Panel) altitude window indicated 50;000; not the pre-takeoff selected altitude of 3;000; and the FO's command bars biased out of view. The PF continued the climbing turn using PFD (Primary Flight Display) raw data in night-time VMC conditions. Cross-checking respective PFDs revealed no flags or indications as to the specific failure.In the busy initial climb segment; confusion as to the cause of current flight instrument condition gave way to confidence in the raw data. Directing the PF to continue to climb using raw data; I attempted to select 3000 ft. on the MCP; the altitude knob spun freely without any effect on the window. I then turned off the FD1 and FD2; reselected 3000 ft. in the MCP altitude window; confirmed the heading bug was at 360; selected heading; and turned the FD switches back on; FD2 first; in an attempt to restore FD2 guidance for the PF. Immediately upon switching on FD2; the MCP altitude returned to 50;000 and no command bars appeared on the FO's PFD.Switching to Departure Control; ATC gave us direct routing to the first fix; ZZZZZ; and continue climb to 11;000. I asked ATC for a heading; mentioning our concern that our navigation might be unreliable. They provided a 010 heading which when selected; had no effect on the FO's heading bug. Changing heading on the MCP failed to change the bugs on the FO's ND (Navigation Display) and PFD compass displays. I confirmed compass heading on the wet compass corresponded with both the Captain's and FO's compasses. They asked if we needed to declare an emergency; I declined as we had good raw data and were still diagnosing the malfunction.I attempted a second reset of FD2 with the same negative result. Leveling at 11;000; the PF reported the autothrottles were not holding commanded airspeed; we disengaged the autothrottles. Turning both FDs off again and selecting FD1 on provided accurate command bars on the Captain's PFD. We agreed that continuing using raw data was possible; and that full FD capability was available from FD1. I transferred aircraft control to myself and agreed with my FO's suggestion of going to the QRH for additional troubleshooting/procedural steps. A satisfactory QRH procedure to handle this malfunction was difficult to find and both FMS1 on the Captain's ND and FMS2 on the FO's confirmed FMC operation. We asked ATC for direct down range and confirmed FMS accuracy using FD1 guidance of MCDU1 entered direct routing. I engaged the autopilot and autothrottles and we continued on course using LNAV/VNAV.We discussed the status of the aircraft and the conditions at our destination; ZZZ. We elected to continue to ZZZ where we completed the trip without incident. I submitted an electronic logbook entry and called Maintenance Control after arrival. Approximately 35 minutes into our hour-long flight; I realized we had not requested [the] planned climb above our initial cruise altitude; FL310; and that contingency fuel had been burned during a slower climb than normal. Burn; alternate; ZZZ1; and 45-minute FAA fuel was still available; though a missed approach would have compelled diversion to ZZZ1. The FD2 diagnosis and distraction lead to the initial loss of SA regarding erosion to our fuel state. Beginning descent and approach planning brought for our new fuel and prepared us for contingencies. Communication throughout was key to understanding the status of the aircraft and mitigated the initial startle and confusion at such a low altitude early flight stage.
column123: We were cleared for takeoff by ZZZ3 Tower with instructions to turn to heading 360 and maintain 3;000 ft. The pilot flying which was me; the First Officer; put 360 in the MCP and deselected LNAV. We took off and as we were climbing through about 500 ft.; the command bars disappeared and altitude went to 50;000 on both the PFD and MCP. We leveled at 3;000 on heading 360. ATC gave us climb to 11;000 and direct to a fix. The Captain told him we needed a heading we were having trouble with the flight director. ATC gave us a head of 010 and climb to 11;000 ft.The heading bug on the First Officer's PFD and MFD was stuck on heading 360 but was 010 on the MCP and on the Captain's displays. The Captain checked the PFD heading with the compass and it matched. We had no flags on the PFD or MFD. The Captain turned off both flight directors and then turned them both back on with the First Officer's being the master. When he turned it back on; the altitude went back to 50;000 and we could not change it. The command bars never came back. We saw that the Captain had a flight director and that his heading bug would turn with the MCP. The Captain then turned the FDs off and put his FD as the master. When he did that; the altitude went back to normal. On the FO's (First Officer) displays there was still no FD and the heading bug was stuck on 360 but now the altitude was correct. We continued the flight to ZZZ with the Captain flying.

column121: Outside the marker [Runway] XXR Captain received call from purser about chemical type smell moving forward from aft cabin. column123: On approach in ZZZ the Captain received a call from the lead Flight Attendant about an acrid chemical smell moving forward from the aft cabin. We started the APU on short final and turned off the engine bleeds after exiting the runway; using the APU to power the packs.  After turning off the engine bleeds the smell dissipated and we turned the recirculate fans back on. No oxygen was used or needed by the crew or passengers.  We parked safely at the gate and briefed me and made a maintenance write up.
