column121: After landing on Runway 22R; we contacted Ground who advised us to taxi via Bravo; November. Since Bravo was directly off the nose of the aircraft; the Captain assumed; and I didn't disagree; that November was somewhere down Bravo closer to our arrival gate. Unfortunately; November was also directly across the nose and nobody noticed it until the Captain has commenced the same turn which resulted in a Boeing 787 taking out some taxi lights the week prior. As we were taxiing northbound on Bravo; Ground gave us a phone number to call which led to an intra-cockpit discussion of what we might have done wrong. Not finding any fault on our own; the Ground Controller advised us of the incorrect turn as we continued to taxi to the gate. This discussion never ceased until we were already into the gate area. No attempt was made to contact the ramp prior to entering the ramp area because ATIS stated (paraphrased) Company extended ramp procedures not in effect". When we read that during the approach briefing; we incorrectly thought it meant "Company ramp procedures effect". If the latter statement had been correct; we would have been correct to taxi to the gate with Ground...who had been talking to us the whole time. The expectation bias of believing that the ramp was closed; combined with the continuous chatter from EWR Ground led to us believing we were OK to taxi to the gate. When Ground finally let us go; I switched to Operations vs. Ramp for gate and we were told to contact Ramp...who was more than a little upset. Apparently the Captain hadn't followed the correct wide-body line but had followed the taxi line which met the one we were already on. The wide-body gate is not well marked as such at the intersection of all these lines to make it readily apparent to us; although a post-incident discussion and analysis showed us that the textual description of WB taxi lines is clearly something we could and should have seen. Despite having sufficient clearance; which was visually confirmed; Ramp was understandably angry with us for not contacting them and for following the eastern; rather than center taxi line."
column123: Landing 22R we exited highspeed B4. During arrival briefing we discussed that the normal ground flow was for arrival traffic to utilize A; as B is used for traffic taxiing out. Exiting B4 ATC said to join N and contact Ground. That intersection is a junction of B4; N; A & B. Obviously a dynamic situation as we are clearing the runway and changing controllers. We joined N and as we switched to Ground Control made the hard right turn onto A consistent with our arrival briefing and consistent with the need to clear the runway rather than stopping leaving the rear of the aircraft still on the runway. After switching to Ground; the controller inquired as to our turn onto A. The controller queried us wondering if the signage was not clear. He referenced a recent incident where taxiway lights had been damaged by a wide body making a similar (or same) turn recently. He suggested that we were not the first ones to make this turn. In a follow up phone call we suggested that the instructions be more specific; such as 'join N and a right turn on B' so that there is no guesswork on anybody's part. EWR ATIS indicated 'Company expanded ramp procedures not in effect'. We were still with Ground discussing our runway exit as we approached the alleyway. Ground control did not switch us to Ramp Control. On our 'late' switch to Ramp Control we discovered we were on the wrong frequency. Upon coming up on the correct Ramp Control; we were admonished for entering the alleyway before contacting them and for being on the wrong line". Contributing factors were 1) missing the note regarding using the center of 3 lines for wide-bodies; 2) the fact that the only graphic depiction of the lines is not on the ramp diagram; not on any of the 10-7's; not on the gate page. It only appears on the secondary JeppPro AMM display of 10-9; and 3) The lead in line from RK ties into the left alleyway taxi line rather than the center as in every other similar situation I have ever seen. 4) There is considerable anxiety and distraction caused by ongoing company responses to Covid. While Covid has knocked the wind out of the travel and airline industry; the company's actions to pile on additional unnecessary restrictions and requirements add a huge level of stress; anxiety and uncertainty; adding completely unnecessary and avoidable threats and distractions to the conduct of our duties across the board! I am making more mistakes and I am witnessing my crew members and others like ground staff; ramp agents and maintenance personnel doing the same."

column121: During the engine start we received an engine 3 start valve caution message. The Captain elected to start the engine 3 more times; finally starting it on the 4th attempt. During this time I suggested that we contact Dispatch to initiate a three-way call between the Captain; Dispatch; and Maintenance Control due to the fact that the engine was not starting. What actually ended up happening was the Captain used the DDG (Dispatch Deviations Guide) Procedure 80-XX-XX to start the engine; which is a maintenance procedure involving tools. He asked the pushback driver to do this procedure; I have no idea if this person was qualified to work on our aircraft or not?We had a Mechanic on board who elected not to go down and do the procedure but instead left someone else to do it. As it turned out; the tug driver outside said the valve moved by itself. However; what concerned me was if this person was qualified to work on our aircraft. I strongly suggested to the Captain before and after the event that we enter this item in the logbook as he'd been operating the engine start as though we were already deferred under DDG 80-XX-XX.After we continued out to the runway; we received a pack 1 caution message. The Captain had me run the checklist and eventually we ended up turning off the pack 1. Then; the Captain announced that the pack was just getting warm and turned the pack back on and turned to me and said; see it was just hot. I further insisted that we call Maintenance and Dispatch to report both of these items and was met with a tirade of sarcasm; trying to put me down. CRM at this time was at an all-time low. He finally agreed to do the 3-way call only as a further attempt to try and put me down. It turned out the items he didn't want to write up; Maintenance still wanted to him to write up in Miami. I think that further irritated him.Takeoff was normal; but as we reached 5000 ft. AGL the Captain turn round to me and expressed his further annoyance at me; saying we're going to have to talk about this. As we were in sterile cockpit; climbing out of mountainous terrain; I responded with let's talk about this on the ground; which I guess further irritated him and he yelled at me he'd take me to the Chief Pilot. I wanted him to concentrate on his flying duties and not lecturing me; that could come later; so I said nothing back. At approximately 17000 ft. we received another pack 1 message. This time; the Captain ended up turning off pack one and it remained off for the duration of the flight.

column123: Pilot not flying is an LCA (Line Check Airman) conducting an Initial Operating Experience flight for pilot flying; who is a transition First Officer from the other aircraft builder.Assigned to fly the ZZZZZ Visual Approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. Installed the RNAV V XX procedure in FMC and briefed RNAV/visual approach procedures. ATC cleared us direct ZZZ1 and cross ZZZ1 at 3;000 ft. While descending on profile; aircraft was slowing to 180 kt. and configuring for landing. PM was tracking the configuration changes and verifying on course with LNAV; and then selected TDZE after passing ZZZZZ2 intersection. Pilot flying was having difficulty finding the runway which was out his right window behind [of] his shoulder line. Pilot not flying looked outside to acquire runway to direct pilot flying to look in the right direction. At that moment; ZZZ Tower Controller called 'Altitude Alert' for our flight. Pilot not flying looked inside and noticed altitude was 900 ft. crossing ZZZZZ1; below the 1;500-ft. altitude that was programmed in the FMC. Pilot not flying then also noticed that VNAV was not engaged but the aircraft was descending in FLCH; so was therefore not on the VNAV descent path. Pilot not flying took control of the aircraft; leveled the descent; and continued to follow the LNAV course to line up with Runway XX. column121: We were given a late hand off by the previous controller to Salt Lake Approach control controlling the LEEHY arrival. On check in Approach Control contacted us first and it was apparent that he was task saturated and that the sector was extremely busy. He told us he needed to give us a 'box pattern for spacing' and gave us a heading westbound over Utah Lake. We complied with this heading and the instruction to descend to 14;000 ft. and reduce speed to 190 KIAS. We were then given another heading turning us to our left and back towards the approach course. It was at this time that we got a traffic advisory of an aircraft that was in the direction we were now turning towards with the latest vector from ATC. The aircraft was climbing towards us as we were descending and turning as per the ATC instructions. Almost simultaneously ATC realized the situation and gave us a traffic alert at the same time the aircraft gave us an RA to descend. The Captain immediately disconnected the autopilot and began to comply with the instruction to descend. At this time I was looking outside doing what I could to see and avoid the traffic. At this point we were in a layer of smoke and visibility was low. I was able to spot the traffic as the aircraft was passing above us. It was very close; only a few hundred feet. It is hard to judge distance without anything to base the measurement on. Just prior to me seeing the traffic the TCAS system made the annunciation to monitor vertical speed and as the aircraft was passing off our right we got clear of conflict. It took us a minute to get back with the controller and he gave us a new altitude and heading to join the final approach course into Salt Lake. We made an uneventful landing on Runway 35 in Salt Lake and once safely parked contacted Company to figure out next steps. I believe the cause of this event mostly had to do with improper instructions from ATC. I obviously did not have the big picture of the traffic environment in that sector like the controller did. However I could tell he was task saturated and had more aircraft to control than he could safely handle. We were not aware of any potential conflict until beginning the turn to the heading the controller gave us which put us in conflict with the other aircraft. In the future I will attempt to be even more vigilant at situational awareness. I believe this event has only renewed my sense of importance on this matter. Furthermore I would suggest that the controller of this sector not be controlling more than one sector as it seemed he was. I believe that the controllers task saturation was potentially the largest contributing factor in the event. I am glad that we responded so promptly to the resolution advisory and were able to resolve the conflict. The training we had at Company prepared us well for this situation and I am glad that I have practiced it many times in training.

column121: Flew a 737 Max from ZZZ-ZZZ1.  During single engine taxi to [runway]; called for the delayed engine start with what I thought was enough time to reach runway at a normal pace and fully prepare for takeoff.  I even briefed the need to take into consideration the slow engine start cycle as part of the workload management process.  The engine start process took so much time that we were finishing checklists (at a normal pace) when we were cleared to line up and wait. As we took the runway; an LCA (Line Check Airman) on the jumpseat pointed out that the 3 minute warm up time was not complete.  We asked the Tower for 30 seconds on the runway and then took off.  The rest of the flight was normal. While the buck stops with the Captain; there were a few factors that led to this inadvertent deviation.  This leg was my 3rd in the Max.  This was a threat that was briefed in preflight.  While I knew we needed more time for the engine to start; it was much longer than I planned for.  Additionally; the FO did not start a timer after the engine start for some reason.  Because the FO did not call out that the warm up time was not finished; it was forgotten.  What I took away from this event was that the start sequence on the Max takes at least 6 minutes - approximately 3 for the start; and 3 to warm up.  Another take away is that even though FO's normally track this time and report it as necessary; I need to monitor this much more closely.

Our approach would take us close to that airport; so I instructed the FO (First Officer) to keep terrain up on his side and I would take a look at the radar on mine. We immediately leveled off; even though we still had the terrain in sight. We discovered the error; re-entered the remaining crossing restrictions; and continued. We should have deleted the 'melded' altitude and then re-entered the correct one. Instead; I just re-entered the crossing altitude and did not re-verify the crossing restrictions. Since we both had verified all the altitudes prior to the descent checklist; it gave us the confidence that they would still be there.While I take full responsibility; the FMS 'issues' are just waiting there for a slightly distracted crew; with weather. column121: Fume event.  We loaded the passengers and had a maintenance issue with my oxygen mask that they had to run to the hanger so we were going to be delayed slightly.  The Captain started the APU.  The Gate Agent came down and asked if Maintenance was there for the smell.  We didn't realize that it smelled on the plane as we were already acclimated to it. I asked the flight attendants about it and they all thought it was from outside also until they walked to the back of the plane and it was getting worse.  They called us and we both decided to turn off the APU bleed and get the people off.  I talked to the agent and she said just send them up and I made an announcement that we had a maintenance issue and everyone needed to deplane.  The total time was about 25 minutes; 15 minutes to realize the extent of the problem which got progressively worse; and 10 minutes to deplane all but one wheelchair that took another 10 minutes to find a wheelchair.  Afterwards; Chief Pilot met us at the gate and we called air medical service. It was a waste; the person couldn't understand us; and told the Captain he was fine.  Name told her that's not what he said as he was sitting next to him.  We debated going to the hospital but went to the company medical center and home. We feel the APU was the factor that caused [the event]. Not having the fumes would be the best; but the agent being aware and speaking up reduced the severity of the event.  It allowed us to act faster than we probably would have not realizing the severity.
column123: During preflight on Aircraft X in ZZZ; we started the APU and turned on the APU bleed air. Soon after that we began to notice a musty dirty air smell throughout the entire aircraft. column121: A lot going on that culminated into a low altitude caution on approach to Runway XXR. The RNP approach was loaded into the FMS in the normal preflight planning. I did not catch this error and thought it was the RNAV XXR that we were flying during the initial descent and approach; which is the approach we were cleared for. On the base leg prior to the ZZZZZ fix; we noticed the error and the box was not sequencing correctly. I instructed the FO to 'handfly' to make the 90 degree turn to final while I went heads down to get the correct approach in the box. The FO started a turn but also a descent and we received a caution obstacle aural warning from the aircraft. I instructed the FO to immediately correct and to climb to the correct altitude. At that time we also received a query from the control tower for a low altitude alert and we were 800-1000 feet below the minimum vectoring altitude at that point on the arrival. We corrected the altitude error and climbed to be at ZZZZZ1 (FAP) at the correct altitude.   I neglected or misread what approach was actually loaded into the FMS. The turn to  final should have been a turn only and not a descending turn. I was removed from monitoring while heads down reloading the approach so I did not monitor the hand flying properly. It was the end of a long day; and the last 45 minutes of the flight was dodging weather in and around ZZZ. This all happened very quick and was a bit of a wake up call to me how quickly it went from normal to a situation that had the aircraft in a low altitude situation. In hindsight; I should have just asked ATC for a vector to buy time and get reestablished on the approach instead of trying to save the approach and fix it while asking the FO to hand fly. The safest course of action would have been to get a vector.
column123: On the late downwind leg of the approach; of the second leg for the day; after multiple deviations due to weather; the CA & I realized the approach loaded in the box differed to that which was briefed. That is; RNAV GPS instead of RNAV RNP . Although this was recognized; changed & executed just after the IAF; the aircraft did not respond accordingly; and as PF I initiated hand flying to correct the base to final turn; of which we momentarily overshot. Whilst hand flying & commencing a 30 degree turn in the descent at the IF; insufficient back pressure was held & the aircraft lost approximately 700-800 ft before establishing on final. This was immediately recognized and corrective action was taken to reestablish the correct altitude; whilst an aural 'Obstacle' warning was heard & moments later; an ATC advisory was received. The approach was stabilized before 1000 ft; we broke out around 900 ft & landed safely. This event was initially due to a combination of complacency & distraction... where we were dodging multiple cells en route; and failed to amend the previously entered approach in the box (*as loaded prior to departure). We held off amending the box; until we were in range to receive the latest ATIS; and at that time; became busy avoiding weather; and then once closer to the field; there was multiple traffic & very busy ATC communications. To ensure this is not repeated; I will also be thoroughly going over the box during the approach brief; and verify my intentions regarding when I shall be arming the approach & what I then expect to see on the FMS.

There was a Company Aircraft Y that was in front of us; joining Taxiway XY from Taxiway XZ at the conjunction of taxiways XX; XZ; and XY. I assumed that the Company Aircraft Y was the aircraft we were to hold for; as ZZZ Ground did not specify an aircraft type; e.g.; 787 or Airbus. I did not realize or expect that it was the aircraft that ZZZ Ground had instructed us to hold for; so I continued taxiing on Taxiway XX. Over the next few seconds; as we approached the conjunction of Taxiway XX and XY; I noticed the Company Aircraft Z on Taxiway XZ had caught up and was parallel with our aircraft; an A320; and was continuing towards Taxiway XY in order to join Taxiway XX in front of our aircraft.During this time; I instructed my FO (First Officer) to start the number 2 engine in order to be prepared for takeoff once reaching the runway. As such; he was heads down and did not notice the taxi conflict with the other Aircraft Z. Both aircraft were nearly at Taxiway XY when ZZZ Ground noticed the conflict and informed us that the Company Aircraft Z on our left was the actual aircraft we were supposed to yield for; vs. the earlier Aircraft Y. I noticed the Company Aircraft Z had initiated a turn towards Taxiway XY and as such; I ended up using firm braking in order to stop our aircraft in order to prevent any possible left wingtip conflict/contact; and in order to comply with ZZZ Ground instructions to hold short of Taxiway XY in order to yield to the other aircraft. During the braking maneuver; [a] FA (Flight Attendant) was facing towards the aft of the aircraft and lost her footing in the aft galley. She then fell backwards; towards the front of the aircraft; striking her left elbow on a quarter turn in the aft galley cart stowage area. Her impact with the quarter turn was hard enough to cause a painful injury to her elbow.I contacted the Purser and asked if the flight attendants were OK. I was informed that [the] FA was injured; and the nature of her injury was serious enough that we needed to return to the gate and to have medical personnel meet the aircraft. We coordinated with ZZZ Operations and returned to Gate XX; our original departure gate. We had paramedics; a Flight Operations Representative; and eventually an Flight Attendant Representative meet us. The paramedics tended to [the] FA and she was taken off the aircraft in their care. During the process; they had arranged for a replacement FA to work the flight segment from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I discussed the overall situation with [the] ZZZ Flight Operations Representative. I called the Chief Pilot and left a message with brief details of the incident. My First Officer and I made the determination that we were fit to fly the segment from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After further consult with [the] Flight Operations Representative and taking care of all necessary actions; we continued with the flight.

column121: I was the First Officer and pilot monitoring on our flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. This was the last leg of a three-day trip. We taxied out on time and parked to wait out a ground stop. ZZZ was just starting to get the worst of a tropical storm. Convective SIGMETs for embedded thunderstorms covered much of the mid-Atlantic states. The ground stop lifted and we were able to depart 2 hours and 2 minutes after pushback.The first part of the flight went fine; and we were clear of weather until contacting Approach Control. The controller gave us good vectors; but we still had to penetrate some moderate rain showers. Our aircraft was an older 321 with CRT screens and the old radar display; and it was night by this point. This made it difficult to know the intensity until we were very close to the depicted weather. We were able to keep clear of magenta turbulence indications on the display; yet we still encountered moderate to severe turbulence with speed indications +/- 20 kt. below 8;000 ft. Upon turning base; we were in a clear area and could see one more cell crossing the final approach course. Traffic ahead that had just flown through the same cell reported moderate rain and smooth ride. Our ride was worse than that; and after configuring we got an aural predictive windshear warning; 'GO AROUND; WINDSHEAR AHEAD.' We initiated a go-around. The ride was moderate and there were big airspeed fluctuations; but we didn't get a reactive windshear alert. Approach vectored us back for another ILS. The downwind took us around more moderate intensity rain and turbulence. Approach informed us that traffic behind us had landed; and that we were the only one to go around so far. I believe two aircraft landed between our first approach and our second attempt.Our second approach also resulted in a go-around. When we encountered the heaviest part of the rain; airspeed loss was unacceptable and we initiated the go-around. We did not get a predictive windshear alert. I don't recall if we had a reactive windshear warning; but almost instantly we had multiple ECAM warnings and cautions. The autopilot disconnected and Captain assumed manual control - he was pilot-flying throughout the event. The ride felt very similar to how the simulator presents a windshear event. Recovery felt like it took forever. With no autopilot and multiple F/CTRL ECAM messages; we were fully caught up in recovering to a normal state. We climbed up to 3000; which was [the] missed approach altitude. Flight director guidance was fluctuating a lot; and we turned off FD 1 and 2.Re-configuring the aircraft after the approach was delayed; the airspeed trend arrow indicated a very imminent flap over-speed condition. I asked the Captain if he wanted flaps up; and then raised them when he indicated in the affirmative. My perception here was that we were in level flight and accelerating rapidly. In retrospect; I misjudged our energy state and failed to follow the prescribed schedule for flap retraction; retracting them too quickly. As the flaps were retracting; we were somewhere around 3;100 ft. correcting for 3;000; in moderate turbulence. These factors all compounded; resulting in a low-energy state and stall warning indication. I'm not sure what the auto thrust was commanding at this point; or if it had reduced thrust for us to descend back to 3000. I believe I yelled; 'Nose down!' and Captain responded that he was full forward stick. I momentarily pushed my flight stick forward and was corrected by the aural 'dual input' alert. Captain recovered the aircraft. I gave ATC a quick description of our flight control computer problems and they climbed us to 5000 on vectors. We began the process of going through the ECAM malfunctions; with me working the ECAM. The autopilot was inoperative for the rest of the flight. F/CTRL ALTN LAW was next. There is no follow-up for this. I believe the next was F/CTRL ELAC 1 PITCH FAULT and F/CTRL ELAC 2 PITCH FAULT. I know that's the checklist I went to; but after the fact I can't say whether it was the ELAC PITCH FAULT or a generic ELAC FAULT. The pitch fault follow-up prohibits resetting an ELAC in flight; and so we did not attempt a computer reset. The ELAC FAULT reset procedure does allow a reset in flight if you do it one at a time and there are no uncommanded maneuvers happening.After follow-ups; I called Dispatch to see if we could go to ZZZ2 or ZZZ3 or ZZZ4. We had around 12;000 lb. of fuel. ZZZ4 appeared to have storm cells at the field but ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 were clear. I expressed that we were hand-flying with degraded flight controls and needed a clear airport. Dispatch gave us a minimum fuel of 8.0 to go to ZZZ4 if we could not get into ZZZ. Ultimately; ZZZ updated us that winds were shifting straight out of the north; and they could turn the airport around for us. The non-normal section of the [manual] confirmed we had enough runway landing distance. The final for XXR was clear of storms; and we were able to shoot the ILS and land.So many factors were at play here. At the time we entered ZZZ airspace we had been on duty for 10 hours. We were navigating around severe weather in a tropical storm with the old-style radar. It was working well; but overall; it just doesn't provide the clarity that the new radar presents. We were in continuous turbulence of varying intensities; occasionally severe; before our first approach. Our picture of what the weather was doing was not as clear as the situational awareness that can be achieved in cruise flight. We were relying on ATC vectors through areas that other aircraft had just previously flown. Reports from other aircraft indicated acceptable conditions; or conditions that we could plan for by following severe weather avoidance guidance. The predictive windshear system did its job the first time and we had a clean go-around. Other aircraft landed after our missed approach and conditions were ok. Startle factor played a huge role on the second attempt. Windshear plus multiple ECAMs and autopilot failure created a complex and dynamic situation. We were getting bounced all over the place. We were struggling to get the airplane under control. The monitoring challenge was huge because of the turbulence and the degraded flight controls. I was making FCU inputs in between running checklist items. I had sent an ACARS to Dispatch asking where we should go and listing our system failures; and got no response. The crew phone app worked well enough; but I was frustrated that the feedback we got was that it would be preferred that we hold for ZZZ or go to our listed alternate. I'm sure the Dispatcher could hear my frustration. I am glad that we were able to safely continue to ZZZ; but I wanted to get the plane on the ground without dealing with any more threats to the flight. Holding between thunderstorms with no autopilot in alternate law is an unnecessary risk. I'm not sure why the ground stop for ZZZ was lifted. After the flight; we learned that there had been 7 confirmed tornadoes in the area right around ZZZ. These storms were moving very quickly. It looked like it was possible that ZZZ would clear up before we got there; but there was a good chance it would not. Our decision to go was based on having a lot of fuel; and two alternates. Our second alternate was ZZZ3; which remained clear. This meant that if at any point the path ahead looked bad; we could turn around and have an escape plan. The weather moving in from the south across the final ended up being the worst that we would encounter. If we had delayed this flight by another hour; I think we would have been better off.
column123: On first approach; got a windshear warning and went around. On second approach with moderate to almost severe turbulence; we hit a heavy rain shower. From what I remember we were configured for landing when we hit turbulence. Right then from what I can remember; the autopilot kicked off with the nose pitching up and the speed tape coming up. I pushed the power to climb and tried pushing the nose down. At first; nothing was happening. We did get a low-energy warning too. The plane did recover and started to respond to control inputs. column123: This was the last leg of a six day pattern. Fatigue was not the primary cause; but certainly a contributing factor. This was an OE flight with the FO (First Officer) being the PF (Pilot Flying) and trainee. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) was a Captain LCA (Line Check Airman) and two other FO's were onboard. The flight was being vectored around weather for a visual approach to Runway XX. The autopilot was engaged; we were above the glideslope; and approximately 5 miles from ZZZZZ our altitude was above 8;000 feet. I mentioned that we seemed high; and soon after the gear and speedbrakes were extended. I also spoke of the pitfalls of getting ALT before G/S capture and that using vertical speed instead of FLCH was the correct way to solve that problem. We did get ALT and the FO disconnected the autopilot which significantly increased the work load. I switched to Tower; and shortly after we went from above glideslope to approximately 1 dot below. Speedbrakes were extended; flaps were going to 25 and then 30. Tower issued a low altitude alert; and the FO responded back to glidepath. We never heard a GPWS glideslope warning. After securing the airplane at the gate; all four of us thoroughly debriefed the event. We emphasized automation management and specifically the result of turning off the autopilot which significantly increased everyone's workload. Another emphasis was situational awareness and how the 787 does not slow and descend as quickly as the 777 the FO had previously flown. We also talked about monitor crosscheck and the need to speak up earlier to address an approach that is becoming high and fast. Finally; I talked about leadership effectiveness and my lack of being more assertive instead of allowing the student to continue into that situation. Additionally; during the debrief for my own knowledge and clarity; I asked the other pilots if the speedbrakes had been retracted by 1;000 feet; the autothrottles had remained engaged; the glideslope was captured and if we had met the stabilized approach criteria. The others agreed that was the case. Finally; perhaps the training center could include a training scenario where the glideslope needs to be captured after the FAF with ALT engaged.

column121: First Officer's Qualification Line Check which concluded First Officer's IOE (Initial Operating Experience). First Officer was Pilot Flying. Check Airman was Pilot Monitoring. Normal arrival via SILCN5.KLIDE for ILS 30L at SJC. Shortly after KLIDE; both pilots became aware of flashes of intense blue laser light illuminating the windscreens for 1 to 2 seconds. Pilot Flying continued the approach referencing the instruments rather than scanning outside. Pilot Monitoring reported the threat to NORCAL Approach. After the handoff to SJC Tower; another burst of the same blue laser light appeared; this time from the right side of the aircraft. The flight leveled off at 3;300 feet and the Pilot Monitoring reported the latest burst to the Tower Controller.The distraction of both the laser events themselves and the reporting of the events to NCT (NorCal TRACON) and SJC Tower caused the Pilot Flying to lose track of the briefed stabilized approach plan. The delay in configuration caused the aircraft to be well above the glide path past the final approach fix. There was no way to continue the approach and remain within stabilized approach criteria; so the crew executed a missed approach. SJC Tower Controller instructed crew to climb to 3;000 feet and to contact NCT. NCT issued vectors for an ILS 30L. The second approach was unremarkable; as no further laser activity was noted. The Pilot Flying drew the sunshades on the right side of the aircraft to mitigate the threat of subsequent laser bursts. The remainder of the flight was normal. Following the termination of the flight; the crew [was] informed that the source of the laser activity was some sort of club establishment. They determined that the lasing appeared to be random and not intentionally targeted at aircraft.
column123: Flight was final leg of First Officer's (Initial Operating Experience) with the Captain as Line Captain. Line Captain was Pilot Monitoring while First Officer was Pilot Flying. This was the First Officer's Qualification Line Check. Flight was descending normally via the SILCN 5 arrival for transition via KLIDE for the ILS 30L approach to SJC. Past KLIDE; the Pilot Monitoring noted a brief (2-3 second) series of flashes of bright blue light. The Pilot Monitoring continued to scan for additional evidence of directed laser illumination and landmarks for reference; but did not mention the initial burst to the Pilot Flying. Several seconds later; a subsequent burst of flashes of light appeared to illuminate the windscreens; at which time the Pilot Flying also saw the light.Pilot Flying reported the incident to the NCT Approach Controller; and passed along generalized street locations of the position of the light. Within a minute; at the time of handover to SJC Tower; the flight was subjected to a third illumination burst viewed peripherally by the Pilot Flying; with the Pilot Monitoring noting the dazzle effect of the light on the flight deck windows. At this point; the flight leveled off at approximately 3;300 feet and the Pilot Monitoring contacted the Tower Controller; reporting the continued laser illumination from the same vicinity.At this time; the Pilot Flying noted that the flight was well above the vertical path and was not yet configured according to the briefed Stabilized Approach Plan. The crew immediately began speed reductions and configuration for approach; but soon determined that the flight was 'well above' the glide path and well past the final approach fix. The crew discontinued the approach at approximately 2;700 feet and climbed to maintain 3;000 feet per Tower instruction; and soon switched back to NORCAL for vectors back to final.Subsequent vectors to final and final approach and landing via the ILS to 30L were uneventful. The Pilot Flying drew the flight deck sun shades as a precaution from possible further laser illumination. There were no further illuminations observed during this second approach.It appeared that the source was from a club establishment that was using a laser light source with some reflective device that was reflecting the light upwards. The illumination appeared to be random and unintentional. The atmospheric conditions were clear with very little particulate in the air; which did not refract the laser light when it was directed away from our aircraft; neither crew noted any laser light being directed anywhere other than at our aircraft.

column121: While on approach to Runway 30 and flying the ILS 30 approach the aircraft automation intercepted the glide slope from below after a momentary fluctuation from the glide slope signal. For a split second the glide slope indicator fluctuated from full up to full down about 15 miles away from the airport. At that moment the aircraft automation captured the glide slope from below and the aircraft started an abrupt pitch up attitude. To fly the glide path and at that moment I disconnected the autopilot and continued the approach manually (there was no deviation from ATC instructions). The glide slope indicator did that a second time right before landing again along with the flight director. It took us a bit to understand why that happened; but here is my theory.When landing west in Miami; the airport uses Runway 30 for landing and 27 for takeoff (intersecting runways). Every time an aircraft was cleared to take off Runway 27 the moment that aircraft passed adjacent to the glide slope antenna there was a fluctuation with the glide slope indicator in the aircraft; and with the flight director since they were coupled. We flew this approach many times and on different aircraft since then and every time the same thing happens. When an aircraft is cleared for takeoff from Runway 27 and passes the glide slope antenna we received a fluctuation (full pitch up and down from the flight director and glide slope signal). My recommendation would be for the FAA to investigate and see if this is true. Also for the time being I would recommend the airport uses the RNAV approach to Runway 30; or publish an amendment to the approach to not allow an autopilot coupled approach. Thankfully we caught this situation early when we got the abrupt pitch up attitude of the autopilot following the flight director and glide slope signal; but it can easily turn into an unusual attitude situation if caught off guard.

column121: Prior to departure we briefed the multiple MEL/CDL (Configuration Deviation List)/NEFs (Non-Essential for Flight) on file for this aircraft including MEL XX-XX-XX AUXILIARY POWER UNIT. While the Form sticker said BLEED APU LEAK; the APU as a whole was deferred; so we briefed and followed the procedures for MEL XX-XX-XX as opposed to MEL YY-YY-YY (which was not listed). While in cruise at approximately XA50Z the EICAS displayed caution message BLEED APU LEAK while the APU was inoperative; off and the APU BLEED button was pushed OUT. MEL XX-XX-XX makes no mention of BLEED APU LEAK being an expected EICAS message but the QRH procedure did not make sense to me in this situation. My FO (First Officer) and I decided together it would be best to contact Maintenance for further insight; so I transferred the radios and flight controls to the FO and proceeded to contact dispatch via ARINC (Commercial Radio) at around XA53Z. After a normal exchange with ZZZ1 Radio and patching into our Dispatcher I requested to talk to Maintenance and the Dispatcher responded that 'Maintenance would not talk to me in flight and to follow the QRH' even after insisting several times. We proceeded to follow the remainder of the QRH and had to descend to FL300 and continue the flight with single bleed. Upon arrival into ZZZ2 I made the appropriate entry into the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) for a BLEED APU LEAK EICAS caution message. In my opinion this was a complete breakdown in CRM between the flight crew and Dispatch/Maintenance. I accept responsibility if this MEL was incorrect and should have been YY-YY-YY; but if that is the case; it has been incorrect for 10 days worth of flights. When I saw the APU deferred as a whole I considered that an acceptable solution to an APU Bleed leak; however there is no mention in XX-XX-XX of any special procedure for BLEED APU LEAK EICAS message. Furthermore; I do not have the full information in flight as to why the APU was deferred as opposed to the APU BLEED over a week prior to this event. I believe our decision to contact Maintenance for further guidance via ARINC was sound; and if they had simply answered our call for help we could have avoided descending to FL300 with a single bleed/PACK. There are numerous examples of NTSB accident reports where a safer outcome was achieved thanks to the pilots communicating with Maintenance while in flight; and throughout my training with Company I have always been trained to use all resources available. While I do not know whether Dispatch refused to talk to Maintenance or Maintenance refused to talk to me; I strongly recommend this practice of not allowing pilots to contact Maintenance during irregular situations in flight cease immediately.

column121: I was flying pilot. Approach was fully briefed. AMOS 1E STAR; transitioning to an RNP approach from HADAS. Descending in VNAV Path. Cleared direct MORIA and cleared the approach. Normal stable descent; normal procedures and speed reduction. MORIA waypoint in the FMC must have had 3;000A instead of 3;600A; because we crossed MORIA between 3;600 and 3;000; when the altitude we should cross MORIA at is 3;600 or above. It is on the chart as 3;600A. We became aware when the controller questioned our altitude at MORIA and if we has visual terrain clearance and the runway in sight; which we did. We landed without incident in a stable configuration throughout the approach. Upon reflection; I do not know how that altitude at MORIA in the FMC was 3;000 instead of 3;600. Fatigue a factor after a long overnight flight. 1st time flying the trip with a 4th pilot; which disrupted expected rest pattern. We had multiple GPS outages on the descent and it was distracting as we were discussing the backup plan of an ILS should the GPS not return. Although this is a known issue of the GPS outages in that area; this particular outage lasted much longer throughout the descent than my previous experience. As a result; I had both approach plates queued and it took away from my normal progressive crosscheck of chart against glass routine on RNAV approaches. Regardless of distractions; as the flying pilot I need to do a better job of progressively checking the progress of the VNAV points on the approach. It is not enough to check the altitudes during the approach briefing and then rely on the data to all be correct. Fatigue after a long flight should have heightened my awareness of potential omissions or errors in the data. I have learned from this event and will increase my awareness and cross-check moving forward.
column123: While descending into TLV we were flying the AMMOS 1E STAR to HADAS and then the HADAS transition to  an RNP Approach.  We were cleared for the approach.  We were proceeding when the controller asked us about our altitude.  I said we were going to cross MORIA at 3;000 feet.  He said it should be 3;600 feet. He then asked if we had the terrain in sight. We said we had the terrain and the airport in sight. We then realized that somehow the FMC altitude for MORIA had switched from 3;600A to 3;000.  We continued to the field and landed without any further problems.  First time into TLV. column121: On climbout of ZZZ Flight ABC we experienced a 1000 pound differential between main tanks on initial departure/climb-out. The CA plotted our fuel to the next waypoint which was ZZZZZ and were 1000 lbs below planned. Within a few minutes our fuel was 1500 lbs below planned fuel to the next waypoint ZZZZZ. The decision was made to request priority handling; shutdown engine #1 per the QRH; and return to ZZZ.   I ran the non normal checklists; cleanup items; and reviewed the evacuation checklist. The CA flew the approach and landing which were uneventful; stopped the aircraft on the runway; and had ARFF check for a visible leak. After confirmation that there were no fuel leaks we taxied the aircraft to parking and shutdown the aircraft normally.There are no causal factors by me that played a role in the event.I believe an aircraft history should be pulled to check for any history of fuel quantity malfunctions or any fuel system maintenance has been   completed for this this tail number.
column123: Fuel imbalance developed during climb of 1000 lbs - left wing low within minutes of departure. Leaving 10;000 feet. Cabin crew was asked to perform a cabin walk through with attention paid to possible fuel emissions visible aft of wing from No.1 engine. No visible fuel leak was evident as communicated by cabin crew. We stopped climb at FL260. Position; time and fuel comparison with Flight Plan Review showed us 1000 lbs low at first fix after level off as we ran QRH IMBAL checklist. Subsequent FMC PROG fix (fix name: ZZZZZ) initially showed us estimating 1000 lbs low crossing the fix; then 1500 lbs low; then 1700 lbs low as we approached ZZZZZ. FMC PROG fuel estimate deterioration occurred rapidly over the course of just a few minutes. QRH IMBAL checklist led to Fuel Leak Engine Checklist - parameters indicated probable fuel leak No.1 engine - which led to Engine No. 1 shutdown. All checklists to include precautionary landing checklist were performed. ATC and Dispatch notified. Flight attendants and Passengers advised of return to ZZZ for a precautionary landing.  Single engine landing was performed - Captain flying. After landing we stopped on the runway; ARFF inspected aircraft; found no leaks or damage; and we taxied to the gate. The following AML entries were made: 1) possible fuel leak leading to engine No. 1 shutdown; 2) info to maintenance item: No 1 engine windmilling time 15 minutes; 3) info to maintenance item: landing was accomplished below maximum landing weight. Report made to Dispatch of engine failure and emergency declaration. FO did a great job - especially so given his approx 100 hours in seat and on type. Comment: cabin crew kept cool and were professional. Comment: I made every effort to be both clear and deliberate during each step of the event; to solicit FO's input; and - as we returned to ZZZ - I slowed the aircraft approximately 20 miles from the field and kept the cockpit CRM 'in the green' to the maximum extent possible.

column121: Pre-flight document review: Flight Plan indicated extra fuel; cruise at FL320 due to APU use. MEL 24.01a also listed on flight plan.Arriving Captain (CA) briefed me on aircraft status; MEL 24-XX-X for #1 IDG: Requires running APU; Max Altitude 33;000 feet. Otherwise there were no other problems with the aircraft (as reported by CA).Once in cockpit; CA & First Officer (FO) review of MEL 24-XX-X indicated a requirement to (M) c) 'Operator ensures the APU oil quantity if adequate for the intended flight.'* Both CA & FO interpreted this to mean APU Oil quantity check prior to each flight.* CA called Maintenance to ensure and APU oil quantity check was accomplished.* Maintenance came; read the log book & MEL; concluded that an oil quantity check was not required.Pre & post-engine start procedures of MEL were successfully accomplishedDuring departure (approx. 8;000 feet) got 'VENT SKIN VALVE FAULT'; accomplished ECAM procedures (Blower & Extract to OVRD). QRH and Supplemental procedures were reviewed; flight continued.At cruise altitude (FL32;000 feet) we started selecting potential divert fields with adequate runway length; putting fixes and 100 nm rings around. We updated them along the path; and pre-briefed our plan in case of generator failure.Approx 80 NM SW of ZZZ; got 'ELEC GEN 2 FAULT'; with IDG temp high.  Accomplished ECAM procedures; including disconnecting IDG.  Now single generator ops.At this point PM (CA) requested immediate assistance'; nature of problem; and told ATC we were turning toward ZZZ; required vectors for immediate approach & landing. At this point; CA tasked PF (FO) to take ATC comm; descend & set up for ZZZ arrival. FO passed SOB and fuel state.CA briefed Flight Attendants; Passengers; then took back ATC radio duties. Crew set up & briefed ILS XX approach to ZZZ; reviewed non-normal procedures; contacted ZZZ OPS for gate assignment. FO flew arrival and landing to ZZZ Runway XX in VFR conditions.After landing taxied to gate XX; wrote up Generator #2; debriefed to Maintenance personnel.Cause -1. Aircraft was dispatched away from a major maintenance base with an inoperative IDG/Generator.2. MEL does not clearly describe APU oil quantity check (one time; or prior to each flight).3. MEL does not require the opposite side IDG oil level to be checked.4. MEL category B allows too much time. Believe this MEL should only be for a single flight (ferry) to a maintenance base.Suggestions -1. Review MEL 24-XX; rewrite to clearly define oil quantity check requirements. Ensure both APU & other IDG are serviced/checked prior to EACH flight.2. Review Airbus failure data for IDG's; consider re-setting MEL 24 from cat B to single flight only.3. Review maintenance records for this aircraft; specifically the IDG servicing. Determine why/how BOTH IDGs on the same plane can fail within 3 flight legs/2 days. Possibly the units were both serviced at the same time but improperly; or contaminated; or serviced with improper fluid.

column121: On takeoff roll ZZZ-ZZZ1 at (XA05L); we went through a large flock of birds. I observed numerous birds illuminated by the landing lights passing by both sides of the aircraft. We simultaneously heard several thumps as birds impacted the aircraft nose area. Considering the quantity of birds and impacts; I expeditiously decided to reject the takeoff in the interest of safety; concerned about the possibility of bird ingestion by the engines. Windshield wipers were on high in moderate rain with somewhat reduced visibility.  Estimated speed at the time of the event was between 105-120 knots. We applied the rejected takeoff procedure; stopping with approximately 2;500 feet remaining; notified ATC; and initiated the rejected takeoff QRH checklist. Initially we expected more moderate brake temperatures; and did a 180 turn at tower's direction; expecting that we would later be able to taxi clear. We stopped; completed the Recommended Brake Cooling Schedule charts in the QRH Performance Inflight section; and monitored the Brake Temperature Monitoring System (BTMS) display. As the temperatures increased and we saw brake temp values increasing above 4-5; a decision was made to remain in place and request fire trucks; which were dispatched to our location; arriving after several minutes. In hindsight; remaining stopped straight ahead may have been the best option; however the turn did enable the fire trucks to approach us from the front; which aided in coordination; and possibly safety. The BTMS indications peaked at 7 on most brakes; 8 on two; and one eventually reached 9. The fire trucks monitored us for a time; seeing no indication of fire or smoke; but eventually informed us that we had 2 flat tires; one on each truck. At this point I shut down both engines and we ran the after landing checklist. We informed [the company] and the duty officer what had occurred; as well as coordinating through tower control; who was helpful at relaying information. The fire trucks continued to monitor us as the brakes cooled to the normal range and we coordinated with maintenance to be towed back to parking. Once the brakes had cooled; and the tug crew was on scene; the fire trucks were released; and maintenance towed us slowly to parking IAW their procedures. Maintenance inspections later found bloodstains on the leading edge slats #2 and #9. I wish to point out that the First officer performed in an exemplary fashion; providing extremely helpful and timely inputs and suggestions; his excellent CRM skills undoubtedly contributed to the safe outcome for this event. Thank you for your time. Multiple Bird Strikes on Takeoff Roll; leading to a rejected takeoff.Bird control at ZZZ; bird strike events are frequent
column123: At (XA05 L) we were cleared for takeoff from runway XX. It was a rainy night after a typhoon had passed through; and although the wind was calm; we needed our wipers on for the rain. We were accelerating normally; I called 80 knots and the captain acknowledged. A few seconds later when my eyes were scanning the engine instruments I heard several thumps against the fuselage and heard the captain say 'Birds.' He later told me he said this when he saw many medium-sized white streaks pass through our lights. I saw the captain pull the thrust levers to idle and say 'Reject.' I believe we were about 110 knots (V1 of 143 knots was well above our speed on the speed scale) but I did not notice the exact speed. After a normal RTO procedure; the captain called and I completed the QRH procedure for Rejected Takeoff.  Tower instructed us to make a 180 degree turn on the runway; and after the turn we noticed that the BTMS was climbing more than expected.I calculated for a 120 knots reject at our takeoff weight (345;000 lbs) we should see a BTMS Indication of 5. When the BTMS indication on several brakes increased above 5; I called Tower and requested the fire services to come check for fire and smoke from the brakes. After the fire services arrived and told us (via Tower because fire services did not have an aviation frequencies radio) there was no smoke or fire; we saw one wheel (#2) indicate BTMS 9; and two wheels (#3 and #4) indicate BTMS 8; so asked fire services if any tires were flat. They told us that one wheel on the left side was flat; and at that point the captain decided to start the APU and shut off the engines as it was clear that we would not be taxiing back. I tried calling Company ramp/maintenance on the frequency on the chart but we got no answer; so we asked Tower to relay information to our maintenance and request assistance. Fire services then relayed to us that a tire on the right side was also flat. Maintenance arrived around time XA50 and plugged in to the intercom to let us know they would inspect and decide on a course of action. At XB25 with BTMS in the range of 1-2; they started slowly towing us back to the ramp. We exited the runway at around XC05 and set the parking brake on the ramp at XC25 Z.Multiple Bird strikes on takeoff roll causing a rejected takeoffAirport authority should be better at controlling the birds at ZZZ airport

column121: Approximately 35 minutes from landing at ZZZ at FL 350 we were given a descent clearance to cross ZZZZZ intersection at FL310 while talking to ZZZ center.  The Captain was the PM and set the alt in the MCP; confirmed by the PF FO.  The MAX 9 was programmed for the descent with winds/speeds and confirmed in VPTH.  This was approximately 30nm from ZZZZZ and a timely clearance.  This was almost 5 hours into a 5:XX all night flight.  We were working on canceling a previous write up that was noticed as being incorrect.  As we felt the aircraft descend we noticed that the A/C had put itself into VSPD and that the VDI showed us being approximately 1100 feet high.  The FO placed the autoflight system in LCHG with increased speed to increase the descent.  The plane did not respond to the inputs so the FO disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the aircraft to FL310 at ZZZZZ but crossed approximately 800 feet high at ZZZZZ.ATC very soon after changed us to ZZZ center and nothing was indicated by ATC; and we felt there were no traffic conflicts since the radio had been very quiet recently.I am writing this scenario in concern that the MAX 9 has been having issues with randomly disconnecting VPTH and putting the Autoflight system in VSPD for no apparent reason.  As we look back to the events prior; the Autoflight system was setup for success but somehow it changed modes on us without us immediately noticing.  Moving forward a takeaway from this event would be to obviously pay more attention to modes especially if distracted with other items such as maintenance writeups.  I would have also been quicker to request relief from the altitude restriction although this would never be assured to be given.  I have seen this mode change happen before but have always caught the change in mode before it becomes a concern.

I had 3 main concerns that the Airframe Technician did not address.There is a note under flight crew that states there are no landing penalties with SEC 2 INOP. Yet in the FM (Flight Manual) under F/CTL GND SPLR 5 INOP for loss of Spoiler 5 for SEC 2; a landing distance procedure applies. The Airframe Technician could not explain the difference. I don't know why these contradict.The following note states Maintenance is required to verify sidestick transducers associated with ELACs (Elevator and Aileron Computer) and operative SECs are operative. This sentence seems redundant to what the flight crew are asked to do in the procedure; which appears to ask the crew to pressurize all 3 hydraulic systems and do a flight control check for each operative ELAC and SEC. I say appears because this was far from clear in my conversation with the Airframe Technician. In fact; the verbiage appears different from the FM's description of the flight control check; which states both engines and generators must be running. So why am I doing this at the gate using the blue system on the aft overhead maintenance panel? At this point I am making educated guesses. The system training we as aircrew are given does not support doing this type of deferral. Having been through 4 full-course for the bus; the switch was identified as being for Maintenance use only. If I need to be able to do this type of deferral; I need better and more thorough system knowledge of what I am doing and why I am doing it; either from the Airframe Technician or ground school. I would propose a Pepsi blind taste test - call 3 different airframe technicians and ask them to explain this deferral. My bet is you would get 3 completely different answers. I just don't think our system ground training program supports this type of deferral.For a deferral of this type there needs to be a one paragraph-big picture of what you as the pilot are trying to accomplish. Pilot-to-pilot. If the Airframe Technician can't explain it to me adequately; and neither myself or the FO (First Officer) understands what is being conveyed; then we as a crew cannot meet the FOM requirements to have a complete understanding of the maintenance status. This leads to the philosophical debate of how much information needs to be taught in ground school; but I would submit for deferrals such as this we need much more. In addition; this day we received an email from ZZZ1 Operations stating there was a large weather system moving through; with the likelihood of diverts. Taking an aircraft that required maintenance action every leg to an alternate could be problematic.

column121: FMS data was up-linked as usual.  Being familiar with the route we noticed we were flight planned much further north than usual.  Captain called Dispatch and asked for briefing and was told the route was due to headwinds.  We noticed 3 fixes; YVQ; FOIRD and DEYEP did not upload.   However we verified the distance on our flight plan was within a reasonable distance of what was loaded onto the FMS.  Both of us had heard from other pilots that many fixes in Canada were not in the database and a common practice was to build the fix using lat/long per FOM.  Due to already being hours late for departure and the fixes in question (YVQ; FIORD; DEYEP) were hours away we concluded we would build those fixes after departure.  The Captain also verbalized that he expected the HRDING3 Arrival and we likely wouldn't need those fixes.  The Captain had added an additional 1000 lbs of fuel and our fuel load was planned with those fixes so I felt comfortable that fuel would not be a concern after adding those fixes enroute.  After departure we were cleared to YVQ much sooner than we expected.  We told ATC that we did not have that fix in our database and we would need a moment to insert the LAT/Long.  ATC then asked if we could proceed to FIORD instead.  We said we could and then began to load that as Lat/long.  After a few moments ATC asked if we were proceeding direct FIORD and we admitted we were still in the process of building the Lat/Long.  He then asked if we could proceed direct CHAPO.  This was in our database and we accepted the cleared direct CHAPO and then to the airport.  We landed without any other issues or concerns.I was fit for duty however I was concerned that due to the late departure; the length of the flight and the time of day; we could become fatigued prior to arrival if we delayed departure much longer.  It seemed reasonable at the time that we could add the fixes enroute without incident and without any concern towards our fuel burn.  The issue I was not aware of was the format of the lat/long on the flight plan does not match the format that the FMS would accept.  It took some time of trial and error to discover the proper format.  We did however load the FMS with the proper LAT/LONG and were capable of navigating to the proper fix as ATC requested.  There was however a small delay between when we accepted the direct and actually could proceed direct. And before actually proceeding direct FIORD we were cleared to CHAPO.More training in the building of a fix as a LAT/LONG.  An iPad hyperlink to the instruction of lat/long FMS inputs.  It should be assumed that the need to build a LAT/LONG is time sensitive therefore training and documents should reflect this need.  Adding all fixes to the Data Base that could be reasonably expected with a regularly scheduled flight.

column121: We were descending on the [arrival] from the northeast for an approach to [Runway] XXR in VMC. We had briefed the extensive military training and the towers in the airport area. We were on a vector of approx 260 and were cleared for the visual. I selected 2800 ft. in the FCU (Flight Control Unit) altimeter (the FAF/ALAMO altitude); and we began to descend and start the big left hand turn (120+ degrees) to final. The runway was actually behind the Captain's head and while I was looking outside and dialing in intercept headings; I noticed we were below 2800 ft. I remarked that 2200 ft. was in the altimeter; but I didn't know why. (In hindsight; I must have bumped or spun the dial as I reached up to make heading adjustments). About this time we received a GPWS obstacle alert for the tower we had briefed and was in sight. By the time we climbed back up to 2800 ft. we were high (ILS NOTAM'ed OTS) and I couldn't see [the] runway in the climb and then was slow to get speed back. We finished configuring; ran the checklist and briefed a go around if not stable by 500 ft. [Cause includes] Lack of recency of experience -- I sat for a year before Airbus training after the [other make/model] was grounded. I was on that aircraft [for about a year]; but flew 2/3 to 3/4 as the [relief pilot]. Prior to that; I was out on a 4 yr leave (not flying). Lack of time in Airbus - [this month] was my third full month of being qualified on the aircraft. Not yet comfortable with [the] concept of 'flying the FCU' on visual approaches. There is no way to 'chair fly' the approaches in an Airbus. I don't enjoy this feeling. I've looked for a simple computer simulation program for the FCU; FMA; PFD and ND that I could purchase so I could chair fly some of these situations and see what happens as different modes of speed; alt; and nav are selected; but have not found one yet.

column121: I was Captain on a flight. Once the flight reached cruise altitude I received a call from the [A Flight Attendant] that discussed with me he had a passenger with mask compliance issue and that he had spoken to the passenger several times. He also had the other crew members check on the passenger who was with a teenage child. I asked him to try again; and issue information for noncompliance if needed. Later he called me and said he had attempted to give the information to the passenger who refused it; and also refused to wear the mask. He had asked the teenager to also wear the mask; but the parent had snapped at him and said it was a child and leave them alone. The teenager was acting as if asleep; but not wearing a mask either. I took note of the names; and contacted dispatch. The dispatcher let the Customer Service (CS) know the details and we were told they would meet the flight. As the flight continued; this became more of a distraction as many other passengers were visibly upset about the passenger not wearing a mask; and several stated that it compromised their safety. Several people wanted to be moved as it wasn't a full flight; however the passenger causing the problem was in a premium seat. When we took a bathroom break; passengers approached my First Officer about the issue even though it isn't allowed for passengers to come up front when the cart is out protecting the cockpit. I noted the passenger's name; and personally made a few announcements regarding mask usage in airports and on aircraft along with my normal announcements. When we arrived at ZZZ a CS agent met the passengers. I debriefed this CS agent as I departed who said the passenger also wouldn't take any info from him; and was not cooperative. He stated he would send the names and info to security and that the couple would likely be banned from travel on our airline. I do hope this is followed through on because it was a distraction and I would say to the point of a safety problem as it distracted all of the crew in critical flight duties.

column121: The MCO ILS 18R procedure has a charted altitude from YAGGO (IAF) of 6;000 feet MSL. In the interim would recommend an ops alert outlining this threat and suggest refusing an approach clearance from YAGGO and instead requesting vectors to final to ensure intercepting below glide slope.

column121: We were coming into Morelia. It was night VMC and we carefully set up and briefed the VOR2 to Runway 5. We reviewed it over and over all the way there and were very prepared. We chose the VOR2 approach because the one other time I flew to Mexico they always have us do the approach with the arc; and the VOR2 approach was the one with the arc. Also; we made our best guess as to which approach we would use because there is no way to get the weather there. We sent an ACARS to our Dispatcher and never received an answer. At about 10 miles out; the Approach Controller gave us the VOR1 approach to Runway 5.  We told him we were all set up for the VOR2 approach and we wanted to do that one. He told us there was no VOR2 approach to Runway 5. We have it in our JEPPS and told him we had the plate and we were going to do that approach.  I explained to him that it was too late to change everything. He kept insisting that there was no VOR2 approach to Runway 5; but I was looking at it. We had gone over it numerous times in cruise and we both knew we were OK on all the altitudes and we both felt the safest thing to do was to proceed with what we planned. We are both unfamiliar; it was night in mountainous terrain; and that is not the time to have a head down making changes in the MCDU.  As soon as we made the turn on a left downwind to head towards the Initial Approach Fix; we got the runway in sight and asked for a visual; and were given a visual. Not only do we have an approach that the approach control/tower doesn't have; the names on the plate compared to the MCDU don't match. We reviewed all of them and they all check out DME wise and match the approach plate; but the names (which are letters and numbers) did not match. This is a huge safety concern. If it were IMC it could have ended a lot worse. The only thing that could have helped was to ask approach what runway they were using farther out so we had time to make changes; but I'm not sure they would have been able to tell us.
column123: While [enroute] to MMMM (Morelia; Mexico); we briefed and prepared for the VOR DME 2 approach to Runway 5. We were advised by Mexico Center to contact Morelia Approach and to descend and maintain 11;000 feet. Morelia Approach asked us to report 25 nm DME from the airport. At 10 nm DME; Morelia Approach cleared us for the VOR DME 1 to Runway 5. Because of high terrain on all quadrants; night time; unfamiliarity with the terrain/environment; low to the ground condition; we decided to ask the Controller to keep us on the VOR DME 2 instead. The Controller claimed to not have such an approach available for that airport. We told him we had all the information we needed to safely execute the approach in our FMS database. We sighted the runway and asked for a visual approach. We were granted clearance for the visual approach and flew the profile corresponding to the VOR DME 2 approach which we were all set up for. The landing went on uneventfully.In the future; I'll make sure to ask the Controller as soon as able for the approach in use (there was no ATIS at this airport) so that we can set up for the right approach and thus avoid last minute changes which could be fatal specially at unfamiliar/high terrain airports.

column121: Roughly 2:30 into our flight I/We were informed by the #1 (flight attendant) [name 1] that our 3 other FA's(Flight Attendant) 'were not feeling to well' I asked some basic questions and asked to be updated as more info became available. Minutes later a rest room break and crew meals were coordinated and Name 1 came in the cockpit. During her time in the cockpit she once again told me that over all the other 3 FA's where 'not feeling well' I suggested hydration; inquired about ingestion of food and suggested portable O2. We talked about the possibility of contact with MedLink and even initiated several attempts on both of our iPads and quickly found out that both phone apps were not working. As she left the cockpit I once again asked to kept informed. I then proceeded to transfer radios and the aircraft to FO (First Officer) while I pursued alternate communication methods (VHF Press To Talk) Once communication was established with [company] I passed on the information of 'not feeling to well' gave [employee info] and requested to have medical personal to meet us upon our arrival into ZZZ (ETA at this time 70 minutes) I asked to be patched to MedLink to obtain some guidance. On my conversation with the medlink rep I gave the broad explanation that I had been told (This due to the lack of the [medical form]; I had requested from Name 1 at her earliest availability; in her absolute defense I understood she was alone handling the initial situation; not to mention later with the Pax occurrence) Simultaneously we had coordinated with ATC Direct routing and had gotten a Direct destination. VHF Press To Talk Communication issues arose and several calls were dropped/disconnected. I then was informed that a female pregnant passenger 'was having trouble breathing and did not feel well' At this juncture I verified all systems related to atmosphere conditions in the aircraft and requested even further decent from altitude to alleviate cabin altitude environment in the cabin.After several inquiries to Name 1 and Name 2 of possible scenarios including unfamiliar smells; I informed them that all relatable cabin atmospheric condition indications were normal and that we had the lowered the cabin Alt by 2;500 feet to alleviate the possible situations (to which I was told they 'felt better'). I continued my efforts to communicate with MedLink and once again requested [medical] sheets. (ETA at this point is apron 50 minutes) Considering the information that was passed along and the proximity to ZZZ and com issues I asked Name 1 to prioritize the [medical] Sheets because I would not have enough time (Proximity and Com. Issues ) to address all 4 situations! I was informed that Name 2 was feeling better and was actually present in the last several Inter-phone communications. At approximately ETA 35 minutes I was handed 3 [medical] forms to proceed communications with MED Link. The com issues continued (comm bleed communications etc etc) on top of the high load working environment; as ATC was starting to bring down the aircraft from Altitude. I started to feel out of the green and decided that due to the proximity of our destination; the expeditious handling (ATC) and the last information relayed to us with adjectives that signaled to stability and no apparent incapacitation; to desist with MedLink and concentrate on the arrival. (Also a Medical professional on board had addressed the patients and used the medical kit on Name 1 initiative.An emergency was not declared and landed uneventfully. We made a PA prior to reaching the gate asking the Pax to remain seated so Med personnel could come on board an attend the patients. On arrival at the gate and after shut down checklist items I proceeded to the galley to access the situation. There were several law enforcement officers meeting us initially and talking to the FA's (all 4) [name 1] then told me they had been authorized to deplane so a deplaning process commenced only to be halted 30 second laterby an apparent intervention of a Med Professional who had just arrived. The Main cabin door of the aircraft on both ends was very crowded with no regards to social distancing; I was overhearing and watching as the medical Professional was interviewing all 4 flight attendants. After the health state questions were answered and 'stability' was diagnosed; the Medical professional rushed off; (I assumed and concurred) advised Name 1 that a medical intervention or continuance would be better suited after deplaning. The female Pax patient was also at the cabin door; I had a brief conversation with her as to how she was feeling; to which she answered 'Much better now thank you.' I proceeded back to the cockpit to establish external electrical power and write in the logbook the need to re service all 3 O2 bottles that were used during the flight. By this time in the deplaning process a Maintenance employee had come on board; I told him that I was writing up the O2 bottles (he knew they were used in the flight) I stood in the cockpit door as the deplaning continued and also had a brief exchange of words with Name 3 and Name 1 in regards to their condition and coordinated follow up actions with Medical personnel. Which both acknowledged. I then expressed my concerns and hope you feel better sentiments. I would like to point out that at NO POINT in this entire situation and after queries on my behalf; was Crew incapacitation informed to me or First Officer. The use of FUMES AND ODORS IN THE CABIN was also at NO POINT reported/mentioned; nor we as the front end crew perceive such . In any of those situations I would have not hesitated to [request priority handling] and divert to nearest suitable airfield do to the obvious reasons. In two occasions in the many cabin inter phone communications I inquired about 'crew incapacitation' and my intentions if that were the case. As the other two crew members in the flight neither First Officer or myself had any symptoms of any kind from the start to the end of the flight. First Officer and myself crosschecked our physiological conditions and deemed we did not require any medical assistance of any kind and proceeded to conclude our duties.[A contributing cause] Air Phone App not working. Broad Communication.  This situation had very Broad Human Physiological State communications breakdown due to the inability (at no ones fault) to have Professional medical evaluations in-place. And all seemed to line up to make things worse and get the entire team out of the green in several different moments and several times. I am not satisfied with the lack of SOPS that we all succumbed to once the aircraft was met at the gate by a Overwhelming amount of personnel. As I watched the medical professional interview the 'Patients' In this case 3 out of 4 FA'S (not the Passenger) considering my/our stable health state I knew I had no place to interfere or nothing to contribute. The well being of the 'Patients' was my main concern and I judged the Medical Professionals to be their best alternative at that moment. The lack of functionality of the Phone App was impacting unwarranted and complicated this situation immensely.
