column121: On the approach into ZZZ; already cleared to land via Tower and under visual conditions; we got a blue message on EICAS that stated 'CRG FWD FIREX HI ARM'.  Me and the Captain discussed our options and decided that continuing to land would be our best option. I called the flight attendants in the back to make sure they didn't smell any smoke or realize any abnormalities which they both confirmed they hadn't! The blue Message on the EICAS actually was cleared away prior to our landing. Upon landing; we advised operations of what happened and told them to proceed with care.  once at the gate; the Captain wrote the event in the logbook for further inspection by maintenance.
column123: We planned and briefed a visual approach to [Runway] XXL. About 20-25 miles from ZZZ; we were cleared by ATC for the visual approach to XXL. We immediately turned direct for the visual approach.Shortly after crossing the far (north) shoreline; at about 12 nm WNW of ZZZ; we were over the water; still on a heading to intercept final; when the following EICAS Advisory (cyan) message appeared: 'CRG FWD FIREX HI ARM'. Associated with this was the illumination (in red) of the FWD CARGO fire extinguisher pushbutton; which indicated that the high-rate cargo fire bottle had indeed armed.We were on the lookout for the EICAS Warning (red) message CRG FWD SMOKE; but this NEVER appeared. Because of the lack of any Warning (red) or Caution (yellow) EICAS message and because there was NO secondary abnormality or indication of ANY kind (no other system failure indication and neither the pilots nor the FAs smelled smoke); we did not press the illuminated FWD CARGO fire extinguisher button. We want to emphasize that if a SMOKE condition HAD been sensed- or if smoke or fire had been reasonably-suspected by the crew; we would have IMMEDIATELY pushed the illuminated FWD CARGO fire extinguisher button (to discharge the high-rate bottle immediately followed automatically by the low-rate bottle one minute later) per the Immediate Action Card (IAC); and then transitioned to the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) checklist. But since there was no Smoke/Fire Condition sensed or reasonably-suspected; we did not go this route.Instead; the PF took the radios and instructed the PM to look in the QRH for anything related to the 'CRG FWD FIREX HI ARM' advisory (cyan) EICAS message; but there was zero guidance. There were also no cargo fire detection system failure messages on EICAS. The PM then called the FAs to inquire as to whether or not they smelled any odors or observed smoke of any kind. Neither the pilots; FAs; nor passengers; sensed nor observed any visible smoke or discernible abnormal odors (NOTE: only FAs were asked about odors; NOT the passengers; but we assume the passengers would have told the FAs if they had sensed something). Indeed; the Advisory (cyan) EICAS message disappeared about 30-40 seconds after it appeared; along with the FWD CARGO fire extinguisher push button ceasing to illuminate. This indicated to us that we had potentially made the right call and a SMOKE/FIRE Condition in the FWD CARGO BAY had indeed NOT BEEN DETECTED.The PM and PF discussed their options; and decided the safest option was to continue with the visual approach without pressing the illuminated FWD CARGO fire extinguisher button; BUT also BE READY TO PRESS that button; Declare Emergency; call for Fire Trucks; and continue for immediate landing IF either the Warning (red) EICAS message or ANY secondary indication were to appear. The existing clearance for visual approach was already the most expeditious landing clearance possible; and would get us on the ground the fastest if anything was to go wrong.After landing; as an additional measure of caution; we told Station to alert Ramp Agents to use extreme caution when opening the FWD Cargo Door; just in case there was somehow smoke; odors; or Halon in that bay. After Block-In and during the regular post-flight walk-around inspection; neither the CA nor any Rampers observed ANY signs of fire; smoke; nor odors in; nor discharged Halon extinguisher into; the Fwd Cargo Bay. After the flight; we debriefed with both Rampers and Flight Crew; called Maintenance Control and also warned the next flight crew (who was swapping into the aircraft) about what we had observed.  We planned and briefed a visual approach to XXL. About 20-25 miles from ZZZ; we were cleared by ATC for the visual approach to XXL. We immediately turned direct for the visual approach.After landing; as an additional measure of caution; we told Station to alert Ramp Agents to use extreme caution when opening the FWD Cargo Door; just in case there wassomehow smoke; odors; or Halon in that bay. After Block-In and during the regular post-flight walk-around inspection; neither the CA nor any Rampers observed ANY signs of fire; smoke; nor odors in; nor discharged Halon extinguisher into; the Fwd Cargo Bay. After the flight; we debriefed with both Rampers and Flight Crew; called Maintenance Control and also warned the next flight crew (who was swapping into the aircraft) about what we had observed.This was a tough judgement call.An argument could be made to press the illuminated FWD Cargo fire extinguisher push button; immediately; as soon as it illuminates; even WITHOUT ANY 'CRG FWD SMOKE' EICAS Warning (red) message; as the arming of the fire bottle may be the sole (or advance) indication of a SMOKE or Fire condition.However; the cargo fire protection system is designed so that if all sensors are operational; several sensors must independently sense smoke before the fire detection system determines that a SMOKE Condition exists (resulting in 'CRG FWD SMOKE' EICAS Warning [red] message). Indeed; the QRH has a checklist for EICAS-annunciated 'CRG FWD SMOKE' Warning [red] message; not for Advisory (cyan) or Caution (yellow) messages related to Cargo Smoke.In addition; blowing the fire extinguisher bottles unnecessarily comes with its own issues (albeit with less serious consequences); such as ruining loss of luggage; death of any live animals in FWD Cargo Bay; and small safety hazard to ground crew opening the FWD Cargo door (due to lingering extinguishing material in the bay); following an in-flight discharge of fire extinguisher(s) into that bay. After a call to Maintenance Control; they suspected some sort of fault in the system; but that is unconfirmed.We believe we made the right judgement call; and the entire fellow flight crew- both the FO and FAs- are to be commended for assisting the CA in making the best decisions for safety of flight and ground crew.

column121: I was made aware by the A [Flight Attendant] that we only had three of our four required emergency checklists for both ditching and land emergency evacuations. As a crew we determined this to be a 'no-go' issue; so the A requested one each of the checklists that were missing. We were initially informed that the station didn't have any. Immediately upon being informed of the situation; the Captain became very agitated and began questioning the A as to why we needed the checklists. After an explanation was attempted; the Captain; again in a very agitated manner; proceeded to get on his cell and call the Chief Pilot. As a crew; we checked the manual to confirm that we were correct in our understanding that we had to have four on board and confirmed this to be accurate; to the best of our interpretation. Someone also called for an Inflight Supervisor to come to the gate; but I am not exactly certain which of the crew made that call. A Supervisor did arrive and informed us that they were looking for one; but she had been informed that we were ok using our [tablets] in the event they couldn't find one. At no point up to this time did I feel like anyone considered this more than an annoyance and an unnecessary interruption to their abilities to board the plane for an on time departure. I was even threatened with termination of my job after I said I would not fly if we didn't have the proper equipment. We as Flight Crew are already on high alert where safety and security was concerned; we all felt like no one else cared about anything else but the flight being delayed. I have never felt less supported or more pressured by a Captain in my time of flying. When all was said and done; they found additional copies in the training room; which was what we had recommended about 20 minutes prior.

column121: During climb out; FA (Flight Attendant) called on intercom to report a very loud banging noise behind the wing area; aircraft right side; row 31. FA said it sounded like someone pounding on the fuselage with a sledgehammer repeatedly. We leveled off at FL280 immediately and reduced speed from 280 KIAS to 250 KIAS. I asked the FO to look for a nearby field with good weather.  FA recorded the noise via video on her cell phone and brought it to the cockpit. After reviewing the video; we decided to divert to ZZZ. We notified dispatch and coordinated with the FA's and informed the passengers. During the descent and configuration of the aircraft for landing at ZZZ; with the flaps at 5deg; I called for Flaps 10 while the aircraft speed was at 209 KIAS. I immediately said 'delay that stay at flaps five.' I believe the FO moved the flap handle out of the 5 detent and returned it immediately. The flaps remained at 5 degrees and I continued to slow the aircraft. I called for gear down an Flaps 15; flaps 25; flaps 30 landing checklist. I noticed the stick shaker indicator on the airspeed tape was in an unusual position and cross checked the configuration to find the flaps were at 5. We were at approximately 1200 feet when I announced 'going around'; but did not hit TOGA as I did not want GA thrust. At this point; the FO and I were convinced that the two problems were related; that there was some structural damage to the flaps.We climbed to 5;000 feet and referenced the Checklist for FLAPS - TRAILING EDGE FLAPS DISAGREE. We returned the flap lever to 5; then selected 2. The flaps retracted to 2. The checklist directed us to 'Proceed normally.' We had a discussion about what that meant and were not comfortable with extending the flaps again; with suspected mechanical damage to the flaps already existing. We got a phone patch with Maintenance Control and dispatch on HF and discussed the two issues and our checklist. They had no additional advice. We discussed the plan to land in the current flap configuration (flap 2); using the flap up speeds with Maintenance Control and dispatch. The FO had already assessed the landing distance and we referenced the FLAPS- TRAILING EDGE FLAPS UP LANDING checklist. We landed on RWY XXL at ZZZ; at VREF 40 + 40 + 5. I used auto brakes 3; and rolled to the end of the runway. We had the fire/rescue look us over for damage prior to proceeding to the gate. They reported a large cable hanging from the satellite antenna. The PSEU (Proximity Switch Electronics Unit) light came on after landing. The FO and I debriefed the events in detail post flight and during the next two flights. It was not until the following morning; that I realized that in all likelihood; I caused the flap malfunction by calling for flaps 10 at 209 KIAS. The SATCOM antenna seal failure noise was significantly concerning; and I assumed the flap issue was directly related.

column121: While making our descent at approximately 8;000 feet on the ZZZZZ1 arrival we noticed the Emer/Parking brake 'on' light and a 'PRKG BRK NOT RELEASED' caution on the EICAS Illuminated with a Master Caution. We responded by requesting a heading with ATC and let them know we were working an issue. As the PM; I accessed the QRH and looked up the EICAS message and competed the procedure. We attempted twice to cycle the parking brake per the QRH procedure with no effect. After reading the note in the QRH that states 'Expected potential tire burst during landing' we opted to request priority handling; requested CFR to be available due to a potential parking brake issue. Upon touchdown there was no indication of loss of steering control. We taxed off the runway and then asked CFR to make a visual inspection of the tires and brakes. During the inspection the engine had reached their cool down period and the APU was on and 100%. I instructed the FO to terminate #2. About a minute later and after the CFR's inspection came up negative for any abnormalities we began taxiing via ATC instruction. As I began straightening out onto the taxi line by making a soft left turn the aircraft responded normally and then after several seconds the aircraft started to make an un-commanded right hand turn. I immediately added more left on the power steering tiller and the aircraft initially responded but then went back to the right. I stopped the aircraft; turned on the HYD pump 1&2 from auto to on. The FO open the HYD status page and saw no abnormal indications but there was a cyan advisory message that read EMER BRK FAULT. The aircraft did taxi normal and we were able to taxi to the gate without issue. Once we deplaned the passengers the FO and I were asked to stay behind to accomplish a taxi check. Later; we terminated the attempt to complete a taxi check due to no ground crew personnel available. Crew scheduling was called and they asked us to be at the airport in the morning for sign in. I left the airport via hotel shuttle to the hotel. The Crew was given an early van time the next morning. When we arrived at the aircraft the next morning I was asked to complete the taxi check.  After completing the taxi check maintenance issued MEL XY-Z and released the aircraft for revenue flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I explained to maintenance that there were issues with the MEL and it does not state that I would have to turn on the hydraulic pumps on and that only by turning the pumps on would I get power steering and asked if they still agreed it was good for revenue flight. With the pump issues maintenance decided that they were not going to release the aircraft for revenue flight. Shortly there after I was asked to do a ferry flight with the loss of directional control being the open write-up and source for the ferry flight permit (I'm not sure if that statement is exactly correct but that is my understanding after maintenance explained the process). Once we received the permit we prepared the aircraft with a manual weight an balance and pushed off the gate. During the takeoff brief both the FO and I spoke about how we would have to turn the #2 electric hydraulic pump from auto to on for taxi; and opted to do so for taxi and landing as well. In addition to that we talked about how we would get a 'no takeoff brakes' aural message while executing the taxi checklist and checking the T/O Config. We were also prepared to get warnings and cautions during the takeoff roll due to the 'no takeoff brakes' status the aircraft thought it was in (some of us may have seen something like this in the sims). Lastly we were prepared for the caution 'PRKG BRK NOT RELEASED' once airborne and that we would disregard all of those as long as they were associated with the parking brake being on. When we executed to takeoff from runway XY R at ZZZ; Literally everything we discussed happened. We received continuous master warning light with chimes and 'not takeoff brakes' aural messages until reaching 80 knots and then shortly after rotation we received the master caution for the 'PRKG BRK NOT RELEASED'. After climbing through 2;000 to 3;000 feet the master caution for the parking brake disappeared and was never seen again for the remainder of the flight. When we landed there was no abnormal emergency brake light on or emergency brake fault advisory on the EICAS. The landing and braking was normal as the night before and we taxi it to the company hanger. We were then taken via van from the maintenance hangar to Gate X where we used the jet bridge to get back into terminal on date; [2 days later]. All but the #1 FA was scheduled to take off on the next company flight due to depart [later that evening.] After about an hour sitting at the airport both the FO and I concluded that for safety reasons it would be best that we remove ourselves from the flight due to fatigue. I called crew scheduling on behalf of the FO and myself and we were both removed from the last turn of our sequenceMidway during a sequence dominated by evening flying with late starts and late ends we had to respond to an Emergency landing with the possible loss of aircraft control. Then during the taxi to the gate after a normal landing onto the emergency runway we lost aircraft directional control. The FO and I stayed were asked to stay late to help maintenance and then given minimum crew rest to come back and again to help maintenance early in the morning which was a disruption of our sleep cycle by several hours. After the uncertainty of continuing with our normal sequence we had to ferry a broken aircraft including dealing with a plethora of false warning; cautions; and advisories that would have normally cause rejected takeoffs and emergency declarations. Upon arrival to the airport we would have concluded the completely abnormal and stressful day with a 3 hour sit follower buy a 3 hour evening flight.

column121: Trip started with FA (Flight Attendant) Brief re: Weather enroute and at ZZZ at Arrival; Passengers got same brief. Twice enroute I had FA's take their seats due to Company Alert; and Weather deviation around Utah; no issues...90nm from ZZZ; I briefed the Passengers of the weather and Arrival info; expecting a bumpy ride on the descent; and that we would be landing; and then parking at Gate XX; at XX:35 ZZZ Time; 30 minutes to landing. 20 minutes to landing; I made a PA for the FA's to take their seats; as a precaution. We were cleared direct ZZZZZ and to keep our speed up. We were then cleared to descend via the ZZZZZ and transition to 310 kts.; as we were #1. We were then given a heading for vectors to the ILSXX Approach; and descend to 12;000 ft.At 12;000 ft.; I cycled the seat belt switch and stated 'Flight Attendants prepare for landing' over the PA; early on purpose. We were then given Descend to 8;000 ft.; followed by a turn to downwind and descend to 4;000 ft. We were IMC; it was 9 degrees Celsius; 29.49; and strong winds and moderate rain. Descending from 5;000 ft. to 4;000 ft.; we encountered severe turbulence; the AP kicked off and the airplane pitched up and down erratically.I hand flew the airplane to regain control of our Flight Path; and we settled down at 4;000 ft. and re-engaged the AP. We were then given a descent to 3;000 ft.; followed by a heading to Intercept the ILSXX Approach Course; and cleared for the approach. We broke out at about 2;000 ft.; configured for a full flap landing; encountered 30 kts. headwind on Final; followed by a 10 kt. tailwind on landing; and made a normal landing.As we were rolling out; we got a call from the back (FA's); and the FO (First Officer) answered as I taxied clear of the runway. She informed me that the #2 FA hit the floor hard on her left side; and could we ask for Medics to meet us at the Gate.We were met at the Gate by 2 ZZZ Airport [Officials]; and they checked out our #2 FA. They recommended that she go to the hospital; as did I; so she could get a proper check out. It was also recommended that at least 1 other FA go with her. The FA's then left the aircraft; as did the FO.I stayed with the aircraft; so I could note in the logbook that an aircraft inspection would be needed do to our encounter with severe turbulence. FA did not go to hospital; and returned to work the next day.The 2 AFT FA's did not take their seats when instructed; by my PA: 'Flight Attendants take your seats'. FA's need to follow instructions; i.e. when told to Be Seated; then Take Your Seat.

column121: Aircraft had MEL XX-XX-XA (Slat/Flap System - Flap Subsystem) for FLAP FAULT Status message. Operations were discussed and conducted in accordance with AFM Supplement (performance Penalties for Operations with Airplane Systems Inoperative).Flaps Halfspeed performance penalties were observed on take off performance numbers. Taxied out for takeoff with no unexpected cautions; warnings or advisory messages. Normal take off performed Runway XX ZZZ1. Climbing thru 500-600 feet AGL 'FLAP FAIL' Caution Message Posted. QRH items were accomplished - Flaps had failed in the Take Off Position (8). ATC was advised that we would stop climb at 10;000 feet whilst Dispatch and Maintenance advised of the issue & formulate the best course of action. An emergency was not declared but the nature of the issue was given. Dispatch was contacted initially via ACARS; given the failure and fuel onboard; then subsequently via ZZZ Radio.After discussions with the dispatcher and calculating the fuel onboard all parties were in concurrence to continue to ZZZ. Requested for the Dispatcher to call ahead and have ZZZ ensure the longest runway was made available for the landing and to provide any assistance to facilitate 'short cuts' and weather avoidance to ensure arrival with sufficient fuel. Final cruise altitude was 14;000 feet and speed was 220 KTS to comply with the flap speed restriction and a 10 kt buffer for turbulence associated with weather. ATC was advised and provided assistance in find the shortest way around weather and direct to points on the arrival into ZZZ.Passengers were than advised via PA due to a performance issue that presented itself on the climb out of ZZZ1 the aircraft will be limited to 14;000 feet and a slower speed than flight planned causing our arrival time to be approximately 15 minutes after scheduled arrival. Additionally Airline was aware of the issues and would be watching and looking at any possible misconnects and proactively make any re-bookings if required in ZZZ. Flight Attendants reported no issues with the passengers and everyone seemed to be in good spirits.Thirty (30) Minutes prior to arrival flight attendants reported a strong 'mechanical/electrical' smell beginning aft of the wing root and extending back towards zone 6 in the cabin. Dispatch and Maintenance was advised; flight attendants asked to monitor and advise of any changes and systems were monitored via the various system pages for any indication of further subsystems degradation to which none was found.Flight was vectored to join final for Runway XYL ZZZ. Items in QRH (prior to landing) were accomplished aircraft landed with no issues; exiting Taxiway X and parking at gate XX in ZZZ.
column123: Climbing out of ZZZ1; immediately after take off; received the 'flaps fail' caution message. Completed QRH and made the decision; with Dispatch and Maintenance input to continue to ZZZ. Flight was limited to 15;000 feet and 230 knots due to the flaps being stuck at 8. A much less fuel efficient route; so we required shortcuts when the weather would allow just to make sure we had plenty of fuel. With approximately 30-45 minutes left in the flight the flight attendants reported a mechanical or electrical smell.  No smoke was observed.  We discussed diverting to another airport but our options were limited since we had to increase our landing distance and roll.  Discussed the fact that the smell was probably associated with the failure and no other indications to suggest a fire so we continued to ZZZ.  Landed on the longest runway in ZZZ without any issues. The training received in the sim helped me be well prepared for a situation like this.

column121: We were briefed by inbound crew that they had spoiler float.  When we got to aircraft; we found out that the number 10 spoiler had been deactivated.    Everything was normal below 10;000 feet.  As our speed increased above 250 knots; we had a very slight yaw/roll to the right and auto pilot put in left rudder.  As we climbed our speed increased further and so did left rudder.  Finally; we got over 320 knots; rudder went left with foot pedals to 3.5 degrees left.  Simultaneously; we received the Yaw/Roll Asymmetry EICAS Warning.  The checklist had no procedure.  It just said to land at the nearest suitable airport. Knowing that we had a deactivated spoiler at takeoff; I sent the First Officer back to look at it.  He was unable to see it even with his flashlight.  We asked to hold at present position because we were about to go over mountains.  We reread the deferral to see if this is one of the expected messages we could get as a result of the spoiler being deactivated.  It was not.  We then called Dispatch and got a phone patch to Maintenance Control.  I told him our situation and that I thought the spoiler was floating.  I asked if the Roll/Yaw Asymmetry EICAS was a possible message for our deferral to which he replied no.At this point; unable to determine the cause of the EICAS; we stopped our climb at 30;000 feet; [notified ATC]; found a new place to hold; got permission to dump fuel; and proceeded back to ZZZZ.  Dump altitude was 30;000 feet down to 18;000 feet.  As our speed decreased; the rudder slowly centered.  By the time we reduced to 250 knots; it was zeroed.  Landing was uneventful at max certified weight except we had hot brakes. After we got back to the hotel; I found the inbound crew.  They said they only had 2.5 units of left trim.  This makes sense because at altitude; the IAS is only around 270 KTS and do to speed restrictions at ZZZZ they never went over 300 knots on descent.  After talking to the inbound crew; I then called Maintenance Control and gave them a full in-depth review of what happened.  I asked him to call me when they found out something so we could prepare our rest cycle.Five hours later; Maintenance Control called me and said the rod on the PCU Actuator was incorrect.  Apparently; our maintenance manual has two ways to lock out a spoiler.  One is to use a Rear End Cap and the second is to use lock out plates.  Our Maintenance manuals don't specify which one to use and apparently; they used the wrong method.  After maintenance talked to Boeing; Company is going revise their manuals to reflect the preferred lockout method for each specific situation.  They suspect we had a sheared shaft but won't know until we bring the aircraft home with the spoiler locked out using the Lock Out Plate Method.  Note: We used all 4 pilots in this event.  We had one flying the entire time and that was his only job.  We had one in the back of the aircraft checking out the spoilers and helping with checklists including the diversion guide.  We had another rereading the Maintenance Required Document and looking up the possible EICAS messages we might receive with a spoiler deactivated and assisting with checklists like fuel dumping and giving the flight attendants the brief.  I was overall in command talking to Dispatch and Maintenance Control and coordinating a plan.

column121: It was the FO (First Officer)'s leg into ZZZ. He had briefed the ILS approach which was the landing runway on the ATIS. A flap 40 degree landing was planned. The weather was VFR at the field with a cloud base at roughly 4;000 ft. MSL. ATC had us on a left downwind and turned us on a 90 degree base to final for Runway XXR. The FO had a 2.0 mile ring around the FAF ZZZZZ in the box to be fully configured for landing by then. And to the best of my recollection we were fully configured by the FAF. Runway XXR was in sight and ATC cleared us for the visual approach which was backed up by the ILS XXR. As we turned on to final for the Runway XXR at ZZZ; an accelerated red airspeed zipper came up on the bottom of the speed tape. There was an 'airspeed low' aural warning. The FO pushed the power in immediately; a stick shaker was felt; and the red airspeed zipper came down for the top of the airspeed tape. The FO disengaged the autopilot. There was very narrow gap on the upper and lower red zippers on the airspeed tape and the FO flew between the narrow gap. The FO stated; 'I'm not sure what is going on'. The chain of events happened at a very accelerated pace. Then the aircraft accelerated and the red zippers opened up and I called out ' watch your speed'. I remember seeing the aircraft accelerate near 159-160 kts. and I saw the red zipper on the top of the airspeed tape at 162 kts. In recovery; the aircraft climbed approximately 200-300 ft. We had Runway XXR in sight and the FO was in good position to land. I asked the FO if he was good with landing or if he wanted to do a go-around. The FO elected to continue the approach. Considering what we had just experienced; I felt that was a good choice. The FO continued the visual approach flying on the ILS XXR glide slope and localizer. At 1;000 ft. the FO made the 'stable' call out. At 500 ft. I made the 'stable' call out. We experienced no more airspeed red zipper indications or aural warnings for the remainder of the approach. The FO had a good landing. Upon landing I saw that the speed brakes did not automatically deploy so I manually deployed them. I noted after clearing the runway that due to the distractions; I failed to finish the 'below the line' checklist which I later mentioned to the FO. After the flight the FO and I decided to call Maintenance Control to discuss what had happened to us. Maintenance Control notified me that our Aircraft X had a 'history' of unreliable airspeed and that the FO's pitot tube was changed out. The Maintenance Representative voiced concern that it may be that our aircraft had a much 'bigger' maintenance issue and he wanted to pressure test the pitot system before releasing the aircraft. I put the 'write-up' in the maintenance book. I notified the outbound crew of what had happened and that my understanding was that Maintenance was on the way. ZZZ Operations was notified as well.I agreed with the Maintenance Representative that Aircraft X possibly had a bigger Maintenance issue at hand. When I called out 'watch your speed' as the airspeed was approaching 160 kts.; the First Officer had the same indication and matched mine. I have never seen anything like this event ever. So it seems possible that the airspeed was correct but the red zippers were not correct. Due to the distractions on final approach; I did not complete the Before Landing 'below the line' checklist and this did not register until touchdown when I had to manually deploy the speed brakes.I did not complete the Before Landing 'below the line' checklist. A go-around could have possibly helped in this situation but I do feel now as I did then; that the safest thing to do was land the aircraft straight ahead.

column121: When the fuel stick calculator was first approved for MD11; I had an aircraft that was not on a level ramp (roll attitude) with a number 3 fuel quantity on deferral. I used the online fuel stick calculator to try and verify the fuel quantity in the #3 tank. The numbers were off significantly. I used the maintenance manual procedure to correctly measure the quantity and it matched the known quantity. Afterwards I did more research and found that the web based fuel stick calculator to be inaccurate with the RH wing tanks of all fleets if the ramp isn't level. The problem stems from the fact that there is only one selection for wing tanks and that selection includes both left and right tanks. The calculator gives the same quantity for left and right tanks regardless of the roll selected. I had sent emails to the website contact and the Director of Maintenance office. Periodically throughout the last 6 years I have been sending emails to the office and discussed with my managers trying to get this corrected. About 6 months ago there was a read and sign about the importance of doing accurately sticking the tanks. This prompted me notifying the Maintenance office about the problems with the calculator again. I checked today and it still hasn't been corrected. I haven't heard back and I'm out of ideas to get this resolved. I believe the FAA would be very concerned if they were aware. Correct the calculator by making each tank a separate entry with its own table of quantities instead of combining left and right wings.

column121: During takeoff roll; the jet's nose began to rise when the First Officer (FO) reduced forward side stick pressure to neutral. I visually noticed the jet's nose rising and holding a nose up pitch. The mains didn't feel as if they had extended struts and lifted off. I checked the side stick indications on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and it had been removed so the jet definitely thought we were in the air. The FO applied forward command of the side stick but not enough to force the nose wheel back to the ground. He didn't want the jet to go into the landing mode with max auto brakes already selected as we do normally for takeoff. By this time I checked the airspeed and it indicated 120 KIAS (approx 40 below V1). We continued to accelerate to V1 and Vr. I told the First Officer to use caution on rotation. He neutralized the side stick and the jet had enough elevator command in neutral position to gain altitude. As we moved into the 2nd segment of the climb; the jet flew normally due to the auto trim adjustment after takeoff. When we reached TOC (Top of Climb); we reviewed our actions including trim settings and performance numbers for takeoff and everything checked out as normal. I even remember checking the performance trim setting against the CG trim setting in the Fuel Pred page of the FMGC after engine start (my normal 'gross error' check on every flight). We could only determine that the jet may have been loaded in error or the load numbers were reported with an error to Maintenance so we sent an ACARS message to the Dispatcher asking for a baggage loading audit on arrival. column121: Aircraft X departing ZZZ the left main gear would not retract. Meanwhile we kept monitoring the engine gauges. Everything seemed to be normal and there were no indications of engine damage nor caution/ warning messages; however; we continued with caution to the field.The Captain contacted the flight attendants and they advised him about hearing and feeling the 'bangs' yet no smoke or fire was present in the cabin. The number one priority at the moment for us was to get back and land as soon as possible as we were not sure about the possible external or internal damages that those bangs might have caused. I contacted tower and made sure to have fire trucks waiting for us down the runway. Shortly after landing; we stopped at the runway and asked fire trucks to inspect the engines. There were no signs of damage so we continued to the gate.As of now we are not aware of the exact cause; but we're expecting it to be a mechanical malfunction.

column121: Approaching ZZZ on the ZZZZZ3 RNAV Arrival Runway XXR transition and while joining an approximate 20 mile final; ATC advised us of traffic joining the [Runway] XXL approach course. Traffic was in sight and within a few moments we received an RA command of 'Descend'. The First Officer; who was the Pilot Flying; disengaged the automation and complied with the RA. I advised ATC of the conflict and we continued our approach for XXR with autopilot/autothrottle disengaged. While continuing the approach; we heard an aircraft executing a 'Go-Around' on XXL due to windshear. The F/O (First Officer) and I communicated with one another to 'Be ready' in case windshear was encountered. During the approach I observed unremarkable wind speeds 7-15 knots; however; winds varied from direction as descent continued. The aircraft was fully configured and on airspeed well before 1;000 ft.; landing clearance was received and the Before Landing Checklist complete. At the 500 ft. call; the traffic that we were following to XXR; had landed and was just clearing the runway. Light unremarkable turbulence was encountered during the approach with little fluctuations in airspeed until approximately 200 ft. AGL. At that point I felt the aircraft sink and observed what seemed to be an instantaneous decrease in airspeed. 'Pull Up' appeared on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and then I called 'Pull Up'.The F/O appeared to have observed the same warning and was initiating the escape maneuver. I called 'Windshear' and as pitch and power was applied; the aircraft performed as commanded. No change to configuration occurred until both the F/O and I agreed that the aircraft was no longer in jeopardy. A normal go-around procedure was then completed. ATC advised several aircraft (after our go-around) of 'Microburst Alert! Loss of 40 knots on short final'. ATC gave a frequency change to Departure Control; that neither the F/O nor I heard. After several minutes of distraction; ie. ACARS Dispatch for alternate; excessive radio traffic; communication with passengers; I contacted Tower and communication with Departure Control was attained. A divert plan was received from Dispatch; however; ATC advised that approaches and landings had resumed in ZZZ. Due to the lengthy delayed vectors; we determined that conditions had improved and enough fuel was on board; to attempt another approach and landing. A normal approach and landing was performed to Runway XXL in ZZZ.As a note; the F/O informed me of the two-tone aural alert and windshear warning. It's quite possible that when I said windshear it was due to what I saw on the PFD and or me repeating what was already said by the aircraft. The event happened so quickly I can't recall.
column123: We began our descent on the ZZZZZ 3 Arrival [Runway] XXR transition. As we approached the ZZZ terminal area ATC vectored us off the arrival with an intercept heading and cleared us for the visual approach to XXR. A descending RA ensued during LOC interception to XXR with the autopilot on. The conflict aircraft was in sight and I disconnected the automation and complied with the RA command. This lasted a few seconds and only descended a few 100 feet; whilst maintaining localizer centerline. Once the RA was clear we opted to continue the approach. As we were configuring on the visual approach to XXR we heard an aircraft transmitting to ATC that they were going around on XXL due to windshear. At that time we received no predictive windshear/or reactive windshear warnings and all indications in the flight deck seemed normal. In fact the aircraft we were following to XXR had not transmitted any adverse conditions as well. We continued fully configured by 1;000 ft. AGL to XXR.At approximately 150 ft. the aircraft felt as if it started to drop/fall and the Captain called 'Windshear' and a 'WINDSHEAR' warning followed. I performed the windshear escape maneuver. The threat only lasted what seemed like a few seconds and we were through the microburst. ATC then issued microburst warnings after our encounter. Once we were in the clear; we were vectored back to ZZZ for an approach to XXL. At that time the microburst was no longer a threat and three or four aircraft already landed XXL. We agreed that returning was the most viable option instead of diverting to ZZZ1. We landed with no further incident. It wasn't until we were getting vectored back to ZZZ that the Captain informed me that a PULL-UP was also received. During the event I did not hear or see a PULL-UP warning. I was so focused on not hitting the ground and executing a WINDSHEAR escape maneuver. Before the event we discussed the possibility of a windshear encounter due to the other aircraft go-around. So when the Captain and aircraft called windshear; windshear was on the forefront of my mind and a WINDSHEAR escape maneuver was executed.

column121: Bird Strike On takeoff out of ZZZZ at XA:21Z on date.  We noted a flock of about 50 to 75 birds that were a little more than halfway down the runway.  The aircraft was about 10 knots below V1.  The flock took off around the aircraft. The only bird the crew physically saw hit the aircraft was one that impacted over the captains windshield.   We continued the takeoff roll and the takeoff and subsequent climb were normal. We notified departure control that we had a bird strike. They asked if we wanted to return. We told then to standby while it was discussed. At approximately 8;000 feet; an abnormal high vibration was noted in the N1 section of he right engine. The vibration was noted to be 5.0. The Captain consulted the Flight Mechanic. The Mechanic stated that he thought he felt a vibration and heard unusual sounds in the back. We opted at that point to return to ZZZZ. The Captain assigned duties to each of the 3 flight crew members.  He had the FO fly the airplane. The Captain worked the checklist to begin a needed fuel dump to prevent an overweight landing. The observer FO was designated to contact the company and talk to the flight attendants about the issue. As the observer; I contacted the company via sat phone. Told them we would be returning to ZZZZ; and that we would be dumping fuel.  After that I contacted the purser to advise her we were a return. I asked if she had any questions. She indicated she did not.  I then; under the direction of the Captain; made a brief announcement about the fuel jettison so passengers would not be alarmed When I was done with my duties; I asked the Captain what I could help with. He had just finished up the dump. Finished the checklist and said that he was caught up.  He had also retrieved numbers for both a normal and a single engine landing to runway XX.  At this point we had descended; descent and approach checks were complete; and we were set up for a left base entry visual runway XX.   The approach and landing were uneventful. On the landing roll we encountered another flock of birds and hear a couple strikes forward. Upon exiting the aircraft; severe damage to the right engine fan and shroud were noted.
column123: At 10 knots prior to V1 we encountered several bird strikes at ZZZZ Airport on takeoff. At least 50 plus birds flew from the right to the left side of the aircraft and one bird hit the airplane just above the Captains head and some on the right side of the aircraft near the right engine. It was my takeoff (FO) and we continued. The Captain reported it to ATC. ATC asked if we needed to return to the airport and the Captain initially said that we do not need to return. We weren't sure of the damage at that moment and shortly there after around 8;000 feet the relief pilot said the right engine FAN vibrations are at a max of 5.0 with all other engine indications normal. The Captain then called ATC to request a level off at FL150 and I maintained a reduced airspeed of 280 knots to avoid any unnecessary stress on the airplane. At that time the relief pilot was communicating with dispatch per the Captains request and the flight attendants as to the status of our aircraft; plus a PA to our passengers to keep them all informed of our situation. The Captain was in constant communication with ATC.The Captain then consulted with maintenance and he told us it was really loud in the aircraft; so we all were in agreement and made the decision to return to the airport.The Captain then told ATC that we wanted to return to ZZZZ; but we need to jettison fuel to be able to land below landing weight. The Captain then requested to jettison fuel with ATC. The Captain was running the QRH to jettison fuel as I followed along and the Captain also was getting our performance numbers for landing.We received authorization to fly in the vicinity of the airport and jettison fuel for 14 minutes. Then the Captain requested runway XX for landing and I (FO) shot the visual approach and landed. As I was rolling out around 130 knots we encountered numerous bird strikes again and reported that to the tower and ground frequency. At 60 knots the Captain took control of the aircraft from me and taxied to our assigned parking. On my post flight walk around I noticed severe damage to the inside cowling and all the fan blades on the right engine. Plus a marking above the Captains L1 window.I would suggest that ZZZZ finds a method of bird control at their airport to avoid this situation from happening again to another aircraft.

column121: During the final climb phase of Aircraft X (ZZZ-ZZZ1); the aircraft experienced a high-altitude decompression event; the result of a L BLEED DUCT Master Warning and subsequent automatic left and right bleed valve closures. The crew requested priority with ZZZ2 [Center]; initiated a descent and diverted to ZZZ3 for a precautionary landing. The process and procedure of preparing and securing the aircraft for the abnormality; as directed by the appropriate priority and QRH Checklists; was complicated and slowed somewhat by a temporary vision impairment of the Pilot Monitoring (myself) due to an unknown dust or contaminate in the smoke goggle portion of the mask during donning. While climbing through FL316 to a filed cruise altitude of FL360; we were alerted to a potential bleed duct leak by a triple chime; aural 'Bleed Air Duct' and red EICAS message of 'L Bleed Duct'.I would STRONGLY suggest that maintenance inspect; clean and blow out the crew o2 masks / smoke goggles on a regular basis. These masks are checked for air pressure and operation by the flight crew every morning; but the condition and cleanliness of the actual mask is widely unknown until it is needed. The white powdery dust that blew all over my face and lap during the initial use of this very important safety gear could have been a lot worse than it was; possibly creating a crew incapacitation during critical emergency operations.

column121: Obviously the instructors and check airmen doing this have no idea of the possible repercussions of this act. To quickly review; like inputs are summed; opposed inputs are cancelled. To actually have your hand on the side stick while the other pilot is flying can have catastrophic consequences. A subtle; unconscious input by the pilot monitoring say during the flare or strong crosswind landing to 'help' the pilot flying may generate a dual input warning but by then recovery may be unattainable. The reason given during training is to be quick to push the take over button. I can have my hand in my lap and in 1/2 second can reach to the button; depress it; and have control of the aircraft. When flying a conventional airplane; one with a control wheel; does the pilot monitoring actually have their hands on the controls while the other person is flying. No! The PM can have their hand on the side console; rubber grommet around the base; or arm rest; but should not be actually on the side stick while the other person is flying. Stop this training practice.This is the X time this year I have flown with a new pilot where they have actually had their hand on the side stick while I was flying the airplane. This is expressly forbidden in the pilots operating manual; 'Only one person will fly the aircraft at a time'. They all tell me that is the policy during training that the instructors and check airmen have been telling them to do this not only during training but on their initial operating ride as well!

column121: Early morning departure from ZZZ Runway XXR. Cleared for takeoff direct ZZZZZ. On the takeoff roll all engine indications were normal. As I pitched up to takeoff and receiving positive rate from my First Officer I asked for gear up. As the gear was in transit we heard and felt a bang. At first we thought it was gear related then the gear was in and another bang is heard. At that point tower tells us that we have 'sparks' coming from our engine. The bangs were intermittent about every 3-5 seconds. As we analyzed the situation we knew the right side engine was the issue sign ITT (Inter-stage Turbine Temperature) was hotter then normal. Once I seen the ITT start to shoot up into the red I put the engine from TOGA to Climb and ITT some what reduced. By this time we were also reaching 3;000 ft. so I was in the process of leveling off and reducing power. At no point did we get any alerts or indications that anything was wrong other then the weird ITT indications. The bangs only happened when throttle was in TOGA position. Once level all indications were green and we quickly decided to return to ZZZ. We requested priority handling and received vectors back to ZZZ. I contacted the Flight Attendants and told them we had issues with the right engine they quickly responded with 'Yeah; we know it was really loud back here'. Asked if any smoke is present they said no. Told them were going back to ZZZ and that everything is good and normal as of now and if that changes I will let them know. Continued to land Runway XXR with no other engine indications. We told the Tower to have fuel trucks waiting just in case of a fire. Upon landing we stopped on the runway; and Tower tells us no fire is visible and I make a PA letting everyone know of the situation and that we will be returning to the gate. Fire Trucks verified no fire and followed us back to the gate. Engines were working as normal on landing and taxi as if nothing happened.

column121: I was PF (Pilot Flying) on this leg; we were cleared to descend via KIDDZ 3 RNAV Arrival into HOU. Winds aloft were light and we were about eight miles behind a Company aircraft also following the same clearance and flight path; which led to some intermittent moderate turbulence. We were at 12;000 ft from the crossing restriction at SNIFY [when we] encountered the wake turbulence. I elected to descend early to 11;000 ft to avoid the conditions.The first attempt to do this I selected the ALT INT option to start the descent early to the next 11;000 ft restriction at RVEEE. That did not work for some reason; and the turbulence was not letting up; so I set the altitude to 11;000 ft from 6;000 ft (from the descend via clearance) and descended in Vertical Speed mode to get the aircraft down. I selected VNAV again once established at 11;000 ft to continue the arrival. Shortly after reaching 11;000 ft and selecting VNAV; we crossed RVEEE and I was expecting the aircraft to descend to make AAHZZ at 10;000 ft. The aircraft did not descend and I couldn't figure out why; and immediately was in the Yellow if not Red per the RRM (Risk and Resource Management) model. I quickly figured out the altitude selection in the MCP (Mode Control Panel) was not reselected to 6;000 ft. I quickly set the lower altitude and initiated a descend as quickly and safely as I could; but the delay in descent put us 700 ft high over AAHZZ. ATC didn't say anything; nor did we as there weren't any other aircraft conflicts.It is vital to maintain situational awareness and vigilance especially when changing descent modes during an RNAV arrival. The turbulence distraction should have been a trigger to do so to avoid errors such as not resetting the clearance altitude after reselecting the original MCP vertical mode VNAV. Another option was to request vectors from ATC or a delay vector to laterally escape and avoid the wake and alleviate the VNAV demand until we were well clear of the rough air.

They can be easily confused for a barrier on the runway if you are not expecting them. This can cause an early rotation or a rejected takeoff. In our case we did and aggressive rotation. It a perfect set up for an accident.My last flight I again took off from Runway 9C and as I was partway down the runway; I noticed the LAHSO lights were if fact on again during takeoff. Knowing that this was the LAHSO lights; I knew this was not a problem but my First Officers were a bit concerned as they had not seen these lights before. We don't need someone making an unnecessary high-speed abort. This is going to cause an accident and maybe get someone killed. These lights should never be on when we are taking off. It is very disconcerting to say the least. We notified tower that they had the lights on when they told us to go to departure frequency.

column121: Upon departure and climbing through 1;500 feet MSL; a Master Caution followed by Speed Trim on the overhead panel alerted us during the acceleration phase from flaps 1 to flaps 0. Shortly thereafter; I believe the autopilot tripped off or I disengaged the autopilot leaving me to manually fly the aircraft. It was then I noticed that my control wheel trim switches were not working. I asked the FO (First Officer) if his control wheel trim switches were working; and he said NO as well.It was then I extended the manual trim handle and proceeded to manually trim the aircraft. I also asked the FO to set speed to our current speed (approximately 210 knots) so to minimized as much trimming as possible. I then asked what Master Caution light illuminated; and the FO responded it was associated with the Speed Trim Light. I then called for the Speed Trim Fail Checklist in the QRH. The FO completed the Speed Trim Fail checklist; but there was no further direction in that checklist other than to continue normal operation. Nothing led us to refer to any other checklist such as Stabilizer Trim Inoperative due to our electric trim was not working.I then asked the FO to look and see if there was an Electric Trim Failure Checklist; because we did not have a jammed stabilizer nor a runaway Stabilizer Trim and the aircraft was flying just fine with the manual trim wheel. With me flying the aircraft and the FO trying to assist with ATC; QRH; while trying to assess the true problem; it apparently created a scenario where he simply overlooked the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative Checklist Condition statement.I was busy hand flying the aircraft; and with the distractions of talking to ATC and keeping the aircraft in trim; I did accidentally allow the aircraft to descend as much as 400 ft. below our assigned altitude of 3000 ft. MSL; but recovered quickly before ATC inquired. After realizing the additional task loading we were creating on ourselves; I elected to return to ZZZ without further troubleshooting. This set in motion a different set of task priorities for the FO in order to coordinate our return with ZZZ Operations and Maintenance. We evaluated our landing weight to be below MGLWT (Maximum Gross Landing Weight) and the only other immediate concern at the time was getting a longer final so we could get the aircraft configured and trimmed without getting behind in controlling the aircraft again.Once we caught up with our duties and were turning on final; I inquired again with the FO as if we had forgotten any possible QRH checklist for our condition. He again confirmed he could not find anything else in the QRH for Electric Trim Failure. That didn't sit at ease with me; as having recently completed the MAX training of runaway stabilizer. I remembered hand flying and trimming the aircraft and there was also something specific with the flap setting chosen; I just couldn't remember at the time. Even selecting flaps 30 for landing; something was still concerning me that I briefed the FO that in the event of the go-around; I may need help trimming the stabilizer through the configuration changes. The landing went uneventfully and taxiing back I still had that feeling we forgot a checklist in the QRH. After reaching the gate we verified; along with the Mechanic; that the electric stabilizer trim was indeed inoperative. I then had time to reach for the QRH myself and search through the checklist choices. It was then I found the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative Checklist; where the Condition and Objective statements under the title clearly stated and matched what our situation was.When I showed the FO the QRH Checklist for Stabilizer Trim Inoperative; he said he completely missed that as he was looking for something about Electric Stabilizer Trim Fail as I had called for; since the Manual Stabilizer Trim was working just fine.In the heat of the moment; sometimes confusion can take place and miscommunications can be amplified. In this case it was a Speed Trim Caution Light that lead us into the QRH; but in a correctly identified non-normal would of kept us into the QRH until all the proper checklists had been completed in this scenario. I recommend [adding] to the Speed Trim Fail Checklist a step prior to '#1 Continue normal operation.' I would word it (Condition: If stabilizer does not respond to control wheel electric trim inputs: Go to the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative checklist on page XX.)

Due to wind shear alerts on the approach; and WX moving toward the field; we elected to do a TOGA take off. We were on the ZZZZZ Departure; but were given a heading immediately after takeoff to avoid a cell. Approximately 5-7 min after takeoff; and cleared to climb to 16k feet; we got a 'DOOR  L EMER EXIT' EICAS message. The First Officer (FO) declared it was his aircraft and we identified the need to level off at 10k. I notified Departure; and they gave us clearance to stop climb at 10k. I told him we were troubleshooting and we would need to return to ZZZ. We requested priority. The FO took over the radio; and I was tying to determine the problem and keep the passengers and flight attendants appraised of the situation. I briefed the flight attendants a couple of times on ALL; and made a PA to the passengers. The number 1 Flight Attendant told me that a cover for that over wing emergency exit had fallen off. I notified the company through ACARS that we were returning to ZZZ and they acknowledged. Meanwhile; the weather had hit the airport; and they asked us if we wanted to land with a tailwind; or if we wanted to wait for the field to be turned around. (Landing west now)We told them we would prefer to land with a headwind. They told us to expect the RNAV to [Runway] XX because the ILS was not up yet.  We accomplished the descent checklist and set up for the RNAV. Approach later told the plane ahead of us that the ILS was working now; so we set up for that while being vectored. The weather was not optimal - there was a strong rain column over the field; about 1/2 way down Runway XX; but we had a good visual on the field.  We discussed the need for a hard go-around if needed.  After an outstanding landing from the right seat; we were met by possibly every priority vehicle at ZZZ as we taxied clear of [Runway] XX. They checked that we did not need any further assistance; and the on scene commander followed us all the way to the recovery gate.  After evaluation by maintenance; we were told that the cover that had fallen off is held in place by a rather flimsy metal clip. There is a magnet on the cover; and when the cover is removed; it causes the alarm that we received. He said that the covers are routinely removed when the plane is in the hanger; and that they can sometimes get loose. They eventually adjusted the clips for both over wing exits and returned the aircraft to service. We flew it to ZZZ1 and back with no further issues.I was told that; had the handle been pulled on the emergency exit; due to the plug nature of the exit; the hatch would most likely not have moved. The slide; however; would have deployed. This would have caused major controllability issues. Additionally; after discussing it with safety; I was told that this is not a common problem; but it is one that could use greater awareness for pilots. The metal clip holding the emergency exit cover in place was either loose or had not been seated properly.  Had the cover fallen off at altitude; the EICAS would have asked for an emergency descent to 10k; which would; obviously be very dramatic. Our air interrupt and any further similar events could be avoided if the pilots were trained to replace the cover before as step one in trouble shooting.

column121: During RNAV (RNP) M approach to ZZZ Runway XX; the crew of Aircraft X was made aware of company traffic (Aircraft Y) approaching ZZZ with a similar arrival time; as well as another company aircraft (Aircraft Z) requesting departure clearance. After descending on the approach to an altitude where the crew could remain VMC; the crew cancelled IFR to allow company traffic to obtain a clearance. Aircraft X crew broadcasted their position and FMC predicted landing time; and stated intentions to land Runway XX on CTAF. ZZZ radio advised Aircraft Z that they were released for departure. However; when Aircraft Z did not immediately depart or make a radio call stating intentions; the crew of Aircraft X queried them on the company frequency. Aircraft Z responded that they were not aware of their release; and then again contacted ZZZ radio to confirm.After receiving confirmation of their release; Aircraft Z announced that they were departing Runway YY. At this time there was a lack of clarity where Aircraft Z was on the airfield; and the crew of Aircraft X became uncomfortable with the developing situation. The crew discussed that there may be a need to discontinue the approach; but made one more attempt to communicate with Aircraft Z. Based on the presumed impending missed approach; the PF delayed calling for further configuration; and continued toward Runway XX visually; while the PM broadcasted Aircraft X's position; and attempted to determine Aircraft Y's position on the airfield. Ultimately; the crew initiated a non-standard missed approach with a climbing left turn; and announced on CTAF that they would be holding visually over the water north of ZZZ at 1;500 ft. During the missed approach turn; the crew experienced a GPWS caution for terrain that they visually determined to not be a factor. However; the PF did increase thrust and pitch to clear terrain by a wider margin. During visual holding; the PF maintained aircraft configuration at flaps 5 to allow for lower air speeds and improved maneuvering. While Aircraft X was completing a visual 360 degree turn north of ZZZ; Aircraft Z departed Runway YY with a left turn to the southeast; and Aircraft X announced their position and intention to land Runway XX on CTAF. At this time additional company traffic Aircraft Y broadcasted their position and estimated landing Runway YY within 1 minute of Aircraft X.Due to weather observed moving in southeast of ZZZ; the crew of Aircraft X determined the prudent action would be to make an additional visual holding pattern north of ZZZ to allow Aircraft Y to land; as opposed to flying a VFR downwind to Runway YY. To ensure Aircraft Y would have enough time to clear and that both aircraft would not be on approach from opposite directions at the same time; the PF of Aircraft X elected to enlarge the visual holding pattern to the north. Again; Aircraft X crew announced their position and intentions on CTAF. During the visual maneuver; the crew received another GPWS caution for terrain north of them and initiated a turn to the west. Visibility and cloud clearances were excellent in the area and the crew had all terrain well in sight. After Aircraft Y landed and while Aircraft X was maneuvering for a visual approach to Runway XX with raw ILS data tuned and monitored in the background; the crew observed that a cloud had blown in from the south across the final approach path to Runway XX; requiring the PF to fly below the glide path to maintain VMC. During this approach on short final; while on visual and ILS centerline but below glide path at approximately 800 feet; the crew received a glide slope alert which was silenced; and a persistent GPWS caution annunciation. Again; the aircraft was observed to be on centerline and well clear of all terrain; but in an attempt mitigate the GPWS alerts; the PF offset slightly left and continued a descent toward the runway. At approximately 600 feet the crew received a GPWS warning and command of pull up. The crew again observed that they were clear of all obstacles and continued to a landing without further incident.After reviewing the event; the crew determined that they should have initiated a missed approach and turn sooner and at the first indication that opposite direction traffic may become an issue. This would have prevented the crew from descending below 1;000 feet without being fully configured; and may have prevented the first GPWS caution. Although the weather supported holding in VMC; the crew could have requested an IFR clearance to climb to a higher holding altitude and follow traffic into Runway YY.

column121: We were descending via the SNDIA 4 for the ILS Runway 8. Passing ASIDE intersection I noticed that my MFD (Multi Function Display) screen when zoomed in didn't exactly match the Captain's side. As we continued down the arrival we received a clearance for the ILS 8 approach. Going through about 8;000 feet both the Captain and I were looking at a very large discrepancy now between our two screens. The autopilot was coupled to the Captain's side so it was still following what we thought was the correct track. I switched to green needles in anticipation for the turn to the localizer off the transition route and now noticed we were flying through the localizer but our FMS still had us at the previous point prior to the turn. Both the Captain and I were unfamiliar with the airport especially at night; so we were planning on flying the full approach. ATC then asked us to report any GPS issues; which I had responded with yes we believe we have lost GPS; looking for vectors.At this time I had gotten visual contact with the runway as well as the Captain who was flying. We both agreed that due to our current location it was best to discontinue the approach and try again. We went around and got vectored around. The second approach had no issues as we got vectors to final off the localizer. It was later found out that the military was jamming the GPS signal. We also received a terrain INOP yellow message displayed on our MFD's for a few minutes but no associated EICAS message. A GPS signal lost was never displayed on either FMS. We do not know how long or how far off course we were on the arrival as it appeared okay on our end; and ended up missing the turn to the localizer as our FMS was telling us we were several miles behind our current position. ATC needs to be aware of potential military GPS jamming so they can provide that information to the pilots. We did not see a NOTAM in ABQ for jamming either. Given it also being night around terrain; ATC should have provided vectors from the beginning and not the RNAV arrival since GPS signal could not be guaranteed.

column121: Winds 140/15 gust 25; Tower broadcast landing aircraft report +-15 kts on final. Regional jet taking off ahead of us showed large downwind drift after rotation. Prior to takeoff I briefed TOGA on takeoff roll if necessary. We tracked center-line until 110 kts then the aircraft weather-vaned 30 degrees to the left (gusts exceeded rudder control). If we rejected we would have departed the runway. I applied full right rudder; right aileron and selected TOGA with the aircraft correcting and the left main gear on the left runway edge striping. Rather than risk further drift to the left I elected to rotate 15-20 kts prior to VR. After becoming airborne the right wing dipped 7-10 degrees; I neutralized aileron and rudder; called for gear up and continued the climbout. We immediately reported the windshear (horizontal) and I believe we were the last takeoff out of ZZZ. We reported the incident to Dispatch and he told us all the airports in the area were ground stopped.I believe we encountered a sudden horizontal windshear; with resulting side gusts; exceeding the aircraft capability to maintain heading at a critical phase of takeoff. I believe a runway change to [Runway] XXR would have aligned us with the wind and prevented this incident.ATC should not hesitate to change runways so that aircraft are taking off into the wind. Especially when the winds are strong and gusty crosswinds.
column123: I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) and we were cleared into position and hold for Runway XYR full length in ZZZ. The winds were gusty but nothing beyond our limits. ATIS reported 140/17G27 with LLWS in the area. In addition Tower had relayed to landing aircraft for XXL reports of +15 kts. on final near 500 ft. As we entered the runway the CA (Captain) PF (Pilot Flying) mentioned; 'We have TOGA available if we need it.' There were no reports by previous aircraft; a company 777 and an RJ; of any airspeed gain or loss on takeoff and there were no LLWS warnings issued. We were cleared for takeoff and I believe Tower reported wind gusting to 24; still well below our limits. The CA PF added power normally and we began the takeoff roll. The engines came up normally. The airspeed moved rather quickly beyond 80 to 90 kts as the engines stabilized at FLEX and I called 90. As I looked up from the engines and the airspeed the aircraft began to move off centerline slightly then began a more rapid turn to the left to the point of the right mains being to the left of the centerline. At this point I called out to the CA PF; 'Centerline; centerline; centerline.' and we continued a drift to the left. I looked down to begin stepping on the rudder with the CA PF to maintain directional control and it appeared full right rudder was applied. I then looked up and was about to call reject when the CA PF began to pitch up as we slowly regained directional control. Our airspeed was not yet at V1; probably 10 kts.; perhaps a little more below. We were approximately 3000 ft down the runway I believe but I'm not certain. At this point a reject was out of the question as we were airborne and turning back towards the centerline. The CA PF held a very slight pitch up and allowed the aircraft to slowly accelerate and fly out of the windshear. As we began a slow climb; speed was still low. The CA PF did an excellent job keeping the airplane from settling back to the ground without excessive pitch and at a very slow airspeed. Somewhere in this event the CA PF went to TOGA. I have no idea when but I believe it was shortly before we became airborne and turned back toward the centerline. The aircraft continued a climb and we climbed out with a normal takeoff out of about 200 ft. There was never a call of windshear by the aircraft or a noticeable change of the airspeed. I was 100% looking outside after 90 kts. to assess where we were and what I could do to help the CA PF control the aircraft. From the time of calling centerline to the time of getting airborne could not have been more than 3 seconds. It all happened incredibly fast. It was very smooth and not a single bump climbing to 800 ft. or so. The entire scenario lasted maybe 10 seconds but it felt like 20 minutes. I'm still not 100% certain what caused the drift to the left. The turn matched with the strong crosswinds. I'm fairly certain they were the cause but it could not have been the same wind speed as what the ATIS reported and what Tower stated. It was as if we entered an area with a significant wind increase that temporarily approached our crosswind limitations. At the slower airspeed and less rudder authority the capabilities of the aircraft may have been briefly exceeded until we accelerated and got more airflow over the rudder. I've taken off near crosswind limits before and I've never had this type of event. Not even close.I'm not sure anything could have been done differently. The CA mentioned the availability of TOGA due to the winds which was crucial to the end result I believe. My call of centerline brought the CA into action to which he stated was a good thing. We were both very surprised by the rapid turn; like the startle effect almost. The only thing I could have done was call reject sooner but it was not necessary until we made the rapid turn to the left and subsequently became airborne.

column121: The Runway Awareness and Advisory System (RAAS) on the 737 MAX is a great Situational Awareness tool. However; I experienced what appears to be a design flaw in its triggers for approaching crossing runways.During takeoff on ZZZ Runway XX; Runway XXR crosses Runway XX about 700-800 feet from the threshold. Following FOM Guidance setting the thrust for takeoff; RAAS alerted us with 'Approaching Runway XXR' during a critical time in the takeoff roll. Coordination between the Pilot Flying and Pilot Monitoring for setting takeoff thrust is absolutely critical and the distraction of an unnecessary warning compromises safety. The trigger for that particular warning to be silenced is 40 knots ground speed or greater. The thrust lever angle/setting or thrust mode in TOGA should also cancel the warning.

column121: For this flight; I was FO PF (LCA) ZZZZ-ZZZ as Aircraft X. We had completed the before start procedure/checklist and were preparing to request a push-start clearance when the Captain noticed a STATUS message; CENTER FUEL PUMP L. The parking brakes had been released; thus initiating the Block-Out phase of flight. Therefore; we were initially planning to address the issue once airborne (write it up in the aircraft logbook).In less than a minute after receiving the STATUS message; we received an amber Advisory message; CENTER FUEL PUMP L; which was quickly followed by an amber EICAS CENTER FUEL PUMP L message with an associated checklist. Per our procedures; the captain asked me to reference the checklist and perform the tasks as required. Note; we were still at the gate with the engines shutdown. Following the checklist as instructed caused the message to blank. At that point; the Captain referenced the laminated flow chart; which stated we could continue and write up the problem upon landing. I recommended to the Captain against following the flow chart; rather to write up the message and to contact dispatch/maintenance; which he and the crew agreed was appropriate.Prior to calling Dispatch; we decided to take a look at the Company Document; as well as the ETOPS Critical systems section of the FOM; to see what guidance they provided; although the flow chart didn't state this was necessary due to the message going blank after completion of the non-normal checklist. What we found was quite alarming.First; this is an ETOPS Critical system; which requires the PDSC to be completed again prior to block-out. Following the flow chart would have missed this important step. Second; per the Document; a reduction of 80;000 pounds of payload was required to comply with the Document ZFW limit reduction. Again; following the flow chart would have caused this to be missed.Last; the Document specifies there needs to be enough fuel in the wing tanks to ensure your ability to reach the suitable airports if the remaining center tank pump fails. There is no way the crew would be aware of this requirement if they simply followed the flow chart; continued as directed (the message blanked after completing the non-normal checklist) and wrote the issue up upon landing; as directed by the flow chart.The flow chart; while a useful tool; needs to be modified.The flow chart states to reference the appropriate Document if a message doesn't blank. I would suggest modifying the flow chart to always reference the Document and reference ETOPS Critical Systems chart when appropriate prior to making a determination to proceed and write up an issue upon landing. Further; it's my opinion to write up any discrepancy occurring before takeoff and have maintenance address/defer it before departing is the safest course of action unless the item is crew deferrable.

column121: We were on a visual approach to Runway 36L in MEM on a clear and light wind day. I was the Pilot Flying and was hand flying. We were lined up with Runway 36L and right on the LOC. Around 100 feet I heard ATC say; '36 left traffic go-around'. There was no call sign but as we were the only traffic besides the Company behind us and as there was no time to discuss it I said 'Go-Around' and we went around. A true startle event. Switching to Departure; they asked the reason for the go-around and we said; We don't know and we were told to go-around!" We went around the pattern and then landed without further event. We asked Tower why we were told to go-around and they said an automated system said we were lined up with Taxiway Mike; the parallel to Runway 36L. And they have to issue a go-around instruction; regardless if they/we appear to be lined up with the runway. We got the Tower number after we got to the gate and the Captain called them after getting back to Operations. The Supervisor said that there is a new part of the ASDE system that provides warnings if airplanes are lined up with taxiways instead of runways. They have had issues with the system and have turned it off on certain parts of the airfield. He asked us to be sure and put in a safety report on our end as they are trying to fix the issues.Faulty alert on ASDE Taxiway Safety Logic. Recommend De-activating the ASDE Taxiway Safety Logic due to the faulty alerts it is giving. Or fix the logic and perhaps have different times it is in use; like IMC; etc."
column123: First Officer was around 100 feet above touchdown zone; clicked off auto throttles. We heard 36L traffic go-around"; without our call sign being used. We went around as instructed. When handed off to Departure (126.7) they asked our reason for going around. I simply stated; "We were instructed by Tower". When back with Tower I asked why we were given the go-around instructions. The Controller told us there is a system called ASDE Taxiway safety logic that gave an alert that showed us lined up with Taxiway M. They visually confirmed we were stable and aligned with the runway center line; but said they cannot override the system and must send us around. A faulty ASDE Taxiway Safety logic computer. This caused a startle event that could cause an accident. Deactivate the system. Common sense should be used to override the system. The runway and taxiways were clear. The go-around could have caused a fuel problem for us at a busier arrival time. Not using our call sign made the event even more confusing."
