column121: We departed ZZZ [Runway] XXR on the ZZZZZ2 departure following Company Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z ahead of them. While attempting to initiate the turn to ZZZZZ; I found that I was unable to roll into a bank to the left. I added more aileron pressure and started adding trim to the left. Though I was not encountering any unusual resistance in the yoke; the aircraft was not rolling left. I reached and maintained about half control travel to the left. After a few seconds of this; I began to suspect a flight control problem and told the FO (First Officer) to select the flight controls synoptic page on the EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System). Almost simultaneously with the selection of the page; the plane began to respond to my aileron inputs. I only had the chance to observe the left side control positions before everything felt normal again; but I saw that the left aileron and both left multi-function spoilers were deflected upward as they should have been. I believe the full event lasted 15-20 seconds; and I believe I was holding half control deflection for 5-10 seconds.I honestly don't understand what happened. My two best guesses are wake turbulence or a transient aileron PCU (Power Control Unit) runaway; but both ideas seem unlikely. I don't believe Aircraft Y would produce enough wake to require that much aileron; and Aircraft Z was two planes ahead of us. It also seems unlikely to me that we would hit wake turbulence perfectly enough to experience such a consistent roll tendency for so long. An aileron PCU runaway seems unlikely to me because I don't know if that malfunction can be transient. Also; while I only had the chance to look at the flight control synoptic page as the event was ending; what I observed there looked normal for the control position I was holding.This probably was not an aircraft malfunction; but if similar incidents are reported; particularly in the same aircraft; I recommend inspecting the aileron system; and possibly the rudder system; although I did not feel any unusual yaw tendencies; nor did I observe anything amiss on my slip/skid indicator.

column121: During our descent into ELP; we noticed 'GPS L & R Invalid' messages on the FMC.  We checked the POS page of the FMC and there were no coordinates displayed in the GPS L or GPS R fields. We also noticed the transponder had a fail indication in both the 1 and 2 positions.  In addition; we had an amber TERR POS indication on both NDs and no green; amber; or red terrain information displayed.  We initially thought these indications may be associated with the frequent GPS jamming that occurs in this part of the country. Our weather packet did not contain a note of that possibility. Later; we talked to Approach Control about the GPS jamming and they told us it happens often; sometimes all night.We used the RNAV Z from WIKKR to align with Runway 22 and then transitioned to an ILS. While on final approach at approximately 500 feet AGL we received a GPWS PULLUP indication. We performed the terrain avoidance maneuver and got vectors back around to Runway 22 again. We couldn't find any guidance in the QRH for our lack of terrain information/amber 'TERR POS' on the NDs. The second ILS to 22 produced the same result with another terrain avoidance maneuver. After the second go-around; the TERR POS indication went away on both NDs and we started seeing green; amber; and red terrain information being displayed on the NDs. We got vectors back around to Runway 22 and landed uneventfully. After talking with Maintenance; we deferred the jet's GPWS.I did not perform an FMC navigation check following the initial 'GPS L & R Invalid' FMC messages. I'm not sure if that would have alleviated the situation. I was more concerned about the amber 'TERR POS' indication and lack of terrain data on the ND which I had never seen before. There is nothing in the QRH on how to deal with that indication. I can't explain why the amber 'TERR POS' indication went away and terrain information returned to the ND while being vectored for the third approach. I also don't know if GPS jamming was a factor; since our weather packet did not have a note about that possibility. I am thankful I was tankering 5500 pounds and the weather was nice.

column121: On Date; I was the Captain of Aircraft X operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The aircraft for this flight was an Airbus A321. The aircraft had NO MEL items and only 1 NEF item - CABIN LT LENSES.The aircraft was properly fuel in ZZZ with our Release FUEL of 43;250 Lbs. Both wings and center tanks were full; and we had the remainder of the fuel in ACT AFT TANK 1.The fuel utilization (burn) was normal with the ACT AFT 1 and the center tank operating normally.After the ACT AFT 1 and center tanks were depleted; the fuel quantity in the RIGHT WING tank started to decrease more than the LEFT WING tank. Both engines showed the same fuel flow and fuel used amounts.The rate in which the RIGHT WING fuel tank was deceasing started to increase over time. When the fuel imbalance exceeded 1;000 Lbs. between wing tanks; First Officer and myself independently preformed the Fuel On Board (FOB) calculation list in the QRH. We both confirmed that we had the correct amount of fuel remaining and there was no fuel leak.At no time did we have any ECAM advisories or alerts.We both came to the same conclusion that somehow fuel was moving from the RIGHT WING tank to supply the left side.The ECAM - Fuel page showed:1) Fuel transfer value in the Closed Position;2) AFT 1 and CTR FUEL TANK empty;3) CRT FUEL TANK PUMPS OFF.Fuel imbalance limitations were check and we well with the limitation.We had an uneventful normal landing at ZZZ1.We arrived at the gate with approximately a 2;400 lb fuel imbalance.After shutdown I called dispatch and talked with Company Maintenance while the dispatcher monitored the phone call. The fuel imbalance / fuel transfer problem was entered into the AML. Maintenance told me on the phone they were going to get one of the fuel computers reset.When the hotel van arrived; the informed the outbound Captain about the fuel problem and informed him at the had called dispatch/maintenance.The outbound flight was delayed while maintenance was working on the aircraft.The next day I was having a conversation with my dispatcher about the routing of our return flight to ZZZ and enroute weather. When I asked if the Dispatched could explain the MEL that was now listed for aircraft X. I explained what had happened the day before with the fuel transferring itself during the flight. The dispatched told me the aircraft had landed that morning in ZZZ with a 3;000 lb fuel imbalance and the crew did a repeat entry in the AML.The aircraft's fuel was checked in ZZZ and the wing tanks did have a 3;000 lb fuel imbalance and it was not just an indication problem. At this time maintenance returned the aircraft to service using MEL 28-XX-X. This MEL has nothing to do with the in-flight problem with the fuel transferring itself. This MEL has to do with refueling the aircraft on the ground. (Indication Problem)The dispatcher called over to maintenance and asked about the issue with aircraft X. He was told that they believe a solenoid that controls the transferring of fuel from ACT AFT 1 tank was at fault. The solenoid was causing the fuel to transfer wing tanks with no indication of the FUEL X FEED valve.The solenoid was replaced the night of DATE1 in ZZZ2.

column121: After landing in ZZZ; we received a message from the out bound crew that an MEL on the aircraft may have been incorrect. I reviewed the release (rev0) and MELs before arriving at the aircraft in ZZZ1. At that time the only MELs where for the Rudder Limiter System; and more importantly MEL 23-XX-X for the CIDS (Cabin Intercommunication Display System) Director system. This MEL had no (O) procedures; and looked fairly straight forward. Upon arrival at the aircraft; Maintenance had the logbook and was in the process of deferring the Mid Lav. On the ECAM status page; in addition to the Rudder limiter INOP message; we had a SMOKE class II message. We discussed if that was part of the CIDS MEL; as I knew that the smoke detector system was connected to CIDS; but we weren't sure; so we called Maintenance. When the Mechanic returned with the book; we related to him that we had the smoke message and weren't sure if it was related to the CIDS deferral or not; and he attempted a reset. While waiting for the reset; I reviewed the logbook; and saw that the deferral 23-XX-X came from a write up of the Lav Smoke Det System on Date1. This confirmed to me that the SMOKE Class II message was likely related to the deferral. I also noticed that either the Log Deferral sheet or placards had been completed for the New LAV deferral; and prompted the Mechanic to complete those. By then the Class II message had extinguished; and besides the rudder limiter INOP message; no messages were displayed.Upon deplaning in ZZZ; we briefly SMOKE class II message; but by the time we exited the only Class II message was CIDS. After arriving at the overnight hotel; the outbound crew informed us that after some digging and questioning Maintenance Control; it was found that since there was a history of Smoke Det faults; this issue should have been deferred under 23-X-XY; which took the aircraft out of service. We then reviewed the MELs; and what we remembered seeing. Without the knowledge that a history of Smoke Det Faults would require a different deferral; nothing stood out to me to question the deferral. The only time I saw an ECAM for SMOKE DET FAULT was during the reset procedure in ZZZ1; and so was disregarded as part of the reset. Insufficient information available to legitimately question the correctness of the deferral. Late arriving log book prior to departure with multiple issues needed to be corrected. I'm disappointed this event occurred; but without the knowledge that a history of SMOKE DET FAULTS required a different deferral; information that I can't find in the manuals available to me; I'm not sure what I reasonably could have done differently. Regardless; this event has re-emphasized the importance of a thorough review of the maintenance log on every flight.

column121: After holding for gate XX at the west cargo pad (PHOG) for 20 minutes we were cleared to taxi via Runway 02 and exit Taxiway Foxtrot due to excessive airport congestion. Once clear and on Taxiway Alpha we [were] cleared by Ground to gate XX. Once abeam the gate I proceeded across the ramp to the gate. Aircraft Y in line in front of us abruptly departed Taxiway A adjacent to gate XY and cut us off to circumvent waiting in line without warning. I was forced to abruptly apply braking to stop. OGG Tower categorizes the ramp area as a non-movement area and advise departing aircraft to push 'at their own risk'. This terminology is not used at any other airport in the US that I am aware of other than Maui and Lihue. I desired to address the issue immediately but there were so many aircraft on the frequency that the Ground Controller was overwhelmed. In fact when he initially cleared us out of the south cargo pad he actually thought we were at the north hold area over 1 mile from our location. I called the Tower Supervisor and expressed my dismay and concern over their lack of control on the tarmac.With the advent of Company serving Maui; ramp congestion at OGG has significantly increased. There were at least 30 airliners including wide bodies at gates and actively taxiing. To designate over 1/3 of the surface area of the airport as 'uncontrolled' is unwarranted; absurd and dangerous . The Tower Supervisor said the early afternoon is extremely busy. It was further aggravated by a bird strike on the runway. They use this unique 'own risk' terminology but yet it is a requirement to call for push and taxi. Is it controlled or not? They were totally unaware of Aircraft Y's departure from Taxiway Alpha to cut across the ramp without warning. It's a free for all at this place.   After speaking to the Tower Supervisor I suggested that the idea of this 'own risk laissez faire' attitude of ramp control has outlived its usefulness.The size of the pavement and the amount of aircraft are creating a hazardous operating environment. I would suggest additional training in the Tower and [they] should be more clear about what is expected from pilots operating there. Their rules seem to be contradictory. There is no mention of the proceed at your own risk policy on the [Jeppesen] 10-9 page or anywhere else including company pages. The FAA should look closely into the specific ground ops procedures in place at OGG. The Local Controller should have positive control over all of there between the gates and Taxiway Alpha which runs parallel.

column121: We departed Runway XXR in ZZZ. The takeoff roll and initial climb out was normal. Shortly into the climb we heard a loud banging noise and felt the airplane shuttering with the noise. No messages showed up on the ECAM. Engine indications for the number one engine were showing high EGTs and surging indications. Above 1;000 feet AGL we reduced power to idle on the number one engine and the noises stopped. We requested priority with ATC and requested vectors to return to Runway XYC. We shutdown the number one engine and completed all ECAMs. I flew while the CA (Captain) looked at follow ups; notified the FAs (Flight Attendants); the company and prepared for an over weight landing. We made a safe landing on Runway XYC and came to a stop on the runway. CFR (Crash fire Rescue Equipment) inspected the aircraft and told us there was no fire smoke or flames and that the plane looked good. We exited the runway and taxied to  Gate XX and parked without further issue. We had good weather; a great experienced CA; and ATC did a great job of working us right back around for a safe landing. I think our training department gets the credit for these events being successful. Although stressful and startling; the control and safety of the aircraft was never in question thanks to the great training.
column123: I was the Captain on Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on DATE. We had X passengers and Y crew members aboard.  Conditions in ZZZ at the time were CAVU with light and variable winds and departures were being conducted to the north. Takeoff was planned with Config 1 Flex on Runway XXR. I was the PF (Pilot Flying) and we had a normal takeoff. At approximately 2;000 ft. MSL; a loud; constant banging was heard from the left side of the aircraft resembling a jackhammer followed by strong vibrations. No ECAM or other alerts were present; and all engine parameters seemed normal. Both engines were producing normal thrust as I called for a straight out to 3;000 ft. climb with ATC. Upon global assessment; I and FO (First Officer) determined that we were experiencing possible compressor stalls on the #1 engine. I instructed him to slowly reduce to #1 engine to idle as I advanced the #2 to MCT so we could climb now to 4;000 ft. I [requested priority handling] and transferred aircraft control to FO and instructed him to coordinate with ATC for a return to landing in ZZZ Runway XYC. I then proceeded to brief the Flight Attendants on what happened and for them to plan for a precautionary landing with no evacuation in approximately twenty minutes. Next; I made a PA to the passengers stating that we an engine issue and we would be returning to ZZZ and to expect to see safety vehicles inspecting us when we landed. When I returned; FO pointed out that the oil level was 2.5 qts and dropping on the #1 engine. After a brief discussion; we both determined out an abundance of caution that the best course of action would be to shut down the #1 engine and secure it to prevent any further damage. I did this as FO was flying and started the APU. Ran all applicable checklists and did a quick landing data assessment. I assumed PF duties and landed on Runway XYC in ZZZ without incidence and stopped on the runway. After setting the parking brake; I made the PA for the passengers to remain seated. FO coordinated with CFR (Crash Fire Rescue equipment) vehicles for inspection. All clear signal was given by CFR and then I taxied under ships power to the gate in ZZZ.Compressor stall and loss of oil pressure in number one engine.

column121: We were departing ZZZ Runway XY. I was the PM and the FO was the PF. After getting clearance to line up and wait; I taxied the aircraft onto the runway; stopped; and handed control to the FO. I said 'your brakes; my radios'. The FO assumed control by stating 'my aircraft' but subsequently realized that the rudder pedals were not locking in position when she applied pressure with her feet. She tried to make an adjustment and it again did not lock. I assumed that she was having problems securing the pedals; and knowing that my rudder pedals were secure; I stated 'my aircraft' and stated something to the effect that I would do the takeoff. I planned to takeoff and hand controls in cruise; but then decided that since I did the takeoff that I would do the landing and she would fly the next leg of the sequence. The takeoff was uneventful. During cruise she tried to secure the rudder pedals and had no issues. After landing while taxiing to the gate; she asked me if she could check the pedals. The pedals again were not staying in position when she tried to lock them. I wrote a maintenance entry in the logbook describing the fact that the FO rudder pedals could not be secured. The FO during cruise had expressed concerns about the rudder pedals on the older Airbus 319 as this had been her 2nd or 3rd flight where the pedals could not be secured.The FO's before takeoff flow does not include a rudder check as the CA does. The only time that the FO notices that the rudder pedals cannot be secured (if not checked at the gate prior to pushback) is when control is handed over prior to the takeoff roll. A suggestion would be to include a rudder position/adjustment check during preflight as it would be difficult to do an FO rudder check during taxi the way the check is done by depressing the button on the tiller.
column123: Date 1This morning we were departing from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  I was the pilot flying departing on Runway XY. I began the takeoff and had my feet on the rudder pedals.The rudders moved and I tried to quickly adjust them. They slipped again and I told the Captain. He quickly took the controls and continued the takeoff roll with normal rudder control on his side.At this point the thought was I had not properly locked the rudder pedals in place when I set them.Once in cruise I started to think about some previous experiences I have had with the rudder pedals over the last year.In-flight I repeatedly pressed on the rudders and confirmed they were in fact locked in place. Although it appeared there was no issue with my pedals at this point the captain continued to be the pilot flying. During taxi in ZZZ1 I asked if I could check my rudders to see if in fact the issue was resolved but once again they would not lock in place I could push them forward and aft freely. A similar scenario happened to me on two other occasions with a different aircraft.Date 2From ZZZ2-ZZZSame scenario however it occurred at V1/R so I rotated and gave the Captain the controls. After passing through 10;000 feet it appeared that my pedals were again working correctly so I became the pilot flying again and continued for landing at ZZZ. On touchdown the position of the pedals went from 1-2 all the way to 12. The Captain took control of the aircraft. We wrote up the malfunction in the logbook and asked maintenance to come out so we could explain what had happened.Date 3I arrive at work to fly another turn to ZZZ3 from ZZZ and immediately checked the logbook.I found that the rudder pedal position was on MEL for positions 0 to 3.Since I set my rudder pedals within that position; I asked the Captain to refuse the aircraft citing safety concerns.I have pictures of the write ups and logbook entries.Date 4ZZZ4-ZZZSame aircraft as Date 2 and similar situation. Just prior to starting the Departure roll the rudders slipped in position and I quickly corrected them for takeoff. The remainder of that takeoff was normal. However; I was certain that I had properly set my rudder pedals back at the gate and checked them.I went back to my records and realized this was the same aircraft I had a problem with approximately six months prior. I briefed Captain on my previous experience. In cruise the pedals remain locked in place as normal. I was the pilot flying and on touchdown on Runway XY in ZZZ as I applied brake pressure the rudder pedals again went all the way to 12.Once again; we entered all the information in the logbook and requested maintenance come to the gate so we could explain the situation. The Captain requested follow up through a report but to my knowledge he had never received any.This morning almost 11 months from the original time this happened and in a different aircraft. I did not expect it to be the same problem. Initial I thought I had made a mistake and not locked the pedals. Unfortunately; it appears it is the same problem as on the other aircraft and I am quite concerned. This is potentially serious malfunction that has happened on two different aircraft. I am happy to provide any further information that could assist in making sure this safety concern does not happen again.Some additional notes- I understand from my systems knowledge there is no difference in the positioning of the rudder pedals whether in the air or on the ground. However; all three times the pedals seem to stay locked in place in the air.- At the gate when I reset my rudder position; I always push on them to confirm they are locked in place. A suggestion my Captain had was to possibly add a rudder check for the first officer during taxi. column121: Aircraft X; ZZZ-ZZZ1. 10 minutes prior to scheduled departure time; briefings and checklists complete; awaiting numbers from Preliminary Weight & Balance. The Ops Agent came down with a NOTAC form requiring Captain signature for two boxes of radioactive material; not in the remarks on the release. I looked up FOM [reference section] Radioactive Pharmaceutical Shipments XXXXXX as Cargo to determine if it was acceptable HAZMAT. I determined from the NOTAC that the Transport Index was in the acceptable range; and that it was stowed correctly. We received an ACARS amendment to the 'Remarks' on the Release 'HAZMAT ON BOARD REFER TO NOTAC (time) XX'. I called the Dispatcher to confirm that; according to what I was reading in the FOM; we were safe and legal to carry the HAZMAT on this flight. He was in concurrence. We got our numbers and departed normally. Approximately an hour into the flight; I was reviewing the NOTAC and realized that although it had the correct 'origin' and flight number; it had ZZZ2 as the destination. The flight was not a through flight. Upon arrival in ZZZ1; I called the Dispatcher to confirm that ZZZ1 was the destination. He looked up the waybill and confirmed that ZZZ1 was the destination. I went down to the A bin and confirmed that ZZZ1 was the destination. I then called the Chief Pilot on Call to relay the information to him and see if he had any questions or additional input.I think there is a certain amount of continuation bias in the way we handle HAZMAT. The Ops Agent assumed that the Dispatcher okayed everything; the Dispatcher assumed that the Ops Agent okayed everything. I am not sure if anyone (other than me) actually looked up the policies regulating our carriage of medical HAZMAT. Introducing this scenario; 10 minutes before departure; greatly decreases the time available to trap errors. I believe that ZZZ2 was a typo. I should have caught it before departure. I caught it after departure; at cruise; where I had more time to examine it without distractions.

column121: I was the relief FO on the flight. Preflight was normal with the exception of a 'SLATS DRIVE' EICAS message which none of us had ever seen before. We called maintenance and they troubleshot the problem for about 30 minutes. Ultimately they were able to extinguish the EICAS message and a new flight release was issued. Taxi; takeoff; and initial climb out were uneventful and I went on first break. As I was climbing into the bunk; I was called back to the flight deck. When I arrived; we were in holding; the SLATS DRIVE message had returned; and the crew was setting up to dump fuel and return to TLV. The Captain had me run landing distance for RWY 12 for max landing weight. In general; I observed the crew manage the situation; and making sure someone was always flying the airplane; and that checklists were complete. As I joined the problem late; I verified they had issued an alert to ATC (they did; both with Nicosia control and Tel Aviv arrival). Because TLV typically jams the GPS; SATCOM was garbled but the Captain was able to communicate with Dispatch via ACARS. Arrival and landing were uneventful other than the expected Brake Temperature EICAS message which we handled per the proper checklist. (We did request vehicles who inspected us upon exiting the runway and followed us to gate.)
column123: Arrived at gate saw unusual EICAS Slat drive message. Entered as MRM code and called TLV Operations to have maintenance come to aircraft. Maintenance worked the issue and cleared the item. Uneventful taxi and takeoff. About 90-120 miles from TLV communication with Nicosia control we got Slat Drive EICAS. We communicated to Nicosia we had a flight control issue; declared emergency and told of our intentions were to return to TLV. We requested hold and informed Nicosia we would have to jettison fuel as well. Nicosia authorized the fuel Jettison. We entered hold about 118 miles North of TLV and worked the Slat drive EICAS and the un-annunciated fuel jettison checklist. Both checklists completed successfully. It had been the FOs leg but after checklists had been completed I opted to fly the airplane back to TLV.We were within 180 miles of TLV which required us to talk to BGN control to request re-entry into their airspace and to also declare the emergency. They asked if we were a priority aircraft and we affirmed. During the hold we tried to Satcom dispatch after we had already notified them of the nature of the issues via ACARS and included our intentions. Satcom was weak so we sent ACARS to dispatch to work out our landing distance needed with our slat drive malfunction. We came up with approximately 7;000 feet runway needed and dispatch came up with 7;200.  After checklists completed and fuel jettisoned down to MLW we requested clearance to TLV. TLV offered us straight in RW 12 which we accepted. Land although fast 182kts at flaps 20 was uneventful (auto brakes 4 used) we rolled to almost end of runway for a slow uneventful turn off.We expected hot brakes and advised Tower to tell CFR trucks to inspect wheels brakes. They noted nothing and we taxied uneventfully to gate. CFR had expressed they were given only 12 minutes notice to roll trucks and wanted to know when we had actually requested priority. We explained well before contact with approach control. Final write up made at blocks was hot brakes. My crew acted like a well oiled machine great CRM; and all was included in the debrief. Dispatch was also a great help throughout the problem.

column121: I am submitting this report because This is the second time I've experienced this situation. After sending an email to [the] Manager the first time and not getting a response; I am submitting this report. It has been a relatively new procedure to leave hydraulic switches off during preflight inspection. It used to be that hydraulics switches were always left on. Because the hydraulic pumps were off during our preflight inspection; we did not observe the hydraulic leak that was present. During the 'Pushback' checklist when the hydraulic switches were finally turned on; we received an 'RF' message on the EICAS within about 4-5 seconds. I then contacted Maintenance Control. Upon Maintenance Technician arriving; he advised we had a serious hydraulic leak spraying fluid all over the wheel well. Long story short; we ended up being almost 2 hours delayed getting the leak repaired. If we had NOT received the 'RF' message; we would've most likely had taken off with this leak and would've gotten a B hydraulic low quantity or even worse loss of hydraulic B pressure inflight!I've asked many people in several chief pilot offices; and sent emails to training and no one has offered a reason; other than standardize with other fleet type. I believe this is a safety issue. Leaving the hydraulic pumps off during preflight makes observing possible leaks impossible.

column121: Leveling at FL240 during descent into ZZZ; ATC asked us to report our altitude because she was not receiving anything from us. When we looked down; the Captain noticed that IFF 2 had a fault and switched it to his side. At about that time we both noticed a power surge which made my clock blank momentarily and the Captain noticed lights on his panel flash. Next we had a series of lights come on spaced apart by a few minutes at first and then began to come on more quickly as time passed. First we had a cooling fan supply light. Then when cleared to descend via the arrival; I pushed recall and noticed the left pack light remained illuminated. Suspecting something wrong with the power distribution system; I cycled through electrical panel wafer switch positions and found no amps coming from TR 2 or 3 and negative 3 amps on the battery. I hacked my clock. About 5 minutes had already passed. I took the radios while the Captain ran the checklist for the pack light next and shortly after; we lost the left aft fuel boost pump. I told the Captain I thought we had a power distribution problem and we were draining our battery. I thought we might be slowly shedding components due to their power sources being associated with the battery. As we passed 10;000 ft. I told the Captain and he put away the book and ran the landing checklist. While on the descent; I recommended [requesting priority handling] so we could land ASAP. I configured early in prep for a slam dunk and the Captain and I agreed to starting the APU just in case. By this time we were on base and more lights had come on. We lost the B Electrical Hydraulic Pump; had a right side window over heat light; battery discharge light; TR fail light; and a few pitot lights had come on. Then while turning to final; I noticed the short vectors would overshoot me so I clicked off autopilot and turned. That's when I noticed I had no electric trim. The Captain manually ran the trim for me as we slowed and configured and we had an uneventful landing. After the fire trucks greeted us and found no hot spots around the E & E bay; we discussed whether we had enough power on the battery and I noted the time had been 17 minutes from when I noticed the negative amps on the battery and started the clock. We continued to taxi to the gate and after the fire crew came up I went with them down to the E & E bays to do my own inspection. I didn't see or smell anything. Aircraft X is an old airplane. The older planes get the more they will have gremlins like this. Maintenance discovered a faulty number 2 generator or regulator with some certainty that an Aircraft phase was not getting to the busses. How many more lights would have come on eventually? Just thank goodness we were so close to landing when it failed.

column121: Aircraft X experienced an upset aircraft state as a result of severe turbulence encountered on approach to ZZZ Runway XXR. The aircraft pitched to approximately 20 degrees nose up and 10 to 15 degrees left bank; disengaging the autopilot and causing the autothrust to increase power toward max. The airspeed decayed from 250 KIAS to 220 KIAS as the aircraft climbed from 10;000 ft. to 10;900 ft. before upset recovery procedures returned it to stable flight at 10;000 ft. and 250 KIAS. There were no injuries as passengers and flight attendants were seated early in anticipation of turbulence. There was no aircraft damage. Aircraft X made an uneventful landing on Runway XXR. The severe turbulence encounter was reported to Air Traffic Control and the Company. A full debrief was conducted with Flight Operations.Prior to descending into ZZZ; the First Officer (FO) and I discussed concerns about thunderstorms and convective activity in the terminal area. We had plenty of gas and I noted that ZZZ1 weather was excellent. I briefed the flight attendants to be seated approximately 20 minutes before touchdown. I then confirmed that they were seated. I made a PA to the passengers that I expected very bumpy conditions and I emphasized the need for them to obey the Fasten Seat Belt sign. The FO and I briefed windshear precautions; indications; and procedures while inbound to ZZZ2 for the ZZZZZ [arrival]. We did not re-brief the Upset Recovery procedures as they had been briefed prior to departure. (In retrospect; I think this could be good to review when windshear concerns are expressed as the windshear could result in an upset.) We were initially cleared on the ZZZZZ arrival. We loaded the Runway XXL ILS approach. Shortly into the descent; we had an AUTOFLT RUD TRIM 1 FAULT ECAM. I wrote it up as we were descending. Shortly after that; ATC vectored us off the arrival. ATC did not tell us what we should expect; but I heard several aircraft ahead of us receiving clearances to ZZZZZ1 for what I assumed would be the remainder of the ZZZZZ arrival. Radio communication congestion was significant. I sensed ATC was struggling to manage the number of arrivals from the north. I did not hear anyone receiving holding clearances. Holding might have alleviated the density of traffic and eased the friction for ATC. Eventually; we were told to do a 360 degree turn. Out of the turn; we were cleared to descend to 10;000 ft and given a heading of 190deg. I had heard another aircraft given a vector toward the ZZZZZ2 intersection; so I put it on the fix page for situational awareness. At that time; I was watching the radar which showed a cell next to the ZZZZZ2 intersection and another cell to the southwest. The two aircraft ahead of us were vectored through that gap. A 777 was behind us. At that time; we still did not know what arrival or approach clearance to expect. As we passed through the gap between the two cells; ATC said to advise when we could take a turn direct to ZZZZZ3. We did not have ZZZZZ3 loaded into the FMC. The FO did not know what ZZZZZ3 was. I asked him to load it and I spelled it out. (We still had Runway XXL loaded.) As we tried to get ZZZZZ3 loaded; along with the remainder of the ILS XXR approach; while still in the gap between the two cells; we experienced the severe turbulence and upset. After recovering the aircraft; I gave direction to the FO to load DIRECT ZZZZZ3 and I spelled it again. He did so; and we turned direct to the fix. He then connected the rest of the approach and it was flown uneventfully.As far as the execution of the Upset Recovery procedure; I did not comply with all the procedures. I also did not verbalize the steps and I did not silence the autopilot aural which resulted from the disconnect for quite some time. I had trouble focusing on the instruments and the 'Startle Effect' was significant.
column123: Descending into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ arrival; we were taken off the arrival. I am assuming it was because of the convective weather in the area. We had flown in from the north and were being vectored west away from ZZZ. It seemed ATC was overwhelmed with all of the aircraft and bad weather in the area. Because we knew there was adverse weather around the airport the Captain sat the passengers and flight attendants well in advance. At one point while being vectored west we were told to fly multiple different headings which eventually made us complete a giant 360 degree turn. At the end of the turn I noticed that ATC was vectoring aircraft towards ZZZZZ2 intersection which seemed like ATC had found a gap they were funneling aircraft through. I pulled up ZZZZZ2 intersection on the fix page so we could see we where it was in relation to our position on the nav display. ATC gave us a heading of 190 that was towards ZZZZZ2 intersection. At this point ATC did not tell us which runway or routing to expect. While flying on a heading of 190 and 250 kts. at 10;000 ft. we flew into a cloud and at that point we experienced an upset event of severe turbulence. The aircraft gained about 900 ft.; dropped 30 kts.; banked 10-15 degrees and disengaged the autopilot. The Captain was flying and immediately returned us to straight and level flight. The Captain reported the incident to ATC and I checked in with the Flight Attendants and no injuries occurred in the cabin. After the event ATC told us to go to ZZZZZ3 intersection and to expect Runway XXR. We landed the airplane and contacted the company about the event.

column121: Operating Aircraft X; ZZZ-ZZZ1 we pushed back from Gate X in ZZZ and were pulled to the top of the alleyway near spot 1. Wasn't immediately sure if it was a concern or not so I notified the Flight Attendants and asked if they could smell anything unusual in the cabin.  They did not.  Then after starting engine 2 as we taxied up to spot 1; the fume smell got stronger in the flight deck.  The First Officer now stated that he could smell strong odors.  I checked with the Flight Attendants again; and they now said they could start to smell something.  We notified ground control from spot 1 that we had to return to the gate and we shut down engine 2.  Ground control had us taxi from spot 1; Taxiway 1; Taxiway 2; and hold short of Taxiway 3 awaiting a gate assignment.  We notified Ramp Control that we needed to quickly return to the gate because of fume smells.  We had donned O2 masks and tried a few times to get a gate assignment but Ramp Control kept asking multiple times what the issue was after we had already told them.  I then [requested priority handling] with Ground Control; and they replied for us to contact Ramp Control.  I also [requested priority handling] with Ramp Control and started taxiing from Taxiway 4 to Taxiway 5 spot 2 in anticipation getting into Gate 2.  Ground Control then asked if we needed [priority] equipment.  We acknowledged yes send the personnel to check the outside of the aircraft.  We parked at Gate 2; shutdown; and deplaned the passengers as soon as possible.  The Flight attendants had left the aircraft with the passengers by the time I had given my report to Dispatch; Maintenance; and the [airport authorities].The First Officer and I both had dull headaches; burning sore throats.  I notified safety and they said to call the Duty Pilot on call and they would facilitate our being examined by a medical professional.  After talking to the Duty Pilot/Chief Pilot; I was told to call a Paramedic if I was concerned about my health.  Both of us stopped by the Airport station and asked if they could have the Paramedics take our vitals.  After this was done; I drove the First Officer to ER where they examined us both. [The cause was] Maintenance issues with older aircraft.

column121: During climb passing approximately FL280 the flight attendant called and informed me that a passenger believed we were trailing fuel out of our #2 engine.  All engine indications appeared normal including engine fuel flow.  Checking our fuel we determined we were showing an imbalance of approximately 1500 pounds with the right wing being low. We continued to monitor to determine if the fuel imbalance remained stable or if the imbalance was increasing. We received a second call from the flight attendant informing us we had a company A320 instructor pass riding. He and I spoke and he told me it appeared to be fuel trailing the #2 engine. I sent the First Officer back to the cabin for a visual inspection and told him to look forward and aft of the wing and specifically any damage he might see on the forward edge of the wing.  While he performed a visual inspection; the flight attendant in the cockpit showed me cell phone video of the leak. I leveled off at FL380 and verified the fuel imbalance was increasing to about 1700lbs with the right wing on the low side.  I referenced the QRH for fuel leak and sent dispatch a message that we had a fuel leak; needed to divert and would be shutting down the #2 engine. The First Officer returned and informed me of the same information and we began running the fuel leak QRH.  Dispatch recommended ZZZZ and looking at our distance and time required for descent I determined it to be a proper divert location. I [requested priority] with ZZZZ Center and requested an immediate turn to ZZZZ and descent to FL 200. The First Officer and I ran the fuel leak QRH which directed an engine shutdown for a fuel leak out of the engine or pylon followed by the engine shutdown checklist.  We shut the engine down in an idle power descent and I started the APU. I then transferred flying duties to the First Officer.  ZZZZ Center handed us off to ZZZZ Approach. ZZZZ is an non radar airfield. They told us to report 30 miles from the airfield and asked if we could maintain VMC.   Weather was scattered to broken with some vertical development but was sufficient to maintain VMC and the field was reporting 6;000 scattered.  Approach gave us a descent to 7;000 and offered the [non-precision] Approach to Runway XX. I asked for the ILS for XX. Approach asked if we could fly a visual to Runway 26 and conditions were sufficient for that and we were cleared for the visual approach. We never received guidance information on our ILS though it was programmed correctly. After an uneventful landing by the First Officer we taxied to a hard stand. Foreign Country aviation authorities inspected our certificates/medical/airworthiness certificate/insurance certificate which the company instructor was very helpful working that while I worked with operations. Operations moved the passengers indoors to a gate seating area. I worked with the Chief Pilot and Maintenance Control. They informed me that the passengers would be taken on a flight from ZZZZ-ZZZZ1-ZZZ. I made several announcements and trips to the gate holding area and informed all passengers of our plan.  Most of the passengers had left carry-on bags on the aircraft; but Foreign Country security wouldn't let them return to retrieve it. I coordinated with Station Operations to have aft air stairs brought up so we could get the passenger to come back and file front to back through the airplane to retrieve their items before their inbound flight arrived and coordinated with Foreign Country security.  Foreign Country security eventually agreed but only allowing 4 passengers at a time.
column123: On climbout from ZZZZ1 we were passing FL280 when the Flight Attendant (FA) called us.  He said a passenger (who is a pilot) said that it looked like fuel was coming out of our #2 engine.  We monitored the fuel page.  The engine fuel used totals were identical; as were the wingtip tanks.  The inboard wing tanks showed an imbalance of 1000 pounds.  Over the remaining 5 minutes of our climbout we watched the imbalance increase to 1400 pounds.  During this time we got another call from the FA.  He put us on with an Airbus Instructor that was non-revving in the back.  He told us it appeared that fuel was coming from the engine exhaust.The Captain took over the aircraft and I went back to look for myself.  There was nothing visible on the front of the wing or the front of the engine.  I went back to row XX and could clearly see a fluid coming out of the exhaust of #2.  I returned to the flight deck and told the Captain.  We ran the Fuel Leak checklist and it directed us to shut down the engine.  After starting a descent to FL200; we did so.  We secured the engine and talked to dispatch.  He directed us to either ZZZZ1 or ZZZZ.  ZZZZ1 was further and the weather was reported as suboptimal.  We chose ZZZZ.The Captain and I turned the aircraft back to ZZZZ and finished the descent to FL200.  We briefed up the approach and I took control of the aircraft.  Approach control informed us there was no radar service.  We used the local MSA to ensure terrain clearance until we were clear of the clouds and could see the airfield.  I maneuvered the aircraft to a 6-7 mile final and we configured the aircraft for landing.  There was no glideslope which we knew; but the localizer wasn't working either.  We confirmed with Tower that they could see us and that we were lined up on the correct airport.  During the confusion we forgot the Before Landing Checklist; but the Spoilers Not Armed message reminded us.  We accomplished the checklist and were fully stable and complete by 500 ft. AGL.Landing was normal; the Captain took the aircraft around 80 knots on the rollout.  We taxied clear to a hard stand near the terminal.  Most of the passengers deplaned into the terminal.  We coordinated with the Foreign Country equivalent of the FAA; as well as dispatch and maintenance.  After the passengers got on the rescue airplane; we closed up the plane and went to the hotel.

column121: The Jeppesen approach plate for Denver RNP to Runway 26 seems to have an inappropriate speed restriction for the initiation of the RF legs from both sides of the airfield. Both speed restrictions require an 'AT 210 knots;' all other RNP approaches similar in design have 'Below 210 knots.' column121: I took off from ZZZ on a reposition flight to ZZZ1. At 900 ft. I turned the autopilot on with the master switch. At no point during the event did I ever engage the autopilot by selecting a mode. The 'ready' annunciation turned on and then it turned off. At the time I was flying runway heading. Approach then gave me a right hand turn at which time I noticed the turn coordinator had frozen and was not turning with me. It had previously worked fine on the ground. I decided to return to ZZZ. Approach gave me another right hand turn and that is when the aircraft controls became very stiff. It was difficult to turn the aircraft and even more difficult to hold altitude. After I leveled out in that turn; approach attempted to make a radio call that was very broken up and I asked her standby. She then informed me I was almost completely unreadable but when I asked her standby a second time she heard me a little better. I recycled the autopilot master switch and it once again showed ready and then the ready disappeared. I turned the autopilot master switch back off and pressed the red autopilot disconnected button but nothing changed. I then leaned over to try to pull the circuit breaker. After a few moments of not being able to pull the circuit breaker; I still couldn't get it. At this time I requested priority handling. I said if [I] could get out of IFR I would like to [have] the Approach Controller turned me again to more of a downwind leg for Runway XX. Another aircraft called and said they had the field in sight at 2000 ft. and 5 miles from the runway. I told Approach to send me there. She gave me a small turn and descended me to 2;000 ft. When I made it to 2;000 ft.; I checked the trim to see if moving forward and back would alleviate the problem. I moved it backwards (towards nose up) and everything with the trim seemed to be working properly but have no affect on the controls stiffness. I pushed the trim wheel forward and then back to level flight. At this time; the aircraft had started a small descent which the VSI also showed but the attitude indicator showed a 10 degree nose pitch up. After returning the aircraft to level; I noted the attitude indicator was becoming sluggish and not matching the movements of the aircraft as quickly as it normally does. The stiffness of the controls wanted the aircraft to pitch nose down and made it difficult to turn; however when I got to just outside the final approach fix flying in the opposite direction; I was still unable to see the runway so I had to shoot the ILS Runway XX into ZZZ. The only reduction in stiffness came when I pulled the power for in range and it lessened the pull I was having to put on the yoke to maintain altitude and heading. All engine gauges including the suction gauge were normal throughout the event. I was met at the hangar after landing by the Airport Support Personnel and [other] airport personnel. I wrote up the aircraft afterwards and discussed everything that happened per [each] instrument with the Mechanic so he could have a better picture of the situation.

column121: During cruise at FL400 the oil filter bypass light for engine #2 EICAS message began blinking and then remained on steady. I told the First Officer to continue flying and to advise ATC of the problem. I said I would reference the QRH 'ENGINE OIL FILTER BYPASS'. Reading the checklist we realized the procedure might have us shut down the engine. We asked for a descent from FL400. There was traffic below us at FL390 so ATC said it would be a minute before we could descend. We started to look for a suitable diversion airport at that time. I sent a message to Dispatch to 'call me'. We waited to retard/reduce the power to idle (as stated by the checklist) until the descent was initiated due to drift down airspeed restrictions at FL400 and traffic right below us. The oil filter bypass QRH required us to shut down the engine because the light did not extinguish when the throttle was brought to idle. We continued the checklist and shutdown #2 engine with the (MAX) 'ENGINE FAILURE OR SHUTDOWN' checklist. We [requested priority handling] with ATC. Dispatch responded within a few minutes but the frequency was garbled and somewhat busy. Communicating with Dispatch we received weather and NOTAMs for ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 and we collectively decided to divert to ZZZ3. Dispatch said they would send landing data for Runway XXR at ZZZ3. I also looked up the non-normal landing distance performance table. So many performance non-normals it was hard to find the One Engine inoperative section. Later I realized the aircraft/config performance non-normals table was alphabetized! It was an idle descent all the way down as the airport was only 80 miles away from where we shutdown the engine so we did not have to consider the drift down QRH. Dispatch stayed on the frequency if we needed any more assistance. I advised the purser [and] communicated with the passengers to advise them of the problem and our need to land in ZZZ3. We asked for extended vectoring with ATC to complete checklists and approach briefings. The First Officer continued to fly as we had discussed this during the descent and he was comfortable landing. Based on the situation and conditions I felt he was more than competent to execute a safe landing. Checklists were completed and an uneventful single engine approach and landing were completed. Airport Fire Department met the aircraft after landing and we taxied to a hard stand where passengers were able to deplane via air stairs. The First Officer and I had a meaningful debrief. I then contacted Dispatch and the Chief Pilot to debrief. A logbook entry was made and I had a discussion with Maintenance regarding the engine shutdown.
column123: We were operating Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on a B737 MAX-9. We had completed a delayed flight from ZZZ4 and had to do a quick turn in ZZZ. I started preparing the flight deck while the Captain did the walk-around and dealt with jumpseaters and a new-hire pilot doing an 'observation ride' with us in the flight deck jumpseat. With the preflight done; we pushed on time and started both engines on push-back due to the long start times on the LEAP engines. Both engines; specifically #2; appeared to start normally. Taxi out; takeoff; and initial cruise was normal. Approximately; 50NM East of ZZZ2; we had a #2 Engine 'Oil Filter Bypass' flashing amber annunciation. I took the radios from the Captain and continued to fly while he looked up the MAX QRH for an oil filter bypass. The first step in the checklist is to disengage the auto-throttles. So we did that. The next step is to retard the affected thrust lever until the bypass light extinguishes or the throttle is closed. The Captain said we needed to descend to close the throttle since we cannot maintain FL400 on a single engine. I looked up the engine out info page on the FMC to see what our target altitude should be. It said FL244. The Captain quickly sent a 'Call Me' ACARS message to Dispatch. While he did that I requested a descent to FL300 with ATC; because we felt there was a chance the bypass light would extinguish as we retarded the throttle on our way down to FL300. This piqued the interest of ATC which appropriately asked if we needed any assistance. At that time; I told them to standby due to us running a checklist. On our descent; we closed the throttle completely and the bypass light did not extinguish. Per the checklist; step 3 says if the light does not extinguish we are to proceed to the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist. We were a little surprised there were not any more steps involved with the checklist; such as checking other engine indications for corroboration. So before proceeding to engine shutdown we re-examined the fault; we made sure we were in the correct checklist; and that we had not erred or missed anything that would prevent an engine shutdown.  Our conclusion was that we had not and an engine shutdown was necessary. After securing the engine; [I requested assistance] with ATC and requested FL240; I also began slowing the aircraft down to a more drift-down speed so we would not get too far away from ZZZ2; which appeared to be VMC; as well as prevent us from having large amounts of asymmetrical thrust at level-flight at a low altitude. While this was occurring; the Captain was briefing the Flight Attendants. He was also coordinating with Dispatch. Dispatch informed us that the weather in ZZZ2 was not VMC and he recommend ZZZ3 instead due to weather. Hearing Dispatch on frequency was a challenge due to the lag in relays; static on the frequency; and other parties transmitting on the same frequency. That is one area specifically that I feel could use improvement. Communicating to Dispatch should be as easy as communicating to ATC in a high stress; time limited situation. After agreeing of diverting to ZZZ3; I notified ATC of our new destination and we received vectors direct to the airport. The Captain made a PA to the passengers to explain the situation and plan. Next; the Captain began running the single engine landing checklist to prepare for landing in ZZZ3. I simultaneously began loading the ILS XXR approach in the FMC and prepared the aircraft for an approach into ZZZ3. We requested a delay vector for an extend final so we had ample time to complete all the checklists. Once we were set up; we completed the deferred items and began configuring the aircraft for landing. We had emergency equipment standing by upon our arrival as a precaution. The XXR runway was plenty long for our brakes 3; flaps 15; increased Ref speed approach; and we made an uneventful single engine landing. We were able to taxi under our own power to the ramp for passenger deplaning via air-stairs and busing to the terminal. We ensured everyone safely exited the aircraft and submitted a maintenance write-up for an engine oil filter bypass annunciation with a corresponding inflight engine shutdown. I feel everyone worked well together with excellent CRM including the Company new-hire observation First Officer; Name. I also feel safety was not in jeopardy at any time.

column121: After starting engines and completing the before takeoff checklist on the ZZZZ Ramp; ZZZZ Tower Control cleared us to back taxi & lineup/wait runway XX; and the I correctly read those instructions back to the controller.  Before taxiing onto the runway from taxiway C--which is approximately 3;500 ft. from the approach end of Runway XX--we verified that both the runway and final approach areas were clear; especially since it was still dark out; wet runway;  and the weather was reported scattered at 2;000 ft AGL.With about 2;000 ft. of taxi distance remaining; both the Captain & I observed an approaching aircraft's landing lights breaking out of the weather.  (Call sign of that aircraft is unknown.)  Captain observed on TCAS that the approaching aircraft was only about 500 ft above our position at field elevation.  At no time did we hear communication between the approaching aircraft and tower prior to observing the landing lights.  This also highlights that the actual weather on approach to Runway XX was significantly lower than the reported 2;000 ft. scattered.I immediately communicated via tower freq 'The approaching aircraft needs to go around; we are still on the runway' at which point we observed a climb from the approaching aircraft while the tower controller and approaching aircraft pilot were communicating in non-English.  With the approaching aircraft go-around underway; we completed our back-taxi; and were cleared for an uneventful takeoff & departure shortly thereafter.We operated strictly IAW flight manual and ICAO procedures; to include maintaining SA of the aerodrome environment which allowed us to see the traffic and direct the go-around; preventing a more dramatic outcome.  The cause is very simply sub-standard Country ATC operations that allowed this situation to arise.  (Regrettably--and even though this was the first experience for me in the dozen or so times I have operated in Country--events like this are purportedly not uncommon in Country based on fellow pilots' accounts.  Country operators do not adhere to the highest standards of ICAO procedures.)  In this case; it is safe to assume that there was a likely ATC coordination breakdown between approach and tower controllers since we were cleared onto an active runway while an approaching aircraft was on final approach.  And for whatever reason; the approaching aircraft was not on tower freq until well inside the final approach fix; otherwise we would have heard the check in.  Also; had it been VMC; we would have likely seen the aircraft on approach and declined to take the runway.NEVER get complacent operating in Country.
column123: We were given clearance to back taxi and to line up and wait on Runway XX in ZZZZ. column121: Wake turbulence encounter following a Boeing 747 on final approach. On radar downwind in VFR conditions we were cleared a visual approach following a 747 that was already established on final.  On the dog leg to final I was descending to arrive at the FAF at what would be a normal intercept for glideslope to runway 07R. Autopilot and autothrottles were connected at this time.  I noted on TCAS that we were 6 miles behind the heavy as we were about be aligned on final. Suddenly we encountered the wake turbulence from the preceding aircraft and the aircraft rolled quickly to the left. I took over controls manually and disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles while simultaneously recovering the airplane from the sharp bank to the left. The event happen very quickly; so I am unsure as to what bank angle we reached but estimating more than 30 and less than 45deg. We received a roll authority alert as the auto pilot had been unable to maintain level flight with the quick onset from the wake turbulence.  The aircraft recovered and we re-established ourselves on final. I mentioned to the First Officer that I was going to climb and maintain above the preceding aircraft flight path and also stay above glide slope for the remainder of the approach; planning to touchdown at 2;000 feet. The rest of the flight was uneventful and we landed normally in Anchorage.Looking back on this event I could have easily avoided encountering the wake turbulence.  When cleared for the visual approach behind the 747 I should've maintained my altitude instead of starting a gradual descent. I had plenty of time to descend later and descending at that time only increased the chances of encountering the wake. At the time; I was considering the fact that our distance was adequate and that we wouldn't have any issues following the 747 using normal visual cues /angle approaching the runway. I was wrong.  Even 6 miles behind the heavy the turbulence was strong and the rolling tendency abrupt. Not worth the risk; not to mention the discomfort to the passengers and crew. In the future I will certainly keep this in mind for a visual behind a preceding heavy aircraft to avoid this type of encounter.

column121: I was Pilot Monitoring (PM) descending for ZZZ Runway XXL ILS while avoiding several storms. While descending from about 11;000 ft on a weather avoidance heading of about 100 degrees I noted we were above the proper profile and suggested we program a direct-to for the IAF; ZZZZZ; ILS XXL at ZZZ. This was to give the VNAV a better calculation as the Pilot Flying (PF) thought we were low (due to VNAV Path indicating so because of extra track miles we now would not be flying because we were not flying to ZZZ then back to the IAF for the full ILS; an extra 35+ miles VNAV was expecting with ZZZ; discontinuity; ILS XXL). We discussed these reasons and probably this extra conversation distracted us. We failed to scan our Vertical FMA (Flight Mode Annunciations) below 10;000 ft perhaps because we had just slowed below 250 kts. Had we scanned the FMAs again; or possibly avoided confirmation bias; we would have recalled that we had just switched to FLCH SPEED instead of VNAV PATH...this of course mattered because the PF then set FAF altitude of 2;100 ft upon receiving approach clearance. I (PM) failed to remind him to return to VNAV or set the issued crossing restriction of 3;000 ft at ZZZZZ; our next fix.    Previously; on being cleared the approach and to descend to 3;000ft; we had both confirmed the Primary Flight Display (PFD) altitude and VNAV Descent page specifically reflected 3;000 ft. Of course we apparently forgot to individually confirm the FMA's. We got a call from Approach; as I recall; switching us to Tower and noting '3;000 ft at ZZZZZ'. I replied that I thought our FMS had sequenced and we were climbing. I misunderstood the deviation; still not realizing then that we had not returned to VNAV (PATH) when setting 2;100 ft. Our altitude had reached a low of approximately 2;250 ft. Per our approach study; I noted to the PF that there is a tower about a half mile east at 1;946 ft which I immediately located visually as clear. We reached about 2;500 ft at ZZZZZ and shortly thereafter; while still climbing back up; captured the XXL glideslope.  I think I will always have to verbally confirm the Vertical FMA every time an approach related altitude is set. I also plan to never again explicitly set FAF altitude once on heading/vector and given an altitude to maintain till intercepting the LOC course. It's just another layer of complexity that's unnecessary; this also is more CDFA compliant and noise avoiding while still allowing early configuration for being Stabilized by the FAF and well above 1;000. Although I realize its possible in VNAV PATH or VNAV ALT prior to configuring (FMS) I'm thinking that a VNAV understanding shouldn't drive me to fly a precision approach like a non-precision just because I'm outside the FAF. This simplified process management is fully my responsibility.  It also will reduce errors and increase consistency in my execution of precision approaches in a non-STAR environment. These techniques can help insure that the FMA being left out will not be the single point of failure. Or in Threat and Error Management language they will force another layer of swiss-cheese to be present hopefully blocking the potential for FMA checking error getting through. This whole repeating situation could also be averted by getting ZZZ Approach Control to allow us to file to an IAF or even for them to build at least one south flow STAR and one for north flow. I've been flying at ZZZ since Year XXXX routinely and this circumstance is constantly a challenge because of the fact we file direct to the airport combined with the facts that Center usually keeps us high due to ZZZ1 traffic and then dives us in steep for an approach. It's not unlike what ZZZZ Approach does. Once again; its entirely my responsibility to execute correctly no matter the set up. These are just ideas I think can help in this location.

column121: As Captain of Aircraft X; inadvertently taxied onto an unmarked; newly constructed taxiway apron at night at South Bend (SBN).  Taxi plan from the company ramp to runway 36 via taxiway B was thoroughly briefed. With an aircraft on 4 mile final for runway 36; ground requested that we expedite taxi across runway 18/36 at B (from west to east) with follow on instructions to taxi B-N-hold short runway 36 at N3. There is a lot of construction on the airfield but no NOTAM regarding construction of a new taxiway just north of the current taxiway B between runway 36 and taxiway N. That area is not lit. Crossing runway 18/36 on the current taxiway B from west to east requires a brief dogleg south on runway 18/36 that is not depicted on the Jepps airport diagram. The new taxiway apron under construction aligns more closely with the current airport diagram.  It was also a very dark night.  Poor construction lighting on the apron barriers; inaccurate taxiway diagrams; darkness; faded taxiway B center lines on the runway; and failure of the crew to stop earlier on the runway due to an 'expedite' crossing clearance for an aircraft on final were the primary factors that contributed to us taxiing straight across Runway 18/36 and partially onto a newly constructed; closed taxiway before poorly lit portable barriers became visible.  Once we realized our mistake there was not enough room before the portable barriers to turn around.  Ground waved off the aircraft on approach because we were not sure if we were fully clear of Runway 36. The Company ramp said they were unable to tow us from that area so airfield operations confirmed that the apron could hold the aircraft weight; moved the portable barriers and allowed us to pull forward and conduct a 180 turn back onto runway 18/36.  The remainder of the taxi and flight was uneventful.Inaccurate airport taxi diagram doesn't show dogleg on runway when crossing runway 18/36 on taxiway B; low light night ops; poorly lit barriers in apron under construction; no mention of apron under construction in NOTAMs; pilot error due to hesitancy to stop on the runway to discuss faded taxiway B markings on runway due to aircraft on 4 mile final and ground controller request to expedite runway crossing. More accurate airport diagram that shows that taxiway B is staggered on each side of runway 18/36; requiring a brief taxi along runway to cross between west and east on taxiway B.  Better lighting on barriers in apron under construction between taxiway N and runway 18/36 north of taxiway B.  Include company note about staggered taxiway B.
column123: On the evening of Date I was the First Officer for Aircraft X; a flight from SBN to ZZZ.  I don't recall the exact reported weather; but it was a low overcast night. There is a lot of construction taking place at SBN so the Captain and I first briefed the taxi plan of how we would get from the Company ramp to runway 36 while in the Company Ops facility at SBN. Reviewing the airport diagram; our plan was to exit the east taxiway departing the Company ramp onto taxiway B.  Once on B; we would have to taxi 'straight' across runway 18/36 onto B; turn south on N which would take us to N3 for a full length departure from runway 36.  During our cockpit departure brief; we once again briefed and reviewed our taxi plan as mentioned above.During our taxi; we exited the Company ramp onto taxiway B.  As we approached runway 36; tower cleared us to cross runway 36 at B and expedite our taxi for an aircraft on a 4 mile. The Captain and I gained visual of the traffic on final; referenced our chart and proceeded to cross runway 36.  Crossing Runway 36 on what we thought was B; we inadvertently taxied onto a new taxi apron under construction.  I informed tower we could not verify if our tail cleared the runway; so Tower instructed the aircraft of final to go-around.  The Captain and I received verification the new taxiway was greater than 120 feet; it was reported to be 150 feet; and we verified the area behind construction was usable. Ops confirmed the area was usable and received permission to move the barriers; and then show us the exact location where the hazard begins. Once the barriers were moved; we had appropriate space to execute a 180 degree turn.  We executed our 180 degree turn and taxied onto 36 where we turned south on 36 to join taxiway B and continue with our flight.  After the incident; the Captain and I reviewed the SBN taxi diagram.  The diagram shows crossing 36 on B is 'straight' across with no turn onto 36 to join B.  In short; the area where B joins 36 from the west; is actually north of where taxiway B joins 36 to the east.  We taxied straight across 36 and ended up in the new construction area.Incorrect airport diagram due to recent construction.  The current airport diagram shows taxiway B is straight across when crossing runway 18/36.   In reality; taxiway B on the east side of 18/36 is approximately 100 yards south of where taxiway B intersects the west side of 18/36.  A turn south to back taxi onto runway 36 is required when crossing B from west to east.

At approximately 1;200 ft MSL Aircraft Y drifted south of course. We had a TCAS TA. We both looked at the Aircraft Y drifting; about that time the TA became an RA. It was a descending RA. I thought I disconnected the autopilot immediately; I did not. I attempted to lower the nose and felt resistance; I immediately disconnected the autopilot correctly and descended complying with the RA. Delay in autopilot disconnect was about 3-5 seconds. Went low on glide slope and ATC issued a low altitude alert. RA ended; Aircraft Y corrected back to [the] localizer and we rejoined the GS to 28L. Approach was stable prior to 500 ft so we continued to a normal landing. We debriefed the event at the gate.
column123: On visual approach (Tip Toe 28L) at approx 11-1;200 feet; we received a TCAS RA due to traffic on visual for 28R overshooting their turn to final. We informed them of the intrusion and informed the Tower we were returning to glide slope. We were stable and continued approach for an uneventful landing.

column121: After a 1-hour maintenance delay in ZZZ; we set off for ZZZ1. The flight was uneventful until we began to descend into ZZZ1. The forecast for our original arrival had been winds 220/6; 6 SM; BKN 100; VCSH. So; while the weather wasn't spectacular; it certainly wasn't something we were concerned about when we departed. Even at the time of the delayed departure; the weather had not changed from the forecast. Prior to top of descent; all briefings were completed. Threats acknowledged (short runway; possibly wet; landing distance; night; go-around into possible weather; autobrakes max and windshear potential). As such we choose Flaps 40; autobrakes maximum; for a landing distance of about 5;000 feet. We only had 2 selections; normal or good braking at MAX AB; after that there were no options for autobrakes; something I remarked during the brief as a definite threat given the short runway. As we descended in ZZZ1 on the arrival; we began to see numerous thunderstorms and lightning; but nothing at the airport. Below 9;000 feet it was clear and we could see the airport; but to the North; South and West; thunderstorms were everywhere and the lightning was out of a movie; turning night into day. With just one aircraft in front of us; we were on vectors to the ILS XXR. Again; no weather or Thunderstorms within 10-15 miles of the airport and the weather that was there was North; South and West of the airport. We were slowed and fully configured by the FAF. The approach was stable throughout; only with some slight deviations due to winds and light turbulence. Throughout the approach I keep thinking about the go-around and possible windshear; but knowing all along; I really don't want to have to go-around into it. As the aircraft in front of us landed and cleared the runway; we were given clearance to land at 600-700 ft. Winds were reported less than 10 knots with no gust. At about 100 feet before landing; I began to feel the airplane start to encounter some gusts; nothing unstable; just making me work for it. I remember thinking to myself; this shouldn't be this hard given the reported conditions. At about 50 feet; I began to feel the airplane sink; I added power; no luck; added more; still no luck. I made the decision in my mind to go-around; and at that exact same moment the GPWS screamed; 'Windshear; Windshear; Windshear'. Without hesitation I slammed the throttles to the forward stops; rotated to approximately 15 degrees; pushed TOGA and held my breath. For a brief moment; it seemed as if nothing happened. I'm honestly not sure if we got the warning again as I became focused on flying the plane and getting away from the ground. Within about 3-4 seconds I could see our airspeed vector immediately start a positive trend and Instantaneous Vertical Speed Indicator (IVSI) was climbing at 4;000-6;000FPM. I immediately felt we were out of the event so I began calling for the go-around configuration changes and cleaned up the airplane. However; our event wasn't over; after telling the Tower of the windshear event; we now needed to navigate the numerous thunderstorms that were West of the airport. We asked for an immediate left turn to a downwind; which was granted and kept clear of the storms. Now; we had a decision to make. Make another attempt; or divert. Having the fuel; we choose to head in the direction of another approach. ATC vectored us behind Aircraft Y who was on approach. We felt that if Aircraft Y was able to land; we would at least consider an attempt. However; as we started the approach; Aircraft Y went around for windshear. At that point; I made the decision to abandon the approach and immediately head to ZZZ2. After we completed the After Take Off checklist (for the second time); declared MIN FUEL; flew some vectors; reviewed the ZZZ2 10-7 and 9 pages; approach brief/threats and deviations for weather; we landed 'uneventfully' in ZZZ2. So; commence the debrief. What went well?  First; my gut told me I should fly this leg. Despite trying to get the training done; it seemed for me to be the safest option. We all have moments like these in our IOE's. Trust yourself; if you think you should fly; then fly. This is where (CRM/TEM) Planning and Decision Making; along with leadership come in. Remember; safety is our number one priority. Next; our threat forward briefing during the descent check was critical (Situational Awareness/Communication). When I briefed the windshear escape; little did I realize I'd be using it.  Also; during the maneuver; I did see my First Officer (FO) ensure the speed brakes were stowed; an outstanding back up. What could have gone better?  The one part of this we didn't review was how the Pilot Monitoring (PM) responds to the windshear escape. They provide key information to you when you are in the middle of a windshear event. This won't be something I'll soon forget to mention when I brief windshear. Next; the actual windshear escape/go-around. It happens so fast in actual operation; yet in the simulator we all know it's coming; as well as; what to do and what to say. Without identifying and briefing it; I would guess the PM might not be saying anything as they are reacting to the event. In our case; the FO; after being startled by the GPWS alert; was back in the loop as I called for the go-around configuration changes. Throughout the actual windshear event; I didn't hear him say anything.  During our debrief; he knew what he was supposed to say; but because of the 'startle' (distraction); by the time he gathered himself; the event was over. Also; since we hadn't reviewed it in the threat forward briefing; it was understandable given his experience. However; he was right there with me on the go-around procedures and clean up. This; I believe; was because we briefed the GA procedure and he was fully aware of his responsibilities (Communication and SA). Now the divert.  Simple right; just tell dispatch and ATC; plug it into the FMC RTE page; load the approach and go (Automation/Workload Management). That is of course would be simple; if you aren't coordinating with dispatch; ATC to deviate for thunderstorms; being almost on top of the airport deviating too; and while all the while watching your fuel state getting lower and declaring MIN FUEL (time compression). This is where we could have reviewed the diversion guide in the FOM; but we choose to forgo that due to time constraints and weather. Also; as diverting airports went; ZZZ2 was the only airport that was not being affected by the weather. Furthermore; we reviewed the ATIS and NOTAMs; but did not ask Dispatch for landing data. We did however; do an evaluation of our landing data per the FM; by reviewing the 10-7 page which lists no special engine out for our landing runway (Rwy XXR; 10;200ft); and we also knew we had the landing distance based on our data from ZZZ1 and the FM. Another not so well; was we forgot to re-cruise the FMC. As a result; we were unable to load the ILS approach. I'm here to say the re-cruise; 'slipped' my mind. That led us to not being able to load the FMC ILS approach due to altitude constraints. However; I did have the FO load the ILS in the FMC; which gave us a white line depiction of the approach despite being unable to execute it. Given the VFR conditions; we were able to fly a visual approach and back it up with the ILS. Next; where is the communication with the Flight Attendants? An area that was really tough. Given the time compression; after the go-around and we deviated away from the thunderstorms; I called the Flight Attendant's and told them what happened; and let them know that we were diverting to ZZZ2. I asked the Purser if she could tell the passengers; as I just didn't have time to make a PA (Workload Management). Once we landed; we still had to coordinate with operations and the passengers upon landing to determine what to do. Keeping the people informed was my biggest concern.  I went into the cabin to let the passengers know I was sorry about not getting them into ZZZ1 and for having a delay in talking to them about the divert. Given the weather everyone saw out the window; no one seemed to mind and most were thankful we were just on the ground safely. The final resolution was the flight canceled in ZZZ2 due to the ZZZ1 curfew and the passengers were bused to ZZZ1. This took almost an hour after we parked.
